How Private Equity Fuels Nonbank Lending
abstract: Abstract We demonstrate how private equity (PE) promotes nonbank lending by substituting for bank monitoring. Relative to non-PE-backed loans, PE-backed loans exhibit lower bank monitoring, smaller loan shares retained by lead banks, and larger shares held by nonbanks. The substitution is strongest when sponsors have greater incentives to engage with portfolio firms, is not associated with weaker loan performance, and persists during borrower distress. Our findings suggest that PE sponsors’ active engagement—through monitoring and support in distress—reduces banks’ need for monitoring and information production, enabling them to retain less skin in the game and sell loans to nonbanks.

title: Networks of Dissent: Social Leaders and Protest in an Autocracy
Regional favoritism and educational attainment in Africa
abstract: Abstract We investigate the impact of regional favoritism on educational attainment in Africa. Using geocoded, individual-level survey data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), we show that men who grew up in areas geographically linked to a national leader attain higher levels of education later in life. In contrast, we observe no beneficial effects of geographical leader connections for women on average; only a subset of women who have additional ethnic ties and are possibly from wealthier families experience such effects. We interpret these results using a discrete choice framework that models decisions regarding whether children continue schooling based on perceived returns to education versus the costs of that education. This framework suggests that preferential educational policies are unlikely to be the primary cause of the higher attainment observed for men and the subset of women mentioned previously. Instead, educational choices appear to respond to expectations of local economic booms in geographically connected regions. Additional evidence, such as regarding the likelihood of skilled employment later in life, supports this interpretation.

title: Social distancing under strategic uncertainty: The role of strategic sophistication in the COVID-19 pandemic
abstract: Abstract This study examines how individuals’ strategic sophistication shapes social distancing during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, when distancing was a costly protective decision under two sources of risk: the private risk of infection and strategic uncertainty about whether others would comply. We develop a weakest-link public goods game with private costs of social distancing, in which agents differ in their level- k depth of reasoning about others. The model predicts that the probability of distancing rises with the level- k type when baseline compliance is low. We test this prediction using large-scale, nationally representative survey data that include incentivized experiments to measure participants’ level- k types. We find that a one-level increase in level- k lowers the probability of leaving home daily by 1.6 percentage points in Singapore and is associated with a 3.4 percentage-point lower probability of maintaining or increasing outdoor activity in South Korea.

title: Entrepreneurial Optimism and Venture Capital: A Quantitative Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT We quantitatively analyze the impact of entrepreneurial (EN) optimism on venture capital (VC) projects in a dynamic calibratable model. VCs and entrepreneurs (ENs) have differing beliefs and risk attitudes about projects. The equilibrium features staged VC investments, progressive vesting of the EN's stake, and intertemporal performance targets. Optimism is a major driver of VC projects. The EN's mean project quality assessment is over twice the VC's mean assessment. Optimism increases pay‐performance sensitivities by 75% and almost doubles project values. We derive quantitative implications for the effects of optimism, project qualities, productivities, and risks on VC contracts and project values.

title: Invisible bridge: Digital infrastructure, energy transition, and energy poverty
Material use and its relationship with per capita income. A panel data analysis at the global level
abstract: Global use of materials has significantly increased over recent decades, causing a wide range of environmental and social concerns. In this study, we use the latest available data from the UN database on global material flows to investigate the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis for two widely used material flow indicators, Domestic Material Consumption and Material Footprint, for a dataset of 147 countries. Using both semiparametric and parametric methods over a longer period than any previous study (1970–2019), we find no evidence in support of the EKC hypothesis. A concerning result is that material-income elasticities are higher after 1989, implying that the situation has not improved. We conclude that major changes have not yet occurred in the income-material use relationship and that strong policy measures remain necessary to reduce material consumption.

title: How Disruptive Technologies Spawn New Industries: Mechanisms, Controversies, and Future Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper reviews the literature on how disruptive technologies catalyze the formation of new industries. We first clarify conceptual boundaries between disruptive technologies and adjacent innovation constructs. Drawing on Schumpeterian innovation theory, evolutionary economics, and industrial organization theory, we develop a four‐dimensional transmission‐mechanism framework to unpack the evolutionary logic of new industry formation. Further, we identify four core academic controversies regarding disruption paths, actor roles, institutional functions, and mechanism heterogeneity, and trace the theoretical roots and empirical limitations behind divergent viewpoints. On this basis, this paper outlines a multi‐dimensional future research agenda covering theoretical integration, empirical expansion, policy research, and scenario extension. This review strengthens the unified conceptual foundation for subsequent studies and offers differentiated insights for firm innovation strategies and industrial policy design across digital, biotech, and energy technology scenarios.

title: Mapping the Signaling Landscape in Crowdfunding: Insights From Profit and Non‐Profit Models
abstract: ABSTRACT Crowdfunding campaigns rely heavily on signals to reduce information asymmetries, yet evidence regarding signaling effectiveness remains fragmented across crowdfunding models. This review examines how and why signaling effectiveness varies across crowdfunding contexts through a systematic narrative synthesis of 97 empirical studies identified within a 2015–2023 review window. The synthesis suggests that signaling effectiveness varies in patterned ways across the reviewed crowdfunding contexts. Rather than functioning as universally effective cues, signals are interpreted through distinct receiver decision problems associated with profit‐oriented and non‐profit‐oriented crowdfunding environments. The review develops a comparative signaling taxonomy that links crowdfunding context, signal portfolios, credibility mechanisms, receiver interpretation, and fundraising outcomes. The systematic narrative synthesis further suggests that signaling outcomes depend not only on signal characteristics but also on how heterogeneous receivers interpret coherent signal portfolios. In addition, credibility may be supported through multiple mechanisms, including costliness and verifiability, reputational exposure, transparency and accountability, third‐party validation, and portfolio consistency. By integrating fragmented evidence across crowdfunding models, the review advances a contextualized understanding of signaling effectiveness and extends signaling theory to heterogeneous digital fundraising environments.

title: Regulating the Artificial Intelligence Economy: A Systematic Search and Mechanism‐based Review of Legal Institutions, Regulatory Mechanisms, Economic Trade‐offs, and Welfare Consequences
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence regulation changes technological risk as well as entry, learning, competition, work, and control. Legal and economic research nevertheless remains divided by instrument and discipline. This article combines a transparent systematic search with a mechanism‐based, purposive synthesis. The corpus contains 84 academic contributions and 20 primary legal and institutional documents, current through August 21, 2026. The search is reproducible, but the corpus is designed to cover mechanisms rather than estimate the prevalence of findings across all scholarship. The Institution‐Mechanism‐Incidence‐Welfare framework connects legal authority to behavior, strategic adaptation, and welfare. Four conclusions follow. Risk rules, assurance, liability, data rights, competition policy, and labor protections operate as complements. Fixed compliance and information costs can favor incumbents even when rules reduce direct harm. Evidence is strongest for narrower shocks involving privacy, workplace rollouts, and pricing technologies. It remains weakest for the aggregate welfare effects of comprehensive AI statutes. Efficiency claims are incomplete unless they report incidence and rights constraints separately. The research agenda therefore pairs safety with innovation, market structure, and distribution.

title: Panel Econometric Approaches to Purchasing Power Parity: A Survey of Methods and Findings
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper surveys the development of panel econometric approaches to testing purchasing power parity (PPP), focusing on how methodological advances have addressed key empirical challenges that limited earlier time‐series evidence. We review the evolution of methods designed to account for cross‐sectional dependence, parameter heterogeneity, and structural breaks, and assess how these developments have influenced conclusions regarding PPP validity. A central finding is that first‐generation panel methods, which assume cross‐sectional independence, tend to provide stronger support for PPP, whereas second‐generation approaches that explicitly model interdependence across economies often yield weaker evidence. The survey also highlights the importance of base currency choice and shows that panel cointegration studies generally support weak PPP while rejecting stricter proportionality conditions. Evidence incorporating productivity differentials and structural breaks tends to strengthen support for PPP. Despite substantial methodological progress, estimates of exchange rate adjustment remain slow, leaving the persistence of real exchange rate deviations‐and the broader PPP puzzle—only partially resolved.

title: Europe’s new geoeconomic cleavages: from capitalist diversity to international vulnerability in European political economy
Situational state capacity for transformative industrial policy in dependent market economies
abstract: The paper engages with ongoing debates in political economy on industrial policy (IP) and economic development in dependent market economies of Central Eastern Europe. More specifically, the paper focuses on how these countries are capable to implement transformative IPs given that they tend to lack important prerequisites of earlier successful developers. To answer this question, the paper synthesizes the existing literature on successful economic transformations into a conceptual framework of state capacity for transformative IP, which comprises of two components – developmental mindset and political mobilization. Based on this framework, one form of state capacity relevant to Central Eastern Europe – situational state capacity – is explored in more details. Building on insights from international relations and from nationalist-constructivist political economy, the paper proposes a model of conditions under which situational state capacity, defined as the ability of the state to mobilize and deploy existing policy and administrative resources effectively and legitimately in response to specific contextual conditions and with economic restructuring in mind, can emerge and result in mobilization of political elites toward pursuing transformative IP. The paper illustrates this model empirically with the recent case of semiconductor technology transfer from Taiwan to Lithuania.

title: Insurance and Assurance: Government Interventions and Depositor Behavior in Crisis
abstract: Abstract We examine how different forms of government intervention - explicit deposit insurance, implicit guarantees from nationalization, and assurance effects from re-privatization - shape depositor behavior during a banking crisis. Using proprietary monthly account-level data, we show that depositors respond to formal insurance limits even in an environment of broad state support, but adjust only partially. Stabilization is markedly stronger after the takeover by a financially strong private bank than during state ownership, despite unchanged statutory coverage. These patterns are inconsistent with a strong bailout-expectations view in which explicit insurance is largely irrelevant and instead point to credibility as a key determinant of depositor behavior. We further show that political trust amplifies the effectiveness of government guarantees. Overall, our findings highlight that the form and credibility of government backstops, rather than coverage levels alone, are central to retail deposit funding stability during crises.

title: Balancing Act: How Unaffiliated Analysts Navigate Private Information Disadvantages
IPOs and Foreign Tax Structures
Synthetic diversity: Racial depictions influence consumer responses to AI ‐generated models in advertising
abstract: Abstract As brands seek to increase racial representation in their advertising, many are turning to AI‐generated images of humans (i.e., synthetic models) as a scalable solution. This research demonstrates that consumer reactions to synthetic models are asymmetric, depending on the racial identity being depicted. Across five studies, we demonstrate that disclosing the AI‐generated nature of models lowers firm evaluations when the featured models are from racially underrepresented groups (e.g., Black, Hispanic, and Asian models), but not when they are White. This effect is driven by reduced perceptions of the authenticity of the firm's inclusion efforts, which in turn elevate inferences of manipulative intent. Importantly, these negative effects can be mitigated when consumers are informed that the firm is owned by members of the depicted racial community, suggesting that credible signals of authentic community ties can neutralize the evaluative penalty of AI disclosure. Our findings extend research on racialized depictions in advertising by identifying synthetic depiction as a novel threat to the evaluative benefits of minority representation, and by theorizing why this threat operates asymmetrically by race. More broadly, our results highlight that technological innovations in advertising cannot be divorced from the social and historical contexts that shape their meaning.

title: Toward Digitalized Circular Economy Practices: Examining the Nexus Between Customer and Technical Requirements
abstract: ABSTRACT The adoption of circular economy ( CE ) practices has become indispensable for countries worldwide to minimize the adverse environmental impacts of waste. Digital platforms for CE practices have been anticipated to improve societal involvement. However, existing digital platforms for CE practices have failed to enhance such involvement. This study investigates the customer requirements (CRs) that improve societal involvement in CE practices through digital platforms and the technical requirements (TRs) needed to meet them. An integrated Fermatean fuzzy set (FFS)–analytic hierarchy process (AHP)–decision‐making trial and evaluation laboratory (DEMATEL)–quality function deployment (QFD) method was employed to determine the weight significance and to reveal the causal interrelationship among the CSFs, and to rank the TRs. The findings indicate that “Actual impact assessment systems,” “Integrated service support,” “Sustainability rewards,” “Opportunity for entrepreneurship,” and “Provision of digital product passport” are the top five CSFs, while “Automated Support System” and “Integrated Payment Gateway” are the important TRs. The findings of this study could help in enhancing the digital platforms for CE practices, which could increase societal involvement.

title: Decoupling Economic Growth From Material Use: A Bibliometric Review and Research Agenda for Business Management Scholarship
abstract: ABSTRACT The imperative to decouple economic growth from resource consumption sits at the heart of current sustainability research, yet the role of businesses in this process has barely been explored. This paper presents a bibliometric analysis of 251 documents from the Web of Science (1998–2025) examining decoupling, the circular economy and material flow analysis. Drawing on co‐citation networks, keyword co‐occurrence, thematic mapping, bibliographic coupling and thematic evolution analysis using the Bibliometrix package in R, we map the intellectual structure and research dynamics of this domain. Three intellectual clusters emerge—planetary boundaries and degrowth, empirical decoupling analysis and social metabolism—alongside two active research fronts, whose intellectual core does not include authors primarily affiliated with business management. This is the central finding of the paper. We are dealing with a domain that has grown at a compound annual rate of 12.66% over nearly three decades, yet has done so without the systematic engagement of business management scholarship. Emerging topics—such as recycling, digital platforms and circular business models—point toward a future convergence. This review offers a business‐oriented bibliometric synthesis of the field and proposes a five‐strand research agenda for management scholars.

title: Climate Policy Stringency, Corporate Energy Efficiency and Sustainable Business Performance: A Synthetic Global Panel Simulation
abstract: ABSTRACT This study develops and demonstrates an integrated analytics framework to examine how climate‐policy stringency could shape corporate sustainability performance through corporate energy behaviour, while accounting for digitalisation as a contextual amplifier. Rather than drawing inferences from observed firm‐level data, the study uses a transparent policy‐calibrated synthetic panel simulation design covering 20 countries, 30 firms per country and 8 years (2017–2024), yielding 4800 firm‐year observations across five sectors. The simulation design is calibrated to plausible ranges and stylised relationships reported in recent climate–energy–ESG research and serves as a reproducible testbed for methodological integration. The simulation workflow combines descriptive diagnostics, clustered‐error panel regressions, a random‐forest prediction model with out‐of‐sample evaluation, a simulation‐based difference‐in‐differences policy‐shock exercise with event‐style diagnostics and mediation decomposition with bootstrap uncertainty. The results show that the framework recovers the directional relationships embedded in the simulation design: Higher policy stringency and renewable‐energy adoption are associated with higher ESG scores, whereas higher energy intensity is associated with lower ESG performance. Digitalisation is positively associated with the policy–energy–ESG linkage within the simulated environment. Feature‐importance rankings indicate that the policy index remains the dominant predictor, followed by financial valuation (Tobin's Q ) and energy intensity. In the simulated policy‐shock exercise, treated countries exhibit a modest decline in energy intensity and a small increase in ESG relative to controls after 2020. These estimated effects are directionally consistent with the programmed treatment structure but remain statistically imprecise, illustrating estimator behaviour within the synthetic simulation rather than providing evidence of real‐world policy impacts. Mediation estimates further suggest that approximately 15% of the simulated policy association operates through the energy‐intensity channel under the assumed structural ordering. The study contributes a transparent and reproducible workflow for integrating regression, machine learning, DiD diagnostics and mediation analysis in synthetic sustainability‐policy research.

title: The Greenwashing Gambit: A Double‐Edged Sword in Crowdfunding Success
abstract: ABSTRACT The paper examines when greenwashing becomes a success factor in reward‐based crowdfunding campaigns aimed at financing environmentally sustainable products. While prior work has identified what drives success in such campaigns, it remains unclear when misleading environmental claims are discounted as cheap talk and when they instead contribute to funding outcomes. Building on signaling theory, the study explores how costly quality signals interact with potentially deceptive environmental messages (greenwashing risk) and jointly may contribute to crowdfunding success. Additionally, the paper investigates whether the “wisdom of the crowd” can act as a mechanism to prevent greenwashing from becoming a success factor. Using fsQCA on 253 Kickstarter and Indiegogo campaigns (2009–2024), for which greenwashing risk was expert‐coded through the Terrachoice seven‐sins framework, we identify configurations associated with funding success. The findings reveal a double‐edged pattern. Greenwashing co‐occurs with funding success when embedded within a rich bundle of costly quality signals and when funding goals are modest; in ambitious campaigns, success co‐occurs with low greenwashing, and the combination of high goals, greenwashing, and absent quality signals constitutes a highly consistent path to failure. An exploratory analysis of high‐participation campaigns further suggests that the “wisdom of the crowd” may not reliably penalize greenwashing when other credible signals are present. Overall, the study contributes to signaling theory by specifying the configurations under which potentially deceptive environmental claims gain or lose traction, rather than treating them as uniformly effective or inert. For practice, it offers crowdfunding platforms an observable screening rule: Campaigns that pair ambitious goals and dense environmental claims with weak quality signals form a high‐risk configuration that warrants targeted review before launch.

title: Sustainable Marketing Orientation and Sustainability Performance of Nigerian Small Medium Enterprises (SMEs)
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable marketing is a strategy for building ethical capabilities, cost optimization, social value delivery, environmental differentiation and competitive advantage. Underpinned by resource‐advantage (R‐A) theory, this paper studied how sustainable marketing orientation (SMO) factors, Eco‐innovation (EI), and operational openness (OO) individually and/or collectively interact to determine the sustainability performance (SP) of 13 major water producing SMEs in Port Harcourt, Nigeria. A sample of 315 managers and officers directly or indirectly involved in marketing and sustainability programmes was studied through cross‐sectional design and self‐administered questionnaire. Analyzing the data and testing the hypotheses using SmartPLS, the results showed that SMO factors and EI significantly affect SP, with strategic integration (SI) having the most critical effect. Similarly, social commitment (SC), ethical capabilities (EC), and SI affect the flow of EI programmes; and EI and SI influence OO. Therefore, integrated systems that ethically and morally address environmental and social issues produce sustainability outcomes beyond the economic pursuit of R‐A theory. Sustainability adoption is no longer optional in modern markets rather a core driver of resilience, value creation, and long‐term application of heterogeneous, imperfectly mobile resources to enrich comparative advantage and R‐A's domain. Managers were advised to invest in social engagement and integrate the different layers of stakeholders in developing environmentally friendly programmes, suggesting a revision of R‐A theory and embedding sustainability into corporate culture and strategic planning processes.

title: Embedded and engaged: how employer branding drives talent retention
abstract: Purpose Employer branding leverages the organization’s image to attract and retain talent. However, the mechanisms linking employer brand to organizational turnover intention among skilled frontline employees (FLEs) remain underexplored. This study aims to examine the moderating and serial mediating roles of job-related factors in employer branding effectiveness. Design/methodology/approach Integrating social exchange theory with job embeddedness and job engagement, this study developed a comprehensive retention framework for the hospitality industry. Using partial least squares structural equation modeling, it analyzed time-lagged data from a convenience sample of talented FLEs. The study recruited participants from 30 leading Iranian organizations, purposively selected across three hospitality sectors. Findings Bootstrapping confirmed that job embeddedness and engagement serially mediate the relationship between employer brand and turnover intention. Furthermore, embeddedness significantly moderated the association between engagement and turnover intention. However, it had no direct effect on turnover intention, nor did it moderate the initial employer brand–engagement relationship. Practical implications Rather than using employer branding solely as a direct retention tool, practitioners may adopt a sequential intervention strategy that strengthens job embeddedness before deploying engagement initiatives. Engagement investments can then target highly embedded, talented FLEs to maximize retention returns. Originality/value This study advances talent management research by explaining talent retention through the synergistic mechanisms of job embeddedness and engagement. It further extends existing paradigms by testing these relationships in a unique context: a hospitality sector navigating both post-pandemic recovery and severe international sanctions.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Tasting responsible luxury: eco-branded fine dining in Macao
abstract: Purpose Drawing on norm focus theory in conjunction with the norm activation model, this study aims to examine how social and personal norms shape consumers’ behavioural intentions towards responsible luxury consumption within the experiencescape of eco-branded fine dining. Design/methodology/approach A two-stage research design was adopted. The ecobranding fine dining (E-BFD) experiencescape construct was first developed on the basis of a field survey conducted at a Michelin Green Star restaurant in Macao; a series of quasi-experiments was subsequently carried out to examine its direct influence on responsible luxury behavioural intention, alongside the mediating role of social norms and the moderating effect of personal norm. Findings Results show that the E-BFD experiencescape exerts an indirect influence on responsible luxury behavioural intention through injunctive and descriptive norms and that personal norm moderates both of these indirect relationships. Practical implications Findings offer fine dining operators practical guidance for encouraging responsible luxury consumption among their guests. Originality/value This study identifies four dimensions underlying the E-BFD experiencescape, namely service quality, food sensory appeal, interaction with other guests and dining atmospherics and links these dimensions to responsible luxury behavioural intention through social norms, thereby extending experiencescape and norm-based research into a new hospitality context. Its principal contribution lies in bringing established norm-based perspectives to bear on eco-branded luxury fine dining, thereby moving hospitality scholarship beyond the conventional focus on green purchase intention.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Qualitative systematic literature reviews: methodological insights and theoretical contributions
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address the methodological inconsistencies prevalent in qualitative-based systematic literature reviews (Q-SLRs) within hospitality and tourism (H&T) and proposes a comprehensive framework to enhance their rigor and replicability. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a quality framework for Q-SLR methodology, outlining best practices for conducting Q-SLRs and a “theorizing from association” approach to guide the development of theoretical implications for Q-SLRs. Findings The framework presents four phases: planning, conducting, extracting and analyzing, providing a step-by-step approach to Q-SLR. The novel “theorizing from association” integrates H&T literature with related fields, including management, organizational behavior and marketing. Practical implications The proposed framework enhances methodological rigor and fosters theoretical advancement, ensuring that future reviews can more effectively contribute to the field. Originality/value This paper addresses a critical gap in the H&T literature by providing a comprehensive guide to conducting Q-SLRs and to theoretical development from Q-SLRs.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Founder experience, intellectual property and corporate venture capital: Rethinking knowledge spillovers in highly valued startups
abstract: Highly valued ventures represent an important subset of entrepreneurial firms that successfully integrate and commercialise knowledge spillovers. While much of the research examines predictors of high growth, less is known about how founders strategically leverage knowledge-based resources during rapid scaling. This study examines how the prior entrepreneurial experience of founders, intellectual property (IP) and corporate venture capital (CVC) partnerships interact to shape a startup’s likelihood of achieving billion-dollar valuations. Using a curated dataset of 1295 startups, we find that the founding team’s prior entrepreneurial experience and the IP of the startup are complementary in driving unicorn outcomes. However, CVC partnerships, while offering some financial and strategic advantages, constrain IP development and diminish the effectiveness of founder-led innovation. We introduce the ‘Paradox of Relational Spillovers’ to capture the tension between accessing knowledge through partnerships and retaining the autonomy to appropriate it. These findings extend the knowledge spillover theory of entrepreneurship to highly valued ventures and highlight how collaboration with CVCs can be a multifaceted process.
journal_name: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship

title: City Digitalization and Employee Welfare: A Stakeholder Empowerment View
abstract: Building on the smart cities and empowerment literatures, this study investigates how city digitalization affects employee welfare expenditure of local firms in China. We develop a stakeholder empowerment view and posit that by empowering local governments, the public, and local workers, city digitalization increases employee welfare expenditure of firms located within the city. Analyzing a panel dataset of Chinese listed firms spanning from 2014 to 2019, our study reveals a positive impact of city digitalization on local firms’ employee welfare expenditure. This positive effect is amplified in regions with stronger legal systems, and for firms that attract greater public attention or have a more educated workforce. These findings provide important implications for policymakers on how to foster employee welfare expenditure in their regimes.

title: Bibliometric insights into the internationalization and strategic growth of premium private labels
abstract: Purpose This study investigates the global intellectual landscape of premium private labels (PPLs) – a nascent yet increasingly influential subfield within private labels (PLs) research. By uncovering its evolution from domestic retail strategies to a recognized dimension of international marketing and branding, the study identifies key foundational works and emerging thematic clusters that advance both theoretical understanding and managerial practice regarding the strategic positioning of PPLs across markets. Design/methodology/approach A bibliometric analysis of 626 peer-reviewed articles and over 26,000 cited references, indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection (1993–2025), was conducted. By applying comprehensive co-citation and temporal trajectory analyses using VOSviewer and CiteSpace, the study systematically maps interdisciplinary connections, identifies global research clusters and traces the international diffusion of key ideas. Findings Research on PPLs has transitioned from early price–quality debates within PLs studies to encompass themes central to global marketing, including cross-border consumer behavior, brand premiumization across cultures and multinational PLs strategies. Emerging areas such as sustainability-led innovation, digital retail ecosystems and global supply chain reconfiguration represent promising yet underexplored international frontiers. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is one of the first bibliometric studies to integrate network-based and temporal mapping tools to systematically examine the global trajectory of PPLs scholarship. The paper synthesizes fragmented literature into a globally relevant framework and highlights pathways for expanding PPLs strategies in emerging markets and international retail ecosystems. The findings offer actionable insights for international marketers, retail strategists and policymakers seeking to leverage PPLs for competitive advantage across markets.

title: Financial stress: a multi-level stakeholder perspective on turnover intentions, job mobility, and retention
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Dynamic political risk and international investment
The paradox of algorithmic disclosure in prosocial campaigns: how utilitarian and deontological moral frameworks divide consumer support
Entrepreneurial bankruptcy as a career-sorting event: income trajectories, re-entry, and risk-taking
The dual impact of cap-and-trade policies on innovations and the moderating role of accumulated resources
Visions, narratives and numbers: How roadmapping enables industrial transformation toward decarbonisation
abstract: The transformation to a low-carbon industry requires different actors to work together and align their strategies. To support this process, policy and industry in many European countries have been driving the development of industry technology roadmaps at sectoral and national levels. However, limited attention has been paid to how visions, narratives and quantitative modelling work together within roadmapping to enable alignment and transformation across organisational, industry and policy levels. We examine industry technology roadmaps in six selected European countries, using secondary material, survey responses and two focus groups. The analysis is based on a conceptual framework that integrates the design and process elements considered important for roadmap development and implementation, complemented by the requirements for promoting industrial transformation rooted in the literature on socio-technical change. While most roadmaps included sophisticated modelling techniques and quantified scenarios, the study shows that a well-articulated narrative is equally important in mobilising stakeholders toward long-term industrial decarbonisation goals. In addition, the case studies illustrate that strategic planning processes of industrial companies benefit from having a forum to assess the future potential of specific technologies with other companies and along the value chain, thereby helping them manage uncertainty in investment decisions.

title: From surviving to thriving: the effect of death reflection on voluntary simplicity and flourishing
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to examine how death reflection and death anxiety influence the adoption of voluntary simplicity, clarify the mechanisms underlying this relationship, and explore its subsequent outcome of flourishing. Design/methodology/approach This research uses five independent studies (total n = 1,831) across diverse methodological paradigms, including experimental manipulation, survey measurement and field intervention, to test the proposed hypotheses rigorously. Findings The five studies show that death reflection increases consumers’ tendency toward voluntary simplicity, whereas death anxiety has the opposite effect. Authenticity mediates both effects, providing initial insight into the underlying mechanism. Exploratory analyses further reveal that death reflection promotes voluntary simplicity by enhancing authenticity, which, in turn, fosters flourishing. Research limitations/implications This study provides a comprehensive examination of the relationship between death awareness and voluntary simplicity, including its mechanisms and outcomes. Although the findings offer valuable insights, future research should consider more diverse age groups, complementing self-report measures with behavioral methods and examine alternative moderators. Practical implications Death-reflection practices (e.g. mindfulness workshops and life-transience discussions) can foster authenticity and voluntary simplicity, thereby enhancing employee flourishing. Simplicity should also be integrated into policies for work-life balance, sustainable consumption and minimalism. Originality/value This study introduces the dual-existential systems model to reveal that death reflection promotes voluntary simplicity through authenticity, whereas death anxiety inhibits it. This extends death awareness research beyond defensive responses to demonstrate a growth-oriented pathway to well-being.

title: De-Sludging High-Friction Frontlines: Designing an AI-Mediated Service Gateway for Mental Health
abstract: Nearly one billion people suffer from mental disorders globally, yet 35 to 85 percent receive no treatment even when services are available, affordable, and known to them. This paradox suggests that the primary barrier to utilization is not only structural supply failure but also behavioral friction at the mental health service entry threshold. Drawing on sludge theory and administrative burden research, we conceptualize these barriers as service sludge—cognitive, emotional, and process frictions preventing vulnerable consumers from crossing the threshold. We adopt a design science research methodology and design MyMatcher, an AI-mediated service gateway—a pre-encounter frontline entity comprising three modules: a sensing engine that infers clinical intent from vernacular distress language, a low automated social presence (ASP) chatbot designed to reduce the social risk of disclosure, and a provider-matching module that collapses provider search into a curated shortlist. Through diagnostic and evaluative interviews with mental health practitioners, complemented by classification validation on a labeled corpus of over 4,000 texts, we derive three design principles and three research propositions for de-sludging high-friction service frontlines. Theoretically, we extend the 3A (Affordability, Access, and Awareness) framework by introducing Agency as a fourth behavioral dimension; we introduce the service gateway as a pre-encounter entity distinct from augmentation and substitution models; and we theorize an inversion of intimacy, the proposition that lower ASP facilitates sensitive disclosure in stigma-laden contexts, which qualifies a central assumption in service technology research. The framework is designed to generalize beyond mental health to high-stigma, high-complexity domains where behavioral frictions prevent consumers from acting on structural access to relevant services.

title: Rethinking Ethical Employment Pathways for People with Intellectual Disabilities: A Systemic Nested Alliances Model
Green Finance, Social Trust, and Corporate Green Innovation Quality
High-Tech Entry and Customer Innovation: Evidence from AI-Augmented Supply Chain Collaboration
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) continues to reshape global supply chain dynamics, understanding how supplier entry by high-tech firms interacts with AI adoption has become a critical pathway for fostering customer innovation. This study develops a theoretical framework that incorporates supplier-side entry, AI-augmented production technologies, and firm-level cost structures, grounded in both production cost and market demand functions. Leveraging a unique panel dataset of 37,631 firm-year observations in China from 2007 to 2023, we employ a difference-in-differences (DID) approach to empirically identify the impact of AI adoption by high-tech suppliers on customer innovation outcomes. Our analysis yields three main findings. (i) After entering customer supply chains, high-tech firms that adopt AI significantly improve the innovation performance of their customer firms. (ii) The effect of AI-enabled supply chain integration is stronger for firms in SME-oriented segments and highly competitive industries, and is mainly reflected in the increase of invention patents. (iii) Mechanism analyses associate AI-enabled supplier entry with lower R&D expenditure per patent application and greater participation in joint innovation alliances, consistent with improved innovation efficiency and interfirm coordination.

title: The Great Reallocation: Geoeconomic Fragmentation, Regional Value Chains, and the Macroeconomic Trade-Off Between Resilience and Efficiency
Policy Optimization or Resource Misallocation? Sports Tourism Development Orientation and Corporate Overinvestment
abstract: Does local government promotion of an emerging industry discipline or distort corporate investment? We measure city-level attention to sports tourism from the work reports of Chinese prefecture-level governments and link it to A-share firms over 2006–2024. Firms in cities with stronger sports tourism orientation overinvest less, and the result survives instrumental variable estimation and robustness checks. Policy attention strengthens government–business connections, which raise overinvestment, and improves expected returns, which lower it, though each channel carries a small share of the effect. The effect is concentrated in southern cities and in the upper half of the overinvestment distribution.

title: Domestic Trade Networks and Export Upgrading: Evidence from China’s Domestic Value-Added Ratio
abstract: Global value chain disruptions have renewed interest in whether domestic market structure is associated with export upgrading. This paper examines how a province’s position in China’s interprovincial trade network is related to the domestic value-added ratio (DVAR) of exporting firms—a question overlooked in existing studies, which treat the domestic market as a homogeneous aggregate. We construct China’s interprovincial trade network from provincial input-output tables and match network centrality indicators to firm-level microdata from the Annual Survey of Industrial Firms and China Customs records, covering 2007, 2010, and 2012. We find that interprovincial trade network centrality is positively and significantly associated with firm-level DVAR, a result robust to instrumental variable estimation and alternative network measures. The effect is heterogeneous: it is stronger in southern provinces, non-labor-intensive industries, non-general-trade firms, and foreign-invested enterprises. Export propensity significantly strengthens this positive relationship, while firm productivity shows a positive but more weakly supported moderating role. These findings provide evidence consistent with domestic trade network integration playing an important role in export value upgrading, distinct from GVC embedding or foreign technology spillovers, and offer a policy-relevant insight for emerging economies seeking export resilience under deglobalization.

title: Digital Finance and Rural Residents’ Income in China: Potential Channels Through E-Commerce and Industrial Upgrading
Voluntary Environmental Regulation and Corporate Greenwashing Behavior: Evidence from China’s Green Factory Certification
How Does Digital Industry Agglomeration Affect the Specialized Division of Labor? Evidence from Chinese Low-Altitude Economy Firms
Intellectual Property Litigation Risk, Debt Financing Costs, and Corporate Financial Risk
Photovoltaic Poverty Alleviation and Bird Biodiversity Conservation: Evidence from China’s Birdwatching Data
abstract: Photovoltaic Poverty Alleviation Project (PPAP), a targeted poverty reduction policy, plays a significant role in China’s anti-poverty campaign. Using panel data for Chinese poverty-stricken counties from 2014 to 2023, this paper measures county-level bird biodiversity based on birdwatching records and employs a difference-in-differences (DID) model to examine the impact of PPAP on bird diversity in these counties. The results show that PPAP significantly enhances bird biodiversity in poverty-stricken counties, and this conclusion remains robust after a series of robustness tests. Mechanism analysis indicates that PPAP enhances bird diversity through two channels: promoting regional population agglomeration and livelihood substitution and improving environmental quality. Moreover, the higher the level of financial accessibility, the stronger the positive effect of PPAP on bird biodiversity. Further analysis reveals that the biodiversity-enhancing effect of PPAP is stronger in counties with larger average photovoltaic power station scale and lower initial environmental protection levels; in addition, the policy mainly increases the species diversity of unprotected birds. These findings suggest that fully leveraging the positive effects of PPAP can help achieve a win–win outcome between poverty reduction and ecological conservation.

title: The Financing Effects of Media Tone: The Asymmetric Impacts of Positive and Negative Tone
abstract: As media coverage becomes an increasingly important source of information in capital markets, systematic evidence remains limited on how the direction of media tone shapes corporate financing. Using panel data for Chinese listed companies from 2001 to 2024, this study applies firm and year fixed-effects regressions to examine the effect of media tone on financing constraints. The results show that positive media tone is significantly associated with lower financing constraints, whereas negative tone is associated with higher financing constraints. More importantly, the penalty associated with negative tone is substantially stronger than the relief generated by positive tone, indicating that external capital providers are more sensitive to adverse information. Reputation capital helps explain this relationship, while disagreement in media evaluations further tightens financing constraints. The relief associated with positive tone is concentrated among firms with lower disclosure quality, whereas the penalty generated by negative tone remains stable across different disclosure environments. These findings reveal an asymmetric financing effect of media tone and provide new evidence on how media information shapes capital allocation.

title: Do Firms Shield Employees from Risk Shocks? Empirical Evidence from China
abstract: This study investigates firm-employee risk-sharing through implicit employment insurance mechanisms within China’s labor market. Leveraging data from Chinese A-share listed firms and employing Double Machine Learning (DML), we document that firms provide significant insurance against unpredictable risk shocks. Specifically, firms offer nearly full insulation against transitory shocks but only partial insurance against persistent ones. Heterogeneity analyses reveal distinct patterns in this risk-sharing. Managers receive substantially stronger job security guarantees compared to rank-and-file employees. Contrary to conventional wisdom, state-owned enterprises do not provide greater employment stability than private firms. Furthermore, family firms offer weaker insurance, attributable to selective corporate social responsibility fulfillment. Critically, employees implicitly accept wage discounts as premiums in exchange for this job security. Although employment insurance strengthens employment rigidity, wage discounts allow firms to flexibly adjust labor input, so they do not bear additional risk from ensuring employees’ job stability. We further identify a significant substitution effect between public unemployment insurance and firm-provided employment insurance: reducing firms’ unemployment insurance contribution burdens incentivizes them to enhance insurance, thereby strengthening employment stability.

title: Digital Finance and Regional Financial Risk: Evidence from Leverage, Default, and Housing-Market Channels in Eastern China
abstract: As digital transformation continues to reshape financial intermediation and resource allocation in emerging markets, maintaining regional financial stability has become increasingly important. Using panel data for 88 prefecture-level cities in eastern China from 2011 to 2023, this study examines the relationship between digital finance and regional financial risk using two-way fixed-effects and instrumental-variable models. The results show that greater digital finance usage depth is associated with significantly lower regional financial risk, with the finding supported by multiple robustness and identification checks. Mechanism analyses provide evidence consistent with household-leverage restraint and reductions in average and tail default risks. Under high-house-price state, positive housing-price shocks exert stronger risk-amplifying effects, while the risk-mitigating effect of digital finance becomes more pronounced. These findings provide city-level evidence on how digital finance may strengthen financial resilience in regions undergoing rapid digital transformation.

title: The Non-Linear Relationship Between Macroprudential Policies and Bank Competition: Evidence from Selected EMDEs
abstract: The nexus between macroprudential regulation and bank competition continues to generate considerable policy debate. Therefore, the study investigates the potential non-linear relationship between macroprudential policies and bank competition using data from 56 emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) over 2000–2022. Applying a dynamic common correlated effects (DCCE) framework, we investigate how credit, capital, liquidity, and tax-based macroprudential policy measures affect bank competition across financial cycles, institutional quality, and macroeconomic contexts. Findings reveal an inverted U-shaped relationship: moderate MaPP tightening enhances bank competition, whereas excessive tightening strengthens market power. Findings further indicate that the dynamics between macroprudential policies and bank competition are primarily influenced by financial structure, monetary policy stance, regulatory quality, and crisis episodes.

title: Fully Unlocking the Consumption Potential of Chinese Households: From “How It Is Possible” to “How It Can Be Achieved” with Digital Finance
abstract: Under the new development paradigm, how digital finance can fully unlock the consumption potential of households warrants an in-depth investigation. Using panel data from the China Household Finance Survey (CHFS) and applying a two-way fixed-effects model, we empirically examine the effects of digital finance on per capita household consumption and the main mechanisms through which digital finance unlocks consumption potential. The main findings are as follows. (1) Digital finance has a significant positive effect on per capita household consumption. Moreover, digital payments, digital wealth management, and digital lending each increase per capita consumption, indicating that digital finance helps unlock household consumption potential. (2) Urban and rural households exhibit markedly different responses to digital finance in terms of releasing consumption potential. Household participation in industry and commerce, the household head’s risk preference, and financial literacy all contribute to the unlocking of consumption potential in urban households through digital finance. (3) Digital payments expand the range of household consumption categories, digital wealth management reduces the need for precautionary savings, and digital lending stimulates household consumption through credit channels. Together, these mechanisms enable digital finance to unlock households’ consumption potential.

title: From Traffic to Retention: Can Digital Marketing Enhance Export Stability?
abstract: Does digital marketing support export stability? Using 26,932 Chinese listed-firm observations from 2012–2024, we estimate firm and year fixed-effects models linking annual-report digital marketing measures to a weighted index of overseas revenue shares. Digital marketing is positively associated with the index across robustness checks. Channel regressions suggest links with supply chain stability and strategic responsiveness, without establishing mediation. Acquisition and retention measures both show positive associations; their coefficients do not differ significantly. The findings connect digital marketing to sustained overseas business engagement, while overseas revenue remains an imperfect export proxy.

title: Supply Chain Contagion: How Customers’ Abnormal Temperature Exposure Amplifies Suppliers’ Debt Default Risk
abstract: Corporate debt defaults are a major source of financial risk and can threaten market stability when they occur on a large scale. Meanwhile, shifts in the global climate and episodes of extreme weather are profoundly altering economies and financial systems. Against this backdrop, examining how temperature-related shocks affect corporate default risk is essential for understanding credit risk transmission under changing environmental conditions. We investigate how customer-side exposure to abnormal temperatures affects suppliers’ debt default risk, using observations for Chinese A-share listed firms over 2008–2023. The findings indicate that suppliers’ debt default risk increases as the annual average temperature in customers’ locations rises further above its long-term historical average. The channel analysis provides evidence consistent with two channels: customers’ abnormal temperature shocks are associated with weaker demand for suppliers’ products and tighter financing conditions, which may help explain the increase in supplier default risk. Heterogeneity tests show that this effect is stronger among suppliers with greater customer dependence or tighter financing constraints, consistent with the demand and financing channels. The effect is also more pronounced for suppliers without green products, whereas stronger ESG performance helps mitigate the adverse impact. Additional analysis links customers’ abnormal temperature exposure to lower subsequent customer concentration among suppliers, suggesting possible adaptation through customer diversification.

title: Can Financial Agglomeration Amplify the Productivity Dividend of Digital Infrastructure? Evidence on New Quality Productive Forces
How Does Regional S&T Planning Affect Urban Green Innovation Diffusion in China? A Spatial Econometric Analysis
abstract: This study examines how Regional Science and Technology Planning (RSTP) relates to urban green innovation diffusion (UGID) using a panel of 284 Chinese cities from 2008 to 2020. UGID is measured by registered green patent transfers aggregated by the transferor’s city. We combine a spatial difference-in-differences framework with a BERT–DNN model that classifies policy sentences into obligatory goals (OG), anticipatory goals (AG), and other categories. In the baseline estimates, RSTP is positively associated with local transfer activity. The coefficient on innovation-network policy exposure is positive and statistically significant at the 10% level, whereas the coefficient on geographical policy exposure is not statistically significant. OG shows a positive own-city coefficient and a negative geographical exposure coefficient. The contemporaneous AG coefficients are not statistically significant, which does not establish the absence of longer-term effects. Regressions show that OG is positively associated with technology-service personnel density, fiscal science and technology expenditure intensity and relative local research and development (R&D) personnel advantage, supporting innovation-resource concentration as a plausible channel. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing local transfer activity from geographical and innovation-network relationships when evaluating regional planning. They also suggest that target design should give greater attention to cross-regional cooperation and the longer-term evaluation of anticipatory goals.

title: Does the Belt and Road Initiative Trigger Corporate Tax Avoidance? Evidence from a Quasi-Natural Experiment in China
abstract: Using a difference-in-difference (DID) model and a sample of Chinese listed firms, we examine whether the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) affects tax avoidance. The results indicate that participating firms have significantly larger book-tax differences after implementing BRI, suggesting that tax avoidance is an unintended consequence of BRI. Our results are consistent across alternative sample periods and withstand both the parallel trend tests and placebo tests, and our conclusions remain unchanged after applying the instrumental variable method to mitigate endogeneity. Furthermore, the effect of BRI on tax avoidance is moderated by cash flow volatility, excessive debt, executive overseas background, tax rate differences, and tax regulatory environment. Our research provides important references for understanding the effect of BRI on tax avoidance.

title: The Heterogeneous Impacts of Digital Transformation on Firms’ Internationalization: Evidence from China
abstract: Using Chinese A-share-listed firms from 2013 to 2023, this study examines whether and how digital transformation affects firm internationalization. We measure internationalization along both the intensive and extensive margins, including overseas revenue share, overseas operating revenue, internationalization participation, and a BERT-based internationalization indicator constructed from annual reports. Digital transformation is mainly measured by firms’ digital intangible assets, and we further use digital patents, digital job postings, and annual-report digital keyword disclosure as alternative measures. The results show that digital transformation significantly promotes firm internationalization. A one-unit increase in the digital transformation is associated with a 1.3-percentage-point higher probability of internationalization and a 0.8-percentage-point higher overseas revenue share. Further analysis based on the Awareness-Motivation-Capability (AMC) framework shows that digital transformation promotes internationalization by improving firms’ awareness of overseas opportunities, strengthening their motivation to expand abroad, and enhancing their capabilities through higher productivity and lower financing constraints. The effect is more pronounced among firms with higher initial productivity, suggesting that preexisting capabilities affect how firms convert digital investment into international expansion. Evidence from recruitment data further shows that digital transformation is associated with higher demand for highly educated workers, indicating that human-capital upgrading is an important part of this process. Overall, this study provides firm-level evidence that digital transformation supports Chinese firms’ internationalization by improving both market expansion and organizational capabilities.

title: Government Data Openness Empowering Enterprise Digital Transformation: The Moderating Role of Enterprise Internationalization
abstract: Using Chinese A-share listed firms over the period 2011–2023, this study exploits the staggered rollout of local government data openness platforms as a quasi-natural experiment and employs a staggered multi-period difference-in-differences model to examine the impact of government data openness (GDO) on enterprise digital transformation (EDT), with particular attention to the moderating role of the enterprise internationalization level (EIL). The results show that GDO increases firms’ digital transformation, with a larger effect among more internationalized firms. These firms appear better able to turn open government data into information that supports digital investment and business operations. The potential mechanism analysis points to two channels. International operations expand firms’ markets and asset bases, which helps them spread the fixed costs of digital transformation. GDO also lowers the costs of cross-border compliance, information search, and commercial data access, leaving more resources available for digital investment. Heterogeneity tests show that the moderating effect of enterprise internationalization is more pronounced among firms located in eastern China, non-state-owned enterprises, low-polluting firms, high-tech firms, and technology-intensive firms. By bringing enterprise internationalization into the analysis, this study shows that the effect of GDO depends partly on firms’ strategic and organizational conditions. The findings also provide evidence for designing more targeted public data policies.

title: Systemic Risk in Chinese Commercial Banking Systems Based on Complex Networks and Deep Learning
abstract: Given the pronounced nonlinearity and time-varying characteristics of risk contagion in modern interbank markets, traditional econometric methods based on linear assumptions and static frameworks are insufficient to effectively capture the tail risk spillover effects under extreme market conditions. Therefore, this article constructs a systematic risk analysis framework integrating deep learning algorithms and complex network theory, builds a directed weighted network of tail risk in the banking system, and analyzes the topological structure of risk transmission by combining Granger causality tests and the Infomap community detection algorithm. Finally, this article introduces time-varying network analysis and the PELT changepoint detection method to endogenously identify structural abrupt changes in risk evolution. The LSTM-CoVaR estimates are validated against linear quantile-regression, copula, and unconditional CAViaR benchmarks through conditional-coverage backtests and an out-of-sample evaluation. The study finds that the Chinese banking system has formed a significant core-periphery asymmetric two-layer structure, with the risk transmission mechanism evolving from early single-center diffusion to a core spillover-driven and regional multi-layered resonance model. Systemically important banks are the main positive sources of risk spillover, and their fluctuations are highly synchronized with policy cycles. Local and rural commercial banks, as net receivers, amplify local shocks in the chain structure of core, regional, and periphery. The surge in network connectivity after 2020 has propelled the system into a highly coupled, globally resonant phase, enhancing overall resilience while significantly increasing the fragility of local structures. These findings suggest that macroprudential monitoring may benefit from extending its focus beyond single hubs to the multi-layered nested structure of risk transmission, where regional disruptions can propagate into broader financial instability.

title: Science and Finance Integration and Sustainable Urban Energy Transition: Evidence from China
abstract: This article tests whether science and technology finance (STF) enhances the urban low-carbon energy structure transition. Treating China’s 2010 pilot policy for integrating science and technology with finance as a quasi-natural experiment, we use panel data for 282 prefecture-level cities (2010–2023) and employ a staggered DID model. The findings show that the pilot policy promotes the low-carbon energy structure transition, and the finding remains robust after a series of tests. Mechanism analysis indicates that the effect operates mainly through credit supply, green technological innovation, and artificial intelligence development. Heterogeneity analysis further shows that the policy effect is more pronounced in regions with stronger resource endowment, higher marketization, and better digital infrastructure.

title: Fiscal Incentives, Fiscal Capacity, and Regional Innovation Efficiency
Regional Legal Environment, Green Investors, and Corporate Performance
abstract: Drawing on new institutional economics and upper echelons theory, this study examines how the regional legal environment affects corporate performance using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2014–2024. The results show that a stronger legal environment significantly improves ROA and ROE and remains robust across alternative estimations, performance measures, sample periods, and instrumental-variable tests. Mechanism analyses reveal that green investors and executive green cognition partially mediate this relationship by reducing information asymmetry and greenwashing risks and strengthening firms’ long-term green orientation. Intellectual property protection further reinforces the positive effect of the legal environment on performance. Heterogeneity analyses show stronger effects among heavily polluting firms, state-owned enterprises, and firms in more marketized regions. These findings clarify how legal institutions promote corporate value creation through green capital allocation and managerial cognition, offering implications for legal business environment reform and sustainable economic development.

title: Does Low-Carbon Transition Disclosure Alleviate Stock Price Crash Risks? Evidence from China
abstract: We examine whether firms’ low-carbon transition disclosure (LCTD) is associated with stock price crash risk in an emerging-market context. Using a sample of Chinese A-share firms in pollution-intensive industries from 2008 to 2020, we construct a firm-level measure of LCTD based on the MD&A sections of annual reports. This measure captures firm-specific transition-related communication beyond broad ESG classifications. We find that firms with higher levels of LCTD exhibit significantly lower subsequent stock price crash risk. The result is robust to alternative measures and model specifications. Further analyses show that the negative association is more pronounced for firms with greater media coverage and analyst following, consistent with disclosure reducing information asymmetry and limiting the accumulation of undisclosed negative information. Overall, the findings suggest that credible transition-related disclosure is associated with greater market stability during the low-carbon transition.

title: The Contemporaneous and Lagged Spillover Effects of Carbon and Energy Markets: Focusing on the Asymmetric Impact of US–China Tensions
abstract: An innovative R2 decomposed connectedness approach is employed in this study to investigate contemporaneous and lagged linkages between carbon and energy markets. The GJR-GARCH-MIDAS model is further utilized to verify the causal impacts of US–China tensions on cross-market spillover effects. The results show that significant return and volatility spillovers exist between carbon and energy markets. In detail, return spillovers are dominated by stronger contemporaneous transmission, particularly for the Wilder Hill and S&P Clean Energy indices. In terms of volatility, the lagged effects are relatively noticeable, especially in the sectors of Renixx Clean Energy, Wilder Hill Clean Energy, and S&P Clean Energy. The analysis outcomes of dynamic spillover effects demonstrate that the spillover effects between carbon markets and energy markets have distinct characteristics and change over time. Ultimately, the paper finds that US–China tensions exert a significant asymmetric impact on the return and volatility spillover effects between carbon markets and energy markets.

title: Geopolitical Risks, Commodity Market Spillovers, and Agricultural Market Instability: Evidence from China
abstract: Geopolitical risks have emerged as a critical force reshaping global commodity markets, posing significant challenges to agricultural market stability, particularly in emerging economies with fragile market infrastructures. This study investigates whether and how geopolitical tensions indirectly influence China’s agricultural commodity market by amplifying cross-market volatility spillovers from other commodity sectors. We employ a two-stage empirical framework that combines the TVP-VAR model and the GARCH-MIDAS model to analyze dynamic spillovers and assess the explanatory power of geopolitical risk. The results show that, since 2008, overall spillover intensity has increased markedly, and the agricultural market has persistently acted as a net recipient of external risk. Geopolitical risk significantly magnifies volatility transmitted from non-agricultural commodity sectors, intensifying agricultural price instability even in the presence of strong domestic regulation. Out-of-sample results further demonstrate that global geopolitical risks, especially geopolitical threats and actions, are more effective predictors of agricultural market spillovers than China-specific geopolitical risk indicators. These findings suggest that agricultural market stabilization should pay closer attention to cross-market risk transmission under geopolitical stress, and that integrated risk management is important for maintaining agricultural market stability and food security in emerging economies such as China.

title: Prehypertension and prediabetes in Rwandan adults aged 18–69 years: insights from the 2022 STEPwise survey
Forecasting risk-factor distributions by sex and age, 1990–2050: a parametric estimation framework using GBD summary exposure values, demonstrated for Australia
Familial factors in SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and COVID-19 severity: a nationwide Danish study of adult twins and their spouses
When the Baseline Is Not Exogenous in Random-Intercept Models
abstract: Researchers routinely adjust for a baseline score in random-intercept models, usually for efficiency or confounding control. Because the baseline is a noisy measure of the same trait as the random intercept, the two are correlated, yet standard multilevel software treats the baseline as exogenous. We examine the consequences. The baseline coefficient does not estimate the structural effect of initial level; it estimates a reliability-weighted blend, the structural effect plus a regression-to-the-mean projection. A structural equation formulation makes explicit when the structural effect itself, rather than this blend, can be identified. The focal predictor’s effect is unaffected when that predictor is uncorrelated with the trait, and otherwise depends on whether its confounding runs through the observed baseline or the latent trait.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: Simultaneous Growth Curve Models and Their Use for Intervention Evaluation: A Practical Instruction to Model Fitting and Parameter Interpretation
abstract: Understanding how an intervention unfolds its effects is as important for its further development as establishing whether it works. This article introduces Simultaneous Growth Curve Models (SGCM) for longitudinal intervention data: separate latent growth curves fitted simultaneously to several repeatedly measured variables and connected by a structural model. It focuses on the multigroup formulation, in which every model matrix is estimated per group. The central argument is that the invariance testing sequence and the decomposition of group differences in expected growth are not two exercises but two views of one analysis: each constraint removes an identifiable component from the decomposition, so the surviving components define the effect structure. We derive this correspondence algebraically and illustrate it with a constructed example containing every type of group difference and with a cluster-randomized classroom intervention in mathematics. Guidance on unequally spaced time scores, control variables, diagnostics, and causal interpretation is given throughout.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: Estimation of Non-Directed Parameters in MIIV Structural Equation Modeling
abstract: Model-implied instrumental variable (MIIV) estimation provides a limited-information alternative to maximum likelihood estimation in structural equation modeling. MIIV estimation proceeds in two stages: directed parameters are estimated first, followed by the remaining variance and covariance parameters. We revisit this second stage from a weighted least squares perspective, showing that it comprises a family of estimators that includes unweighted least squares, generalized least squares, two-step reweighted least squares, and fully iterated reweighted least squares. All but the fully iterated reweighted least squares estimator have closed-form solutions. We also establish the relationship between model-based and unrestricted standard errors for the directed parameters. An exploratory simulation study illustrates the promising finite-sample behavior of these estimators. All estimators are implemented in the R package lavaan.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: Probabilistic GSCA: A Likelihood-Based Approach to Component-Based Structural Equation Modeling
abstract: This paper introduces probabilistic generalized structured component analysis (pGSCA), a likelihood-based framework for component-based structural equation modeling. pGSCA embeds GSCA within a generative model by incorporating multivariate normal disturbances into its submodels and is estimated by direct maximum likelihood, using expectation–maximization estimates as initial values. This formulation enables formal statistical inference, including asymptotic standard errors, information criteria, and likelihood-ratio tests (LRTs)—capabilities unavailable in conventional GSCA. Simulation results show that pGSCA performs comparably to GSCA in recovering component weights, loadings, and path coefficients, while additionally providing accurate estimates of disturbance covariance matrices. The asymptotic standard errors exhibit well-calibrated Type I error rates and confidence interval coverage, and LRTs yield well-controlled Type I error rates and high empirical power for model comparison. An empirical example illustrates formal likelihood-based model comparison. Overall, pGSCA substantially expands the inferential scope of GSCA while retaining its component-based nature.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: Nested Cross-Validation for Model Selection in Structural Equation Modeling

title: A One-Stage Approach for Estimating a Meta-Analytic Continuous-Time Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model
abstract: This article describes, evaluates, and applies a meta-analytic random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). The model enables meta-analytic study of temporal relations between two variables while separating stable between-person differences from within-person fluctuations. The RI-CLPM has been proposed as an alternative to the cross-lagged panel model and has recently motivated many reanalyzes of longitudinal datasets. To support flexible, integrative reanalysis across multiple datasets, we introduce a Bayesian one-stage approach for fitting a meta-analytic RI-CLPM using correlation matrices from longitudinal primary studies. The method combines Bayesian meta-analytic structural equation modeling with continuous-time modeling. The continuous-time framework allows us to account for different time lags across studies, a common challenge in longitudinal meta-analysis. We propose four model variants that differ in their random-effects structures for capturing between-study heterogeneity. A simulation study compares their performance, and an empirical example from educational psychology examines reciprocal relations between academic self-concept and achievement, illustrating their application.

title: Fatigue in head and neck cancer survivors after radiotherapy – prevalence, risk factors, and radiation dose correlates
abstract: Abstract Purpose To determine the prevalence of fatigue in head and neck cancer survivors and identify associated factors, including potential associations with radiation dose to cerebral organs at risk (OAR). Methods This cross-sectional observational study included survivors treated with curative radiotherapy between 2005 and 2023 at a tertiary cancer center. Fatigue and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) were assessed with the EORTC QLQ-C30. Dosimetric analyses evaluated associations between fatigue and radiation dose to intracranial OAR (brainstem, cerebellum, posterior fossa, medulla, pituitary gland, basal ganglia, hippocampus), including voxel-based analysis (VBA). Results One hundred fifty-eight patients were included. The most common tumor site was the oropharynx (38.6%). Median time from radiotherapy completion to study participation was 41 (IQR, 22–61) months. The mean fatigue score was 44.7 (SD, 28.0), exceeding the fatigue levels in the age- and sex-adjusted German general population (29.7); 51.3% of patients showed clinically relevant fatigue (≥ 39 points). Fatigue was inversely associated with HRQoL (ρ = − 0.59, p < 0.001), and positively with distress (ρ = 0.54, p < 0.001) and fear of cancer recurrence (ρ = 0.41, p < 0.001). Higher fatigue was found in patients with impaired performance status and in those with laryngeal and hypopharyngeal cancers. Neither cerebral OAR radiation doses nor skeletal muscle mass index was associated with fatigue, and VBA revealed no relevant subregions. Conclusions Clinically relevant fatigue affects about half of head and neck cancer survivors. Implications for Cancer Survivors The absence of a correlation with cerebral OAR doses suggests that other, probably multifactorial somatic, psychological and lifestyle-related factors play a more central role in the genesis of fatigue than the radiation-related brain exposures investigated.
