The paper contrasts this productivity-based selection with the traditional cost-based selection studied in prior work and discusses the distinct empirical tests each implies.

title: A BOOTSTRAP SPECIFICATION TEST FOR SEMIPARAMETRIC MODELS WITH GENERATED REGRESSORS
abstract: This article provides a specification test for semiparametric models with nonparametrically generated regressors. Such regressors are not observed by the researcher but are nonparametrically identified and estimable. Applications of the test include models with endogenous regressors identified by control functions, semiparametric sample selection models, or binary games with incomplete information. The statistic is built from the residuals of the semiparametric model. A novel wild bootstrap procedure is shown to provide valid critical values. We consider nonparametric estimators with an automatic bias correction that makes the test implementable without undersmoothing. In simulations, the test exhibits good small sample performance, and an application to women’s labor force participation decisions shows its implementation in a real data context.

title: Slavery and Northeastern Industrialization
abstract: Abstract From the 1820s through the 1850s, parts of New England began industrializing. Over the same period, slavery expanded in the southern states in terms of the number enslaved, the geography it encompassed, and the amount each enslaved worker produced. While many scholars have looked at the connections between northern industrialization and southern slavery, it is our aim in this paper to better identify the links between these two crucial developments in our nation's history by estimating the importance of the southern market for northern textiles – the key manufacturing industry during the early antebellum period. As we will see, the South was a crucial market for cotton textiles produced in America's first factories.

title: Building without income mixing: public housing quotas in France
abstract: Abstract We study the effects of the SRU law introduced in France in December 2000 to support scattered development of public housing in cities and favor social mixity. This law imposes 20 per cent of public dwellings to all medium and large municipalities of large-enough cities, with fees for those not abiding by the law. Using exhaustive fiscal data, we evaluate the effects of the law over the 1996–2008 period using a difference-in-differences approach at the municipality and neighborhood levels. We find that the law stimulated public housing construction in treated municipalities, but only slightly increased the presence of low-income households. Indeed, new public dwellings enter categories to which medium-income are eligible and most additional occupants are not poor. Within municipalities, the policy decreased public housing segregation but it barely decreased low-income segregation. This comes from local authorities increasing over time the presence of public dwellings in neighborhoods away from existing public housing but in places concentrating low-income households.

title: A Particle-Kalman Double Filtering Method for State Space Models with Superposed Latent States
Less is more: Decision-making under increasingly complex ambiguity
Vanishing Borders: Ethnicity and Trade Costs at the Origin of the Yugoslav Market
abstract: This article uses the creation of a paradigmatic multi-ethnic state, Yugoslavia, in 1918, and a novel large dataset of grain prices to examine the effect of ethnicity on trade costs when borders changed. Controlling for transport costs and import tariffs, we find a large but transitory border effect. Ethno-religious differences initially significantly increased price gaps, but their negative influence vanished over time as well. The decline was virtually complete about 16 years before unification and involved city-pairs divided by the border, supporting the hypothesis that Yugoslav unification nationalism fostered trust across ethno-religious networks of international traders.

title: Testing capacity-constrained learning
abstract: Abstract We introduce a general test of capacity-constrained learning models. Learning has capacity constraints when the set of possible ways to learn is exogenously fixed, as in the widely used fixed-capacity versions of rational inattention (Sims, 2003) and efficient coding (Woodford, 2012). With such models, changes in incentives do not alter the extent of attention, only how individuals decide to allocate their scarce attention. We show that choice data are consistent with capacity-constrained learning if and only if they satisfy a No Improving (Action or Attention) Switches (NIS) condition. Based on existing experiments in which the incentives for being correct are varied, we find strong evidence that participants fail NIS for a wide range of standard perceptual tasks: identifying the proportion of ball colors, recognizing shapes, and counting the number of balls. We further show that violations of NIS occur systematically in response to higher incentives, suggesting that incentives often expand attention beyond what capacity-constrained models allow. However, we find that this is not true for all existing perceptual tasks in the literature, which offers insights into settings where we do or do not expect incentives to impact the extent of attention.

title: Hot–cold reciprocation gaps
abstract: Abstract We study whether and why the mode of decision-making affects reciprocation in a binary trust game, using three preregistered online experiments. Trustees – some of whom were exogenously induced to be surprised by trust – either decided whether to reciprocate after observing their partner’s choice ( hot mode) or committed in advance to a contingent response plan ( cold mode). In our Baseline experiment, once participants gained experience, reciprocation became more likely under hot than under cold decision-making, especially when trust was unlikely – consistent with a model in which positive surprise at being trusted increases the utility of reciprocating. Results from the other two experiments show that surprise promotes reciprocation only when trust reflects an intentional choice by the trustor and when cognitive load in the decision environment is not too high.

title: Despite the odds: assessing Africa’s new social welfare landscape
abstract: Over the past decades more attention has been given to the growth of social welfare related programs in sub-Saharan Africa. However, to date there are still insufficient empirical observations, which makes it difficult to assess these changes or the factors behind them. This article introduces the Structure of Social Welfare (SSWA) dataset. Rather than rely on spending data, which is sporadically reported, the SSWA gathers data on the design elements of diverse social welfare programs for 44 African countries between 1960 and 2022. These data are used to create indexes of social welfare that take into consideration intended coverage as well as institutional and fiscal sustainability. The SSWA data demonstrates that despite difficult material conditions there is considerably more social welfare in Africa today, but that there is also important variation across countries in terms of the level of commitment. The utility of the SSWA data is then demonstrated by reevaluating the contested impact of democratization on welfare expansion in Africa. The results indicate a positive yet underexplored relationship.

title: “Made in heaven, matched by parents”: Can arranged marriage restrict labour market autonomy and participation of women?
abstract: This paper investigates whether parent-arranged marriage causally reduces women’s post-marriage labour market autonomy and participation. We conceptualize and separately estimate two distinct dimensions of women’s labour market engagement: autonomy (the power to decide whether to work) and participation (the actual decision to work), a distinction overlooked in the existing literature. Using a nationally representative sample of approximately 30,000 currently married women from the India Human Development Survey (2011–12), we estimate causal effects using an instrumental variable strategy that exploits the intergenerational persistence of community marriage norms. Our primary instrument uses lagged marriage-type prevalence within state-caste cells; a second, Leave-One-Out instrument—constructed from other-caste groups’ historical patterns—serves simultaneously as a robustness check and a falsification test, with both instruments yielding statistically indistinguishable estimates. Relative to parent-arranged marriages, self-matched marriages causally increase labour market autonomy by 30 percentage points and participation by 14–16 percentage points; jointly-arranged marriages yield gains of 22 and 10–11 percentage points, respectively. These effects are large, given that only 42% of women in our sample report autonomy over work decisions. Heterogeneity analysis suggests that the pronounced asymmetry between autonomy and participation arises from structural barriers rather than women’s preferences. Our findings imply that policies targeting marriage norms must be complemented by supply-side labour market interventions to achieve commensurate gains in women’s economic participation.

title: Informed options trading and stock price crash risk
abstract: Abstract This study investigates the relation between informed options trading and stock price crash risk. Higher options to stock trading volume ratio ( O/S ), used as a proxy for informed options trading, is associated with lower future crash risk. This negative relation is more pronounced for firms with tighter short‐sale constraints, riskier firms, and firms with greater information asymmetry, and when the options market is more liquid. The finding is robust to tests exploring quasi‐natural experiments and instrumental variable analysis. Further results are consistent with firm‐specific information incorporation and managerial bad news hoarding serving as potential channels for the O/S –crash‐risk relationship.

title: Taming the narcissist
abstract: Abstract We investigate whether corporate governance constrains the agency costs associated with CEO narcissism. Narcissistic CEOs are linked to lower earnings quality, greater risk‐taking, and inefficient overinvestment. However, these effects vary substantially with board structure. Boards characterized by low diversity and excessive director compensation are significantly less effective at constraining the adverse consequences of CEO narcissism, whereas more diverse boards with appropriately incentivized directors mitigate these effects. The strongest adverse outcomes occur when low board diversity and excessive director compensation coexist. Our findings highlight the central role of governance design in limiting personality‐driven distortions in corporate decision‐making.

title: Debt-for-nature swaps: the state of play and scaling-up options
Sovereign debt in developing countries: old challenges in new settings
Nature at risk, debt at risk: towards integrating nature into the Low-Income Country Debt Sustainability Framework
Aging Out of Coverage: Lessons From the West Virginia $1,000 Adult Dental Benefit
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies the utilization of dental services during the recent implementation of an adult (age 21 and over) Medicaid dental benefit in West Virginia. We analyze claims data and find: (1) before implementation, quarterly utilization of preventative and restorative services falls from 8% at age 20 to virtually 0% at age 21; (2) post‐implementation, utilization falls from 8% at age 20 to 5% at age 21, implying a net increase of 50% of baseline utilization; (3) the net effect of the dental benefit is significantly larger in counties with a larger number of oral health care provider practices. Our results provide evidence that public health insurance expansions are dampened in markets with a limited supply of provider practices.

title: The peripheralisation of Europe’s battery industry: derisking regimes, productive models, and the geography of green industrial policy
abstract: Why has Europe’s battery boom bypassed the fiscally powerful core and clustered in the continent’s peripheries? The answer, this article argues, lies in the fit and misfit between national derisking regimes, through which states absorb investment risks, and the productive models through which firms organise industrial production. Because the EU created an electric-vehicle market without imposing a dominant battery-production model, three rival configurations emerged to supply European carmakers: a venture-capital configuration backing European startups in North-Western Europe, an FDI-attractor enclave configuration hosting Asian manufacturers in Central and Eastern Europe, and an FDI-broker configuration assembling Sino-European ventures in the Southern semi-peripheries. Production stabilised where derisking absorbed the risks firms faced and collapsed where it did not, above all in the EU core. Bridging the state-centred literature on green industrial policy and firm-centred global production network analysis, it shows Europe achieving green industrialisation through integration with, not strategic autonomy from, Chinese firms.

title: Kalman Filter Learning, Bounded Rationality and Informational Consistency
abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a behavioural New Keynesian model with rational (RE) and boundedly rational (BR) agents. The latter are anticipated utility learners and use simple heuristic rules to forecast aggregate variables exogenous to their micro‐environment. For the RE agents, we study two information assumptions: standard perfect information and imperfect information (II‐involving Kalman‐filter learning). We show that a consistent set of II for the modeller and the private sector generates endogenous persistence of decisions in response to unobserved exogenous shocks and thus RE under II dominates the BR specifications in empirical comparisons. We reveal substantial evidence of composite RE(II)‐BR structure with estimated proportions of RE and BR agents. Our results highlight the importance of informational consistency for the analysis of behavioural heterogeneity.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Childbirth Effects of the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper evaluates the effect of in utero exposure to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami on birth outcomes in Indonesia. Exploiting variation in the timing of exposure, we find that the probability of a successful pregnancy drops by 5.4 percentage points (pp), while miscarriages increase by 5.0 pp for those exposed in the first trimester of pregnancy. Gestation length shortens by 0.28 months, and the likelihood of preterm birth rises by 5.4 pp. We find suggestive evidence that post‐disaster health investments by households may have shielded later cohorts from harmful effects, while measures of maternal health and socioeconomic status have limited explanatory power. Our results suggest the importance of considering fetal loss as a first‐order cost in natural disasters and highlight that facilitating household investment in health through various policies may mitigate negative birth effects in the aftermath.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Estimating Hysteresis Effects in Times of Crises
abstract: Abstract One of the most puzzling facts following the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) is that output in both advanced and emerging economies did not return to its pre‐crisis trend, contrary to the predictions of standard macroeconomic models. This paper analyzes the factors behind output hysteresis, with a special focus on the role played by financial crises. The paper shows that financial crises are associated with medium‐term output and total factor productivity (TFP) losses, suggesting that these crises lead to “scarring” effects on the supply side of the economy. The paper also examines how additional factors, such as persistently low investment rates, research and development (R&D), and the effects of currency and debt crises, contribute to these permanent losses. Our empirical findings are broadly consistent with models featuring endogenous productivity and capital‐embodied technological change, which suggest that a contraction in investment is a key factor that limits the adoption of new technologies, ultimately reducing medium‐term TFP and output.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: Return on AI (RoAI): A framework for assessing AI investments in the marketing organization
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing as firms increasingly delegate activities and decisions previously performed by marketers to AI systems. As AI assumes a greater role in market-facing decisions, understanding the value firms realize from these investments becomes increasingly important. Building on marketing accountability and resource-based theory, we develop a Return on AI (RoAI) framework that conceptualizes AI investment through the people, processes, and capabilities that enable its deployment and governance. RoAI evaluates incremental benefit while accounting for value retention, evidence durability, and the full costs of deployment over time. The framework identifies a distinctive consequence of delegated judgment, wherein AI can improve current performance while reducing the experiential practice through which marketers develop and maintain the judgment required to evaluate and redirect the AI solution. This mechanism helps explain heterogeneity in AI returns across firms and over time. We develop seven testable predictions and an agenda for research on creating, appropriating, and sustaining value from AI.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Identifying and managing milestones in consumers’ goal journeys
abstract: Abstract Understanding consumers’ holistic journeys as unfolding events is paramount for managing service design and delivery. Touchpoints, “moments of truth” and critical incident research primarily focus on firm-facing events and consumers’ evaluations of firm encounters, rather than critical events in consumers’ own goal pursuit. This article introduces and uncovers the significance of milestone events in consumers’ journeys. Milestones are significant events that mark a major step or turning point in a consumer’s journey. Multi-stage, multi-context qualitative consumer journey research is used to inductively identify the key features and implications of milestones. They are distinct from other service events and consequential for consumers’ lives. This research fills a significant research gap in understanding consumer goal journeys. Identifying and understanding consumers’ milestone events enables service firms to support and improve goal progression; increase confidence in success; help consumers prepare for and interpret milestone outcomes; and manage risk by adjusting or pivoting from the goal.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Buffering institutional erosion: organizational ties and SME exports under populism
abstract: Abstract We argue that pre-existing organizational ties can partially buffer against the adverse effects of populist deinstitutionalization. In contrast with the chronic institutional weakness emphasized in prior literature, populist deinstitutionalization reflects a politically driven weakening of institutions that firms had previously relied on. This disrupts established routines and increases the transaction costs of cross-border exchange. For SMEs, which are highly dependent on external institutional support for internationalization, pre-existing ties to government actors, international suppliers, and foreign owners can provide partial buffering by replacing some of the coordination, information, and enforcement functions lost through institutional erosion. We test these arguments using data on 10,399 SMEs across 29 economies in Central and Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The results support our theoretical expectations: while populism is negatively associated with SME exporting, pre-existing organizational ties attenuate this adverse association, with foreign ownership providing the strongest buffering effect. Our findings extend institution-based research by identifying politically driven institutional erosion as a distinct challenge for international business and by showing that organizational ties can function as selective, imperfect buffers rather than substitutes for formal institutions.

title: Belief Traps Hinder Small Business Climate Action
abstract: Climate (in)action by small business owners is not driven only by policy or economic considerations but also by sociological and psychological factors, as leaders mimic the behaviors they perceive among their peers. We find that these social inferences about what others believe are often incorrect. In this registered report of 4,432 small-to-medium business owners and leaders across seven countries, we observe a persistent gap between perceived and actual beliefs. And this gap matters: small-to-medium enterprise owners exhibiting a larger gap have fewer sustainability policies in place. These results highlight how peer effects can spur climate action among business leaders.

title: Framing the unknowable: The role of language and frame multiplicity in early‐stage startup pitches
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Early‐stage startup pitches must make largely unknowable futures plausible. As such, they bear a rhetorical burden. This study theorizes how multiple frames jointly shape this burden and, consequently, affect investor evaluations. Specifically, it considers how future growth frames interact with concreteness and novelty frames. Evidence from 618 startup pitches and ad‐hoc investor evaluations reveals that growth frames relying more on entrepreneurs' own assertions than on established grounds tend to receive lower investor evaluations. This evaluative discount is alleviated when growth is expressed concretely but becomes more pronounced when the pitch emphasizes novelty. These findings extend framing theory by explaining the relevance and possible implications of frame multiplicity in pitches and entrepreneurial communication more broadly. Managerial Summary Mobilizing support for a new venture is difficult because founders must often describe a future that does not yet exist. This study of 618 startup pitches shows that growth‐related messages can shape investor evaluations even at the earliest stage, but only if configured well. Because growth frames must appear plausible amid the uncertainty surrounding new startups, framing early‐stage startups around growth is rhetorically burdensome. Findings show that pitches are evaluated less favorably when they rely more on founders' own projections and reasoning than on established grounds such as market analyses. Concrete language can alleviate this burden, while novelty framing intensifies it. As such, this study reveals intricate and potentially unintended interactions among multiple frames within a single pitch.

title: Share Issues vs. Share Repurchases
abstract: Almost all firms repurchase shares through open-market repurchase programs. In contrast, issue methods are more diverse; at-the-market offerings, analogous to open-market repurchases, and seasoned equity offerings, analogous to rarely used tender-offer repurchases, are both used by significant fractions of firms. Furthermore, average seasoned equity offerings are larger than at-the-market offerings. We show that this asymmetry in the diversity of transaction methods in issuances and repurchases and the size-method relation in issuances are natural consequences of the single informational friction of a firm having superior information to investors. Moreover, although this friction always leads firms to issue inefficiently little, it leads firms to repurchase too little if they maximize long-term shareholder value but too much if the primary goal is to boost short-term share prices. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: Y. Yuan acknowledges support from the Paul Woolley Centre, the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Projects 72342020 and 72495152], and University College London. H. Zhong acknowledges support from the Economic and Social Research Council [New Investigator Grant ES/T003758/1]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03301 .

title: Filtering the Labor Pool: How Digitalization Redistributes Hiring Costs
abstract: I theorize that candidate filters, a core technology in digital labor markets considered central to cost-effective matching, redistributes costs from the search-and-screening stage to the job-offer stage of hiring. Filters cause employers to focus on applicants who display common preferred characteristics. At the search-and-screening stage, filters reduce the number of applicants interviewed and alter the composition of the interviewed pool by removing both lower- and higher-quality candidates. At the job-offer stage, filters lead employers to make job offers to candidates with easily observable signals of quality and higher wage demands. Additionally, I theorize that if many firms target the same signals of quality, they may all pursue similar candidates. This increases bargaining power for those applicants, leading to more rejected job offers and higher wage demands. A randomized field experiment in a large online labor market confirms that filters redistribute hiring costs. The experiment shows that employers with access to filters interview 3.4% fewer applicants. Using a machine learning algorithm to proxy for unobservable-to-the-employer applicant quality, I show that filters cause employers to interview 28.9% fewer lower-quality applicants and 36.9% fewer high-quality applicants per job. Among employers who actively used filters, I find suggestive evidence of worse job-offer outcomes: offers are 8.9% more likely to be rejected, and contracted wages are 2.5% higher. I discuss the implications of this cost redistribution for organizations, labor markets, and strategy research.

title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
abstract: While structured search interfaces—such as filters and sorting tools—help consumers reduce search frictions on digital platforms, they also shape how consumers encounter product information during search. This paper studies how search interface design influences revealed preferences and market outcomes. We develop a theoretical framework linking interface design to attribute preferences through salience reallocation and information-based preference updating. The framework generates two predictions that can be formally derived: restricting faceted filters reduces the concentration of attribute importance weights (i.e., preference dispersion) and increases the diversity of products chosen (i.e., choice diversity). We test these predictions using a randomized, incentive-aligned online experiment in which 1,200 participants searched for wireless headphones on a custom-built e-commerce platform. Restricting filters led consumers to explore more broadly and resulted in more evenly distributed attribute importance weights and more diverse, higher-priced product choices. Mediation analysis further suggests that increased exploration was associated with shifts in attribute preferences. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences.

title: Media Review: Disintegrated Organizing and The Problem of Integrative Capacity in Collective Action
Local Faces of Global Employment Practices: Media Discourses on Uberization of Labor and Institutional Adaptation
abstract: Uberization has become a paradigmatic case of how platform-mediated work arrangements disrupt labour markets and existing institutional structures, yet we know little about the discursive processes through which such models are reworked within divergent capitalist systems. This article investigates how Uber’s employment model is received, contested and reshaped in the United Kingdom, Germany and Mexico. Linking translation theory and Varieties of Capitalism within a discursive legitimation perspective, we examine how global platform employment practices are received, contested, and evaluated across national institutional contexts. Empirically, we conduct a longitudinal analysis of 3,771 newspaper articles (2012–2023) from the three countries, combining sentiment classification with thematic analysis. We identify discursive waves of (de)legitimation around Uber’s labour practices in distinct institutional constellations. The analysis reveals three trajectories: reactive accommodation under competitive and consumer pressures in the United Kingdom as a liberal market economy; proactive regulatory resistance rooted in labour institutions in Germany as a coordinated market economy; and delayed but intense contestation in Mexico as an emerging market economy characterized by hybrid, fragmented and highly informal arrangements. The study extends the discursive legitimation perspective by linking institutional theory and industrial relations theory to show how institutionally conditioned media discourses shape the (de)legitimation of global employment practices, while bringing emerging markets and informality more centrally into Varieties of Capitalism debates.

title: Strategic Adaptation or Strategic Confusion? Fashion Organisations' Engagement With Sustainability Certifications
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite considerable costs associated with environmental certifications, fashion organisations consistently adopt multiple schemes to address sustainability challenges. As key mechanisms of sustainability governance, certifications expand legitimacy signalling opportunities, yet questions remain about their practical implementation and outcomes. This study examines this pattern through the diffusion‐impact paradox, drawing on interviews with 30 participants and archival analysis of certification communications from Australian fashion organisations. We find that the paradox operates through the following three interconnected mechanisms: certification proliferation, economic exclusion and a shift towards more demanding governance frameworks. Rather than acting independently, these mechanisms form a cumulative sequence. Organisational size shapes how firms navigate these dynamics, with large, medium and small organisations pursuing distinct strategies. By reframing the diffusion‐impact paradox as a dynamic sequence rather than a static trade‐off, this study extends paradox theory and offers certification bodies and managers concrete guidance for improving certification accessibility and impact.

title: Industry 5.0 Orientation and ESG Performance: Evidence From European Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether Industry 5.0 orientation is associated with environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance among European firms. Drawing on a socio‐technical perspective, the study conceptualises Industry 5.0 orientation as a firm‐level orientation that integrates advanced digital technologies with human capability, sustainability, resilience and transparent information systems. Using Bloomberg panel data for 1682 European Union‐listed firms over 2020–2025, the findings show that Industry 5.0 orientation is positively associated with overall ESG performance and with the environmental, social and governance pillars. The results further indicate that workforce capability and ESG information transparency partially mediate this relationship, suggesting that Industry 5.0 becomes ESG‐relevant through human‐capital and information‐accountability pathways. The association is largest in lower factor market development contexts, suggesting that Industry 5.0 orientation may have greater ESG relevance where external market support is weaker. The study contributes by distinguishing Industry 5.0 orientation from generic digitalisation and by identifying the organisational mechanisms and contextual conditions through which socio‐technical transformation is linked to ESG performance.

title: Dynamic Capabilities and Strategic Performance Under Polycrisis: The Roles of Strategic Flexibility and Regenerative Capability
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms increasingly face polycrisis environments in which geopolitical, climate, technological, and supply chain disruptions interact and cascade. Drawing on the dynamic capability view, the study examines how strategic flexibility and regenerative capability relate to strategic performance and how their values vary with polycrisis intensity. Survey data from 780 Indian manufacturing firms are analyzed using partial least squares‐based structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) and permutation‐based multigroup analysis. Both capabilities are positively associated with strategic performance. Strategic flexibility has its strongest performance effect at intermediate polycrisis intensity, significantly exceeding its effects at low and high intensity. Regenerative capability is also strongest at intermediate polycrisis intensity, although the cross‐group evidence provides only partial support. The study extends dynamic capability research by conceptualizing polycrisis intensity as a boundary condition and positioning regenerative capability as a strategic mechanism that links socio‐ecological renewal to strategic performance amid polycrisis.

title: An investigation of the neglected serial mediators and moderators of green inclusive leadership in the hospitality industry
abstract: Using social exchange and social identity theories as the theoretical umbrella, our paper proposes and tests the neglected serial mediators and moderators of green inclusive leadership (GIL) using time-lagged data gathered from hospitality employees. The findings from the partial least squares structural equation modeling disclose that employees’ perceptions of green organizational climate (GOC) mediate the influence of GIL on their corporate social responsibility (CSR) judgments. GOC and CSR judgments serially mediate the impact of GIL on their in- and extra-role CSR performances. More importantly, organizational identification strengthens the indirect positive impact of GIL on said CSR performances via GOC and CSR judgments. Our paper augments hospitality literature by extending the understanding of underlying mechanisms (GOC, CSR judgments) and boundary conditions (organizational identification) through which the GIL and CSR outcomes relationship unfolds and contributing to research on sustainable development goals associated with “decent work and economic growth-8” and “responsible consumption and production-12”.

title: Generative artificial intelligence and international green supply chain performance: dynamic capabilities as strategic enablers
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GAI) adoption is associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage in cross-border e-commerce enterprises. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory and the Technology–Organization–Environment–Human framework, the authors examine absorptive capacity and transformative capacity as intermediate capability mechanisms and artificial intelligence turbulence as a contingency. Design/methodology/approach The authors use an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. The quantitative strand combines survey data from 334 Chinese cross-border e-commerce enterprises with partial least squares structural equation modeling, fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis and importance-performance map analysis. The subsequent qualitative strand draws on semi-structured interviews with ten managers and executives directly involved in GAI implementation, which are integrated with the quantitative evidence at the interpretation stage. Findings GAI adoption is positively associated with absorptive and transformative capacities, which are in turn positively associated with international green supply chain performance and international competitive advantage. International green supply chain performance shows the largest estimated association with international competitive advantage. Artificial intelligence turbulence positively moderates the relationships between GAI adoption and both capacities, and the configurational analysis identifies five equifinal configurations sufficient for high international competitive advantage. Practical implications Managers should develop absorptive and transformative capacities alongside GAI implementation, integrate sustainability requirements into artificial intelligence-enabled supply chain decisions and pursue internally coherent implementation routes rather than a single ideal template. Originality/value This study integrates variance-based, configurational and qualitative evidence to explain the capability pathways through which GAI adoption is associated with environmental and competitive outcomes in cross-border supply chain settings rather than in dyadic buyer–supplier relationships.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: Avatars, fashion and the metaverse: a cross-cultural analysis of young consumers’ digital identity and self-expression
abstract: Purpose This study examines, from a cross-cultural perspective, how young consumers engage with fashion brands in the metaverse through avatars. It aims to understand how young people build their digital identity and how they interact with other users, brands and experiences, comparing consumers from a Western country (Italy) and an Eastern one (China). Design/methodology/approach The study employs a qualitative, cross-cultural design based on semi-structured interviews with Italian (N = 12) and Chinese (N = 26) Gen Z and Alpha consumers. It explores how young users engage with the metaverse and social gaming platforms such as Roblox, Fortnite and Zepeto, with particular focus on the role of avatars, immersive brand environments and interactive gaming formats. Findings The findings highlight cross-cultural differences in the ways Italian and Chinese experience virtual brand encounters. Based on level and engagement and on socioeconomic access, four avatar users' profiles have been identified: dreamers, collectors, explorers and pragmatists. Originality/value This study contributes to international marketing research by offering new insights into the way in which fashion brands can leverage metaverse platforms to connect with digitally native consumers. It expands the understanding of brand engagement beyond traditional advertising, emphasising the strategic role of virtual environments and interactive experiences in shaping consumer-brand relationships across different cultures.

title: Applicants’ perceptions of AI in personnel selection across Chile, Germany, and India
abstract: The increasing use of AI evaluations in personnel selection raises fundamental questions about how applicants interpret these recruitment signals in different institutional contexts. In particular, little is known about whether applicants across countries perceive AI evaluation in the same way. Drawing on signaling theory and North’s institutional perspective, we examine applicants’ perceptions of AI evaluation across Chile, Germany, and India, proposing that country-level differences in formal and informal factors shape applicants’ perceptions of opportunity to perform, consistency, innovativeness, and ultimately organizational attractiveness. Using a between-subjects vignette experiment (N = 252), we found that AI evaluation, compared to human evaluation, negatively affects perceived opportunity to perform and positively affects innovativeness. Both perceptions mediated the effect of AI evaluation on organizational attractiveness, whereas consistency did not. Applicants from Chile and India perceived AI evaluation as less consistent than those from Germany. Moreover, German applicants perceived AI as more innovative than Indian applicants, while no significant country-level differences emerged for opportunity to perform. Our findings advance theoretical understanding by showing that AI-based recruitment signals are interpreted differently across national contexts due to countries’ formal and informal factors, and practically highlight the need for organizations to tailor AI-based selection processes to sustain positive applicant perceptions.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: The Impact of Intellectual Property Protection “Distance” on Collaborative Innovation Quality: Evidence From Chinese Listed Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT Cross‐regional collaboration plays a growing role in firm innovation, yet interregional institutional differences create frictions that undermine the quality of collaborative outcomes. Whether institutional distance in intellectual property protection (IPP) reduces collaborative innovation quality and whether professional intermediaries can alleviate these frictions remain open questions. This study investigates how interregional distance in IPP (DIPP) affects interregional collaborative patent quality (ICPQ) using extensive 2007–2022 collaborative invention patent data from Chinese A‐share listed firms. We find that greater DIPP significantly reduces ICPQ, as divergent IPP regimes erode mutual trust, hinder knowledge sharing, and raise coordination and enforcement costs between partners. Patent agency experience effectively mitigates this adverse effect, suggesting that professional intermediaries help bridge institutional gaps between collaborating regions. These findings hold across a range of robustness tests and an instrumental variable analysis addressing endogeneity. The study contributes to the institutional distance literature by identifying patent agency expertise as a mechanism through which firms can navigate interregional institutional frictions. It also offers practical guidance for firms and policymakers seeking to leverage patent agency services to support high‐quality cross‐regional innovation.

title: International comparisons of institutions and innovation: Assessing the role of institutional coherence
Consumers Overestimate How Much Others Value Valenced Content
abstract: ABSTRACT Consumers often decide what to share by estimating how much others will value a piece of content. We show that these estimates are systematically miscalibrated for emotionally valenced material. Across four studies spanning controlled tasks and naturalistic contexts, people overestimated others’ valuation of valenced, especially negative, content relative to others’ self‐reports and willingness to pay. Process evidence indicates that valence makes highly affected exemplars salient; focusing on these recipients inflates beliefs about audiences’ valuations, which in turn predicts higher sharing intentions. A lightweight focus‐switching prompt that asks senders to consider a specific close friend reduces this bias to narrow the valenced–neutral sharing gap. These findings recast the spread of valenced content as a judgment bias about what audience value, not reducible to other established drivers of sharing, integrating value‐based sharing with projection biases in consumer judgment. Managerially, interface prompts and audience‐specification defaults can rebalance sharing toward content that audiences actually value, with implications for engagement quality, customer decisions, and consumer welfare.

title: Auspicious Names, Social Aims: The Psychology Behind Souvenir Gift‐Giving
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research has shown that auspicious product names can enhance consumer attitudes and purchase intentions, but less is known about the psychological processes and relational conditions through which such culturally symbolic names influence gift choice. This research examines how auspicious naming shapes tourists' decisions to purchase souvenirs as gifts. Across four studies and two supplementary experiments, we show that auspicious naming enhances gift purchase intention through two mechanisms: gift‐social goal congruence and gift‐selection self‐efficacy. Relational closeness strengthens the indirect effect through gift‐social goal congruence, whereas recipient relative status strengthens both indirect pathways. Together, these findings show how culturally symbolic product names operate in socially situated gift‐giving by shaping both meaning‐purpose fit and gift‐selection capability, and by showing how these processes vary across giver‐recipient relationships.

title: Balancing Artificial Intelligence Autonomy and User Control: Threat‐Contingent Appraisal Pathways to Consumer Responses
abstract: ABSTRACT AI–enabled products increasingly delegate decision authority to autonomous systems, yet consumer responses to such autonomy depend on whether users retain meaningful control and how threatening the technology is perceived to be. Drawing on both Technology Threat Avoidance Theory (TTAT) and a risk–benefit appraisal perspective, this research examines how AI autonomy and user control shape consumer responses under different levels of perceived technological threat. Across one qualitative study and three experiments, the findings reveal distinct appraisal patterns. Under high perceived technological threat, AI autonomy and user control interact to shape perceived product risk, with greater autonomy associated with lower risk when user control is high, which in turn influences consumer responses. Under low perceived technological threat, greater AI autonomy enhances perceived relative benefit, which in turn promotes favorable consumer responses. A within‐category manipulation of technological threat provides a more controlled test of these patterns. The research also extends the evidence beyond purchase and usage intentions by examining product choice, information seeking, test‐driving decisions, and willingness to pay. Overall, this research provides a threat‐contingent account of consumer responses to AI autonomy by highlighting the role of retained user control under technological threat and identifying distinct risk‐ and benefit‐based appraisal pathways across threat contexts.

title: The Fragile Encounter: Service Interaction Vulnerability in Emergency Department Care
abstract: This paper investigates service interaction vulnerability (SIV) within emergency departments, where both patients and providers are susceptible to heightened vulnerability. Providers face exhaustion from long shifts, high patient volumes, challenging patient behaviors, and systemic constraints contributing to emotional exhaustion. Patients, meanwhile, feel vulnerable due to illness or injury and their dependency on providers, compounded by the ways in which presenting certain characteristics, such as intimate partner violence, substance use, or suicidal ideation, can shape how they are perceived and treated in the system. These dynamics often result in unintended negative consequences that exacerbate perceived vulnerability for both patients and providers. Employing a mixed-method approach, including hospital data analysis and netnography, this study introduces a theoretical framework for SIV that illuminates how patient–provider interactions can exacerbate or mitigate vulnerabilities. By examining how these interactions shape the likelihood of service failure or successful service encounters, the study advances understanding of dual vulnerability in high-stakes service contexts.

title: Inventory adjustment under global supply chain pressure: the moderating role of working capital structure
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to investigate how global supply chain pressure affects firms' inventory adjustment and how this relationship depends on their working capital structure, specifically supplier trade credit, customer credit exposure, and liquidity. Design/methodology/approach We draw on organizational information processing theory and real options theory to develop hypotheses about how global supply chain pressure and working capital structure shape firm inventory adjustment. The hypotheses are tested using a panel of 214,674 firm-quarter observations from 6,499 publicly listed US manufacturing firms over 1998–2025. We employ a shift–share panel design with firm and quarter fixed effects for the empirical analysis. Findings The results reveal that firms increase inventory as global supply chain pressure rises, but the average buffering response masks substantial heterogeneity in how firms manage supply uncertainty. Firms with higher supplier trade credit and customer credit exposure respond more strongly by increasing inventory. Liquidity has the opposite effect. It weakens the inventory response and, at high levels, reverses it, indicating a shift toward flexibility preservation. Liquidity further conditions the role of supplier trade credit and customer credit exposure, such that supplier financing matters most when liquidity is scarce, whereas customer credit exposure becomes more consequential when liquidity is abundant. Originality/value This study contributes to inventory management research by integrating the buffering and flexibility preservation perspectives on inventory under uncertain supply chain conditions. It shows that rising global supply chain pressure does not uniformly lead firms to build inventory buffers. Instead, the balance between buffering and flexibility preservation depends on the working capital structure that supports or constrains inventory commitment. The study also advances a liquidity-centered account of inventory adjustment by showing that liquidity changes both the inventory response to global supply chain pressure and the roles of supplier financing and customer credit exposure in supporting inventory buffers under strained supply conditions.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Spanning boundaries to boost network engagement along implementation processes of digital technologies: evidence from a multiple case study in hospitals
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how boundary spanners realise network engagement during the implementation of digital technologies in healthcare operations, focusing on how actors connect diverse stakeholder groups across organisational, functional and professional boundaries. Design/methodology/approach A multiple case study was conducted in two hospitals implementing comparable digital technologies with contrasting outcomes. Data were collected through archival documents and two rounds of semi-structured interviews. By means of inductive analysis, we identified boundary-spanning roles and their contribution to network engagement across organisational, functional and professional boundaries. Findings The findings show that boundary-spanning roles operate not in isolation, but as a constellation that jointly activate, embed and legitimise across diverse groups of actors. Through this constellation, actors cross organisational, functional and professional boundaries, thereby supporting the implementation of digital technologies in healthcare operations. Originality/value This study contributes to healthcare operations literature by moving beyond single-organisation adoption models and introducing a network-based perspective on technology implementation. It advances boundary-spanning theory by conceptualising how boundary-spanning roles enable engagement across multi-actor networks, addressing a gap at the intersection of digital technology, healthcare operations and implementation. Practical principles are provided to guide managers in defining, supporting and leveraging boundary-spanning roles during technology implementation in healthcare operations.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Cohort Profile: A Scottish population-level study on the outcomes of people released from prison (RELEASE)
Calls to action and voter engagement on Facebook: a comparative study of eight European election campaigns
abstract: This study examines the use of Facebook by political actors across eight European countries – Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Kosovo, Norway, Portugal, Spain, United Kingdom – as they attempt to engage voters through calls to action. By analysing what is often referred to as the supply and demand of political communication, the paper conceptualizes three primary types of calls to action: informing, mobilizing, and interacting. Our findings reveal that mobilizing calls are the most prevalent, reflecting the central mission of election campaigns to secure voter turnout. However, such calls do not necessarily result in higher user engagement compared to informative content. Despite the potential for interactive features to enhance dialogic communication, they remain underutilized, with political actors apparently favouring controlled interactivity to maintain message control. The study highlights significant cross-country differences, with variations in the degree of engagement reached by different calls to action as influenced by national political contexts and campaign cultures. The research underscores the importance of considering both the strategic priorities of political actors and the cultural and institutional factors that shape voter engagement on social media.

title: Data visualisation as an ‘emotional repository’
abstract: Understanding the role of emotions in engagements with data visualisations (graphs, charts, maps) is important given their increasing circulation in everyday life and their influence on how people make sense of social and political issues. This paper builds on sociological perspectives on emotions and advances existing research on the interplay between data visualisation and emotions by proposing the concept of ‘emotional repository’ to describe data visualisations. I argue that data visualisations do not simply evoke emotional responses but become sites where emotions attach to, accumulate around, and acquire meaning through specific visual, data, and socio-political contexts. To explore this, the paper draws on empirical research, analysing thirty-four semi-structured interviews and thirteen follow-up interviews with diverse social media users who responded to climate data visualisations published on social media by environmental organisations. The paper makes an original contribution to the limited existing research on data visualisation in society by showing how data visualisations are socially and politically structured through their embedding within broader socio-political contexts. Moreover, it argues that data visualisations have the potential to make distressing topics, such as climate disaster, more palatable and aesthetically enjoyable, thereby influencing how social media users emotionally engage with and respond to the information presented in the data visualisation. The findings suggest that approaches to data visualisation should extend beyond clarity and accuracy to consider the social, political, and emotional contexts that shape how people engage with data.

title: Quantifying lifetime risk of Lyme disease: a population-based modelling study in the United States
Sleep health and uterine leiomyomata incidence and growth: a prospective ultrasound study
abstract: Abstract Poor sleep may negatively impact reproductive outcomes, yet its role in uterine leiomyomata (UL) development has not been studied. We estimated prospectively the association of self-reported sleep health with ultrasound-detected UL incidence and growth in the Study of Environment, Lifestyle, and Fibroids, a prospective cohort of Black individuals aged 23-35 years in Detroit, Michigan. At each of five clinic visits (2010-2020), participants reported sleep duration, frequency of trouble sleeping, and sleep quality, and underwent transvaginal ultrasound to detect incident UL. We used Cox proportional hazards regression models to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and applied inverse probability weights to adjust for time-dependent confounding. Among 1,137 participants, 351 developed UL (10-year cumulative incidence: 30.9%). Short (<6 hours/day, HR=0.30 95% CI: 0.17, 0.55) sleep duration and consistently poorer sleep quality (<4 days/week feeling well-rested, HR=0.78, 95% CI: 0.56, 1.08) were associated with lower UL incidence. Increased frequency of trouble sleeping was positively associated with UL incidence (≥15 days/month, HR=1.96, 95% CI: 0.76, 5.09). Sleep health was not associated with UL growth. In this prospective ultrasound study, sleep measures were inconsistently associated with UL incidence and not associated with UL growth.

title: Husband smoking, smoking cessation, and fecundability among couples with non-smoking wives
abstract: Abstract Among couples with non-smoking wives, the relationship between husband smoking and fecundability remains uncertain. Evidence is limited regarding whether smoking cessation before conception is associated with improved fecundability. We included a total of 4,569,530 reproductive-aged couples with non-smoking wives from the National Free Pre-conception Check-up Project in China from 2015 to 2017. Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate fecundability hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Among 4,569,530 eligible couples, 1,228,222 (26.88%) husbands reported smoking at baseline. Within 1 year, 3,046,804 couples (66.68%) conceived, with a median TTP of 2.76 cycles. Husband smoking was associated with lower fecundability (HR=0.97, 95% CI, 0.97-0.97), demonstrating a dose-response relationship. Among 781,481 couples in which the husband smoked and conception occurred within 1 year, 507,530 (64.94%) reported smoking cessation. Smoking cessation was associated with higher fecundability (HR=1.23, 95% CI, 1.23-1.24), with consistent benefits across prior smoking levels, although the magnitude of improvement was smaller among husbands who smoked more heavily. Associations varied by age and were more pronounced in older couples. These findings support the inclusion of husband smoking cessation in preconception care and highlight its potential role in promoting smoke-free households and broader tobacco control efforts.

title: Driving Simulation Methods for Assessing Post-Injury Driving Performance After Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: A Scoping Review
abstract: Driving is a cognitively demanding task that involves the continuous integration of attention, executive control, visual processing, and motor coordination. Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) may disrupt these functions and affect driving performance during recovery. Driving simulation is increasingly used to examine post-mTBI driving performance, yet substantial heterogeneity exists in simulator platforms, task designs, and outcome selection. This scoping review characterized driving simulation methodologies used to assess post-mTBI driving performance and examined patterns of mTBI-related findings across reported outcomes. A systematic search of seven electronic databases identified 12 eligible publications between 2017 and 2026. Publications were synthesized by participant characteristics, time since injury, simulator platform, task demands, and outcomes. Across publications, mTBI-related findings were most frequently reported for vehicle control metrics, particularly lane position variability and speed regulation. mTBI-related differences were most often condition-specific, including differences during curves, hazard events, and manipulated cognitive load or dual-task conditions. Cognitive measures also demonstrated mTBI-related differences and associations to driving performance, particularly those assessing executive functioning and processing speed domains. Differences were observed across all post-injury intervals, including ≥ 15 days, with a small number of related publications reporting performance differences after symptom resolution. However, the predominantly cross-sectional evidence does not establish whether these differences persist over time within the same individuals. Findings suggest that driving simulation can provide a useful controlled method for examining functional driving performance following mTBI across varying road environments and task demands. Future work should prioritize standardizing simulator outcomes and validating simulator performance against on-road, naturalistic-driving, and crash-related outcomes.

title: Exploring pathways between childhood parental abuse and adulthood generalized anxiety disorder: The roles of neuroticism, extraversion, and conscientiousness
abstract: Background Childhood parental abuse is an established risk factor for adulthood generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), but the personality mechanisms explaining this pathway are underinvestigated. Based on developmental psychopathology and triple vulnerability models, this study evaluated whether neuroticism, extraversion, and conscientiousness mediated the 18-year prospective paths from maternal and paternal abuse to adulthood GAD severity. Each abuse source was tested independently. Method Community adults ( N = 3293) ( M age = 45.61 years, standard deviation [ SD ] = 11.41, range = 20–86; 54.95% women; 89.7% non-Hispanic White) participated in three Midlife Development in the United States (MIDUS) study waves. A parallel latent variable mediation analysis estimated all three personality traits as mediators. Covariate-adjusted analyses controlled for age, sex, race, education, and body mass index (BMI). Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs) and residualized-change models differentiated trait-level from within-person effects. Results Greater maternal, but not paternal, abuse significantly predicted higher neuroticism, which, in turn, significantly mediated the path to GAD symptoms ( B = 0.051, p = .008). This effect remained significant after covariate adjustment and in unadjusted and covariate-adjusted RI-CLPMs ( Bs = 0.074 and 0.060, p s < .001), though paternal abuse showed a smaller effect. Change-based mediation was attenuated ( B = 0.007, p = .014). Conscientiousness and extraversion did not mediate any path. Discussion Neuroticism mediated the 18-year path from childhood maternal abuse to GAD symptoms, mainly via trait-level differences, but pre-existing personality differences are still potential confounders. Neuroticism-focused prevention approaches, possibly optimized via transdiagnostic strategies, require assessment.

title: Maternal childhood emotional abuse and prosocial behavior in Chinese preschoolers: Roles of parenting and children's social information processing
Unpacking the Gender Wage Gap: Integrating Gradational Measures of Gender Perceptions
abstract: The wage gap between men and women remains a durable form of gender labor market stratification. In this article, we integrate gradational measures of gender perceptions with standard models of the binary gender wage gap. Specifically, we articulate two pathways through which gradational gender perceptions may assist in explaining the disparity in wages between people who identify as men and women: the “gender atypicality” perspective and the “masculinity premium” perspective. Drawing on original survey data from more than 4,000 workers in the low-wage service sector in the United States, we find that, on average, men and women receive higher wages when they are perceived as more masculine and that differences in perceived masculinity assist in explaining some of the binary gender wage gap. While this main set of findings aligns with the “masculinity premium” perspective, we show that this pattern is far from universal. It holds only among woman-dominated jobs and does not hold for tips. Additionally, women who are perceived as more masculine also report higher levels of gender discrimination and sexual harassment. Together, these findings contribute to our understanding of the gender wage gap, encourage the use of more gradational and perceptual measures of gender, and point to important heterogeneity in the ways that these processes operate.

title: Data-driven design of hybrid energy systems: Insights from a high-resolution nationwide geospatial assessment
abstract: In the United States, roughly 95% of hydrogen is produced via steam methane reforming (SMR) and natural gas is becoming increasingly valuable for other applications such as power generation and export. This study evaluates pathways to diversify supply and lower hydrogen costs through a high-resolution, physics-based, open-source assessment of off-grid hybrid energy systems for electrolytic hydrogen. We resolve plant design, nonlinear electrolyzer performance and degradation, and hydrogen storage across 58,225 sites, executing approximately 173 million simulations that sweep 198 wind-solar-battery configurations, five hydrogen storage options and three electrolyzer CapEx scenarios, to produce geographically resolved design guidance. Key findings: (1) Hybrid and hybrid-battery plants minimize levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) at nearly all sites, with optimal designs consistently oversizing generation relative to electrolyzer capacity. (2) Declining electrolyzer costs simplify plant designs by eliminating batteries, this change in plant design leads to lower capacity factors and shorter stack lives. (3) Electrolyzer cost reductions yield larger LCOH reductions without storage than with buried pipe. (4) Optimal storage adds approximately $0.64/kg on average; buried pipe is never the least-cost option but is widely considered deployable today. Together, these results show that off-grid hybrid energy systems can become increasingly competitive with SMR as electrolyzer CapEx costs fall and indicate where that competitiveness emerges first. Future work should assess advanced dispatch to limit degradation and LCOH, optimize for fixed delivery profiles, and expand to additional electrolyzer types and dispatchable generators to map broader hybridization benefits.

title: An LLM-guided multi-objective optimization framework for cluster-aware electric vehicle charging management toward sustainable grid operation
abstract: The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) is increasing stress on power distribution networks by amplifying peak demand and reducing charging-station utilization under uncoordinated charging. This study proposes a Large Language Model-guided Hyper-Heuristic (LLM-HH) for adaptive EV charging coordination. The framework uses a lightweight LLM-based meta-controller that monitors compact optimization feedback signals, including hypervolume (HV) improvement, population diversity, and stagnation, to orchestrate a portfolio of multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) through constrained solver selection and bounded parameter updates. Under an hourly coordination model, the framework coordinates a portfolio of MOEAs to jointly optimize three competing objectives: reducing on-peak demand, improving charger utilization, and preserving a cluster-level energy-per-session proxy across three behaviorally distinct charging regimes: Quick Top-Up, Home-Based, and Public-Stay. Experiments on a real-world Korean EV charging dataset demonstrate that the optimization-feedback-driven LLM-HH consistently improves Pareto front quality, achieving statistically significant improvements in Pareto-front quality over strong MOEA baselines and adaptive HH comparators, reducing on-peak demand by up to 18%, and incurring negligible runtime overhead ( < 2 % ). The framework also supports practical deployment through auditable, guardrail-constrained control actions grounded in optimization feedback. These results demonstrate that LLM-guided HH can improve the robustness, efficiency, and scalability of coordinated EV charging for more sustainable grid operation.

title: Calibrated uncertainty quantification for prosumer flexibility aggregation in ancillary service markets
abstract: Reliable forecasting of prosumer flexibility is critical for demand response aggregators participating in frequency controlled ancillary service markets, where reliability requirements such as the P90 standard are enforced. Limited behavioural data and dependence on exogenous forecasts introduce uncertainty into flexibility estimates, which can lead to reserve overestimation and financial penalties. This study applies and systematically evaluates established uncertainty quantification approaches based on Monte Carlo dropout (MCD), conformal prediction (CP), and conformalised quantile regression (CQR) to construct prediction intervals for aggregated prosumer flexibility and support uncertainty-aware aggregator bidding. The approaches are evaluated for a behind-the-meter aggregator participating in the Danish manual frequency restoration reserve capacity market. A large-scale synthetic dataset is generated using an industry-grade home energy management system, combined with publicly available load, solar, price, activation, and device-level data. Multiple multivariate CP strategies are evaluated using MCD predictions, alongside CQR using a separately trained quantile regression model. Under nominal synthetic test conditions, conformal methods substantially improve joint coverage compared with uncalibrated MCD baselines. More conservative methods satisfy the 90% lower-tail reliability requirement, while CQR and MCP provide comparatively narrow intervals and higher retained economic value. CQR and MCP retain approximately 69% and 68% of perfect-information profit, respectively, under the stricter penalty interpretation. A controlled robustness analysis further shows that increasing perturbations of load, solar, price, and activation inputs increase overbidding and reduce empirical coverage and economic performance. The results highlight the trade-off between reliability, economic value, and robustness to input uncertainty when applying established uncertainty quantification approaches to aggregator bidding.

title: Entropic risk-aware end-to-end learning for stochastic optimization of renewable-rich integrated energy systems
Constraint-first energy-efficient indoor environmental control with multi-agent device coordination and knowledge-graph memory
A region-aware field reliability prediction method for power batteries under heterogeneous conditions using improved deep clustering
abstract: Power batteries, as core components of new energy systems, exhibit significant regional variability in field reliability under heterogeneous operating conditions. However, accurate prediction of region-specific reliability remains challenging due to the scarcity of comprehensive field failure data across diverse regions and the homogeneity assumptions commonly adopted in existing regional reliability modeling. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel region-aware field reliability prediction method for power batteries under heterogeneous conditions, leveraging an improved deep clustering algorithm. First, environmental factors and a macro-level socioeconomic covariate associated with regional field reliability are systematically analyzed and identified, and a dynamic panel dataset is constructed. Mutual information is employed to quantify their statistical associations with regional field reliability. Second, an improved Transformer-based multi-kernel ensemble spectral clustering (TMESC) algorithm is developed to enable intelligent regional classification driven by heterogeneity in observed regional characteristics. Third, based on the derived regional clusters and available failure data from observed regions, a nonlinear mapping model is developed to quantitatively link field reliability with regional characteristics, facilitating accurate prediction of field reliability in unobserved regions. Experimental results show that, guided by TMESC clustering, the proposed method estimates power battery failure rates and has accurate predictive ability at the regional aggregate scale, improving regional reliability assessment and providing support for data-driven warranty and maintenance strategies.

title: Resource flows in the UK’s foundation industries
abstract: The UK foundation industries supply essential materials but remain difficult to decarbonise because of high-temperature processing and process emissions. This study implements a gate-to-gate resource flow mapping, integrating material and energy inputs and outputs, by-products, and direct emissions, for selected cement, ceramics, chemicals, glass, metals, and paper products in 2019, benchmarked against global averages and product-mix-adjusted energy best practice. These products totalled 33 Mt/yr, used 330 PJ/yr of fuels and purchased electricity, and emitted 27 MtCO 2 /yr (Scope 1): 12.5 Mt from process reactions, 12.3 Mt from fossil fuels, and 2.1 Mt biogenic. Recovered materials (e.g., scrap), not counting by-products (e.g., slag), supplied 14% of material inputs excluding water and oxygen. UK energy intensity was 13% above the global benchmark. The gap to energy best practice is 28% in energy use but only 15% in direct emissions, mainly due to process-reaction emissions. This baseline can inform sectoral decarbonisation priorities and monitoring.

title: Hippocampal Meis2+ Interneurons Remodeling Involved in the Chronic Pb Exposure-Induced Learning and Memory Impairment: Single-Nucleus and Spatial Multiomics Evidence
abstract: Abstract Lead (Pb), recognized as the second greatest global environmental risk factor, is associated with lifelong and irreversible learning and memory impairments resulting from chronic exposure. However, the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. We integrated single-nucleus transcriptomics, spatial multiomics, neuroelectrophysiological, and morphological techniques to systematically delineate the susceptible neuronal cells and their interaction networks within hippocampal subregions following Pb exposure. The results indicated that Pb exposure led to a significant increase in the proportion of Meis2+ interneurons in the CA1 and CA3 regions of the hippocampus, and dysregulated calcium signaling. This subtype may affect PV+ and SST+ IN subtypes as well as CA3 excitatory neurons via abnormal intercellular NRG and EPHA signaling, contributing to E/I imbalance and impairing learning and memory. Moreover, reduced NRG signaling output from oligodendrocytes and microglia to IN subtypes likely exacerbates the impairment. Our findings highlight Meis2+ interneurons as a core IN subtype that may drive a cascade of “transcriptional changes – calcium signaling dysregulation – impaired neuronal interactions – reduced glial support”, offering potential targets for intervening in environmental Pb neurotoxicity.

title: Correspondence on “Kidney Urate Underexcretion Mediates the Relationship between Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances and their Alternatives and Uric Acid Levels: Evidence from a Case–Control Study and an Animal Study”
abstract: reports that decreased fractional excretion of uric acid (FEUA%) mediates the association between exposure to perand polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) and increased serum uric acid levels.While the authors integrate epidemiological and experimental data, the direction of causality in their findings warrants more careful consideration.A primary concern is reverse causality in epidemiological study.Although it was described as a "case-control study" in the title, this research essentially functions as a "cross-sectional analysis" because serum PFAS concentrations and FEUA% were measured simultaneously using the blood samples at recruitment. 2 A common misconception is to regard a casecontrol study as merely a comparison between "case" and "control" groups.The critical distinction from a cross-sectional study lies in whether the exposure can be ascertained to have occurred prior to the outcome, i.e., whether a temporal origin of the exposure in the past can be clearly identified.Consequently, the temporal relationship between FEUA% and blood PFAS levels remains unclear in the study design.1 Several PFASs have long biological half-lives, 3 and they may reflect exposure in the past.However, PFASs are eliminated primarily through renal excretion, and their serum concentrations are strongly influenced by renal clearance efficiency.It is highly plausible that reduced renal function leads to the accumulation of both PFASs and uric acid in blood, meaning decreased FEUA% may be confounded, rather than a result (Figure 1).This concern is supported by the study's data.The hyperuricemia group had significantly higher serum creatinine levels (88.43 μmol/L) than the control group (79.84 μmol/L), suggesting baseline differences in renal function.Furthermore, the metabolisms of urate differ fundamentally between rodents and humans.In humans, uric acid is the terminal metabolic product of purines because of the evolutionary loss of the uricase enzyme.Conversely, mice possess functional uricase, meaning uric acid is an intermediate metabolite that is further degraded into allantoin.4 This significant species difference complicates the extrapolation of urate-related mechanisms from mice to humans.We suggest that the authors more extensively discuss the potential for reverse causality, the limitations of their study design, and the extrapolability of animal study based on the biochemical differences.

title: From Equality to Equity: The Dual Socioeconomic Inequalities of Mobility-Based Exposure and Exposure Avoidance Options during Urban Floods
abstract: Abstract Urban pluvial flooding creates unequal risks that are not fully captured by residence-based exposure measures. We developed a framework that jointly evaluates mobility-based flood exposure (MFE) and exposure avoidance constraint (EAC), defined as the additional travel distance required to reduce flood susceptibility. Within Beijing’s Fifth Ring Road, we combined AlphaEarth Foundation Embeddings with mobile phone signaling data to quantify flood exposure and flood-avoidance routing constraints for 614,510 residents. EAC is measured by constructing Pareto frontiers through Monte Carlo path simulation, while multinomial logit models with interaction terms are used to examine the relationships between socioeconomic status (SES) and the dual inequalities. The results show: (1) residence-based assessment suffers from the Neighborhood Effect Averaging Problem, leading to systematic bias relative to mobility-based measures; (2) low-SES groups experience dual disadvantages, characterized by higher MFE and higher EAC; and (3) the interaction between exposure and avoidance constraint is state-dependent, reinforcing the relative disadvantage of low-SES residents beyond an additive pattern under finite EAC, while limiting further socioeconomic differentiation under infinite EAC. We argue for a shift from an equality-oriented to an equity-oriented perspective, providing actionable insights for disaster risk reduction and the achievement of SDGs 3, 10, and 11.

title: Emissions of Respirable Magnetite from the Coal-Fired Power Sector in China: Spatial Inequalities and Mitigation Pathways
