title: EXPRESS: The Dark Side of Competition for Market Share: Competitive Pressure May Trigger Corporate Misconduct
abstract: There is an ongoing debate about the role of market share and market share–based competition in shaping corporate behavior and performance. This study advances the discussion by analyzing how a firm’s specific competitive situation drives corporate misconduct and how such misconduct affects future market share. Based on a theory-in-use approach, the authors propose the Theory of Market Share–Based Competitive Pressure (TMCP) and introduce four new market share–based constructs that reflect different dimensions of competitive pressure. Using a global sample of 2,145 firms across 254 industries over 11 years, they find that firms that are closer to market leadership and more closely followed by competitors are more prone to misconduct. The results demonstrate that misconduct systematically weakens the very market positions that created the pressure in the first place, with particularly strong penalties for environmental and governance–related misconduct incidents. Importantly, organizational characteristics such as compensation design, board composition, and marketing capabilities condition the extent to which competition translates into corporate misconduct. Together, these findings demonstrate that while misconduct may appear as a shortcut to defend competitive positions, it ultimately undermines them, and there are ways to reduce incentives for misconduct in the first place.

title: “Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source AI for entrepreneurship
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
abstract: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .

title: Looking Under the Hood of Commodity Currency Predictability
abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate predictability of commodity currencies through the lens of market efficiency. Focusing on currencies with strong contemporaneous exposure to commodity prices, we show that changes in country-specific commodity export or import prices predict exchange rate fluctuations both in sample and out of sample. We establish four empirical facts: (i) the sign of the predictive relationship runs counter to standard risk-based explanations; (ii) predictability is concentrated at short horizons; (iii) predictability is driven by a small set of thinly traded currencies; and (iv) even sophisticated speculative traders adjust positions sluggishly in response to commodity price shocks in these currencies. Together, these findings suggest that predictability arises from the slow incorporation of information in less actively traded currencies, which is likely due to liquidity and position-building constraints, rather than from compensation for risk. The results also clarify the sources of commodity-based predictability in carry trade returns. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07249 .

title: Recomposing Management Education Under Climate Crisis: Towards a Composting Heuristic for Epistemic Change
abstract: Abstract Management learning and education (MLE) is increasingly critiqued for its reliance on anthropocentric and profit‐maximization paradigms, which fail to adequately address the escalating ecological and climate crises. In this article, we call for an epistemic shift in MLE by introducing the metaphor of composting as a lens for collective reflexive critique. We propose a composting heuristic inspired by the social practices of managing organic matter—landfill, industrial composting and community composting—to help MLE educators critically examine the epistemic foundations, limitations and possibilities that shape their teaching and learning practices. This metaphorical framework highlights an epistemic transition towards a multispecies and regenerative pedagogical paradigm, grounded in relational ontology, care and embodied practice. We argue that engaging with the metaphor of composting—and reflecting critically on one's positioning within the landfill‐industrial‐community composting heuristic—can catalyse a collective endeavour to drive epistemic change in MLE in response to the urgent demands of climate and ecological breakdown.

title: EXPRESS: Interactive Blind Lead-In Ads and Purchase Conversion: The Roles of Completion and Creative Design Features
abstract: Interactive display advertising increasingly employs delayed product disclosure in multi-stage formats, yet little is known about how they affect purchase behavior when exposure to the reveal depends on users’ interaction. This article studies interactive blind lead-in (BLI) ads with a randomized field experiment: over 109,000 customers of a book retailer were assigned to a BLI ad with delayed reveal or a static ad with immediate disclosure. The experiment identifies a boundary condition on the transfer of prior interactivity findings to user-controlled delayed-reveal advertising: assignment to the BLI format does not increase average purchase conversion, as interactivity’s positive mechanisms need not produce a conversion gain when most exposures end before the reveal. Using random assignment as an instrument, completing the BLI sequence increases long-term purchase conversion among compliers (a 46.6% lift; 437 completions per incremental purchase), indicating that delayed-reveal interactivity is effective only when users meaningfully interact with the ad. Completion varies across ads consistent with a Cost-of-Progress framework: early informational cues predict higher completion, late-stage textual and visual complexity predicts lower completion, and social cues predict higher completion when placed before the final stage. A supplementary study shows that the downstream impact of BLI interaction depends on overall hedonic experience.

title: Forward‐Looking ESG Relevance and Corporate Performance: Evidence From Credit Ratings
abstract: ABSTRACT How does the relevance of ESG issues relate to firm performance, and does ESG relevance moderate the relationship between ESG engagement and firm financial outcomes? Using a novel indicator introduced by Fitch Ratings, we provide new empirical evidence to answer these questions. The forward‐looking indicator measures the relevance of ESG issues to firms' credit ratings. It captures firms' financial sensitivity to ESG‐related issues from a credit‐rating perspective. Utilising a sample of 663 firms from 55 countries, we examine the relationship between ESG relevance, its subcategories and firm performance. We find that environmental relevance has a significant negative association with firm performance. The results are economically meaningful as a one‐standard‐deviation increase in the environmental relevance score associated with decreases in Tobin's Q and return on assets ( ROA ) by 5.7% and 11.9%, respectively. Furthermore, we investigate how ESG relevance interacts with ESG performance in explaining firm performance. We find that environmental relevance significantly weakens the positive association between environmental performance and firm financial performance. The association between ESG relevance and firm performance is primarily concentrated in environmental relevance, while the moderating effect is concentrated in Tobin's Q . The findings remain broadly robust to instrumental variable regressions, propensity score matching and alternative measures of firm performance. Further analysis of the disaggregated components of environmental relevance indicates that the negative association is primarily concentrated in the relevance of greenhouse gas emissions. Our findings provide important insights into why ESG relevance matters for investors and firm performance, an issue that is often neglected in the literature.

title: Silent Strategies: CEO Populism, Supply Chain Opacity, and Biodiversity Disclosure
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether CEO populist rhetoric is associated with corporate biodiversity disclosure and whether supply‐chain opacity conditions this relationship. Using an unbalanced panel of 1828 nonfinancial listed firms from 12 European countries over 2014–2022, the analysis comprises 15,842 firm‐year observations in the baseline estimation. Firm fixed effects, two‐stage least squares, and two‐step system GMM models are used to account for unobserved heterogeneity, potential endogeneity, and dynamic persistence. The findings show that CEO populist rhetoric is negatively associated with biodiversity disclosure and positively associated with supply‐chain opacity, indicating that stronger populist rhetoric coincides with less visible, specific, and verifiable publicly reported upstream supply‐chain information. The moderation analysis provides qualified evidence that lagged supply‐chain opacity strengthens the negative association between CEO populism and biodiversity disclosure, suggesting that executive rhetoric is more strongly related to lower nature‐related transparency when upstream information is less visible and verifiable. These findings extend the understanding of biodiversity disclosure beyond a predominantly technical reporting perspective by showing that nature‐related transparency is associated with both executive rhetorical framing and the informational conditions surrounding upstream supply chains. Integrating upper echelons theory with stakeholder and institutional perspectives, the study explains how CEO rhetoric may shape the interpretation of external accountability demands while supply‐chain opacity affects the informational conditions under which such interpretations are reflected in disclosure. The study contributes to research on executive communication, sustainability governance, biodiversity reporting, and the credibility of corporate environmental disclosure.

title: When Eco‐Innovation Backfires: Governance Thresholds That Reverse Green Business Strategy in Sub‐Saharan Africa
abstract: ABSTRACT Sub‐Saharan Africa is attracting an increasing share of international climate finance, yet whether eco‐innovation consistently translates into environmental improvements remains unclear and highly variable across the region. This study examines the effect of eco‐innovation on carbon intensity and identifies the governance and infrastructural conditions under which its environmental benefits materialise. Using a balanced panel of 32 Sub‐Saharan African countries from 2002 to 2024, the study employs two‐way fixed‐effects estimation with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, Hansen threshold regression, interaction models and two‐stage least squares estimation to address cross‐sectional dependence, nonlinearity and endogeneity. The results show that eco‐innovation reduces carbon intensity on average, but its effectiveness is highly governance‐dependent. Although eco‐innovation lowers carbon intensity in West and Southern Africa, it is associated with higher carbon intensity in East and Central Africa, revealing an eco‐innovation paradox. Threshold analysis identifies a critical governance breakpoint at a Worldwide Governance Indicator score of −0.35, below which eco‐innovation increases carbon intensity and above which its environmental effect becomes negative. Approximately 42% of country‐year observations fall below this threshold. The findings further show that digital infrastructure strengthens the environmental benefits of eco‐innovation, whereas renewable energy consistently reduces carbon intensity irrespective of governance quality. The study advances the eco‐innovation literature by identifying a measurable institutional threshold that explains heterogeneous environmental outcomes and provides a practical governance benchmark for firms, policymakers and development finance institutions seeking to maximise the environmental returns to green investment in Sub‐Saharan Africa.

title: Does Corporate Water Performance Matter to Investors?
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates whether corporate water performance matters to investors, using water consumption, withdrawals, and discharge as three proxies of performance. Based on a sample of 2141 US firm‐year observations with available water data in the CDP annual surveys over 2014–2019, we find that poor corporate water performance is consistently associated with lower market value. This valuation penalty is weaker among firms that voluntarily disclose their water performance data to the CDP, but stronger among firms with a dedicated CSR committee on the board. Our results are robust to potential endogeneity issues. Overall, our findings suggest that investors reward sound water management and penalize weak practices more heavily when governance structures raise expectations for environmental stewardship. The study offers policy‐relevant insights by highlighting the financial benefits of transparent water reporting and contributes to the emerging literature by showing that water stewardship is a value‐relevant corporate strategy.

title: The Influence of Voluntary Environmental Disclosure on the Environmental Impact of Waste Reduction Activities
abstract: ABSTRACT Using the Attention Based View (ABV) as a theoretical framework, this study investigates the moderating influence of firm voluntary environmental disclosure on the effectiveness of waste avoidance and waste management to improve two environmental metrics that have received differing levels of attention: carbon emissions and water usage. Employing a panel fixed effects estimation strategy, the results provide two key findings: (1) differing effectiveness of waste reduction strategies to reduce environmental harm and (2) voluntary disclosure moderates the effectiveness of waste reduction strategies to reduce environmental harm, though not always beneficially. Voluntary disclosure improves the environmental benefit of waste avoidance while attenuating that of waste management. Moreover, the moderating influence is more pronounced for water usage, showing that concerns receiving less external attention may benefit more from internal changes in managerial attention.

title: Corporate Governance and Sustainability Disclosure in Environmentally and Socially Sensitive Industries
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how corporate governance relates to environmental and social sustainability disclosure in environmentally and socially sensitive industries and whether these relationships differ from low‐impact industries. Drawing on stakeholder–agency and resource dependence theories, we analyze 3276 firm‐year observations from 503 European Union‐listed firms during 2011–2021 using OLS, instrumental‐variable, and two‐step system‐GMM estimations. Board size and gender diversity are positively associated with both disclosure dimensions. Board independence is positively associated with social disclosure, whereas CEO duality is negatively associated with social disclosure. Supplementary analysis of 6097 observations from 965 firms shows that most relationships between governance and disclosure do not differ significantly by industry sensitivity. However, CEO duality has a significantly more negative association with social disclosure in sensitive industries than in low‐impact industries. These findings identify industry sensitivity as a selective boundary condition and underscore the need to distinguish environmental from social disclosure when evaluating board effectiveness.

title: From Smart Waste Management to Environmental Performance: The Mediating Roles of Blockchain Transparency and Corporate Image in the Textile Industry
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital investment in smart waste management does not automatically translate into environmental performance (EP) gains, and this technology–performance gap is acute in the textile and apparel (T&A) industry, the world's second most polluting sector. Drawing on the resource‐based view, institutional theory, the technology acceptance model, the technology–organization–environment framework, and technological determinism as a rival baseline, this study tests whether smart waste management system (SWMS) adoption improves EP directly, and whether blockchain technology (BCT) and corporate image (CI) mediate this relationship, with environmental management system (EMS) as a moderator. Survey data from 294 T&A professionals in Bangladesh were analyzed using PLS‐SEM (SmartPLS 4) across eight hypothesized paths. SWMS shows no significant direct effect on EP; instead, the SWMS–EP relationship is fully mediated through a serial BCT–CI pathway, and this pathway is strengthened by EMS. The findings indicate that technology adoption alone is insufficient for environmental gains without complementary reputational and governance mechanisms, offering both a theoretical refinement of technology–performance models and practical guidance for green business strategy and circular economy activation in global apparel supply chains.

title: Who Benefits from Climate Investment? Gendered Employment Quality and Asymmetric Effects in the Green Transition
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate investment is widely expected to generate a “double dividend” by improving environmental sustainability while promoting inclusive development. However, its labor market consequences remain insufficiently understood. Using panel data from 28 OECD and European economies over the 2001–2023 period, this study examines how climate investment affects employment quality and gender inequality. The findings reveal a significant asymmetry: Climate investment substantially reduces female vulnerable employment, while its effect on male vulnerable employment is statistically insignificant. The resulting change in the female–male gap is therefore driven by improved female employment outcomes rather than deterioration in male outcomes. Mechanism analysis indicates that these effects operate through structural shifts toward service‐oriented sectors and improvements in female human capital. The effects are more pronounced in lower‐income, labor‐market‐flexible, and highly digitalized economies. These findings suggest that climate investment does not generate uniformly inclusive outcomes, but instead reshapes employment quality through gender‐differentiated access to emerging economic opportunities during the green transition.

title: Foreign knowledge spillovers and new product development speed in boundary-spanning teams: A sufficiency–necessity perspective on digital interoperability and collaborative conflict resolution capabilities
Understanding the spillover effect of personal AI use on service innovation: the role of psychological capital and conscientiousness
abstract: Purpose As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life and workplace operations, research has begun to document numerous organizational benefits, including enhanced efficiency and productivity. However, employees’ personal experiences with AI and how these experiences spill over into the work domain remain underexplored. Using sociomateriality as a sensitizing lens, we propose and test a sequential process in which personal AI use increases work-related AI use, further enhancing employees’ psychological capital, ultimately improving their service innovation performance. We further examine conscientiousness as an important boundary condition that moderates this pathway. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 uses a three-wave survey of 438 service employees and employs structural equation modeling to test the hypothesized serial mediation. Study 2 extends this investigation by examining within-person dynamics using a daily experience sampling design with 121 participants and testing the moderating role of conscientiousness. Findings Across both studies, personal AI use positively predicts employees’ work-related AI use, which in turn increases their psychological capital and subsequently service innovation performance. Moreover, employees lower in conscientiousness benefit more from AI use. Originality/value This paper contributes to our understanding of personal AI use’s spillover effect in the work domain, suggesting AI use may introduce psychological affordances that were less evident in earlier technologies. Our research demonstrates that individual personality differences can influence the effectiveness of human–AI collaboration.

title: Stakeholder salience: The empirical role of stakeholder multiplicity, stakeholder proximity, and social capital in SMEs
abstract: The stakeholder salience model is integral to understanding the entrepreneurial process. However, despite its contribution to stakeholder research, existing research on the model has stagnated, offering limited theoretical refinement and insufficient empirical attention to the relational, proximal, and interdependent nature of stakeholder interactions. Building on calls to develop the model’s explanatory richness, we examine how stakeholder multiplicity, stakeholder proximity, and structural social capital shape entrepreneurs’ perceptions of stakeholder salience in small-to-medium enterprises (SMEs). Using survey data from technology-enabled SMEs in Canada and Nigeria, we find that higher levels of stakeholder multiplicity, proximity, and social capital are associated with stronger perceptions of stakeholder salience. However, these relationships varied between the two country contexts, a difference we interpret through the lens of environmental dynamism. By integrating relational and network-based mechanisms into the stakeholder salience model, we enrich stakeholder theory by demonstrating that stakeholder salience relies on SMEs’ embeddedness in broader stakeholder networks.

title: Job crafting under pressure: roles of mindfulness and self-efficacy in the relationships between performance and citizenship pressure, job crafting, and service performance
abstract: As performance and citizenship pressures intensify for frontline service employees (FSEs), their roles in shaping job crafting behaviors and proactive service performance remain unclear. We seek to address this theoretical and empirical gap by examining a three-way interaction between performance and citizenship pressure, mindfulness, and self-efficacy in predicting FSEs’ job crafting—specifically task and relational crafting—as well as their proactive service performance. Using a three-wave longitudinal survey design, we collected data from 318 South Korean FSEs over a six-month period. The analyses revealed that the positive association between performance pressure and task crafting was significantly stronger among employees exhibiting high levels of mindfulness and self-efficacy. Similarly, citizenship pressure predicted relational crafting only when these personal resources were concurrently high. Moreover, mindfulness and self-efficacy jointly amplified the indirect effects of performance pressure on proactive service performance through task crafting, and of citizenship pressure via relational crafting. By elucidating the complex interplay between contextual demands and individual psychological resources, the findings offer important theoretical contributions to understanding how FSEs manage workplace pressures through adaptive behaviors.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Mapping Digital Platforms and Their Infrastructural Foundations for Biodiversity: A Bibliometric Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Biodiversity loss is increasingly recognized as a grand challenge requiring new forms of innovation, coordination, and knowledge integration across organizational and institutional boundaries. While digital technologies have substantially advanced how biodiversity is monitored, measured, and managed, less is known about how digital platforms and their underlying infrastructures can support innovation processes aimed at biodiversity protection and regeneration. This paper offers a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research connecting digital platforms, their infrastructural foundations, and biodiversity, based on a dataset of 528 scientific publications. Using co‐citation and keyword co‐occurrence analyses, the study maps the intellectual structure and evolution of this emerging field and identifies five promising research frontiers: platform governance for collective action, biodiversity data infrastructures, innovation for biodiversity, digital platforms as innovation intermediaries, and the orchestration of scalable nature‐based solutions. Building on these findings, the paper develops an integrative framework explaining how platform design and governance shape organizational coordination, knowledge integration, and innovation mechanisms, ultimately influencing biodiversity outcomes. The findings reveal that existing research remains largely technology‐driven, with a strong emphasis on monitoring and biodiversity data generation, while questions related to platform governance, ecosystem orchestration, and biodiversity valorization remain comparatively underdeveloped. By repositioning digital platforms as organizational infrastructures for biodiversity‐oriented innovation, rather than merely technological tools for ecological monitoring, this study contributes to the literature on digital innovation, platform ecosystems, and R&D management, while outlining a future research agenda for designing innovation ecosystems capable of supporting biodiversity‐positive transformation.

title: Matching for impact: a dyadic process model of mentor–venture alignment in entrepreneurial support organizations
abstract: Business incubators and accelerators (BIAs) play a central role in regional entrepreneurial ecosystems by providing mentoring to support new venture development, yet mentoring outcomes vary considerably. While prior research documents mentoring benefits, limited attention has been paid to how mentors and ventures are matched or how these processes shape outcomes. This study conceptualizes mentor–venture matching as a dyadic, co-constructed process and examines how alignment between mentors and ventures shapes the formation and evolution mentoring relationships and their outcomes. Drawing on a multi-stage qualitative research design involving interviews with program managers, twenty mentors, and twenty-one new ventures across twelve Belgian BIAs, as well as follow-up interviews with ventures, the study identifies distinct yet complementary selection criteria on both sides of the dyad. Mentors evaluate ventures based on experiential alignment, deep-level personal characteristics, and venture-specific attributes, whereas ventures assess mentors based on expertise, interpersonal qualities, and value alignment. The findings show that alignment across these dimensions is associated with different mentoring outcomes, ranging from short-term problem solving to access to networks, investment opportunities, and long-term professional collaborations. This study develops a process model explaining how early-stage matching conditions shape the depth, durability, and strategic value of mentoring relationships over time. By linking matching processes to differentiated outcomes, the study advances a dyadic perspective on entrepreneurial mentoring and contributes to research on entrepreneurial ecosystems by demonstrating how BIAs act as intermediaries shaping how mentoring relationships influence access to resources within entrepreneurial ecosystems.

title: Adapting to extreme heat: how corporate responses enhance customer stability
abstract: Purpose This paper examines the impact of extreme heat risk on corporate customer stability in the Chinese market. Design/methodology/approach Using a comprehensive dataset from 2012 to 2023, we find that greater exposure to city-level extreme heat risk incentive firms to adopt adaptive adjustments, thereby enhancing customer stability. Findings This effect is mainly achieved through three channels, including optimizing human capital, advancing digital transformation and strengthening supply chain finance. Cross-sectional heterogeneity test reveals that the impact is more pronounced in firms with lower labor intensity, fewer high-skilled employees and limited trade credit access. These findings provide novel evidence on how firms transform climate-related risks into opportunities to strengthen resilience, and offer important implications for corporate adaptation strategies and policy support in the context of global climate change. Originality/value Our research makes several contributions in three major aspects. First and foremost, our findings extend the literature on the economic consequences of extreme heat; furthermore, our research enriches the literature on the determinants of customer stability; last but not least, by examining the mechanism linking extreme heat risks at firm locations to customer stability, our study extends organizational adaptation theory to the context of climate risk and supply chains, enriching the theoretical framework on how climate factors influence corporate supply chain networks.

title: Covered interest rate parity in the presence of time-varying transaction costs: an application of the fractional integration approach
abstract: Purpose We demonstrate that fractional integration offers an improved framework for assessing the reliability of the covered interest rate parity condition compared with traditional unit root tests. Specifically, in the presence of transaction costs, the parity condition will tend towards one of the arbitrage bounds, making the process fractionally integrated at that bound which renders traditional unit root tests unsuitable. Given the widespread adoption of parity conditions in practice, in areas such as risk management and foreign exchange rate forecasting, an approach which permits an assessment of the reliability of these models, particularly for volatile markets such as emerging markets, is crucial. Design/methodology/approach We propose a threshold autoregression framework that more effectively identifies near-unit-root behaviour and improves market classification relative to conventional approaches. The analysis uses data from the industrialized markets of Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, New Zealand and Singapore, as well as the emerging markets of India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand, with the USA serving as the reference market. Findings Our results show that shocks to covered interest rate parity are asymmetric and that the parity conditions tend towards one of the arbitrage bounds. Originality/value The fractional integration approach is well established in the econometric literature, though we are the first to apply this in this context. In relation to the international finance literature on tests of parity, recent attention has been almost exclusively on the causes of parity deviations than on assessing the reliability of the condition as an exchange rate forecasting instrument.

title: Explainable medical artificial intelligence: The impact of agent and explanation types on health persuasion
I deserve better: beauty work increases consumer preference for advanced products
abstract: Consumers often engage in beauty work to improve their physical appearance. Prior research has largely focused on how such efforts shape others’ perceptions and inferences about the focal individual. However, little is known about its impact on consumers’ self-perception, particularly how these shifts influence subsequent product preferences. This research demonstrates that beauty work increases consumers’ preference for advanced products by heightening their perceived deservingness. Specifically, after engaging in beauty work, consumers are more likely to choose products featuring premium packaging, upgraded hardware, advanced services, and superior auxiliary functions. This effect occurs because beauty work uniquely generates a sense of “I deserve better”, a mechanism not observed in a general self-improvement activity. Additionally, we identify three boundary conditions: the effect dissipates (1) when beauty work does not produce visible appearance enhancement, (2) among entity theorists, and (3) when consumers make choices for others. Together, this research contributes to the literature on beauty work and offers practical implications for promoting advanced products.

title: Why some countries lead and others lag: The political economy of promoting battery electric vehicles
abstract: This study examines how macro-socioeconomic and institutional factors shape government policy orientations toward battery electric vehicle (BEV) promotion within the broader context of technological transitions. Using a political economy lens, we identify eight key factors — car industry, car infrastructure, car culture, oil and gas industry, energy sector, income per capita, air pollution and health, and environmental awareness — through an extensive literature review and a Delphi-based case study of Australia. A structured descriptive synthesis across 12 diverse countries indicates that BEV policy promotion is weak where multiple high-impact factors, such as a resistant auto industry, powerful oil and gas interests, and an entrenched car culture, converge unfavourably. Conversely, where environmental consciousness, pollution concerns, supportive infrastructure, and industrial ambitions align, as in Denmark, China, and Germany, pro-BEV policies are more robust. The study contributes to the analysis of low-carbon technological transitions by developing a diagnostic framework for assessing how differing macro-socioeconomic and institutional conditions relate to BEV policy orientations. Composite scores range from −10 to +21 across the sample, with 5 countries classified as supportive, 3 as ambivalent, and 4 as constraining; for example, Denmark exhibits strongly supportive conditions, while South Africa reflects strongly constraining structural factors. This offers a pragmatic tool for policymakers to assess national contexts and for researchers to interpret transition pathways, highlighting how both formal structures and informal political dynamics—such as lobbying, legacy industry influence, and cultural attitudes—shape the trajectory of sustainable mobility.

title: Investigating pro-environmental policy effectiveness from a consumer perspective
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the consumers’ perceived policy effectiveness to advance understanding of how environmental policies are evaluated across policy attributes, levels of attributes and contexts from a consumer perspective. Design/methodology/approach Three choice-based conjoint experiments were conducted to assess consumers’ perceived policy effectiveness for environmental policies varying in policy attributes (informational, economic and regulatory), levels of attributes (facilitating, constraining or absent) and contexts (plant-based food, electric vehicles and sustainably sourced clothing). Data were collected from student and general population samples. Conditional multinomial logit (cMNL) models were used to estimate the effects of policy attributes and attribute levels on choices of the most effective policy. Findings This research shows that consumers consistently perceive facilitating policies as more effective than constraining policies across different policy attributes (informational, economic and regulatory) and contexts (plant-based food, electric vehicles and sustainably sourced clothing). Findings highlight a fundamental misalignment between consumer-perceived and empirically assessed policy effectiveness. Research limitations/implications This study draws on Australian samples, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other cultural and institutional contexts. Future studies should examine whether this study’s findings can be extended to other cultural settings or conduct comparative research across countries with different cultural values. Practical implications The research advises policymakers and social marketers to avoid equating policy preference with perceived policy effectiveness. The findings help policymakers in identifying which policies are likely to face public resistance and where policy design or communication may be needed to better align public perceptions with empirical effectiveness. Originality/value The findings contribute to the policy and consumer behavior literature by establishing perceived policy effectiveness as a distinct construct worthy of investigation in its own right and by demonstrating that it is jointly shaped by policy attributes, levels of those attributes and contexts.

title: Rethinking human–AI agency in tourism and hospitality: A framework for the agentic AI era
Resolving the “privacy paradox” in digital tourism: A decision process lens
abstract: In digital tourism, travelers frequently disclose personal data despite expressing privacy concerns (i.e. “privacy paradox”). Although mandatory consent explains some disclosure, tourists retain meaningful choice across many encounters. Existing research offers limited insight into how tourists actually navigate these decisions. Drawing on narrative interviews with forty experienced Chinese digital tourists analyzed via the Gioia methodology, this study reconstructs disclosure as a process and identifies five qualitatively distinct decision modes—risk-benefit analysis, anchoring-adjustment, habitual, peer-influenced, and social norms-driven. These modes are linked through two experiential trajectories, analytically reconstructed from participants’ retrospective accounts: a self-centered path from deliberate analysis toward habitual automation, and an other-centered path from peer mimicry toward normative internalization. Both outcomes arise from accumulated disclosure decisions, but only one constitutes privacy cynicism. The paradox is thus mechanistically plural, reframing privacy theory and platform design in tourism.

title: Extreme environmental distance and global sustainability engagement: Evidence from the United Nations Global Compact
Giving Beyond Borders: Antibribery Enforcement and Philanthropic Giving Overseas
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study investigates why and how US multinational enterprises (MNEs) engage in philanthropic giving to foreign countries, exploring whether enforcement actions under the US Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) influence such giving behavior. Research Findings/Insights Using FCPA enforcement actions as reputational and enforcement shocks, we find that while firms directly implicated in violations (focal firms) do not alter their foreign philanthropic giving, peer MNEs operating in the same host countries significantly increase their donations. This increase is consistent with peer firms using philanthropy strategically to mitigate reputational spillovers, manage heightened enforcement risk, and build reputational capital. We establish these findings using a stacked difference‐in‐differences design. Theoretical/Academic Implications The study advances the literature on corporate philanthropy by identifying cross‐border enforcement shocks and peer effects as key determinants of international corporate philanthropy. We further contribute to research on nonmarket strategies by demonstrating that philanthropy can serve as a strategic response to regulatory and reputational risks. Practitioner/Policy Implications Our findings suggest that antibribery enforcement can influence corporate social behavior beyond focal firms, prompting philanthropic responses among peer MNEs operating in the same host country. Policymakers and regulators should consider these spillover effects when designing enforcement strategies. Likewise, corporate practitioners should recognize international philanthropy as a strategic tool for managing global compliance and legitimacy.

title: Employee Communication and Silence: The Role of Managers' Voice Solicitation
abstract: ABSTRACT The aim of this study is to explore employee communication as a distinctive Human Resources (HR) practice and its relationship to employee silence. Building on signalling theory and drawing on a nationally representative sample of 1200 respondents from the UK workforce, our findings reveal that effective employee communication is negatively related to employee silence via the mediating role of managerial voice solicitation. Our study makes significant contributions to the theory of Human Resource Management. Specifically, we depart from studies exploring bundles of HR practices to focus on employee communication as a distinctively important HR practice. In addition, our findings shed light on the existence of a signalling chain, highlighting the important role managers can play in dampening employee silence and its negative workplace repercussions. Furthermore, in contrast to previous work focusing on structural factors promoting employee silence, our study turns the spotlight on ways to alleviate it. Given the harmful effects of employee silence on both employees and organisations, our study offers actionable insights into how such a behaviour can be diminished in the workplace.

title: The Prestige Catalyst: How CEO Awards Accelerate Corporate Green Transformation Through Institutional Channels
abstract: Integrating reputation incentive theory with neo-institutional perspectives, this study explores the impact of CEO awards on corporate green transformation. Using data from Chinese A-share listed companies from 2008 to 2022, the study employs the Propensity Score Matching-Difference-in-Differences (PSM-DID) method. The findings indicate that CEO awards can promote corporate green transformation. Further analysis reveals that institutional pressures play a positive moderating role between CEO awards and corporate green transformation, with institutional pressures divided into three levels: regulatory pressure, normative pressure, and mimetic pressure. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the impact of CEO awards on green transformation is more significant for nonpolluting firms, non-high-tech firms, and non-capital-intensive firms. The study deepens the understanding of the executive recognition mechanism as an institutional tool and offers policy recommendations for integrating award mechanisms with sustainable governance in emerging economies.

title: Regularized Government Accounting Supervision and Suppliers’ Cash Holdings: Evidence from Supply Chain Spillover Effects
abstract: This article takes the reform pilot of strengthening accounting supervision carried out by the Ministry of Finance in selected provinces and municipalities at the end of 2020 as a quasi‑natural experiment, and adopts the difference‑in‑differences method to investigate the supply chain spillover effect of regularized government accounting supervision on the cash holding level of supplier firms. The study finds that when midstream firms are located in regions with the accounting supervision reform pilot, the cash holding level of their supplier firms decreases significantly. Mechanism tests show that regularized government accounting supervision functions mainly through two channels, namely reducing supply chain risks faced by suppliers and increasing the supply of trade credit. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the above effect is more pronounced among supplier firms that are state‑owned enterprises, have high customer concentration, and belong to high‑tech industries. This research expands the research boundary of the economic consequences of government accounting supervision, reveals the microeconomic effects of external regulatory institutions transmitted through supply chain relationships, and provides empirical evidence for improving China’s accounting supervision system and enhancing the financial resilience of supply chains.

title: Industrial policy in times of market power
abstract: We explore the effects of different industrial policies in a macroeconomic agent-based model calibrated to reproduce the decline in US business dynamism over the last half-century. R&D subsidies to innovators raise GDP growth but exacerbate the trend toward rising market power, while financial subsidies to adopters and standard capital-replacement schemes have negligible aggregate effects. A meaningful reversal of market power emerges only when innovation support is paired with adoption-oriented measures that relax the knowledge constraints of small adopters, e.g. the establishment of a National Competence Center providing technology transfer and knowledge upgrading. The effectiveness of each policy is dependent on the underlying technological regime: the growth–dynamism trade-off is sharpest in science-based regimes and attenuated in scale-intensive and supplier-dominated ones.

title: Follow the Money: The State and the Architecture of Union Funding
abstract: ABSTRACT Trade unions need money to sustain the staff, infrastructure and activities on which all forms of union power depend, yet the financial dimensions of unions and their power have been largely overlooked in the comparative study of industrial relations. This article addresses the gap by using unions’ financial means as a revealing lens for understanding the role of the state in shaping union power. The comparison distinguished two ideal‐typical logics of state action behind union funding. Under indirect action, the state enables unions to convert membership into income, producing a tight coupling between union funds and organisational power. Under direct action, the state channels funds to unions on the basis of their recognised societal roles, decoupling income from membership. Systematised during the early decades of the twentieth century, these two action paths present fundamental transformations through liberalisation, leading to the financialisation and politicisation of union funding. By analysing the structures and changes in unions’ financial sustainability, this framework reveals the state's constitutive role in shaping and transforming union power.

title: Nudging citizens to use chatbots: an information and default option approach
abstract: Governments are increasingly adopting chatbots to reduce administrative burdens and improve service quality, yet citizens’ willingness to use them remains limited. Drawing on nudge theory, this study examines how information framing and default options influence citizens’ willingness to use chatbots in public services. Using a survey experiment in China, the results show that participants exposed to a loss frame were more willing to use chatbots than those exposed to a gain frame. The default option alone did not significantly affect willingness. However, the interaction between information framing and default settings was significant. Specifically, the positive effect of loss-framed information on citizens’ willingness to use chatbots was stronger when a default option was presented, suggesting that defaults amplify the effect of loss framing. Overall, the study offers practical insights into designing strategies to promote chatbot adoption in public services.

title: What Is a Terminal Disease? Hidden Expansion of Medically Assisted Death in the United States
abstract: Medically assisted death (MAD) in the United States is legally restricted to adults with a terminal disease. When these laws were debated and adopted, the term “terminal disease” was used by lawmakers and the public with a common sense understanding: an incurable disease that would inevitably cause death in the near term, regardless of treatment. Since then, published case reports, government correspondence, annual report data, and professional discussions indicate that some clinicians now apply the terminal disease criterion to cases where death is expected primarily because the person refuses or cannot access food, water, or standard medical care. This constitutes a de facto expansion of MAD eligibility, likely enabled by excessive clinician discretion and weak state oversight, with significant implications for the legal, ethical, and democratic foundations of terminal illness-based MAD regimes.

title: Cohort Profile Update: The Spanish Longitudinal Study on Ageing and Health (Edad con Salud)
Differences in SARS-CoV-2 rapid diagnostic testing usage by COVID-19 vaccination status can bias vaccine effectiveness estimates against symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection from a test-negative design
Data-driven exploration of occupations and lung cancer risks using regularized regression models
Beyond health: loneliness and productivity growth across countries
abstract: Abstract Objectives: Loneliness is an established risk factor for poor health, yet its macroeconomic consequences remain unclear. We examined whether country-level loneliness is associated with productivity and long-run productivity growth. Methods: We combined 2023 Gallup World Poll data (145,072 respondents from 105 countries) with productivity measures from the Penn World Table. Country-level loneliness prevalence was based on respondents who reported feeling lonely for much of the previous day. Ordinary least squares models estimated associations between loneliness and total factor productivity (TFP), TFP growth, and related outcomes, adjusting for income, age, health problems, urbanization, and region fixed effects. Results: Loneliness was not associated with contemporaneous TFP levels but was consistently linked to lower long-run TFP growth. A one-standard-deviation increase in loneliness was associated with a 0.48-percentage-point lower annual TFP growth rate (0.37 standard deviations). These associations were robust across alternative growth periods. Loneliness showed weak evidence of greater TFP growth volatility but was not associated with human capital, physical capital, or aggregate output growth. Conclusions: Countries with higher loneliness exhibit slower long-run productivity growth but not lower productivity levels. Public Health Implications: Reducing loneliness may improve population health while potentially supporting economic resilience and productivity.

title: Is segregation bad for your heart?: a natural experiment for residential racial segregation exposure during childhood and cardiovascular disease risk
abstract: Abstract Background: Residential racial segregation is hypothesized to cause inequities in cardiovascular disease. Yet existing work is largely associational and has rarely tested longitudinal effects of childhood segregation on later CVD. Here, we leverage quasi-random urban planning decisions in Northern US cities prior to the Great Migration as an instrument for segregation as Black families moved North, providing a natural experiment. Methods: We followed Ananat’s work showing railroad track configurations serve as an instrument for segregation at the metropolitan area level. We linked Ananat’s data to the birthplaces of participants in the Panel Study of Income Dynamics (1968-1994, n=829 Black & 1,262 White), following them through 2023. Race-stratified accelerated failure time models used an instrumental variables design and cluster bootstrapping, progressively adjusting for other railroad features, socioeconomic status, and birth year. Results: Estimates suggest childhood residential segregation causally delays the onset of CVD or hypertension for White people but speeds it up for Black people, though confidence intervals and instrument strength varied across model specifications. Non-instrumented models directly adjusting for confounders yielded strongly attenuated results in the same direction. Conclusion: Segregation is likely a cause of Black-White CVD inequities, not just a correlate. Causal designs across the life course are needed.

title: The French Paradox 2, a remake for Norway ?
Driver-initiated takeover in highway tunnels: effects of non-driving-related tasks on driving workload and takeover risk
Authorization environments for climate policy: a public value–based typology across countries
Understanding the influence of education and training on policy analytical capacity development
Differences in reporting child abuse by mothers and young adults
abstract: Background Measuring violence against children (VAC) requires understanding competing sources of bias, with evidence suggesting caregivers underreport abuse. Objective This study examined differences in reported child abuse by respondent using longitudinal data and identified factors influencing maternal reporting. Participants and settings Using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), we analyzed mothers' cumulative prospective reports of physical and psychological abuse experienced by their children, alongside young adults' retrospective self-reports. Methods Difference between prevalence of abuse by respondents was estimated using McNemar's test for paired proportions. Concordance between respondents was assessed using Cohen's kappa and Prevalence-Adjusted Bias-Adjusted Kappa (PABAK). Multivariable logistic regressions identified maternal characteristics associated with reporting. Results Physical and psychological child prevalence was 6.23% (95% CI 5.51–7.02), and 11.77% (95% CI 10.80–12.81) among young adults, with significant differences by respondent ( p < 0.05). Mothers reported higher prevalence of psychological abuse and lower physical abuse than young adults. Cohen's kappa was 0.11 and 0.16 for physical and psychological abuse. PABAK showed higher agreement: 0.82 and 0.63. Mothers had lower odds of reporting physical or psychological abuse when the child was a female, 0.69 (95% CI 0.51–0.93). Conclusion While reports from mothers and children showed limited concordance, there was no consistent evidence that mothers systematically underreported abuse when identical questions were used. However, mothers' reporting varied by the child's sex and maternal characteristics. This work underscores the importance of considering identity and social norms in VAC measurement, by triangulating data from multiple respondents to improve accuracy in prevalence estimates.

title: Surveillance Path Dependence: Technological and Institutional Lock-In of Digital Surveillance Infrastructures in China
abstract: Digital surveillance infrastructures are widely critiqued for their use-side problems of access, privacy, and discrimination, but meaningful intervention requires understanding how these infrastructures are developed and stabilized in the first place. This paper examines China’s health code systems (HCSs) as a revelatory case of path dependence in the development of digital surveillance infrastructures. Drawing on news, first-hand interviews, and fieldwork, we trace how local governments chose to embed contact-tracing systems within the pre-existing digital ecosystems of Alipay and WeChat, primarily at the local level. Such choices persisted despite the central government’s openly cautious stance toward private tech giants and its subsequent attempts to develop independent alternatives. We describe this trajectory as surveillance path dependence, in which the convergence of pre-existing technological foundations, tight temporal pressure, and institutional incentives within a fragmented authoritarian institutional context locked new applications into established digital surveillance paths. This study suggests that mitigating the adverse societal impacts of large-scale digital surveillance requires intervening directly in the foundational design and institutional deployment of digital ecosystems rather than at the level of use-side effects.

title: We have come a long way, but…..not far enough
Assessing physical activity using Fitbit trackers and the association with quality of life among newly diagnosed patients with hematologic cancer
On the Presumption of Linearity in Behavioral Media Effects Research
How to Talk with the Academic Community about Contested Knowledge: A Confrontational-Reflexive Interview Model
abstract: Interviewing academics about contested knowledge presents significant methodological challenges, as the interview situation often activates “official” professional repertoires that conceal ambivalence and the active construction of epistemic boundaries. To address these limitations, the authors propose and evaluate the confrontational-reflexive interview model (CRIM), a research design aimed at systematically eliciting reflexivity and analyzing boundary-work in situ . The model treats the interview not as a neutral information extraction tool but as a structured sequence of meaning-making occasions. Stage 1 establishes a baseline narrative in expert interviews and focus groups, which is subsequently disrupted by a standardized “confrontation stimulus”—a scholarly text explicitly challenging the dominant disciplinary consensus—forcing participants to negotiate their position against a credible internal critique. Stage 2, conducted approximately one month later via asynchronous written correspondence, introduces temporal distance to test the stability and revisability of these accounts outside the immediate pressure of the face-to-face interaction. Drawing on a study of political scientists’ discourse on conspiracy theories, the authors demonstrate that although standard interviewer probes often fail to unsettle “official” narratives, the combination of a third-party textual confrontation and delayed reflection successfully reveals the specific conditions under which experts reproduce, repair, or redraw the boundaries of legitimate knowledge. The authors argue that CRIM contributes to sociological methodology by offering a replicable framework for observing expertise as a contingent, interactional performance.

title: Better together? Exploring factors of effectiveness and efficiency of mandatory intermunicipal cooperation
abstract: An important reason for municipalities to collaborate in intermunicipal cooperation (IMC) is the supposed performance benefit of IMCs in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. Studies mainly focused on voluntary IMC and presented mixed results about the effectiveness and efficiency gains of IMCs compared to independent task performance. However, evidence on mandatory IMCs is lacking. Therefore, this study extends earlier research by identifying and examining factors affecting the efficiency and effectiveness of mandatory IMCs. Based on an extensive analysis of 143 reports and 12 interviews with key actors in mandatory IMCs in the Netherlands, the study highlights the struggle of IMCs to report beyond output measures to identify outcomes. It also finds that next to their mandatory nature and the horizontal relationships between municipalities, vertical alignment between IMCs and ministries in national government is critical.
