title: The Effects of Health Shocks on Time Spent in Home Production
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the causal impact of health shocks on time spent in home production among retired individuals. Two channels with opposite predictions motivate the analysis: health shocks may tighten household budgets, inducing substitution toward home‐produced goods (income effect), or they may reduce the physical and functional capacity to perform domestic tasks (impairing effect). Using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study, I estimate condition‐specific causal effects of ten health conditions on home production in a staggered difference‐in‐differences design. Conditions that impair functional capacity, such as psychiatric conditions, depression on the Center for Epidemiological Studies Depression (CES‐D) scale, and adverse self‐reported health, reduce home production substantially. Psychiatric conditions reduce weekly home production by 3.2 hours, a 16% decline; CES‐D depression and self‐reported health shocks each reduce it by approximately 1 hour per week. Conditions that raise out‐of‐pocket medical costs but impose modest functional limitations produce no increase. The evidence therefore supports the impairing effect and gives no support to the income effect. The decline is not fully offset by increased help utilization or by spending on market substitutes such as housekeeping services, prepared meals, and yard work. Health shocks thus impose welfare costs beyond what monetary measures alone capture, with direct implications for the design of home‐ and community‐based support services for retirees.

title: How Green Work Characteristics Drive Pro‐Environmental Behavior: The Mediating Role of Green Self‐Efficacy Among Hotel Employees
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the influence of green work characteristics on hotel employees' pro‐environmental behavior and the mediating role of green self‐efficacy. Drawing on the job demands–resources (JD‐R) model and social cognitive theory (SCT), this study conceptualizes green work characteristics as comprising green job demands, green job autonomy, green supervisor support, and green coworker support. Data were gathered from 374 hotel employees in two waves with a 1‐month time lag and were analyzed using consistent partial least squares–structural equation modeling. Results indicate that green job autonomy and green coworker support positively influence green self‐efficacy, whereas green job demands and green supervisor support have no significant effects. Green self‐efficacy is a strong predictor of pro‐environmental behavior and mediates the effects of green job autonomy and green coworker support but not those of green job demands or green supervisor support. These results highlight the importance of green self‐efficacy as a psychological mechanism that links green work characteristics to employees' pro‐environmental behavior. This research contributes to the literature by integrating the JD‐R model and SCT into a comprehensive framework and by demonstrating that different dimensions of green work characteristics do not operate through a common motivational pathway in promoting employees' pro‐environmental behavior.

title: Do ESG‐Oriented Common Institutional Investors Reduce ESG Strategic Dissimilarity? Evidence From Multinational Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether ESG‐oriented common institutional ownership reduces strategic dissimilarity among multinational rival firms. Prior research primarily examined common ownership in relation to competition, firm performance, ESG disclosure, and ESG ratings, with limited attention to its role in shaping strategic ESG convergence among commonly owned firms. Using a global sample of 7766 listed firms and 110,490 firm‐dyad‐year observations from 2010 to 2024, we employ a dynamic panel system GMM approach to investigate this relationship. The findings show that ESG‐oriented common institutional ownership significantly reduces ESG strategic dissimilarity, indicating that such ownership promotes convergence rather than differentiation in firms' ESG strategies. This convergence effect is stronger in industries with high ESG materiality, where ESG issues are more visible, financially relevant, and reputationally sensitive. Furthermore, additional analyses show that reputational risk avoidance and ESG disclosure coordination explain this convergence effect, while cross‐national distance shapes the effectiveness of ESG coordination across countries. This study contributes to common ownership, institutional investors, and ESG strategy research by showing that ESG‐oriented common institutional ownership serves as a portfolio‐level governance mechanism that promotes ESG coherence among multinational rivals.

title: Environmental, Social, and Governance Performance as a Driver of Green Innovation: Evidence from Green Patent Data
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the relationship between environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance and firms' green innovation (GI), positioning ESG as an organizational context potentially conducive to sustainable technological transformation. Using a patent‐based methodology, GI is measured through firms' granted green patent outputs, providing a tangible indicator of green technological innovation. Based on 3314 firm‐year observations from 17 countries over 2002–2021, baseline estimations use OLS models with multiple fixed effects, complemented by count‐data and alternative specifications. The findings show a positive and statistically significant relationship between ESG performance and GI, which remains consistent across alternative specifications. The environmental, social, and governance dimensions are each positively associated with green patent output, with the environmental dimension exhibiting the largest coefficient in the baseline estimates. Additional mechanism analyses indicate that R&D intensity and analyst coverage serve as significant partial mediating channels. R&D intensity represents a firm‐internal innovation input, whereas analyst coverage captures external information and monitoring environment. Overall, the findings provide cross‐country evidence that ESG performance is associated with tangible green technological outcomes and suggest that this relationship may operate through both internal resource allocation and external information and monitoring channels.

title: Profit, Purpose and the ‘Price of Change’: Evidence From Benefit Corporation Transitions
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the short‐term financial consequences of transforming into a benefit corporation, a hybrid organisational form that embeds a dual mission of profit and public benefit. Drawing on the Social Resource‐Based View and sustainability‐oriented change management, we argue that the transition entails a reconfiguration of organisational priorities and resource allocation, which may temporarily affect firms' financial performance. Using a longitudinal event study on Italian firms, we compare transformed benefit corporations with a matched sample of non‐benefit firms. The results reveal lower performance in revenues, more tentative evidence on total assets, together with a reconfiguration of the debt structure following the transformation. Rather than signalling structural weakness, these dynamics may reflect transitional adjustment costs associated with the development of social and relational capabilities. The study contributes to research on hybrid organisations by clarifying the financial implications of benefit transformation and offers managerial insights on the need for careful financial planning during the transition process.

title: How Are Strategic Orientations Related to Environmental Performance? Empirical Evidence From Moroccan Manufacturing Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT In an era of intensifying competition, escalating environmental uncertainties, and heightened regulatory and societal pressures, firms, particularly in developing economies, face significant challenges in improving their environmental performance (EP). Grounded in the relational view and dynamic capabilities perspectives, this study examines how market orientation (MO) and entrepreneurial orientation (EO) are associated with EP. It tests a model in which supply chain integration (SCI) serves as a key mediator and organizational ambidexterity (ABX) acts as a crucial moderator. The empirical analysis draws on survey data from 275 Moroccan industrial businesses using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS‐SEM). The findings show that SCI significantly mediates the positive relationships between MO and EP, as well as between EO and EP. Furthermore, ABX significantly moderates the SCI‐EP nexus. This study supports the proximity argument of MO while emphasizing the crucial role of collaborative relationships and capabilities for achieving environmental outcomes in developing countries.

title: Advancing Circular Economy Measurement in Agri‐Food: An Updated Dashboard of Indicators
abstract: ABSTRACT The increasing relevance of the circular economy in the agri‐food sector highlights the need for systematic tools to assess environmental, economic and social performance. Despite the proliferation of studies, literature still presents fragmentation and lacks comprehensive sets of indicators across certain thematic areas. This study develops an updated version of the Dashboard of circularity indicators for the agri‐food sector, reflecting recent advances in research and policy and addressing previously identified gaps. The methodology builds on prior work through a systematic literature review on the Scopus database, covering publications from 2020 to 2025. Out of 44 retrieved articles, 18 were selected for full‐text analysis, leading to the extraction of 156 indicators, harmonised into a final list of 116. Indicators were classified into eight thematic scopes, of which seven are populated with indicators, three spatial dimensions and the three pillars of sustainability. Further categorisation distinguished product and organisation‐level indicators, while also identifying cross‐linked and cross‐sectional metrics. Findings reveal significant quantitative and qualitative expansion, particularly in the economic and social domains, largely due to the integration of Common Agricultural Policy indicators. Nonetheless, gaps persist in air, water, knowledge and innovation. The updated dashboard provides a more coherent and multidimensional framework, supporting evidence‐based decision‐making and advancing the circular transition.

title: From intra-disciplinary synthesis to problematizing theorization: Rethinking MNE sustainability in local markets
abstract: This study conducted an intra-disciplinary review exploring how multinational enterprises (MNEs) contribute to sustainability in local markets within the fields of international business (IB) and strategy.It comprehensively examines four key themes of corporate social responsibility, economic (regional) development, social performance, and environmental sustainability of MNEs.By doing so, it seeks to consolidate fragmented findings from existing independent studies while broadening understanding through problematizing assumptions made in research.In addition, it sheds light on the complexities that MNEs face to address sustainability challenges, and how to strategically integrate economic, social, and environmental goals while adapting to global and local pressures.In turn, we propose new research directions and draw implications for MNEs in addressing grand challenges.Overall, this study contributes to deepening sustainability research in IB and strategy fields, and provides valuable insights for MNEs' sustainable business practice.

title: Cultural intermediation through indigenous values-based accountability: the case of Bangarra Dance Theatre
abstract: Purpose This paper examines how Indigenous values shape the accountability practices governing cultural intermediation. It investigates how accountability enables Indigenous relational governance to be sustained as Indigenous cultural knowledge circulates through cultural intermediation while remaining aligned with Indigenous custodial authority. Design/methodology/approach The study draws on a qualitative, longitudinal case study of Bangarra Dance Theatre, an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisation operating as a cultural intermediary in Australia. Data were collected over twelve years through a combination of participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and documentary materials. Findings The analysis identifies Indigenous Values-Based Accountability as a set of interconnected accountability practices through which Indigenous relational governance is sustained. Through permission seeking, cultural observation, creative obligation, and return and renewal, IVBA organises Bangarra's continuing accountability as Indigenous cultural knowledge circulates across public and cross-cultural domains while sustaining Indigenous custodial authority. The findings further demonstrate how IVBA structures participation in cultural circulation by making engagement by sponsors, partners, and other external actors conditional upon Indigenous custodial authority. Originality/value This paper advances Indigenous accounting and accountability research by conceptualising accountability as a culturally embedded governance arrangement through which Indigenous values are enacted beyond Indigenous organisational and community settings. It demonstrates how Indigenous relational governance organises authority, reciprocity, and custodial responsibility as cultural knowledge circulates across public and cross-cultural domains. The paper further positions cultural intermediation as a distinctive accountability setting that, in our case, involves Bangarra remaining accountable to recognised custodians while Indigenous authority structures participation, representation, and engagement with non-Indigenous actors.

Data-driven approach to estimate ambient ammonia concentrations
abstract: The Netherlands experiences significant environmental impacts from reactive nitrogen, particularly ammonia (NH 3 ), whose long-term deposition harms soil, water, and biodiversity. NH 3 is emitted mainly from agriculture and its levels can be very high and variable in intensive livestock areas. Although monitoring stations are set up across multiple locations, data gaps may still arise due to issues with measurement instruments. Therefore, there is a need for models that can reliably fill in these missing observations. In this study, we first applied Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) models to predict one day ahead NH 3 concentrations at six sites (De Zilk, Valthermond, Vredepeel, Wekerom, Wieringerwerf, Zegveld) in the Netherlands. All models captured daily NH 3 trends, with Random Forest initially performing best (R 2 up to 0.59 at Valthermond). Predictions were strongly driven by lagged NH 3 values with wind speed and precipitation contributing moderately. After correcting for prediction lag caused by autocorrelation, the linear regression performed best at most sites (with best performance observed at Zegveld with R 2 of 0.84) and was used for gap filling. It maintained reasonable accuracy despite sparse observations (every 2–7 days), with most sites (De Zilk, Valthermond, Vredepeel, Wekerom, Zegveld) exhibiting a significant correlation of almost or more than 0.5 even at 7 days measurement gaps. Additionally, we noted that historical data from existing sites could be effectively used to fill gaps at newly established locations that exhibited similar distributions of NH 3 .

Potential influence of landscape structure on water quality and phytoplankton community in highly degraded urban lakes: Implications for restoration
abstract: Urban lakes are of particular concern in urban landscapes, as they provide ecological, social and economic benefits, but are under strong human pressure. The current study examined eleven urban lakes that differ in their morphometric and hydrological characteristics and were located across various macroregions of Poland. The aim was to examine potential relationships among landscape structure, water quality, and phytoplankton communities across three buffer zones (10 m, 100 m, and 1000 m), selected to reflect different spatial scales of land use/land cover (LU/LC). The urban lakes were characterised by different phytoplankton biomass, with a maximum of 181.3 mg/l. Most of them were dominated by toxic or potentially toxic cyanobacteria. Land use/cover explained the greatest percentage of variability (24.3%) in phytoplankton composition in the 100 m buffer zone. However, this relationship was only suggestive and did not reach the conventional level of statistical significance. In contrast, LU/LC explained little of the variation in physicochemical parameters across three spatial scales, accounting for up to 0.6% in the 10 m buffer zone, but with no statistically significant relationships. Phytoplankton play a more important role than other water quality parameters and can serve as a more sensitive indicator, providing complementary information for assessing the impact of landscape structure. Despite the large proportion of forest and seminatural areas, the urban lakes were classified as highly degraded, exhibiting poor or bad water quality, which can be more related to historical pollution than to current landscape structure. Our results indicate that a 100 m wide buffer zone may be a useful study-specific spatial scale for considering shoreline and surrounding LU/LC management. They can be prioritised for protection and restoration activities, as well as for planning future spatial development. Restoring natural vegetation within this zone may reduce the nutrient inflows and slow the process of cultural eutrophication. However, further studies with a larger number of lakes are needed to confirm these relationships.

A national dataset of downtown business district boundaries for pre-automobile U.S. cities and towns
abstract: The downtown business district is a fundamental unit of analysis in urban revitalization research, yet no nationally consistent, publicly available dataset of downtown boundaries exists for small and mid-sized U.S. cities and towns. This paper introduces an open data product containing 6,551 downtown polygons for pre-automobile-era places spanning 47 contiguous states. The dataset is constructed from a fully reproducible, open-source R workflow: a national universe of historically significant places is assembled using historical census records, contemporary population data, and metropolitan classification criteria; points-of-interest data from the Overture Maps Foundation are collected within each place boundary; and a kernel density estimation algorithm identifies the highest-concentration commercial cluster as the downtown core. The resulting boundaries are validated against Main Street program districts, which the polygons cover at high rates in the two states examined. The polygons are deposited at Harvard Dataverse under a CC0 1.0 license, with all R code available on GitHub. The dataset supports research on downtown revitalization, Main Street commercial activity, and the economic geography of small and mid-sized American cities.

Optimal avoidability in cross-border minimum taxation
abstract: Many tax regimes collect revenue to the extent that other governments do not. This paper develops a theory of how such cross-border minimum taxes should be designed, focusing on choices that affect avoidance of the regime. Making a minimum tax more difficult to avoid retains more firms within the regime but weakens competition among tax havens. Havens then raise their rates toward the minimum, reducing the top-up tax rate on shifted profit. As a result, an avoidable minimum tax can raise more revenue for the governments that impose it than an unavoidable one.

title: Pricing climate risks: Evidence from wildfires and municipal bonds
abstract: How are public finances affected by climate-driven changes in wildfire risk? Using high-resolution meteorological forecasts, land use data, and US municipal bond spreads, we find that municipalities facing greater future wildfire exposure already incur higher borrowing costs: A one standard deviation increase in future wildfire risk is associated with a 7 (8) basis point rise in primary (secondary) market spreads—over 15% of the sample mean. Impacts appear larger in areas with higher minority populations and greater reliance on local revenue. Our study contributes to the broader literature by introducing a new approach to evaluating the capitalization of evolving physical climate risks.

title: The impact of preference programs in public procurement: Evidence from veteran set-asides
Geopoliticizing the Firm: Embraer, Corporate Nationality, and the Geopolitical Constitution of Contracts, Capabilities, and Markets
abstract: Transnational corporations (TNCs) drive fast-changing global economic geographies amid fraught geopolitical relations. However, three influential theoretical accounts of the firm, the nexus of contracts, the resource-based view, and Global Production Networks 2.0, still underspecify how corporate nationality and home–host state geopolitical agendas constitute TNCs’ formation, operations, and strategic management. This omission creates a gap in explaining the connections between geopolitical conditions and TNC operations. This article addresses this gap by geopoliticizing the firm. To this end, it integrates key aspects of the three theoretical accounts into a novel conceptual framework that comprises three analytical mechanisms: geopolitical agenda alignment, territorially defined capability formation, and territorially differentiated product development. Empirically, the article primarily draws on twenty-two interviews with elites across different firms and institutions to examine how Embraer, an aerospace producer, evolved following its establishment in 1969 as an integral part of Brazilian state developmentalism. After privatization in 1994, Embraer simultaneously (dis)engaged with multiple state geopolitical agendas to straddle US–China geopolitical tensions and compete internationally. Such proactive geopolitical (dis)engagement augmented Embraer’s ability to secure contracts, create capabilities, and capture markets across multiple countries. Through this case study, the article demonstrates the importance of conceptualizing the entwinement of TNC activities with both corporate nationality and variegated geopolitical contexts.

title: The Weight of Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement, Banking Sector Composition, and Lending
abstract: Abstract We examine how strengthened anti-money laundering (AML) enforcement affects the U.S. banking sector. Heightened enforcement disproportionately raises compliance costs for small banks, especially in counties more exposed to money laundering. In these areas, small banks contract while large banks expand, increasing standardized, government-supported, and secured lending. While aggregate county-level credit does not decline differentially, local outcomes improve. Small establishments grow, non-tradable employment and wages rise, and real estate prices increase. The evidence is consistent with a reallocation mechanism in which AML enforcement shifts activity toward large banks, potentially improving intermediation quality through changes in the composition of local financial intermediation.

title: A Century of Stock Market Liquidity and Trading Costs
abstract: ABSTRACT I assemble and examine an annual time series of bid–ask spreads on Dow Jones stocks from 1900 to 2000 and average commission rates for trading NYSE stocks since 1925. Spreads are cyclical, especially during periods of market turmoil. The sum of half‐spreads and one‐way commissions, multiplied by annual turnover, estimates the aggregate cost of trading and drives a wedge between gross and net equity returns. This difference explains only a small part of the observed equity premium, though I show that the gross equity premium is perhaps 1% lower today than it was early in the 1900's. Finally, I find that the transaction cost measures (spreads and turnover), which serve as a proxy for liquidity, predict stock returns 1 year or more ahead and dominate traditional measures such as the dividend yield. The evidence suggests aggregate liquidity is a determinant of expected stock market returns.

title: The Impact of Early Investments in Urban School Systems in the United States
abstract: Cities in the United States dramatically expanded spending on public education after WWI, with the average urban school district increasing per pupil expenditures by over 70 percent by 1924. We provide the first evaluation of these unprecedented investments in public education using a new dataset and plausibly exogenous growth in school spending generated by anti-German sentiment. We find that school resources significantly increased educational attainment and wages later in life, particularly for less advantaged children. Increases in expenditures can explain about 40 percent of the sizable increase in educational attainment of cohorts born between 1895 and 1913. “Every great war in which the United States has played a part has been followed by educational developments of supreme national importance…Although the United States was engaged in the World War less than two years, the effects upon education resulting from this brief period of warfare will perhaps prove to be as far-reaching and as important as those growing out of any previous war…Undoubtedly the World War was the most important factor in awakening the American public to the inadequacy of its educational provisions and in arousing the States to vigorous efforts to improve educational conditions.” —Fletcher Harper Swift, Biennial Survey of Education 1920–1922, Volume 1, (1924, pp. 1–2).

title: School timing, sleep, and adolescent behavior: Evidence from lottery-assigned start times
Revisiting the price elasticity of charitable giving: Meta-analysis of tax incentives and matching donations
abstract: This paper presents the first quantitative meta-analysis of the price elasticity of charitable giving under both rebate and matching schemes. We compile 137 elasticity estimates from 26 experimental papers and synthesize them using random-effects and multilevel models. Charitable giving is highly price-responsive: the pooled meta-analytic mean elasticity of total donations is −1.75, indicating that lowering the effective price of giving substantially increases charitable revenue. Although we observe considerable between-study heterogeneity and some evidence of publication bias, bias-adjusted estimates remain negative. Furthermore, elasticity is substantially more negative under matching (−2.44) than under rebate (−0.73), contradicting the theoretical prediction of equivalence but aligning with the original experimental findings in this literature. The rebate-matching difference is attenuated when moving from laboratory to field settings, although it persists.

title: Human rights economics
abstract: This article proposes a theoretical framework that systematically integrates human rights and economic analysis, addressing gaps in previous attempts linking theory and policy. Rather than developing a new theoretical approach, we work within a standard social planner setting in which a social welfare function embeds both fiscal constraints and rights-based valuations, ensuring Pareto-efficient outcomes while guaranteeing minimum rights. Conceptually, we link principles, policy instruments, and outcomes, highlighting shared structures across disciplines and enabling policy design that balances efficiency, equity, and transparency. Empirically, a case study of universal social protection strategies in South Africa illustrates how economic, human rights, and integrated approaches produce different priorities: targeted basic income maximizes fiscal efficiency, the universal transfer maximizes equality and rights, and the integrated perspective favors the expansion of the existing system as the second-most rights-consistent and most cost efficient option. This fully integrated framework demonstrates that human rights economics is not a slogan, nor merely the economics of human rights or rights within economics, but a true integration of both—practically applicable, context-sensitive, and offering a pathway to fiscally sustainable, socially inclusive, and administratively feasible policies.

title: Economic impacts of pasture degradation at the municipal level: Evidence from Minas Gerais, Brazil
Government positions and climate change: paradigmatic conflict versus consensus in environmental performance
abstract: Historically, environmental policy was framed as a fundamental trade-off between economic growth and ecological preservation. Since the mid-1980s, however, this dichotomy has been largely replaced by the paradigm of ecological modernization, expressed in concepts like “green growth” and “sustainable development,” which hold that economic growth and environmental protection are mutually reinforcing. This shift was accompanied by the assumption that a broad political consensus on reconciling economic growth and environmental protection would lead to superior environmental outcomes. Yet, the persistent gap between climate targets and actual emission trends necessitates a critical re-evaluation of this “consensus” approach and of whether the original antagonism between environmental protection and economic growth has genuinely been overcome. To assess this claim, this study tests six distinct conceptualizations of government ideology and policy focus, analyzing government positions across 35 advanced democracies from 1990 to 2021. The findings show that neither the focus on technocratic environmental issues, nor the classic left-right divide, nor the newer, more encompassing green-alternative versus traditional-authoritarian dimension predicts emissions performance. Instead, emissions decline where governments adopt growth-critical positions and even more where environmental ideology contrasts growth-oriented productionism with growth-critical environmental protection. This suggests that the depoliticization of climate policy may be part of the problem: ideological contestation over growth itself, not environmental consensus, emerges as the more effective driver of decarbonization.

title: The effects of R&D tax credit and market competition policies on firms’ zero-leverage behaviour
abstract: Abstract Motivated by the characteristics of R&D and its co-movement with the rising prevalence of zero-leverage firms over the past four decades, we investigate the effects of US R&D tax incentive and import tariff policies on zero-leverage behaviour. We find that the number of R&D-intensive firms has increased since the introduction of the R&D tax credit in 1981, and that zero-leverage firms are disproportionately concentrated among R&D firms. Both the increase in R&D investment and the rising sensitivity of leverage decisions to R&D contribute to this pattern. In addition, intensified market competition driven by tariff reductions significantly increases the likelihood of zero leverage among R&D firms, but not among non-R&D firms. Overall, our findings suggest that R&D tax incentives and trade liberalisation policies have played important roles in shaping the long-term trend of zero-leverage behaviour in the United States.
journal_name: Review of Quantitative Finance and Accounting

title: Emerging Research Frontiers in Business Cycle Synchronization: A Review of Measurement, Evolution, and Driving Forces
abstract: ABSTRACT Offering new evidence on business cycle synchronization (BCS) has received special attention in recent decades owing to the structural shifts witnessed in the world economy. Hence, this study provides a survey of the literature on business cycle synchronization. The study aims to understand: (a) the definition, (b) measurement, (c) evolution, (d) determinants/driving forces, and (e) propose future research directions. This study highlights that correlation, dynamic correlation, the concordance index, the absolute growth differential, the decoupling index, and the network approach are the key measures of synchronization. While trade integration, financial integration, specialization, and policy similarity have emerged as key drivers, other factors, such as the global financial cycle, geographical proximity, and political factors, also drive synchronization. To track the evolution, this study delves into historical evidence, conventional wisdom, the world business cycle, sectoral and regional business cycles, the financial crisis perspective, the euro area, and the decoupling hypothesis. Finally, this study reveals that although economies are broadly synchronized during a specific period, they exhibit distinct synchronization patterns across different economies and groups at various time periods. Given the long‐standing and unsettled literature, these findings are highly relevant for policymakers, and the suggested research directions open avenues for future research.

title: Review of Literature on Corporate Cash Holdings and Future Research Agenda in an ESG Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT This study synthesizes the literature on corporate cash holdings under an ESG framework and develops a theoretically grounded future research agenda. Based on a systematic review of 116 studies screened from Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection, the literature is categorized into five streams: impacts of aggregate ESG, environmental, social, and governance factors on cash holdings, and reverse effects of cash holdings/financial slack on ESG‐related outcomes. ESG reshapes three established cash‐holding motives: the insurance value of liquidity, the financing wedge between internal and external funds, and agency costs of retained cash. The E, S, and G pillars present distinct mechanisms tied to environmental commitments, stakeholder/labor claims, and liquidity governance. Stronger ESG can reduce cash by lowering risk, financing frictions, or agency costs, while strategic liquidity needs, stakeholder commitments, and adverse ESG shocks may increase cash demand. Reverse evidence shows accumulated liquidity funds ESG investment and supports employment resilience, forming a dynamic bidirectional ESG‐cash relationship. Methodologically, OLS and fixed‐effects regressions dominate the literature, while quasi‐experimental, structural, and machine‐learning approaches remain rare. Future research could explore nonlinear, co‐determined ESG‐cash dynamics via E‐DSGE modeling, real‐options analysis, AI‐enabled liquidity management, and ESG contagion in strategic alliances.

title: Mitigating time-varying buyer power through farmer commodity storage
abstract: Abstract Buyer market power is a significant concern in many agricultural product procurement markets. Research almost exclusively treats such buyer power as a static element of agricultural market structure, despite evidence that buyer power varies across the marketing season for many commodities and locations. We study buyer power as a time-varying phenomenon and analyze the role of commodity storage in mitigating such power and increasing farmer incomes. Data-driven simulations show that strategic storage can generate significant farm income gains and risk reduction. Key factors determining welfare impacts are magnitudes and expected changes in buyer power and farmers’ storage efficiency and risk preferences.

title: Corridors in Shallow Lakes: The Case of Intermediate Pollution
abstract: Abstract We study optimal management of the standard shallow lake model with special attention to the damage caused by the accumulated phosphorus in the water of the lake. The occurrence of a tipping point leads to a stronger increase in the damage after moving from the low-damage to the high-damage regime, because of the loss of ecosystem services. We modify the standard quadratic damage function by introducing a jump in marginal damage when moving from the low-damage to the high-damage regime. Connecting the lower and the higher marginal damage functions yields a continuous piecewise linear marginal damage function with a strong increase around the jump. In addition to the well-known oligotrophic and eutrophic steady states, we find that a third steady state can occur, separated by two Skiba points. This implies that a corridor or a basin of attraction arises between these two Skiba points where optimal management of the lake stabilizes the amount of phosphorus somewhere in the middle instead of either moving to the low-damage or to the high-damage regime, as is the result in the standard knife-edge case with one Skiba point.

title: A Cross‐Country Study of Carbon Risk and Financial Constraints: The Role of Carbon Disclosure Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether firm‐level carbon risk affects financial constraints and whether the quality of carbon disclosure moderates this relationship. Using 16,274 firm‐year observations from 50 countries from 2007 to 2023, we find that higher carbon risk is associated with greater financial constraints. The result is robust to entropy balancing, Heckman correction, instrumental variables and a quasi‐natural experiment based on the 2013 UK carbon disclosure regulation. High‐quality disclosure weakens this association, suggesting that transparency reduces financing frictions by lowering information asymmetry. Additional analyses show that governance, monitoring and institutional context shape the financing consequences of carbon risk.

title: The Effect of a Miscarriage Compared to a Completed Pregnancy on Mental Health Care Use, Labour Market and Family Outcomes
abstract: ABSTRACT Miscarriages occur in about 15% of recognised pregnancies and often cause grief and stress. We investigate the effect of a miscarriage on mental health care use, labour market and family outcomes of women and their partners using an event study framework applied to Dutch linked administrative data. After a miscarriage, women's use of mental health care temporarily increase compared to before the miscarriage, while their partner's use is unaffected. Furthermore, miscarriages affect labour market trajectories and reduce the probability of living together. Results are similar when comparing the effects of a miscarriage with the effects of having a child using a matched sample of women with a completed pregnancy.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Do Tax Incentives Enhance Entrepreneurship? Evidence from Value‐Added Tax Reform in China
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the causal effect of tax incentives on entrepreneurship. Using a staggered Value‐Added Tax (VAT) reform in China as an exogenous shock to conduct difference‐in‐differences estimation, we find that tax cuts have a considerable positive effect on local entrepreneurship. A plausible mechanism driving our findings is the ease of financial constraints. Our results are robust to a battery of endogeneity and robustness tests. We find that regions with high levels of institutional quality, trust, or a commercial culture undergo greater entrepreneurship after the VAT reform. Overall, this study provides a timely policy evaluation of the importance of tax incentives in promoting entrepreneurship in a typical emerging market.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: The Tipping Point: Interest Rates and Financial Stability
abstract: Abstract This paper studies the impact of interest rates on bank stability in a standard bank‐run model. Banks invest in long‐term assets, whose value decreases with interest rates, and set deposit rates to optimally insure depositors' liquidity risk. Liquidity‐risk insurance implies banks earn interest margins, which increase with interest rates. Hence, interest rates have two countervailing effects: they reduce the value of banks' long‐term assets while widening their margins. First, the paper characterizes the parametric condition under which an effect dominates. The condition implies interest‐rate risk is captured by banks' maturity mismatch adjusted for deposits' effective duration. Second, the paper solves for the interest‐rate level that tips banks into instability. Quantification points to the possibility of a negative effective maturity mismatch, making the tipping point a lower bound on interest rates.

abstract: The subject of this very interesting book is the consumer society, which gradually emerged along with the industrial economy. According to Collantes, productive consumption increased as long as it ...

title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
abstract: Abstract Drawing on visual complexity theory and the arousal properties of color, this paper challenges the prevailing assumption that only warm (longer wavelength) or highly saturated colors can induce arousal in consumers. Instead, we propose a novel pathway: multicolor logos with cool hues can elicit arousal through triggering curiosity. Across a total of eight experiments (seven preregistered with a total of 1,724 participants recruited), of which six experiments are reported in the main text, including a behavioral lab study employing biometric measures (eye tracking, galvanic skin response, pupil dilation), and three studies utilizing real product choices, we consistently find that multicolor cool logos are more arousing than single cool color designs. This heightened, curiosity-driven arousal subsequently impacts marketing outcomes, including willingness to pay and choice. These findings offer marketers alternative strategies for inducing arousal in brand communications and provide actionable guidelines for effectively designing logos.
