Renewable fuels for hard-to-abate transportation: Exploring the impact of biomass availability and variable renewable potentials
abstract: Decarbonising the hard-to-abate maritime and aviation transport sectors will be challenging. Alternative renewable fuels, such as biofuels and E-fuels, show promising potential for substituting traditional fossil fuels, but carry challenges regarding the expansion of variable renewable energy (VRE) and the availability of sustainable biomass. This study assesses these challenges and regional impacts using a comprehensive sector-coupled energy system modelling framework applied to Europe. Under high biomass availability, a documented substitution effect allows the share of E-kerosene and biokerosene to shift with VRE accessibility, whereas this flexibility declines under biomass scarcity. These differences are reflected in fuel costs: aviation fuel prices are more sensitive to biomass scarcity, while maritime fuel prices are more sensitive to VRE restrictions. Regional resource availability reshapes renewable fuel production and trade. Under the modelling assumptions, accessible VRE resources favour E-fuel supply-chains from Spain, while lower VRE accessibility increases the role of biomass-rich countries, including Germany and Poland, as exporters. Constrained VRE deployment results in increased infrastructure needs, lowers average renewable capacity factors, and raises total system costs by up to 9%. Finally, increasing scarcity increases the importance of carbon management. Biomass is prioritised for fuel production and industrial applications coupled with carbon capture, while direct air capture and carbon reuse become increasingly important for meeting fuel demand. These results highlight the need for coordinated policies on biomass utilisation, VRE deployment, carbon management, and infrastructure planning to achieve cost-efficient decarbonisation of Europe's hard-to-abate transport sectors.

title: Life cycle engineering for battery production within absolute environmental sustainability targets: a climate change case study
abstract: Battery production is growing rapidly, yet whether its environmental impacts remain within planetary boundaries requires investigation. We develop a four-step life cycle engineering framework integrating 1) prospective and probabilistic target derivation, 2) parametric and prospective life cycle assessment, 3) Sobol index-based selection of mitigation measures, and 4) marginal abatement cost curves for cost-effectiveness evaluation. The framework builds on a review of 28 studies and 36 reviews, addressing six of the seven identified research demands. Applied to NMC811 battery production under three SSP-RCP scenarios and two allocation principles (2024–2050), current impacts (138 kg CO₂-eq/kWh) exceed the SSP2-RCP2.6 justice-based and grandfathering targets by factors of 6.2 and 1.9, respectively. Under SSP2-RCP2.6, combined foreground and background improvements reduce impacts by 75% to 34 kg CO₂-eq/kWh by 2050. Sixteen mitigation measures are derived to reach net-zero; 70 kg CO₂-eq/kWh can be abated at negative marginal costs, yielding net savings of €70/kWh (−51%).

title: The sense and sensibility of the circular material use rate: a case study of EU's key circularity indicator
abstract: The Circular Material Use Rate (CMUR) has become a flagship indicator for monitoring progress towards a circular economy in the European Union. Promising in its conceptual simplicity, CMUR is widely employed in policy evaluations, international comparisons, and national target-setting. Yet despite its prominence, the indicator has been subject to limited empirical scrutiny. This paper examines the performance and interpretive validity of CMUR through a case study of Iceland, an economy characterized by high levels of imported materials, large-scale aluminum production, high percentage of renewable energy, significant biomass flows, and substantial domestic extraction of rock, sand and gravel. Based on a calculation of Iceland’s CMUR for 2024 and six policy-relevant scenarios—those being transport-related fossil fuel phase-out, increased recycling of household waste, food-waste reduction, material-efficiency measures in cement use, sufficiency scenarios for electronics and textiles, and all measures combined—the analysis shows that CMUR exhibits limited responsiveness to core circular economy interventions in this particular case. In some scenarios, such as food-waste prevention, CMUR decreases when environmental performance improves. The paper identifies one main structural reason for this behavior: the overwhelming dominance of a few inert and/or structurally non-circular materials in domestic consumption. To address this, the paper explores a contextualization of CMUR by modifying the boundary conditions for those materials. The findings highlight the importance of contextual interpretation when CMUR is used to evaluate circular performance and to inform policy. The analysis further suggests that similar interpretive challenges may arise in other European economies with comparable material-flow structures.

title: Deriving Organism-Relevant Nanoparticle Safety Exposure Limits from In Vitro Toxicity Data
abstract: Abstract Establishing human safety limits of engineered nanoparticles remains a challenge. In vitro assays have become a major toxicity data resource, driven by the demand for new approach methodologies (NAMs) that reduce animal testing. However, robust tools that bridge in vitro data with in vivo outcomes are still lacking. Here, we present an integrated computational framework using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling to derive organism-level BMD10-based dose estimates directly from in vitro liver toxicity data. For 4 nondissolvable nanoparticles (TiO2, SiO2, Au, and graphene oxide), we curated in vitro toxicity data sets spanning 7 liver-relevant cell systems (5 human and 2 mouse) across 24 assays and estimated in vitro effect thresholds using the benchmark dose for a 10% response (BMD10). Mouse in vitro BMD10 values were then reverse-translated into predicted BMD10IVIVE values using a validated mouse PBPK model and benchmarked against available mouse-derived in vivo effect threshold (BMD10eq) data to ensure consistency. The resulting nanoparticle-specific BMD10IVIVE ranges showed qualitative concordance with animal-derived reference doses, supporting the biological plausibility of these screening-level dose estimates. We further applied the same workflow to human liver cell systems to derive human-relevant BMD10-based points of departure. This approach establishes a scalable and prospective animal-free workflow for human nanoparticle risk assessments, overcoming a critical translational gap.

title: Nanoconfinement Decouples Calcium-Enhanced Phosphate Capture from Calcium Phosphate Crystal Maturation
abstract: Abstract Calcium phosphate (Ca–P) scaling, which is ubiquitous in nature and in water systems, has been shown to interfere with the capture of phosphate by ferric oxide-based sorbents, thereby deteriorating their decontamination performance in repeated cycles. Here, we show that a specifically designed gel-type nanocomposite, namely HFO@N201, enables Ca-enhanced phosphate sequestration while restricting Ca–P scaling via nanoconfinement. Increasing the initial Ca2+ concentration from 0 to 160 mg/L improved phosphate uptake from ∼4.5 to ∼6.2 mg/g in the first cycle. After 20 adsorption-regeneration cycles, phosphate uptake remained at ∼6.4 mg/g in the Ca-containing system, twice that of ∼3.2 mg/g in the Ca-free system. In fixed-bed tests, the presence of Ca2+ enhanced the working capacity from ∼1350 to ∼1800 bed volumes, which could be observed again in the subsequent cycle. Asynchronous release of Fe, P, and Ca during acidic elution of P-loaded HFO@N201 indicates heterogeneous and nonstoichiometric Ca-associated phosphate retention rather than formation of a mature bulk Ca–P phase. XRD, TEM, EXAFS, and Mössbauer spectroscopy further show that the retained Ca–P species remained weakly ordered and that the nanosized ferrihydrite-like Fe phase persisted during cyclic operation. Thermodynamic analysis, classical nucleation theory, and molecular dynamics simulations further support that the nanoconfinement structure of HFO@N201 (∼2 nm) creates a low-mobility hydration environment that restricts solvent exchange, ion rearrangement, and long-range ordering, thereby stabilizing Ca–P species in a weakly ordered interfacial state. Our work demonstrates nanoconfinement as a strategy to exploit Ca-enhanced phosphate capture while reducing Ca–P scaling in regenerable sorbents.

title: Influence of COVID-19 Lockdown on Atmospheric Nitrate Sources and Chemistry in the Northeastern US
abstract: Abstract The outbreak of COVID-19 and subsequent lockdowns caused widespread restrictions on human activities. This presented a unique opportunity to track atmospheric chemistry changes under rapid emission reductions. Using stable nitrogen (δ15N) and triple oxygen isotopes (δ18O and Δ17O) of particulate nitrate (pNO3) collected from 2019 to 2020 in the northeastern US, combined with 0-D box-model simulations, we investigate the response of atmospheric nitrate chemistry during the COVID-19 lockdown period (March 2020) in the northeastern US. Triple oxygen isotope measurements indicate that emission reductions altered the relative contributions of NOx oxidation pathways, with a shift toward the NO2 + OH pathway and a reduced contribution from N2O5 hydrolysis. This shift was consistent with the modeled increase in OH concentrations and the observed and modeled decrease in O3 during the COVID-19 lockdown, which limited N2O5 formation and subsequent heterogeneous nitrate formation. Moreover, nitrogen isotope-constrained sensitivity analysis suggests that a reduction of approximately 40(±10)% in transportation NOx emissions relative to the annual emission inventory estimates may be required to reproduce the observed decrease in δ15N(pNO3) during the COVID-19 period. These findings highlight the utility of isotopes to detail the complex interactions between emission reductions, atmospheric oxidation chemistry, and secondary aerosol formation. Understanding these interactions is critical for effectively determining air pollution mitigation strategies and testing air-quality models, particularly under rapidly evolving emission conditions associated with energy transitions and policy interventions.

title: Unveiling Seven-Decade Disparities of Methane Emissions across China
abstract: Abstract China’s century-long economic transition generated substantial methane emissions, yet the trajectory and factors of this evolution remain poorly quantified. A systematic understanding is essential for reconciling China’s economic growth with emission mitigation targets and for informing Global South nations. Using a bottom-up estimate of subnational methane emissions (1949–2022), we uncover a fundamental shift from agriculture-dominated to industry-dominated methane emissions in China. Nationwide emissions peaked in 2012, declining 3.8% by 2022, yet provincial disparities widened by 48%. While superficially reflecting heterogeneous fossil fuel use, these disparities are attributable to a shift in explanatory dominance from purely economic to dual economic-policy factors, particularly carbon policies. The long-term stability in agricultural sectors reflects nationwide efforts to food security, which maintains a baseline level of production across provinces. Recent regional decoupling masks the disproportion between emissions and economic gains. Western provinces (e.g., Shanxi, Ningxia, Guizhou) continue to exhibit high-emission but low-return economic profiles. The average of their methane emissions per GDP was 4.8 times that of eastern regions in 2022, with extremes reaching 150-fold differences. For equitable mitigation, future focus should shift from “who emits” to “why emits”, establishing a scientific basis for fair compensation between resource-dependent and resource-consuming regions.

title: Subsoil versus Topsoil Straw Addition Shifts Microbial Carbon Allocation for Enhanced Carbon Sequestration and Emission Mitigation
abstract: Abstract Subsoils (>20 cm) represent an underutilized sink for soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration because C inputs in subsoil are typically limited. To clarify how organic inputs regulate subsoil SOC accrual and C emissions in rice paddies, we combined a 2-year field experiment with 13C-labeled straw incubation and validated the results with a global meta-analysis. Results showed that compared with no addition and topsoil straw addition, subsoil straw addition increased SOC stocks by 10.5% and 2.2%, respectively, primarily via enhanced mineral-associated organic C (MAOC) formation at 0–30 cm. The 270-day incubation revealed that subsoil addition accelerated microbial conversion of straw C into amino sugars, evidenced by 13C-phospholipid fatty acids, promoting MAOC formation. Relative to topsoil addition, subsoil addition reduced CH4 emissions by 15.3%, driven by improved root growth and enhanced CH4 oxidation, and decreased CO2 emissions by lowering topsoil C availability and peroxidase activity. Meta-analysis confirmed that C emissions decrease progressively with increasing incorporation depth, and machine-learning models indicate that deeper incorporation (>20 cm) mitigates global C emissions by half under future climate change. Overall, compared with topsoil addition, subsoil addition represents a win–win strategy that simultaneously enhances SOC sequestration and reduces C emissions, with potential applicability beyond paddy systems.

title: The Subclinical Cardiovascular Effects of Nonoptimum Ambient Temperature: A Longitudinal Study in 15 Chinese Cities
abstract: Abstract Short-term ambient temperature is linked to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, but subclinical responses remain unclear. Using repeated health examinations from 247,641 adults in 15 Chinese cities (2013–2020), we assessed 20 cardiovascular indicators with linear mixed-effects and distributed lag nonlinear models. The indicator-specific sample sizes ranged from 1119 to 219,090 participants. Exposure–response relationships were near-linear or inversely J-shaped for ten indicators, U-shaped or inverted U-shaped for seven, and atypical or unclear for three. Low temperature was associated with 18 indicators, peaking at lags 0–5 days, whereas high temperature was associated with seven, peaking at lags 0–6 days. Relative to the reference temperatures, extremely low-temperature exposure (P1, −9 °C) was associated with cumulative increases over lag days 0–10 of 6.52%–13.99% in blood pressure, 4.63%–46.23% in inflammatory markers, 5.11%–10.48% in cardiac-associated enzymes, and 6.29% in homocysteine, as well as cumulative changes ranging from −2.68% to 5.36% in hemorheological parameters and from −4.96% to 12.05% in lipid-related indicators. Extremely high-temperature exposure (P99, 32 °C) was associated with cumulative changes ranging from −1.47% to 4.84% in hemorheological parameters and increases of 1.62%–1.91% in lipid indicators and 1.32%–15.13% in cardiac-associated enzymes. These findings provide multicenter evidence that nonoptimum temperature is associated with early cardiovascular alterations.

title: Correction to “Exposure to Intermittent Environmental Hypoxia Promotes Vascular Remodeling through Angiogenesis in the Liver of Largemouth Bass ( Micropterus salmoides )”
Nontargeted Identification and Prioritization of Organic Contaminants in Biosolid-Amended Soils across the United States
abstract: Abstract The widespread use of biosolids as an agricultural soil amendment has raised concerns about the release of organic contaminants into the environment. This study identifies biosolids-associated organic contaminants (BOCs) in soils from municipal biosolid-amended plots across the United States. Soil samples were collected from 18 sites in 15 states, representing biosolids applications from the 1980s to the present. Samples were taken at three depths (30, 90, and 180 cm) from plots with no, low, and high application histories. Samples were extracted using QuEChERS and analyzed by liquid chromatography–high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS) using a nontargeted analysis (NTA) approach. A total of 111 BOCs were detected across biosolid-amended plots. BOCs were detected most frequently in surface soils (30 cm), with significantly fewer detections at subsurface depths (p < 0.001). Cumulative loading rate and application frequency were significant predictors of the number of BOCs detected (p = 0.003 and p = 0.017, respectively). Quality-adjusted hazard scores for human health, ecological impact, and environmental fate identified 4-nitrophenol (44%), PFBS (41%), and miconazole (38%), among others as the highest-priority BOCs. This NTA-hazard prioritization workflow provides a strategy for identifying compounds warranting further evaluation for potential environmental and human health risks.

title: Unraveling the Bound-Water Removal Mystery: Preoxidation Enhances Sludge Dewatering via Cell Permeabilization and Transformation of Intracellular Polymeric Substances to Extracellular Polymeric Substances
abstract: Abstract The effect of oxidation degree on sludge dewaterability during oxone-induced preoxidation was investigated. The optimal oxone concentration increased free cells and membrane permeabilization while limiting cell lysis, releasing bound water, and producing a drier sludge cake without reducing the filtrate volume. Dewaterability enhancement was mainly driven by the shift of low-molecular-weight proteins and polysaccharides (<20 kDa) from intracellular polymeric substances (IPS) to extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), along with selective degradation of hydrophilic glucose and peptidoglycan in EPS. Organic matter transferred to the outer EPS layer was mainly derived from the cellular constituents of Gram-negative bacteria in sludge. Importantly, IPS was found to exert a distinct and non-negligible influence on sludge dewatering with its oxidative response fundamentally differing from that of EPS. As the oxidation intensity increased, the ratio of protein to polysaccharide rose in loosely bound EPS but declined in IPS, whereas carboxyl and lactone groups decreased in both soluble and loosely bound EPS fractions, while carboxyl groups concurrently increased within IPS. IPS contained more hydrophobic components than did EPS at all oxone concentrations. Excessive oxidation induced cell disruption and hydrophilic debris, impairing sludge dewaterability. Cell membrane permeabilization, rather than cell lysis, was the key factor affecting sludge dewaterability.

title: Electron Transfer at Microbe–Mineral Interfaces: From Molecular Mechanisms to Ecosystem-Scale Biogeochemical Cycling and Remediation
abstract: Abstract Microbe–mineral electron transfer (MMET) drives key microbial processes and biogeochemical cycling, but linking these microscopic interactions to ecosystem-scale dynamics remains a major challenge. MMET couples intracellular metabolism to extracellular mineral transformations. The resulting changes in mineral redox state and reactivity can, in turn, influence microbial energy conservation and metabolism. MMET flux could therefore provide a quantitative link between nanometer-scale electron exchange and larger-scale biogeochemical processes. In energy-limited and contaminated environments, electroactive microorganisms may transfer electrons to or acquire electrons from redox-active minerals, depending on their metabolic capabilities and local redox conditions. These interactions can support energy conservation, mitigate toxic stress, and generate localized zones of high biogeochemical activity. As their effects accumulate across space and time, microscale electron transfer may influence ecosystem-scale elemental cycling, microbial community succession, organic carbon stabilization, and contaminant fate. Building on established modeling approaches, we suggest that integrating individual-based models (IBMs) with genome-scale metabolic models (GSMMs) could translate spatially heterogeneous, genome-informed microbial responses into collective MMET fluxes across scales while accounting for key thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. More broadly, progress requires characterizing electroactive microbial diversity and mechanisms, engineering microbe–mineral interfaces through computational design and synthetic biology, and translating MMET principles into scalable environmental applications.

title: Longitudinal Multiomics Reveals Core Microbiome Disruption and Potential Keystone-Associated Recovery Following Pesticide Exposure
abstract: Abstract Pesticides have become indispensable in modern agriculture, serving as a primary tool to minimize crop loss amid increasing human population pressures. While the negative effects of pesticides on the soil microbiome have been reported, the temporal dynamics of soil microorganisms under pesticide use remain underexplored. Specifically, limited knowledge exists regarding how the soil microbiome responds to pesticides before and after the manufacturer-labeled ‘safe period’ of 21 days after application. We conducted a longitudinal microcosm study to investigate the temporal impacts of herbicide, fungicide, and insecticide on soil microbial diversity, composition, network complexity, and functional pathways across five time points. Our results show that soil microbial communities are negatively impacted by pesticide applications, but there is a trend of recovery after 21 days. We found a significant impact of the temporal persistence of pesticides on both bacterial and fungal community composition, with a stronger effect on fungi. Network analysis revealed that core microbiome networks were negatively impacted by pesticide applications, with the core microbial nodes, raw associations, and modularity declining in pesticide-treated soils, and this negative effect was particularly strong for pyrethroid insecticides. We identified several differentially abundant taxa, including Xanthobacteraceae and Vicinamibacteriales among bacteria, and Mortierella, Mytilinidales among fungi, which could serve as useful biomarkers for pesticide-affected soils. Results from microbial co-occurrence network analysis revealed that one ASV assigned to the Methyloligellaceae family consistently emerged as a keystone taxon in pesticide-treated soils. Using genome-resolved metagenomics, we assembled the genomes (MAGs) of Methyloligellaceae members and found these taxa harbor putative genes associated with pesticide degradation and antimicrobial resistance, suggesting their possible role in community recovery. Given the remarkably dynamic nature of soil microbial communities, our findings bridge an important knowledge gap regarding the short-term dynamics of microbial structures and functional pathways in response to major pesticides.

title: Mapping the Carbon Footprint of Organic Chemicals in Commerce
Novel NIR-II Imaging Reveals Gut-First, Brain-Later Inorganic Mercury Signals with Structural Injury in Zebrafish
abstract: Abstract Mercury (Hg) neurotoxicity has generally been assessed by organic methylmercury, whereas inorganic mercury [Hg(II)] is often considered less likely to cause direct brain exposure. Conventional approaches cannot resolve the in vivo spatiotemporal distribution of Hg(II) across tissues. In this study, we first developed an Hg(II)-responsive aggregation-induced emission sensor for second near-infrared (NIR-II) fluorescence imaging, which was then employed to track Hg(II) signals in live zebrafish. The sensor produced enhanced NIR-II signals in the presence of Hg(II), allowing low-background, noninvasive, and real-time imaging. We observed that Hg(II)-responsive sensor signals first appeared in the intestinal region and later increased in the brain region, revealing an intestine-first and brain-later temporal pattern in living zebrafish. During a 48-h continuous exposure followed by depuration, brain-region Hg(II)-responsive sensor fluorescence increased with exposure concentration and time and remained detectable during the depuration phase. Expansion microscopy further showed that low-dose Hg(II) exposure reduced the brain cell density and average cell size, and disrupted the local tissue organization. These results provided in vivo evidence of Hg(II)-responsive sensor in the brain region and its association with structural brain injury during development. Thus, inorganic Hg should also be considered in the assessments of developmental brain exposure and neural structural injury.

title: Solar Activation of Peroxymonosulfate by Chromophoric Dissolved Organic Matter Enables Predictable Micropollutant Attenuation in Real Waters
abstract: Solar-driven activation of peroxymonosulfate (PMS) is a promising advanced oxidation process for water and wastewater treatment; however, the kinetics of emerging contaminant removal in real water matrices remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated PMS photosensitization in three environmentally relevant water matrices and evaluated its role in the abatement of 42 pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs). Under simulated solar irradiation, CDOM promoted PMS transformation and generated multiple photochemically produced reactive intermediates (PPRIs). A multiple-probe chemical method was employed to quantify the cumulative exposure doses of HO•, SO4•-, Cl2•-, CO3•-, and 1O2. Across the tested matrices, PPRI exposure doses followed the order CO3•- > 1O2 > Cl2•- ∼ SO4•- > HO•. The measured PPRI exposure doses, together with second-order rate constants, reasonably predicted PPCP removal in the solar/PMS/CDOM system. For several phenolic and aniline-containing PPCPs, DOM-mediated inhibition was observed and was attributed to reductive back-reaction of one-electron oxidation intermediates; incorporating inhibition factors improved the agreement between calculated and experimental removal efficiencies. Furthermore, four commonly detected PPCPs, sucralose, metformin, caffeine, and carbamazepine, were first identified as practical indicator compounds for estimating PPRI exposure without adding external probe chemicals. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for predicting PPCP attenuation during solar/PMS treatment in CDOM-rich waters and highlight the importance of secondary radicals in real aquatic matrices.

title: Upcycling agricultural biomass waste into sustainable carbon dots with dual-color emission for optical security applications
Quantitative evolution of unfixed dyes, clearing mechanism, and universality of low-pollution sulfonated polymer-assisted reduction-free clearing of disperse-dyed polyester fabrics
Life cycle assessment for disposal of polypropylene food packaging plastic waste
Bio-based gelatin supramolecular microcup arrays via molecular engineering towards sustainable electrophoretic displays
Power-reduction detection and classification in photovoltaic modules using clustering of parametric deviations
abstract: Power reduction in photovoltaic modules may be caused by environmental conditions, faults, and degradation mechanisms, whose correct identification is essential to improve the reliability, safety, and energy yield of photovoltaic systems. This article proposes a classification approach for power-reduction scenarios based on parametric deviations extracted from a Global Nonlinear Model (GNLM) derived from the Single-Diode Model (SDM). The methodology starts with the construction of a GNLM representative of a healthy reference photovoltaic module, capable of describing its electrical behavior under different irradiance and temperature conditions. For each evaluated experimental current–voltage ( I–V ) curve, selected SDM parameters associated with this healthy reference model are adjusted to approximate the electrical behavior of the analyzed module. The deviations required for this adjustment, calculated with respect to the healthy reference condition, are used as diagnostic markers for clustering-based classification. Different power-reduction conditions were evaluated, including soiling, short-circuited bypass diodes, open-diode conditions under different shading levels, front-glass breakage, and partial shading (PS). To reduce the overlap between scenarios with distinct electrical behaviors, the samples were initially separated according to the number of maxima in the power–voltage ( P–V ) curve, denoted by N peak , distinguishing cases with N peak = 1 from those with N peak > 1 . Based on these diagnostic markers, two strategies are investigated according to the set of SDM parameters used in the classification process. Strategy 1 uses deviations in the diode ideality factor ( n ) and photogenerated current ( I p h ), achieving the best performance, with an overall accuracy of 99.6%. Strategy 2 uses deviations in the n , series resistance ( R s ), and shunt resistance ( R s h ), achieving an overall accuracy of 98.3%.

title: A decoupled dual–stream CNN–LSTM with adaptive attention mechanism for joint multivariate forecasting of solar irradiance and wind speed
Investigation and parametric optimization of external spray cooling for gas turbine inlet air via computational fluid dynamics simulation and response surface methodology
Microplastics as vectors and reservoirs of pharmaceuticals and drugs of abuse: experimental evidence, mechanistic predictions and analytical challenges
Strategic phosphorus recovery clusters in Europe: Linking geospatial resource availability with thermochemical recovery potential
abstract: Phosphorus (P) is an essential, non-substitutional resource, yet Europe's supply of elemental P (P 4 ) - classified as critical raw material – remains highly vulnerable. This study assesses whether Europe's secondary organic P resources can support centralized P 4 recovery by linking demand, resource availability, spatial distribution and thermochemical recovery potential. European P 4 demand was estimated at 34.7 kt(P 4 )/a from foreign trade statistics for 2017–2022. Sewage sludge alone contains an estimated 190.9–220 kt(P)/a across the EU-27 and the United Kingdom, demonstrating that resource availability exceeds current demand but is spatially distributed. Geospatial clustering identified nine phosphorus resource centers (PRCs) containing 19.5% of the European sewage-sludge-derived P 4 potential, while 80.5% remains distributed outside these hotspots. The PRCs differed substantially in plant size and feedstock distribution, highlighting spatial aggregation, not P availability, as a key constraint for centralized recovery. Highest P-flux Ruhr-area PRC was subsequently evaluated using a METSIM-based FlashPhos digital twin. Co-processing sewage sludge with Category 1 meat-and-bone meal (MBM) reduced the Fe:P ratio and increased the modeled P 4 recovery from 73.42% to 78.09%, corresponding to a potential output of up to 5350 t(P 4 )/a, or 16.5% of European demand. MBM co-processing provided an additional gross economic contribution of 4.02–5.25 million€/a through increased P 4 production and avoided CaO expenditure. The results demonstrate that Europe possesses sufficient secondary P resources to substantially exceed current P 4 demand, but their decentralized distribution makes spatial aggregation a principal constraint. High-density PRCs combined with complementary feedstocks therefore represent promising targets for future site-specific logistical, techno-economic and experimental assessment of centralized P 4 recovery.

title: Pesticide-driven bacterial adaptation: biodegradation pathways and co-selection of antibiotic resistance
abstract: The intensive use and misuse of pesticides has increased the chemical pressure exerted on soil microbiomes. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the global pesticide used in agriculture in 2023 reached 3.73 million tonnes of active ingredients, highlighting the magnitude of environmental exposure. Soil bacteria can adapt to pesticide contamination through catabolic pathways encoded by chromosomal genes and/or mobile genetic elements (MGEs), enabling pesticide transformation and sometimes supporting bioremediation. In parallel, a growing body of evidence indicates that non-antibiotic chemicals including herbicides and insecticides can contribute to the emergence and persistence of antibiotic resistance through co-selection. Mechanisms include cross-resistance mediated by multidrug efflux pumps and permeability changes, stress-induced responses and enhanced horizontal gene transfer (HGT) that facilitates the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) and MGEs in environmental ecosystems including soil, water and others. In this review, we summarise current knowledge on biodegradation pathways, genetic determinants and documented evidence linked to antibiotic resistance for five selected pesticide case studies: glyphosate, atrazine, cypermethrin, chlorpyrifos and paraquat. We identify where evidence is strongest (e.g., herbicide-associated AMR outcomes) and where major gaps remain, particularly regarding causal attribution under environmentally realistic concentrations and the frequency of ARG co-localisation with catabolic loci. We further propose an explicit mechanistic framework in which biodegradation and antibiotic resistance are examined as potentially interconnected components of bacterial adaptation, connected by a shared mobilome, a shared efflux and stress-response, the reactive intermediates of incomplete catabolism, and nutrient-driven community restructuring.

title: Relevant disruptions in critical mineral supply chain sustainability: A systematic literature review
abstract: Critical mineral supply chains are central to the energy transition but are increasingly exposed to disruptions that affect their economic, environmental, and social performance. Existing research has quantified the sustainability outcome, examined tier-specific research, and identified the wide range of disruption risks. However, these concepts remain fragmented and rarely integrate into a single analytical framework. Furthermore, few studies systematically prioritise the disruptions' relevance based on their tier's prevalence and the strength of their sustainability evidence within the supply chain. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic literature review of 103 Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed articles on critical mineral supply chain disruption and sustainability. The review descriptively classifies the literature by mineral type, geographical focus, research method, disruption category, supply chain tier, and sustainability dimension, using a full-text-coded article. It then develops a two-parameter, structured content analysis to assess which disruptions are most relevant in the literature, based on tier-based prevalence and sustainability-impact evidence. The finding indicates that price volatility and supply-demand imbalance are among the most prominent disruptions affecting supply chain sustainability performance, while logistics and transportation-related have received comparatively limited attention. The finding also reveals further research avenue to address county- and mineral-specific studies, a dynamic approach that integrates social performance and robust disruption assessment.

title: Integration of third-generation concentrated solar power and solid oxide electrolysis for dispatchable solar hydrogen production: Multi-variable optimization and techno-economic assessment
Performance analysis of waste heat utilization system for magnesium smelting flue gas
Co-pollutant mortality effects of short-term exposure to fine particles and ozone: A global systematic review and meta-analysis with omitted variable bias correction
Sustainability assessment of low-carbon soil stabilization strategies for cold region transportation infrastructure: an integrated life cycle and multi-criteria decision-making framework
Integrated Prediction and Analysis of Soil Erosion and Soil Organic Carbon Loss in the Dayekou Watershed, Qilian Mountains
abstract: ABSTRACT Soil erosion poses a critical threat to ecological security in mountain watersheds worldwide. Predicting its dynamics and associated soil organic carbon (SOC) loss remains an ongoing challenge during the 21st century due to complex interactions among climate, land use, and topography. This study developed an integrated modeling framework by combining Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks, Cellular Automata‐Markov (CA‐Markov), and the InVEST Sediment Delivery Ratio module to predict soil erosion and SOC loss in the Dayekou Watershed in northwest China's Qilian Mountains. LSTM accurately forecasted 48 months of rainfall (RMSE: 177.9–211.7) using 300 months of historical data (2000–2024), while CA‐Markov simulated land use patterns (2024–2028) with high precision (Kappa = 0.85). Results revealed that severe erosion areas (< 9% of watershed) contribute > 97% of total soil loss, concentrated above 3750 m elevation of the watershed. Land use type dominated erosion spatial distribution ( q = 78.8%), with glacier/snow and bare land exhibiting the highest erosion modulus. Average SOC loss increased from 9.877 to 21.524 t/(km 2 ·a) (2000–2023), with forested areas experiencing disproportionate carbon depletion despite lower erosion rates. The coupled framework demonstrates its robustness in predicting dynamic erosion in complex mountain systems, providing strong evidence‐based conservation support for protected areas in northwest China.

title: Trade‐Offs Between Maize Productivity Improvement and Topsoil Salinization Risk Under Shallow Burial Drip Irrigation in Semi‐Arid Regions
abstract: ABSTRACT Drip irrigation is widely used to conserve water and maintain crop production in water‐limited regions. However, how contrasting drip irrigation systems shape soil water‐salt movement, water and nitrogen (N) use, and maize productivity in semi‐arid environments remains poorly understood. Here, we conducted a two‐year field experiment (2019–2020) with a randomized complete block design to compare shallow buried drip irrigation (SBDI) and mulched drip irrigation (MDI). Relative to MDI, SBDI increased grain yield, dry matter accumulation, and N uptake by 5.86%, 3.11%, and 9.58%, respectively, contributin to greater water and N use efficiency. Soil salinity dynamics were closely coupled with soil water movement, representing a remarkable accumulation in the 0–20 cm soil layer under SBDI compared to MDI, owing to higher evapotranspiration. Although both irrigation systems resulted in soil salt accumulation, SBDI was more conducive for chloride ion elution. Partial least squares path modeling, Random forest, and Mantel tests suggested that water N utilization and salt dynamics were highly related to maize productivity. Our findings enrich the theoretical framework for preventing secondary soil salinization by inhibiting soil resalinization via water regulation or interlayer installation. In the future, the integration of SBDI with desalination measures may be a crucial strategy for enabling sustainable high‐yield maize production in semi‐arid regions.

title: Producing spatial justice: Scalar governance and territorial differentiation in coastal China’s nuclear development
abstract: Nuclear infrastructure development highlights an important empirical case in environmental governance: nuclear facilities concentrate environmental and social burdens locally, yet many projects proceed without sustained opposition. In the context of China, this paper argues that such outcomes are produced through county-level scalar governance strategies. Focusing on the Zhangzhou Nuclear Power Project, the study reconstructs how local authorities designed four concentric governance zones (20 km, 10 km, 2 km, 200 m) and calibrated distance-based interventions—compensation and relocation, tiered emergency planning and monitoring, graded communication and participation, and differentiated infrastructure and welfare investments—so that governance intensity corresponded to spatial exposure. Drawing on archival materials, policy documents, and semi-structured interviews with officials and project actors, corroborated by administrative records and implementation milestones, the analysis shows that scalar governance pursued distributive, procedural, and recognition objectives across zones. Importantly, the absence of organized resistance is interpreted not as conflict resolution but as the managed incorporation of grievances into institutional channels within a constrained political environment. By reframing nuclear legitimacy as the outcome of territorially differentiated state action, the paper contributes to debates on territory, scale, and environmental governance and positioning spatial justice as a conditional mechanism for managing uneven infrastructural risk.
journal_name: Environment and Planning C: Politics and Space

title: Matching on Gender and Sexual Orientation,
abstract: Abstract We study the mating patterns of non-heterosexual individuals, who represent a significant and increasing portion of the population, particularly among the youth. We estimate a multidimensional matching model of the marriage market where partner’s gender is endogenously chosen conditional on the agent’s sexual orientation, and is subject to trade-offs that depend on both the agents’ preferences and the pool of potential partners. We show that same-sex couples experience lower gains from live-in relationships, a “same-sex penalty”. Absent this penalty, the share of same-sex couples in the U.S. would increase by about 50% (from 1.36% to 2.04% of all couples).
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Union Membership and Native-Immigrant Labour Market Gaps
abstract: Abstract We estimate the causal effects of union membership on labour market outcomes for natives and immigrants, exploiting quasi-experimental variation from large increases in Norway’s tax deduction for union dues. Union membership raises earnings and improves employment protection for native workers, while the private returns for non-Western immigrants are substantially smaller and often close to zero. Complementary survey evidence suggests that this gap is not explained by differences in information, preferences, or engagement with unions: immigrants receive similar information when joining, report similar preferences over job amenities, and are more likely than natives to seek union assistance. Instead, the combined administrative and survey evidence is consistent with differences in union-side behaviour. Immigrants report lower satisfaction after contacting unions for support and are more likely to believe that native workers and those with strong local networks receive greater benefits from membership. The impact is most pronounced in concentrated labour markets, indicating that relying on unions to address monopsony-based market failures may unintentionally amplify group inequalities.

title: Production-Based Option Pricing
abstract: We show that a structural model incorporating firms’ real options and financial leverage decisions can generate forward-looking equity distributions of various shapes, resulting in highly flexible implied volatility surfaces. In contrast, exogenously specified models with stochastic volatility and jumps can only generate smiles and downward-sloping curves. We explain the observed negative relationship between downward sloping implied volatility surfaces and the value of real options: real options contribute positively to equity skewness, and more so the more convex their payoff, which is the case when the real option is “at-the-money” and has the lowest value.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Enjoying more years of good life while reducing resource use and emissions? A global panel analysis 1990–2019
authors: Duro, Juan Antonio; Galiana, Pau; Soldevila, M. Victòria; Piñol, Josep M.; Martín, Mónica; Sardà, Jordi; Ponce-Alifonso, Xavier; Farré Albendea, Fco Javier

title: Reconfiguring labour regimes in the Eastern industrial peripheries of the EU: a labour perspective on European industrial reorganisation within geoeconomic rivalry
Influence of Geopolitical Risk on Energy Transition and Climate Change
abstract: ABSTRACT Geopolitical tensions can influence energy transition, which, in turn, can impact climate change. Thus, we construct a framework that integrates these processes, analyzing 17 economies from 1990 to 2020 using a GVAR model. We hypothesize that geopolitical risk shocks affect economies through domestic financial markets. The results demonstrate that geopolitical risk shocks (i) hinder national energy transitions and contribute to increased carbon emissions; (ii) induce fluctuations in financial markets; (iii) have a minor direct impact on energy transition, except in Scandinavia and the United States; (iv) indirectly influence economies through financial markets (particularly stock markets); and (v) generate spillover effects and heterogeneities. We corroborate our findings through shock identification, treating financial markets as conduits for the geopolitical risk shock. Additionally, we conduct a battery of robustness checks addressing structural breaks, time‐varying bilateral trade, and bilateral financial flows (instead of bilateral trade), all of which confirm the consistency of our results. We conclude by discussing fiscal policies aimed at counterbalancing the negative effects of geopolitical risk on energy transition and climate change, emphasizing the importance of international cooperation for the effectiveness of these policies.

title: Navigating Climate Risk for Resilience: A Roadmap of Research Patterns and Emerging Trends
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate risk has become a defining challenge for business strategy, yet its research landscape remains fragmented across disciplines. This study maps the intellectual structure of climate risk research through a bibliometric analysis enriched with latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) topic modeling of 2715 peer‐reviewed articles. Our analysis first identifies the following six consolidated research patterns: (1) climate adaptation and community resilience, (2) climate risk and insurance mechanisms, (3) climate finance and green investment, (4) climate extremes and scenario modeling, (5) climate impacts and agricultural resilience, and (6) climate mitigation and energy transition. Analysis of the 2020–2024 literature reveals four emerging trends: urban climate adaptation, climate risk and financial stability, extreme climate events and climate modeling, agriculture, food security and household security. The findings indicate a shift toward integrated approaches connecting the physical, social, and financial dimensions of climate risk. The resulting roadmap identifies converging risks and strategic priorities for organizational resilience while providing policymakers with an evolving evidence base to support climate governance and informed decision‐making under deepening uncertainty.

title: Structural Dynamics of the European Circular Economy Through a Consumption–Circularity–Efficiency Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT The transition toward a circular economy requires analytical approaches capable of capturing the interdependence between resource consumption, material circularity, and economic efficiency rather than assessing these processes through isolated indicators. This study develops and empirically evaluates the Consumption–Circularity–Efficiency (CCE) framework as an integrated representation of circular‐economy performance across the EU‐27. A balanced panel of 378 country–year observations covering 27 Member States over 2010–2023 was constructed from 10 harmonized Eurostat indicators. Principal component analysis (PCA) was used to identify the dominant multivariate structure, followed by robustness and alternative‐retention analyses, construction of dimension scores and a composite CCE index, country‐level and temporal assessment, and complementary observed‐variable structural equation modelling (SEM) with country‐clustered robust inference. Three retained PCA components explain 71.44% of total variance and correspond to Consumption, Circularity, and Efficiency, although substantive cross‐loadings show that these dimensions are interconnected rather than empirically isolated. The variance‐weighted CCE index proved highly robust to equal weighting ( r = 0.983, p < 0.001), indicating that comparative positioning is not driven by the aggregation rule. Country‐level results reveal pronounced structural heterogeneity: Similar composite CCE scores arise from markedly different combinations of consumption intensity, circular‐resource performance, and efficiency. Temporal analysis indicates an overall improvement in relative EU‐27 CCE performance between 2010 and 2023, accompanied by non‐linear evolution and persistent divergence in national transition pathways. SEM provides complementary structural corroboration by identifying RMC, resource productivity, and GDP per capita as interconnected interfaces between material throughput, circularity, and economic performance; several relationships operate through significant indirect pathways rather than direct associations alone. Global SEM fit is mixed, supporting structural compatibility rather than complete confirmatory fit or causal interpretation. The study contributes to circular‐economy research by integrating dimensional identification, composite measurement, structural configurations, temporal dynamics, and pathway analysis within a single empirical architecture. The CCE framework therefore provides a configuration‐based diagnostic approach that can support differentiated circular‐economy strategies while preserving the structural information concealed by conventional aggregate rankings.

title: Transitioning to Circular Beauty: the Sense–Trust–Adopt (STA) Framework for Scaling Upcycled Ingredient Integration in Sustainable Cosmetics
abstract: ABSTRACT The cosmetics industry faces increasing pressure to integrate upcycled agro‐food by‐products, yet consumer adoption remains constrained by contamination concerns that are strongest for products applied directly to the body. Linear attitudinal models offer limited insight into how meaning is constructed around novel “waste‐derived” claims. This study therefore examines how consumers interpret, evaluate, and negotiate trust in cosmetic formulations containing upcycled ingredients. Thirty‐one in‐depth interviews with UK consumers were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis, combined with close attention to the language participants used, and structured by the FRASE elicitation framework (familiarity, reflection, articulation, sentiment, engagement). The findings show that evaluation unfolds in stages rather than as a single attitudinal judgment: Most participants initially misunderstood the category, typically assuming that upcycled cosmetics are made from recovered used products, and this misreading—rather than weak environmental motivation—constituted the first barrier to acceptance. Trust was then negotiated on two fronts: whether the product is safe and effective, and whether the claim itself is credible and independently verifiable. Acceptance thresholds varied by application zone: A majority of participants demanded stronger evidence for facial products than for body products—a pattern termed contextual gatekeeping—although a substantial minority applied uniform standards across zones. These insights are integrated into the sense–trust–adopt (STA) framework, advanced as a provisional interpretive framework rather than a tested model of behavior. Implications are developed for communication strategy, certification design, market‐entry sequencing, and policy support for circular business models aligned with SDG 12. The contribution lies in locating the barrier to circular adoption in comprehension and trust negotiation rather than in environmental attitudes alone.

title: Examining the Relationships Between Sustainability Orientation, Entrepreneurial Orientation, and SME Financial Performance in the Italian Agri‐Food Sector
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between sustainability orientation, entrepreneurial orientation (EO), and financial performance of Italian agri‐food SMEs, using panel data (2017–2022) and random‐effects models. The analysis identifies three sustainability dimensions—social, environmental, and external stakeholder‐oriented—examined alongside EO dimensions through a multidimensional approach. Results show that environmental sustainability is not significantly associated with financial performance. Social sustainability is negatively associated with operating and net income, while external stakeholder‐oriented sustainability is negatively associated with operating and net income, ROI, and ROA. EO dimensions show heterogeneous associations: innovativeness is positively associated with ROA, proactiveness with operating and net income, and risk‐taking is negatively associated with ROE. Competitiveness and autonomy show no significant associations with financial performance. Overall, the findings highlight heterogeneous relationships between sustainability and EO dimensions and different measures of financial performance, underscoring the value of examining both strategic orientations at the dimensional level over time.

title: Modeling ESG Performance Drivers in the Shipping Industry: An LLM‐Assisted q‐ ROFRS‐Delphi‐WINGS‐FCM Framework for Causal Analysis and Simulation
abstract: ABSTRACT The shipping industry plays a vital role in global trade and also exerts significant environmental and social pressures due to high fuel consumption, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and intensive port activities. Implementing environmental, social, and governance (ESG) practices offers a strategic pathway to enhance sustainability performance in this sector; however, it remains difficult to determine which managerial and operational actions can most effectively drive improvements in ESG performance. To address this challenge, this study proposes a novel framework that integrates a large language model (LLM), an extended q‐ rung orthopair fuzzy rough set ( q‐ ROFRS)‐based Delphi‐weighted influence nonlinear gauge system (WINGS) model, and a fuzzy cognitive mapping (FCM) simulation. This approach systematically identifies critical success factors (CSFs), analyzes their cause–effect relationships, and simulates their dynamic influence on ESG performance in the shipping industry. The findings reveal that six CSFs, including structured board oversight, global policy engagement, comprehensive legal compliance framework, employee‐centric culture, effective communication strategy, and integrated water resource management, serve as key causal drivers within the ESG system. FCM‐based scenario simulations suggest that full activation of these modeled drivers could substantially improve projected ESG performance under the assumed scenario conditions. This research offers a dual contribution: Theoretically, it extends fuzzy decision‐making and AI‐driven causal modeling to complex sustainability systems; practically, it provides actionable guidance for shipping companies and policymakers to strengthen ESG integration, meet the International Maritime Organization's net‐zero targets, and advance the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).

title: From Friends to Filings? Social Connectedness and the Demand for Public Information
abstract: Exploiting social network data from Facebook, we show that investors acquire more publicly disclosed information about firms located in counties that are more socially connected to their home counties. Using significant information events as shocks to private communication within social networks, we find that this relation is stronger in the weeks leading up to these events, consistent with private communication via social networks stimulating investors’ demand for public information. The relation is also stronger when there is greater scope for complementarity between private communication and public information. Furthermore, we provide evidence that stock prices respond to earnings announcements more rapidly for firms headquartered in more socially connected counties, suggesting social networks improve price discovery. Overall, our study provides new insights into how social communication shapes investors’ acquisition of public information.

title: The great slowdown? Trajectories of sustainability reporting boundary change from a value chain perspective 1990–2020
abstract: Purpose As sustainability has become an increasingly urgent and critical challenge, firms have faced growing expectations to broaden the scope of accountability by extending their sustainability reporting boundaries. This article analyses sustainability boundary change from a value chain perspective across different phases of sustainability reporting. Design/methodology/approach We analysed sustainability boundaries, i.e. the extent to which a firm accounts for impacts across its own operations and wider value chain, in a single value chain of steel-adjacent firms in Sweden, using a firm- and value chain-level assessment framework developed in the article. Reports from 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020 were analysed qualitatively and quantitatively to identify boundary trajectories based on an institutional theory framing. Findings Boundaries expanded significantly between 1990 and 2020; however, this trajectory slowed between 2010 and 2020 as sustainability reporting became stabilised as a practice, with extensions primarily occurring upstream rather than downstream or societally. No firms were found to use holistic reporting by including a full value chain perspective. Research limitations/implications Firm-centric reporting is shown to be the dominant approach over time; this sits in tension with mounting expectations to report on sustainability topics more broadly. It is suggested that future studies explore other institutional contexts, countries and value chain configurations to support and expand on the findings. Studies on a more granular level than the 10-year increments used in this study could also reveal nuances of boundary extension over time. Originality/value We distinguish between scope and depth, two dimensions of sustainability boundaries, to develop a framework of boundary approaches: firm-limited reporting, insular reporting, value chain aware reporting and holistic reporting. Based on these, we identify opportunities and challenges for adopting a value chain perspective in sustainability reporting, noting that, while the number of topics (i.e. depth) can be increased by using reporting frameworks like Global Reporting Initiative, incorporating topics at the value chain level (i.e. scope) remains a key challenge for firms due to the firm-centric logic used in both financial and sustainability reporting.

title: Accounting for the working conditions of social compliance auditors investigating modern slavery in supply chains
abstract: Purpose This study explores the working conditions of social compliance auditors who investigate modern slavery in global supply chains. This issue is important for understanding how auditors' working environment shapes audits as a key mechanism for detecting modern slavery. Design/methodology/approach We conducted 32 interviews with actors involved in social compliance auditing, including auditors, certification bodies, NGOs and accreditation agencies. Drawing on labour process theory and the complex role of multi-principal employment networks, we analyse how the work of auditing, the objects of that work and the instruments that structure it organises control, dependency and risk across external modern slavery audits. Findings Our findings show that social compliance auditing can be intensive, under-resourced work in remote, often hostile settings, producing heightened vulnerability for auditors. We also find that auditors periodically face physical harm and managerial coercion, including intimidation, violence and efforts to manipulate or suppress critical findings precisely because those findings pose a threat to business interests when non-compliant labour practices are found. Nonetheless, we show how auditors draw on “buffers of culpability” which include micro-resistance, safety-driven adaptation and agentic use of informal tools, relationships and planning, to preserve some investigative integrity despite these adverse conditions. Originality/value Businesses are increasingly held accountable for labour conditions in their supply chains and rely on social compliance auditors to independently assess operating facilities, yet auditors' own working conditions and structural vulnerabilities remain poorly understood. We specify implications at both agentic (micro) and structural (macro) levels for the governance and reform of social compliance auditing in the context of fragmented and multi-principal employment networks.

title: The Role of Institutions in the Relationship Between Informal Competition and New Product Development in Emerging Economies
abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Research has argued that informal competition (IC)—the competitive pressure from firms that are unregistered but derive income from the production of legal goods and services—increases formal (i.e., legally registered) firms' engagement in new product development (NPD) in emerging economies. However, other studies have suggested that IC may decrease such engagement. Drawing on an institutional perspective, we argue that the relationship between IC and NPD is contingent on the level of IC and the influence of formal and informal institutions. A multilevel analysis of 29,520 formal firms across 21 emerging economies indicates an inverted U‐shaped relationship between IC and NPD probability. Low to moderate levels of IC increase NPD probability, whereas higher levels reduce it. The findings also reveal that this relationship varies across emerging economies, with significant cross‐level interactions between IC and elements of formal (e.g., regulatory control, availability of finance) and informal institutions (e.g., survival vs. self‐expression and traditional vs. secular‐rational values) shaping NPD probability. Managerial Summary Informal competition can stimulate formal firms' new product development at low to moderate levels, but high levels of IC can discourage it. Because informal firms spur innovation among their formal counterparts, policymakers should not automatically seek to eliminate IC. Instead, they should consider IC as a changing condition and adapt enforcement to its intensity. At low to moderate levels of IC, minimal enforcement may be appropriate as the innovation and consumer benefits associated with IC may outweigh its costs. As IC becomes more intense and begins to undermine formal firms' NPD, policymakers can tighten enforcement while offering informal firms incentives to formalize. For managers, the findings suggest that the strategic response to IC should also depend on its intensity. When IC is low, formal firms may continue to innovate despite financial constraints; managers can therefore pursue low‐risk, affordable products using frugal innovation methods, while policymakers can support these efforts through improved access to finance. Managers are also well‐advised to consider the institutional context. Unlike their counterparts in countries leaning toward survival values (e.g., India), formal firms operating in societies that lean toward self‐expression values (e.g., Uruguay) are more likely to engage in NPD when IC is low; the probability decreases as IC becomes higher.

title: Pathways Out of Cybercrime: Perceived Desistance From Criminal Hacking
abstract: The present study seeks to understand how criminal hackers self-report to desist from the world of cybercrime. In doing so, we address significant gaps in criminological literature, as little is known about pathways out of cybercrime offending. Interviews were conducted with 22 individuals involved in cyber-dependent crime, primarily from the Netherlands. Of these, 15 respondents were justice-involved youth and 7 respondents self-identified as criminal hackers. The interviews offer unique insights into the stages offenders navigate following their involvement in cybercrime. Findings reveal that young hackers may be susceptible to behavioral change through various mechanisms. Desistance from cybercrime is a process that warrants a multidisciplinary perspective, influenced particularly by social bonds, prosocial daily routines, and deterrent experiences. A combination of police intervention and alternative approaches that emphasize ethical application of skills may be a promising route for young hackers in particular, although actual intervention effects remain unverified. We encourage evaluations of current programs for hackers as well as additional quantitative assessments of protective factors among cybercrime offenders.

title: The Cost of Capturing: How Smartphone Photo-Taking Alters Memory Performance and Cognitive Self-Esteem: The Role of Smartphone Self-Expansion
abstract: Taking photos to manage memories with smartphones is a routine strategy in the digital era. However, it remains unclear how smartphone photo-taking affects memory performance and self-evaluation. This research examined whether smartphone photo-taking is associated with a pattern consistent with the “Google effect,” and whether these associations vary with self-expansion via smartphone use. Across three experiments ( N = 363), participants photographed or observed materials before completing memory tests and measures of cognitive self-esteem. Study 1 tested the basic photo-taking effect; Study 2a examined device ownership as a contextual proxy for smartphone self-expansion; and Study 2b examined trait self-expansion as a continuous moderator. Results showed a photo-taking-impairment effect on memory, alongside higher cognitive self-esteem following photo-taking. Moreover, higher smartphone self-expansion was associated with stronger increases in cognitive self-esteem and greater memory overestimation, whereas its role in objective memory impairment remained inconclusive. Altogether, the findings suggest that smartphone photo-taking can reduce memory performance while increasing cognitive self-esteem.

Pesky Metals: Historical Perspective, Advances, and Challenges for Remediation of Problematic Metal Contaminants
abstract: Abstract Persistent and problematic toxic metal and metalloid pollutants (in particular, As, Hg, Pb, Cd, and Cr) have long been challenging and expensive remediation targets in contaminated surface and subsurface environments. Since the advent of environmental regulations and cleanup in the late 20th century, much progress has been made to address sites of legacy metal pollution and limit new contamination. Despite this, metal pollution remains a global problem, particularly in soils and sediments, with many large legacy sites inadequately remediated, metal contamination widespread in developed and developing nations, and new pollution occurring from informal and often illegal extraction and recycling processes. In this perspective, we highlight advances and challenges in science and technology, and key economic and social factors, that have influenced remediation of these “pesky” metals over the last ∼50 years. Through this lens, we consider emerging challenges and opportunities associated with legacy and critical metals, climate resilience, and sustainability.

title: A Framework for Time-Explicit Life Cycle Optimization
abstract: Abstract Life cycle optimization (LCO) selects optimal processes and supply chains from a set of alternatives given environmental constraints and objectives, supporting the design of sustainable systems and their transitions. However, current approaches rely on static assumptions, overlooking two interacting temporal dimensions: temporal distribution (flows are spread over time) and temporal evolution (processes and supply chains change over time). Because distribution and evolution jointly dictate the magnitude of a flow at a given time, both must be considered simultaneously to accurately optimize against cumulative environmental impacts and time-specific environmental constraints. We present a framework for time-explicit LCO that captures these interdependencies to determine optimal transition pathways. The framework tracks flow timing relative to process installation and dynamically determines flow magnitudes from time-specific process parameters and background supply chains. A case study on integrated methanol and pig iron production demonstrates how time-explicit LCO enables optimization against time-resolved environmental impacts and constraints, revealing mitigation strategies inaccessible to static approaches: prioritizing early high-efficiency technology installation to idle older processes as operational savings outweigh embodied impacts of stranded assets, and avoiding transient resource bottlenecks through diversification. To facilitate widespread application, we provide the open-source Python package optimex, enabling practitioners to design transition pathways that rigorously respect environmental limits.

Tree Species Configuration Shapes Soil Phosphorus Fractions and Microbial Communities in Uneven‐Aged Multilayered Chinese Fir–Broadleaved Mixed Forests
abstract: ABSTRACT Chinese fir ( Cunninghamia lanceolata ) plantations in southern China are often limited by phosphorus (P) availability, constraining productivity and sustainable management. We hypothesized that multi‐species, multilayered, uneven‐aged configurations would enhance soil P availability by regulating P fractions and microbial P transformation. This study aimed to identify the optimal tree species configuration for alleviating P limitation and improving soil quality. Four configurations were compared: pure Chinese fir (M0), Chinese fir + Phoebe bournei (M1), Chinese fir + P. bournei + Taxus wallichiana var. chinensis (M2), and Chinese fir + P. bournei + T. wallichiana var. chinensis + Schima superba (M3). Soil samples were collected from the 0–20, 20–40 and 40–60 cm layers and analysed for P fractions, acid phosphatase (ACP) activity, soil properties, and bacterial and fungal communities. Multivariate analysis, network analysis, structural equation modelling (SEM), and soil quality index (SQI) analysis were used to identify regulatory pathways. Different tree species configurations significantly altered soil P pool composition and its vertical distribution. Mixed configurations increased organic phosphorus (Po) and available phosphorus (AP), mainly enhanced surface soil organic matter (SOM) and total nitrogen (TN), and reshaped bacterial and fungal communities. M1 was enriched in P‐activating fungi such as Penicillium and Trichoderma , whereas M2 exhibited the highest fungal network complexity and SQI value, as well as higher AP content than the pure plantation. SEM indicated that available Fe (AFe) was an important driver of AP formation, while Al‐bound P (AlP) and occluded P (OP) negatively affected AP. Overall, M2 was the most favorable configuration for improving soil P availability and soil quality.

title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.

title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning–assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth–based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.

title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface
abstract: Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. We discuss implications of these observations for adsorption on Pt nanoparticles.

title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development—its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

title: A commensally regulated immune rheostat fine-tunes skin barrier fitness
abstract: At the skin’s surface, the epidermis must balance stem cell renewal with barrier maintenance to withstand environmental stress and shield against pathogens. In this study, we identify a microbial-immune-epithelial feedback mechanism that integrates environmental information into stem cell regulation in mice. Specifically, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), an intraepithelial macrophage population, orchestrate this circuit by producing prostaglandin E 2 , which restrains stem cell proliferation, promotes epidermal differentiation, and maintains barrier integrity during homeostasis. Upon pathway disruption, stem cells become overactivated, hindering terminal differentiation and weakening barrier function. Upstream, LC activity is tuned by the local microbial environment in a rheostat-like fashion, coupling commensal sensing to stem cell dynamics. Our findings provide a general framework for how barrier tissues achieve adaptive homeostasis amid continual external fluctuations.

title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

title: Altermagnetism revealed by polarized neutrons in MnF 2
abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. It is this feature that clearly demonstrates altermagnetism in MnF 2 . This finding highlights the potential for polarized INS to characterize altermagnets through its sensitivity to fine structure in magnon spectra.
