title: The effects of national security assessments in public procurement on competition, sustainability, innovation, and critical technology procurement
abstract: By strategically leveraging public procurement, governments can harness market competition to drive business innovation and sustainable development. It remains unclear, however, how this premise is affected by heightened security awareness due to increasing geopolitical tensions. Focusing on European Union (EU) member states, we examine how security-oriented practices in public procurement affect tender outcomes. Using data from a recent pan-European survey of 1613 procurement projects, coupled with data from the EU's tender platform Tender Electronic Daily, we test the effect of using national security assessments (NSAs) during tender preparation on competition, innovation, sustainability, and critical technology procurement. We find that conducting such assessments has positive effects on innovation and on critical technology procurement, but only for tenders won by domestic suppliers. NSAs can thus create urgency and mobilize resources to innovate through public procurement, but possibly in a way that reinforces national rather than EU-wide technological development. We identify a tension between the need for research and coordination of NSA development at the EU level to avoid market distortions arising from uncontrolled NSA proliferation versus a heightened bureaucratic burden for suppliers. We also argue that stimulating joint cross-border innovation procurement, particularly of critical technologies, is key to fully leveraging the benefits of the EU internal market when pursuing strategic policy goals.

title: Dueling Political Fictions and Public Administration and Democracy in an Era of Populism and Authoritarian Impulses
abstract: ABSTRACT The political fictions used in political discourse, during the English Civil War period, remain relevant to contemporary public policy and administration. Mainstream public administration discourse has too often employed the fiction of a singular and unbounded popular sovereignty that emerged during this period, leaving public administration ill‐equipped to deal with the authoritarian impulses of contemporary populist governments. What is needed in public administration discourse, in dealing with these authoritarian impulses, is not an ethic of administrative neutrality, such as has traditionally dominated much of our field, but an ethic of constitutionalism that draws on the fiction of the individual that was also articulated during the English Civil War period by the English Levellers and subsequently by the founders of the American Constitution.

title: Form Before Capability? AI Governance Adoption, Functional Capability, and the Limits of Index‐Based Evidence in the Global South
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments across the developing world have adopted artificial intelligence governance instruments at high speed, though the relationship between formal adoption and the capability to operate those instruments remains poorly understood. This article asks whether the expansion of AI governance architecture across the Global South has been matched by the functional capabilities on which regulatory effectiveness depends, and what explains the answer. Drawing on panel data for 82 countries across five Global South regions and six waves of the Government AI Readiness Index, it reports that within the period of stable index architecture (2020–2024) measures of regulatory form rose by 20.3 points on a 0–100 scale while measures of functional capability rose by 0.4 points, a within‐country differential present in 90% of sample countries and surviving removal of the single step‐scored indicator of national strategy adoption. The pattern of the differential discriminates among explanations: formal adoption rose four times faster in states in the top quartile of administrative capacity than in the bottom quartile, where capability fell; the most aid‐dependent states adopted least; and the differential is unrelated to regime type. This is inconsistent with the view that legislation is simply quicker to produce than infrastructure and with the view that adoption is decoupled from performance for external audiences, and consistent with adoption conditioned on administrative capacity, in which capability in the weakest states erodes while capability in stronger states grows more slowly than the instruments that depend on it. Vietnam and India are developed as confirming and deviant cases. Cross‐national dispersion widened on both dimensions, and patterns that appear only when the 2025 wave is included cannot be separated from the redesign of the index in that year.

title: Roger Detels, 14 October 1936 to 25 July 2026
Discrimination in Bureaucratic Recruitment Under Civil Service Exams
abstract: ABSTRACT Meritocratic recruitment is a central tenet in Weber's theory of bureaucracy, which states that employees should be hired based on merit. However, extensive research has shown evidence of hiring discrimination against minorities, breaking with basic principles in bureaucratic selection. This paper examines whether ethnic and racial minorities are discriminated against when bureaucratic organizations use civil service exams to assess candidates' merit and fitness for positions. Drawing on data from the local government of New York City and a candidate list fixed effects approach, we find that Black and Hispanic candidates are slightly more likely to be hired than White candidates with similar exam scores, suggesting that these ethnic minorities hold a small advantage in bureaucratic selection. However, examining the starting compensation levels of new hires, we show that minorities are hired at lower salaries and are compensated less for high exam scores than comparable White hires. Our findings suggest that civil service exams might be an important lever for securing fair and unbiased bureaucratic selection but also that they do not prevent discrimination in later steps of the recruitment process.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Participation in the smart city: disability and autonomous public transport in Singapore
abstract: Amidst the increasing interdependency between bodies and technology in smart city space, this article examines the extent to which disabled people can participate in the development and discursive construction of smart city technology. While citizen participation in urban planning and decision-making processes is ostensibly a key pillar of the smart city concept, the actual and meaningful capacity for citizens – especially disabled citizens – to translate their interests into smart city technology systems remains limited. In this article, we focus on the weaving of autonomous vehicle technology into Singapore’s city space as autonomous public transport is situated as an integral part of the country’s imagined future as a ‘driverless vehicle city.’ Findings from a qualitative content analysis of 86 newspaper articles about autonomous public transport, published from August 2013 to August 2025, and a series of online focus group discussions with 20 people with ambulatory disability indicate few opportunities for disabled people to democratically participate in autonomous public transport development and hold a stake in Singapore’s smart, driverless future, as well as a disappearance of disability from public communication about the technology. Reading technology communication and design as critical mediums that concretise standards for citizenship in smart city space in both material and symbolic ways, we emphasise the need for meaningful citizen participation, informed by disability, to develop smart city technologies in line with more democratic and emancipatory agendas.

title: The making of cloud computing: an antecedent of scalability
abstract: This paper offers a historically situated analysis of cloud computing. Cloud computing is a paradigm for provisioning computing infrastructure that now has enormous reach. It is defined by its unique scalability. This unique scalability has proven to be enormously impactful in the digital economy and beyond, shaping the emergence of platform ecosystems, the development of AI, and the process of digitalization in the 21st century. As important as it is to grapple with this scalability, it is easy to reify. This paper examines emergent sociotechnical practices that sought to make the computer more flexible. The study focuses on specific efforts within the Research Department of a major US technology company. The analysis of scalability I offer is based on interviews with former engineers in this Lab as well as archival material. I trace projects and practices as teams forayed into making a relatively fixed machine more dynamic and more scalable. This paper advances emerging literatures on cloud computing and digital infrastructure by offering a grounded analysis of scalability-in-the-making.

title: Correction to: Caution in handling switchers in pharmacoepidemiologic studies estimating treatment effects: the example of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors and inflammatory bowel disease
abstract: CorrectionCorrection to: Caution in handling switchers in pharmacoepidemiologic studies estimating treatment effects: the example of dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors and inflammatory bowel disease

title: Causal Inference with Missing Exposures and Missing Outcomes
What matters in pre-crash driving behavior modeling? An evaluation of state representations via imitation learning
Is greater engagement with a gamified app associated with greater improvements in safe driving behaviour? A naturalistic study from the i-DREAMS project
Configuring hidden and visible camera enforcement for risky driving deterrence
abstract: Road rule violations such as speeding and mobile phone use while driving remain major contributors to road crashes worldwide. Camera-based enforcement is widely implemented to address these behaviours, yet the relative and combined effects of overt and covert enforcement remain insufficiently understood. This investigation develops and tests a deterrence-based framework for identifying the perceived effectiveness of hidden and visible camera enforcement, focusing on key mechanisms including perceived certainty of apprehension and punishment avoidance. A cross-sectional, scenario-based survey was conducted with 1,167 licensed drivers in Australia. Participants evaluated four enforcement configurations (no enforcement, covert cameras, overt cameras, and combined covert and overt cameras). Outcomes included deterrence perceptions, willingness to engage in offending behaviours, and attitudes towards enforcement. Ordinal random forest models were used for variable selection, followed by cumulative link mixed-effects models to estimate effects while accounting for repeated measures. Covert enforcement was associated with higher perceived certainty of apprehension, whereas overt enforcement reduced punishment avoidance and willingness to offend. Punishment avoidance emerged as a central behavioural mechanism, showing stronger associations with willingness than perceived certainty. Combined enforcement aligned these mechanisms, increasing perceived certainty while reducing opportunities for undetected violations. Visible enforcement was also associated with more positive attitudes, indicating a complementary role in supporting legitimacy. The findings demonstrate that deterrence is not a property of individual enforcement mechanisms, but an emergent outcome of how enforcement is configured. Effective strategies should therefore balance uncertainty, visibility, and communication across the road network. These results extend deterrence theory by showing that key mechanisms are co-produced through enforcement configurations and provide practical guidance for designing more effective and publicly acceptable enforcement systems.

title: Reactive safety-critical scenario generation for autonomous driving via interaction-adaptive diffusion
The relationship between child protection training and teachers' self-reported contact with authorities
Youth Engagements with Pornographic Stereotypes: A Systematic Scoping Review
abstract: Pornography is a pervasive influence on young people’s understandings and experiences of sexuality, raising critical questions about how they engage with its stereotypical portrayals. While most research approaches this issue from an “effects” perspective, far less is known about the more agentic, interpretive, and contextual ways in which youth make sense of and position themselves in relation to pornographic stereotypes. To address this gap, this systematic scoping review synthesizes empirical insights into how youth (aged 16–25) in OECD countries interpret and navigate such stereotypes. Following the PRISMA-ScR framework, a systematic search across eight academic databases identified 27 studies relevant to our research question. The findings show that youth engagement with pornographic stereotypes is heterogeneous, ranging from uncritical adoption of stereotypical scripts to various forms of detachment and transformation. These modes of engagement reveal both a capacity for evaluative reflection and the relational character of sexual socialization, with transformation, in particular, emerging through dialogue and boundary setting within peer and intimate relationships. By integrating dispersed findings, this review advances scholarly debates on media and sexuality while offering practical insights for interventions such as porn literacy programs.

title: Beyond fossil fuels: ensuring food and energy security in low-and-middle-income countries amid recurring geopolitical tensions
abstract: Abstract The increasing dependence of smallholder agriculture on fossil fuels not only constitutes an energy challenge but also a structural threat to domestic food security in world’s low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where a majority of the rural population still relies on small-scale agriculture for food and income, yet rapid urbanization has increased food and energy demand. Recurring geopolitical crises, such as the recent Strait of Hormuz crisis, expose one fundamental vulnerability of the food systems in the LMICs: their dependence on imported fossil fuels. Such a dependence leaves both agricultural production and food security vulnerable to energy supply and price shocks. In this Opinion article, we argue that these crises actually could open the ways to, and accelerate, a strategic transition toward renewable-energy-powered agri-food systems. Renewable energy offers proven pathways to enhance domestic food security. Success, however, requires coordinated actions from governments, NGOs, research institutions, and global development stakeholders guided by a systems view, translated in economic terms by comprehensive benefit–cost frameworks, which account for long-term public benefits (e.g. increased food-system resilience, reduced fossil fuel dependence, and environmental footprints), in addition to short-term private benefits.

Modeling the electricity system in integrated assessment models - a time-series clustering approach for diverse futures
abstract: The growing role of variable renewable electricity calls for high time resolution when modeling the electricity sector. However, this can be computationally too expensive for models that combine different sectors and run over long timeframes, such as Integrated Assessment Models (IAMs). The computational burden can be reduced by, e.g., timeslicing or time-series clustering. Clustering approaches have the benefit of maintaining chronology and thus enabling electricity storage modeling; however, which hourly-level features clustering should capture for the diverse long-term scenarios calculated with IAMs have remained unclear. This paper makes a two-fold contribution to address these challenges. First, we propose an hourly-resolution electricity sub-model that links to the annual level of a suitable IAM, and uses time-series clustering to reduce the hourly dimension to a small number of representative periods. Second, we propose a new clustering approach – the multi-scenario clustering – that functions robustly across a range of future scenarios that might be calculated with an IAM. In this approach, outputs from multiple model runs covering different future scenarios are used in clustering to define representative periods. Our results show that this approach produces a clustering that works for a wide range of future scenarios nearly as accurately as a-posteriori clustering tailored for each scenario individually. Therefore, the multi-scenario clustering approach provides a robust way to save on computational burden while offering a relatively good level of accuracy in comparison to using the full, multi-year, hourly time-horizon, which would be prohibitively costly to use in IAMs.

Towards European hydrogen market design: Perspectives from transmission system operators
abstract: Despite hydrogen being central to Europe's decarbonisation strategy, only a small share of renewable hydrogen projects reached final investment decision. A key barrier is uncertainty about how future hydrogen markets will be designed and operated, particularly under Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin requirements. This study investigates the extent to which future hydrogen market design can be adapted from existing natural gas markets, and the challenges it must address. The analysis was based on a survey on future hydrogen market design targeting European gas transmission system operators, the stakeholder group responsible for operating the network and implementing the Network Codes. The survey provided an assessment of mechanism transferability and identified challenges for the early development of the hydrogen market. Core market design principles and trading frameworks are broadly transferable from natural gas markets, as entry-exit systems and virtual trading points. Capacity allocation requires targeted adaptation to improve coupling with electricity markets. Tariffs require adaptation through intertemporal cost allocation, distributing infrastructure costs over time to protect early adopters. Balancing regimes should be revisited to reflect hydrogen's physical characteristics and different linepack flexibility usages. Key challenges for early hydrogen markets include: temporal mismatches between variable renewable supply and expected relatively stable industrial demand, limited operational flexibility due to scarce storage and reduced pipeline linepack, fragmented regional hydrogen clusters, and regulatory uncertainty affecting long-term investment decisions. These findings provide empirical input to the hydrogen Network Codes and offer guidance to policymakers designing hydrogen market frameworks.

title: Understanding demand-side flexibility characterisation and barriers to effective deployment: A Dutch case study
abstract: Demand response is a critical component of future energy systems, as it provides a significant contribution to the cost-optimal integration of renewable energy. However, a variety of barriers inhibit its deployment and utilisation. While the research on barriers to demand response is wide and varied, it is often unsystematic and incomplete, with studies focusing on parts of the demand response ecosystem such as specific sectors, technologies or stakeholders. To bridge this gap, this study builds upon existing literature to develop a consistent and comprehensive framework for systematically identifying, classifying and analysing barriers across the demand response ecosystem, with the aim of providing input for the design of policy incentives. We develop an integrated framework that is based on the underlying nature of the identified barriers. We identify four overarching categories: technical, economic, regulatory and behavioural, along with multiple sub-categories and elements. This framework is tested on the Dutch energy system. We find that the most significant technical barriers faced by the Dutch energy sector are process and operational constraints and network limitations; the main economic barriers are financial uncertainty and distorted market signals due to taxes and tariffs; the main regulatory barriers are policy ambiguity and information insufficiency; and the main behavioural barriers are lack of expertise and incompatible individual preferences.

title: Decommissioning and repowering of utility-scale solar photovoltaic systems: A review of policy, economics, technology, environment and social dimensions
abstract: The rapid global expansion of solar photovoltaics (PV), rising to nearly 3 TW in 2025, has outpaced planning for end-of-life (EoL) management. The first wave of large-scale solar farms, commissioned in the early 2010s, is now in its second decade of operation, making EoL decisions increasingly urgent. Existing literature has focused primarily on panel recycling, overlooking balance of system components, civil works, grid infrastructure, and regulatory and contractual obligations. In mature industries such as oil and gas, decommissioning frameworks and financial assurance were developed over decades after environmental harms became visible, and liabilities such as abandoned wells remain unresolved. Solar PV is younger and growing rapidly, and can establish EoL frameworks before most of its fleet reaches EoL. This review provides the first cross-domain synthesis of EoL pathways for utility-scale PV systems, spanning policy, economics, technical practices, environmental impacts, and social dimensions. Drawing on 85 sources and 36 case studies, it examines decommissioning and repowering as the primary EoL strategies. The literature reveals fragmented regulatory frameworks, inconsistent cost estimation methods, and limited empirical evidence. While repowering offers economic benefits, it presents environmental trade-offs, while social impacts are underexplored. The evidence is concentrated in the U.S. and Europe and limited to English language sources, so findings on costs, incentives and permitting may not transfer to other regions. No framework exists to compare EoL options across these factors. These findings highlight the need for structured, site-specific decision frameworks, and for evidence from more regions, to support transparent and consistent EoL planning.

Lipophilic Redox Mediators Reprogram Intracellular Electron Flow to Promote Arsenic Methylation in Soil Fermentative Bacteria
abstract: Abstract Anaerobic arsenic (As) methylation by fermentative microorganisms, particularly Clostridium-related populations, controls As speciation, mobility, and volatilization in flooded paddy soils, yet the mechanisms promoting this process remain poorly understood. Here, we reveal that phenazine- and phenoxazine-like redox mediators can enhance anaerobic As methylation via reshaping the intracellular electron allocation in a representative As-methylating fermentative bacterium. We integrated As speciation analysis, metabolite profiling, proteomics, and metabolic-flux modeling to determine how resazurin, as a represenative lipophilic redox mediator, reshapes fermentative metabolism and methylated As (MeAs) formation. The membrane-permeable redox mediator resazurin increased the apparent rate constant of MeAs formation by up to fourfold relative to the hydrophilic mediator anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonic acid (AQDS). Unlike AQDS, resazurin enhanced dimethylarsine formation while establishing a more reducing intracellular environment by diverting electrons from hydrogen evolution, indicating altered intracellular electron disposal. At the proteomic level, resazurin induced coordinated increases in As(III) methyltransferase (ArsM) and proteins involved in S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) biosynthesis, representing the primary molecular responses associated with enhanced As methylation. Proteins involved in amino-acid-fueled energy conservation and redox homeostasis were also enriched, potentially creating favorable cellular conditions for SAM-dependent As methylation. In a paddy-soil-derived fermentative consortium, resazurin likewise enhanced MeAs production and increased transcript levels of Clostridium-associated arsM and the SAM synthetase gene (metK). These findings identify lipophilicity-dependent, redox-compound-mediated intracellular electron flow reprogramming as a previously underappreciated control on anaerobic As methylation and provide a mechanistic basis for predicting MeAs formation in flooded soil environments.

title: Industrial Solid Wastes Recycling from Steel and Power Sectors Delivers Climate and Net Societal Benefits
abstract: Abstract Sectoral decarbonization can substantially reshape the quantity and composition of industrial solid waste and its associated resource recovery potential, yet how these changes evolve along decarbonization pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we develop a sectoral transition framework linking future waste generation, recycling technologies, life cycle environmental impacts, and societal benefits. We focus on the steel and power sectors, which represent major industrial solid waste sources and distinct decarbonization pathways across six major producing regions from 2025 to 2050. By 2050, steel sector wastes remain at 0.61–0.78 Gt, whereas power sector wastes decline from 1.11 Gt in 2025 to 0.17–0.50 Gt. Under four scenarios, cumulative mitigation ranges from 25.68 to 53.39 Gt CO2-eq, with discounted net societal benefits of USD 11.24–23.81 trillion. Steel sector benefits are sensitive to recycling technology shares, whereas power sector benefits are more strongly shaped by transition-driven changes in the waste generation and composition. These findings highlight the importance of integrating evolving waste flows and technology choices into long-term decarbonization and circular economy strategies.

title: Proteomic Profiling for In Situ Exposure in a Sentinel Freshwater Species to Describe the Crustacean Reproductive Effects of Aquatic Contamination
abstract: Abstract Complex mixtures of contaminants can affect aquatic organisms through diverse modes of action, making extrapolations of laboratory findings to field conditions complex. Here, we show that proteomics combined with active biomonitoring may inform about reprotoxic effects in the sentinel species Gammarus fossarum. Proteomic responses provide information on the diversity of underlying mechanisms and may serve as a sensitive early warning signal of reprotoxicity. Females were exposed in situ in 18 French surveillance sites and analyzed for reproductive end points and proteomic levels in the caeca and the ovaries. This study aimed to assess links between reproductive impairment and molecular responses, using the complementary information provided by both tissues. Protein coexpression analysis identified protein clusters associated with organ functions, reproductive impairments, or field exposure. Several modules were significantly associated with field condition or females’ physiological integrity. Interestingly, we identified a large diversity of biological pathways modulated in impacted females exposed to reprotoxic sites, with reproduction-related proteins as potential early biomarkers of reprotoxicity. These results highlight the relevance of considering field conditions and individual physiology within the eco-exposome framework and demonstrate the value of integrating omics and active biomonitoring to uncover diverse molecular signature behind field-induced reprotoxicity in this sentinel species.

title: Unregulated Disinfection Byproducts from de facto Water Reuse: Molecular Evidence for EfOM-Induced Redirection of Chlorination Pathways
abstract: Abstract Unplanned potable reuse introduces effluent-derived organic matter (EfOM) into drinking water sources. While conventional coagulation partially removes EfOM, the residual fraction undergoes chlorination and may form toxic disinfection byproducts (DBPs) that escape current monitoring. However, the molecular mechanisms by which EfOM alters DBP formation pathways remain poorly understood. Here, we combine ultrahigh-resolution mass spectrometry with reaction network analysis to reveal that EfOM significantly redirects chlorine pathways. Compared to EfOM-free surface water, the presence of 20% EfOM decreases direct halogenation pathways (addition and substitution) from 4.2% to 1.8% of total transformation events. This shift occurs because EfOM introduces reduced, high-molecular-weight, heteroatom-rich molecules that cannot be directly halogenated; they require HOCl-driven oxidative fragmentation to generate halogenation-susceptible intermediates. Consequently, chlorinated finished water accumulates sulfur-containing DBPs (CHOS compounds, with relative intensity increasing from 35% to 60%) and complex “orphan” DBPs lacking identifiable precursors (with molecular features linked to elevated toxicity). These findings highlight an urgent need to update DBP monitoring frameworks to include unregulated sulfur-containing and orphan byproducts in de facto reuse scenarios.

title: Enhancing sustainability in greenhouse agriculture through chemical analysis–driven characterization of boiler biogas fuel strategies
abstract: Greenhouses can enhance sustainability and productivity by integrating renewable energy and CO 2 enrichment, which improves photosynthesis and reduces environmental impact. However, existing studies on biogas and methane combustion have not addressed how combustion-derived CO 2 can be strategically managed to meet the coupled thermal and photosynthetic demands of greenhouse crops. In this context, the present study is the first to conduct a parametric analysis of biogas utilization for greenhouse applications, offering a proposed adaptive fuel management strategy hypothesized to support both environmental and economic benefits. To achieve this, a counterflow flame configuration is employed to investigate the combustion characteristics of a greenhouse boiler operating with various methane–biogas fuel mixtures. The detailed Gas Research Institute Mechanism (GRI-Mech 3.0), comprising 53 species and 325 reactions, is utilized to model the reaction kinetics. Detailed thermophysical and transport properties based on fundamental thermodynamics are integrated to accurately capture flame structure and species transport. The model was validated against experimental methane/air flame data, demonstrating good agreement and confirming its predictive accuracy. The effects of (1) CO 2 enrichment, (2) operating pressure, and (3) strain rate on flame temperature and species concentrations (CO 2 , CO, NO, and NO 2 ) are systematically investigated. Findings demonstrate the potential of biogas as a sustainable fuel under characterized conditions: Biogas substitution lowers peak in-flame NO x and CO concentrations while increasing peak CO 2 concentration, highlighting its potential for CO 2 enrichment. A pressure-sensitivity analysis (1–10 atm) and a proposed adaptive diurnal fuel-switching strategy are also presented. Practical guidelines are proposed to support greenhouse growers in enhancing thermal efficiency and environmental performance.

title: Village and farm ponds differ in contaminant retention and mobility: Implications for sustainable management of rural agricultural landscapes
Consumer willingness to pay and farmers’ adoption intentions for pesticide-reducing technologies in European orchards
abstract: Reducing synthetic pesticide use remains an EU sustainability objective, yet uptake of pesticide-reducing technologies remains limited in high-input orchard systems. This study examines whether information on consumer willingness to pay (WTP) for products with reduced pesticides is associated with farmers' adoption intentions. We focus on four pesticide-reducing innovations: smart mapping variable rate (VRA) application systems, robotic weeders, bio-based solutions with low sulphur and copper formulations, and cover crops. Evidence is drawn from a structured survey experiment involving 354 olive and vine growers across five European Union countries. Using a within-subject design with randomised presentation order and a Cheap Talk script to mitigate hypothetical bias, we compare farmers' adoption intentions before and after exposure to estimated consumer WTP premiums for wine and olive oil produced with reduced pesticide use. Non-parametric tests and multinomial logit models indicate that consumer WTP information is positively associated with both partial and full adoption intentions across all four technologies, with stronger associations for smart mapping VRA and robotic weeders than for bio-solutions and cover crops. Farm structure and behavioural factors, including perceived costs, subjective norms, and perceived effectiveness of existing pest management practices, exhibited technology-specific associations with adoption intentions. Although the study design does not permit causal inference, the findings suggest that consumer-driven market signals could complement existing policy approaches to support the transition towards more sustainable agricultural production.

title: Major olive mill aqueous effluents as industrial sources of hydroxytyrosol, 3,4-dihydroxyphenylglycol and tyrosol for circular valorisation
abstract: The selective recovery of valuable chemicals from waste streams is a central objective of Green Chemistry, particularly when waste prevention and the use of renewable feedstocks can be combined. In two-phase olive oil extraction systems, several aqueous effluents are generated that are commonly treated as waste despite their significant organic and phenolic content. In this work, four industrial effluents—olive washing water (OWW), hopper drip water (HDW), vertical centrifuge water (VCW) and oil decanting water (ODW)—were systematically characterised in six olive oil mills over two consecutive production seasons to evaluate their potential as sources of bioactive phenolic compounds. HDW exhibited the highest phenolic concentration, reaching up to 3.5 g/L, together with elevated sugar contents, identifying it as the most promising stream for the recovery of hydroxytyrosol (HT) and 3,4-dihydroxyphenylglycol (DHPG). VCW, although more diluted, was generated in the largest volumes and contained substantial amounts of both compounds, while ODW showed an unusual predominance of DHPG over HT, enabling selective recovery. An industrial chromatographic process was optimised to maximise phenolic retention and HT purity in the most concentrated streams. Based on national production data, the valorisation of these effluents could enable the recovery of up to 80 t/year of HT and 56 t/year of DHPG. Overall, this study highlights the potential of phenolic recovery to support waste valorisation strategies and facilitate subsequent wastewater management within a circular-economy framework.

A novel Solar-Driven Molten-Salt methane pyrolysis system with direct Particle-to-Reactor-Wall heat Transfer: Design and Techno-Economic assessment
abstract: This study proposes a solar-driven methane pyrolysis system in which a particle-based concentrating solar power (CSP) plant supplies heat directly to an array of molten-salt (MnCl 2 –KCl) bubble-column reactors through the reactor wall, without an intermediate heat-transfer fluid or electric heating step. An hourly-resolved CSP model over a full year, comprising a heliostat field, a free-falling particle receiver, and two-bin thermal energy storage, is coupled to a reactor model that includes reaction kinetics, bubble hydrodynamics, particle-to-salt heat transfer, and equipment sizing. The integrated plant is assessed through a techno-economic analysis for a site in Daggett, California. At the baseline design (hot and cold particle temperatures of 1100 and 950 °C, 14 h of storage), the bulk salt temperature is 936 °C, the plant reaches a capacity factor of 69% and a single-pass methane conversion of 45%, and it produces about 6700 t/yr of hydrogen at a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH 2 ) of $3.87/kg without carbon credit and $3.52/kg with credit for the co-produced carbon. Raising the reactor temperature increases the cost of solar heat but lowers LCOH 2 through faster kinetics and fewer reactor modules, so the CSP and reactor subsystems must be designed jointly. Natural gas accounts for about 54% of LCOH 2 , and the particle-to-wall heat transfer coefficient is the most influential design parameter. At an assumed hydrogen price of $4/kg, the project has a positive 30-year net present value of $53 M with the carbon credit and without Section 45 V or LCFS policy support. At a gas price of $6/GJ and a hot-particle temperature of 1200 °C (bulk salt temperature of 1021 °C), approaching the conditions of earlier studies, LCOH 2 falls to $1.9–2.3/kg depending on the carbon credit. The configuration is a conceptual design: experimental validation of the particle-to-wall heat transfer, corrosion, creep, thermal cycling, abrasion, and liner compatibility in molten chloride is required.

title: Multi-seasonal assessment of soil contamination and metal mobility following the Jagersfontein tailings storage facility failure event in South Africa
abstract: The failure of the Jagersfontein tailing storage facility (TSF) in South Africa on 11 September 2022 released ~5.8 million m 3 of kimberlite tailings into a semi-arid wetland, representing one of the largest such spillages in history. This study investigates the chemical evolution of the deposited tailings and their impact on soil geochemistry over three seasons (18 months). Geochemical and statistical analyses identified two broad elemental groupings: Group 1 elements (B, Na, Mg, Cr, Mo, Co, and Ni) were primarily introduced into the landscape by the tailings, whereas Group 2 elements (V, Mn, Cu, Zn, As, Sn, Cd and U) were mainly enriched through landscape-driven processes, particularly groundwater discharge, and material redistribution during flood events. Sodium migrated rapidly through the soil profile, contaminating soils down to bedrock, and showed no signs of recovery even where surface tailings had been removed. In contrast, Mg, Cr, Co and Ni migrated primarily via colloidal-facilitated transport, resulting in the progressive enrichment of the upper soil horizons. The tailings' sodic and metal-laden nature is particularly problematic in an environment naturally enriched in Na, B, As and Mo. Chemical mass transfer analyses indicate that pedogenic processes are unlikely to reverse contamination within ecologically meaningful timescales. Immediate remediation, including tailings removal, is recommended to mitigate long-term environmental and health impacts. Overall, the findings demonstrate that environmental impacts extend far beyond surface contamination, revealing complex subsurface enrichment pathways that offer new insights into contaminant behaviour following large-scale tailing failures in dryland environments.

title: A 4000-year record of parallel collapse in the ecological niche of Black Sea top predators
abstract: Marine ecosystems face multifaceted threats stemming from historical overexploitation and environmental degradation. Despite existing research, there are notable gaps in understanding the long-term dietary dynamics of marine organisms in the context of anthropogenic impacts. To address these gaps, we utilized stable isotope analysis as a proxy for dietary niche and examined changes in the Black Sea over a 4000-year period, focusing on ancient and contemporary samples from cetaceans ( Phocoena phocoena , Delphinus delphis , Tursiops truncatus ) and fish ( Scophthalmus maximus ). Among the ancient samples, the isotopic data from all four species revealed a wide and generally overlapping average dietary niche. In contrast, contemporary cetacean and fish samples exhibited niche compression, indicative of a fundamental shift in the Black Sea marine ecosystem from Antiquity to the present day. Our analyses provide ecologically significant temporal perspectives, shedding light on critical trends and changes essential for conservation efforts aimed at addressing contemporary ecological challenges in degraded marine systems.

title: Experimental assessment of rotational speed stability in a micro turbojet engine for unmanned aerial vehicles based on fuel physicochemical properties, engine performance, and vibration analysis
abstract: This study investigated the rotational speed stability of a micro turbojet engine operating with three different fuels through physicochemical fuel characterization, engine performance testing, and vibration-based stability analysis. Experiments were conducted on a micro turbojet engine used in unmanned aerial vehicle applications under five steady-state operating regimes. Key performance parameters—including thrust, turbine inlet temperature, fuel flow rate, and specific fuel consumption—were investigated. Engine stability was evaluated using two triaxial accelerometers installed near the compressor and turbine bearing planes, while rotational speed variations were analyzed from vibration signals and encoder measurements using short-time Fourier transform, root mean square, and kurtosis indicators. The results showed that diesel fuel containing 5 vol% lubricating oil provided engine performance comparable to Jet A containing 5 vol% lubricating oil, with thrust and fuel flow variations generally below 3%. In contrast, biodiesel containing 5 vol% lubricating oil increased the specific fuel consumption by up to 17%. For all tested fuel–lubricating-oil formulations, kurtosis values remained below 3, indicating no pronounced impulsive or shock-like behavior in the measured vibration signals. However, at high operating regimes (approximately 110000 rpm), biodiesel and diesel fuel containing 5 vol% lubricating oil produced slightly higher vibration amplitudes than Jet A containing 5 vol% lubricating oil. The standard deviation and coefficient of variation ranged from 27 rpm to 869 rpm and 0.06% to 2.01% for engine speed, from 0.11 N to 0.78 N and 0.59% to 7.89% for thrust force, and from 0.07 L/h to 0.20 L/h and 0.38% to 2.91% for volumetric fuel flow rate, respectively. Overall, the diesel fuel formulation containing lubricating oil exhibited performance and vibration characteristics closest to those of Jet A formulation containing lubricating oil under the investigated conditions, while the biodiesel formulation containing lubricating oil resulted in higher fuel consumption and slightly increased vibration amplitudes at high operating regimes. These findings are limited to the short-duration operating conditions investigated in the present study.

title: Pragmatic muddling as an enabler for coastal adaptation? Implementation of seawalls as protection against sea-level rise in Aceh, Indonesia
abstract: There is growing scholarly interest in pragmatic approaches to local-level implementation of climate change adaptation. However, hard coastal protection arguably requires a coordinated approach across time and space, and a high level of technical knowledge. Our objective is therefore to assess the extent to which pragmatic approaches can enable effective local adaptation to sea-level rise through hard coastal protection, with a specific focus on seawalls. We use the analytical framework of pragmatic muddling to evaluate how local government officials in Aceh, Indonesia realise the construction of seawalls within a complex governance landscape, drawing on data collected from interview and site visit methods. Our principal findings are that local officials in Aceh do indeed draw on aspects of pragmatic muddling to support seawall implementation, especially by framing projects differently to draw down multiple funding sources; but that the scale and complexity of coastal change can exceed the level of protection that can be realised through local-level pragmatic approaches. The key implications of our findings are: reduce complexity in adaptation governance through better coordination mechanisms, so that local officials can use their context-specific knowledge within a wider programme of interventions; support the development, resourcing and retention of capable personnel at local levels of government who know what the challenges are and what needs to be done; and strengthen mechanisms for systematic evaluation of interventions, including those undertaken on a piecemeal or pragmatic basis, to create a pathway from pragmatic muddling to more transformative adaptation outcomes.

title: Free to Fail? Paternalistic Preferences in the United States
abstract: Abstract This paper examines paternalistic preferences in two large-scale experiments with participants from the US general population. Participants decide whether to intervene when a stakeholder is about to make a choice misaligned with the stakeholder’s own preferences. Willingness to intervene depends on which intervention is available: only a minority implements a hard intervention, which restricts the stakeholder’s choice set, while a majority implements a soft intervention that provides information without restricting choice. A substantial share of participants does not defer to the stakeholder’s stated preferences when evaluating welfare. Our framework estimates that about half are welfarists and a third libertarian paternalists.

title: Who pays for decarbonizing homes?
abstract: The decarbonization of the residential building sector requires large upfront investments in heating system replacement and thermal renovation that fall disproportionately on lower-income households. Faced with political constraints on carbon pricing and technology mandates, investment subsidies have become the main policy instrument.This paper analyzes the distributional effects and fiscal costs of this policy approach for Austria. We develop a microsimulation model that links household-level investment needs to landlord wealth distributions,allowing us to assign the incidence of subsidies and financial burden across homeowners and landlords within a unified empirical setting.We find total investment needs amount to 78–92 billion euros over the transition period to 2040 (approximately 1% of GDP annually), implying fiscal costs of 33–40 billion euros under the 2023 subsidy scheme. Despite a targeted low-income component, approximately 45% of subsidy outlays accrue to the top three income deciles. Net investment burdens remain strongly regressive when thermal renovation is required, exceeding three annual incomes for low-income single-family homeowners. We further document substantial horizontal disparities within income groups and show that Austria's fragmented housing law is a first-order determinant of investment feasibility in the multi-apartment (rental) sector.Addressing distributional and feasibility concerns under fiscal constraints may require a policy mix combining mandates, income-contingent transfers, liquidity-support instruments and housing law reform.

title: Do the trophic impacts which jaguars have on wildlife communities matter to farmers? Diverging farmer preferences for jaguar-associated benefits and costs
Actualizing entrepreneurial futures: Imaginaries, Visions, and the Olivetti Corporation
In Value Creation: The Mediating Roles of Lean Sustainability and Sustainable Quality Culture in Linking Values‐Based Leadership to Organizational Outcomes
abstract: ABSTRACT This research investigates the mechanisms by which value‐based leadership (VBL) impacts critical organizational outcomes, namely, operational performance (OPP), business performance (BSP), and business survival (BSV). Specifically, it examines the mediating roles of lean sustainability (LES) and sustainable quality culture (SQC) in translating leadership into tangible results. The research employs a quantitative research design using survey data collected from 402 middle and senior‐level managers. The proposed research model and hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) with SmartPLS 4. A two‐stage analytical approach was followed, involving the evaluation of the measurement model (reliability and validity) and the structural model (path coefficients and mediating effects). The direct effect of values‐based leadership on sustainable quality culture (β = 0.759; t = 26.912; p < 0.001) was identified as the strongest relationship in the model. In the mediation analysis, the indirect effect of values‐based leadership on lean sustainability through sustainable quality culture (β = 0.395; t = 12.494; p < 0.001) emerged as the most prominent mediation mechanism. All seven proposed hypotheses (between H1 and H7) were statistically supported, with coefficients excluding zero within the 95% confidence interval and significance levels of p < 0.001. While the research uses a robust sample of 402 managers, the use of non‐probability purposive sampling may limit generalizability. Future research could adopt longitudinal designs to further validate causal links over time or examine these dynamics across different sectors to determine whether sectoral nuances affect the mediating effect.

title: Who Governs Carbon? Board Diversity and Incentive‐Linked Pay as Key Drivers of Disclosure in FTSE 100 Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT Corporate boards are increasingly expected to drive climate accountability, yet evidence on which governance mechanisms shape carbon transparency remains contradictory. Using an unbalanced panel of 618 firm‐year observations from 62 FTSE 100 nonfinancial firms (2015–2025), this study examines how board structure, composition and incentive design shape both the decision to disclose carbon emissions via the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the depth of that disclosure (a 0–8 quality scale). Combining pooled OLS, fixed‐effects, random‐effects and logit regressions with structural equation modelling, we find that gender diversity and sustainability‐linked executive compensation are the only governance mechanisms consistently and robustly associated with both disclosure outcomes; board size is positively associated with disclosure depth but not with the disclosure decision itself. Board independence, meeting frequency, attendance and sustainability committees show no material effect once firm‐specific heterogeneity is controlled for. Structural equation modelling further reveals a negative covariance between governance and financial‐capacity constructs, suggesting a long‐term sustainability trade‐off. These findings extend recent cross‐country meta‐analytic evidence by showing that, once structural governance adoption is near‐universal, incremental gains in carbon transparency come from incentive alignment and compositional diversity rather than additional structural apparatus. For policymakers, investors and boards, the implication is that diversity targets and ESG‐linked pay are more reliable levers of carbon transparency than procedural governance metrics.

title: Business Model Innovation Under Institutionalized ESG Regulation: An Ontological Account of Paradox Closure
abstract: ABSTRACT Institutionalized environmental, social, and governance (ESG) regulation is reshaping how firms justify value, responsibility, and viability across industrial value chains. This paper examines how Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive requirements enter business model innovation in SMEs embedded in five industrial value chains. Drawing on a 3‐year longitudinal qualitative study of 25 SMEs, the findings show that ESG was initially treated as an external layer associated with documentation, compliance, and customer demands. When translated into business model reasoning, ESG surfaced persistent tensions among economic, environmental, social, and governance logics. These tensions were frequently closed through sequencing, commensuration, deferral, and compliance‐oriented reasoning. Artifact‐mediated workshops were associated with moments of provisional copresence, while the wider analysis identified governance constraints arising from the separation of ESG responsibility and decision authority. Building on these patterns, the paper advances the abductively grounded proposition that assumptions embedded in dominant BMI frameworks may reinforce ontological closure under institutionalized ESG conditions. It introduces the E 2 SG Flower as an analytically grounded paradox‐navigation proposition whose effects and transferability beyond the studied industrial value chains require further empirical validation.

title: AI‐Enabled Capabilities for Open Circular Innovation and Industrial Symbiosis: Towards Agentic AI Orchestration
abstract: ABSTRACT Industrial symbiosis supports circular economies through resource exchanges. Yet, this collaborative approach faces information asymmetries, fragmented networks and coordination challenges. This study synthesises the extant literature and examines five industrial symbiosis initiatives with varying levels of digital maturity. Cross‐case analyses identify five interconnected capabilities, including knowledge discovery, ecosystem orchestration, resource matching, resource‐exchange facilitation and value‐chain integration. The findings indicate that, for the time being, existing platforms remain AI assisted rather than fully autonomous. Building on these empirical insights, the study proposes an agentic industrial symbiosis (AIS) framework that conceptualises how these capabilities could support future agentic AI orchestration. The framework extends existing research on industrial symbiosis by clearly explaining the potential transition from AI‐enabled capabilities towards autonomous ecosystem coordination. It offers novel theoretical and practical implications for circular innovation. Moreover, it provides a foundation for future empirical research.

title: Human resources governance and human capital management disclosure following the SEC mandate
abstract: When do board-level governance mechanisms enhance human capital management (HCM) disclosure? Drawing on the concept of governance complementarity, we argue that individual human resources (HR) governance mechanisms, i.e., committee with HR oversight mandate and board-level HR expertise, lack sufficient organizational capacity to improve HCM disclosure on their own; rather, they become effective when configured together. Using a measure of HCM disclosure transparency that integrates readability, numerical intensity, and specificity for S&P 500 firms following the SEC's, 2020 mandate, we find that neither mechanism individually is associated with greater transparency, but their joint presence relates positively with HCM transparency. Partitioning the sample indicates that this relation reflects internal capabilities rather than external incentives to disclose transparently. A falsification test confirms this relationship is specific to HCM disclosure and does not extend to non-HCM portions of Item 1 in 10-K filings. More transparent HCM disclosure is related to better labor market outcomes. This study contributes to the governance literature by highlighting the importance of calibrating governance mechanism bundles for effective governance. From a regulatory perspective, this study informs policy discussions about the board's role in overseeing HCM.
journal_name: Journal of Accounting and Public Policy

title: Constructing sustainability expertise: capital conversion and the making of a sustainability CFO
abstract: Purpose This paper examines how a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in a Sri Lankan state-owned bank constructed sustainability accounting as a new domain of professional expertise. Extending Baxter and Chua's (2008) conception of accounting expertise as an organisational accomplishment, the paper asks how entirely new forms of accounting expertise are constructed before organisational legitimacy, evaluative criteria and professional jurisdiction have been established, drawing on Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital to explain this process. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a longitudinal qualitative case study of a CFO in a Sri Lankan state-owned housing bank, whose sustainability agenda developed during the country's post-tsunami reconstruction. Data were collected across two phases (2013–2014) using 44 semi-structured interviews with 25 participants, supplemented by field notes and documentary analysis of sustainability reports, policy documents and media coverage. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, proceeding from inductive coding through temporal coding to theoretical interpretation via Baxter and Chua (2008) and Bourdieu, tracing the sequential conversion of cultural, symbolic, social and positional capital. Findings Sustainability accounting expertise was constructed through a cumulative process of capital conversion. An entrepreneurial habitus generated the disposition to recognise emerging opportunities, enabling the accumulation of cultural capital through learning, authorship and reporting innovation. This cultural capital was converted into symbolic capital through managerial endorsement and award recognition, which expanded social capital through strategic alliances, and was ultimately converted into positional authority, redefining the finance function's organisational jurisdiction. However, this expertise construction did not automatically translate into institutionalisation: sustainability expertise remained concentrated in a single individual rather than becoming embedded in organisational systems and routines. Research limitations/implications The single-case design prioritises theoretical development over statistical generalisation; future research should examine whether similar processes of expertise construction occur across different organisational, professional and national settings. The case also centres on an unusually entrepreneurial CFO, and alternative trajectories may emerge where sustainability initiatives are collectively led or externally mandated. The longitudinal design captured the construction of expertise but not its longer-term reproduction following leadership succession, pointing to a need for future research on how such expertise diffuses, evolves or declines once its original architect departs the organisation. Practical implications Organisations should not equate the success of a prominent sustainability champion with the institutionalisation of sustainability capability. Individual actors can mobilise resources, secure legitimacy and accelerate organisational innovation, but sustained transformation depends on converting individually held expertise into collective organisational capability. Building durable sustainability capacity therefore requires deliberate investment in knowledge sharing, succession planning and cross-functional learning, alongside organisational systems that embed expertise beyond the individual who originally constructed it, reducing organisations' dependence on any single actor for the continuity of their sustainability agenda. Originality/value The paper offers a distinctive contribution by reconceptualising accounting expertise as something that must first be constructed, rather than simply organisationally accomplished, in emerging domains such as sustainability accounting. By integrating Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital with Baxter and Chua's (2008) framework, it identifies cumulative capital conversion as the specific social mechanism underlying this process – a mechanism not previously articulated in the sustainability accounting literature. It further offers the original insight that expertise construction and organisational institutionalisation are analytically distinct, showing that individually constructed expertise can achieve legitimacy while remaining fragile and undiffused across the organisation.

title: Cisnormative accounting organizations: recording the experiences of transgender people in Brazil
abstract: Purpose This study aimed to record, understand and problematize, in the light of transfeminism, the experiences of transgender people who have transited and/or are transiting through accounting organizations in Brazil. Design/methodology/approach This article provides detailed information on the oppression present in accounting offices in Brazil and how oppressive actions impact the experiences of trans workers in the workplace. Six semi-structured interviews were conducted with: a) two transgender women, b) two transgender men and c) two non-binary people, with various identity markers in relation to gender, race, sexuality, age, disability and socio-economic class. The stories were categorized and analyzed using Dialogic Thematic Analysis. After the analysis, we present a map of resistance strategies in the Brazilian accounting environment. Findings The participants reported negative experiences in organizational accounting environments in Brazil, marked by prejudice, discrimination, disrespect for gender identity, erroneous pronoun treatment and physical and psychological violence committed by cisgender managers and co-workers, mainly cisgender men. We identified the use of resistance strategies in these environments in the participants' narratives, including the development of technical skills, professional experience, remote training and the use of cisgender passability as a coping mechanism. Originality/value This study makes significant contributions to understanding the experiences of transgender workers in accounting organizations in Brazil, the most oppressive country for this population in the world. Our findings fill gaps in the literature on the experiences of non-cisgender gender identities in accounting and can help improve corporate actions for the inclusion, permanence and belonging of diverse people in accounting organizations. This study also contributes to the gap in the literature, encouraging the development of new studies so that the voices of trans workers can be heard, stories can be told and recorded and oppression denounced.

Small Modular Electrochemical Containers for Decarbonization of AI Data Centers
abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) is increasing data-center electricity demand and reinforcing the near-term role of fossil-fuel power generation. Decarbonizing this infrastructure requires carbon capture systems that are efficient, compact, modular, and compatible with space-constrained data centers. Here, we evaluate Small Modular Electrochemical Containers (SMECs) as a deployment-oriented application of a two-stage, membraneless electrochemically mediated amine regeneration (EMAR) process. The design integrates CO2 absorption and electrochemical desorption within one gas-diffusion-electrode cell, eliminating absorber columns and ion-exchange membranes. Single-cell experiments were conducted under simulated natural-gas and coal-derived flue gas. Polarization mapping identified optimized operating conditions, which were then used in a 300-cycle, 50-h accelerated stability test with periodic polarity switching. The cell maintained repeatable voltage and CO2 absorption/desorption profiles, with absorption and desorption efficiencies of ∼90% under optimized conditions. The energetics ranged from 50–85 kJe/molCO2, and GC/IC analyses showed no detectable gaseous or liquid side products. The paper further includes theoretical modeling of SOx and NOx effects on the absorbent. In a case study for a 360 MW data-center power plant, the TEA showed that fewer than 20 SMEC units could achieve near-complete decarbonization, increasing the levelized electricity cost from about \$58/MWh to \$74/MWh.

How to manage meadows effectively? Flagship, keystone & diagnostic species perspective
abstract: We investigated the long-term effects of meadow management regimes (abandonment vs. mowing, and its frequency), plant invasion, and habitat availability on three different meadow ecosystem components. The system consists of (1) native plant Sanguisorba officinalis , (2) ant assemblages, and (3) butterfly species of the genus Phengaris , known as flagships for biodiversity conservation. The investigated wet meadow communities responded quite similarly to management regimes. In general, declining biodiversity was related to either complete abandonment or more intensive management (with mowing more than once per year). The focal native plant cover was affected by management and invasive plants. Mowing frequency did not affect ant diversity or population fluctuations of Phengaris butterflies over a five-year period. Low frequency mowing (one cut per year) is crucial to long-term persistence of the studied species, and S. officinalis cover is a good indicator for assessing habitat condition of studied meadows. The establishment of non-intensive management and occasionally more intensive mowing for active control of invasive plants is needed to preserve the investigated wet meadows of high conservation value and complex system of organisms inhabiting them.

Assessing the association between street view–derived perceived liveliness and street thefts
abstract: Crime geographers are attentive to how the spatial characteristics of the environment affect criminal behaviors. Recently, scholars have found that aside from physical and social attributes, the perception of the environment, such as safety perception, is also associated with crime occurrence. However, perceived liveliness, a visual perceptual proxy for potential routine activity settings that are closely linked to routine activity theory and crime pattern theory, is rarely explored in prior research. This study examines the association between perceived liveliness and street thefts in the City of Cincinnati, the United States. The liveliness perception scores are derived from street view imagery using a support vector machine model trained on the MIT Place Pulse V2 crowdsourcing image survey. Negative binomial regression models are used to test the relationships between perceived liveliness and street theft, with social and physical environmental attributes controlled. Results show that perceived liveliness significantly improves model performance and is positively associated with street theft. This study provides the first evidence that perceived liveliness helps explain crimes. The positive relationship between perceived liveliness of the built environment and crime adds a new dimension to the routine activity theory and the crime pattern theory. It also offers a scalable and cost-effective measure that can assist urban planners and law enforcement in identifying potential theft hotspots using readily available street view imagery.

Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
A Theory of Redistribution and Public Good Provision under Nondemocracy
The Evolution of the Market for Corporate Control
abstract: ABSTRACT We consider an informed large shareholder who can choose between making a takeover bid herself and initiating a sale to another acquirer. Such takeover activism complements direct takeovers because the very choice mitigates the asymmetric information problem, thereby improving efficiency. As more investors enter the market for corporate control, takeover activism increasingly replaces direct takeovers as the prevailing mode of disciplinary control change, matching the evolution in practice. Our model shows how this evolution, characterized by a symbiotic relationship between investor activism and private equity, arises to overcome asymmetric information and collective action problems through intermediated transactions.

title: Does ridesharing affect external-cause mortality? Evidence from U.S. Vital Statistics Data

Maximum likelihood estimation of fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with discretely sampled data
Information Aggregation With Delegation of Votes
abstract: ABSTRACT Liquid democracy (LD) combines elements of direct and representative democracy: voters can either vote directly or delegate their votes to others. We study its information aggregation properties in a setting with heterogeneously and privately informed independent and partisan voters. We establish that LD always has equilibria that improve welfare and information aggregation relative to direct democracy, identify economically interpretable conditions under which these gains are strict, and characterise optimal delegation for salient classes of committees. However, while delegation improves the best‐equilibrium, it can also introduce robust inefficient equilibria that perform worse than direct democracy.

title: Launching for the “Greater Good”: Spillover Effect of ESG Funds
abstract: We examine the incentives for mutual fund families to launch ESG funds. Our analyses reveal that introducing a new ESG fund leads to a significant increase in capital inflows to sibling non-ESG funds in the family. This flow spillover accounts for a significant portion of the monetary awards for families to offer ESG funds. We also find that spillover is stronger among retail funds and cannot be attributed to changes in the ESG profiles or abnormal returns of the sibling funds. Further evidence suggests that affect-based judgments, particularly the halo effect, are the key drivers of this spillover effect.
