title: Predicting food waste from dynamic inconsistency
abstract: Household food waste imposes substantial economic and environmental costs, yet its behavioral determinants remain imperfectly understood. Because food consumption unfolds over multiple stages, it creates scope for dynamically inconsistent choices that may turn good intentions into waste. We investigate this relationship using a nationally representative survey from Germany that combines targeted measures of food purchasing, consumption, and waste with individual present-bias parameters elicited from monetary intertemporal trade-off questions. More present-biased individuals waste significantly more food: a 10% increase in dynamic inconsistency is associated with roughly 2% more waste. This relationship is robust across specifications, replicated using a self-reported procrastination proxy, and stable several weeks later in a second survey wave. We also identify and empirically validate the mechanism linking present bias to food waste: dynamically inconsistent individuals are more likely to deviate from their own consumption intentions, and these deviations are strongly predictive of food waste. Our findings identify present bias as a systematic and previously overlooked driver of avoidable household food waste, suggesting that food policies need to address behavior along the full consumption chain.

title: The power of tolerance: First environmental violation exemption and air quality
Peripheral monopoly capital: business groups, class power, and the reproduction of dependency in Chile
abstract: Although the past decade has seen renewed interest in theories of monopoly capital, debates have largely focused on the leading knowledge-intensive corporations of the Global North, paying far less attention to monopoly power in dependent economies. Addressing this gap, this paper develops the concept of Peripheral Monopoly Capital (PMC) to theorize concentration, centralization and class power in contemporary peripheral capitalism. We elaborate PMC through an analysis of diversified, pyramidal, and interlocking business groups in the reproduction of dependency in Chile, arguably a paradigmatic case of centralization under dependency. Focussing on four major business groups, each representing a distinct configuration of monopoly power, we show how these groups articulate circuits of rent-based accumulation in antagonistic cooperation with global capital. Our main contribution is to reconnect monopoly capital theory with dependency analysis and to locate the organizational foundations of dependency in the business group itself. By conceiving business groups as class projects that link global and domestic circuits of rent-based accumulation, PMC offers a new lens on monopoly power in the Global South.

title: Globalization unravelling? ASML and the geopolitics of Europe-China tech decoupling
abstract: This article investigates the geopolitical dynamics driving Europe’s emerging technological decoupling from China. Focusing on the semiconductor industry and the Dutch semiconductor firm ASML, it examines how technonationalism emanating from the US has shaped a small European member state’s policy response amid intensifying US–China rivalry. The article analyses how national security arguments and US strategic influence aimed at undermining China’s advances in high-tech has reshaped the Dutch semiconductor export control regime in a way that seemingly contradicts both ASML’s corporate interests and Dutch long-term economic interests. Moreover, cutting the dependency ties of China to one of the few chokepoint industries and tech firms in the EU arguably undermines its commitment to ‘technological sovereignty’. We explain these puzzling outcomes through the inherent contradictions within technonationalism and the tensions between state and corporate actors strategizing around different national security and profit-oriented interests. As such, we argue that the case of ASML offers a useful prism through which to study the ongoing ‘geoeconomic’ shift in the global political economy in which the alignment of the geopolitical and capital logics characteristic of neoliberal globalisation is coming apart, with state and corporate actors attempting to realign these logics into different configurations.

title: Do Inflation Expectations Improve Model‐Based Inflation Forecasts?
abstract: Abstract Those of professional forecasters do. For a wide range of time‐series models for the euro area and its member states, we find a higher average forecast accuracy of models that incorporate information on inflation expectations from the ECB's Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) and Consensus Economics compared to their counterparts that do not. The professional forecasters expectations seem to help to correct the upward forecast bias in the low inflation period and to make the model forecasts more robust. By contrast, incorporating expectations derived from financial market prices or those of firms and households does not lead to systematic improvements in forecast performance.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: Consequences of Fiscal Risk to Optimal Monetary Policy
abstract: Abstract We study the optimal monetary policy of a New Keynesian economy on the brink of fiscal dominance. The model features a Markov switching structure to incorporate regime uncertainty. Switching probabilities can be either exogenous or endogenous. We find that a fiscal risk entails a welfare loss and breaks the “divine coincidence” because perfect price stabilization becomes counterproductive when monetary policy affects debt dynamics and agents anticipate regime changes. In this environment, the optimal inflation coefficient in the Taylor rule is decreasing on the fiscal risk, and the optimal regime choice ultimately depends on government credibility.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: Who Do You Vote For? Same-Race Voting Preferences in Director Elections
abstract: Abstract This paper highlights racial and ethnic preferences in corporate director elections. Using a comprehensive dataset of mutual fund voting records, we discover that mutual fund managers are more likely to vote for director nominees who share their racial or ethnic identity. Funds managed by White-dominated teams exhibit the strongest same-race preferences, particularly those in fund families with scarce minority representation. Same-race voting preferences have detrimental implications for the career outcomes of minority director candidates, and are associated with worse fund performance primarily when fund managers operate under weaker accountability. We investigate various potential mechanisms—including statistical discrimination, value maximization, conflicts of interest, social networks, and taste-based biases—and find that the evidence aligns most closely with a taste-based explanation for same-race preferential voting. JEL Classification: G23, G34, G41, J71

title: When great minds do not think alike: Pasinetti and Samuelson on Ricardo
abstract: Taking advantage of the recent opening of the Samuelson Archive and the Pasinetti Archive, we scrutinise a hitherto unpublished correspondence between Pasinetti and Samuelson concerning their almost contemporaneous mathematical treatments of Ricardo’s economics: Samuelson (Citation1959) and Pasinetti (Citation1960). We focus on three inter-related issues: the labour theory of value, Ricardo’s attempt to “get rid of rent,” and the role of final demand. We assess the respective arguments by Samuelson and Pasinetti both in their published and unpublished contributions, and we highlight their radically different perspectives on value and distribution theory.
journal_name: The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought

title: Optimal reserve prices under seller uncertainty
abstract: Abstract We justify the prevalence of small reserve prices in real-life auctions despite empirical findings that suggest optimal reserve prices in those contexts should be higher. We reconcile such a discrepancy without modifying the standard assumptions about bidders’ preferences, information, or the market environment. Instead, we introduce a form of uncertainty on the seller’s side regarding the distribution of valuations. This uncertainty may arise when the bid sample lacks variables necessary to determine the valuation distribution or when its point estimate differs from the true distribution. We show that the optimal reserve price under uncertainty decreases as the number of bidders grows, and the revenue gain from the optimal reserve price relative to any smaller reserve price—including zero—disappears at an exponential rate. We then show that the reserve price decreases further as the amount of uncertainty, as represented by the integrated variance of the valuation distributions, increases. Finally, we extend the analysis to a risk-averse seller and show that risk aversion reinforces the effect of uncertainty, further lowering the optimal reserve price as the seller trades off expected revenue against revenue volatility.

title: Competitive Dormancy in Interfirm Rivalry: Consequences for Rival Actions
abstract: In this study, we examine the implications of competitive dormancy, defined as a situation in which a focal firm’s observed time span of inaction following its prior action has exceeded the firm’s typical duration between successive actions. We argue that competitive dormancy may be perceived as inconsistent with a rival’s expectations and may be associated with an interpretive process concerning the rival’s subsequent actions. Integrating expectancy violation theory (EVT) and competitive dynamics research, we propose that the relationship between a focal firm’s competitive dormancy and the likelihood of rivals’ subsequent actions varies with their relative market standing and strategic resource commitment. Using a sample of 78,055 daily observations from 28 firms across 14 industries from 2000 to 2017, we find support for our hypotheses.

title: A Moral Foundations Perspective on CEO Political Ideology
abstract: As a reflection of their fundamental value systems, CEOs’ political ideology has come to be regarded as a major predictor of their strategic decision-making. Among the most persistent characterizations in this literature, liberal-leaning CEOs are considered to exhibit a distinct preference for evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices due to their ideological endorsement of equality—an association derived from the conceptualization of political ideologies along the motivated cognition perspective and routinely used to differentiate them from their more conservative peers. Yet, moral psychologists increasingly call for a broader understanding of the moral values differentiating liberals and conservatives. We therefore introduce moral foundations theory to the study of CEO political ideology, according to which liberal- and conservative-leaning CEOs differ in their focus on individual- versus group-centric concerns but, contrary to the existing consensus, should both endorse evenhanded outcomes and pro-social corporate practices. We find evidence for corresponding U-shaped rather than linear effects of CEOs’ political ideology in a sample of over 1,600 S&P 1500 CEOs. As such, we offer a novel theoretical perspective on CEOs’ political ideology and its organizational ramifications.

title: Leveraging social legitimacy to navigate geopolitical fragmentation and populist polarization
abstract: Abstract Although earning political legitimacy helps MNEs manage political risk, association with governments and political elites can become liabilities when regimes, alliances, and public sentiment shift. Reflecting on our study of MNE survival during abrupt regime change, we revisit social legitimacy as a complement to, and sometimes a substitute for, political legitimacy. We distinguish two foundations of social legitimacy: relational legitimacy, built through broad ties across societal constituencies, and material legitimacy, earned by providing products, services, and investments perceived as valuable by non-elite society. Although long recognized as a part of earning and maintaining a license to operate in any country, social legitimacy has become an increasingly important hedge against the ebbs and flows of political power driven by geopolitical fragmentation, populism, and polarization. Indeed, as geopolitics and populism make political affiliations more noticeable and more volatile, we suggest that efforts to earn social legitimacy play an increasingly important role in MNE nonmarket strategy. We identify theoretical and empirical questions concerning the sources, usefulness, and limits of earning social legitimacy; urge researchers and leaders to learn from and connect to non-elite sectors of society; and suggest ways that investment in social legitimacy can help MNEs navigate political turbulence worldwide.

title: Strategy as a theory of change
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state. Focusing on theorizing as a thought process of model creation, we propose a framework to specify hypothetical causal links and analyze their structure as a directed graph connecting inputs, activities, and indicators of problem resolution. We then propose a set of metrics operationalizing key theory attributes: complexity, equifinality, interdependence, and circularity. We discuss the strategic relevance of these attributes in terms of a theory's ability to promote comprehensive problem resolution as well as implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed solution. Our work represents a step toward operationalizing model creation in the theory‐based view and informs the design of strategic theories of change. Managerial Summary Strategists often theorize how to move their organizations toward an improved performance state. Yet most strategic analysis tools describe the organization's external environment or the internal components of its business model, without precisely specifying forward‐looking interventions that might cause the desired changes. In this paper, we represent strategic theories as a chain of causal interventions—inputs and activities that address relevant problems and lead to desirable outcomes. We propose a structured framework that helps managers develop theories and measure key attributes that influence comprehensive problem resolution and the ability to implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed interventions. In this sense, our work helps managers mentally create their strategic theories and assess their usefulness as a roadmap to superior performance.

title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research.

title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
abstract: Tip request messages are marketing communications that can help digital platforms balance customer spending with worker effort and compensation. We report the first field experiments testing how three appeals based on tipping motivations—injunctive norms (“It’s customary to leave a tip for the seller’s service”), personalized reciprocity, and impersonal reciprocity—affect tipping and future demand in a global freelance marketplace. Overall, the norms message increased tipping the most, and did so without reducing returning demand, showing that tip request messages can motivate customer tipping to better incentivize and compensate gig workers.

title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure human preferences and opinions, but their outputs can diverge from human responses. We introduce human mimicry calibration (HuMCal), a post hoc, model-agnostic method that uses aggregate human benchmark data to learn how to combine LLM outputs from different prompts, personas, and model checkpoints. In applications to consumer transaction data and public opinion surveys, HuMCal improves agreement with human benchmarks over standard aggregation rules, and the calibrated weights often remain useful across time, geography, industry, and question clusters.

title: Experimental Evidence on Structural State Dependence in Demand
abstract: The paper provides nonparametric estimates of structural state dependence from a natural field experiment for 223 brands.

title: Mandatory Disclosure and Peer Firms' Learning From Stock Prices
abstract: ABSTRACT Theory posits that mandatory disclosure influences peer firms' learning from stock prices in two non‐mutually exclusive ways: intra‐industry information transfers and the reallocation of information acquisition efforts. Using mandatory segment disclosure as our setting, we document a decrease in investment‐ q sensitivity for peers of disclosing firms. This effect is stronger among peers with greater economic links to disclosing firms and peers with the greatest incentives to glean information from prices. Our findings provide novel evidence that mandatory disclosure can have significant negative externalities on peer firms' investment efficiency via a managerial learning from the stock price channel. These insights inform regulators assessing the economic consequences of mandatory disclosure, while also assisting managers who rely on information from stock prices to guide investment decisions.

title: Whose Job Is It, Anyway? The Effect of the Review Process on Employee Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT Companies have widely adopted a system of work‐product reviews whereby the work of one individual is subsequently reviewed by another to ensure its quality. We examine how managers can effectively implement a review of employee work to improve performance. Organizations review employees' work to identify mistakes and improve work quality. However, reviews may also reduce employees' effort and initiative if they expect reviewers to identify and correct their errors for them. We use an experiment to examine how employee performance depends on who conducts the review and how feedback is provided. Specifically, participants' work was reviewed by either a superior or a peer, and the reviewer provided either general, high‐level guidance (autonomy‐oriented) or specific corrective information about errors (dependency‐oriented). Employees performed best when superiors provided high‐level guidance or when peers provided specific corrective feedback, with these benefits emerging over time. Guidance from a superior increased employees' sense of responsibility, whereas corrective help from a peer strengthened feelings of teamwork and cohesion. Review approaches that did not fit these combinations offered no clear performance benefit relative to having no review. The findings show that review effectiveness depends on matching the feedback approach to the reviewer's organizational rank. These results have important implications for managers, accountants responsible for internal controls, and audit professionals involved in designing and implementing the review process.

title: The trap of appearing perfect: When servant leaders accidentally intensify follower over-commitment and workaholism
abstract: Can striving to look perfect backfire when your leader puts you first? We examine this question through the concept of perfectionistic self-presentation (PSP), an impression management (IM) motivation to appear flawless to others. Drawing on IM theory, we argue that employees high in PSP may feel compelled to appear flawless to their leaders, increasing their tendency to overcommit to them as salient evaluative audiences and, in turn, have higher workaholism. We also propose that servant leadership, a leadership style that emphasizes serving and cultivating followers, amplifies the relationship between followers’ PSP and overcommitment to leaders. Across three time-lagged field studies, two conducted in China and one in the United Kingdom, we find that individuals high in PSP are more likely to report workaholism through overcommitment to the leader, particularly when reporting to servant leaders. Our findings show how a normally positive form of leadership can have unintended costs when interpreted through followers’ self-presentational motives, extending understanding of PSP, IM, and the boundary conditions of positive leadership.

title: Teaching for Wonder: Pedagogical Openings for Epistemic Change in the Climate Crisis
abstract: Abstract The accelerating climate crisis demands profound changes in how management learning and education prepares students to engage with uncertainty and ecological interdependence. While recent scholarship calls for epistemic transformation in business schools, there is limited understanding of how pedagogy might cultivate the orientations required for such change. This paper advances wonder as a critical yet under‐theorized pedagogical orientation for climate‐responsive management education. We conceptualize wonder as an epistemic–affective orientation of attentional widening and humility in response to the more‐than‐known, capable of disrupting instrumental habits of knowing and sustaining openness to uncertainty. Drawing on an interpretive qualitative study of an arts‐based pedagogical collaboration with the Birmingham Royal Ballet, we develop a processual framework comprising five interrelated moments: encounter, suspension, engagement, refiguration and return. Together, these moments show how wonder reshapes students’ relationships to knowledge, enabling them to engage with complexity beyond instrumental frames. In doing so, the paper provides an empirically grounded theorization of wonder as a pedagogical mechanism for epistemic transformation and advances debates on what climate‐responsive management education could look like.

title: EXPRESS: THE SOUND OF WORDS: VERBAL AND VOCAL CUES IN CUSTOMER SATISFACTION
abstract: Technology-mediated service interactions, such as phone calls, generate rich behavioral signals that firms currently struggle to monitor in real time. Post-interaction surveys provide delayed and unrepresentative feedback, leaving satisfaction invisible as calls unfold. Satisfaction judgments depend on how evaluative meaning is communicated across two channels, verbal content and vocal delivery, whose relative contribution varies by outcome type. The authors analyze 1,144 real-world service calls, each coded as dissatisfied, neutral, or satisfied, using text-only, audio-only, and multimodal deep learning models. Dissatisfied calls are identified from transcripts alone as accurately as by multimodal models, since customers articulate problems and remedy expectations explicitly. Neutral and satisfied calls depend more strongly on vocal interpretation, and cross-attention models outperform text-only alternatives precisely where verbal content is absent or insufficiently distinctive to separate outcomes. The findings identify a boundary condition on interactivity, whereby vocal cues add predictive value when evaluative meaning is absent or insufficiently distinctive between outcomes, not when it is explicit and clearly distinguishes outcomes, as is the case for dissatisfied calls.

title: Forecasting and Explaining Environmental Fiscal Capacity: How Informality and FinTech Shape Environmental and Biodiversity Finance
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the impact of the shadow economy (SE) on environmental fiscal capacity (environmental tax revenue, public environmental expenditure, and biodiversity expenditure) and the moderating role of financial technology (FinTech) across OECD countries over 2004–2022. Using second‐generation econometric techniques, with robustness assessed through the CCEMG estimator, Driscoll–Kraay fixed effects, and one‐step GMM, and complemented by machine‐learning forecasting (tensor double machine learning and a graph‐inspired machine learning model) compared using the Diebold–Mariano test. The analysis yields three main findings. First, the SE significantly reduces environmental tax revenue and public environmental and biodiversity expenditures, consistent with the hypothesis that informality constrains the fiscal capacity required for environmental protection. Second, FinTech adoption directly enhances environmental revenue and mitigates the adverse effect of the SE on environmental revenue through a transaction‐formalization channel that expands the observable tax base, although its direct association with biodiversity expenditure is negative, reflecting a countervailing frontier‐expansion effect. Third, the forecasting evidence reinforces this structural account: Environmental tax revenue is strongly forecastable and public environmental expenditure moderately so, whereas biodiversity expenditure resists accurate prediction across both models. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of digital financial innovation as a complementary instrument for reducing informality, strengthening environmental governance, and advancing biodiversity conservation in OECD economies.

title: Board Gender Diversity and Environmental Activity in Family Firms: The Role of Female Directors
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how female board representation relates to environmental activities in family firms, distinguishing family from nonfamily female directors and considering the curvilinear shape of the relationship and the role of industry. Drawing on upper echelons theory and socioemotional wealth, we argue that women's influence depends on their ties to the controlling family, that the marginal effect diminishes as representation grows, and that this varies by sector. Using panel count models on large US family firms in the Fortune 1000 during the 2018–2022 period, we find that female representation is positively associated with the number of environmental activities in family firms. Family and nonfamily female directors show similar linear associations, but only nonfamily directors display a concave pattern. The turning point occurs at a lower level of representation in manufacturing than in nonmanufacturing firms, again only for nonfamily directors. Board gender diversity should not be viewed as a uniform attribute, as its association with corporate environmental engagement varies depending on the heterogeneity of board members and the industry in which the firm operates.

title: Corporate Biodiversity Reporting and Firm Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Strategic Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT This study provides a systematic literature review of emerging research on biodiversity, synthesising evidence on ownership structures, corporate innovation, biodiversity regulation, biodiversity risk, reporting practices, firm performance, national culture and governance quality. As nature‐related risks become increasingly financially material, biodiversity has gained prominence within accounting and corporate governance research. However, existing studies remain fragmented, largely atheoretical and methodologically narrow. Using a three‐stage systematic review of peer‐reviewed articles published between 1970 and 2025 across Scopus, Web of Science and EBSCO, we identify and analyse 40 high‐quality studies. The review integrates theoretical perspectives, research designs and empirical findings to examine the antecedents and consequences of corporate biodiversity reporting. Evidence suggests that biodiversity risk has economically significant effects on firm value and investor behaviour, while reporting is shaped by governance mechanisms, ownership structures and institutional pressures, often reflecting legitimacy concerns. Innovation emerges as a strategic response to biodiversity exposure. We conclude by outlining methodological gaps and proposing a multi‐theoretical, cross‐country research agenda.

title: Drawing more complete and valid interpretations of mediation in human resource management: Beyond the sole focus on indirect effects and their statistical significance
Challenging assumptions in supply chain management accounting and reporting: a metamodern sustainability transformation
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to use a metamodern approach and a problematization lens to challenge the assumption that transparency driven accounting of historical social and environmental harms is sufficient to achieve the scale of sustainability transformation of supply chains required by scientific evidence. It argues that sustainability measurement, accounting and reporting must also encompass future orientated, positive and absolute sustainability contributions enabled by transformative product, business model and supply chain redesign. Design/methodology/approach A metamodern approach is introduced and used in the paper. Drawing on metamodernism, the paper develops a framework for oscillating between incremental, transparency-based measurement and more fundamental assessments of business development. Through problematization of existing literature, it identifies limiting assumptions and advances accounting and reporting for sustainable supply chain transformations. Findings The analysis reveals four dominant assumptions in sustainability accounting and reporting that constrain sufficiently far-reaching sustainability transformations of supply chains: backward looking transparency, supplier assessment logics, harm reduction framing and incremental improvements. The proposed metamodern framework broadens the role of accounting by integrating multiple intelligence sources to support monitoring of existing supply chains and identification of redesign opportunities aligned with planetary boundaries and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Research limitations/implications The paper provides a metamodern foundation for future empirical development and testing of transformative sustainability measurement and accounting that embraces different intelligence sources. Practical implications Measurement and accounting informed by metamodern theory oscillates between different intelligence sources, comprising data, information and knowledge, to support both monitoring of existing supply chain relationships and identification of transformative redesign opportunities. Social implications The argument supports development of supply chain strategies and designs capable of addressing the easing of social and environmental harms as well as development of transformative sustainability opportunities. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first paper to apply a metamodern lens to sustainability accounting and reporting for supply chain management. It shows how oscillation between modernist and postmodern logics opens new pathways for theorizing transformative measurement and positions accounting information as a catalyst for strategic redesign rather than incremental optimization.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: Pleasure or annoyance? The opposing effects of food-service rituals
abstract: Purpose Food-service rituals are increasingly prevalent in hospitality practice, yet their effects in real-world settings remain underexplored. Drawing on Interaction Ritual Chain theory, this research aims to investigate when and why food-service rituals enhance versus undermine encounter satisfaction. Design/methodology/approach Three video-based experiments were conducted in a restaurant setting. Findings Study 1 shows a positive main effect of food-service rituals on encounter satisfaction. Study 2 demonstrates that food-service rituals enhance satisfaction by evoking pleasure among customers with hedonic consumption goals but elicit annoyance among customers with utilitarian goals. Study 3 further reveals that food-service rituals exert a positive effect under communal customer-brand relationship norms, but backfire under exchange relationship norms. Practical implications This study offers valuable guidance for restaurant operators. Businesses should consider customers’ consumption goals and customer-brand relationship norms when implementing food-service rituals. Originality/value This study enriches the hospitality management literature by developing a more balanced understanding of food-service rituals and highlighting the conditions and emotional mechanisms that shape customer reactions.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Reshoring: Governance, knowledge, and capabilities
abstract: An increasingly uncertain global landscape is inducing firms to reconsider some of their previous location decisions. Among the relocation options, reshoring has emerged as a relevant strategy to cope with changing environmental conditions and strategic needs. A key, yet underexplored, factor in reshoring is how governance decisions, specifically whether activities are managed in-house or outsourced in the host and home country, shape the knowledge transfer processes triggered by relocation. To address this, we adopt a knowledge-based approach and develop a typology of four reshoring types based on governance mode, each characterized by a distinct knowledge transfer process: backward, brokered, inward, and outward knowledge transfer. Further, we build on this to elucidate the knowledge strategies and capabilities underlying each type of reshoring. The study advances reshoring research by showing how different governance configurations generate distinct knowledge transfer processes and their inherent dynamics. It also contributes to knowledge transfer literature by contextualizing transfer processes within reshoring, a context characterized by high organizational change, and by showing how governance structures influence the nature and strategic outcomes of knowledge strategies, supported by specific capabilities.

title: Managing critical raw materials supply chains: aligning capabilities and strategic levers for effective strategy formation under uncertainty
abstract: Purpose This study examines how firms should design supply chain strategies to secure Critical Raw Materials (CRM), which are scarce, geographically concentrated, and exposed to geopolitical and institutional interference. These features generate structural uncertainty that amplifies normative and mimetic pressures on strategic decision-making, exposing firms to strategic isomorphic bias and leading organizations to replicate legitimized sourcing templates rather than formulate strategies calibrated to their specific dependence structure. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Resource Dependence Theory, the study links key strategic levers (Supplier Substitutability, Discretion over the Resource, and Importance of the Resource) to underlying supply chain capabilities (resilience, agility, flexibility, sustainability, efficiency). A rank-ordered logit choice experiment with supply chain managers elicits preferred capability configurations in CRM supply scenarios, allowing the inference of the associated strategic levers while reducing strategic isomorphic bias in self-reported strategies. Findings Results show that Supplier Substitutability emerges as the dominant strategic lever for CRM-intensive supply chains. Resilience and sustainability are identified as the core capabilities underpinning this lever, supporting rapid reconfiguration of the supply base and the maintenance of legitimacy and stakeholder support under uncertainty. Originality/value The study theorizes an inside-out, bottom-up capability-driven strategy formation process, in which supply chain capabilities serve to infer effective strategic postures. It also demonstrates the value of experimental choice designs to reduce strategic and institutional bias in supply chain management research, particularly in politically sensitive domains such as the energy transition.
journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

title: When Autonomy Collides With Control: Leveraging Strategic Alignment by Boundary‐Spanning for Business Model Innovation in Corporate Ventures
abstract: ABSTRACT Corporate ventures (CV) must reconcile entrepreneurial discretion with parent‐firm accountability, yet how venture actors experience this contradiction and how it relates to business model innovation (BMI) performance remain unclear. Drawing on paradox theory, we examined whether perceived autonomy–control tension is associated with BMI performance through strategic alignment and whether boundary‐spanning leadership conditions its associations with strategic alignment and BMI performance. We tested a moderated mediation model using two‐wave survey data from 196 South Korean CV leaders and partial least squares structural equation modeling. Perceived autonomy–control tension was negatively associated with BMI performance and exhibited a negative indirect association through strategic alignment at mean boundary‐spanning leadership. Boundary‐spanning leadership attenuated the negative associations with strategic alignment and BMI performance, and the indirect association was no longer statistically distinguishable from zero at high leadership. Supplementary estimates showed negative associations of boundary‐spanning leadership with both outcomes under low tension and positive associations under high tension. The study shifts attention from formal governance architecture to actor‐experienced governance strain, positions strategic alignment as a relational pathway to BMI performance and identifies governance strain as a boundary condition on the relevance of boundary‐spanning leadership. It extends boundary‐spanning leadership to authority‐sensitive parent–venture interfaces and theorizes internal political translation as a possible process. The findings suggest diagnosing recurring governance strain, sustaining strategic compatibility, and using perceived strain to guide when boundary‐spanning capability is mobilized.

title: Foreign technology adoption, democracy and SME innovation
abstract: Abstract This study investigates how foreign technology adoption and the institutional context of democracy interact to shape innovation outcomes among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Drawing on World Bank Enterprise Survey data covering 45,542 SMEs across 63 developing countries (2006–2022), we find that both foreign technology adoption and democratic institutions independently stimulate SME innovation. Moreover, democracy moderates the returns to innovation from foreign technology. Specifically, democracy reduces the positive impact of foreign technology adoption on SME innovation. These relationships remain robust to alternative measures and endogeneity checks. By demonstrating that democratic governance not only fosters innovation directly but also amplifies the innovation-enhancing effects of foreign technology, this study advances theory on institutional environments and capability development in SMEs. The results highlight the importance of policies that jointly strengthen democratic institutions and facilitate cross-border technology diffusion to enhance SME innovation in developing economies.

title: Do sustainable business models scale differently than business model configurations with lower environmental ambitions? A comparative analysis of business model scaling performance among sharing-mobility providers
abstract: As it has developed into a defining paradigm of the 21st century, the sharing economy is widely regarded as providing opportunities for environmental and social benefits in addition to economic advantages. Yet, it remains unclear whether sharing business models that incorporate environmental ambitions and public alignment require supplementary changes to other business model elements to scale successfully. Drawing on configurational theory and the business model literature, we model market scaling as a function of five business model design choices: environmental ambitions, alignment with public stakeholders, value-proposition portfolio size, digital intensity, and revenue-stream diversification. Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of twenty-one sharing-mobility providers identifies six configurations (four associated with successful scaling, two with scaling failure) and yields three implications. First, business models with strong environmental ambitions and close public alignment can scale as successfully as their counterparts that lack these characteristics. Second, irrespective of a firm’s level of environmental ambitions and public alignment, value-proposition portfolio size and revenue-stream diversification consistently emerge as the keys to successful scaling. Third, successfully scaled business models exhibit congruence between environmental ambitions and public alignment. Overall, business models with strong environmental ambitions and close public alignment and business models without these characteristics share similar paths to scale: multiple value propositions or diversified revenue streams. These findings advance configurational business model theory, resolve ambiguities in the sharing economy literature, and offer a cautiously optimistic message for management practice: Designing a business model with genuine environmental ambitions neither requires sacrificing scalability nor defying the common commercial logic.

title: Beating the crowd: The interplay of firm experience and industry dynamics in radical innovation
abstract: The technology transition driven by artificial intelligence is causing new patterns of technological change. Some firms design their entire products or business models around AI, while others employ it moderately or not at all. We therefore explore the firm- and industry-level antecedents of AI entry. We hypothesize that new ventures are more likely to engage in artificial intelligence in synchrony with industry competitors. Yet, at the firm-level, broad pre-entry experience leads to differentiated opportunity recognition, which enables distinctive market entry. We find support in data on 1258 new ventures in 47 industries. In industries with low AI entry, ventures with broad pre-entry experience have a higher degree of AI entry. Conversely, in industries with high AI entry, ventures with broad pre-entry experience have a lower degree of AI entry. Hence, we contribute to theory on technology transitions with a firm-level view of industry life cycles, and to entrepreneurship theory with insights on the industry-level conditions influencing pre-entry experience.

title: The Power of Review Contiguity: How Sequential Viewing Shapes Consumer Judgment
abstract: ABSTRACT Online reviews are a prominent source of information in consumer decision making, yet little is known about how review presentation and order jointly affect consumer judgments. Drawing on eWOM literature and working memory theory, we propose that sequential presentation makes consumers more sensitive to the grouping of reviews. Across four experiments, we show that when reviews are viewed sequentially, grouping minority reviews into a contiguous run increases their perceived prevalence and in turn shifts product evaluations accordingly, whereas scattered minority reviews have weaker effects. This grouping effect emerges for both positive and negative minority reviews, is attenuated under cognitive load, and is stronger under mobile than desktop viewing conditions. Perceived minority prevalence mediates the effect on product evaluations. Our findings identify structural contiguity as a distinct source of review order effects and demonstrate how ostensibly functional choices about review presentation and sorting can shape consumers' perceptions and judgments.

title: How followers build Instafame: an ego-network analysis of user-generated hashtags about influencers
abstract: Purpose While social media influencers (SMIs) are often theorized through self-branding and micro-celebrity lenses, this study reconceptualizes their identity formation as a networked and co-produced process. This study aims to investigate how follower-generated hashtag networks function as semantic infrastructures that shape influencer identities on Instagram. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a mixed-method design, integrating ego-network analysis with qualitative content analysis. The analysis is based on 15,000 Instagram posts (5,000 posts for each of three mega-influencers) collected during late 2020. Ego-network analysis was used to identify the structural relationships among follower-generated hashtags, while qualitative content analysis of follower-generated captions examined the symbolic and cultural meanings embedded within these hashtag networks. Findings The results demonstrate that follower-generated content produces hierarchical hashtag networks that act as symbolic scaffolds for influencer brands. Eponymous hashtags are not merely metadata but serve as semantic hubs, linking influencers to genres, celebrities and relational personas (e.g. family, romance). This structure reveals followers’ active role in shaping cultural meaning through affective and symbolic labor. Practical implications Network analysis offers brands and influencers strategic tools for identifying influential hashtags and understanding audience-driven narratives. This approach enables more authentic engagement strategies by uncovering how followers frame influencer identities beyond curated self-presentation. Originality/value This study contributes to theory by bridging network theory with cultural branding to show that influencer identity is coconstructed within digital infrastructures of meaning. Hashtag networks reflect not just popularity but public symbolic expression, advancing theory on cultural production, platform dynamics and influencer–audience relationships.

title: Co-branding as a strategic factor in achieving a sustainable brand image: managerial and theoretical implications from a literature review
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to comprehensively and systematically review and analyse the use of endorsement co-branding and label co-branding strategies in the creation of a sustainable brand image. It concludes by identifying potential topics for future research. For marketing managers, this paper offers a normative guideline for managing the speed–stability trade-off in establishing a sustainable brand image. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a systematic literature review of 38 journal articles published between 2012 and 2026. It offers an in-depth analysis of important literature related to the development of a sustainable brand image. Findings This paper develops a theory-driven conceptual framework that identifies four strategic factors crucial for the development of a sustainable brand image and proposes potential research topics associated with each factor. Research limitations/implications The implication of this paper is to broaden the scientific understanding of sustainable marketing, and report that a systematic and credible development of a sustainable brand image can contribute significantly to the brand value. Practical implications This paper outlines essential actions for managers to effectively establish a sustainable brand image, prioritizing them by importance. Social implications The findings facilitate wider societal engagement with sustainability in marketing. Originality/value The research provides a comprehensive and insightful analysis of the important co-branding literature relevant to sustainable marketing and offers an up-to-date research agenda for co-branding researchers.

title: Translating sustainability into tourism investments: Green growth and budget allocation in NextGenerationEU
Collective Sensemaking When Purchasing Complex B2B Services: How Buying Centers Construct and Align Interpretations of Vendor Service Offering
abstract: Buying centers evaluate complex B2B service offerings not by aggregating independent assessments but through collective interpretive processes that buying center theory has documented structurally without explaining. This study introduces collective service offering sensemaking as a theoretical lens that explains how buying centers construct, contest, and align interpretations of a vendor’s service offering. Drawing on a multi-phase qualitative multiple-case study of six organizations (24 interviews, 3 focus groups, 5 procurement-meeting observations; 2022–2024), we show that service evaluations originate in identity-rooted interpretive frames that differ across technical, financial, procurement, and operational roles. Through interpretive bridging, narrative negotiation, controlled dissent, and evaluative rituals, buying centers transform fragmented meaning structures into interpretive sufficiency, a threshold that enables collective action despite persistent misalignment. The central contribution is interpretive sufficiency: buying centers act on negotiated adequacy rather than consensus, convergence, or shared understanding, through three forms of service value alignment. Three supporting elements explain how the threshold is reached: identity-rooted frames generate the divergence, four interactional mechanisms convert it into workable evaluations, and contextual anchors condition which interpretations gain authority. These elements are not unique to services; what changes under service conditions is their function, salience, and intensity once value-in-use cannot be verified before adoption.

title: The Sound of Good Service: How Dominant and Submissive Language in AI Voice Assistants Shapes Consumer Responses Across Service Settings
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) voice assistants (VAs) function as service agents, delivering information and recommendations tailored to users’ specific needs. VA agents can engage in voice conversations, in which they may convey dominance or submissiveness in response to consumer requests, thereby shaping consumer experiences across service settings. Drawing on the notion of master–servant relationships from assemblage theory, this research examines how, and in which contexts, VAs should use dominant and submissive language to shape consumer interactions. Across six experimental studies, we find that VAs’ submissive language increases usage intentions and perceived interaction value by enhancing rapport and, in turn, comfort, which ultimately drives these consumer responses, even in authority-oriented service settings. However, under time pressure, VAs’ use of either dominant or submissive language equally predicts rapport, thereby disrupting the serial pathway through comfort that leads to usage intentions and perceived interaction value. Together, these findings help specify how service managers can best design VA language to enhance the value of consumer interactions with this technology in service contexts.

title: Interesting and impactful research avenues emerge from teaching operations management
abstract: Purpose This article reflects on how teaching operations management (OM) to graduate students and executives provides a rich source of interesting and impactful OM research avenues. Design/methodology/approach While it is common to hear that the latest research should keep teaching fresh and relevant, this article flips this advice to discuss interesting and impactful OM research topics emerging from the challenges of teaching an MBA core course. Findings This article suggests six avenues for future research that emerged from teaching – how company operations pertain to its strategy, the role of chief operating officer (COO), enterprise processes, process improvement, performance measurement, and automation/artificial intelligence (AI) – and specific research questions within each avenue. Research limitations/implications The proposed research questions are exemplary and not comprehensive. Practical implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to interesting, practically relevant and impactful results. Social implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to socially relevant and impactful results. Originality/value This article reverses the typical admonition to let research inform teaching, showing how considering the counter-relationship illuminates interesting and impactful research avenues.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Every Mile Counts: Geographical Distance as Administrative Burden in Intellectual Property Services
abstract: Abstract While existing research has examined procedural and informational sources of administrative burden, this paper examines how organizational design choices about the geographic location of administrative authority institutionalize spatial burdens on firms. We leverage China's decentralization reform in trademark registration services as a natural experiment to test this theory. This reform reduced geographic distance by establishing local acceptance windows across the country from 2016 to 2019. Prior to this reform, trademark applications had to be submitted exclusively at the centralized Beijing office, imposing substantial geographic barriers on firms nationwide. Using a unique dataset covering over 37 million trademark applications from 294 Chinese cities, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach to estimate the causal effects of reduced geographic distance on trademark filings. We find that establishing local acceptance windows increased trademark applications by approximately 4.4 percent, or roughly 209,000 additional filings in 2019 alone. Moreover, the reform generated compound distributional outcomes: small and medium-sized enterprises responded more strongly than larger firms, and the new applicants drawn into the trademark system were concentrated in cities with thinner infrastructure. Mechanism analysis confirms that this increase is primarily driven by distance reduction rather than improvements in administrative efficiency or reductions in corruption. The findings provide large-scale causal evidence on the behavioral consequences of redistributing administrative service delivery across space, demonstrating that physical accessibility remains crucial for equitable service uptake even amid the digital transformation of administrative services.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: An Informational Letter From the Federal Government Increases Naturalization Submissions
abstract: ABSTRACT Citizenship offers enhanced opportunities for immigrants, but the complex naturalization process can be a barrier. We evaluate a preregistered, large‐scale randomized trial that tested the impact of a low‐cost letter that combined informational content with active encouragement from the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) to potentially eligible Lawful Permanent Residents (LPRs) to apply for naturalization. Within a nationwide population of 1,861,178 individuals in LPR status for 6 to 9 years, we find that the letter increased naturalization applications by 1 percentage point (12%). This increase was positive across all groups tested, though the effects were larger for families in higher income zip codes and those who did not submit the fee waiver application, suggesting that financial and time constraints, along with administrative burdens, play a role in naturalization submission rates.
journal_name: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management

title: Cue production and evaluative uptake: prompt framing and user judgments in AI-Mediated health communication
abstract: Conversational AI systems are increasingly embedded in everyday information and support-seeking practices, including health-related interactions in which users seek advice, reassurance, or emotional acknowledgment. Yet less is known about how users’ own communicative framing shapes what AI systems produce, and whether such AI-generated emotional and supportive cues are subsequently taken up in users’ evaluations of the interaction. Drawing on research on human-like social cues and cue-based credibility processing, this study distinguishes between cue production and cue uptake in AI-mediated communication. Using a randomized, naturalistic prompt-based experiment, participants engaged in a brief two-turn exchange with ChatGPT using one of three prompt exemplars about sleep difficulty that varied in solution orientation, distress expression, and help-seeking structure. The study combined experimental manipulation, computational analysis of AI-generated responses, and pre–post measures of perceived emotional understanding, credibility, trust, and intended future use. Prompt framing shaped the emotional and supportive cues of AI responses: distress-expressive prompts elicited higher anxiety-related language scores, solution-oriented prompts produced more positive emotional tone, and mixed help-seeking prompts elicited more reassuring language. However, variation in these features was not reliably associated with differential pre–post changes in users’ evaluations. Across conditions, users reported modest increases in perceived emotional understanding, credibility, and intended future use after the interaction. The findings suggest that conversational AI can adapt its language to users’ framing, but such cue production does not necessarily lead to credibility uptake. The study contributes to research on AI-mediated communication by examining emotional cueing in a live, ecologically realistic interaction context.

title: Joint trajectory prediction in complex traffic scenarios using causal behavior analysis and risk potential fields
Driving operation state transition prediction under moving bottleneck scenario via Graph-Attention LSTM with Bayesian survival features
Does permanent basic farmland affect the income and inequality of urban and rural residents? Evidence from China’ s Yangtze River Delta
Agreement Helps, Disagreement Matters: Scaling Framing Function Annotation With Large Language Models
abstract: Framing research has long relied on human annotation, but many aspects of framing – especially framing functions such as defining problems, identifying causes, making moral evaluations, or proposing solutions are difficult to label consistently and at scale. We demonstrate that large language models can reliably identify these framing functions, achieving levels of agreement comparable to those of human annotators. We evaluate three state-of-the-art models (GPT-5, Claude 3.7, and DeepSeek) alongside three trained human coders on a new dataset of social media posts about electric-vehicles, a highly topical and contested issue that holds many interpretations. This setting provides a strong test of both agreement and meaningful disagreement in framing-function annotation. Across models and humans, we find not only substantial convergence but also patterns of valid disagreement – differences that reflect legitimate alternative interpretations rather than annotation error. Recognising and preserving these cases enhances construct validity and provides a more realistic portrayal of how framing functions operate in contested debates. Our results demonstrate that large language models can scale framing function analysis while capturing the variability inherent in human interpretation, enabling forms of communication research that were previously impractical with human-only coding.

A promising approach for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery black mass recycling for fertilizer production
abstract: The manufacture of agricultural products has recently gained attention, particularly in the search for practical methods to replace traditional mineral-based raw materials. Therefore, this investigation presents an innovative hydrometallurgical process for producing fertilizers from spent lithium-iron phosphate batteries. Additionally, this work developed a method to produce lithium phosphate as a subproduct. To extract lithium, sodium hydroxide (NaOH) was used; with 2 M NaOH, 20 g/L, 60 min at 25 °C, 98% of lithium was dissolved. Lithium phosphate (purity >98%) was then obtained by precipitation. The solid residue from the alkaline leaching was treated with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA). 98% Fe and ∼96% Cu were extracted (0.3 M EDTA, 60 °C,120 min); therefore, these leachates are promising for fertilizer production. Furthermore, the content of electrolyte solvents and fluoride was analyzed. Electrolyte solvents decomposed in alkaline media, and fluoride concentration was significantly lower than levels found in natural soils, yielding products free of impurities.

title: Resuspension of Micro- and Nanoplastics Trapped in Coastal Sediments: Insights into Their Cross-Interface Transport and Environmental Fate in Transitional Zones
abstract: Abstract Changes in environmental conditions may drive the transfer of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) between sediment layers and overlying waters, yet their resuspension behavior in coastal transitional waters and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study comprehensively investigated the resuspension dynamics of MNPs from sediments with different properties, as well as the effects of aquatic environmental conditions, including salinity, sediment water content, and hydrodynamics, on MNP resuspension. Sediment grain size and mineralogical composition played a dominant role in governing MNP resuspension. Differences in resuspension behavior between microplastic and nanoplastic particles were identified. MNP resuspension showed a nonlinear response to salinity, with increasing salinity generally suppressing resuspension. Resuspension was highly sensitive to salinity changes within the low-salinity range. A U-shaped pattern was observed in PSNP resuspension, with the resuspension rate initially decreasing as sediment water content declined and then increasing as sediments became drier. Positive correlations between MNP resuspension and fluid shear rate were observed, while sediment-trapped MNPs exhibited distinct sensitivities to hydrodynamic disturbances between freshwater and marine conditions. Trapped MNPs were more susceptible to hydrodynamic disturbance under freshwater conditions. These findings offer valuable insights into MNP resuspension and advance understanding of their vertical transport and overall environmental fate in coastal regions.

title: The End of Uniformity: Spatial, Climatic, and Toxicological Redefinitions of Air Quality
abstract: Her research interests focus on air pollution and human health.Her group combines field measurements, laboratory experiments, and computational simulation to study oxidative potential, environmental persistent free radicals (EPFRs), and chemical and cellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) in particulate matter to understand the sources, reaction mechanisms, toxicity, and health effects of air pollutants.

title: Dual-Isotope Tracing Reveals Substantial Postanthesis Foliar and Panicle Contributions to Grain Cadmium Accumulation in Hydroponically Grown Rice
abstract: Abstract Cadmium (Cd) accumulation in rice grains occurs through multiple exposure pathways, yet the relative contributions and associated transport mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we applied dual stable isotope labeling (112Cd/113Cd) in hydroponically grown rice under controlled conditions, with root exposure through nutrient solution as well as foliar and panicle exposure through direct solution spraying. Source apportionment was complemented by sap analysis and triple-quadrupole LA-ICP-MS imaging to examine vascular transport and allocation in the first node under the panicle (node I). Direct Cd contact with aboveground tissues inhibited growth more strongly than root exposure, inducing antioxidant responses and stomatal limitation. Isotopic mass balance revealed that under controlled hydroponic root/foliar exposure, postanthesis Cd inputs contributed 80% and 90% of grain Cd, respectively. Under triple exposure, grain Cd averaged 0.558 mg kg–1, comprising 40% foliar, 24% panicle, and 36% root contributions, demonstrating that aboveground contributions were comparable to root contributions. Transport routes diverged: root uptake elevated xylem sap Cd, whereas foliar-derived Cd showed phloem-associated localization in node I and enrichment in phloem exudates. These results highlight the role of aboveground sources in grain Cd accumulation and suggest that risk assessment in deposition-affected areas should consider both root and aboveground Cd inputs, especially during reproduction.

title: Fog Intensity and Droplet Size-Resolved Aqueous Secondary Organic Aerosol (aqSOA) Formation in Polluted Winter Fog: New Insights from a Combined Observational and Modeling Study
abstract: Abstract Fog is a chemically active aqueous medium in which dissolved organic gases and particles are converted into highly oxidized aqueous secondary organic aerosol (aqSOA). Its magnitude is difficult to constrain, and most published estimates rely on models. We analyzed size-resolved fogwater collected over two winters at Kanpur, India, by offline high-resolution aerosol mass spectrometry and apportioned by positive matrix factorization (PMF). Three highly oxidized factors (O/C 0.95–1.19) were summed as an aqSOA proxy. Combining this proxy with colocated liquid water content and water-soluble organic carbon yielded 3.1–8.4 μg m–3 aqSOA across seven events. The droplet aqSOA accounts for a median of about 7% of ambient SOA and 5% of ambient OA, reaching 13% of SOA in the densest fogs. Fine droplets carried the largest aqSOA share (43–84%), driven by higher concentrations of dissolved Fe and Cu and longer residence times. Ambient OA was less oxidized during dense than light fog (O/C 0.52 versus 0.61). Returning aqSOA after dissipation gave direct-radiative-effect increments of −0.048 W m–2 (dense) and −0.032 W m–2 (light). These size- and intensity-resolved observational constraints quantify fog–aerosol interactions and their air quality consequences in a heavily polluted region.

title: Unraveling the Differentiated Roles of Reactive Chlorine in Regulating Atmospheric Oxidation and Secondary Formation
abstract: Abstract Reactive chlorine species significantly perturb atmospheric oxidation, yet systematic observations of multiple chlorine species and comprehensive assessments of their distinct photochemical roles remain limited. Here, we present concurrent field measurements of four reactive chlorine species (ClNO2, Cl2, HOCl, and NCl3) in a coastal urban atmosphere. Cl2 photolysis dominated Cl• production (40.2%), whereas HOCl photolysis served as a dual source of Cl• and OH•, a mechanism previously overlooked, and most effectively elevated ROx• levels. Temporally, ClNO2 photolysis enhanced early morning oxidation, Cl2 prevailed around noon, and HOCl dominated the afternoon radical budgets, while NCl3 photolysis contributed minimally throughout the diurnal cycle. Incorporating chlorine-induced volatile organic compounds (VOC) consumption in the box model amplified O3 and PAN production by up to 43.4 and 43.8%, respectively, without altering the VOC-limited regime. Our findings underscored that regulating coastal atmospheric oxidation required a species-specific, time-resolved treatment of chlorine chemistry, with direct implications for air quality management.

Early post-emission particle decay dynamics of E-cigarette aerosols under controlled conditions
abstract: Thirdhand smoke consists of residual pollutants that remain on indoor surfaces after smoking or vaping and may contribute to later exposure through desorption and gas-particle-surface partitioning. However, the early post-emission aerosol dynamics that precede and may contribute to residue formation remain poorly characterized for electronic cigarettes. Here, we quantify particle-number decay following a single controlled electronic-cigarette puff in a controlled small-volume chamber under defined airflow and surface conditions. Particle concentrations showed a consistent two-stage decay pattern: a shorter initial decline, potentially driven by airborne removal and surface deposition, followed by a long-tail post-emission particle-decay phase potentially influenced by surface-related and gas-particle processes. Across triplicate experiments, the tested surface configurations produced no consistent change in the fitted decay parameters, whereas increased airflow accelerated particle clearance. These results characterize the early post-emission behavior of electronic-cigarette aerosols and establish a quantitative baseline for processes that may contribute to subsequent thirdhand residue formation.

title: Dual-parameter self-updating predictive energy management strategy for PHEVs based on bidirectional temporal fusion

Post‐Mining Conservation Measures for Erosion Control: A Global Assessment of Their Effectiveness on Runoff and Soil Erosion Reduction
abstract: ABSTRACT Mining activities severely disturb land surfaces and hydrological processes, intensifying hillslope erosion and soil loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of post‐mining restoration measures and identify the factors regulating their performance, we compiled a global dataset of runoff and soil erosion yield from 58 studies spanning multiple mine types, climatic zones, and restoration practices, and conducted a weighted meta‐analysis using random‐effects models. Overall, restoration measures reduced runoff by 49.0% and soil erosion yield by 67.6%, with consistently greater reductions in soil erosion. Combined measures were most effective, whereas soil amendment alone showed the weakest runoff reduction (21.1%). Runoff reduction increased with restoration duration, while soil erosion control was strong initially but showed a transient decline before recovering. Restoration effectiveness also varied substantially among mine types and environmental conditions. Soil erosion reduction was more sensitive than runoff to climatic and topographic factors, with higher rainfall intensity and steeper slopes generally weakening both runoff and soil erosion control. Slopes longer than 15 m sharply reduced soil erosion control (56.9% vs. > 70% on shorter slopes). Vegetation cover further revealed contrasting responses: runoff reduction plateaued at approximately 40% cover, whereas soil erosion reduction continued to increase up to 80%–100% cover. These findings demonstrate that post‐mining restoration effectiveness is jointly regulated by restoration strategy, recovery duration, and site conditions, highlighting the need for context‐specific combinations of restoration measures, vegetation targets, and landform configurations.

title: What defines the linear city? Examining accessibility premises with novel flow-based linearity indices
abstract: This study re-examines the widely held assumption that the linear city model enhances both efficiency and equity of accessibility. From a space syntax perspective, we introduce two flow-based linearity indices: the Morphological Linearity Index, which captures how strongly path-implied trips align along a single axis, and the Structural Linearity Index, which captures how strongly paths converge on shared street segments. We then relate these indices to accessibility measures that are likewise derived from network configuration alone. Applying these indices to 60 South Korean cities, we find that corridor-centered structures alone do not guarantee efficient or equitable accessibility. Networks with higher morphological linearity show lower mean detour rates yet no corresponding reduction in average trip distance, a directness-distance trade-off that can offset net efficiency gains. Higher structural linearity is associated with both greater detour rates and longer trip distances, suggesting that corridor-centered designs can undermine overall accessibility. By translating the “linear city” into measurable indices, this study provides an operational basis for evidence-based road network planning and assessment.
journal_name: Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science

title: Generative AI for urban planning: Designing streetscapes from street-view imagery using diffusion models
abstract: Street-view imagery (SVI) is widely used to quantify key indicators of urban environment, such as greenery, sky, or road view indices. However, relatively few studies have examined controlled SVI synthesis that combines explicit target proportions of trees, sky, buildings, and roads with road-layout masks, while also testing conflicts between textual and spatial controls. To address this gap, we propose a generative multimodal AI framework that synthesizes alternative streetscapes conditioned on targeted visual metrics, enabling direct visual exploration of urban scenarios. We first construct a multimodal dataset that aligns SVIs with textual descriptions, segmentation maps, road masks, and quantitative metrics of visual elements in Chicago and Orlando. Using this dataset, we demonstrate that diffusion models can produce realistic and semantically consistent streetscape imagery while responding to both textual and imagery controls. Our quantitative evaluations show that incorporating visual controls can improve semantic consistency, reducing the LPIPS index by approximately 6% while maintaining global visual realism. In addition, overall semantic consistency increases by 23.7% in Orlando and 46.4% in Chicago, as measured by the mIoU index, with class-wise gains exceeding 100% improvement for building view indices. Streetscape generation shows directional and interpretable responses to both visual and textual prompts, and when textual and visual controls conflict, imagery controls tend to dominate, indicating a clear control hierarchy and the importance of further developing visual controls for urban scene generation. Overall, this work establishes an important benchmark for streetscape generation using SVIs and diffusion models, and illustrates how generative AI can support controllable and exploratory urban scenario visualization.
journal_name: Environment and Planning B: Urban Analytics and City Science

title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
abstract: Abstract Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

title: Correction to: The Financial Channel of the Exchange Rate and Global Trade
The Distributional Impacts of Time-Varying Electricity Pricing: A Novel Approach to Estimating Household Income,
abstract: Abstract As interest in the distributional effects of climate policies gains prominence, designing electricity tariffs that are both efficient and equitable becomes critical. Efficiency often favors the shift from time-invariant to time-of-use (ToU) or real-time prices (RTP), but this transition may have distributional implications. We develop a framework to assess the implications and the channels through which distributional impacts manifest. Central to our approach is a novel method that infers individual household income by combining zip-code-level income data with household-level electricity consumption. We demonstrate the value of this method in the Spanish context. First, we show that using more granular estimates of income has an impact on the distributional assessment of electricity tariffs. Second, we find that the potential distributional impact of RTP is very modest compared to the impact of ToU. The most salient effect of RTP is to increase bill volatility, particularly so for the low-income group.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: The cultural origins of the demographic transition in France
abstract: Abstract This research shows that secularization accounts for the early fertility decline in France. Why the demographic transition began in France a century before any other country is one of the big questions of history because it challenges traditional explanations and because of data limitations. Using a novel dataset crowdsourced from online genealogies, I comprehensively document the decline and its timing. Then, I document the loss of influence of the Catholic Church and find a strong and robust association with the timing of the transition. Finally, I explore the drivers of secularization and discuss the transition’s impact on economic growth.

title: Asylum granted: The integration and well-being benefits of obtaining refugee status
