Agroforestry development drives a progressive shift from physicochemical to microbially mediated organic matter cycling in tropical soils
abstract: Land-use change in tropical soils alters dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry and carbon cycling, however, linkages to microbial functions remain unresolved. We tested whether microbial carbon-degradation potential is associated with DOM composition along an Amazonian agroforestry chronosequence (10, 20, and 30 years), using adjacent pasture and primary forest as references. We integrated shotgun metagenomics with high-resolution mass spectrometry to couple carbohydrate-active enzyme (CAZymes) profiles to DOM composition. Soil chemistry explained 41.6% of the variability in microbial composition, while land-use type accounted for 28.5% of DOM variability. Seasonality did not affect microbial composition but was a significant source of variation in DOM. Relative to pasture, agroforests showed higher potential for sucrose and α-glucan degradation and a greater abundance of aliphatic DOM, indicating enhanced microbial processing. Older agroforests were enriched in genes targeting lignin and microbial-derived substrates such as peptidoglycan, resembling primary forest, whereas younger agroforests had higher abundances of GH36, GH5, and CE3 genes linked to cellulose and hemicellulose degradation, resembling pasture. Soil pH and available P were marginally associated with microbial-derived compound degradation, while pH, P, and Ca showed a stronger association with plant-derived compound processing. These results suggest that as agroforestry develops, carbon cycling may shift from physicochemical to microbial regulation, while DOM remained related to vegetation inputs and seasonality. Soil management of pH and available P during early establishment could support this transition, but the recovery may take decades.

title: Pilot study testing varenicline combined with a behavioral intervention for promoting smoking cessation and pain management among patients with cancer
abstract: Abstract Purpose Many patients with cancer smoke and also experience pain. Smoking offers short-term pain relief but exacerbates pain long-term. We pilot tested the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of adding varenicline to a combined behavioral treatment that addresses smoking cessation and pain management. Methods We conducted a single arm pilot study in which we provided varenicline paired with a 4-session behavioral treatment that uses the same techniques to help people quit smoking and manage their pain. Our primary outcome was 7-day point prevalence abstinence at 6-months post-randomization. Results We recruited 19 patients with cancer. 80% of the patients who received the intervention rated it as extremely useful (4 or 5 out of 5) in helping them quit smoking; 60% rated it as helpful in managing their pain. Further, 81% would recommend the program to other patients with cancer. Over one-third (35%) reported biochemically validated abstinence at 6 months post-randomization. We did not see improvements in reported pain but did see improvements in pain self-efficacy. Conclusions Our pilot data suggest the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of this approach for promoting cessation. We need to refine aspects to help address pain, yet addressing pain in addition to smoking cessation might motivate more patients with cancer to join the program. The next step is to conduct a large randomized controlled trial to fully test the efficacy of the combined behavioral program with varenicline. Implications for Cancer Survivors: A combined smoking cessation and pain program paired with varenicline might help patients with cancer quit smoking.

Environmental, circularity, and criticality assessment of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries: Implications for management strategies in Mexico
abstract: Mexico's rapid growth in battery electric vehicle (BEV) adoption has not been accompanied by a regulatory framework for the end-of-life management of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), creating environmental risks and limiting the recovery of strategic materials. This study evaluates four end-of-life management strategies for BEV LIBs in Mexico (controlled disposal, hydrometallurgical recycling, pyrometallurgical recycling, and repurposing) using an integrated framework that combines Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), the Material Circularity Indicator (MCI), and a criticality-weighted extension (MCI-c). The proposed MCI-c incorporates material criticality into the circularity assessment, allowing resource recovery to be evaluated not only in terms of material recirculation but also considering the strategic importance of recovered materials. Repurposing achieved the best overall environmental and circularity performance, while hydrometallurgical recycling consistently outperformed pyrometallurgical recycling among recycling alternatives. Incorporating criticality into the assessment altered the prioritization of management strategies under increasing lithium criticality, demonstrating that criticality can influence end-of-life management priorities. These findings highlight the importance of integrating environmental performance, material circularity, and criticality into the evaluation of end-of-life LIBs management strategies. For Mexico, they support the development of a dedicated regulatory framework that prioritizes higher-value recovery strategies and incorporates criticality into end-of-life decision-making. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a practical approach for evaluating end-of-life LIBs management in countries facing similar challenges in battery circularity and critical material supply.

title: A comparative TEA–LCA study of biomethane production through anaerobic digestion and five upgrading technologies: Amine scrubbing, water scrubbing, membrane separation, PSA, and cryogenic separation
abstract: Producing grid-quality biomethane from sewage-sludge biogas is promising, yet selecting an upgrading route remains uncertain because mature technologies differ in energy use, cost, methane losses in off-gas or vent streams, and the fate of biogenic CO 2 . This study evaluates anaerobic digestion integrated with five commercial upgrading technologies: amine scrubbing, water scrubbing (WS), membrane separation (MEM), pressure swing adsorption (PSA), and cryogenic separation (CRYO), modelled for a municipal wastewater treatment plant. All configurations deliver grid-quality biomethane, while separated CO 2 is compressed and liquefied where feasible; venting is assumed for the dilute CO 2 stream from WS. Aspen Plus simulations were coupled with techno-economic analysis (TEA) and consequential life cycle assessment (LCA). The results show clear trade-offs. Amine scrubbing has the highest thermal demand (1207 kW), whereas CRYO and MEM have the highest upgrading-unit electricity demands (257 and 201 kW, respectively). Economically, without an additional emission charge, WS is the most attractive option, with the lowest levelized cost of biomethane (LCOM) of 436 €/t, while amine scrubbing is the most expensive (652 €/t). Hypothetical charges on vented biogenic CO 2 and CH 4 progressively increase the LCOM of WS above those of MEM, CRYO, PSA, and amine scrubbing at approximately 36.5, 37.7, 43.2, and 120.4 €/t CO 2 -eq, respectively. From an environmental perspective, consequential LCA shows that PSA, MEM, and CRYO outperform solvent-based routes in human health, ecosystem, and climate performance due to efficient CO 2 liquefaction and avoidance of upgrading-stage venting. In the deterministic base case, PSA delivers the highest net human-health savings and the largest net GHG reduction, whereas WS shows the weakest climate performance. The economic preference for WS depends on emission-pricing assumptions, while PSA, MEM, and CRYO are more suitable for carbon-circular biorefineries.

Greenwashing or Sustainability Misalignment? Analysing Organisational, Workplace and Real Estate Strategies Through an Iceberg Lens
abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental sustainability and the broader Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) agenda have become prominently proclaimed organisational priorities, yet their integration into core decision‐making remains uneven. While greenwashing research has largely focused on communication and disclosure, it has paid less attention to the internal strategic dynamics that underpin sustainability outcomes. This paper examines how environmental sustainability and ESG shape organisational decision‐making in workplace and corporate real estate (CRE) strategies. Drawing on organisational culture and institutional theory, the study adopts an iceberg perspective, conceptualising sustainability as a visible commitment underpinned by less visible strategic, cultural and institutional dynamics. Using a mixed‐methods design, the study combines quantitative analysis of two waves of large‐scale survey data from senior CRE professionals with qualitative insights from semistructured interviews with employees, senior executives and CRE managers. The findings show that sustainability and ESG considerations may be unevenly associated with workplace and CRE strategies. It revealed that sustainability may be largely peripheral to future strategic decision‐making, with stronger links to workplace adjustments than to fundamental CRE portfolio decisions. Qualitative evidence further shows that economic, operational and social priorities dominate stakeholder workplace considerations, while organisations weakly prioritise environmental sustainability in routines. The study shows that sustainability may be rhetorically prominent yet strategically peripheral, reframing sustainability misalignment as an underlying strategic integration challenge that spans business, organisational strategy and sustainability research, and offering insights for organisations seeking to align ESG commitments more effectively with asset‐intensive strategies.

title: Global Manufacturers' Approaches to Managing Waste in Their Production Networks
abstract: ABSTRACT This research investigates how global manufacturers organize local waste management within their global production networks to aid the implementation of circularity. This study aims to identify the approach to managing waste in the global production network and the extent of engaging in waste‐to‐resource activities. We methodologically study this through six industrial case studies in the household electronics industry, which we explore through qualitative analysis of archival data, such as sustainability and annual reports. Our findings reveal how bottom‐up and top‐down approaches to managing waste in the global production network are characterized. We further identify relationship management with external actors in the waste‐based supply chain. We identify and discuss how these two factors affect the global manufacturer's extent of engaging in waste‐to‐resource activities. This research contributes to academic understanding on global operations by identifying the factors that are required to enable circularity implementation for global manufacturers.

title: Generative AI in ESG Reporting: A Case Study and Process Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is found to have a remarkable impact on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) reporting. Although there is abundant literature on ESG reporting, very few studies have examined the adoption of GenAI in ESG reporting. As a result, this study examines how companies can use GenAI to generate value in ESG reporting. We obtain the following three findings that we articulate in this paper: (i) GenAI drives digital innovation in ESG reporting via automated data extraction, accelerated analytics, and dynamic reporting; (ii) GenAI‐powered platforms enhance stakeholder engagement by integrating diverse data sources and improving information accessibility; and (iii) organizations encounter significant challenges in data governance and human‐AI collaboration. We also propose a framework for adopting GenAI in digital ESG platforms.

title: The Immortality Paradox: One‐Party Dominance, Political Tenure, and Organizational Continuity in Japanese Agencies
abstract: ABSTRACT In his classic 1976 study on organizational survival, Kaufman argued that public organizations are “immortal”. More recent research, however, has come to the opposite conclusion, finding that public organizations are frequently terminated. These findings largely relate to contexts where changes to the ruling party occur regularly. In contrast, this study examines the survival of government agencies in Japan, where the postwar political system has been characterized by one‐party dominance and short‐lived political leadership. The findings suggest that Japanese agencies remain largely “immortal,” and that when they do undergo transitions this tends to be linked to prime ministers with longer tenures who are able to implement minor, cosmetic changes; hence agencies typically persist even after such events. This study thus sheds new light on how political–administrative relations shape patterns of agency transition and highlights the importance of leadership tenure in sustaining commitments to organizational change.

title: Urban Digital Twins as Spatiotemporal Synchronization Systems: A Four-Layer Framework for Sustainable and Resilient Cities
A New Approach to Household Flood Resilience Assessment using the Recovery-Damage Ratio (RDR) Index
abstract: Flood resilience is the ability of a system to withstand and efficiently recover from flood damage. Although resilience has become central to disaster research, most household-level flood assessments remain focused on estimating immediate damage, offering limited understanding of post-flood recovery dynamics. To address this gap, this study develops a new approach that extends conventional flood damage assessment toward resilience, capturing variations in household recovery trajectories across different resilience properties. The novelty of this research lies in the formulation of a new index that quantifies the dynamic nature of post-flood recovery relative to the damage incurred. We achieve this by coupling empirical flood damage curves with a time-dependent Recovery–Damage Ratio (RDR) index, creating the flood resilience curve. As a proof of concept, we utilized survey data from Marikina City, Philippines, and set the longitudinal information of income, post-flood financial aid, and house type as surrogate indicators of the four properties of resilience, namely robustness, redundancy, rapidity, and resources. This analysis reveals disparities in recovery speed associated with income class and external assistance. This also uncovers a paradox that while structural robustness dictates initial damage, low-flood depth households may delay repairs, whereas highly inundated households rapidly mobilize reconstruction. Furthermore, the comparison of paired flood events shows a shift in household resilience after experiencing severe flooding, consistent with localized flood adaptation and preemptive actions. Ultimately, this approach offers a reproducible framework to quantify post-flood recovery through the lens of interdependent resilience properties.

Smart-city pilot vs. non-pilot cities: Long-term trends in urban resilience in China
abstract: Urban resilience has become a critical component of sustainable urban development under increasing climate risks and disaster uncertainty. Smart city initiatives have been widely promoted as a strategy to enhance urban governance and resilience. However, their long-term relationship with urban resilience remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the resilience evolution of 300 Chinese cities, including 155 smart city pilot cities and 145 non-smart cities, from 2004 to 2023. A multidimensional resilience evaluation framework consisting of four dimensions and 48 indicators was constructed, and social network analysis was used to calculate resilience index for each city group and year. The results indicate that pilot cities had a mean resilience index of 0.795, compared with 0.478 for non-pilot cities, and permutation tests showed that this difference was significant in every year. However, the difference was largest in 2004, before the pilot program began, and narrowed mainly before 2013, as the resilience of non-pilot cities increased, and did not widen after the pilot program began. Given the non-random selection of pilot cities, these differences should be interpreted as an association that mainly reflects pilot selection rather than a direct causal effect of smart city policies. Early smart city pilots showed higher and comparatively stable resilience (mean 0.935) than the second (0.621) and third (0.180) batches. Institutional and infrastructure resilience increased in both groups, agent resilience changed little, and environmental resilience declined in both pilot and non-pilot cities, suggesting persistent challenges in ecological sustainability. The findings suggest that smart-city policy evaluation should account for baseline differences, and that future resilience-oriented policies strengthen environmental integration and support for less developed cities alongside technological advancement.

Surviving Rome: The Economic Lives of the Ninety PercentKimBowes, Princeton University Press, 2025. Pp. 512. Hbk £35. ISBN 9780691273334.
abstract: In Surviving Rome, Bowes sounds a clarion call for researchers to focus on the understudied economic lives of the majority 'ninety percent' inhabitants of the early Roman Empire.The dramatis personae of her book are the potters, hustlers, weavers, small holders (emphatically not peasants!),sex workers, children, and drovers.Here, we have the masses, the rustics and urban mob, decried and denigrated by Roman elite writers.It was these masses -the agricultural producers, craftspeople, and purveyor of services -who literally built the Roman Empire and its material world.In many ways, the volume is an antidote to our imaginary Romes and the preconceptions, drawn from textual sources, hazy economic theory, and the odd ethnohistoric analogy, that have sketched their outlines.Sacred cows are slaughtered, and strawmen are burnt along the way.The consumer city, autarkic peasants, 'Cicero & Co', and calculating ancient GDP are definitely out.In their place is a series of micro-narratives: pieces of lives glimpsed through the waste paper bin of Egyptian papyri and the boxes of pottery sherds, animal bones, and burnt seeds recovered by archaeologists.We learn that the 'ninety percent' were exploited -by the state, landlords, and others.They led hard, gruelling lives and made choices in a struggle to surf the wave of precarity.These individuals and families were faced with choices that are unenviable to modern eyes -prostituting a close relative or sending their small children out to work -but these strategies, along with others, enabled those individuals to survive and more at a level greater than that of modern economists' idea of 'subsistence'.The seven chapters are a joy to read.Bowes' prose is compelling, written with a simple clarity that is both elegant and seductive.It is easy to be carried along, and the reliance on the Egyptian textual evidence is a case in point.The papyri and ostraca provide vignettes of past lives that are fascinating and have an immediacy that is hard to ignore.Yet, they stand as a proxy for All rights reserved, including rights for text and data mining and training of artificial intelligence technologies or similar technologies.

title: Peripheral participation, metropolitan ownership: core and periphery configurations in Japan’s Green Transformation technological paths
abstract: Abstract Research on innovation beyond metropolitan cores has paid less attention to whether peripheral participation is matched by formal ownership of patents on key technological paths. We distinguish spatial and network participation from the headquarters geography of patent applicants, and apply kernel density, core–periphery network, and main-path analyses to sixty-two Japanese Green Transformation technologies. Four technology participation configurations emerge. Yet most main-path patent–firm links involve firms headquartered in Japan’s three major metropolitan areas. The study highlights that participation in main technological paths differs from ownership, which marks the tensions between core and peripheral configurations of inventive activity.

Forecasting seasonal changepoint models utilizing changepoint uncertainties
abstract: Forecasting in the presence of changepoints is a challenging task. However, if changepoints occur regularly across seasons, we want to utilize that information in our predictions for the next season. In this paper, we develop a framework for forecasting seasonal data that contain within-season changepoints. In our forecasts, we account for uncertainty in the changepoint locations both within and across seasons via a weighting approach across changepoint uncertainties. The framework is very flexible across different changepoint model assumptions and approaches to identifying changepoint confidence sets. We demonstrate the improvement in forecasting performance of our framework for atmospheric pressure with a multivariate changepoint approach, and for air pollution ( PM 2.5 ) with a univariate changepoint approach.

Military experience and ethical restraint: Evidence from CEO insider trading
abstract: Abstract We examine the relation between CEO military experience and insider trading in U.S. public firms. Military CEOs earn significantly lower insider trading profits than non‐military CEOs, particularly those who attained commissioned ranks or served in the Air Force, Army, or Marine Corps. The negative relation holds for both purchase and sale transactions. Military CEOs also exhibit longer investment horizons and are less likely to trade in the month preceding earnings announcements. Overall, the findings are consistent with military socialization promoting discipline, rule adherence, and ethical restraint in exploiting informational advantages for personal gain.

Water Markets for Climate Change Adaptation: Trade, Storage, and Investment Under Stochastic Water Supply
abstract: Abstract It is widely accepted that water markets can support adaptation to climate change. However, quantifying this adaptive capacity is difficult as it requires models that represent both stochastic water supplies and forward-looking behaviour by market participants. We develop a stochastic dynamic model of the Murray-Darling Basin water market in which irrigators form rational expectations over future water prices, and make monthly water use, annual crop planting, and long-run investment decisions. The model is solved using reinforcement learning methods to approximate expectations, combined with mathematical programming to estimate market equilibrium. We validate the model against observed prices and irrigation activity from 2008 to 09 to 2021–22 and apply it to an ensemble of 37 CMIP6 climate projections for the southern Basin. Under drier future climates, water markets support adaptation through increased inter-regional trade flows into the downstream Murray, and larger storage reserves through more conservative crop planting. However, under the driest projections, inter-regional trade constraints bind, price differences widen across zones, and long-run irrigation development contracts by up to 16 per cent. The results highlight both the value and the limits of market-based adaptation, with implications for the design of water market institutions under a non-stationary climate.

title: Do Protected Areas Affect the Income Levels in Remote Regions? Evidence from Italian Inner Areas
abstract: Abstract The economic impact of protected areas (PAs) on local development remains a debated topic in regional economics, particularly in peripheral regions facing demographic and economic decline. While protected areas provide essential ecological benefits, their effects on local economies remain debated, with concerns about land-use restrictions potentially limiting economic opportunities alongside potential gains from tourism and ecosystem services. This study investigates the causal effect of PAs on per capita income in Italian municipalities classified as inner areas under the National Strategy for Inner Areas. We exploit variation in the share of municipal land covered by protected areas using a Difference-in-differences approach with continuous treatment in a dose-response framework. The results show a robust, positive, and statistically significant relationship between PAs and local economic growth. The expansion of protected areas is associated with increased per capita income, suggesting that environmental protection contributes to development in Italy’s marginalized inner regions.

title: Policy uncertainty shocks and farm investments in Europe: Evidence from a newspaper‐based index
abstract: Abstract In order to quantify the impact of agricultural policy uncertainty on European farmers' investment behavior, we construct a newspaper‐based monthly index of European agricultural policy uncertainty from 2013 to 2023. We use 327,224 newspaper articles to assess and compare the trends in policy uncertainty across five top agricultural producers in Europe, that is, Germany, the United Kingdom, France, Spain and Italy. We connect this index of policy uncertainty to bookkeeping data from 13,706 farms in these five countries over the period 2014–2018 ( N = 68,530) to estimate the relationship between policy uncertainty and investment decisions. We find an increasing trend in agricultural policy uncertainty, with significant peaks around key events such as the COVID‐19 pandemic, the introduction of the European Green Deal and Brexit. Despite the presence of a common policy environment, agricultural policy uncertainty is heterogeneous across countries and captures country‐specific uncertainties such as elections and weather shocks. Anticipated policy uncertainties, such as those arising from Brexit and the European Green Deal, allow farmers to analyze optimal responses and make investment plans, and therefore, if they affect farm investment, they do so smoothly over time (e.g., bringing investment forward). In contrast, unanticipated uncertainties, or policy uncertainty shocks, like those caused by the Russian food import ban of 2014 or the US‐China trade war are negatively correlated to farm investment.

title: Navigating the Family Support Dilemma in Female Entrepreneurship: An Embeddedness Perspective
abstract: Drawing on family embeddedness and gender performativity, we examine how family support is enacted and governed through gendered norms, and how female entrepreneurs navigate these dynamics. Based on indepth interviews with female entrepreneurs and family members in Ethiopia, we introduce the family support dilemma: a process in which support enabling female entrepreneurship simultaneously generates explicit or internalized obligations that constrain sustained engagement and growth over time. Our findings show that family support is embedded in gendered social structures, functioning as a site of norm enforcement where support is granted or withdrawn based on women’s enactment of gender role expectations.

title: From Contested Endogenization to Regulatory Unravelling of Mandatory Human Rights Due Diligence: Extending the Endogeneity of Law Framework
abstract: Abstract Drawing on the endogeneity of law framework, this study examines how business, legal, public, and civil society actors constructed the meaning and practice of mandatory human rights due diligence in the context of the German garment industry and the German Supply Chain Act. Using interview, document, and observation data spanning the period 2019 to 2026, our findings reveal a two‐stage process: an initial phase of contested endogenization in which actors experienced with private regulation prevented convergence on a managerialized interpretation of the law, followed by regulatory unravelling in which changes in the political‐economic climate provided avenues for substantively weakening the law and preventing its implementation. We discuss how the dual processes of managerializing a law and legalizing of organizations is complicated by three boundary conditions: the complexity of the regulatory issue, the field's regulatory maturity, and the degree of regulatory uncertainty. Connecting the endogeneity of law framework with research on the public and private governance of global supply chains allows us to theorize refinements to this framework when applied to contested, complex governance fields, and to derive a set of theoretical and practical implications for public supply chain regulation.

title: The coevolution of trust and behavioral uncertainty: Toward a theory of vulnerability acceptance in entrepreneurial ventures
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This conceptual study develops a process theory of vulnerability acceptance explaining how trust and behavioral uncertainty coevolve as entrepreneurial actors form, interpret, and realize opportunities. Trust is frequently invoked to explain creativity, exploration, and opportunity formation, yet remains theorized through predictability and evaluability, which entrepreneurial opportunities often lack ex ante. We distinguish three forms of vulnerability acceptance: uncertainty creating, releasing, and decreasing trust. Each transforms the uncertainty it engages, which in turn reinforces or unsettles that form, so no form is terminal. Their salience shifts across opportunity formation, interpretive recombination, and realization, and misalignment between a form and the conditions it confronts impairs entrepreneurial progress. Trust thereby becomes a means through which epistemic conditions are produced, not only a response to them. Managerial Summary Entrepreneurship exposes forms of vulnerability that cannot be explained by risk‐based models of trust alone. Entrepreneurs often face the practical question: “Trust them to do what?” The answer depends on the kind of agency they are willing to be vulnerable to, and it changes as an opportunity takes shape. That may mean backing people to take the work somewhere no one can yet specify, relying on others' expertise to make sense of what is emerging, or counting on them to deliver what was agreed. Trust is therefore not only a way of reducing uncertainty but a means of transforming it, and progress depends on recognizing when the prevailing form fits the conditions and when it does not.

title: Swap and Save: How a Button Shapes Lasting Online Grocery Shopping Behavior
abstract: A well-documented phenomenon in the literature is that consumers exhibit persistence in their choices. Using data from the mineral water category on a price comparison platform that delivers real-time prompts of cheaper alternatives through "swap and save" buttons, this study examines whether and how these prompts influence persistent product choices in online grocery shopping. The findings reveal that shoppers who switched to an alternative product after receiving a prompt were 23.7 percentage points more likely to select that alternative product in subsequent visits, with this effect lasting for up to 10 shopping trips. Our analysis suggests that this sustained impact is driven not by long-term cost savings but by product discovery enabled through these real-time prompts.

title: The psychodynamics of contemporary careers: Anxieties and defenses in deconstructed work
abstract: To gain flexibility, organizations increasingly deconstruct jobs, shifting from relatively stable bundles of tasks and titles to dynamic task–project constellations matched to employees’ skills. Yet this redesign also weakens the psychological containment through which jobs have historically stabilized workers’ lived experience of work inside organizations. Drawing on systems psychodynamics, we theorize that as the job’s psychological containment function weakens, workers experience three shared anxieties—about finding their place in shifting configurations of work, having their competence recognized, and forming and maintaining secure work relationships. Workers respond, collectively and often unconsciously, with social defenses: projecting familiar roles and rules onto deconstructed work, splitting off the generalist competence such work demands, and falling back on safe relationships. These defenses provisionally contain anxiety, but they also reorient workers toward familiar ways of organizing, evaluating, and relating that job deconstruction is meant to transform, keeping the redesigned work system in defensive stasis. By reconceptualizing job deconstruction as both a design property of work and a lived condition of shared anxiety, we explain why flexible work redesigns, though fluid in theory, are often frozen in practice, and how organizations can intervene to contain anxiety in new ways as they transition to the new world of work.

title: Do Geopolitical Risk, Economic Policy Uncertainty, and Trade Policy Uncertainty Drive Corporate Carbon Transition Risk in China?
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the effects of geopolitical risk (GPR), economic policy uncertainty (EPU), and trade policy uncertainty (TPU) on corporate CTR in China from January 2010 to December 2022. Using a combination of complementary quantile‐based approaches, including quantile‐on‐quantile regression (QoQR), quantile‐on‐quantile Granger causality (QoQGC), and wavelet quantile correlation (WQC), this study reveals substantial nonlinear, asymmetric, and time–frequency‐dependent relationships between external uncertainty and corporate CTR. The QoQR results show that GPR, EPU, and TPU generally increase corporate CTR as uncertainty rises from low to moderate levels; however, their marginal effects weaken and, in some regimes, become negative at extreme uncertainty levels. The QoQGC results reveal that predictive causality varies across uncertainty regimes: GPR and EPU exhibit strong predictive relevance at extreme uncertainty levels, whereas TPU shows predictive relevance across a broader range of low‐to‐moderate uncertainty regimes. The WQC results demonstrate that the uncertainty–CTR relationship also varies across both the CTR distribution and time‐frequency dimensions, with stronger positive co‐movement generally observed at middle‐to‐upper CTR quantiles and over medium‐ to long‐run horizons. Overall, the findings demonstrate that external uncertainty does not affect corporate CTR uniformly; rather, its transmission is regime‐dependent and time‐varying, highlighting the importance of uncertainty‐specific and adaptive strategies to support China's low‐carbon transition.

title: Emissions Performance as a Capability‐Based Organizational Outcome: Evidence From Interpretable Machine Learning in Hospitality and Tourism
abstract: ABSTRACT Reducing corporate greenhouse gas emissions has become a central strategic challenge for firms, yet substantial heterogeneity persists in emissions performance even among organizations facing similar regulatory and market conditions. Existing research has largely attributed emissions outcomes to governance mechanisms, ESG initiatives, or financial capacity, often assuming linear and additive effects. This study advances a capability‐based perspective by conceptualizing firm‐level emissions performance not as a capability in itself, but as an emergent organizational outcome reflecting how effectively firms deploy and coordinate capability‐related workforce, operational, and managerial systems. Using firm‐level ESG and financial data from 110 publicly listed hospitality and tourism firms over the period 2015–2024, we apply ensemble machine learning techniques, bagging, random forest, and boosting, to model emissions performance. Boosting models consistently outperform alternative approaches and are analyzed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and partial dependence plots (PDP) to ensure interpretability and theory development. Across four progressively enriched model specifications, the results show that workforce quality, resource‐use efficiency, and managerial effectiveness, the empirical proxies for underlying organizational capabilities, are the most influential and stable predictors of emissions performance. Governance mechanisms and financial performance display patterns consistent with conditioning rather than substitutive roles, being associated with the effectiveness of capability‐related systems without independently determining emissions outcomes. The analysis identifies nonlinear relationships, asymmetric predictive patterns associated with weak capability‐related organizational indicators, and joint partial‐dependence patterns consistent with complementarity among organizational systems, suggesting that emissions‐related performance may be sensitive to organizational deficiencies and the alignment of related practices. By focusing on the hospitality and tourism industry, where emissions are embedded in continuous service operations, the study highlights the central role of organizational execution in shaping environmental outcomes. The findings contribute to sustainability and strategic management research by explaining emissions performance as an observable outcome of capability deployment, coordination, and complementarity rather than as the direct product of isolated ESG policies, governance structures, or financial resources.

title: From Entrepreneurial Orientation to Environmental Performance: Dynamic Capabilities and Institutional Weaknesses in an Emerging Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how entrepreneurial orientation is associated with environmental performance in manufacturing firms, focusing on the mediating roles of dynamic managerial capabilities and dynamic technological capabilities and the conditioning role of institutional weaknesses. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory and institutional theory, the study adopts a capability‐based and context‐sensitive perspective to explain how entrepreneurial strategies translate into environmental outcomes in an emerging economy. Survey data were collected from 320 manufacturing firms located predominantly within Ghana's Southern industrial zone and analysed using a two‐step approach involving confirmatory factor analysis and regression‐based bootstrapped estimation of direct, indirect and conditional indirect associations. The results show that entrepreneurial orientation is positively associated with environmental performance, primarily through dynamic managerial and technological capabilities. Moreover, the indirect associations are stronger under higher levels of institutional weakness, indicating that internal capabilities become more salient in challenging institutional environments. The study contributes to the entrepreneurship and sustainability literature by demonstrating that entrepreneurial orientation is associated with environmental performance mainly through capability‐based mechanisms and that institutional context shapes the strength of these mechanisms. The findings offer context‐specific insights for managers and policymakers seeking to enhance environmental performance among manufacturing firms operating in weak institutional settings, although the geographic concentration of the sample requires caution in generalising the results to less industrialized and resource‐constrained regions.

title: Organizational Rootedness, Territorial Dynamic Capabilities and Environmental Priorities: Evidence From European Regional Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines organizational rootedness as the degree of territorial integration that differentiates environmental priorities in regional firms. Although its constitutive function in shaping environmental engagement is recognized, its ordering function in determining which initiatives become more salient is less clear. We examine whether higher‐ and lower‐rooted regional firm patterns prioritize environmental initiatives differently, how their priorities vary under social and economic pressures, and how these pressures are associated with eco‐innovation orientation in higher‐rooted patterns. The conceptual framework integrates organizational embeddedness with territorial dynamic capabilities: the first conceptualizes the different degrees of firms' territorial integration, whereas the second explains how this integration supports readaptation processes and eco‐innovative development under pressures. Using a novel database from 145 EU regions, we identify distinct priorities in environmental initiatives, reordered under contextual pressures. Furthermore, in higher‐rooted patterns, eco‐innovation orientation tends to be stronger under economic than social pressures. The findings suggest that managers should treat environmental sustainability as a territorially ordered portfolio of initiatives.

title: Leader humility and employee psychological well-being: the roles of relational age and supervisor gender
abstract: Purpose The study aims to apply the social information processing (SIP) theory to examine the three-way interaction of leader humility, supervisor-subordinate relational age and supervisor gender on hospitality employees’ psychological well-being (PWB) through job crafting. Design/methodology/approach Data were gathered from 235 US hospitality employees through a time-lagged, multiwave survey design. Confirmatory factor analysis was used to validate the measurement model and PROCESS analyses were used to examine the hypothesized mediation and moderation effects. Findings Leader humility is positively associated with hospitality employees’ PWB directly and indirectly through job crafting. Leader humility, relational age and supervisor gender interact to impact employees’ job crafting and PWB. The positive association between leader humility and job crafting was strengthened for female supervisors across both relational age conditions. The positive relationship between leader humility and PWB was strengthened for female supervisors regardless of relational age. The indirect effect of leader humility on PWB via job crafting was positive when employees perceived female supervisors as younger or similar in age or male supervisors as older. Research limitations/implications The study extends SIP theory by showing that leader humility is interpreted through the combined social information signaled by supervisor gender and relational age. These social cues jointly influence the effects of leader humility on hospitality employees’ job crafting and PWB. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is among the first to investigate the joint moderating roles of supervisor gender and relational age in the effects of leader humility and to examine their conditional indirect effect on PWB via job crafting.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Perceived authenticity in ethnic and cultural restaurants: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Purpose This study aims to address fragmented evidence on perceived authenticity in restaurant contexts by developing an integrated understanding of its key antecedents and customer outcomes in ethnic and cultural dining settings. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review identified 100 studies, with 50 meeting the inclusion criteria for meta-analytic synthesis. Effect sizes were synthesized using random-effects models, and moderator analyses were performed to examine the roles of culture, age and gender. Findings Perceived authenticity is strongly shaped by tangible cues, particularly brand image and food quality. In turn, authenticity exerts robust positive effects on customer satisfaction, revisit intention and word of mouth. Moderator analyses further show that individualism strengthens the authenticity–positive emotion relationship, that older consumers place greater emphasis on authenticity in forming memorable dining experiences and that female customers are more sensitive to interpersonal cues. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for restaurant managers on developing and communicating authentic dining experiences in ways that support favorable customer responses. They also highlight the value of considering cultural and demographic differences when designing and delivering authenticity-related experiences. Originality/value This study clarifies how key antecedents differentially shape perceived authenticity and how authenticity influences customer outcomes. It also identifies boundary conditions across cultural and demographic contexts.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Consumer misbehavior in tourism and hospitality contexts: a framework-based systematic review and future agenda
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to synthesize the fragmented literature and develop an integrative framework to advance understanding of the emergence, consequences and management of consumer misbehavior in tourism and hospitality. Design/methodology/approach A framework-based systematic review is conducted. Drawing on 83 peer-reviewed articles retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science, this paper uses an Antecedents–Enactments–Consequences–Interventions (AECI) framework to synthesize the literature. Findings Consumer misbehavior is primarily shaped by external situational factors and consumers’ psychological catalysts. Negative feelings, defensive regulation and threat evaluation emerge as key enactment mechanisms linking antecedents, consumer misbehavior and stakeholder responses. Consumer misbehavior generates consequences for employees, other consumers and residents. These individual-level impacts may lead to organization- and destination-level outcomes. Research on interventions has focused more heavily on precautionary strategies than on coping strategies. In particular, coping strategies addressing the impacts of consumer misbehavior on employees and residents remain largely overlooked. This review identifies theoretical fragmentation and under-researched areas, including contagion effects and post-incident recovery for employees and residents. Practical implications Effective management of consumer misbehavior requires both precautionary and coping strategies. Managers should tailor interventions to the severity and context of misbehavior. Organizations and destinations should also provide active post-incident management and immediate psychological support to facilitate employee and resident recovery. Originality/value This paper offers a comprehensive synthesis of consumer misbehavior in tourism and hospitality using an AECI framework. This paper clarifies conceptual ambiguity, integrates dispersed evidence and proposes a future research agenda.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Mindful eating and sustainable dining behaviors: a psychological resources perspective
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the psychological mechanisms linking mindful eating (ME) with sustainable dining behaviors in restaurant contexts. Drawing on Hunecke’s psychological resources perspective for sustainable lifestyles, the study explains how self- and other-focused psychological resources are associated with green restaurant selection and dining-out leftover prevention across pre- and post-consumption stages. Design/methodology/approach A dual-pathway sequential mediation model was developed and tested using data from 611 Taiwanese consumers who had dined out within the previous three months. Structural equation modeling was used to examine the hypothesized paths and mediating relationships. Findings The findings support two sequential pathways linking ME to sustainable dining outcomes. The self-focused pathway operates through self-compassion and subjective vitality, whereas the other-focused pathway operates through altruistic values and food gratitude. Together, these complementary psychological resources connect ME with green restaurant selection and dining-out leftover prevention across pre- and post-consumption stages. Research limitations/implications The findings advance sustainable hospitality research by highlighting psychological resources as mechanisms through which ME is associated with sustainable dining behaviors. From a practical perspective, mindful dining experiences may encourage self-focused resources, while appreciative communication may strengthen altruistic concern and food gratitude. Originality/value This study extends Hunecke’s psychological resources perspective to hospitality by specifying complementary self- and other-focused pathways. It advances research on the intention–behavior gap and broadens ME as a dining-specific antecedent associated with sustainable decisions through downstream psychological resources.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI: A Theoretical Framework for Memory, Metacognition, and Consumer Decision-Making
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. Drawing on cognitive offloading research from cognitive psychology, we develop the CogOffload framework to explain when consumers delegate cognitive work to Gen-AI and what consequences follow. A seven-stage delegation continuum maps increasing levels of offloading, and a value-based cost-benefit framework identifies its antecedents and the moderators that shape how consumers weigh them. We propose three clusters of outcomes. First, offloading weakens memory for brands and product attributes while strengthening memory for AI-generated summaries. Second, it inflates metacognitive self-esteem and decision confidence, producing AI-induced overconfidence that reduces further information-seeking. Third, effects on decision quality depend on AI reliability: when AI is unreliable, verifying AI recommendations imposes cognitive and emotional costs but can restore impaired memory and recalibrate inflated confidence. Seven propositions and three long-term conjectures extend these effects to consumer autonomy, competence erosion, and brand loyalty. Together, the CogOffload framework positions advertising in the era of Gen-AI as operating within a distributed system of human and artificial cognition.

title: Crafting Mixed Methods Research in Procurement and Supply Chain Management
journal_name: Journal of Purchasing and Supply Management

title: Standard setters’ use of qualitative characteristics in fair value standards: a Derridean analysis
abstract: Qualitative characteristics (QCs) are accounting concepts stated in standard setters' conceptual frameworks, which are intended to guide their standard-setting decisions. This paper explores how the FASB and IASC/IASB used their primary QCs (relevance, reliability and faithful representation) in their fair value standards. Drawing on Derrida's notion of iterability, we analyse how and why these QCs were reiterated in different contexts to promote, defend and retreat from fair value. Our findings show that QCs are not fixed concepts, but rather evolve through reiteration across different standard-setting contexts. This malleability enables the Boards to justify standard-setting decisions as their preferences evolve. Our research contributes to the literature on conceptual frameworks by identifying the flexible use of QCs in standard setting as a subtle mode of standard setters' legitimacy work, while also showing that these reiterations shape, and sometimes subsequently reverse, revisions of conceptual frameworks. Ultimately, we reveal that neither conceptual frameworks nor standards act as fixed reference points for the meanings of QCs, which are mutually deferred in an endless process of reiteration.

title: Algorithmic justice in AI-driven human resource management: Implications for workplace well-being and affective commitment
abstract: Human resource functions are increasingly mediated, and sometimes directly governed, by algorithmic systems, yet little is known about how employees’ fairness perceptions of these systems relate to their workplace well-being and affective commitment. Drawing on organizational justice and social exchange theories and survey data from 307 employees in the Australian financial and insurance sector, we establish algorithmic human resource management (AHRM) justice as a multidimensional construct comprising distributive, procedural, interpersonal, and informational justice. We argue that AHRM does not simply place these dimensions in a new context but reconfigures the social exchange conditions under which justice perceptions form. AHRM justice was positively associated with workplace well-being and, both directly and indirectly through well-being, with affective commitment; informational justice emerged as particularly salient. Self-perceived AI understanding did not moderate these relationships. The findings extend the ensemble view of algorithmic HRM and support a human-centric approach to AI-driven people management.

title: Restoring legitimacy under resource constraints: The impact of data breaches on corporate social responsibility
Enhancing or Transcending the Pipeline? How Incumbents Transition Toward Marketplace Platforms
abstract: ABSTRACT Business‐to‐business incumbents whose value creation rests on pipeline business models increasingly launch their own marketplace platforms. Yet how these business model transitions toward marketplace platforms unfold, and what they imply for the pipeline model, remains poorly understood. Adopting a cognitive perspective on managerial interpretations and decisions, we conduct a comparative case study of five marketplace platforms launched by incumbents in the European industrial products industry. We find that platform competition and the opportunities managers perceive in business‐to‐consumer platforms trigger platform creation, after which incumbents follow one of two pathways. In pipeline‐enhancing transitions, managers locate future value in the existing pipeline model and adopt platform features that strengthen it, resulting in cognitive alignment and interconnected platform–pipeline business models. In pipeline‐transcending transitions, managers locate future value in the marketplace platform and use business‐to‐consumer marketplaces as a reference point. This generates cognitive tensions with the pipeline model that ultimately resolve into independent pipeline and marketplace platform business models. Which pathway unfolds depends on the customer segments served, which shape managers' reference points for interpreting the evolving platform business model. Our process model explains these divergent outcomes and contributes to innovation management research on business model transitions toward platforms and their cognitive dynamics.

title: Orchestrating inter-organizational technology networks to build data analytics capability: the case of a professional service firm
abstract: Purpose This study examines how professional service firms (PSFs) orchestrate inter-organizational technology networks to develop data analytics capability. Adopting an organizational information processing perspective, we examine how PSFs vary orchestration modes across networks to mobilize distributed resources and increase their information-processing capacity. Design/methodology/approach We conducted a longitudinal single-case study of a global PSF in the UK construction sector, triangulating 37 interviews with observations and project documentation. Using an abductive theory-elaboration approach, we explain how the PSF accessed, bundled and leveraged network-embedded resources to build analytics capability. Findings We identify three interrelated components of analytics capability: data capture, data transformation and processing, and data visualization and interpretation. Closed-mode orchestration enabled standardized data capture across the supply network; hybrid orchestration combined broad open engagement with selective closure to integrate technological expertise from SMEs; and open-mode orchestration within the client network fostered use-case elicitation, sensemaking and interpretive alignment. We theorize how inter-organizational network orchestration enables PSFs to assemble information-processing capacity from distributed data, technical expertise and interpretive requirements, thereby improving fit between information-processing needs and capacity. Originality/value We conceptualize analytics capability as a composite inter-organizational capability assembled across organizational boundaries. We extend Organizational information processing theory by showing how information-processing capacity can be assembled across networks of external actors through inter-organizational network orchestration, and advance network orchestration research by identifying a contingency logic linking orchestration mode to the coordination conditions surrounding distributed resources.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: The Organizational Benefits of Neurodiversity: A Strategic Human Capital–Based Systematic Review and Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT There is growing interest in neurodiversity across multiple research domains, including human resource management (HRM). Within HRM research, discussions of neurodiversity have increasingly extended beyond inclusion as an ethical concern to raise questions about potential organizational benefits. However, there is limited clarity regarding how such benefits have been examined within the HRM literature. This paper addresses this issue through a strategic human capital–informed systematic review of 88 studies on HRM and neurodiversity. Our findings show that existing research provides a growing body of insights into potential organizational benefits. However, empirical evidence at the organizational level remains limited and uneven. Building on these findings, we propose a future research agenda focused on the organizational value of human capital associated with neurodivergence and the processes through which such value emerges, highlighting the need for more quantitative studies assessing organizational‐level outcomes and qualitative research unpacking emergence processes. We further develop an extended emergence perspective by showing how the recognition, creation, and realization of value shape the transformation of neurodivergent individual capacities into organizational‐level human capital resources. In doing so, the paper contributes to strategic human capital theory by offering a structured framework for understanding emergence processes, while highlighting neurodiversity as a particularly informative context for examining the conditions under which they occur.

title: How economic policy uncertainty spreads across borders: The case of Latin America
abstract: Latin America’s growth has been hindered by institutional instability and volatile economic policies, often driven by political cycles. These shifts generate uncertainty that deters investment and disrupts productivity. We analyze this phenomenon using Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) indices, assessing their impact on domestic macroeconomic variables via regional spillovers - spurred by regional proximity - and also considering the global transmission of EPU shocks to key trade and financial partners. To do so, we assemble a comprehensive and comparable database of EPU indices for the region: first, we construct new indices for Bolivia, Ecuador, Paraguay, Uruguay and Venezuela, and second, we update the ones available in other papers for Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru using a comparable methodology. Our results show that: (i) regional EPU shocks reduce regional GDP growth, deter capital inflows and spark exchange rate instability; (ii) Brazil and Mexico are key sources of uncertainty spillovers within the region; and (iii) EPU shocks in Latin America affect financial and real variables in major partner economies, with Spain being particularly exposed.

title: A heterogeneous-agent model for the latin american financial market
The Effect of Clients’ Financial Resources, Mental Health, and Motivation on Frontline Workers’ Burden Reduction and Prioritizations
abstract: Abstract The street-level bureaucracy literature shows that frontline workers’ decisions about clients are shaped by perceptions of deservingness based on clients’ demographic characteristics and behavioral conduct. Yet, we know little about whether frontline workers also act on clients’ financial resources and mental health, despite the administrative burden literature identifying these two factors as central to how citizens experience compliance demands. We contribute to both literatures by developing and testing preregistered hypotheses that examine how information about clients’ financial resources and mental health shapes frontline workers’ burden reduction and client prioritization. To do this, we run a large-scale vignette experiment with 775 caseworkers across 39 Danish unemployment agencies, manipulating client age, financial situation, mental health, and motivation but holding gender constant (all clients were male). We find strong evidence that caseworkers reduce burdens and prioritize clients with mental health issues and–consistent with prior work–clients displaying high motivation, alongside some evidence for clients struggling with financial hardship. Importantly, mental health appears more consequential than motivation and financial resources. Contrary to our preregistered expectation, clients with mental health issues received the most support when they also displayed low as opposed to high motivation. Rather than indicating that frontline workers reward low motivation, this pattern most likely reflects that caseworkers interpret low motivation as a symptom of the underlying condition, and thus as a signal of greater need. Our findings show how frontline discretion can operate as a redistributive mechanism that channels support toward clients signaling the greatest need.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Crossing the Design–Use Divide: How Organizations Select Innovations to Adopt
abstract: Prior scholarship on technology and organizations has focused either on how innovations are designed or how they are used, often assuming that successful selection stems from successful design. But this assumption has limited our understanding of patterns of resistance and advocacy that can influence how and whether innovations reach organizations in the first place. To explore these patterns, this study asks, how does selection unfold within organizations, and what are the consequences of this process for the design and use of innovations? Drawing on a two-year ethnographic study, I examine how entrepreneurs piloted their AI-based innovations with potential adopting organizations. Rather than testing for learning or generalizability, organizations set up committees that engaged in process manipulation by narrowing the scope of pilots, controlling conversations, assigning pilot responsibility, and using goal claiming to align pilot outcomes with committees’ majority preferences. Committees with more adversarial members designed pilots that tested advanced aspects of entrepreneurs’ innovations, hoping for failure. Committees with a majority that championed the innovations tested basic aspects, ensuring success. While pilots run by champions mostly succeeded, these innovations faced more resistance later, during implementation, than did innovations piloted successfully by adversaries. This study shows that innovation is endogenous to selection, and reveals that champions can temper innovation, while adversaries can enable it.

title: Organizational sensemaking and AI adoption in U.S. local governments
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering public administration, yet adoption across U.S. local governments remains uneven. Existing explanations emphasize structural capacity, expecting internal barriers to constrain adoption. Drawing on Weick’s sensemaking perspective as an interpretive lens, this study examines AI adoption as shaped by how organizations interpret technological opportunity and enact deliberate responses. Using the 2024 ICMA Artificial Intelligence Survey, this study tests whether internal barriers, AI potential, and organizational initiative explain variation in adoption. Findings show that internal barriers are not significantly associated with adoption, whereas AI potential and organizational initiative are positively associated with it. These findings suggest that in equivocal technological contexts, structural conditions operate through interpretive processes, and that what organizations possess shapes adoption through how they make sense of emerging technologies and mobilize action. This study demonstrates the analytical value of sensemaking as a framework for understanding public sector responses to technological change.

title: Resolving institutional fragmentation in a multilevel governance system: configurational logics of social health insurance integration in China
abstract: Institutional fragmentation poses a significant challenge to effective social governance, particularly in the health sector. Prevailing literature often examines the drivers of integration – such as fiscal capacity and political will – in a linear, isolated manner, failing to capture their complex interplay. This study argues for a configurational approach to understanding institutional integration. Using the integration of China’s fragmented social health insurance system as a critical case, we employ fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to analyse a large sample of 251 cities in their varying integration pathways. The analytical framework captures capacity and incentives as critical factors for institutional integration. The QCA analysis identifies four distinct configurations: the Capacitor, the Stabilizer, the Risk Manager, and the Negotiator. These findings suggest multiple equifinal pathways to successful institutional integration, highlighting the crucial conjunctural effects of economic strength, administrative status, coordinative capacity, and financial conditions.

title: When negative control exposures fail to detect bias
abstract: Abstract Researchers increasingly utilize negative control exposures (NCEs), variables known to have no effect on the outcome, to detect residual confounding. However, an NCE analysis may provide little evidence of confounding despite substantial bias in the estimated exposure effect. We study, analytically and via simulations, how the magnitude and source of exposure-NCE association affect the large-sample NCE coefficient and statistical power of regression-based bias-detection. We show that the power does not always increase with bias, and that stronger confounder-exposure associations can increase bias while reducing the NCE coefficient and power. Furthermore, the correlation between the exposure of interest and the NCE is insufficient to characterize how well the NCE will detect confounding. Additional exposure-NCE common causes that affect the outcome only through the exposure can attenuate the NCE coefficient toward zero or reverse its sign, even when confounding bias remains unchanged. These changes can occur even when the overall exposure-NCE correlation is fixed. Adjusting for such common causes alleviated sign reversal in our simulations but did not uniformly improve power. Negative controls can be a powerful tool to detect unmeasured confounding. Researchers should consider the sources of exposure-NCE association and interpret null or counterintuitive NCE findings with caution.

title: Prevention of mpox by JYNNEOS vaccination: a case-control study comparing test-negative and alternative-disease control populations
abstract: Abstract Risk-based vaccine recommendations complicate observational studies of vaccine effectiveness (VE), since recipients and non-recipients may differ in infection risk and likelihood of testing. For JYNNEOS—recommended for men who have sex with men at high mpox risk—prior studies have used differing control populations to estimate VE, with uncertain comparability. We conducted a multi-armed case-control study enrolling mpox cases (N=198), monkeypox virus (MPXV)-negative controls (N=208), and gonorrhea controls (N=155) reported to the California Department of Public Health between November 2022 and October 2024, conducting telephone interviews to capture behavioral risk data typically absent from surveillance and administrative records. Among recipients of 2 pre-exposure JYNNEOS doses, adjusted VE was 89.9% (95% CI, 69.6–96.7%) versus test-negative controls and 92.0% (70.6–97.8%) versus gonorrhea controls. Without behavioral adjustment, however, VE estimates using MPXV-negative controls were lower (50.4–65.4%) than those using gonorrhea controls (61.3–71.3%). Controls diagnosed with an alternative sexually transmitted infection may offer a better comparison group than test-negative controls for JYNNEOS VE studies based on disease surveillance or administrative records, although collection of risk factor data may be necessary to mitigate bias under either design.

title: Why some emergency maneuvers succeed: Interpretable behavior graphs from expert drivers to automated control
The impact of an attorney guardian ad litem program on case disposition and custody agreements in domestic violence protective order cases
Effectiveness of school-based interventions in preventing violence against girls in low- and middle-income countries: Systematic review
abstract: Background Violence against girls remains a major public health challenge in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), and schools represent a critical platform for primary prevention. Objective To review the effectiveness of school-based interventions for preventing violence against girls in LMICs systematically. Methods Seven databases were searched from inception to April 5, 2025, supplemented by grey literature searches. Eligible studies were intervention trials or longitudinal observational studies with a control arm in LMICs reporting sex-disaggregated outcomes for school-based interventions targeting physical, sexual, emotional violence, bullying and cyberbullying against girls. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; narrative synthesis and vote counting based on direction of effect were conducted. The review is registered with the Open Science Framework. Results Twenty-seven articles reporting 29 interventions met the inclusion criteria: 11 curriculum-based, seven multilevel, six single-component, and five multicomponent interventions. Evidence from curriculum-based empowerment self-defence programmes indicated the most consistent favourable effects on sexual violence victimisation. By contrast, multicomponent and multilevel interventions had broader but more heterogeneous potential to prevent victimisation and perpetration. Across intervention types, effects on bullying were predominantly favourable direction. Measurement of victimisation and perpetration was unbalanced, with sexual violence perpetration substantially underrepresented. No eligible studies were identified from the Central Africa, Caribbean, or Pacific Island countries. Conclusions School-based interventions show potential to reduce violence against girls, with curriculum-based approaches offering the most consistent short-term benefits in preventing sexual violence victimisation. Effectiveness of multilevel and multicomponent interventions remains heterogeneous, and evidence on sustainability and scalability is limited across intervention types.

title: The Art of Masturbation: An Analysis on the History and Theory of Self-Pleasure in the Renaissance
Measurement Invariance and Prevalence of Sexual Harassment Among University Students in Jordan
Assessing the Role of Board, Culture and Environmental Complexity on Performance Information Use in Nonprofit Organizations
abstract: Despite growing expectations for Nonprofit Organizations to implement performance measurement, empirical research on its actual use remains limited. To address such a gap, this study investigates the decision-facilitating use of performance information focusing on environmental complexities, the role of the board of directors, and organizational culture. The empirical setting is provided by Nonprofit Organizations located in the province of Bergamo (Italy) to which a survey was administered. The analysis shows that environmental complexity does not directly increase the use of performance information. Rather, it operates indirectly through an externally oriented board and a flexible culture, both serving as bridges that connect external pressures to internal systems.

title: Emulate the Leader? Explaining Crisis Policy Change in the Canadian Federal System
abstract: ABSTRACT In times of crises, do governments coordinate or do they make their own choices independent of what others do? Convergence of COVID‐19 policy at the beginning of the pandemic has been widely studied in federal countries. Yet, there is limited literature looking at the mechanisms that made policy between jurisdictions so similar. Utilizing Canada's decentralized federal system, this paper posits that convergence can be explained by a process of policy diffusion through emulation and a series of leader‐follower relationships. Drawing on the policy diffusion literature, this paper proposes three hypotheses for why some jurisdictions take on leadership roles in crisis policy while others follow. Synthesized as proximity, capacity, and urgency, these hypotheses are tested using a series of pairwise vector autoregressions identifying significant leader‐follower relationships between Canadian provinces. The findings suggest that policy primarily flowed from only a small number of large provinces (Quebec and Ontario), lending partial evidence, but also exceptions to the hypotheses proposed.

Compound effects of traffic and climate on electric vehicle HVAC energy consumption: a spatiotemporal framework with city-level attribution
abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) energy consumption in real-world driving departs significantly from rated values due to the joint influence of ambient temperature, traffic congestion, and route characteristics. Existing studies typically evaluate these factors in isolation or under static conditions, leaving their compound effect on HVAC energy unquantified. This study develops a spatiotemporal simulation framework that couples traffic-aware driving speed, location- and time-specific ambient temperature, and physics-based energy submodels (cabin HVAC, traction, and battery thermal management) at the segment level, and decomposes HVAC energy variability into its temperature and trip-duration components per route. The framework is applied through a structured comparative design across seven UK cities and eight radial routes, varying departure time, regional climate, and road-network type. While total energy consumption varies by 14% across cities, the HVAC component varies by up to 89%, identifying cabin thermal management as the primary differentiator between routes in winter. The decomposition attributes 79–85% of London’s above-average HVAC energy to its extended trip duration rather than to temperature, the range reflecting how the temperature–time interaction is allocated; a same-route counterfactual shows that departure-time congestion accounts for about half of this excess duration and the network’s typical operating speed for the remainder. These attributions are robust to temperature, parameter, and correlated stochastic uncertainties, and the inter-city spread collapses in summer as heating demand vanishes. The decomposition yields a closed-form model estimating HVAC energy from three inputs (ambient temperature, average speed, and trip distance) with physical interpretability and negligible computational cost. Demonstrated for a heat-pump vehicle under UK winter conditions, the framework transfers to other vehicles and regions by re-fitting three coefficients, although the dominance of trip duration is specific to the narrow temperature range and high congestion studied. These findings indicate that the energy intensity of real-world EV operation, and hence achievable range, is substantially shaped by traffic and road-network characteristics.
