Conservation governance challenges in the Karakoram: Analyzing the institutional transitions of Central Karakoram National Park, Pakistan
abstract: Global commitments to conserve 30% of land by 2030 place renewed emphasis on protected areas (PAs), yet governance shortcomings and distributional conflicts often undermine both conservation and socio-economic development outcomes. This paper examines PA governance in Central Karakoram National Park (CKNP), Pakistan’s largest national park in Gilgit-Baltistan (GB), a region marked by constitutional ambiguity, contested land tenure, and infrastructure-driven market integration. Using a historical institutionalist lens, we examine CKNP’s historical trajectories and critical junctures, institutional continuity and change, input and output legitimacy, and implications for co-management. We combine archival and institutional analysis of legislation and management plans with field observations, semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions involving state agencies, park authorities, NGOs, and local communities in seven buffer-zone valleys. We find that administrative reforms and departmental restructuring shifted conservation authority to GB, while participatory, zoning, sustainable-use, and benefit-sharing provisions were layered onto a centralized, exclusionary 1975 legal framework. Input legitimacy remains constrained by uneven consultation, limited decision-making influence, and inadequate information for meaningful participation, whereas output legitimacy is weakened by limited implementation capacity associated with chronic understaffing, project dependence, and limited public financing. Dispersed implementation responsibilities and unresolved property and access rights concerns undermine both decision-making processes and governance performance, leaving co-management largely consultative and uneven. We conclude that co-management could be advanced through valley-level forums with clear decision-making mandates and representation, strengthened and trusted field staffing, sustained public resourcing, and transparent and equitable benefit-sharing. The study highlights how frontier conditions, historical institutional legacies, and valley-specific dynamics shape PA governance.

title: Harnessing wind energy for rural development: the state-orchestrated approach to realizing community energy in rural China
Wind energy acceptance and forest owners’ land-leasing intentions: The role of beliefs and attitudes
abstract: The expansion of wind power plays a crucial role in the European Union's decarbonization strategy. However, the social acceptance of wind power projects, particularly among landowners and non-landowners, remains a significant concern. Drawing on behavioural insights of the social acceptance literature, this study examines the beliefs, attitudes, and behavioural intentions of these groups towards wind power. We focus on the national context of Finland, where wind energy development has accelerated in recent years. Utilizing survey data from 2,103 respondents, including forest owners and non-forest owners, the study employs Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) and regression models to explore how beliefs shape attitudes, policy support and forest owners' behavioural intentions. The acceptance measures indicate that non-forest owners held more favourable attitudes towards wind power, associating it with environmental benefits and economic opportunities, while forest owners expressed greater concerns about landscape changes, land ownership, and economic impacts. The SEM model reveals that attitudes toward wind power were strongly influenced by beliefs about energy production and local impacts, which, in turn, shaped policy support. Additionally, forest owners’ willingness to lease land for wind turbines was associated with higher income level, owned land area size, and positive attitudes towards wind power. These findings highlight the need for tailored landscape-orientated policies that address explicitly address landowners’ concerns while fostering broader societal support for wind power. Enhancing procedural and distributive justice, improving compensation mechanisms, and integrating participatory planning processes could help accommodate resistance and facilitate a just energy transition.

Highly Selective Lithium Extraction from Shale Gas Wastewater Using Al- and F-Doped LiMn2O4 Electrode in Rocking-Chair Capacitive Deionization
abstract: Abstract Selective lithium extraction from shale gas wastewater (SGW) offers a promising strategy to expand lithium supply while reducing wastewater-management burdens. However, low Li+ concentrations and overwhelming competition from Na+ and Mg2+ make selective and energy-efficient extraction challenging. Lithium manganese oxide (LMO) is attractive for electrochemical Li extraction but remains limited by insufficient cycling stability and selectivity in complex ionic matrices. Here, we investigate the effects of Al and F modification of LMO on lithium extraction in a rocking-chair capacitive deionization system. Structural and spectroscopic characterizations show that the optimized modification contracts the spinel lattice and produces near-surface enrichment of F-containing species, improving electrochemical reversibility. Electrochemical analyses and density functional theory calculations further indicate favorable Li+ transport and stronger migration restrictions for Na+ and Mg2+ after lattice entry. In a simulated SGW matrix with a Li/Na/Mg molar ratio of 1:100:1, LMO-Al-F achieves a Li adsorption capacity of 9.54 mg g–1, Li/Na and Li/Mg separation factors of 2216 and 1509, and an energy consumption of 4.21 Wh mol–1 Li. Strong Li selectivity is also maintained in real SGW. After 100 competitive-ion cycles, 78% of adsorption capacity is retained, supporting repeated Li-selective extraction under high-salinity conditions.

title: Water Footprint and Scarcity Risks of Low-Carbon Fuels
abstract: Abstract Production of ammonia, methanol, and hydrogen is key to decarbonizing hard-to-electrify sectors but is also water-intensive. However, the water implications of scaling these energy carriers under low-carbon pathways remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate direct water consumption with facility-level geospatial analysis and hydrological modeling to quantify water-scarcity exposure across each production facility in North America. Low-carbon production routes require more direct and indirect water consumption than conventional pathways, with electrolytic hydrogen and e-methanol increasing water-intensity by up to 5-fold in regions with limited renewable availability─a trade-off further amplified by supply chain effects, particularly for solar PV-based electricity and direct air capture-based CO2 feedstocks. Water scarcity already affects about 58% of methanol production in Mexico, 2% of ammonia production in the U.S., and 5% and 27% of refinery production in the U.S. and Mexico, respectively. Under midcentury climate scenarios, exposure increases in both magnitude and spatial extent. Although irrigation accounts for over 80% of local water consumption in various fuel production facilities, municipalities and manufacturing often exert the greatest pressure on low-carbon fuel production, depending on the product and country.. These results demonstrate that technology choice, system design, and facility siting are as important as hydrology considerations in determining water risks. Incorporating water availability in low-carbon fuel projects is therefore essential to ensure that decarbonization pathways are scalable, operationally resilient, and truly sustainable.

title: Calibration of Passive Sampling Eyewear to Assess Inhalation Exposure
abstract: Abstract Calibrated wearable passive air samplers are critical tools for accessibly quantifying individualized and population exposures to airborne pollution, a leading cause of chronic disease. Our lab recently introduced passive sampling eyewear (PSE) to address gaps in tools tailored for measuring and mitigating risks from inhalation exposure. The PSE, like most existing designs of wearable samplers, is largely uncalibrated. An exception is the polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) brooch, and mini-polyurethane foam (PUF) samplers, which have been calibrated for only 27 compounds. Here, we calibrate PSE against active air samplers codeployed in both stationary and wearable forms in office and home environments to capture a wide range of exposure scenarios. We report sampling rates (RS) and inhalation exposure for over 200 features covering diverse physical-chemical properties measured using the Orbitrap gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC–MS) system in both targeted and nontargeted modes. RS were 0.70 ± 0.62 m3 day–1 dm–2 for stationary and 0.85 ± 0.68 m3 day–1 dm–2 for wearable deployments, with no significant difference (p = 0.06) between the deployment types. Wearable calibration captured higher RS and variability, as expected for personal sampling, because participants’ movement and daily activity can alter airflow and disrupt the stagnant air-boundary layer around the sampler. In terms of analysis mode, RS derived from targeted and nontargeted analysis (NTA) were reasonably comparable for a given compound, differing by ∼1.5-fold, boosting confidence in using NTA approaches for expanding databases of RS. Applying the wearable RS, the profiles and levels of inhalation exposure varied widely between participants when at home versus in offices, reflecting differences in exposure sources and dynamics between the two environments. Overall, the findings from both the calibration and field studies represent a significant step toward quantitatively assessing inhalation exposure using PSE.

title: Atmospheric Aging Modifies the Toxicological Profile of Biomass Burning Particles in Epithelial Lung Cells
abstract: Abstract Wildfire activity and associated smoke emissions are increasing globally, leading to widespread exposure to biomass burning particulate matter (PM). Although people are mainly exposed to aged wildfire smoke rather than fresh emissions, the effects of atmospheric aging on wildfire particulate toxicity remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how atmospheric processing (“aging”) modifies biological effects of biomass burning particles (BBPs) generated under controlled flaming and smoldering combustion conditions. BB emissions were produced in the Photochemical Large Aerosol Chamber (PHOTO-LAC) and aged under alternating photochemical and dark conditions. Fresh and aged BBP extracts were subsequently sampled and tested in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B). We assessed cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, oxidative DNA damage, genome-wide transcriptional responses, and inflammatory and extracellular matrix-related protein expression. Atmospheric aging substantially altered BBP toxicity in a combustion-dependent manner. Aged BBP enhanced intracellular reactive oxygen species formation and oxidative DNA damage, particularly for smoldering emissions, while cytotoxicity remained largely unchanged. In contrast, inflammatory and matrix-remodeling responses were attenuated with aging in smoldering particles but remained stable for flaming BBP. These findings demonstrate that atmospheric aging can simultaneously amplify oxidative and genotoxic stress while dampening inflammatory signaling, underscoring the need to incorporate aging state into health risk assessments of wildfire smoke exposure.

title: Coupled Geophysical and Technoeconomic Industrial Growth Constraints on Geological Carbon Storage Scale-Up: Application to UK Offshore Resources
abstract: Abstract Geological carbon dioxide storage is central to meeting many national climate change commitments, but large-scale deployment may be limited by both techno-economic rates of growth and physics-based processes imposed by subsurface geology. We develop a modeling framework for the assessment of feasible CO2 storage scale-up trajectories that unifies constraints arising from industrial rates of growth, dynamic injection rate limits from reservoir pressurization, and static maximum cumulative storage resource. We employ logistic and Gompertz models to represent policy-compliant deployment trajectories, parametrized by the total cumulative storage resource. We then use a simplified physics model to estimate the resulting regional subsurface pressurization along these trajectories. Growth curves where reservoir pressurization exceeds safe limits are updated by reducing the static storage resource until residing in the safe deployment range. The result is both a growth trajectory and static storage resource achievable subject to injectivity limits. Applying the framework to the United Kingdom (UK), we find that offshore storage resources are sufficient to accommodate all government midcentury deployment rate scenarios up to 175 Mt yr–1. Cumulative storage of up to 78 Gt, representing a reference estimate of the UK storage resource base used in national planning, can be achieved under Gompertz growth trajectories. The more aggressive logistic trajectories are constrained by reservoir pressure, limiting the achievable resource base to 69 Gt. The framework is transferable to other regions to assess the feasibility of policy-driven CO2 storage pathways under coupled industrial growth and geophysical constraints, informing national decarbonization planning and global integrated assessment models.

title: Fingerprints of Airborne Plastics in Urban PM2.5: Applications and Implications
abstract: Abstract To better identify emission sources of airborne plastics, we employed nine plastic-associated chemicals (PlsACs) in 240 daily PM2.5 samples collected in Singapore during 2018–2020. A unique PlsAC, tris(2,4-ditert-butylphenyl) phosphate (I168O), is most abundant, accounting for 90% of the total quantified PlsACs and identifying at least 40% more PM2.5 linked to respirable airborne PlsACs. A newly resolved source of plastic production, use, and burning (PlasticPub) accounts for the highest fraction (37%) of the quantified PlsACs among the seven apportioned PM2.5 sources. Nearly all di-iso-butyl phthalate (DIBP) and more than half of di-n-butyl phthalate (DNBP) are attributed to two factors of Background and Marine aerosols, indicating their potential worldwide transport. More than 90% of diethyl phthalate (DEP) is associated with transported peat forest (PF) burning smoke, demonstrating involvement of anthropogenic activities. Following PlasticPub, Traffic & road dust is the second predominant source responsible for >20% of the near-range PlsACs and featured with a DNBP/di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP) concentration ratio of 2.2. The DNBP/DEHP concentration ratio higher than 1 can indicate nonexhaust emissions from on-road traffic due to abrasion of tires, brakes, and road markings. The average enrichment ratio of quantified PlsACs within PM2.5 (ng PlsACs per μg PM2.5) for each resolved source provides a basis for assessing strategies to cocontrol airborne plastics and PM2.5.

title: Free-Radical Cascade Mediates Humus Formation in Mineral-Rich Organic Matrices
abstract: Abstract Humus formation in nature is traditionally viewed as a lengthy microbial enzymatic process, yet the abiotic pathways remain unclear. Here, by employing iron-mineral-rich composting as a model system that amplifies and accelerates natural humification, we reveal a free-radical cascade that drives abiotic humification. Magnetite addition amplified hydroxyl radical (•OH) production 1.5-fold (1289.4 μmol·kg–1) and enriched humus precursors (amino acids, polyphenols, reducing sugars), ultimately yielding 1.5 times more humic acid (135.6 mg/g) with higher molecular weight and stronger aromatic condensation. Mass spectrometry combined with density functional theory calculations identified multiple environmentally persistent free radicals (EPFRs), including semiquinone and phenoxy radicals as key intermediates that couple precursors into macromolecular humus. Simulated transformation experiments with selective microbial inactivation and •OH scavenging demonstrated that the abiotic radical pathway contributed approximately 33.4% to humus formation. We propose a free-radical cascade: •OH-driven oxidative fragmentation of organic matter followed by EPFR-mediated humus precursors coupling. These findings establish an unrecognized abiotic dimension of humification, reshaping our mechanistic understanding of organic carbon stabilization and offering nature-based strategies for soil carbon sequestration and remediation in organic-mineral interaction environments.

title: Context-Aware Multitask Learning for Aquatic and Soil Ecotoxicity Prediction from Fragmented ECOTOX Records
abstract: Abstract Large ecotoxicity databases contain extensive evidence, yet heterogeneous reporting and sparse coverage across chemicals, species, end points, and conditions limit predictive use. From relational U.S. EPA ECOTOX, we linked 1,234,077 traceable records and constructed model-ready aquatic and soil data sets of 219,818 and 11,532 records. We developed a context-aware multitask model that preserves end point-specific responses while sharing information across molecular, biological, and experimental contexts. On held-out condition keys and parent-species-task combinations, four-seed ensembles achieved pooled R2 of 0.758/0.751 for aquatic toxicity and 0.628/0.537 for soil toxicity. Compared with same-input single-task models, multitask fitting reduced soil task-macro mean absolute error (MAE) by 0.136/0.156 across 16 task heads; aquatic point estimates also favored sharing, although uncertainty across all aquatic task heads was not estimable. Under canonical-parent holdout, frozen shared representations reduced task-macro MAE by 0.170–0.180 in aquatic and 0.093–0.125 in soil tree models versus molecular-only inputs, indicating reusable predictive information. Multidimensional training support stratified parent-holdout errors, meeting prespecified criteria fully for soil and partially for aquatic predictions; benefits weakened under stronger structural separation. These results show model-ready ECOTOX data can support context-aware toxicity prediction across a sparse experimental matrix, helping prioritize informative measurements and providing a predictive evidence base for environmental hazard assessment.

title: Modeling Decadal Organosulfates in Particulate Matter to Improve Estimations of Aerosol Hygroscopicity in the United States
abstract: Abstract Organosulfates (OSs) can comprise a substantial fraction of secondary organic aerosol and exhibit significantly different hygroscopicity than inorganic sulfates, yet their spatiotemporal prevalence and climatic impacts remain poorly constrained because speciated measurements are sparse and common chemical transport models do not explicitly represent OS formation. This study develops a flexible and robust modeling framework to quantify isoprene-derived OS (iOS) concentrations and OS impacts on aerosol hygroscopicity (κ) across the contiguous United States (U.S.) for summers spanning 2013–2022. Using the Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) model with updated iOS chemistry, simulations reproduce Interagency Monitoring of Protected Visual Environments (IMPROVE) network-derived organosulfur and inorganic sulfate and agree with speciated iOS measurements from filter analyses. OS concentrations are elevated in the eastern U.S., with summertime mean values up to 0.51 μg m–3. OS formation produces a net 5.6% decrease in κ (direct OS contribution, +2.8%; indirect, −8.4% via sulfate reduction). We apply an interpretable machine-learning surrogate to identify predictive features associated with OS variability and enable efficient estimation without rerunning CMAQ. These results provide the first observation-validated, high-spatial-coverage OS reconstruction and nationwide quantification of OS-driven κ changes, underscoring the importance of representing OS formation and expanded observations to improve aerosol-cloud radiative effect assessments.

title: Molecular Insights into a Precursor–Chlorine Trade-Off Governing Divergent Formation Pathways of PCDD/Fs and Emerging Cl-PAHs in Waste Cocombustion of Cellulose, PET, and PVC
abstract: Abstract Co-combustion of industrial and municipal solid waste (ISW/MSW) is widely practiced, yet PCDD/Fs and emerging chlorinated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (Cl-PAHs) formation under mixed-feedstock conditions remains poorly understood. Here, cellulose, polyethylene terephthalate (PET), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) were combusted individually and cocombusted with MSW to elucidate how feedstock chemistry regulates chlorinated pollutant formation. Comprehensive mass-spectrometric profiling of target pollutants, aromatic precursors, and the top 50 combustion intermediates, combined with DFT calculations, revealed a precursor–chlorine trade-off governing pollutant formation. PET preferentially generated oxygenated aromatic intermediates, particularly dibenzofuran; PVC supplied the most PAHs and reactive chlorine, and cellulose primarily contributed carbon skeletons. Accordingly, two distinct pathways were proposed: dibenzofuran-centered, chlorination-limited formation of PCDD/Fs and stepwise aromatic growth followed by site-selective chlorination of Cl-PAHs. The higher HOMO energies of two representative PAHs, anthracene and phenanthrene, relative to dibenzofuran indicated their greater susceptibility to electrophilic chlorination. Consequently, Cl-PAHs exceeded PCDD/Fs by 1–3 orders of magnitude and accounted for 83.4% of estimated TEQ. Increasing chlorine availability alleviated the kinetic constraint on dibenzofuran chlorination, causing an approximately 42-fold increase in PCDD/F emissions at 20% PVC blending. These findings establish a molecular basis for feedstock-chemistry-guided management and broaden emission-control priorities from regulated PCDD/Fs to emerging Cl-PAHs.

title: Hydrophilic Nanoisland Interface Engineering for Conquering Activity–Stability Trade-Off in High-Efficiency Salt Lake Lithium Extraction
abstract: Abstract The adsorption-based lithium extraction technology from ultralow-grade salt lake brine is severely restricted by the inherent activity–stability trade-off of traditional granular Li/Al-LDHs adsorbents (GLDHs). Herein, a nanoisland encapsulation strategy integrated with hydrophilic interface engineering is developed to fabricate Li/Al-LDHs composite granules with tailored hydrophilic interfaces (HILDHs), breaking the long-standing bottleneck of conventional aluminum-based lithium adsorbents used in the salt lake industry. Systematic experiments and multiscale simulations reveal that the strong water affinity of polyacrylonitrile cyano groups (−C≡N) creates a highly hydrated microenvironment for rapid Li+ transport, while the nanoisland-confined structure anchors Li/Al-LDHs nanosheets to preserve the layered framework under harsh deep desorption conditions, thus enabling excellent cycling stability. The optimized HILDHs deliver a 3.02-fold higher working adsorption capacity (7.25 mg g–1 vs 2.40 mg g–1 for GLDHs) in actual Qarhan old brine within 60 min, along with a 13.36-fold increase in adsorption rate constant, 40% lower rinsing water consumption, and excellent cycle stability. It is calculated the nanoisland encapsulation strategy can achieve a nearly 5-fold increase for the annual Li2CO3 production capacity from salt lake lithium industrial lines.

title: Polyethylene Terephthalate Oligomers in Disposable Diapers: Occurrence, Dermal Exposure and Health Assessment
abstract: Abstract Disposable infant diapers commonly use multicomponent nonwoven fabrics containing polyethylene terephthalate (PET), from which PET oligomer byproducts may be released and transferred to infant skin. In this study, 6 cyclic PET oligomers (C[TPA+EG]2–7) were detected in the top sheets and absorbent cores of 37 disposable diapers. ∑C[TPA+EG]2–7 averaged 198 ± 98.7 μg/g (top sheets) and 66.6 ± 49.2 μg/g (absorbent cores), dominated by C[TPA+EG]3 (95.9% and 92.3%). Oligomer levels positively correlated with diaper PET content, confirming an in situ polymer source. During a 3-day in-use study, 1348–2318 ng of oligomers migrated to infant buttock skin and remained partially after water washing, corresponding to an estimated C[TPA+EG]3 exposure of 8.80–182 ng/kg BW/day. Network toxicology and molecular docking identified potential targets and pathways associated with local skin effects, including inflammation, barrier regulation, apoptosis, and extracellular matrix remodeling, suggesting potential local skin-health implications. Our results establish diaper dermal contact as a critical infant plastic oligomer exposure route and raise health concerns for vulnerable infant skin.

Environmental and economic assessment of olefin synthesis from waste as an emerging alternative to conventional light olefin production routes
abstract: Light olefins such as ethylene and propylene are essential petrochemical intermediates but remain highly energy- and carbon-intensive to produce using conventional fossil-based technologies. We conduct the life-cycle environmental and economic assessment (LCA/LCC) of seven olefin production pathways, such as coal-based, natural gas-based, shale gas-based, crude oil-based, bio-based, waste-to-olefins and waste-to-olefins with sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis, to understand trade-offs and identify decarbonisation opportunities. A cradle-to-gate LCA employs nine EF 3.1 midpoint indicators, using foreground data from industrial sources, Aspen Plus V14 modelling, and ecoinvent v3.10 inventories. Results show that coal-based olefin production exhibits the highest environmental burdens, particularly for climate change, freshwater ecotoxicity, eutrophication, and water use. Natural gas-based and crude oil-based routes perform better across non-climate categories but remain carbon-intensive. Bio-based olefin production route provides partial climate benefits but is penalised by large land and water requirements. In contrast, waste-to-olefins and waste-to-olefins with sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis achieve net-negative greenhouse gas emissions due to biogenic carbon uptake and integrated CO 2 capture. Sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis further reduces energy demand via in-situ water removal and process intensification, yielding lower GHG emissions (47%), reduced water use by 64%, and improved selectivity compared with conventional waste-to-olefin routes. However, higher impacts persist in ozone depletion and ionising radiation categories, driven by upstream electricity supply chains. Economic analysis indicates that gasification and CO 2 management dominate overall costs, while the sorption-enhanced synthesis adds only a modest incremental cost to waste-to-olefin pathways. Total life cycle costing for waste-to-olefins with sorption-enhanced olefin synthesis falls within EUR 2130 to 3550 t −1 olefin, including environmental cost, competitive with emerging green olefin pathways. Overall, the findings demonstrate that combining waste feedstocks, CO 2 capture, and sorption-enhanced process intensification offers a promising pathway for low-carbon, resource-efficient olefin production, especially within future decarbonised energy systems.

Between symbols and substance: Voluntary impact reporting of funds
abstract: Impact investing has emerged as a prominent investment approach to addressing social and environmental challenges while generating financial returns. Given its dual mandate to generate impact and financial returns, impact investing faces heightened pressures on its legitimacy, making transparent impact reporting essential to counter allegations of impact-washing and to safeguard the credibility of the approach. Despite the growing relevance of impact reporting, little is known about the underlying motivations and reporting strategies of fund managers who voluntarily publish impact reports. Drawing on legitimacy theory, the paper investigates the motivations and reporting strategies behind voluntary impact reporting by fund managers using a sequential exploratory design. First, 13 semi-structured interviews with impact-reporting professionals were analyzed following Grounded Theory principles. Second, a qualitative content analysis of 141 publicly available impact reports was conducted to analyze how reporting strategies are implemented in practice. The findings of the interviews reveal that fund managers’ motivations are driven by a need to show the alignment of profit with purpose, move beyond institutional compliance, and foster impact reflexivity. These motivations are operationalized through six reporting strategies: rationalization, contextualization, verification, institutionalization, participation, and transformation, which cluster around the dimensions of justification, integration, and adaptation. The content analysis assesses the potential for more substantive forms of legitimation in individual reporting elements. The paper contributes to legitimacy theory in the context of reporting by demonstrating that reporting strategies are interdependent and to practice by offering practitioners and standard setters a starting point for critically reflecting on the design of impact reporting.

title: Study on variable-speed operating characteristics of the SCO2 Brayton cycle under different shaft configurations
Effect of active grout irrigation in ground heat exchangers with helical-shaped pipe
abstract: Improving the efficiency of ground source heat pumps during their operation is a key aspect to foster their diffusion, and grout irrigation strategies could be valuable solutions to implement for this purpose. However, this strategy is still largely unexplored and needs thorough study. In this work, it is investigated whether the active irrigation of the grout surrounding helical borehole heat exchangers can improve the heat pump seasonal efficiency, and under which conditions this benefit is not offset by the consumption of the irrigation system itself. The effect of variable water content on the properties of a sandy grout was taken into account through empirical correlations reported in the literature and implemented in an open-source CApacity-Resistance Model, named pyCaRM, in order to be updated at each time step. Three main strategies, adopted only in the summer season, were compared against a baseline case over a twenty-year simulation, including the electricity consumption of the auxiliary water supply system. Results showed that, in the best-case scenario, the heat pump seasonal efficiency during cooling mode can improve by about 5.3%, dropping to 4.5% if considering the auxiliary system, at the end of the 20 th year, and that 96 m 3 /borehole/year were necessary to reach these values. As for the energy efficiency in heating mode, its relative reduction is about 2%. The total volume pumped and its source should therefore be taken into account when assessing the strategy, and the different strategies should be implemented according to the building load characteristics to achieve the highest rate of improvement.

title: Soil nitrogen availability as a metabolic switch between microbial autotrophy–heterotrophy balance and soil carbon sequestration
Shotgun metagenomic surveillance of airport wastewater reveals microbial community restructuring and persistence of antimicrobial-resistance determinants after treatment
abstract: Airport wastewater has emerged as a valuable matrix for wastewater-based epidemiology, providing insights into microbial circulation and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) among highly mobile populations. However, the effects of wastewater treatment on the microbial community structure and resistome of airport wastewater have not been comprehensively characterized. Here, we present the first comprehensive metagenomic assessment of paired influent and effluent airport wastewater, enabling characterization of treatment-induced changes in microbial community composition and antimicrobial resistance determinants. Paired influent and effluent wastewater samples were collected from the wastewater treatment plant serving Catania–Fontanarossa Airport (Sicily, Italy). Wastewater treatment significantly reduced microbial richness and induced a consistent shift in community composition, as demonstrated by paired beta-diversity analyses. Proteobacteria became the dominant phylum after treatment, whereas Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes markedly declined. Differential abundance analyses showed enrichment of treatment-associated taxa, including Thauera, Aliiarcobacter and Pseudomonas , accompanied by depletion of gut-associated genera such as Bacteroides, Prevotella and Alistipes . Qualitative resistome profiling indicated partial reduction of several ARG classes but persistence of clinically relevant resistance determinants, particularly those associated with beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, macrolides and sulphonamides. Functional profiling indicated treatment-associated metabolic restructuring; however, no functional features remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. Overall, these findings demonstrate that airport wastewater treatment acts as an ecological filter that substantially restructures microbial communities without completely eliminating antimicrobial resistance signatures. Shotgun metagenomic surveillance of airport wastewater may therefore provide valuable complementary information for monitoring AMR dissemination and microbial dynamics within a One Health framework.

title: Conceptualising corruption in the extractive industries: Evidence from a systematic review
Process-based Monte Carlo cost simulation for offshore wind farm decommissioning: A scenario analysis for the German North Sea
abstract: The decommissioning of offshore wind farms (OWFs) involves complex, multi-stage processes whose costs are subject to substantial uncertainty. With over 2,000 turbines approaching end-of-life in the German Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) alone, reliable cost estimation is essential for operators, regulators, and financial planning. Existing cost models are predominantly deterministic and lack industry-informed input parameters, correlation structures among risk drivers, or comprehensive scenario comparisons. Using a process-based Monte Carlo model with correlated operational and market risks, we estimate the cost distribution of offshore wind farm decommissioning across ten technological and logistical scenarios. Expected net costs in prices of 2022 range from approximately € 242,000 to € 543,000 per decommissioned MW across scenarios. Foundation removal dominates overall costs, accounting for roughly half of total expenditures, while partial decommissioning strategies significantly reduce expected costs. Vessel charter costs dominate. Partial decommissioning scenarios reduce expected costs by 18–27 % relative to the baseline. Feeder logistics concepts increase costs by 48–65 % due to additional vessels and amplified duration uncertainty. The widely used “installation backwards” approach is neither the most cost-effective nor the least risky option. Incorporating correlated risks substantially increases tail risk compared to deterministic estimates, suggesting that current provisioning approaches may underestimate financial exposure. ​

Reparative soil science: Soil, colonialism, and environmental justice between scientific knowledge and local cultures
abstract: Soil is a repository for historical accounts of power, dispossession, and cultural continuity. This paper proposes the development of “reparative soil science,” a new paradigm that combines soil remediation with theories of environmental justice, decolonization, and multi-knowledge systems. We define it as an orientation within soil science that treats the discipline’s own concepts, classifications, and survey conventions as historical products, and that couples the biophysical repair of degraded soils with repair of the rights, relations, and forms of knowledge that colonial land regimes displaced. By analyzing examples from around the world, the paper shows how colonialism and postcolonial land governance have resulted in the devaluation of local epistemologies and the transformation of socioecological systems. Results indicate that successful integration of scientific and Indigenous knowledge requires mutual legitimacy, long-term trust-building, and equitable sharing of decision-making authority and benefits. It is argued that reparative soil science should extend beyond the purely technical rehabilitation of degraded soils to challenge existing structural inequalities and help restore cultural and ecological relationships between humans and the land. Soil is our entry point, but the same reasoning extends to land, territory, and natural resources more broadly. The perspective positions soil science within global agreements such as the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, the Sustainable Development Goals, and Land Degradation Neutrality, and argues for a pluralistic, participatory, and politically aware practice serving both ecological resilience and social repair.

title: An expert-informed framework for participatory soundscape design: From Interviews to co-design application
Urban form typologies in Seoul since 1960: A framework for block-level classification and their changing prevalence over time
abstract: This study proposes a framework for classifying urban form typologies at the block level and examining changes in their prevalence in Seoul since 1960. The study identifies major typologies aligned with urban planning trends and analyzes their morphological characteristics. Key questions addressed include: how many distinct urban form types can be identified in Seoul; what unique features define each type; and how changes in the prevalence of these types over time reflect broader urban development trends. The analytical procedure consisted of three steps. First, block units were defined based on infrastructure boundaries such as arterial roads. Second, eight indicators were established to capture the morphological features of blocks, parcels, streets, and buildings—the fundamental components of urban structure. Third, Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering was applied to classify blocks with similar numerical indicators into five distinct types. The result effectively captures how many morphological features aligned with Seoul’s urban planning objectives by era. Compared with previous typologies, the study integrates multiple scales of urban form and examines changes in typology prevalence across different periods, providing a basis for interpreting the historical process of urbanization.

title: Saving lives or freeing territory? Sacred values and tragic trade-offs in wartime Ukraine
abstract: President Zelensky has asserted: “We do not trade our lands and our people.” Both territorial integrity and human lives are considered ‘sacred values’ in wartime Ukraine, values beyond cost-benefit and exchange calculations. Yet, the human costs of continuing war to retake territory are so great in Ukraine that these sacred values are forced into a tragic trade-off. Using a survey of frontline Ukrainians from 2022 made up of residents and displaced persons equally (n = 1800), this paper shows that how the ‘lives versus territory’ dilemma divided respondents. We examined the degree to which wartime hatred of the Russian leadership and material insecurity explain people’s choices, and the role that personal stress plays as a mediator for these attitudes. The results reveal that respondents with higher levels of stress were more likely to prioritize saving lives over freeing territory. Displaced persons were also more likely to prioritize lives. The respondent’s material insecurity had modest impacts. For those most stressed during wartime, lives come before land.

Fatty acid desaturation controls cellular fate decisions between senescence and ferroptosis
abstract: Summary When subject to damage or stress, cells develop responses in order to maintain tissue homeostasis. Two such decisions are ferroptosis and cellular senescence, but how cells decide between these outcomes remains unclear. Here we show that senescent cells increase levels of multiple membrane-bound polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs), but a specific PUFA, dihomo-gamma-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3 ω -3) is reduced. Exogenous repletion of DGLA or inhibition of delta-5-desaturase, the enzyme that metabolizes DGLA, instead results in cell death by ferroptosis. Senescent cells had elevated levels of other fezzroptosis sensitizers, including labile iron and expression of lipoxygenases – but also increased Gpx4 levels to prevent ferroptosis. Oral DGLA lowered senescent cell burden in aged mice and improved age-related functional outcomes. Finally, obese humans with lowered DGLA desaturation rates showed lower markers of adipose tissue senescence. Together, our data implicate DGLA and its desaturation as a major driver of decisions between senescence and ferroptosis.

title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
abstract: Understanding how host lifestyle and industrialization shape the human gut microbiome and intestinal physiology requires multimodal analyses across diverse global host contexts. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, IgA-sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations lose accuracy in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results suggest profound restructuring of host-microbiome interactions due to industrialized lifestyles, and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
abstract: To what extent gut bacteria respond to the distinct ecological pressures imposed by human lifestyle remains unclear. Here, we investigate how genomic adaptation in gut bacteria differ between industrialized and non-industrialized human populations. We generated a broad collection of isolate genomes spanning diverse host geographies, lifestyles, species, and strains. We first found that compared to MAGs, paired isolate genomes recover more functional elements and signals of horizontal gene transfers (HGTs). Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent events of HGTs. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as stress response, cell envelope remodeling and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization imprints evolutionary signatures on gut bacterial genomes, illuminating the effects of rapidly changing environments on human biology.

Influence of Digital Resources and Information Sharing on Supply Chain Sustainability
abstract: ABSTRACT Although supply chain digitalization has received considerable research attention, the mechanisms through which digital resources contribute to sustainability outcomes are not fully understood. This study examines how digital technologies, particularly big data analytics (BDA), support sustainability practices and performance in supply chains through information sharing. Building on the resource‐based view (RBV) and the dynamic capabilities perspective, a conceptual framework is developed and empirically tested using cross‐industry survey data from Finland and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM). The results show that digital resources and BDA indirectly contribute to supply chain sustainability by enhancing information sharing among supply chain partners. More effective information sharing improves transparency and coordination across the supply chain, thereby supporting the achievement of sustainability goals. This study makes two contributions. First, from an RBV perspective, it shows that information sharing is a key resource through which digitalization translates into sustainability outcomes. Second, from a dynamic capabilities perspective, it extends the emerging literature by showing how digitally enabled capabilities support sustainability transitions in supply chains.

title: How Green SMEs Combine Resources for Financial Performance and Environmental Action: Multiple Pathways in Weak Institutional Contexts
abstract: ABSTRACT This study explores the key determinants of green small‐ and medium‐sized enterprise (SME) performance in economies that have performed inadequately concerning global sustainability goals. Drawing on the dynamic capabilities view (DCV) as a theoretical lens and utilizing qualitative comparative analysis (QCA), we examined which configurations of resources are associated with higher financial performance and environmental action intensity. Our analysis identified financial, technical, human, and institutional resources that combine in complex ways and are associated with high financial performance in four equifinal configurations: (1) a knowledge‐intensive pathway that combines technical know‐how with private sector support, (2) an institutionally supported pathway that leverages technical know‐how with public sector support, (3) a human capital‐centered pathway that emphasizes green workers with financial resources, and (4) a comprehensive pathway that integrates all resource types. For high environmental action intensity, three configurations are sufficient, with public‐ and private‐sector support jointly associated with broad adoption of energy and waste routines even when internal assets are limited. The study advances beyond “why” entrepreneurs pursue green opportunities to examine “how” these configurations are associated with higher financial performance and environmental action intensity. These findings are also significant to policy and SME managers for highlighting strategic sustainability approaches that enable pathways to competitive advantage through environmental performance while strengthening business resilience in resource‐sensitive and competitive environments.

title: Binding the present and orchestrating the future: accounting as a technology of government in water sustainability
abstract: Purpose The paper explains how water sustainability becomes governable in fragmented hybrid settings. It shows how accounting and accountability hold together diverse actors, competing obligations and different rationalities, enabling sustainability aspirations to translate into coordinated action. The paper illuminates the fragile character of this process, showing how accounting and accountability partially stabilise tensions without resolving them. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an interpretive case study of an Italian water utility undergoing regulatory and organisational changes. It applies Dean's analytics of government framework to analyse data from interviews, sustainability reports and publicly available documents. Findings The study identifies four regimes of practice through which water sustainability was rendered governable. Across these regimes, accounting and accountability perform “binding” and “orchestrating” roles in governing water sustainability. These practices establish norms, responsibilities and incentives (binding) and align actors and activities (orchestrating), thereby stabilising but not resolving inter-regime tensions. Practical implications The study helps multiple actors, such as managers, policymakers and stakeholders, to understand how accounting and accountability can support the organisation of collective responsibility for water sustainability. Social implications The study shows how accounting and accountability redistribute responsibility for water sustainability across organisations and communities in hybrid public–private settings. In doing so, they can promote collective responsibility for water conservation but may also normalise particular ways of valuing water. Originality/value The paper introduces the concepts of binding and orchestrating to explain how accounting and accountability render sustainability governable in fragmented hybrid settings. Its value lies in showing how accounting enables collective action while leaving unresolved tensions among economic, public-service and environmental commitments visible.

title: Strategic Revenue Model Choice of a Video-Sharing Platform: Content Provision and Welfare Implications
Regulatory Rationales in the Face of Emerging Technologies: A Systematic Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Technology is evolving, and so is the discussion of regulation theory among academics. Taking a unique approach to legal research, this paper utilizes the systematic literature review methodology to uncover quantitative evidence on the current consensus among academics on regulation theory, in particular, regulatory rationales. This paper seeks to determine whether the narrative assumptions that social solidarity‐based regulatory rationales have become more prevalent as technology has evolved are correct. Based on the data gathered, this article asserts that the discussion of regulatory rationales is facing a tonal shift as a result of artificial intelligence. Academics are shifting away from a traditional economic view of regulation toward discussion of regulatory rationales based on protecting the common good. This should be welcome. Social solidarity should serve as a foundational principle of good technology regulation. Through applying the principles of social solidarity, regulators can better balance the risks and benefits of modern technology.

Global Steel Decarbonization under Policy, Technology, and Resource Constraints: A Process-Unit Agent-Based Model
abstract: Abstract Deep decarbonization of steel requires low-emission technologies to be deployed through a long-lived and heterogeneous asset fleet without disrupting steel supply. We developed a country-resolved agent-based model that follows global steel process units annually from 2023 to 2060. Units choose among continued operation, renewal, retrofit, conversion, retirement, and new construction, subject to construction time, linked upstream capacity, national production pathways, and annual supplies of scrap, hydrogen, natural gas, and pellets. Four scenarios distinguish stronger climate policy from improved technology and resource availability. Global process-chain CO2 emissions decline by 67–79% by 2060, reaching 0.476–0.737 Gt. The integrated case achieves the lowest emissions, but the two-component interventions do not independently outperform the reference case. Stronger policy changes when assets enter a finite transition queue, whereas technology and material conditions determine whether replacement routes can be built and operated at that time. By 2060, Scrap-EAF supplies 74–80% of crude steel, but residual unabated blast furnaces and coal-based direct reduction keep national steel pathways above their allocated levels in many countries. Deep decarbonization, therefore, depends on coordinating asset turnover, construction, and complementary material systems, rather than on technology availability or carbon-price pressure alone.

Critical mineral supply chain readiness for commercial fusion energy: A framework with applications to the ARC and EU-DEMO tokamaks
abstract: Private fusion energy companies are targeting commercial electricity generation within the next two decades, yet the material supply chains required to build and operate these reactors have received limited systematic assessment. This paper develops and applies a Supply Chain Readiness Level (SCRL) framework to evaluate 13 materials for the ARC compact tokamak, arguably the most detailed publicly documented commercial fusion design. The framework assesses each material across three dimensions: demand (bottom-up engineering estimates from published design parameters), supply chain maturity (geographic concentration, volume adequacy, and specification gap), and timeline criticality (investment lead times measured against deployment scenarios). The analysis uses the Hillesheim et al. (2026) Version 3A engineering baseline as the primary reference case, the Sorbom et al. (2015) original concept as a historical comparator, and the published EU-DEMO material assessment as a cross-design benchmark. Five materials essential to the ARC design score Critical. Four share a single failure mode, fusion-grade production that has not yet been established at any scale: enriched lithium-6 for tritium breeding, REBCO superconducting tape, FLiBe molten salt, and vanadium alloy V-4Cr-4Ti. The fifth, beryllium, is Critical on volume grounds, with single-reactor demand approaching 40% of global annual production. The specification gap between the commodity form and the fusion-grade product, rather than raw material scarcity or geographic concentration, is the dominant constraint across the material set. Under deployment timelines stated by leading private developers, decision windows for several critical materials are already closed or closing. Industry survey evidence from the Fusion Industry Association's 2026 supply chain report independently confirms both rising materials concern among developers and the coordination failure between developers and suppliers that prevents timely investment. The SCRL framework provides the quantified, material-specific demand signals needed to bridge this gap.

title: Balancing ecological benefits and feasibility in large-scale restoration planning: A multi-objective optimization decision-support framework
abstract: Ecosystem restoration requires decision-support tools capable of balancing ecological benefits under limited resources while explicitly accounting for the long-term likelihood of restoration success. Despite its recognized importance, ecological feasibility has rarely been formulated as an optimization objective in spatial planning, typically being treated only as a constraint or biophysical filter. Here, we present a multi-objective optimization framework for large-scale restoration planning that explicitly incorporates ecological feasibility alongside biodiversity and ecosystem service objectives. The framework is grounded in Systematic Conservation Planning and formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming model. We jointly optimize four criteria—extinction risk reduction, carbon storage, water provision, and ecological feasibility—under a fixed restoration area budget and land suitability constraints. Optimization proceeds in two steps: single-objective benchmark solutions are first obtained to define aspiration levels, which are then integrated using Goal Programming to generate balanced compromise solutions and characterize trade-offs. Ecological feasibility is modeled as a socio-ecological property linked to recurrent disturbance regimes, operationalized through spatial proxies of wildfire frequency, anthropogenic pressure, and invasive species richness. Applied to continental Chile using 812,910 units at 1 km² resolution, incorporating feasibility leads to significant spatial reconfiguration: approximately 16.6% of selected units (under a 30% restoration target aligned with Target 2 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework) are replaced relative to solutions that ignore feasibility. This shift preserves total restored area while increasing feasibility performance by 11.1 percentage points, with minimal reductions (below 5%) in the remaining objectives (−4.1 for carbon storage and −2.4 for water provision). Spatial diagnostics based on selection frequency reveal that compromise solutions are anchored in a "backbone" of multipurpose planning units (˃ 80% of selected units), complemented by specialized units that resolve localized trade-offs. Overall, the proposed framework provides a transparent and transferable approach for integrating ecological feasibility into spatial restoration planning, enabling more robust and policy-relevant decision-making.

Advancing acid and metalliferous drainage characterisation, prediction, and monitoring in mine waste systems using electrical methods: Challenges and future directions
abstract: Acid and metalliferous drainage (AMD) is one of the most persistent environmental liabilities faced by the mining industry, owing to its potential to cause long-term contamination. AMD encompasses acidic to neutral, metal-rich waters generated by the oxidation of sulfide minerals upon exposure to oxygen and water. With the energy transition, the volume of mine wastes stored in large-scale facilities is projected to increase, and the magnitude and complexity of AMD-related risks are likely to intensify. Consequently, early assessment and effective monitoring of the geochemical stability of mine wastes are critical for mitigating environmental impacts, avoiding unforeseen closure and remediation costs over the mine life cycle. At present, AMD assessment and monitoring largely rely on conventional geochemical testing methods, which are constrained by inherent uncertainties and provide point-scale data with limited spatial representativeness across heterogeneous mine waste structures. In this context, geophysical techniques, particularly electrical methods, offer a complementary, non-invasive, spatially continuous, and cost-effective alternative for the assessment of AMD potential. This review critically synthesises current knowledge on the application of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) and induced polarisation (IP) methods for AMD investigations in mine waste systems. The review highlights the predominance of qualitative investigations and key barriers that limit the transition to quantitative and predictive AMD assessments, including the lack of validated petrophysical relationships and limited field-scale calibrations. By identifying critical knowledge gaps and future research priorities, the review provides a framework for advancing quantitative AMD prediction, monitoring, and risk-based mine waste management using electrical methods.

abstract: Abstract We measure investors’ short- and long-term stock-return expectations using both options and survey data. These expectations at different horizons reveal what investors think their own short-term expectations will be in the future, or forward return expectations. Across data sources, investors’ forward return expectations are countercyclical, especially when measured as forward risk premiums. This countercyclical variation is, however, excessive, as changes in forward return expectations are too large relative to subsequent realized short-term expectations. The excess variation in forward return expectations can help account for a meaningful share of the stock-price declines during the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 crisis. (JEL G10, G12, G40)

title: Middlemen as an exchange technology in international production networks
Pork, Infrastructure and Growth: Evidence from the Italian Railway Expansion,
abstract: Abstract We study the political economy of transport infrastructure placement and its long-term impact, exploiting quasi-random variation in political factors. Using unique data from XIX-century Italy and deploying a regression discontinuity design, we focus on close races to show that towns in marginal districts supporting winning candidates were more likely to be reached by a railway. Using alignment with the government as a natural instrument for infrastructure placement, we then show that over the following century, services - rather than manufacturing - grew faster in connected municipalities. Our results also indicate that political allegiances likely helped towns with lower growth prospects.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Consistency and convergence rate bounds of initial sequence type variance estimators for reversible Markov chains
ASYMPTOTIC PROPERTIES OF APPROXIMATE MAXIMUM LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATOR IN MARKOV-SWITCHING STATE-SPACE MODELS
abstract: For Markov-switching state-space models, it is practically infeasible to compute the likelihood function through the Kalman filter because of the path dependence on regimes. A widely applied approximation algorithm uses a collapsing step to average out the most dated regime and truncates the regime path. This algorithm’s performance, however, has not been examined analytically. This study fills the gap. We characterize the parameters that affect the approximation error, derive the upper bounds of the errors in likelihood computation and latent variable inference, and investigate the asymptotic properties of the approximate maximum likelihood estimator. We also provide a practical procedure for measuring approximation errors and selecting the number of regime periods to keep in the truncated path. All the analysis is based on our new collapsing step, which removes a nonlinear adjustment term in the existing method to facilitate theoretical derivations.

title: Equity equilibrium for cooperative games
Life‐Cycle Wage Growth and Firm Productivity in Developed and Developing Economies
abstract: ABSTRACT Life‐cycle wage growth varies substantially across countries. We study the firm productivity distribution's role in a random‐search model with learning and labor‐market frictions, estimated for Brazil, Colombia, and the United States. Brazil has a long left tail of low‐paying firms, and Colombia has a highly compressed firm ladder. Replacing each country's firm distribution with that of the United States closes most of the cross‐country gap in wage growth, raising Brazil's relative wage growth from 73 to 103 percent and Colombia's from 52 to 115 percent. The results are robust to alternative distributional assumptions and additional sensitivity checks.

title: Energy shocks and the climate transition
abstract: We present a two-sector growth model in which a representative agent invests in fossil fuel-based energy and renewable energy. These differ in capital intensity and project duration: fossil fuel investments require lower upfront investment and have shorter duration, whereas renewables are more capital-intensive with longer-lived assets. We show that a negative economic shock (such as an energy supply shock or recession) leads to both cuts in total investment and to a shift in the composition of the remaining investment toward fossil fuel projects. This delays the clean energy transition, even if renewable energy is cost-effective on a levelised cost basis, implying a role for policies to sustain clean investment during recessions. We discuss how this mechanism can be amplified by higher interest rates, pro-cyclical climate policies, perceived risk, and financial frictions, and we relate our findings to recent empirical episodes (e.g. the 2022-23 energy crisis and post-2008 recession).
journal_name: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

title: Polycrisis and labour agency in global production networks: evidence from Bangladesh’s apparel industry
abstract: Abstract This article explains how temporally uneven polycrisis reshapes labour agency within apparel production networks. Developing a spatial–temporal analytical framework, it shows how interactions, amplification, and acceleration across crises reconfigure workers’ opportunity structures through legitimacy, profitability, and social reproduction pressures. This qualitative case study of Bangladesh’s apparel industry examines how the Rana Plaza accident, COVID-19, and the climate crisis interacted to produce cumulative effects that enabled openings and constrained mobilization, shifting labour agency across associational, coalitional, and micro-practices over time. The study advances labour regime analysis by demonstrating the temporal contingency and spatial situatedness of labour agency during polycrisis.

title: The impact of geographical and technological proximity on knowledge spillovers from formal standards
abstract: Abstract Proximity is traditionally viewed as crucial for overcoming the search and transfer costs associated with imperfectly codified knowledge. But does proximity still matter when formal standard publication jointly enhances the codification, certainty, and accessibility of technical knowledge? Evidence from the U.S. Information and Communication Technology industry shows that technological proximity drives substantial spillover gains, largely irrespective of location. Conversely, geographical proximity confers a compensating advantage when technological proximity is low. We reveal a nuanced interplay of proximity in knowledge spillovers: while formal standardization effectively flattens the world for the technologically proximate, co-location remains vital for their less proximate counterparts.

title: Does the Salience of Climate-Related Risk Affect Asset Prices?
abstract: Abstract Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs to compare prices of California homes across a new wildfire risk zone boundary, I identify null effects in the immediate vicinity of the new risk zone boundary. In contrast, prices of homes newly assigned to a riskier zone drop by 5.7% further away from the new risk zone boundary. These findings suggest that households do not respond to the risk salience triggered by the new risk zone assignment. Instead, they update their risk beliefs in response to rezoning in a way that is consistent with the actual wildfire risk.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Does Climate Change Affect Firm Sales? Identifying Supply Effects
abstract: Abstract We estimate the supply-side effects of climate change on firm sales by exploiting variation in local average temperature across suppliers of the same client. A 1°C increase in temperature leads to a 2.5% decline in annual sales. This effect is nonlinear, with stronger effects among suppliers in regions with the largest temperature increases and in cooler regions. Manufacturing and heat-sensitive industries are more affected, consistent with a reduction in labor productivity and labor supply when local temperatures rise. Nondiversified and financially constrained firms are also more affected, supporting the importance of operational and financial flexibility in adapting to climate change.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: How does geographic expansion reconfigure innovation networks? Evidence from collaborative innovation

Sorting, training, and careers: public and private universities as complementary providers of doctoral education
abstract: The growth of private providers has increased heterogeneity in doctoral education, raising questions about how university types contribute to advanced skill formation. Using linked administrative labour-market data on PhD graduates in economics and business studies in Germany, we analyse how pre-doctoral employment histories relate to the choice between public and private universities and how careers unfold during and after the doctorate. We find strong sorting: candidates with stable private-sector employment disproportionately enroll in private universities, while those embedded in academic workplaces select public universities. Many private-university candidates complete the doctorate alongside non-academic employment, whereas public-university candidates typically hold academic positions during training. After graduation, public-university graduates are more likely to remain in academia and sustain research activity, whereas private-university graduates more often advance into high-income and leadership positions outside academia. Public and private universities thus operate as organizational complements, serving distinct segments of a heterogeneous doctoral population.

title: Local Returns and Beliefs about the Stock Market
On the optimal location of public charging stations in a monocentric city
abstract: This study examines how the location of public charging stations (PCS) shapes the spatial equilibrium of a monocentric urban economy. We develop a linear urban model in which commuters endogenously choose vehicle type (conventional or electric), charging mode (public or home), and residential location. We show that the PCS location affects these choices, which in turn determine urban spatial structure, traffic-related emissions, and social welfare. We find that placing the PCS in non-ideal locations may exacerbate urban sprawl, reduce electric vehicle adoption, and lower social welfare. We derive closed-form solutions for the optimal PCS location under alternative policy objectives and quantitatively illustrate how deviations from the optimum affect equilibrium outcomes.

title: EXPRESS: When Marketers Get the Top Job: How Marketing CEOs Influence Firms’ Product-Market Strategy
abstract: Research on upper echelons in marketing has primarily focused on the CMO, yet the CEO ultimately bears responsibility for key strategic decisions, including those related to marketing. This study examines how CEOs with marketing experience (i.e., “marketing CEOs”) influence firm stock market performance by shaping product portfolio decisions. Drawing on upper echelon theory and in-depth interviews with business practitioners, we argue that marketing CEOs are more effective at selecting customer segments and implementing competitive strategies, leading to more differentiated portfolios and, consequently, higher shareholder returns. Our analysis of the main research question combines a qualitative study, a natural experiment involving CEO turnovers, large-scale panel data analysis, and an experiment with executives. Our results show that marketing CEOs positively impact shareholder returns through portfolio differentiation. Furthermore, the positive effect of marketing CEOs on portfolio differentiation is strengthened by their larger professional networks and a strong customer orientation within the firm but is diminished by CEO overconfidence and high firm financial leverage. Our findings highlight the distinctive value of CEOs with marketing experience and provide insight into the conditions that enhance or constrain their ability to generate firm value.

title: From Slack to Staff: Managers' Allocation of Slack Resources to Hiring
abstract: Abstract Prior research views cash holdings, or high‐discretionary slack, as a buffer against shocks or a catalyst for strategic change. Drawing on stakeholder salience theory, we argue that cash can also reshape managers' interpretation and prioritization of employee hiring‐related claims, thereby increasing hiring, and that this effect is more pronounced when structural influences heighten the salience of those claims. Study 1, a large‐scale field study of Belgian firms, finds a positive but diminishing relationship between cash and hiring. This relationship strengthens under conditions of greater firm dependence on specific employee groups or following an exogenous legal reform, both of which are hypothesized to make the salience of specific employee groups more apparent. In Study 2, a vignette experiment offers causal support for the hypothesized mechanism, with employee salience cues strengthening how managers translate cash into hiring allocations. Combined, our findings contribute to research on slack resources and stakeholder salience by showing that managers use high‐discretionary cash not only for buffering or strategic change but also to respond to salient stakeholders.

title: EXPRESS: Impatient for Impact: Intertemporal Preferences for Earlier Donation Impact Timing
abstract: Impatience when choosing for oneself has been widely documented, but are people also impatient when making prosocial decisions about benefits to unknown others? The authors study whether and why people care about a donation’s “impact timing,” the time when the benefits of the donation would reach the beneficiaries. In seven pre-registered experiments (N = 2,462) and an analysis of GoFundMe secondary data, they show that people consistently prefer to donate to a charitable program with an earlier impact timing, across different causes, donation amounts, timeframes, charity sizes and tradeoffs between impact timing and other considerations (impact magnitude, number of prior donors, remaining cost to complete, quality rating, and overhead). They find that decreased perceived benefits of delayed donation impact provides an incomplete explanation of the impact timing preference. Beyond less discounting of less delayed benefits, people also infer greater donation efficacy-based trust from earlier impact timing, increasing donation preferences. Together, the strong preference for earlier impact timing is an important and largely overlooked aspect of prosocial decision-making, with implications for building trust in prosocial organizations.

title: National Audit Oversight and Foreign Investment
abstract: ABSTRACT Public audit oversight bodies have become ubiquitous following the establishment of the U.S. PCAOB in 2002. However, despite their cost and prominence, little is known of their economic implications, if any. We examine the relation between establishment of public audit oversight bodies (POBs) and cross-border investment. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that after a country establishes a POB, the country attracts more foreign capital. Our results suggest that total foreign portfolio investment (FPI) increases by approximately $11 billion for the average country that establishes a POB. The impact of POBs on foreign investment is dependent on the effectiveness of the POB in improving audit quality and the strength of a country’s existing institutional environment. Our study provides evidence of real economic effects of public audit oversight around the world, which adds to the literature on auditor oversight and to the broader literature on economic consequences of regulation. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M42; M48; F21; L51; G15; G18.

title: The Cost of Regulatory Inaction: Evidence from IFRS Nonadoption
abstract: A growing literature has examined the benefits and costs of implementing new disclosure regulations. However, little is known about the consequences when regulators fail to take action. Using IFRS adoption in 2005 as the setting, we examine the costs of regulatory inactions among non-adopting countries. We find that firms located in non-adopting countries with a higher overlap of common investors with firms in IFRS-adopting countries experience a significant decline in liquidity. Employing a within-firm-time design, we further demonstrate that analysts and institutional investors shift their attention from non-IFRS firms when other firms in their portfolios adopt IFRS. Moreover, the decline in liquidity and the associated reduction in information production by analysts and institutional investors are particularly pronounced in non-adopting countries with weak reporting enforcement actions and increasing accounting distance from IFRS standards. Overall, our findings highlight the potential costs of regulatory inaction. Valuable information production resources are diverted to the new regime, resulting in a worsened information environment for companies in the old regime.

title: Accounting Comparability and Common Owners
abstract: Abstract We examine the relationship between accounting comparability and common ownership. Accounting comparability can reduce information asymmetry between firms and investors by lowering information acquisition and processing costs. At the same time, greater comparability can reduce the private information advantages that sophisticated investors, such as common owners, exploit. Which of these opposing forces dominates is ultimately an empirical question. Using a sample of US firms for 1999–2021, we find that accounting comparability is positively associated with common ownership, particularly non‐transient common ownership. Further analyses indicate that this relation is driven by a reduction in information asymmetry and is significantly stronger among firms with weaker information environments.

title: The Recycling Illusion: How the Mobius Loop Fuels Greenwashing
abstract: ABSTRACT Globally used labelling systems regulated by governments can inadvertently greenwash packaging. We show that the Mobius loop and plastic resin identification numbers are misleading consumers about recyclability. This is because not all plastic packaging can be recycled. Across three experiments, we demonstrate that the Mobius loop system is inadvertently greenwashing packaging for consumers as it signals recyclability irrespective of other messaging. Packaging displaying the Mobius loop was consistently rated positively and perceived as recyclable and environmentally friendly, even when it was not. The symbol also enhanced brand image. This occurred irrespective of the color of the Mobius loop and product category used. This system will perpetuate the plastic waste problem even though it is not intended. We extend the greenwashing concept by presenting evidence that regulation can greenwash.

title: When leaders prioritize health: Investigating when and how health-oriented leadership shapes employee in-role and extra-role behaviors
