More Than a Bind That Ties—Introducing the Family Meta-Logic in Single-Family Offices When Navigating Financial and Social Welfare Logics
abstract: Single-family offices (SFOs) must balance financial, social welfare, and family logics. Drawing on institutional logics research, this multi-case study of German SFOs examines how the family logic shapes the relationship between financial and social welfare logics in investment decisions. We find that the family logic acts as a meta-logic. Depending on power distribution, value alignment, and governance design, it enables centrality, compatibility, or pseudo-compatibility of the two logics, and it works as an exit barrier that keeps tensions from escalating. We contribute by conceptualizing the family meta-logic and by showing how power dynamics and generational differences shape decision-making in SFOs.

title: More AI, better coordination? Comparing AI incorporation and institutionalized project management practices in project work
Beyond the bottle: decoding the wine list architecture and ordering decisions
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the wine lists’ influence on restaurant customers’ ordering decisions and the role of wine ordering in shaping the overall dining experience. Design/methodology/approach Based on 27 in-depth interviews with restaurant patrons who ordered wine from a wine list, this study employed a grounded theory methodology (GTM) to analyze data. Findings The findings reveal three core categories influencing wine ordering experiences: wine list architecture, wine ordering process and wine-centric experiences. Within the wine list category, wine attributes, menu designscape and cognitive navigability emerged as key subcategories shaping wine list architecture. The wine ordering process is shaped by wine-specific factors, restaurant-related factors, personal factors and food-wine pairing. Notably, a wine-centric experience, characterized by wine fascination, culinary enhancement and relational enjoyment, significantly impacts the overall dining experience. Practical implications These findings inform restaurant managers about the complex wine-ordering process. To optimize diners’ decision experience, managers should prioritize key wine attributes, such as grape variety, price, type, serving size, region, taste profiles and the wine list’s design. Originality/value This study provides an exploratory conceptualization of the wine list as a decision-making interface that shapes consumers’ wine-ordering decisions in restaurant settings, offering conceptual insights with implications for research and practice.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Designing employee wellness programs in hotels: a prioritized resource framework
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how employee wellness programs (EWPs) function in high-demand service environments, addressing the limitation that prior research assumes wellness resources automatically improve employee well-being. Design/methodology/approach A four-stage mixed-methods design was adopted, including literature review, expert content validation, Fuzzy Delphi analysis with 28 experts and a survey of 507 hotel employees analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings A six-dimensional EWP framework comprising 26 validated indicators was confirmed. The results show that EWP dimensions are not functionally equivalent but operate within a structured system. Organizational resources, particularly healthcare support and health management policies, play a foundational role, while other dimensions contribute to recovery and longer-term development. The findings suggest that the effectiveness of wellness initiatives depends on employees’ capacity to use available resources. Research limitations/implications By integrating conservation of resources theory with the well-being-as-capability perspective, this study reframes EWPs as a capability-enabling system that emphasizes resource usability rather than mere provision. Practically, hotels should prioritize foundational organizational resources before expanding other wellness initiatives, using the proposed three-stage implementation roadmap to guide strategic investment and promote sustainable employee well-being. Originality/value This study provides a mechanism-based explanation of how wellness resources function in practice, offering a more nuanced framework for understanding employee well-being in the hospitality industry.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Unveiling the dark side of workplace community: knowledge hiding in frontline hospitality
abstract: Purpose Grounded in Deutsch’s theory of cooperation and competition, this study aims to explain the paradoxical effect of psychological sense of community at work (PSCW) on knowledge hiding (KH) in frontline hospitality. It tests knowledge-based psychological ownership (KBPO) as the explanatory mechanism and prosocial motivation (PSM) as a motivational contingency. Design/methodology/approach Time-lagged data were gathered in three waves from frontline hospitality employees in Pakistan, yielding 632 usable responses. The hypothesized moderated mediation model was tested using covariance-based structural equation modeling with bias-corrected bootstrapping. Findings Contrary to the prevailing assumption that positive workplace social contexts suppress KH, PSCW was positively associated with KBPO and KBPO with KH, producing a significant indirect effect. PSM dampened the PSCW–KBPO link, weakening the indirect pathway among more prosocially motivated employees. Research limitations/implications The study extends KH theory by conceptualizing PSCW as an integrative antecedent, identifying KBPO as the mechanism explaining why KH persists within cohesive workplace communities and specifying PSM’s moderating role in this pathway, thereby questioning the view that positive workplace dynamics necessarily curbs KH. Practical implications Hospitality managers should pair efforts to strengthen workplace community with practices that frame knowledge as a collective rather than a personal resource, such as cross-training, team-based rewards and promotion criteria that recognize knowledge contribution over exclusive expertise and should recruit and develop prosocially motivated employees. Originality/value The study offers three contributions to KH research. It positions PSCW as a theoretically integrative antecedent, moving beyond the fragmented relational constructs of prior work; provides time-lagged evidence that strong workplace community can give rise to ownership-driven KH, revealing its dark side; and shows PSM to be the motivational contingency that determines when workplace community reduces protective hiding in frontline hospitality.

title: A supply chain life cycle framework using social exchange theory
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this research is to develop supply chain life cycle theory using the concepts of supply chain uncertainty, supply chain orientation and social exchange theory. Design/methodology/approach This research employs conceptual research methodology to develop theoretical propositions of the relationships that are fundamental to supply chain processes, while following established theory-building guidelines in supply chain management. Findings Supply chain processes must be examined longitudinally, sequentially and as multiple cycles of events and conditions of multiple firms. Doing so can provide theoretical insights into the birth, continuance and dissolution of supply chains. Originality/value This research offers a temporal, process explanation of how supply chain uncertainty may generate supply chain orientation and supply chain management responses, how those responses subsequently alter uncertainty and how this recursive process may help explain the emergence, continuation, adaptation and dissolution of SCM activities and supply chains.

title: Political risk insurance in the digital age: How CPA moderates negative investor reactions following head of government attacks on social media
From financial constraints to performance via innovation: Evidence from Indigenous‑owned SMEs
abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that financial constraints hinder innovation and firm performance, yet emerging research hints at a more complex relationship. Building on Indigenous entrepreneurship and cultural entrepreneurship theory, we examine how and why financial constraints translate into innovation, and subsequent consequences for firm performance. Drawing on a nationally representative sample of 1,101 Indigenous-owned SMEs in Canada and matching with mediation analysis, we find that financial constraints are associated with weaker firm performance, yet are simultaneously associated with a higher likelihood of product and process innovation. Innovation, in turn, offsets up to 32% of the negative association between constraints and performance. We explain this pattern through the notion of culturally purposeful innovation—which channels scarcity into market‑ and mission‑relevant solutions. In Indigenous entrepreneurship contexts characterized by structural constraints and strong cultural logics, innovation emerges as a culturally grounded mechanism linking adversity to sustained performance outcomes. We contribute to strength-based Indigenous entrepreneurship, cultural entrepreneurship, and financial constraint literature. We also offer implications for entrepreneurship practice.

title: Decoding the influence of the reviewer's country of origin on eWOM adoption: a transnational perspective
abstract: Purpose Prominent travel platforms like Booking, TripAdvisor and Hotels.com increasingly publish electronic word of mouth (eWOM) worldwide, with reviewers' information including country of origin (COO). However, research that analyzes the role of culture in the context of e-WOM remains scarce. Our study addresses this gap by investigating the effects of reviewers' COO and the country stereotypes evoked – based on the degree of a nation's development and culture – on eWOM adoption. Design/methodology/approach Two quantitative studies were conducted using a 3X2 between-subjects factorial design. The manipulated factors were reviewer category according to country-of-origin (COO) culture and level of development (same nationality, developed country with a different culture, developing country with a different culture) and positive or negative eWOM valence. In Study 1, 323 American participants were randomly assigned to one of the experimental conditions. Study 2 extends Study 1 by examining the moderating role of national identification with a sample of 303 British participants. Findings Across both studies, the results demonstrate that for reviewers from other countries, COO positively influences perceptions of reviewer competence when the latter is from a developed country and is perceived as an outgroup member, thereby increasing eWOM adoption. Additionally, Study 2 shows that at higher levels of national identification, ingroup members are perceived as more competent than outgroup members from developed countries. These findings offer valuable insights for both marketing researchers and practitioners. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is the first to empirically examine how COO stereotypes shape perceptions of reviewer competence and eWOM adoption. It also breaks new ground by investigating the moderating role of national identification in shaping perceptions of reviewer competence.

title: Decision inertia in emergencies: Reasons to be cheerful ten years on
abstract: Abstract A decade on from the publication of Decision inertia: Deciding between least worst outcomes in emergency responses to disasters , this commentary reflects on the paper's contribution to understanding decision‐making in high‐stakes environments and its subsequent theoretical, methodological and practical impact. The original paper identified decision inertia as a cognitively active form of indecision, where decision makers in critical incidents get trapped in redundant deliberation rather than committing to a least‐worst course of action. Since its publication, research has advanced understanding of the cognitive, behavioural, affective, social and contextual factors that contribute to decision inertia, while methodological developments have provided increasingly more sophisticated and ecologically valid approaches for studying complex operational settings beyond the practitioner community. However, important questions remain regarding how decision inertia should be measured and how its antecedents and mechanisms can be integrated into a comprehensive multi‐dimensional theoretical model. Moreover, despite advances in the science and recognition in policy, translation into operational practice has been comparatively limited. We argue that greater collaboration and co‐production between researchers and practitioners would ensure that advances in understanding decision inertia lead to meaningful, evidence‐based changes on the ground. Ten years on, there are reasons to be cheerful, but the challenge for the next decade is to translate what we now know into better decision‐making on the ground.
journal_name: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology

title: How Does Board Composition Shape Tax Effectiveness?
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate whether having various nationalities represented on a board of directors is associated with effective tax planning at the firm. We rely on upper echelons theory, which argues that an individual’s experiences, values, and personalities influence their interpretations of the situations they face and their decisions. We use a new tax effectiveness measure developed in prior literature that gauges a firm’s tax effectiveness using tax and non-tax costs. We find a positive association between board nationality heterogeneity and tax effectiveness, consistent with our hypothesis and the proposed role of board scrutiny in tax-relevant business decisions. Our study extends the research on board composition, tax-related decision-making, and how tax outcomes are determined. Data Availability: All data used in this manuscript are publicly available.
journal_name: The Journal of the American Taxation Association

title: Learning While Working: How Do Early Litigation Experiences Affect Managers’ Disclosure?
From exponential extrapolation to regime-aware foresight: A Cognitive Scaling Framework for long-run AI progress
Crafting Persuasive Environmental Messages for Virtual Influencers: The Role of Anthropomorphic Conversational Style, Persuasion Appeal, and Behavioral Context
abstract: The use of virtual influencers (VIs) has emerged as an alternative to human influencers for marketing initiatives. Prior studies have focused primarily on the visual characteristics of VIs and their use in advertising settings, with limited attention given to their capacity to drive pro-environmental behaviors (PEBs). We have developed an integrated persuasive framework, grounded in the Elaboration Likelihood Model and Congruity Theory, that links VI characteristics, message appeals, and behavioral context to persuasion outcomes. Study 1 examined VI message strategies and found that competence (vs. warmth) anthropomorphic conversational style and influencing (vs. de-influencing) appeal enhanced message persuasiveness. Study 2 explored the effectiveness of VIs in promoting plastic waste reduction behaviors across different behavioral contexts and found that messages pertaining to difficult (vs. easy) and private (vs. public) behaviors significantly enhanced message persuasiveness, but that messages promoting easy and private behaviors generated stronger behavioral intentions. The insights from these studies can provide valuable guidance to businesses, marketers, and environmental advocates on effective VI message strategies for addressing challenges related to climate change.

title: Buyer green innovation volatility and the supplier bullwhip effect: a signalling theory perspective
abstract: Purpose Buyers' green innovation does not remain confined within the firm; its volatility may ripple upstream and reshape suppliers' operations. Drawing on signalling theory, we examine how buyers' green innovation volatility (GIV) affects the supplier bullwhip effect (SBE), and how buyers' green supplier management (GSM) and inventory utilisation efficiency (IUE) moderate this effect. Design/methodology/approach We construct a dyadic dataset covering 436 Chinese buyer firms and 871 global suppliers from 2012 to 2022, and employ fixed-effects models to test our hypotheses. Findings There is a U-shaped GIV–SBE relationship: compared with both low and high levels of GIV, moderate GIV leads suppliers to adjust production more cautiously in response to unstable demand, resulting in lower SBE. When buyers' green innovation is on an overall downward trend, GSM helps suppliers interpret demand and operational changes more accurately, curbing GIV-induced increases in SBE. Higher IUE enables suppliers to detect GIV-related requirement changes more promptly, prompting stronger production responses and widening the SBE gap between moderate and low or high GIV. Originality/value By introducing GIV, our study identifies a novel antecedent of SBE and provides insights into how buyers can help suppliers accurately interpret GIV and calibrate their operational responses.

The virtue paradox: how perceived organizational social responsibility and organizational shame fuel resistance to change among motivated public servants
abstract: Public organizations increasingly adopt corporate social responsibility frameworks, yet little is known about how employees react emotionally when their organization falls short of its professed standards. Drawing on appraisal theories of moral emotion, we examine whether organizational shame links perceived organizational social responsibility (OSR) to resistance to change, and whether public service motivation (PSM) moderates this process. Three-wave data from 113 French local government employees show that lower perceived OSR is associated with greater shame, especially among high-PSM employees, and that shame relates to greater resistance to change. Paradoxically, responsibility initiatives may fuel resistance among the most committed public servants.

title: Towards more impactful co-design: insights from a systematic review of food loss and waste solutions
abstract: Co-design, as a component of broader co-production processes, has gained attention in public policy as a means of addressing complex policy challenges. Yet comparative research remains limited on what occurs under participatory and design-led approaches labelled co-design, what policy solutions these processes produce, and how they are expected to generate change. We address this gap through a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of 38 studies on food loss and waste (FLW). Findings indicate that co-design labels inconsistently reflect participatory and iterative design practices; creative engagement methods remain underutilized. Co-designed outputs remain at ideation and prototyping stages, while interventions often lack a clear theory of change. We introduce a coding scheme to document co-design implementation and propose CIMO (Context, Intervention, Mechanism, Outcome) as an ex ante evaluation heuristic to articulate the theory of change of co-designed interventions. We conclude with a research agenda emphasizing enhanced reporting practice, theory-building, and implementation-focused research.

title: Beyond Convergence and Model Fit: Structural Guidance in CFA, EFA, ESEM-T, and Penalized SEM
abstract: This study examines how alternative forms of structural guidance shape latent-variable solutions under dense-loading conditions in which all indicators have systematically nonzero cross-loadings. Near-population analyses (N = 1,000,000) compared exact restrictions, empirical rotation, target-guided rotation, and penalization while minimizing sampling fluctuation. CFA produced increasing distortion as departures from independent-clusters structure increased. EFA recovery depended strongly on the rotation criterion, with Geomin ε = 0.50 performing consistently well across both populations. Exploratory structural equation modeling with target rotation recovered the generating structure accurately when targets were sufficiently aligned and remained highly accessible. Penalized structural equation modeling recovery likewise depended on structural alignment, although accurate retained solutions could be difficult to access across starting values. Supplementary repeated-sampling analyses at N = 500 and 2,000 showed that numerical convergence and excellent fit did not guarantee corresponding factor orientations. Overall, the form and alignment of structural guidance jointly shaped admissibility, accessibility, recovery, and orientation stability, with important implications for practice.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: ‘Like going out at night without pepper spray’: responses to cyber-victimization among LGBTQIA+college students in the United States
abstract: The internet has reshaped the nature of social interactions, providing new environments for people to connect in both prosocial and, too often, antisocial ways. The lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, questioning, intersex, asexual, and associated (LGBTQIA+) communities are among those who studies reveal are most at risk for cyber-victimization. For young people, already the most vulnerable to being targeted, being openly LGBTQIA + serves to compound the likelihood of online harassment. This study reports on three focus groups conducted with LGBTQIA + college students at a mid-sized university in the United States northeast, who discussed their experiences with cyber-victimization. The findings indicate a lack of faith in systemic platform-based responses, and a consensus that young LGBTQIA + people are forced to take personal responsibility for their own online safety. This includes curating their online profiles and feeds, as well as (to a lesser extent) taking direct action to combat anti-LGBTQIA + abuse.

title: Learning enhanced game theoretic decision-making for interaction-aware autonomous driving in urban traffic scenarios

Does a maternal history of childhood maltreatment influence prevention program impact on child outcomes? Exploratory findings from a randomized controlled trial in British Columbia, Canada
abstract: Background Nurse-home visiting programs starting prenatally are a promising approach for preventing child maltreatment including injuries. Understanding which families benefit the most can inform policies to ensure greater impact and efficiency. Objective We investigated whether maternal history of childhood maltreatment (CM) moderated Nurse-Family Partnership (NFP) impact on child outcomes. Participants and setting We utilized secondary data from the Canadian NFP randomized controlled trial (RCT) involving 739 mothers aged 14–24 years and their 737 children in British Columbia (data collected 2013–2019). Methods Baseline data, including maternal CM history, were collected during pregnancy and before random assignment to existing services or NFP plus existing services. Data on main child outcome indicators: injuries (emergency department events), problem behaviour and language (maternal report) and language and cognition (in-home observations) were collected at age two years. Results Many maternal participants reported CM exposure (73.1%), including 57% medium-to-severe and 41.8% severe thresholds. CM history significantly moderated NFP impacts on selected child outcomes including injuries (adjusted differences in rate differences =102.92, 95% CI: 15.18, 193.45) and language via maternal report (adjusted differences in mean differences = −82.52, 95% CI: −150.77, −14.27). Conclusions A maternal history of CM moderated NFP impacts on injuries and language, but not all child outcomes examined. Researchers are encouraged to harness existing RCT data to learn how prevention program outcomes vary across populations. Policymakers may then apply this nuanced guidance to inform the refinement of prevention programs for families with unmet needs, fulfilling the ethical obligation to ensure that programs are effective for all.

title: Variations in Sexual Function and Behaviors by BDSM Self-Identification versus BDSM Practice Frequency in the General Population
China’s Conservative Turn: The Origins of Xi Jinping’s New Era Lin Le. Boulder, CO: Lynne Rienner, 2025. 256 pp. £86.50 (e-book). ISBN 9798896160137
Delegating Digital Policing: The Evolution of China’s Security-Industrial Complex
abstract: Abstract How did China build its formidable digital policing apparatus so rapidly? While prevailing narratives emphasize top-down state direction, this statist perspective obscures critical local dynamics. This article argues that China’s security-industrial complex actually emerged from decentralized administrative pressures. Burdened by unfunded, time-sensitive central security mandates, resource-strapped local security agencies abandoned state-led technological development and outsourced to the private sector. Drawing on extensive field interviews (2017–2022) and policy analysis, this study traces the complex’s evolution through three interrelated mechanisms: the decentralization of internal security politics, the formation of hybrid public–private partnerships, and the varied transactional behaviour exhibited by capitalists, as well as between government and business, in a multi-layered system. By demonstrating how localized security projects inadvertently catalysed technological innovation, this research reveals the hidden market-driven roots of China’s security-industrial complex. It offers a novel framework for understanding how the party-state adaptively leverages capital for building a digital security state.

title: Enacting and negotiating institutional rules in participatory budgeting: how institutional rules shape inclusion and exclusion in democratic innovations
abstract: Local governments increasingly experiment with democratic innovations to strengthen local democracy and decision-making power of residents. This article examines how the institutional rules of a specific democratic innovation – participatory budgeting – shape who is included or excluded. Participatory budgeting holds the potential to empower and emancipate underprivileged citizens through firsthand knowledge and experience with decision-making practices, but it can also reinforce existing inequalities and power disparities. Drawing on institutional theory through a public encounters lens, this study analyzes how rules regarding position, boundary, scope and authority affect the emancipatory potential of participatory budgeting in practice. Particular attention is given to how participants in different positions engage with and shape these rules, as to understand how decision-making within participatory budgeting works. The findings show that institutional rules are continuously contested and that rules intended to empower disadvantaged participants often, in practice, benefit those who already have a dominant position.

Carbon Source Diversity Shapes DOM Chemodiversity and Antibiotic Resistome in Earthworm Casts
abstract: Abstract The earthworm gut acts as a hotspot for reprocessing ingested organic matter, thereby altering carbon availability. These changes reshape microbial communities and competitive interactions, potentially affecting the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in the gut. Beyond substrate amount, substrate diversity shapes these processes, yet its role remains unknown. We established microcosm experiments with a substrate-diversity gradient, combining FT-ICR MS and metagenomics to investigate dissolved organic matter (DOM) chemistry, microbial traits and ARGs in earthworm guts. Higher substrate diversity enriched carbon-centered metabolic genes and increased gut DOM availability, possibly through the proliferation of polysaccharide-degrading microorganisms with larger genomes. However, higher carbon availability may have increased microbial nutrient demand, accompanied by reductions in CHON-containing compounds and stronger microbial competition. ARG enrichment was associated with greater potential for microbial competition, as indicated by stronger negative microbial interactions and higher competition indices derived from genome scale metabolic models. In vitro monoculture of gut-derived pathogenic Klebsiella pneumoniae showed that substrate diversity enriched multidrug- and β-lactam-resistance genes and reshaped the resistome. Collectively, these findings suggest that increased substrate diversity modifies earthworm-driven carbon reprocessing, may reshape microbial resource competition and promote ARG enrichment, providing insights into the linkage between organic matter processing and resistome in soil fauna.

title: Mitochondrial-Endocrine Axis Dysfunction Mediates Diet-Dependent Susceptibility to Nanoplastic Ovarian Toxicity and PCOS Risk
abstract: Abstract Nanoplastics (NPs) pollution represents an emerging threat to reproductive health, yet how dietary habits modulate this toxicity remains largely unexplored. Here, mice were assigned to a control (CD), high-fat (HFD), or high-fiber (HFib) diet and received oral doses of deuterated polystyrene nanoparticles at 0, 5, or 25 mg/kg/day over an eight-week period. Ovarian NP accumulation was dose-dependent under CD, reaching 23.33 ± 5.39 μg/g tissue at the highest dose. HFD markedly elevated this burden to 96.87 ± 13.44 μg/g, whereas HFib significantly reduced it to 7.77 ± 1.32 μg/g. Functionally, HFD synergized with NPs to disrupt estrous cyclicity (only 13% regular cycles), suppress anti-Müllerian hormone by 74%, and increase follicular atresia rate, while HFib maintained near-normal ovarian physiology. Transcriptomics identified steroid hormone biosynthesis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) as core pathways convergently dysregulated by NPs across all diets. Mechanistically, HFD amplified NP-induced ovarian oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial OXPHOS impairment, culminating in hyperandrogenism and profound estradiol deficiency. Conversely, HFib preserved aromatase expression and mitochondrial respiratory capacity, thereby restoring steroidogenic homeostasis. Mendelian randomization further linked human orthologues of these dysregulated genes, including UQCR10 and COX4I1 encoding mitochondrial complex III and IV subunits, to elevated polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) risk, highlighting the central role of OXPHOS disruption. These findings establish a diet-NP interaction pattern with implications for reproductive health guidance in populations.

title: Environmental Mechanochemistry: From Force-Induced Reactivity to Aqueous Reaction Platforms
abstract: Abstract Mechanochemistry is increasingly used in environmental research, but is still commonly treated as a material synthesis or pretreatment step rather than a mode of driving reactions that directly affects pathways relevant to pollution control and resource recovery. This Perspective argues that its environmental significance is most evident when force not only changes material properties before use, but also alters how reactions proceed during operation. We compare how force becomes chemically effective in inorganic and organic systems and classify environmental applications according to its primary role. Using zerovalent iron (ZVI) as a representative example, we show that mechanochemistry can simultaneously alleviate multiple bottlenecks in ZVI preparation, storage, and application. Earlier studies have shown that force can regulate ZVI lattice structure, surface state, and interfacial charge transfer. The wet-milling mechanochemical reactor (MCR) extends these effects into aqueous operation by applying force during rather than before reaction. This intensifies solid–liquid contact, accelerates heterogeneous kinetics, and, in some systems, shifts target transformation from surface-confined pathways toward subsurface redistribution and lattice-associated capture. Future advances should identify systems in which force can strengthen reactions sufficiently to open pathways that conventional treatment processes do not readily access.

title: Implementation Gap in Global Power Capacity Expansion to meet Paris Agreement Climate Targets
abstract: Abstract Meeting the Paris Agreement’s climate targets demands an unprecedented expansion of renewable energy. Despite global commitments, significant implementation gaps persist due to economic, policy, and technical uncertainties. Here, we develop a Global Power Capacity Dynamics Framework, integrating facility-level data, machine learning and transition modeling to assess the feasibility of global power expansion. Analyzing 215,849 power plant units across five status modes (operating, planned, canceled, standby, retired), the framework explicitly incorporates the likelihood of planned capacity realization and the conversion of existing fossil assets. We find that by 2030, only 51% [40%–61%] of announced planned capacity is expected to become operational, while 26% [19%–36%] is likely to be canceled, with fossil fuel projects, especially coal, facing a cancellation rate of about 35%. Global operational capacity is projected to reach 9727 GW [9626–9848], including 178 GW [159–198] of existing fossil units requiring conversion or replacement (e.g., coal-to-gas, fossil-to-biomass). Although renewables dominate the planned pipeline, they are projected to constitute only 52% of the global energy mix by 2030, well below levels needed to meet climate goals. Regional disparities are pronounced: Asia, despite its relatively low cancellation rate, faces the world’s largest implementation gap, requiring an additional 2488 GW of solar and contending with 523 GW of stranded coal capacity to remain on a 1.5 °C pathway. This study provides the first probabilistic, facility-level assessment of global power capacity trajectories, revealing critical shortfalls in planned deployment and underscoring the urgency of aligning capacity expansion with climate targets.

Why Phytate Persists: Mechanisms of Exceptional Binding and Stability on Soil Mineral Surfaces
abstract: Abstract Phytate, a six-phosphate compound that stores plant phosphorus, is a stable component of soil phosphorus, yet mechanisms underlying its persistence remain unclear. Here, we combined adsorption experiments, spectroscopy, X-ray scattering, and molecular modeling to investigate phytate interactions with five soil minerals: goethite, hematite, quartz, montmorillonite, and kaolinite. Iron oxides exhibited up to 5-fold greater adsorption capacities than quartz and clays. Natural organic matter caused negligible desorption of mineral-bound phytate, whereas phytate displaced adsorbed natural organic matter, demonstrating competitive and stable phytate-mineral associations. Adsorption capacities normalized to orthophosphate binding-site densities implied multiphosphate coordination for phytate on iron oxides, but binding beyond nominal orthophosphate sites on montmorillonite. Molecular dynamics simulations captured one to three phosphate groups in phytate associations with iron oxides; metal cation screening of electrostatic repulsion facilitated binding on negatively charged quartz and montmorillonite. Infrared spectroscopy revealed coupled vibrational responses of phosphate and inositol ring moieties on goethite, but primarily phosphate responses on montmorillonite. X-ray total scattering determined a feature at 2.7 Å, supporting inner-sphere coordination on iron oxides and consistent with quantum mechanics-based energy calculations, whereas quartz and clay features indicated interfacial reorganization. These findings establish mineral-specific mechanisms of phytate stabilization, with implications for persistence and bioavailability in soils.

title: Climate-Driven Sink-to-Source Transitions for Microplastics in Terrestrial Systems
abstract: Abstract Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as pervasive contaminants in terrestrial environments, where soils act as major dynamic reservoirs that retain particles but can also release them through hydrological, erosional, and atmospheric pathways. Climate change is altering the physical, hydrological, and biogeochemical controls that govern the MP retention-release balance. This review develops a climate-driven sink-to-source transition framework in which terrestrial systems shift episodically from retention-dominated to export-active states. We synthesize evidence that changes in freeze–thaw regimes and drought-rewetting reorganize pore networks and preferential flow; extreme rainfall and runoff can exceed hydrological retention and redistribute MPs vertically and laterally; and warming and salinization reconfigure interfacial interactions, polymer aging, aggregation behavior, and microbially mediated transport processes. Atmospheric entrainment and snowpack-snowmelt pathways further connect terrestrial MP reservoirs with other environmental compartments. Across these climate drivers, MP mobility depends on the coupled evolution of pore architecture, water flux, particle properties, and biogeochemical conditions rather than on any single forcing factor. By integrating laboratory studies, field observations, and emerging modeling perspectives, this review provides a mechanistic foundation for predicting terrestrial MP redistribution and associated environmental risks under ongoing climate change.

title: Recovering Rare Earth Elements from Mining Effluent via Synergistic Angstrom-Scale Confinement and Phosphate-Mediated Coordination in MXene Membranes
abstract: Abstract Recovering rare earth elements (REEs) from complex aqueous streams is essential for advancing sustainable resource recovery but remains hindered by low REE concentrations and strong competition with impurity ions. Herein, we introduce a biomimetic MXene membrane that integrates phosphate-based molecular recognition with angstrom-level control of interlayer spacing to achieve the selective and continuous recovery of REEs from wastewaters. By intercalating aminophosphonic molecules within Ti3C2Tx layers, the membrane precisely tunes the nanochannel size and establishes coordinatively active oxygen sites that preferentially bind trivalent lanthanides under nanoconfinement. Such a design enables a synergistic mechanism in which steric exclusion and ligand–metal coordination coregulate ion transport, leading to markedly improved selectivity toward REE recovery. The optimized 2-AEP-M membrane exhibited a Ca2+/Dy3+ selectivity of 243.47 in simulated solutions and 130.69 in actual REE mining wastewater. After membrane separation and subsequent precipitation and calcination, REEs constituted 90.2% of the quantified cationic species in the recovered solid products. Experimental and computational analyses reveal that phosphate groups promote Dy3+ coordination, underpinning the observed ion discrimination. The membrane also demonstrates antiswelling stability and antibacterial properties, supporting its potential for long-term deployment. This work integrates chemical affinity with angstrom-confined transport, offering a platform for precise ion separation and sustainable REE recovery.

title: Targeted Coupling of Electrogenerated Reactive Oxygen Species for Deep Pollutant Mineralization
abstract: Abstract Electrochemical oxidation technology holds great promise for wastewater treatment. However, the inherent limitations of single-component reactive oxygen species (ROS) and their low yield impede thorough mineralization of organic pollutants and elevate energy consumption. Herein, we develop a directed ROS coupling oxidation (DRCO) system, which employs a Ni–Sb–SnO2 anode that leverages Ni(III)/Ni(II) redox cycling for highly selective OH generation, coupled with a CrMn@C anode for 1O2 production, significantly enhancing the coexisting ROS yield. By leveraging the electron-withdrawing and donating synergistic effect of •OH and 1O2, the DRCO system removes 61.2–78.5% total organic carbon (TOC) for diverse organics within 20 min. The observed kinetic constants are 1.4–52.6 times higher than those of systems that use •OH or 1O2 alone. Furthermore, the DRCO system achieves 85.4% TOC removal for actual pharmaceutical wastewater and sustains operational stability over a 120 h continuous flow period. Compared to commercial anodes, the DRCO system reduces energy consumption by 72% (to 12.02 kW·h·kgTOC–1) while effectively suppressing the accumulation of toxic intermediate products. This work demonstrates that high-selectivity •OH generation and the elucidated dual-ROS synergistic mechanism jointly offer a viable strategy toward efficient and energy-conscious electrochemical water purification.

title: Biogeochemical Control Points for Mitigating Metal(loid) Risk in Rice under Global Change
abstract: Abstract The uptake of arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), and mercury (Hg) in rice is a global health concern. The variable biogeochemical processes that govern contamination risk, along with increased anthropogenic pressures, present significant obstacles to implementing mitigation strategies. This perspective highlights the biogeochemical processes governing the mobility and rice uptake of metal(loid)s across the soil-rice continuum and provides recent insights into mitigation strategies. An overview of anthropogenic stressors that may further exacerbate rice contamination, particularly climate change, is also provided. Finally, in the context of historical knowledge, we identify and discuss a future roadmap for research priorities and mitigation strategies, including (1) addressing variability in soil-rice systems that alters metal(loid) uptake dynamics, (2) investigating practical applications and mitigation strategies for farmers, and (3) expanding research into the myriad effects climate change may have on metal(loid) cycling.

title: Mechanistic Insights into Humic Acid-Mediated Photosensitized Activation of Mn(VII) under UVA Irradiation
abstract: Abstract Ultraviolet A/permanganate [UVA/Mn(VII)] is a promising advanced oxidation process (AOP), while few studies have noticed that humic acid (HA) could enhance microcontaminant degradation in the process. For the first time, the promotive effect of HA and the underlying mechanisms were investigated in UVA/Mn(VII). HA significantly enhanced the generation of hydroxyl radical (HO•) and reactive manganese species (RMnS). Consequently, the pseudo-first-order reaction rate constants for microcontaminant degradation in UVA/Mn(VII)/HA were several to tens of times those in UVA/Mn(VII). The promotive effect of HA was attributed to the enhanced Mn(VII) activation by photogenerated reactive intermediates derived from irradiated HA. Among them, the excited triplet state of HA (3HA*) played a major role, which was also supported by benzophenone (BP), a model triplet state photosensitizer. The second-order reaction rate constants of Mn(VII) with 3HA* and 3BP* were determined to be 2.54(±0.31) × 108 and 2.88(±0.10) × 109 M–1 s–1, respectively. Spectroscopic analysis and theoretical calculations supported an electron transfer mechanism for the reactions of Mn(VII) with 3HA* and 3BP*. Mn(VII) accepted one electron from 3HA*/3BP* and was reduced to Mn(VI), which underwent disproportionation to form Mn(VII) and Mn(V), followed by HO• and other RMnS generation. These findings provide novel perspectives for the application of UVA/Mn(VII) in practical water treatment.

title: Constructing Prospective Multiregional Input-Output Tables via Scenario-Constrained Optimization for Future Environmental Footprint Assessment
abstract: Abstract Prospective multiregional input-output (MRIO) tables that integrate scenarios from integrated assessment models (IAMs) support forward-looking environmental footprint analysis, but the trade-off between historical structural fidelity and scenario compliance has not been quantified. We constructed 12 prospective MRIO tables from EXIOBASE 2019 and the IMAGE SSP2 scenario for 2035, including a Leontief-based projection and 11 optimization-based projections under different combinations of scenario constraints on GDP, value added, sector outputs, as well as energy and agriculture consumption. Among the constraints, those on energy and agriculture consumption were satisfied at the highest cost in coefficient deviations from the Leontief-based projection and shifted the corresponding transaction flows most significantly. Regional shares of the global carbon footprint remained stable, but sectoral attribution within each region was substantially reshuffled, and the identification of high-growth consumption hotspots was sensitive to scenario compliance level. Some hotspots persisted at all levels of compliance. The consumption-based carbon footprint driven by China’s final energy demand grew the fastest and emerged as a major new hotspot in 2035. The footprint of livestock consumption showed persistent high growth in multiple regions and India and the Rest of Asia rose in environmental significance through their industrial sectors.

Experimental investigation of a multi-buoy cooperative point-absorber wave energy
abstract: This study presents a proof-of-concept experimental investigation of a multi-buoy cooperative point-absorber wave energy converter (WEC). The proposed concept consists of an array of surface-penetrating buoys connected through a shared closed-loop hydraulic power take-off (PTO) system. Energy is extracted through the collective motion of the buoy array, where pressurised flow generated by individual buoys drives a turbine within the hydraulic circuit. A 1:40 scale model was tested in the wave tank facilities at the University of Oslo. Experiments with regular and irregular long-crested waves at two different incident angles were conducted to assess power absorption, wave period response, and interaction effects. Two array configurations were investigated: an eight-buoy array with an axis-to-axis spacing of 1.5 buoy diameters, and a four-buoy array with a 3.0 diameter spacing. Although piston head leakage affected the power measurements, our results demonstrate that the WEC absorbs incoming wave energy and produces measurable power. The eight-buoy configuration achieved the highest power output per buoy compared to the four-buoy configuration, but exhibited increased sensitivity to wave period and wave heading, due to buoy-buoy interactions, such as collisions. This study highlights buoy count and internal buoy spacing as key design parameters for cooperative point-absorber wave energy systems. The results indicate that higher buoy counts enhance hydraulic cooperation, and increased buoy spacing improves robustness to wave heading and reduces destructive interaction effects. We also suggest that a lower system inertia can improve responsiveness to shorter waves. These insights provide a foundation for further optimisation and future full-scale development.

Reindeer habitat selection and movement change with cumulative impacts from mining and wind power development
abstract: Industrial expansion often occurs in landscapes already affected by multiple disturbances, leading to cumulative impacts on biodiversity and local communities. With the societal pressure for an rapid ‘green transition’, land-use changes intensifies, yet most impact assessments remain local and project-based, disregarding cumulative impacts. We conceptualized and disentangled key dimensions of cumulative impacts and integrated them within habitat selection, calving site selection, and movement analyses in a case study of reindeer and Sámi reindeer husbandry in Scandinavia. Using GPS data collected before, during, and after the construction of four wind power plants, we quantified the effects of mining, wind power development, and other infrastructure across snow-free seasons and behavioural processes. We found strong avoidance of mines and wind power plants, with zones of influence extending up to 5-10 km at landscape scale and up to 5 km at patch scale. Impacts were strongest during calving but also present in summer and autumn. Wind power plants affected movement by acting as semi-permeable barriers, with reindeer avoiding crossing them and moving faster and more directionally near turbines during construction. At patch scale, cumulative impacts of several wind power plants were evident during calving. Our results highlight the need for regional and integrative land-use planning that accounts for cumulative impacts from multiple existing and planned developments. The framework we present here provides a general approach to quantify zones of influence and cumulative impacts of multiple features and infrastructure types across landscapes and ecological processes.

title: Assessing commuting-related heat exposure deviations from Neighborhood effect averaging in a megacity
abstract: Urban heat exposure in highly mobile cities cannot be fully characterized by residential conditions alone. Existing mobility-based assessments quantify absolute exposure or residential-to-mobile differences, but do not separate population-level exposure averaging from individual departures around that relationship. We develop a three-layer framework distinguishing absolute exposure, time-matched out-of-home thermal contrast, and conditional deviation from the Neighborhood Effect Averaging Problem (NEAP) relationship. NEAP-adjusted heat exposure deviation (NAE) measures the difference between observed mobile heat exposure (MHE) and the MHE expected given residential heat exposure (RHE). Using reconstructed hourly land surface temperature and mobile-phone trajectories for 179,588 commuters in Shanghai, we identify clear population-level averaging between RHE and MHE ( β = 0.730 ). NAE and the direct out-of-home contrast differed in direction for 32.3% of commuters. Elevated NAE formed a distinct peri-core and commuting-transition geography rather than reproducing absolute heat hotspots; 26.8% of upper-decile NAE grids were not simultaneously identified by high RHE, MHE, or direct out-of-home contrast. Higher NAE was associated with longer home–work paths, longer commuting duration, and more time spent away from home, whereas greater mobility entropy was associated with lower NAE. Higher-rent residential contexts and grids with mean commuter ages in the early-to-mid 30s also showed elevated NAE, while greater functional richness and development intensity were associated with lower NAE across parts of their observed ranges. These findings establish NEAP as an empirical reference for revealing structured mobility-related exposure deviations that remain hidden in conventional absolute or direct-contrast assessments.

Impact of AI robotics, income, clean energy subtypes, and energy transition on environmental progress: An incremental analysis for China by KRLS model
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied in economies, understanding its environmental implications is highly critical. Consistent with this phenomenon, this research uncovers the impact of AI robotics (AIR), income, clean energy subtypes, and energy transition (ETI), along with traditional factors (namely, trade openness, urbanization, and financial development), on environmental progress. In this vein, the study focuses on China, the leading carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emitter, uses CO 2 emissions (sustainable development index) in the main (robustness analysis) as the dependent variable, uses AI robotics as a novel proxy for AI, and performs novel Kernel-regularized least squares (KRLS) model on the most recent data from 2000 to 2024. The results suggest that (i) AIR, income, ETI, trade openness, and urbanization are not helpful to decrease CO 2 emissions, while financial development has an insignificant increasing impact; (ii) among clean energy subtypes, only nuclear energy has a reducing impact on CO 2 emissions at lower percentiles; (iii) in terms of interaction of AIR with clean energy subtypes, only hydro (other renewable) energy is statistically significant (insignificant) decreasing impact on CO 2 emissions at lower percentiles; (iv) KRLS model obtains successful estimation results, reaching ∼99.73%; and (v) the robustness checks using an alternative dependent variable confirm the empirical results. Therefore, the research empirically attests to the inefficient use of AIR, an unsuccessful ETI approach, and ineffective use of clean energy subtypes in China. At the same time, the marginal impacts of the factors considered on CO 2 emissions differ across percentiles. Based on these findings, we outline relevant policy implications for China.

title: Evolutionary game theory for environmental governance: Theoretical foundations, multi-stakeholder dynamics, and policy design strategies for sustainable resource management
abstract: Environmental governance fails less often for want of instruments than for want of an account of how stakeholders revise their choices once instruments are in place. This review asks what evolutionary game theory (EGT) can and cannot establish about that revision process, for problems in which populations differ in position, payoff exposure, and adaptation speed. The apparatus—evolutionarily stable strategies, replicator dynamics under heterogeneous learning rates, and multi-population stability criteria—is assembled first, its representational limits stated alongside its capabilities. Two governance settings are then examined in depth. In transboundary water allocation among upstream, midstream, and downstream jurisdictions, positional asymmetry produces stratified rather than uniform cooperation: upstream and midstream converge to high cooperation while downstream collapses under the baseline payoffs, and upstream and downstream paths correlate most strongly at a lag of about 25 years, set by infrastructure investment cycles and institutional adaptation. In tripartite industrial pollution control, single instruments leave the system in the low-cooperation basin (equilibrium near 0.01–0.02), whereas penalties and abatement-cost relief applied jointly move it to an equilibrium near 0.73; enterprise adjustment lags the regulatory shock by about 15 years and community mobilization by about 25 years. Such regularities are projections of a specified model rather than measurements of behavior, and the conditions under which they would fail are stated with them. For policy, instrument combination takes priority over instrument intensity, commitment horizons measured in decades over electoral cycles, and measures that lower participation costs for the actors whose monitoring extends enforcement reach.

title: Microbial Respiration in Subtropical Urban Soils Depending on Vegetation Type
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban vegetation combines invasive and introduced species with native relics, whose litter is the primary source of organic matter inputs in urban soils. Plant litter quality regulates both organic carbon (C) storage and microbial activity in urban soils. Here we examined the microbial respiration and organic C stocks in the subtropical urban soils depending on plant litter decomposability. Five urban areas differing in vegetation (deciduous forest, shrubland, grassland, ruderal area, and turfgrass) were used for kinetic analysis of plant litter decomposition over a 12‐week incubation, and CO 2 efflux and microbial biomass C in soil were analyzed. The plant litter decomposability decreased as its C/N ratio increased. The decay constant of potentially mineralized litter components decreased progressively from turfgrass and grassland to shrubland and ruderal area, and finally to forest. Higher litter decomposition was associated with a faster rate of soil microbial respiration per unit of organic C content. Soil organic C stocks were 20%–38% larger in urban forest and areas with ruderal vegetation than in turfgrass. This was caused by the greater biostability of forest litter and lower microbial activity in the soils of semi‐natural areas compared with those of completely transformed and managed urban ecosystems such as turfgrass. Consequently, the decrease in decomposability of plant litter increased organic C stocks and reduced microbial respiration rates, highlighting the importance of vegetation type in managing C storage in urban soils.

title: Microplastic‐Induced Shifts in Soil Leachate Chemistry, Redox Response, Biochemistry, and Biofilm Dynamics
abstract: ABSTRACT Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as soil contaminants, yet their time‐dependent associations with dissolved organic matter characteristics, redox behavior, biochemical constituents, and biofilm‐associated responses are often investigated separately. This study evaluated these responses within an integrated soil‐exposure framework using particles derived from three commonly used consumer products—surgical masks (predominantly polypropylene, PP), plastic water bottles (polyethylene terephthalate, PET), and cardboard cups (cellulose‐rich composites containing a polymeric barrier layer)—at three nominal loadings (0.1, 0.5, and 2.0 g per 200 g soil), three exposure periods (1, 3, and 7 weeks), and two extraction media (distilled water and phosphate‐buffered saline, PBS). UV–Vis‐derived aromaticity‐related (AR), humification‐related (HI), and spectral slope factor (SF) indices were assessed alongside DTT‐based redox responses, CUPRAC‐based extractable reducing capacity, extractable carbohydrate and protein contents, and crystal‐violet‐based biofilm‐associated responses. The investigated materials exhibited distinct material‐, loading‐, time‐, and extraction‐medium‐dependent patterns across these endpoints. At week 1, several treatments showed relatively elevated HI and SF ratios compared with matched soil controls. These responses generally declined by week 3, whereas selected PET‐bottle‐ and cardboard‐cup‐derived treatments exhibited renewed increases in aromaticity‐ or humification‐related optical indices at week 7, particularly in PBS extracts. DTT‐based redox responses also varied substantially across conditions, although these measurements did not directly quantify DTT consumption rates or ROS formation. Extractable carbohydrate contents and CV‐stainable biofilm‐associated material showed pronounced responses in selected cardboard‐cup and PET‐bottle treatments, whereas protein responses were generally modest. Overall, the findings demonstrate condition‐dependent changes in soil‐extract optical characteristics, redox‐related analytical responses, and extractable biochemical constituents, without establishing a consistent monotonic relationship with particle loading or a causal link between redox changes and biofilm formation.

title: The material infrastructure of privatization, dispossession and resistance at the Zambian land frontier
abstract: The privatization of communal lands continues to be a central tenet of capitalist and settler-colonial appropriations with devastating implications for the dispossessed and land denied. This article traces how dispossession and resistance become bound up in the material infrastructure of privatization – fences, concrete, rebar and survey lines – and the colonial histories sedimented within them. In dialogue with legal-geographical work on property and materiality, I show how such artefacts become the nodes through which law’s abstraction gives way to struggle; once law is materialized in objects, these become susceptible to alteration and enrolment in new lives of legal association that can subvert – and creatively invert – the power trafficked through property. The analysis draws from ethnographic fieldwork in Mulonga village, central Zambia, where a privatization scheme evolved into a localized struggle between creative cultivators who reworked the things of property to resist displacement, and a bureaucracy that struggled to make them perform the political work assigned to them. Abstract property, I conclude, must be read alongside the contingency and resistant reworkings of its material articulation, which creates new legal surfaces upon which people can act, redirect legal signs, and unsettle translations through which private property achieves exclusionary effect.

The influence of private equity investment on firm transaction costs in offshore emerging economies
abstract: This study focuses on the transaction cost of share trading for listed firms with private equity ownership within emerging economies. We build on a recently advanced emerging market private equity business model (Taussig & Delios, 2016) and complement this model by applying the ownership competency theory of Foss, Klein, Lien, Zellweger & Zenger (2021). Our study draws on a unique sample of listed firms from eight national securities exchanges across the Caribbean region. We find that private equity ownership increases firms’ transaction costs, as reflected in higher estimated bid-ask quoted share price spreads. However, this association is negatively moderated by (1) the firm having a related party located in an offshore jurisdiction and (2) the firm adopting a shareholder value enhancing corporate governance model. In a broader context, our analysis highlights the importance of institutional fit of private equity in the local institutional fabric within which investee firms are embedded

title: Rethinking Supplier Integration in Humanitarian Supply Chains: Feasibility and Constraints From an International Humanitarian Organization Perspective
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite the widely recognized importance of integrative practices in commercial supply chain operations, their application in humanitarian supply chains (HSCs) remains underexplored. HSCs differ from commercial supply chains in their relational dynamics and integration processes, operating under extreme uncertainty, demand volatility, infrastructural disruption, and resource scarcity across a complex web of actors. Using an embedded single‐case design, this study assesses supplier integration (SI) in humanitarian operations in a leading international humanitarian organization (IHO), as well as the IHO's relationships with eight key suppliers. Drawing on the relational lenses of power, trust, and commitment, distinct integration patterns were identified across different supplier types. The findings highlight humanitarian‐specific contextual constraints and are used to inform a typology of SI feasibility encompassing feasible, selectively feasible, and low‐feasibility integration. This typology provides a foundation for guiding supplier relationship management in complex humanitarian contexts. This study offers a framework for understanding how relational and structural conditions shape integration in humanitarian settings and underscores the need for IHOs to adopt context‐appropriate supplier management approaches that reflect the unique dynamics of humanitarian operations.

title: Navigating Circular Economy Challenges in the Internationalization of Food Companies: MCDM‐Based Investigation
abstract: ABSTRACT In today's rapidly changing and highly competitive environment, internationalization has become a strategic necessity. It is no longer merely a source of competitive advantage, but a fundamental requirement for organizational survival. This need is particularly pronounced in the food industry, which faces stringent quality requirements and growing pressure to comply with international regulations. However, the internationalization of these firms brings significant challenges related to circular economy (CE) practices. The main goal of this study is to identify and evaluate the most important challenges and obstacles to implementing CE in small and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) in the food industry. This study was conducted in three phases. In the first phase, through a literature review, the barriers to implementing CE in the internationalization process of food SMEs, along with the evaluation criteria related to these barriers, were identified. In the second phase, the identified criteria were weighted using the hesitant fuzzy best–worst method (HF‐BWM) in order to determine their relative importance. Finally, in the third phase, the barriers were ranked based on the obtained weights by applying the hesitant fuzzy CoCoSo (HF‐CoCoSo) technique, which is a rigorous multicriteria decision‐making (MCDM) method. The findings indicate that criteria “Loss of foreign customers' trust,” “Loss of sales and revenue,” and “loss of market share” received the highest weights. Moreover, the barriers “Financial constraints in implementing CE,” “Lack of successful business models and frameworks,” and “Uncertainty in reverse flows” were ranked as the most significant. The findings of this research contribute to enriching the existing body of knowledge on the internationalization of food industry enterprises by addressing the barriers associated with CE. Furthermore, the results provide decision‐makers with valuable insights to overcome the influential CE ‐ related obstacles affecting the internationalization process.

title: Innovation Environment Matters More Than Policy? Evidence on Technology Adoption From Chinese Manufacturers
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how policy regulation and external innovation environment jointly influence manufacturing firms' adoption of emerging technologies and subsequent operational performance. Drawing on institutional theory and the resource‐based view, we analyse survey data from 451 Chinese manufacturing firms using structural equation modelling. The results show that policy regulation does not directly drive technology adoption. Instead, it significantly shapes the external innovation environment, which fully mediates the relationship between policy regulation and technology adoption. Emerging technology adoption further improves operational performance. These findings reveal an institution‐resource conversion mechanism: Policy enables the environment, and the environment drives technology adoption. The study extends institutional theory by moving beyond the linear pressure‐response framework and theorising the external innovation environment as a conversion interface between institutional and resource logics. For practice, firms should embed technology adoption into long‐term capability building, while policymakers should shift from direct intervention to cultivating an innovation environment that supports resource coordination.

Ion Valence Difference Governs Membrane Charge Preference in Nanofiltration-Based Radionuclide Separation
abstract: Abstract Selective separation of radionuclides with varying environmental hazards is critical for mitigating the disposal burden of high-level radioactive wastewater. Although positively charged (PC) membranes are generally considered effective for cation pair separation, the applicability of negatively charged (NC) membranes for separating cations with large valence differences remains unresolved. In this study, Ag+/Zr4+ and Ag+/Sr2+ were used as representative radionuclides with large and small valence differences, respectively, to evaluate the separation performance and underlying mechanisms of PC and NC membranes. Notably, NC membranes maintained near-complete rejection of Zr4+ while simultaneously exhibiting higher Ag+ permeability, thereby achieving superior Ag+/Zr4+ selectivity relative to PC membranes. DFT calculations and MD simulations revealed that strong ion–membrane interactions facilitated preferential partitioning of Zr4+ at the NC membrane interface, whereas differences in hydration energy governed the competitive transport of Ag+ and Zr4+. Furthermore, Zr4+ accumulated at the membrane surface induced incomplete dehydration of Ag+, reducing interfacial transport barriers and promoting Ag+ permeation. Comparative analysis of Ag+/Zr4+ and Ag+/Sr2+ systems further demonstrated that ion valence difference governs the preference of membrane charges: NC membranes are preferred for M+/M4+ separations, whereas PC membranes are preferred for M+/M2+ separations, which was further validated by Li+/Mg2+ and Li+/Ti4+ separations. These findings clarify the mechanistic distinction between co-ion and counterion competition, providing guidance for the selection of membrane charge types for energy-efficient radionuclide separation and selective resource recovery beyond the nuclear industry.

title: Market-Average Data Can Misrepresent Supply Chain Environmental Impacts and Their Uncertainty
abstract: Abstract Market-average data sets are often used in life cycle assessment and carbon accounting when the production route of a procured good is unknown. The uncertainty this introduces is commonly characterized using generic pedigree matrix factors, which do not reflect how variability across production geographies and technologies differs between goods. Here, we develop a hybrid method that combines pedigree matrix uncertainty characterization within individual production routes with market-share-weighted Monte Carlo sampling between known production routes to represent uncertainty about which route supplied the good. We compare it with conventional market-average uncertainty analysis for 30 economically important goods. For climate impacts, conventional 5th–95th interpercentile intervals are narrower than route-weighted sampling intervals for 25 goods, at least 50% narrower for 14 goods, and up to 82% narrower. Conventional intervals exclude the central climate impact estimates of 44% of possible production routes. Route-weighted sampling captures these outcomes and reveals multimodality and impact-category-specific uncertainty profiles that conventional analysis does not. Variance decomposition distinguishes geographical and technological differences between routes from uncertainty within routes, helping prioritize supplier data collection. These differences show that conventional uncertainty estimates can mislead and may not capture how substantially initial estimates could change when supplier-specific data become available.

Interactions among land use, climate, leaf litter traits, and consumers shape large-scale patterns of decomposition in streams of SW Europe
abstract: Habitat degradation is one of the primary drivers of biodiversity loss and ecosystem alteration. In streams, leaf litter decomposition plays a key role in energy and nutrient cycling, which is influenced by leaf litter quality, microbial and invertebrate consumers, and environmental conditions. Land use changes alter stream habitats and can modify decomposition rates and dynamics, but large-scale assessments of these anthropogenic impacts remain limited. We explored the consequences of major land use changes (tree plantations, agricultural land, and urban settlements) on stream ecosystems by comparing sites in human-impacted catchments with reference unimpacted sites (i.e., surrounded by native vegetation) across several regions of southwestern Europe encompassing a wide climatic gradient. We quantified decomposition rates of multiple leaf litter types to evaluate the interaction between leaf litter traits and environmental variation, exploring changes in associated invertebrate assemblages. Overall, land use changes reduced total and microbial decomposition rates, with agriculture exerting the strongest effects, and caused marked shifts in invertebrate assemblages including replacement of sensitive by tolerant species and reduced detritivore richness, mainly in urban streams. Climatic variability seemed to modulate these responses, with seasonal climates showing higher vulnerability to impacts. Lastly, leaf litter types differed in their sensitivity to detect degradation, although no consistent trait-based patterns were observed. Our results show that land use changes alter stream ecosystems across climatic gradients, highlighting the urgent need to integrate environmental and biological drivers across spatial scales in watershed management and to provide actionable baselines to optimize riparian restoration and buffer the effects of ongoing climate change.

title: Operationalising connectivity in the spatial management of mangroves
“Waste treats waste”: Upcycling spent Zn–Mn battery zinc into carbon-modified ZnO photocatalyst for sunlight-driven methylene blue mineralization

Metal enrichment and downstream concentration gradients in an agricultural ditch draining a long-term fertilisation experiment
abstract: Agricultural sediment surveys seldom quantify the downstream extent of metal enrichment. We measured Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Ni, Pb and Zn in 24 surface sediment samples below the Palace Leas long-term fertilisation experiment at Cockle Park, UK. Eighteen samples formed a 452.5 m ditch transect, with three samples each from the receiving stream and an adjacent diffuse runoff line. Concentrations declined downstream, with the strongest enrichment near the ditch head. Metal-specific segmented-fit breakpoints were 104 m for Cd (5–95% resampling interval, 78–129 m), 159 m for Co (129–185 m) and 159 m for Cu (104–236 m). These do not establish a shared boundary. Cr and Ni breakpoint positions were poorly constrained. The first 150 m contained 66.3–96.7% of the distance-integrated excess concentration for six metals, an index of profile shape rather than stored metal mass. Cd contributed 73.9% of a partial seven-metal risk index, while Ni exceeded its freshwater probable effect level in one third of samples. As and Hg were not measured, so the screening may underestimate multi-element hazard and cannot establish the overall priority contaminant. Missing grain-size and organic-carbon measurements leave sediment sorting and carrier mixing unresolved. Uniform concentration scaling preserves within-metal spatial contrasts, but absolute concentrations and screening classifications remain conditional on unmeasured digestion recovery. Detection-limit-aware uncertainty was therefore used for risk-score scenarios. The upper reach is a candidate for follow-up monitoring; a 150 m mitigation zone requires validation with sediment-flux and repeated sampling data.

title: Multi-target machine learning prediction of constructed wetland effluent quality with model interpretation and experimental validation
A machine learning approach to understanding freshwater salinization dynamics and winter season controls in the Northeast United States
abstract: Freshwater salinization is an increasing concern in colder regions where road-salt application, watershed development, hydroclimatic factors, and anthropogenic activities influence river salinity. This study evaluated winter freshwater salinization across six rivers in New York and New Jersey. We hypothesized that winter salinity reflects both shared watershed-scale relationships and site-specific dynamics, with predictor importance varying among watersheds with contrasting hydroclimatic, land-use, and anthropogenic characteristics. The study included 2570 daily observations across three winter seasons from November 2021 to March 2024. Spatial patterns were assessed through principal component analysis (PCA) and geospatial watershed characterization. Multiple linear regression (MLR), random forest (RF), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) were applied in pooled and site-specific models using snowfall-lag predictors, while SHAP explained the predictor importance. PCA identified climatic-salinity and hydrologic-flow gradients. The pooled XGBoost model achieved a strong test performance (R 2 = 0.79), with developed land identified as a dominant predictor. Site-specific ensemble models generally outperformed MLR, with XGBoost reaching R 2 = 0.81 at Cattaraugus Creek, a highly forested watershed. Larger drainage-area stations showed limited predictive skill, while highly urbanized watersheds performed moderately. Dominant predictors differed among stations and included discharge, pH, and turbidity. In the Bronx River case study, RF achieved R 2 of 0.56, with two-day lagged road-salt application as the most influential predictor, highlighting road-salt monitoring needs in highly urbanized watersheds. Overall, the findings advance understanding of winter stream salinity dynamics across diverse watersheds and emphasize the need for road-salt monitoring and management.

title: Magnetite nanocomposites for pharmaceutical-contaminated water and wastewater: An evidence-maturity framework for design, treatment, recovery, and translation
The driving role of proteins in enhancing lactate and propionate production during food waste fermentation: metabolic constraints and kinetic modeling
abstract: This study aimed to quantify the fraction of lactate, derived from the fermentation of Food Waste (FW) attributable to proteins. Infact, recent studies based on cellular resource allocation suggest that proteins can promote the growth of lactic acid bacteria and enhance lactate production. The experiments were conducted in a chemostat, at a HRT of 20 h and a pH = 5 and 5.5, using a synthetic substrate composed of glucose and albumin in a 4:1 COD ratio, mimicking household FW composition. A pure glucose solution was used for comparison. Although lactate was detected at low concentrations, the glucose-albumin substrate produced a considerable amount of propionate, even when albumin was not consumed, in contrast to the pure glucose solution. It was hypothesized that most propionate was generated via the acrylate pathway, rather than glycolysis, thus confirming the significance of the lactate metabolic pathway. A mathematical model based on the variable stoichiometry approach was adopted as a tool to investigate this hypothesis. The model accounted for the metabolic constraint imposed by the conservation of electron carriers (NADH) throughout the fermentation process. The metabolic constraint made it possible to estimate that propionate production occurred with high probability via the acrylate pathway, thereby revealing that proteins were crucial in driving the metabolic shift of glucose fermentation toward lactate; model calibration estimated that lactate accounted for 35 – 65 % of the total electron flux. Furthermore, lactate was separately supplemented to the substrate in additional experiments, inducing a metabolic shift from acrylate pathway to chain elongation.
