Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1–8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9–13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and continuous repression, and nominate safeguard repressors as candidate therapeutic targets that are distinct from differentiation-inducing activators, with potential relevance across cancers in which phenotypic switching drives therapy resistance.

title: AI agents run this automated biology lab that sequences DNA and more
Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics
Carbon radical generation by irreversible metal-to-ligand charge transfer
Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
abstract: Abstract Fibrous materials, ranging from connective tissues 1–4 to engineered composites 5–8 , are vital to many biological and man-made systems, optimized to withstand complex in operando or in vivo loading. The load-bearing capacity of intervertebral discs (IVDs) of the spine depends on a hierarchical extracellular matrix, where plywood-like lamellae of collagen fibres in the annulus fibrosus contain nanometre-scale fibrils built from staggered triple-helical monomers 4,9,10 . How intact IVDs couple fibril-scale mechanics to fibre-scale organization under load remains unresolved. Here we introduce TomoSAXS, a full-field 3D small-angle X-ray scattering tomography that maps fibril-to-fibre mechanics across an intact tissue. We show that intrafibrillar molecular pre-strain (D-period stagger) is lamellar textured and tightly correlated with microscale fibre strain. Pre-strain is inversely related to fibril strain and its variability, consistent with load-sharing through molecular unwinding. Radial strain bridges and high-curvature zones at the annulus fibrosus–nucleus pulposus interfaces emerge as critical regulators of local mechanics. These findings reveal concerted fibril–fibre interactions that sustain mechanical equilibrium in the IVD, preserving elasticity and shape. More broadly, TomoSAXS establishes a platform to visualize nanoscale-to-microscale matrix mechanics across biological and synthetic fibrous materials, with applications in ageing and disease, therapeutic evaluation and the design of bio-based and bio-inspired materials.

title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
abstract: Abstract Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au (ref. 1 ) but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation 2,3 , effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation 4 . Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation 5,6 . Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories 7 . Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff) 8 to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) 9–11 coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2–15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b (ref. 12 ) at 4.3 μm. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.

title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
abstract: Abstract The Great Unconformity marks a globally extensive erosive surface linked to climatic shifts 1 and environmental transitions 2 that preceded the Cambrian explosion of life. The processes proposed to explain the formation of the Great Unconformity include glacial erosion during the Snowball Earth 1,3,4 , rifting and plume activity 5–7 , sea-level fall 8 and mantle-driven dynamic topography 6,9–11 . However, the dynamics of these processes have not been tested. Here we show that continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography 12 due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity. Our models predict prolonged continental-scale Neoproterozoic uplift and long-term Phanerozoic subsidence for Laurentia, Baltica and North China. This vertical motion scenario is ideal for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity, which is a first-order surface expression of deep Earth processes. The predicted prolonged continental uplift throughout Cryogenian times would have resulted in marked erosion due to the action of glaciers 13 . The large area of Laurentia and limited deformation at its margins explain why the Great Unconformity is best preserved and documented there. Our models predict cycles of dynamic topography that are broadly reflected in preserved sediment volume across continents 1,14 , and open new avenues for understanding the environments of Cambrian animal diversification.

title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
abstract: Abstract Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age 1–3 . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested 4 , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts 5–8 . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory 9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
abstract: Abstract Mating decisions are often attributed to the sensory signalling between prospective sexual partners. Yet these interactions are also shaped by the broader environmental context in which they unfold, to appropriately align sexual arousal with reproductive opportunities 1–6 . Here we show that in Drosophila erecta mating is strictly contingent on the ecological and social environment generated as flies densely aggregate in groups on a food patch. We find that food volatiles directly promote male sexual arousal, triggering individuals to sample and pursue potential mates, giving rise to dynamic interactions across the group. The ensuing visual motion transforms each male’s visual field, which in turn further amplifies his arousal, generating a multisensory feedback loop that coordinately promotes courtship across individuals. D. erecta ’s strict dependence on environmental cues appears latent in related species, such as Drosophila melanogaster , where food odour can promote arousal 7 but is dispensable for vigorous courtship. Comparative circuit analyses show that species-specific thresholds for sexual arousal reflect variation in how olfactory input modulates conserved nodes controlling courtship drive, rendering food volatiles a strict sensory gate only in D. erecta . Together, our findings highlight how environmental cues not directly tied to sexual signalling can profoundly influence reproductive behaviour and reorganize the social landscape to ensure mating occurs in contexts where reproductive opportunities are abundant.

title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
abstract: Abstract The VEGF ligand and its main receptor VEGFR2 are considered to be essential for endothelial differentiation, proliferation, sprouting and survival. Blood vessels cannot form in growing embryos or tissues when VEGF/VEGFR2 signalling is compromised in all cells. The Anti-VEGF blocking antibody is one of the most widely used antibodies in the clinics, blocking angiogenesis in cancer, wound healing or in ischemic diseases. However, vascular resistance to Anti-VEGF has been reported. Here we used iFlpMosaics and iSuRe-HadCre to induce and track genetic mosaics of endothelial cells (ECs) lacking VEGFR2 during the entire embryonic and postnatal development. Surprisingly, Vegfr2 KO ECs adapt, proliferate normally and compete with wild-type cells over time, ultimately forming a substantial portion of the capillary network in most organs. We found that Vegfr2 KO ECs are not able to sprout during the first wave of angiogenesis in most tissues, because it is highly VEGF-dependent and favours the growth and mobilization of wild-type ECs. However, due to their inability to respond to VEGF, over time Vegfr2 KO ECs become dominant in veins, which provide for a long term and continuous source of ECs for subsequent waves of VEGF-independent angiogenesis. Comparative scRNAseq analysis of ECs with acute and long-term loss of VEGFR2, revealed both common and organ-specific molecular mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to VEGF signalling loss. This included significant endothelial venousization and the upregulation of ligands for VEGFR1 and VEGFR3. VEGFR1 only partially compensated for VEGFR2 loss in capillary ECs, whereas VEGFR3 only compensated in arterial ECs. Loss of the three VEGF receptors did not compromise venous growth. This work changes our understanding of the role of VEGF signaling and its receptors in angiogenesis and reveals mechanisms of adaptation and resistance to their loss.

title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
abstract: Abstract Hydrogen-bearing materials are central to low-carbon energy technologies 1 , but hydrogen itself is difficult to detect and localize at the nanoscale 2–6 . This hinders the development of advanced materials with better efficiency. Atom probe tomography (APT) can map hydrogen in three dimensions and at high resolution, yet characterization of dilute, mobile, interstitial hydrogen in metals has remained challenging because of low solubility, the ambiguity owing to hydrogen trapping by structural defects, as well as the artefacts introduced during hydrogen introduction 4–6 . Here we address whether interstitial hydrogen in solution in materials can be distinguished from defect-trapped hydrogen in APT. Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, together with face-centred cubic (FCC) multi-principal-element alloys (MPEAs) containing coherent FCC precipitates, we show that deuterium atoms reproducibly concentrate in hydrogen-affinitive phases in a manner consistent with theoretical predictions. We further resolve differences in deuterium content between phases with distinct local chemistries and crystal structures, consistent with their different calculated hydrogen solution energies. These findings demonstrate that APT can move beyond identifying hydrides and solute-decorated defects to examine hydrogen in solid solution, providing new insights into hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys and informing materials design for hydrogen-related applications.

title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
abstract: Abstract The importance of the gut microbiome in human health has been widely recognized, with alterations in species abundances now reported for many different diseases. In recent years, observations of within-species genetic diversity and strain-level functional differences have urged the field to transition to analyzing microbes at the genetic level, taking advantage of genetic variants in the metagenome to pinpoint relevant genes and pathways. Here, we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) of 12.7 million gut microbial single nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from six independent cohorts from Europe and Africa. We found 3,018 associations supported by at least two cohorts for 105 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Moreover, we found 34,927 significant associations in single-cohort analyses where SNV–phenotype pairs were only available for one cohort. All identified associations are detailed in an online catalog (https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/). The associated microbial SNVs inform mechanistic hypotheses about microbial functionality in human health and provide insights into microbial adaptation and evolution in response to changes in the environment and host physiology. For example, we identified 718 age-associated gut microbial SNVs across multiple cohorts and used these microbial SNVs to accurately predict host age. We also identified SNVs in microbial genes associated with lipid concentrations and BMI, including SNVs in the isoleucine-tRNA synthetase gene of Clostridium phoceensis and an α-Melanocyte-stimulating hormone-mimicking clpB gene of Alistipes ihumii. Mediation analysis provided evidence that microbial genetic variations may be under selection enforced by environmental factors, but also that they mediate the effects on the host, e.g. the isoleucyl-tRNA synthetase gene of C. phoceensis mediated dietary effects on four phenotypes. Overall, this study identifies new biological connections between human host and microbial genetic variants, exposing the functional layer of gut microbiome data hidden at base pair resolution and revealing microbial adaptation and evolution in relation to host lifestyle and physiology.

title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
abstract: Abstract RNA language models have achieved strong performances across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by its hierarchical structure, making the integration of structural information into pre-training essential. Existing methods often depend on noisy structural annotations or introduce task-specific biases, limiting model generalizability. Here, we introduce structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model that is pre-trained on millions of RNA sequences and secondary structures data by integrating base pairing interactions into masked language modeling through a novel pair matching operation. The structure-guided mask and nucleotide-level mask are further balanced by a dynamic masking ratio. structRFM learns joint knowledge of sequential and structural data, producing versatile representations, including classification-level, sequence-level, and pairwise matrix features, that support a broad spectrum of downstream adaptations. structRFM ranks among the top models in zero-shot homology classification across fifteen biological language models, and sets new benchmarks for secondary structure prediction. structRFM further derives Zfold, which enables robust and reliable tertiary structure prediction, with consistent improvements in estimating 3D structures and their accordingly extracted 2D structures, achieving a pronounced 19% performance gain compared with AlphaFold3 on RNA Puzzles dataset. In functional tasks such as internal ribosome entry site identification, structRFM achieves a whopping 49% performance gain in F1 score. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight a promising direction for developing multi-modal RNA language models in computational biology. To support the broader scientific community, we have made the 21-million sequence-structure dataset and the pre-trained structRFM model fully open-source, facilitating the development of multimodal foundation models in biology.

title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
abstract: Abstract Rubella virus (RuV) causes rubella and, when acquired during pregnancy, congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). Despite its clinical significance, the cellular entry mechanism of RuV remains poorly characterized owing to limited knowledge of host receptors, hampering pathogenesis studies and therapeutic development. Here, we identify Nectin-4 as a functional RuV entry receptor through proximity biotin labeling-based proteomics coupled with CRISPR/Cas9 validation. Notably, Nectin-4 is shared with measles virus, revealing convergent evolution in viral entry despite the different viral families. Nectin-4 directly interacts with the RuV envelope glycoproteins through its ectodomain, facilitating receptor-mediated endocytosis following initial calcium-dependent viral attachment. In polarized respiratory epithelial cells, Nectin-4 mediates basolateral viral entry and subsequent apical release of progeny virions, enabling efficient respiratory transmission. Using human placental organoid models, we demonstrate that syncytiotrophoblasts serve as primary targets for transplacental RuV infection, with viral entry significantly inhibited by Nectin-4 blockade. These findings establish Nectin-4 as critical for both horizontal respiratory transmission and vertical maternal–fetal transmission of RuV. Our results provide fundamental insights into RuV pathogenesis and identify Nectin-4 as a promising therapeutic target for CRS. Importantly, the discovery of shared receptor utilization between RuV and measles virus opens new avenues for integrated elimination strategies targeting both pathogens.

title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
abstract: Abstract Cancer cells display highly heterogeneous and plastic states in glioblastoma, an incurable brain tumour. However, how these malignant states arise and whether they follow defined cellular trajectories across tumours is poorly understood. Here, we generated a deep single cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma that pairs transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling of 12 tumours across multiple regions. We identify that glioblastoma heterogeneity is driven by spatially-patterned transitions of cancer cells from developmental-like states towards those defined by a glial injury response and hypoxia. This cellular trajectory regionalises tumours into distinct tissue niches and manifests in a molecularly conserved manner across tumours as well as genetically distinct tumour subclones. Moreover, using a new deep learning framework to map cancer cell states jointly with clones in situ , we show that tumour subclones are finely spatially intermixed through glioblastoma tissue niches. Finally, we show that this cancer cell trajectory is intimately linked to myeloid heterogeneity and unfolds across regionalised myeloid signalling environments. Our findings define a stereotyped trajectory of cancer cells in glioblastoma and unify glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity into a tractable cellular and tissue framework.

title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
abstract: ABSTRACT Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD 1–3 . Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge 4 . Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in males than females 5 , and autistic females tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared to autistic males 6,7 , but the biological basis of this “female protective effect” (FPE) is unknown 8,9 . Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network (GRN) enabled the identification of central transcriptional regulators, including the prominent ASD gene CHD8 as well as novel candidates such as REST , that drive this transcriptomic convergence. Furthermore, the X-linked transcription factor ZFX , which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in females 10 , emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the FPE. Together, these results reveal how key GRNs can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
abstract: Abstract Mycobacterium tuberculosis , the causative agent of tuberculosis, remains the world’s deadliest pathogen 1 . Despite intensive study, many of its genes remain uncharacterized, which limits the insight that can be gained into tuberculosis biology and constrains drug development. Genetic interaction (GI) mapping is a powerful strategy to define functional relationships between genes by quantifying how the phenotypic effects of combined perturbations deviate from expectations based on single-gene perturbations 2,3 . Here we develop a dual-sgRNA CRISPR-interference platform that enables high-throughput GI mapping in mycobacteria. We address key technical challenges in library construction and data interpretation by incorporating unique barcodes for each sgRNA pair and implementing a robust statistical pipeline for GI detection. Focusing on essential genes, we generate comprehensive GI maps in the model mycobacterium Mycobacterium smegmatis and the pathogen M. tuberculosis . These maps recapitulate known biology, uncover thousands of previously unrecognized interactions and identify functional connections between essential genes and drug targets. By generating AlphaFold3-based protein–protein interaction predictions 4 for all gene pairs in our GI maps, we show that a subset of GIs is likely to reflect underlying physical associations. Validation of selected GIs confirms both novel biological relationships and opportunities for synergistic targeting. Overall, this work establishes a generalizable framework for dual-gene perturbation and defines the architecture of essential-gene networks in mycobacteria, advancing both our understanding of tuberculosis biology and the rational design of combination therapies.

title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
abstract: ABSTRACT The ability to observe the social behavior of others and use observed information to bias future action is a fundamental building block of social cognition 1,2 . A foundational question is whether social observation and experience engage common circuit mechanisms that enable behavioral change. While classic studies on social learning have shown that aggressive behaviors can be learned through observation 3 , it remains unclear whether aggression observation promotes persistent neural changes that generalize to new contexts. Here, to directly compare the effects of aggression experience and observation at brain-wide scale, we develop a strategy to perform large-scale cell-type specific recordings across subcortical networks for social behavior control and learning. We record longitudinally while animals “train” through direct experience or observation, then probe shared differences in behavior and neural activity in a novel “hard” aggression context. Using supervised and unsupervised methods for behavioral quantification, we detect unique signatures of a shared behavioral strategy not present in animals with no training. During observation, we find widespread activation that mimics experience in networks for behavior generation, with critical differences in signals associated with reward and threat learning. After observation, we observe that changes persist into the novel aggression context, with increased similarity in the neural dynamics between experience and observation groups. Network-level modeling reveals persistent shared changes to a core aggression network, with widespread decoupling of inhibition from a key hypothalamic output region. This demonstrates that “experience-like” activity during observation can recruit a shared plasticity mechanism that biases behavior toward adaptive defensive strategies in new contexts.

title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe2
Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
abstract: Algal blooms are hotspots for diverse microbial interactions affecting bloom dynamics. Viral infections often regulate the demise of these blooms, recycling >25% of oceanic fixed carbon. Although these blooms collapse synchronously, only 10-30% of algal cells show active viral infection, suggesting additional mortality agents. Using microbial communities from natural coccolithophore blooms, we discovered that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-mediated algal mortality. We quantified this interaction using two novel metrics: the Synergy Index (SI) measuring viral-bacterial interaction strength, and the Benefit Index (BI) assessing changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral-bacterial coinfection, with consistently high SI and BI. In natural communities, Alteromonas exhibited chemoattraction towards infected algal cells, leading to their enrichment in bloom demise particles. This viral-bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent controlling bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, likely influencing global carbon cycling.

abstract: An image-processing framework for detecting exoplanets directly has been developed. The technique overcomes the telescope-stability barrier that has limited previous methods, reveals fainter exoplanets than other approaches can detect and could make imaging exo-Earths easier for future observatories. A physics-based model enables the observation of exoplanets that were undetectable using standard techniques.

abstract: The duration of short ångström-wavelength X-ray pulses, which lasted merely 170 attoseconds, has finally been measured accurately. The optical system designed for precision pulse duration metrology can be used as a ‘stopwatch’ to measure the rapid motion of electrons inside atoms and molecules, too. Short pulses generated by the system could be used to observe electrons moving around atomic nuclei.

Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
abstract: ABSTRACT We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

The Political Economy of Propaganda: Evidence from US Newspapers,
abstract: Abstract This study examines whether racial outrage in the media can result from the incentives of elites who seek to divide society for political gain, focusing on the late 19th century Southern United States. At this time, the Democratic Party had strong political incentives to incite racial outrage, and local Democratic elites exercised considerable influence over newspapers, the only mass media at the time. Using high-frequency historical newspaper data and difference-in-differences and triple-difference estimation strategies, we find evidence consistent with Democratic elites orchestrating a racist propaganda campaign to sway white voters. Supporting analyses are consistent with Democrats benefiting from anti-Black propaganda in the subsequent elections.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: The price of geoeconomic dependence: Sanction intensity and corporate credit spreads
Local Crime and Prosocial Behaviours: Evidence from Charitable Donations
abstract: Abstract We study the relationship between local crime and residents’ charitable donations and explore the mechanisms underlying this relationship. The analysis combines longitudinal postcode-level data on charitable donations made through a UK giving portal with publicly available data on local crime and neighbourhood characteristics. Our main results suggest that an increase in local crime corresponds to a significant rise in the size of unscheduled charitable donations. This pattern is primarily driven by the donation choices of female and gender-unclassified donors. The strength of the relationship between local crime and donation amounts also varies with postcode-specific population characteristics, such as religiosity, age, and mental health.

title: Marital sorting, household inequality and selection
abstract: Using CPS data for 1976 to 2025, we explore how wage inequality has evolved for married couples with both spouses working full time full year, and its impact on household income inequality. We also investigate how marriage sorting patterns have changed over this period. To determine the factors driving income inequality we estimate a model explaining the joint distribution of couples’ wages that accounts for spouses’ employment decisions. This requires a multivariate distribution regression model that incorporates a double selection rule. We find that income inequality has increased for these households and increased wage sorting has exacerbated the inequality resulting from individual wage growth. We find that positive sorting partially reflects the correlation across unobservables influencing the wages of both members of the marriage. We decompose the changes in sorting patterns over the 50-year sample into structural, composition and selection effects and find that the increase in positive sorting primarily reflects the increased skill premia for both observed and unobserved characteristics.

title: Two-stage least squares with treatment-covariate interactions for treatment effect heterogeneity
Agricultural Trade and Industrial Development
Anchoring and Cost Vector Design in Discrete Choice Experiments:Testing Rational Choice, Coherent Arbitrariness, and Discovered Preferences
abstract: This study revisits and extends the discussion by Bateman et al. (2008) regarding potential deviations from Rational Choice Theory, focusing on two hypotheses – Coherent Arbitrariness (CAH) and Discovered Preferences (DPH) – and their manifestations in Discrete Choice Experiments (DCEs). Using data from 5,917 Polish respondents, we implemented multiple treatments varying the cost vector, choice set size, priming techniques, and the placement of a contingent valuation Willingness To Pay (WTP) question either before or after the DCE. Our findings show that the design of the cost vector systematically influences stated preferences and that attempts to mitigate this anchoring effect (e.g., by presenting an open-ended WTP question prior to the DCE) were unsuccessful. The persistence of cost vector effects over time aligns with CAH, while the lack of any discernible preference refinement challenges DPH. Further analyses reveal systematic variations in cost sensitivity and show that excluding respondents who violated the Weak and Strong Axioms of Revealed Preferences did not reduce cost vector effects. In light of these results, we recommend using diverse cost vectors to verify the robustness of DCE-based welfare estimates and call for further research into the broader impacts of heuristic behaviors in stated preference methods.
journal_name: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

title: Urban densification to support climate adaptation: balancing costs and agglomeration benefits in the Netherlands
abstract: Abstract Where should we build new housing under growing climate hazards? This study develops a framework that balances the economic benefits of density against the geographically varying costs of climate adaptation. We apply it to the Netherlands, where demand for new housing is high, but much of the land lies in floodplains or subsidence-prone areas. Agglomeration benefits are proxied by land values, while adaptation costs are derived from engineering estimates of flood protection and soil subsidence. Combining these data allows us to map spatial trade-offs and identify where development remains welfare-enhancing. Our findings show that dense cities continue to generate strong net welfare gains, even in places with high costs, while low-density settlements generate a welfare loss for new housing. We identify density thresholds above which housing development becomes feasible. Many medium-sized Dutch cities already exceed these thresholds, making densification more beneficial than peripheral expansion. Climate adaptation thus strengthens—rather than weakens—the case for urban densification.

title: Towards an Ambivalence framework: decision-making on skills and training in global reproduction networks

Housing Yields
abstract: Abstract We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects. When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.
journal_name: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis

title: Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective
abstract: Abstract The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.

title: The Effects of Prohibiting Marriage Bars: The Case of U.S. Teachers
abstract: Married women in the early twentieth-century United States faced “marriage bars,” a form of employer discrimination that barred them from paid employment. However, because the end of marriage bar use coincided with shifting social norms and labor market conditions, it is unclear how the end of marriage bars affected women’s employment. We study the effects of the state-level prohibition of marriage bars in teaching during the 1930s. A difference-in-differences design shows that the prohibitions increased the share of white married women teachers by 4.1 p.p. (26 percent), with no effect on Black teachers.

title: Information in the First Globalization: News Agencies and Trade
abstract: This paper documents the effect of information frictions on trade using a historical large-scale improvement in the transmission of news: the emergence of global news agencies. The information available to potential traders became more abundant, was delivered faster and at a cheaper price between countries covered by a news agency. By exploiting differences in the timing of telegraph openings and news agency coverage across pairs of countries, we are able to disentangle the pure effect of information from the effect of a reduction in communication costs. Panel gravity estimates reveal that bilateral trade increased by 30% more for pairs of countries covered by a news agency and connected by a telegraph than for pairs of countries simply connected by a telegraph.

title: Incentives and strategic behaviour: an experiment
abstract: Abstract How do incentive levels affect strategic behaviour? We address this with an experiment that separately identifies own- and opponent-incentive effects in two dominance-solvable games that differ in strategic complexity. Higher own incentives favour more strategically sophisticated actions and increase best responding to stated beliefs. Beliefs shift in a parallel direction and participants expect more sophisticated opponent actions. Furthermore, although higher own incentives increase belief accuracy, opponents with higher incentives are harder to predict. Higher incentives also increase response times, and longer response times are associated with better performance and more sophisticated actions and beliefs. Taken together, the evidence suggests that incentives affect strategic behaviour through two main channels: by reducing payoff-dependent mistakes and by increasing the effort devoted to reasoning, with the returns to that effort shaped by strategic complexity of the environment.

title: Echoes of hyperinflation: The link between past exposure and formation of expectations
The behavioral structure of one-shot cooperation in small and large groups
abstract: Cooperation is essential for realizing collective benefits in both small and large groups. In modern societies, many interactions are one-shot and differ in the magnitude of collective benefits. This paper identifies the unified behavioral structure underlying one-shot cooperation. Using online public goods games (N=2,136) and two versions of the strategy method, we examine how attitudes toward cooperation—the causal relationship between one’s own cooperation and others’—and beliefs about others’ cooperation explain cooperative behavior across group sizes (3, 9, and 30) and collective returns (low vs. high). Our ABC framework (Attitudes and Beliefs explain Cooperation) reveals a consistent structure: average attitudes toward cooperation are equally conditionally cooperative across all settings, while beliefs increase with the collective benefit of cooperation but not with group size, although beliefs become more important the larger the group. These results suggest that the ABC framework provides a parsimonious behavioral foundation for understanding one-shot cooperation.

title: Do commodity prices signal inflation under quantitative easing? Evidence from interest rate co-movements
abstract: This paper examines the dynamic relationship between real commodity price changes and interest rate changes during the U.S. Federal Reserve’s quantitative easing (QE) and COVID-19-era policies. Employing wavelet coherency and phase difference analysis over the period from January 2003 to December 2025, we provide a time–frequency characterisation of how these variables co-move under unconventional monetary regimes. We find robust short-term positive correlations between interest rate changes and real price changes across metals, energy, agriculture, and food commodities during both the QE and COVID-19 periods. Precious metals exhibit negative correlations during the subprime crisis, reflecting demand for value preservation. Critically, real price changes in hard-to-store commodities frequently lead interest rate changes, consistent with commodity prices anticipating monetary policy actions. To distinguish inflation-related channels from broader confounders, we implement partial wavelet coherency conditioned on money growth and core inflation. The significant attenuation of correlations under these conditions supports the quantity theory of money and the Fisher effect, indicating that the observed co-movements are substantially linked to inflation expectations. Our findings carry a direct policy implication: when the zero lower bound stifles conventional interest rate channels, commodity prices act as high-frequency barometers of evolving inflation expectations. This necessitates that policymakers treat energy, metals, and food markets as primary leading indicators during episodes of unconventional monetary policy. Complementing this policy insight, we introduce a wavelet-based methodology that significantly advances the literature by exposing the nonlinear, time-varying dynamics that standard econometric approaches systematically suppress.
journal_name: Journal of International Financial Markets, Institutions and Money

title: Are dairy cows replaced too early? Evidence from a structural model and cow‐level data
abstract: Abstract In past analyses of animal replacement decisions, studies have claimed that dairy farms often replace dairy cows too early to be maximizing profits. I estimate a structural model of asset replacement to determine the motives behind early replacement of dairy cows. I specifically test whether the costs from premature removal, an event where cows are removed off‐schedule due to health problems, explain replacement ages on dairy farms that are considered by previous studies to be unprofitable. Using data from over 1000 Wisconsin dairy farms, I find that a cow prematurely leaving the herd costs $2300 per removal, totaling $75 million in lost profit over the sample period. This cost is larger than what has been previously assumed, especially for dairies with less than 200 cows, suggesting that replacement rates appear unprofitable because previous analyses underestimated these costs. Dairy farms may benefit from prioritizing cow longevity and health over productivity to both cut costs and address environmental externalities from dairy. These results highlight the economic damages from poor cattle health on US dairy farms and the extent to which there may be cost savings from increasing cattle resilience to conditions that cause unexpected removal.

title: The effect of extreme wildfire exposure on energy poverty: Evidence from Australia's Black Saturday bushfires
abstract: Abstract This study assesses the effects of the 2009 Black Saturday Bushfires (BSB), which primarily occurred in rural regions of Victoria and represent the deadliest bushfire event in Australia's history, on household energy poverty. Using a linear panel event‐study, an entropy‐balanced event‐study, and a staggered difference‐in‐differences (DiD) design, applied to matched longitudinal household and geographical data, our results suggest a significant increase in the likelihood of experiencing energy poverty among households residing within 15 km of wildfire areas. Specifically, we find that for households directly affected by the fires, the likelihood of being in energy poverty increases by 9.9–11.3 percentage points in 2010 and by 13.2–16.7 percentage points in 2011 across specifications, compared to 2005–2007, which is the reference period. We find that the data are statistically consistent with life satisfaction, perceived safety and quality of life fully mediating the effect of BSB exposure on energy poverty in 2010, and with perceived safety fully mediating the relationship in 2011. We also find that adopting longer‐term financial planning mitigated the adverse effects of BSB exposure on energy poverty.

title: Contextualization of Numbers in Earnings Conference Calls
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research generally finds that using numbers in financial disclosure is beneficial. However, numbers can also be strategically proffered due to their perceived precision and informativeness. We find the use of undercontextualized numbers in earnings conference calls is associated with short‐term benefits but negative longer‐term consequences. Specifically, undercontextualization is associated with a short‐term positive market return, positive analyst forecast revisions, and a more positive tone in analysts’ questions. Furthermore, we find undercontextualization is associated with a longer‐term negative market return, a decrease in year‐over‐year earnings, and a higher incidence of restatements. In additional analyses, we find evidence consistent with the intentional use of undercontextualization, as it is associated with conference call casting, insider trading, and internal information quality. Given the uniqueness of our measure, we provide evidence of its validity by documenting its association with analyst scrutiny and other proxies for strategic call behavior. Finally, we examine a mechanism underlying our results and find evidence that undercontextualized numbers have a greater influence on retail investors.

title: Assessing the common ownership hypothesis in the US banking industry
Demand‐Driven Propagation of Job Losses: Evidence from the Great Recession a
abstract: Abstract This paper presents evidence for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses in the context of the United States during the Great Recession. Using county‐level tradable job losses driven by aggregate shocks as an instrument, it shows that retail and restaurant (R&R) employment fell by 0.37% for every 1% of job loss in the rest of the county's economy. The finding is not driven by the house price decline or by credit supply problems. Moreover, the spillover is more severe for R&R industries that are most affected by consumer demand shocks during the Great Recession, which strengthens the argument for the demand‐driven propagation of job losses.
journal_name: Journal of Money, Credit and Banking

title: A Conditional Shrinkage Method for Portfolio Selection
abstract: Abstract We develop a conditional shrinkage method for portfolio selection. Our approach builds on a decomposition of the mean-variance portfolio into the 1/N portfolio and an alpha component that offers large efficiency gains but is exposed to substantial estimation risk. We show that a linear shrinkage covariance matrix determines the portfolio’s relative exposure to these components, and our framework allows the shrinkage intensity to depend on a state variable that predicts their relative performance. We implement the method using investor sentiment and find that the estimated relation predominantly leads to greater shrinkage toward 1/N when sentiment is low, improving mean-variance efficiency while maintaining low turnover. JEL Classification: G11, G12.

title: Neighborhood mismatch and visits
Trust in Financial Services
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine how generalized trust relates to investing, building on previous literature by simultaneously considering different accounts, assets, and the use of financial advice. We find that account ownership and financial advice are positively correlated with trust. For types of assets, we find mixed results: a positive relationship for assets that involve delegation of decision making; no relationship for cryptocurrency; and a negative relationship for precious metals. We find a positive relationship with having a financial professional take action on your behalf. Our results are consistent with a model where nontrusting investors perceive greater risk of loss. JEL Classification: D14, G11, Z13

title: Beyond Leaderism: Recentering Leadership Science Towards Relationships in Action
abstract: Abstract The historical origins of ‘Great Man’ theories of leadership, and their contemporary offshoots, have produced an accumulated literature in which the leader's behaviours are the focal unit of analysis. This Point article surfaces five theoretical assumptions underlying the leader behavioural paradigm: leaderism, individualistic attribution, behavioural universalism, democratization of leadership, and individual‐level ontology. We discuss theoretical counterfactuals to each assumption and call for a shift in the scene of scholarly conversation, from individual leaders to relationships that incorporate context and stakeholders. This shift in the focal unit of analysis from individual leader behaviour to relationships represents a foundational theoretical pivot built on multidisciplinary foundations, attention to levels of analysis, and a deep grounding in context. By questioning the assumptions underlying 85 years of leader behaviour research, we argue that the science (episteme), skill development (techné), and contextual judgement (phronesis) of leadership could be more tightly coupled by directing the spotlight towards relationships in context rather than individual leaders. In doing so, we move the focus from leaders in action to leadership as relationships in action .

title: Learning‐by‐twinning: Organizational digital twins and the future of search
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Entrepreneurs and managers often need to evaluate strategic choices, such as redesigning an incentive plan or entering an unfamiliar market, before committing scarce resources. Existing offline search tools, including mental models, analogical reasoning, model building, and simulation, allow managers to weigh alternatives without acting, but each is limited by what a single decision maker can specify, recall, or imagine. We argue that advances in generative AI, combined with the growing availability of firm‐specific digital trace data, are transforming this tradeoff. We introduce the organizational digital twin (ODT), an infrastructure combining firm‐specific data, AI‐based behavioral simulation models, and governance rules which facilitates a new form of offline search that we call learning‐by‐twinning: search conducted by observing how a strategic choice unfolds within a digital replica of the firm. We identify three mechanisms through which learning‐by‐twinning creates value, namely expanded search, safer experimentation, and richer system‐level feedback as well as specify certain conditions under which these benefits may attenuate. Managerial Summary Strategic entrepreneurship depends on discovering and refining opportunities through search and experimentation under uncertainty. Enabled by advances in generative artificial intelligence and organizational data infrastructures, we theorize that a new form of entrepreneurial search—learning‐by‐twinning—allows managers to conduct systematic virtual experimentation prior to real‐world implementation. We introduce the concept of the organizational digital twin (ODT) as the technological infrastructure that makes this search and experimentation possible: an evolving simulation environment built from firm‐specific digital trace data and multi‐agent AI models capable of reproducing organizational routines, interactions, and decision processes. We argue that learning‐by‐twinning alters the traditional tradeoffs of offline search by expanding the set of alternatives managers can explore, enabling low‐risk experimentation, and revealing second‐order organizational consequences before strategic commitments are made.

title: The Emergence of Sustainability Reporting in a Family Firm: A Case Study in the Luxury Fashion Industry
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the emergence of sustainability reporting in a family‐owned luxury fashion firm. Using a qualitative case study and drawing on socioemotional wealth theory, it focuses on the preparation of a firm's first sustainability report. Findings show that reporting is not initiated as a technical compliance exercise but as a sustainability conceptualization process involving the translation of longstanding values and practices into a communicable, formal structure. This process unfolds through interrelated stages, with a specific configuration of socioemotional wealth dimensions shaping its development. The family influences this development through concerns for authenticity, control, and continuity. Sustainability reporting evolves through negotiation between internal identity and external expectations, supported by a governance core and cross‐functional collaboration. Rather than using disclosure instrumentally, the firm adopts a cautious and value‐driven approach, gradually moving toward selective transparency. In a context dominated by quantitative research, this study offers qualitative, process‐based insights into the micro‐dynamics through which sustainability reporting emerges in a family firm.

title: Greenhushing and Reputational Threat: Theory and Evidence
abstract: ABSTRACT Motivated by the importance of credible sustainability disclosure and concerns about reputational risk, this study investigates greenhushing—the deliberate under‐communication of strong corporate sustainability performance. As stakeholders increasingly demand transparent and reliable ESG disclosures, firms face a strategic dilemma: how to communicate progress without triggering skepticism, regulatory scrutiny, or accusations of greenwashing. We develop a theoretical framework that extends voluntary disclosure theory by incorporating uncertainty about the outcomes of external scrutiny, explaining why highly active firms may greenhush. Using a panel dataset of 17,012 firm‐year observations from 2003 to 2022, we analyze the relationship between internal and external sustainability actions and find an inverted U‐shaped pattern. Companies initially increase sustainability disclosure as internal efforts rise, but those with the most intensive sustainability activities reduce reporting—consistent with greenhushing. Moreover, high‐reputation firms face heightened scrutiny, leading to greater perceived risks and lower thresholds for greenhushing. These insights reveal that regulatory pressure and fear of misinterpretation can distort corporate transparency.

title: Green Marketing Orientations and Differentiation Advantage in Hospitality: Mediating Effects of Supply Chain Collaboration and Green Product Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT Green marketing is increasingly central to hospitality strategy, yet how different orientations translate into competitive advantage remains unclear. The study examines how strategic, tactical, and internal green marketing orientations, green supply chain collaboration, and innovative green product development affect competitive differentiation advantage in the hospitality industry. The study collected data from 412 hotels, including 198 in the US and 214 in Saudi Arabia, using convenience sampling. Results indicate that strategic green marketing influences innovative green product development but not supply chain collaboration. Tactical green marketing influences innovative green product development but not green supply chain collaboration. Internal green marketing orientations influence green supply chain collaboration and innovative green product development. Innovative green product creation and green supply chain collaboration boost competitive distinctiveness. Innovative green product development links all three green marketing approaches to competitive differentiation. In contrast, green supply chain collaboration merely links internal green marketing orientations to competitive differentiation. Green supply chain collaboration does not mediate the links between strategic and tactical green marketing orientations and competitive differentiation benefits. This study advances the green marketing and hospitality literature by demonstrating that internal execution and innovation are necessary for competitive advantage.

title: Scaling Sustainability: A Process Eco‐Innovation Model for Food Waste Reduction
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how foodservice management companies respond to sustainability pressures through process eco‐innovation (PEI) in food waste management. Using interview data from mid‐ to senior‐level managers, we develop a PEI model leveraging institutional theory. The model explains how institutional directives, including the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, drive organizational change. The findings reveal that institutional learning, compliance monitoring, and stakeholder engagement are key mechanisms that translate global directives into operational improvements. This study further identifies adaptive sourcing, whereby organizations dynamically reconfigure the boundary between external technology partnerships and internal solution development as legitimacy expectations and operational fit evolve. Financial, cultural, and operational barriers further shape PEI implementation and scaling. By linking institutional pressures with organizational adaptation, the PEI model contributes to understanding how service‐intensive firms can embed sustainability into core processes while maintaining legitimacy. The results offer actionable guidance for advancing sustainability in on‐site foodservice management.

title: Corporate Biodiversity Disclosure Under SDG 15: The Role of Internal and External Governance in Emerging Asian Economies
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how internal (corporate) and external (country‐level) governance mechanisms jointly influence corporate biodiversity disclosure under SDG 15 (CBD_SDG15) in emerging Asian economies. Drawing on stakeholder theory and institutional theory, the study conceptualises internal and external governance as complementary governance mechanisms operating across organisational and national levels. Using a balanced panel of 1800 firm‐year observations from five emerging Asian economies over 2016–2017 to 2021–2022, CBD_SDG15 is measured through manual content analysis based on GRI‐2016 biodiversity indicators aligned with SDG 15 targets. The findings reveal an increasing trend in biodiversity disclosure over the study period. Panel Tobit estimation, supported by robustness analyses using fractional logit, IV‐2SLS and System GMM estimators, indicates that both corporate governance and country‐level governance positively influence biodiversity disclosure. Furthermore, stronger country‐level governance enhances the effectiveness of corporate governance, whereas additional sectoral analysis shows that the influence of corporate governance is particularly pronounced among environmentally sensitive firms. The study contributes to the biodiversity disclosure literature by demonstrating that the effectiveness of corporate governance depends on the surrounding institutional environment and the environmental context in which firms operate, offering practical insights for policymakers and firms seeking to advance SDG 15 through improved biodiversity disclosure.

title: The Survival Signalling Paradox: How Financially Constrained Firms Defend ESG Under Climate Stress
abstract: ABSTRACT Does climate pressure lead financially constrained firms to cut environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance or to defend it? Using 28,439 firm‐year observations from 44 countries over 2005–2023, we show that the answer depends on the firm's dependence on external capital. Managerial climate salience, measured from earnings calls, is associated with lower ESG performance on average, but the penalty is borne by unconstrained firms and reverses among constrained ones, a pattern we call the survival signalling paradox. We argue that capital dependence is a boundary condition separating two established logics: where ESG decisions are private, slack‐resource theory applies and stress produces retrenchment; where lenders observe them, withdrawing the visible ESG flow is read as evidence about viability, so the firms least able to afford ESG have the strongest reason to maintain it. Three results support this reading. Constrained firms retrench selectively, shielding ESG while cutting research and development. Among constrained firms, ESG performance under climate salience is associated with debt access in the same year. The constraint gradient also appears when climate pressure is measured by the frequency of recorded country‐level weather disasters, though not by their severity. Institutional quality and market flexibility temper the penalty but do not reproduce the firm‐level reversal. The climate–ESG relationship therefore depends on how the firm is financed.

title: Standardization with nuance: Selective cultural buffering in Michelin-starred luxury dining
Stop honeying me: Endearing language works in human service recovery but backfires for (machine-like) robots
When Do Family Firms “Walk the Talk” in Sustainability? The Role of Socioemotional Wealth
abstract: A central debate concerns under which conditions sustainability orientation—a firm’s attitudinal disposition toward creating social and environmental value alongside economic value—translates into concrete environmental practices in some family firms but not others. Drawing on socioemotional wealth (SEW) theory, we argue that specific socioemotional priorities shape whether family firms “walk the talk” in their environmental practices. Using survey data from 182 Turkish family firms, we find that sustainability orientation is more strongly associated with environmental practices when owning families emphasize preserving the business across generations (renewal of family bonds), but not when they show stronger emotional attachment to the firm.

title: Multiple Family Offices and Stock Price Crash Risk
abstract: Drawing on principal–principal agency theory, we examine how multiple family offices (MFOs) affect stock crash risk of family firms owned and managed by at least two founding families or family lineages. In a study of publicly listed Korean firms where principal–principal agency conflicts are prevalent due to substantial control by family owner-managers, we find that MFOs help reduce stock crash risk by enhancing governance mechanisms that facilitate the alignment of divergent principal interests, especially in non-business-group-affiliated family firms and those facing unfavorable investment environments. Overall, we contribute toward the understanding of the governance function of family offices.

title: Family Management Control and Trade Credit Utilization: The Influence of Financial Constraints and Supplier Monitoring
abstract: We examine how family management control affects trade credit utilization. We find that firms with family management control use significantly lower trade credit, reflecting both lower financial constraints and a stronger preference to preserve control. More importantly, we show that the effect varies across family firms, becoming stronger with deeper family involvement and under first-generation control. We also note that institutional ownership and competitive environment encourage greater trade credit utilization, whereas independent directors and nonfamily Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) exert limited influence. Overall, our findings indicate that substantive family control matters more than formal governance structures in shaping family firms’ short-term financing decisions.

title: Trust gained, trust lost: how service robot anthropomorphism shapes consumer trust in tight and loose cultures
abstract: Purpose This paper aimed to examine the dual pathways through which service-robot (SR) anthropomorphism shapes consumer trust in service robots (CTSR), specifically the positive serial mediating effect of perceived warmth (WA) and perceived competence (CO) and the negative serial mediating effect of perceived identity threat (TH) and discomfort (DI). It further explored cross-cultural differences in consumer attitudes and their underlying reasons from the perspective of cultural tightness-looseness. Design/methodology/approach Five scenario experiments were conducted across three sets of SR picture stimuli, two service settings (hotel and hospital) and two cultures (China and the United States). Findings Both study 1 and study 2 found that anthropomorphism had a double-edged sword effect on CTSR across different sets of SR picture stimuli, service settings and cultures. An exploratory analysis in study 1 further revealed that among Chinese consumers, CTSR and its antecedents did not show significant differences across different service settings. Study 2 results further indicated that Chinese (versus. American) consumers had higher WA, CO and CTSR, along with lower TH and DI and that region-level cultural tightness influenced CTSR and its antecedents, potentially explaining these cross-cultural differences. Practical implications For hospitality managers, this paper offers insights on how to deploy anthropomorphic SRs across different cultural contexts. Originality/value This study developed a dialectical framework that integrates cognitive and affective serial mediation pathways and considers both the country- and region-level effects of cultural tightness on attitudes toward SRs.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Ethical signals attract job seekers when backed by representative leadership
abstract: Purpose Labor shortages in the hospitality industry have intensified reliance on online recruitment strategies, making diversity cues a critical signal to potential employees. This study aims to examine how diversity cues in hospitality recruitment influence applicants’ intent to apply. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts an exploratory mixed-methods design across three studies. Study 1 used focus groups with 12 job seekers to explore perceptions of diversity cues. Study 2 (n = 291) examined relationships among diversity beliefs, endorsed diversity rationales and applicant intentions using survey data. Study 3 (n = 187) experimentally manipulated leadership diversity levels (3%, 23%, 53%) and message rationale (moral vs instrumental). Findings Job seekers preferred morally framed diversity cues over instrumental ones and perceived superficial messaging as insincere. Although endorsing an instrumental rationale was unexpectedly associated with higher application intentions in the survey study, experimental results showed that moral messaging paired with higher leadership diversity increased organizational attractiveness, whereas instrumental messaging reduced perceived mobility as leadership diversity increased. Practical implications Hospitality organizations should prioritize authentic, morally grounded diversity communications to strengthen employer attractiveness and perceived advancement opportunities. Superficial or instrumental messaging may undermine organizational attractiveness and limit application intentions. Originality/value This study advances hospitality recruitment research by integrating signaling theory with organizational legitimacy theory to show how diversity cues shape applicants’ perceptions and behavioral intentions. It provides a multi-method examination of authenticity in diversity signaling, offering insights into how organizations can effectively signal inclusivity in competitive hospitality labor markets.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: The symbolic divide: how human and robotic service rituals shape perception of brand symbolism
abstract: Purpose The rapid adoption of service robots in tourism and hospitality raises questions about their ability to generate brand-related meaning compared to human-led service rituals. Drawing on interaction ritual theory, this study aims to examine how human and robotic service rituals influence perception of brand symbolism through emotional energy and memory and how these effects differ for customers with varying levels of social phobia. Design/methodology/approach Using a multistudy design, this research uses five experiments across airports, hotels and restaurants to test the hypotheses. The inclusion of both Asian and Western respondents across varying service contexts provides preliminary evidence regarding the generalizability of the findings. Findings Human-led service rituals create a stronger perception of brand symbolism than robot-led rituals, with emotional energy and memory as sequential mediators. For high-social-phobia customers, perception of brand symbolism did not differ significantly between the two ritual types, although human-led rituals generated higher emotional energy; for low-social-phobia customers, human-led rituals produced greater perception of brand symbolism and higher emotional energy. Originality/value This study contrasts human and robotic service rituals, identifies sequential mechanisms (emotional energy and memory) and extends interaction ritual theory by specifying when the symbolic outcomes of robot-led rituals do not significantly differ from human-led rituals. The findings also guide managers in designing inclusive rituals that balance emotional richness and social comfort.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Sensing through simulation: Alt-Text descriptive granularity and digital embodiment for visually impaired consumers
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how alternative text (Alt-text) descriptive granularity influences purchase intention among visually impaired consumers in digital restaurant environments. This study further investigates the roles of message framing, health consciousness, restaurant trust and perceived healthfulness through the lens of digital embodiment. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative pretest with 18 visually impaired participants informed stimulus development, followed by four between-subjects experiments (n = 868). The studies manipulated Alt-text descriptive granularity and promotion- versus prevention-focused framing, while health consciousness was measured in Studies 2–4. Studies 3 and 4 tested restaurant trust and perceived healthfulness as mediating mechanisms. Findings Highly descriptive Alt-text increases purchase intention. The effect is stronger under promotion-focused framing and becomes stronger as health consciousness increases. Restaurant trust and perceived healthfulness emerge as complementary relationship- and product-oriented mediating mechanisms. The overall pattern is consistent with an embodied-cognition account of accessible descriptive information. Originality/value This research extends digital accessibility beyond technical compliance by conceptualizing descriptive Alt-text as a basis for digital embodiment. It also shows that accessibility quality can shape both persuasive communication and consumer evaluations of service providers and menu items.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: The future of interaction, relationships and networks: Reshaping interdependencies in a changing world
Modern slavery governance, digital transformation and financial distress risk: evidence from legally grounded text-based accounting measures
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to develop and validate a legally grounded accounting measurement framework for modern-slavery governance and examines whether the resulting governance measures are associated with firms' financial distress risk. Existing research predominantly relies on ESG ratings, disclosure proxies, or qualitative assessments that do not clearly distinguish externally specified governance obligations from firms' disclosed governance architecture. We address this measurement gap by translating mandatory modern-slavery governance requirements into reproducible firm-level accounting measures and evaluating their informational relevance for accounting-based risk assessment. Design/methodology/approach This research adopts a two-corpus measurement framework. The first corpus comprises mandatory modern-slavery legislation and internationally recognised institutional frameworks issued between 1930 and 2024, including the Tariff Act (1930), California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, UK Modern Slavery Act, French Duty of Vigilance Law, Australian Modern Slavery Act, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, Norwegian Transparency Act, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and complementary institutional frameworks including the ILO, OECD, PRI, and the United Nations Guiding Principles. Rather than serving as institutional background, these sources are used to define the governance construct by identifying legally codified organisational obligations and harmonising them into a unified governance ontology representing implementation-oriented governance mechanisms.The second corpus comprises more than 5,000 annual reports of S&P 500 firms covering the period 2010–2022. Artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and supervised machine-learning techniques operationalise the predefined governance ontology to identify disclosed evidence of implementation-oriented governance mechanisms within corporate reports, thereby generating firm-year Modern Slavery Index (MSI) measures. A complementary Digital Transformation Index (DTI) captures disclosed digital capability. The empirical design combines firm and year fixed-effects estimation with 2SLS endogeneity-sensitivity analysis and additional tests addressing disclosure intensity and boilerplate reporting, institutional validity, digital-capability interactions, competing explanations and potential mechanisms. Findings The findings show that firms disclosing stronger implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance mechanisms exhibit lower financial distress risk, although the strength of this association varies across the underlying institutional architectures. Among the four governance measures, the California-based MSI2 provides the strongest evidence, indicating that disclosed governance mechanisms centred on supplier verification, monitoring, accountability, and supply-chain oversight are associated with lower financial distress risk. Digital transformation, by contrast, does not independently reduce financial distress risk and is associated with lower Altman Z-scores in several specifications, a pattern consistent with – but not establishing – the organisational costs and implementation challenges that may accompany technological transformation. Importantly, digital capability also conditions the association between disclosed modern-slavery governance and financial distress risk, with the positive MSI4 × DTI interaction indicating that the financial relevance of governance disclosure varies with firms' digital capabilities under particular institutional arrangements. Overall, the findings indicate that legally grounded measures of disclosed modern-slavery governance contain economically relevant information for financial-distress assessment, while their associations vary across governance architectures and according to firms' digital capabilities. Originality/value This paper makes four contributions to the accounting literature. First, it develops four transparent, legally grounded, and fully reproducible Modern Slavery Indices (MSI1–MSI4), each derived from distinct regulatory and institutional governance frameworks, providing researchers, practitioners, managers, auditors, and policymakers with standardised accounting measures of implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance. Second, it introduces a novel two-corpus measurement framework that explicitly separates construct definition from empirical observation by deriving the governance construct from mandatory legislation and internationally recognised frameworks before operationalising it through AI-enabled textual analysis of corporate reports. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and supervised machine-learning techniques can operationalise externally defined governance obligations into scalable firm-level accounting information while preserving construct validity. Finally, it provides evidence that these legally grounded accounting measures contain decision-useful information for accounting-based risk assessment, advancing research on non-financial accounting measurement, governance architecture, disclosure credibility, internal control systems, and corporate resilience under emerging mandatory reporting regimes.

title: Ethics and climate litigation: from case law to knowledge networks
