abstract: Purpose This article examines how climate litigation has evolved from a policy instrument into a legal mechanism for enforcing ethical obligations, positioning climate change as an ethical issue and identifying human rights as a litigation outcome. Design/methodology/approach Adopting the design of an integrative literature review, the study combines bibliometric mapping of Web of Science citation data, processed using Bibliometrix and Biblioshiny, with conceptual and doctrinal analysis of key climate litigation case law. Findings Climate change litigation is maturing not only in scope but in ethical grounding, with human rights emerging as a strategic outcome courts increasingly pursue. Using bibliometric analysis, this article maps the intersection of climate litigation and ethics, identifying five research areas: greenhouse gases as pollutants, duty of care, climate science, global climate policy and intercountry equity. Cross-jurisdictional themes show that judicial decisions do more than resolve individual disputes – they shape, legitimize and accelerate transnational governance responses to climate change, positioning courts as meaningful actors in addressing climate change as an ethical imperative. Social implications This study maps the acceptance of ethics within legal spheres as part of the climate debate. Originality/value The article is among the first to integrate bibliometric mapping with doctrinal and ethical analysis of climate litigation, and proposes a tiered research agenda that addresses the interplay between government objectives and the interests of litigants.

title: Firms’ carbon disclosure and low-carbon product sales: A perspective from the three-factor theory of customer satisfaction
Neither elevating nor degrading? Technology, job characteristics, and workers' role in manufacturing production
A Perfect Time to Recalibrate Frontlines Research
abstract: Technology continues to transform firm-customer interactions, creating increasingly complex configurations of human and machine interfaces. Orchestrating the actions of widely distributed actors and systems has proven difficult. Agentic commerce, involving interactions between autonomous machines, will add complexity, shift points of marketing influence, and require new tactics. The frontlines have changed faster than scholars’ approaches to studying them, and the gap is widening precisely when decision makers need guidance. Closing this gap requires four imperatives: adopt empirics-first thinking, provide more credible evidence, lead practice – inform decisions, and be prescient.

title: Rethinking Customer Service Digitalization: Incongruent Frames and Alignment Mechanisms in Retailing
abstract: This multilevel study investigates customer service digitalization (CSD), the customer-facing transformation of service processes through digital technologies, in retailing through fifty-two expert interviews with twenty-seven headquarters (HQ) managers, eleven store managers (SMs), and fourteen frontline employees (FLEs). Grounded in a theories-in-use approach and guided by Technology Framing Theory (TFT), the study identifies systematic framing differences between HQ and stores. While HQ managers frame CSD as digitalization, human augmentation, and a continuous “journey,” FLEs perceive CSD as digitization, human substitution, and a fixed “destination.” As boundary spanners between HQ and FLEs, SMs can reinforce these frames and are seen as either enablers or barriers. The study introduces four collective congruence framing mechanisms (CCFMs), namely Ba, Psychological Safety, Redundancies, and Nudging, that buffer the negative consequences of frame incongruence on CSD success and, ultimately, customer service interaction quality; SM boundary spanning strengthens their effectiveness. These findings extend TFT to a multi-actor, multilevel service context. For managers, they suggest diagnosing frame incongruence before rollout, deploying CCFM instantiations such as HQ store days or temporary redundancies, and developing SMs as translators between HQ strategy and frontline practice.

title: Do Disclosures of Corporate Transformative Service Initiatives Signal Enhanced Financial Outcomes? Moderating Roles of Firm-Level Factors
abstract: Corporate transformative service initiatives (CTSIs) are service-led initiatives by for-profit firms that serve communities experiencing vulnerability and articulate an explicit well-being intent. When disclosed, as with other corporate disclosures, they can function as market-facing signals of firms’ enacted service-oriented societal engagement. However, it remains unclear whether such signaling improves financial outcomes and whether firm-level factors moderate this effect. To address this gap, this study examines the impact of CTSIs disclosures on firms’ financial outcomes and the moderating roles of chief marketing officer (CMO) presence, relative firm size, and firm type. A systematic automated content analysis of sustainability reports, cross-checked with annual reports from 2010 to 2019 for U.S. S&P 500 firms, identifies three main forms of CTSIs disclosures: corporate commitment, corporate giving, and employee volunteering. Dynamic panel analyses show that CTSIs disclosures and their components positively impact firms’ financial outcomes (Total q , return on equity), with stronger effects when a CMO is present. Relative firm size matters, with firms with greater relative asset size benefiting more strongly when a CMO is present, and smaller firms showing broader gains across CTSIs disclosure dimensions. The signaling effects of CTSIs disclosures are consistent across service and non-service firms, suggesting that market responses are driven by the communication of service-oriented transformative initiatives rather than by industry boundaries. These findings extend transformative service research and signaling theory by showing how CTSIs disclosures can position service-led initiatives as financially relevant market signals, with implications for managerial disclosure practice.

title: Generative AI Identity Duality: The Mediating Effects of AI Connection versus AI Resistance on Generative AI Acceptance
Guidelines for Employing Large Language Models in Information Systems Research
Toward an “Identity Turn” in Public Service Motivation Theory: A Problematizing Review and Research Agenda
abstract: Abstract Since its inception, Public Service Motivation (PSM) has been recognized as a key driver of behavior in public institutions. Despite its prominence, skepticism has emerged. In response, research has primarily focused on empirical analysis and measurement refinement rather than on conceptual development. This conceptual path dependency has become problematic as mixed empirical results increasingly challenge core theoretical propositions of PSM theory. We argue that one potential cause lies in a dominant assumption shaping the field: its positioning within motivation theory. To address this, we conducted a problematizing review across concepts and disciplines, comparing how PSM is understood in Public Administration with related concepts–such as motivation, altruism, and identity–in Management, Psychology, Sociology, and Economics. Based on this analysis, we propose a novel theoretical framework that reconceptualizes PSM as a social identity. In doing so, we outline a research agenda that (i) revises PSM’s core conceptual features and develops a new measurement approach informed by identity theory; (ii) introduces new ways of understanding PSM's functioning through identity work theory; and (iii) situates PSM theory within the broader debate on the “identity turn” in motivation research, highlighting its potential contribution to this multidisciplinary discourse.
journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

title: Looking the Part? How Candidates’ Race and Attire Shape Employers’ Hiring Decisions in a Low-Wage Labor Market
abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. We test these arguments using data from a gig-staffing platform comprising over 1 million job applications with profile photos, supplemented by a preregistered experiment that manipulates attire within candidates, using two photos of each candidate: one in professional attire, one in casual. The results converge across field and experimental data. Professional attire improves hiring prospects overall but yields substantially smaller returns for Black candidates. Moderated mediation tests confirm that perceived professionalism drives this disparity, such that race discounts how attire translates into perceived professionalism and how perceived professionalism translates into hiring. The racial gap attenuates in customer-facing roles in which appearance is task relevant. These findings challenge supply-side accounts of hiring inequality and reveal how a demand-side interpretation of equivalent signals perpetuates racial disadvantages.

title: Cardiometabolic dysfunction and age at natural menopause: a prospective study
Estimating Marginal Effects on Survival Outcomes for Clinical Interpretations and Decision Making
abstract: The Cox regression model is the most widely used method in survival analysis, but the hazard ratio has limited clinical interpretability. Survival or cumulative incidence curves are often used to illustrate treatment effects, yet there is no consensus on the most appropriate methods for generating these curves, particularly in the presence of confounding and competing risks. We reviewed original research articles published in a general medical journal in 2025, identified limitations in common practices, and describe a marginal effects framework to generate adjusted cumulative incidence curves that are coherent with the analysis model, anchored in absolute risk estimates, and adaptable to competing risks and clustered data. The framework targets the population-average difference in cumulative incidence between exposure groups, under the assumptions of no unmeasured confounding, positivity, and non-informative censoring. As a demonstration, we applied the framework to real-world data from Yek et al. (2025) and showed that it produced clinically interpretable estimates of hospital-acquired antimicrobial resistance risk that a single hazard ratio could not convey. To facilitate implementation, we describe each analytic step in detail, discuss available software, and share an R program with core routines written in C for computational efficiency.

title: Exposure, constraint, and repair: How child abuse pediatrics fellows navigate strain and restore purpose
abstract: Background Child Abuse Pediatrics (CAP) fellows train in a subspecialty marked by repeated exposure to child maltreatment and high-stakes clinical and legal demands. Objective This qualitative study examined how CAP fellows describe and make meaning of emotional strain and restorative experiences during training. Participants and setting Participants were 13 fellows enrolled in U.S. CAP fellowship programs, all practicing in urban settings. Methods Semi-structured interviews were conducted via Zoom between May and August 2024 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Vicarious resilience sensitized the analysis to restorative experiences; the job demands-resources model informed interpretation after themes were constructed. Results Three themes were constructed. Carrying What Cannot Be Left Behind described secondary traumatic stress as an accumulating presence that affected relationships and prompted protective silence. Procedural Continuity, Eroding Presence captured accounts of emotional numbing, constrained agency, and cumulative exposure that strained emotional presence even as fellows described continuing clinical tasks. When the Work Gives Back described how children's recovery, family recognition, and perceived accountability renewed meaning. Conclusions Fellows linked strain and restoration to exposure, supervision, and opportunities for recovery. Their accounts identify workload organization and supervisory support as areas for evaluation alongside individual coping.

title: Symptom trajectories in head and neck cancer from diagnosis to long-term survivorship
abstract: Abstract Purpose Patients with head and neck cancer (HNC) experience substantial symptom burden related to both disease and intensive treatments. Understanding long-term symptom patterns may help identify patients at risk for persistent emotional and physical symptom burden. This study evaluated symptom trajectories of anxiety, depression, fear of cancer recurrence (FCR), and oral pain among patients with HNC from diagnosis through long-term survivorship. Methods This secondary analysis included 5411 patients with HNC from the Head and Neck 5000 study in the UK. Latent class growth analysis (LCGA) and growth mixture modeling (GMM) were used to examine changes in symptoms, predictors of class membership, and within-class variability. Results The majority of patients were classified into a mild symptom class for depression (58%), anxiety (48%), and oral pain (62%), whereas the largest FCR class (44%) represented moderate symptoms. Anxiety, FCR, and oral pain followed recovery trajectories characterized by symptom improvement, while depression demonstrated a distinct pattern of worsening symptoms. Across symptoms, nearly 20% of patients belonged to an elevated symptom trajectory. These patients were more likely to be younger in age, have lower income, and report greater weekly alcohol consumption. Patients with HPV-positive HNC experienced faster reductions in anxiety and FCR but greater increases in depression over time. Conclusions Distinct symptom trajectories were observed into long-term survivorship among patients with HNC. Although most patients experienced mild-to-moderate symptoms, a clinically important subgroup remained at elevated risk for persistent symptoms. Implications for Cancer Survivors Early identification of patients at risk for persistent symptoms may facilitate targeted supportive care and behavioral interventions to improve long-term survivorship outcomes.

title: Visual Sexual Health Communication Assisted by AI: The Case of Synthetic Menstruation Images
abstract: Abstract Public communication about sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) relies on both text and images. A recent development is the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) image generators, which enable rapid, cost-effective, and highly customizable images with appealing aesthetics based on textual requests (prompts). To examine the opportunities and challenges of AI-generated images in SRHR communication, we used the topic of menstruation and developed six research questions (RQs) anchored in the current state of research on AI-supported visual health communication. These questions addressed key areas of concern, such as unsuccessful image creation (RQ1), objective image flaws (RQ2), lack of diversity of human representation (RQ3), stereotypical portrayals of women (RQ4), use of visual symbols (RQ5), and image valence (RQ6). Our study applied 15 AI image generators, 2 user accounts per generator, 5 menstruation-related prompts, 2 prompt languages, and 2 images per prompt, resulting in a sample of N = 600 AI outputs generated in Autumn 2025. All outputs were manually coded using a reliability-tested codebook developed through both deductive and inductive approaches. In 20.0% of cases, menstruation prompts did not produce the requested image but only text output (RQ1). When images were generated, they often (78.1%) exhibited visual and/or textual flaws (RQ2). The images showed a lack of diversity in some human attributes (e.g., body type) but not in others (e.g., skin tone; RQ3). Stereotypical depictions of women were observed but not predominant (RQ4). Common menstruation-related visual symbols (e.g., blood, pain) were identified (RQ5), but most images did not convey a negative portrayal and instead a neutral or positive portrayal of menstruation (RQ6). While results show that initial outputs from AI image generators are often not directly suitable for visual sexual health communication, they might work with targeted refinement. Further research is required to examine the production, characteristics, consumption, and effects of AI-generated images in SRHR communication.

title: Post-Soviet Brides in the China Dream: Migration, Marriage, and Geopolitics Across Borders Elena Barabantseva. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 244 pp. £95.00 (hbk). ISBN 9781009600170
Safeguarding online panel surveys from LLM pollution: evidence from Canadian federal survey contracts
abstract: Bots and large language model (LLM) agents can now complete online surveys convincingly enough to pass as real respondents, a risk long flagged in other fields but rarely addressed in public management research. Drawing on disheartening empirical findings from previous efforts to validate responses to online panel surveys, this research note offers a portrait of efforts to ensure the integrity of data collected by firms that survey citizens on behalf of Canadian federal departments and ministries, a case study likely representative of the challenges facing online survey practices across countries and levels of governments.

title: Optimization of power allocation scheduling and component sizing in battery-assisted electrolyser systems
abstract: This paper presents a co-design optimization framework for battery-assisted electrolyser systems aimed at improving the cost-effectiveness of green hydrogen production. As renewable energy sources (RES) increasingly strain electricity grids, decentralized power-to-hydrogen (P2H) production can mitigate grid imbalance while supplying a clean energy carrier, yet its financial viability remains uncertain. The proposed framework integrates models of battery energy storage systems (BESS), electrolysers, RES, and grid connections, and optimizes them on two levels: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) determines the operational strategy that maximizes operating profit, while Bayesian Optimization (BO) selects the component sizing that maximizes net present value (NPV) over a continuous three-year horizon. The framework is applied to two real-world cases: a grid-limited 2 MW solar site (case A) and a more balanced solar–wind site (case B). For case A the optimal design pairs a 964 kW electrolyser with a 220 kWh battery, whereas case B favors a 475 kW electrolyser without a battery, showing that battery storage is decisive only when the grid connection is small. At a hydrogen price of €8/kg both systems are near break-even (NPV €−0.1 to €−0.9 million) and become clearly profitable at €16/kg (NPV €3.9–4.3 million); a sensitivity analysis shows they remain firmly loss-making across the €3–5/kg range projected for 2030. The electrolyser operates with an average efficiency of about 80% (HHV), at a levelized cost of hydrogen of about €10/kg. These results quantify how hydrogen price, grid capacity, and component sizing jointly govern the techno-economic feasibility of P2H systems, and provide a transferable framework for their cost-effective design.

title: Unlocking flexibility in buildings through batteries: a case study of the Netherlands
abstract: Residential buildings account for a significant share of energy consumption and emissions, and heating electrification and rooftop photovoltaic (PV) generation create new challenges for distribution grids: import peaks from heat pumps and export peaks from PV surpluses. Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) can reduce peak demand and increase self-consumption. We report a multi-objective optimization of BESS sizing and dispatch in a 58-apartment positive-energy building in Utrecht, using a full year of measured smart-meter data. A linear-programming model with a Wöhler-based degradation cost trades off peak shaving and self-consumption across a capacity sweep, under two scenarios: a hypothetical configuration in which all 58 apartments and the facilities share one ± 110.4 kW connection instead of their individual connections (Scenario 1), and the current configuration, in which the BESSs serve only the facilities (Scenario 2). Consolidation rather than operational savings dominates the economics: once the BESS dispatch eliminates the 122 hours of PV export violation (the summed apartment exports exceeding the shared connection, purely from aggregation), the avoided cost of the 58 individual connections becomes accessible. The installed 70 kWh BESS crosses this threshold, with a payback of 0.55 years; the economic optimum lies near 280 kWh. Scenario 1 is notional: its economics depend on contractual and regulatory consolidation of the 58 connections, which is not addressed in this study. In Scenario 2, where peak-shaving has no value, the BESS adds modest self-consumption gains. The results show the value of measured multi-apartment data and of institutional drivers alongside technological ones in residential storage economics.

title: Shipping big data informed maritime decarbonisation strategies for green and digital shipping corridors
A network-aware combinatorial auction mechanism for local multi-energy markets with coupled conversion
Distributionally robust configuration optimization of climate-resilient active distribution networks for enhancing flexibility dispatchability
Comparative field deployment of model-based reinforcement learning and model predictive control for residential HVAC
A hypergraph-based constrained reinforcement learning method for electric vehicle charging navigation in coupled power-transportation networks
Vulnerability assessment of buildings-power distribution networks under compound heatwaves and power outages
A model-uncertainty-aware fault location method for active distribution networks with high-penetration renewable energy sources
The heterogeneous transmission of geopolitical energy shocks: A structural framework
Social acceptance of a green ammonia hub in a remote coastal community – the case of Ísafjörður in Iceland
abstract: The International Maritime Organisation targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions from international shipping by 2050, considering green ammonia to be a promising fuel for decarbonisation. However, development and deployment of this fuel is contingent not only on aspects such as techno-economic feasibility and supportive policy frameworks, but also on social acceptance (SA). This study examines the community-level SA of a potential green ammonia hub for maritime uses in Ísafjörður, Iceland, a remote coastal settlement with a strong maritime history. Based on sixteen semi-structured interviews with local stakeholders, the study identifies the key drivers and barriers influencing SA. It reveals that perceived benefits such as job creation and environmental protection function as drivers, while barriers stem from perceived concerns regarding safety, cost, and lack of clear governance. Guided by a community-adapted corporate sustainability classification and a PESTLE lens, identified themes are mapped across political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental dimensions. The findings indicate that political and governance conditions function as an important enabling condition for SA, particularly through the perceived need for clear legislative frameworks and government incentives. Rather than operating independently, these political conditions were closely intertwined with economic and technological considerations, influencing investment risk, infrastructure development, affordability, safety, and equitable benefit distribution. The study concludes that for a just maritime energy transition to succeed, national policymakers must prioritise the implementation of robust incentive mechanisms and strategic roadmaps that satisfactorily address local socio-economic realities and contexts.

title: Life cycle assessment of floating offshore wind anchors: A state-of-the-art review
abstract: Floating offshore wind (FOW) is moving from demonstration projects towards commercial-scale deployment, but the lifecycle greenhouse-gas implications of its anchoring systems remain poorly resolved. This paper presents a state-of-the-art review of how FOW anchors are represented in life cycle assessment (LCA) studies, focusing on system boundaries, functional units, lifecycle-stage coverage, anchor disaggregation, and the links between environmental impacts and engineering function. The review shows that anchor-related emissions are controlled by coupled drivers: material demand, fabrication route, installation-vessel logistics, mooring configuration, load direction, soil conditions, and end-of-life treatment. These drivers are often hidden in current LCAs because anchors are aggregated with mooring lines, foundations, substructures, or farm-level inventories and are commonly normalised by electricity production. To address this mismatch, the paper proposes a complementary component-level functional unit, the provision of 1 MN of holding capacity under stated reference conditions, and an associated capacity-normalised carbon-intensity indicator expressed in tCO 2 eq/MN. The indicator is meaningful only when reference conditions are stated, including soil class, load inclination, static or cyclic capacity basis, capacity definition, and lifecycle boundary. Applied to the four studies in the review that report both anchor-level emissions and holding capacity, the indicator can preserve material- and installation-related trends. This quantitative base is, however, too narrow to rank anchor technologies, and the demonstration is presented as a proof of concept rather than as a benchmarking result. The paper concludes with a practical reporting framework intended to support transparent anchor-level benchmarking and low-carbon anchor selection in future FOW projects.

title: Assessing 50 Years of Salt Effects in Heterogeneous Photocatalysis
abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous photocatalysis has been studied for the treatment of recalcitrant compounds for half a century, but one of the severe limitations for practical oxidation treatment continues to be the inhibitory effect of salt found in real water matrices. The negative impact of Na+, K+, Cl–, and other ionic species is rarely quantified, as there has been no systematic way to discuss salt effects, making the evaluation of photocatalysis performance across studies difficult and imprecise. In analyzing 50 years of literature for this review, we identified >1,200 publications on heterogeneous photocatalysis in different water types, such as seawater, brackish water, and industrial brines. Just 84 studies reported degradation rates in deionized and salt-containing water, with nearly all involving TiO2 as the photocatalyst composition and charged dye compounds as the model contaminant class. To analyze the kinetic data extracted from these studies, we introduce the photocatalysis salt-effect (PSE) metric as calculated through the relative salt-effectiveness evaluation (RSEE) method, quantifying the percent change in degradation rate when the water matrix contains a salt species. We identified an unexpected correlation between PSE and ionic strength (IS), irrespective of the contaminant, at solution pH values less than the TiO2 point-of-zero-charge (PZC), which is the plausible result of salt-induced particle aggregation at high ionic strengths during photocatalyst testing. While most published results showed salt inhibition of photocatalysis (−100% < PSE < −5%), there is evidence for salt promotion (PSE > +5%) and salt tolerance (−5% < PSE < +5%), which challenges the notion that salinity is always detrimental to photocatalytic activity. These findings highlight the opportunity to study fully and systematically the relationships among contaminant structure, photocatalyst PZC, solution pH, IS, and salt type. The PSE-based framework would be critical in understanding the effects of more complex water matrices and in ultimately developing salt-tolerant and salt-promoted heterogeneous photocatalysis for practical water treatment.

title: Mild Oxidant Regulation of *H Coverage Promotes Electrocatalytic Nitrate Reduction to N2 in Low-Conductivity Media
abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) has attracted growing interest for converting nitrate (NO3–) into ammonium (NH4+), yet NH4+ production from dilute, low-conductivity waters is constrained by high energy consumption, limited NO3– availability, and costly product recovery. Steering NO3RR directly toward benign N2 therefore represents a more practical route, but this pathway is often suppressed by excessive surface *H coverage, which drives the overhydrogenation of nitrogen intermediates to NH4+. Here, we report a mild oxidant-assisted coelectrolysis strategy that regulates interfacial *H coverage and promotes NO3–-to-N2 conversion in a Cu nanoparticle-decorated Ni cathode membrane electrochemical reactor. This reactor separates a highly conductive electrochemical chamber from a NO3–-containing chemical chamber, enabling NO3– reduction in low-conductivity media while maintaining a less negative cathodic potential. Mild oxidants, including H2O2, O2, CH3COOOH, and KIO4, consumed excess *H and redirected the reaction pathway toward N–N coupling. With H2O2 as a representative oxidant, N2 selectivity increased from 13.47% without H2O2 to 87.25% at 100 mM H2O2. Mechanistic analyses revealed that H2O2 decreases interfacial *H abundance, which suppresses NH4+ formation and facilitates the dimerization of nitrogen-containing intermediates. Verification in real low-conductivity groundwater further supports this strategy as a mechanistic basis for designing selective, low-energy electrochemical denitrification systems for low-conductivity NO3–-contaminated media.

title: Waste as Feedstock, Electrolyte, and Target: Closing the Loop in Electrochemical H2O2 Water Treatment
abstract: Abstract Electrochemical H2O2 production is increasingly positioned as an on-site route for water oxidation, disinfection, and resource recovery. However, its environmental translation remains constrained by a basic design mismatch between catalyst development in clean electrolytes and deployment in chemically variable waste streams. This Perspective argues that progress should move beyond catalyst-centered performance metrics toward a closed-loop, waste-centered framework. The key issue is not how to isolate H2O2 electrosynthesis from wastewater complexity but when and how that complexity can be engineered. Solid and liquid waste streams can provide carbon, heteroatoms, and metals for impurity-resilient electrodes. Meanwhile, wastewater constituents can regulate interfacial ion distribution, water structure, oxygen transport, proton availability, intermediate stabilization, and side reactions. Electrogenerated H2O2 can be routed to contaminant transformation, disinfection, detoxification, and metal recovery. We discuss design principles for converting heterogeneous waste feedstocks into catalytic interfaces, defining wastewater operating windows, matching reactor architectures with real water matrices, and evaluating circularity through life-cycle and techno-economic accounting. We identify critical benchmarks─matrix descriptors, durability mechanisms, byproduct control, reactor-treatment matching, and transparent environmental safeguards─needed to turn circular H2O2 concepts into verifiable water-treatment technologies.

title: Evaluating Individual Infection Risk: The Interplay between Air Mixing Intensities and Occupant Dynamics
abstract: Abstract Aerosol transmission remains a critical route for the spread of respiratory infectious diseases, yet real-time exposure mapping in complex public spaces is computationally demanding. This study presents a robust and adaptable framework for estimating dynamic individual exposure (i.e., viral dose) by integrating high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with computer vision (CV) analysis. By overlaying validated steady-state viral aerosol plumes onto dynamic human interaction data, we evaluated the interplay between airflow patterns and human behaviors under two distinct air change rates (ACH: 25 h–1 and 3 h–1). Each scenario was simulated both with and without MERV-13 filtration. Applications in both a stochastic-movement hotel meeting room and a stationary-occupant office demonstrate that while high turbulence due to high ACH limits the spatial extent of plumes, sustained close proximity in structured settings can result in disproportionately high viral doses for specific individuals. MERV-13 filtration effectively reduced exposure within high-concentration zones. We propose a Reynolds number (Re)-based modeling guideline: steady-state CFD-CV for moderate mixing (900 ≤ Re ≤ 2300), a well-mixed assumption for high mixing (Re > 2300), and transient CFD-CV for low mixing (500 ≤ Re < 900) during breathing and speaking, and steady-state CFD-CV for coughing and sneezing regardless of Re value. This framework supports real-time monitoring and targeted interventions, providing a data-driven foundation for indoor occupant safety.

title: Light-Induced Formation of Volatile Organic Compounds from Bleach Cleaning in Indoor Environments
abstract: Abstract Surface bleach cleaning is a common indoor activity that releases abundant strong oxidants, including hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and chlorine gas (Cl2), which can significantly influence indoor chemistry. While bleach-driven chemical transformations are recognized, the specific role of illumination remains poorly understood. This study combines field measurements and laboratory flow tube experiments to investigate volatile organic compound (VOC) formation from reactions between bleach emissions and surface-sorbed species, e.g., kitchen-derived organic films, under illuminated conditions. In real-world indoor settings, we observed that bleach cleaning under light predominantly generates oxygenated VOCs (OVOCs), accounting for ∼92% of total emissions. Saturated carbonyls contributed the most (∼82%), such as C6H12O, C9H18O, and C2H4O. Flow tube experiments using surrogate compounds and kitchen-collected surface films confirmed that OVOCs are generated via heterogeneous reactions between surface-bound organics (e.g., fatty acids, amides, amino acids) and radicals produced from photolysis of bleach-derived oxidants. VOC production was found to depend on surface accumulation and aging, with more accumulated and aged surfaces producing greater quantities and more diverse products. These findings provide important insights into VOC production from indoor surface chemistry initiated by bleach cleaning under typical indoor lighting conditions, advancing our understanding of volatile byproduct formation from indoor bleach photochemistry.

title: Ammonia Triggers Interfacial Breakpoint Chlorination to Enhance Micropollutant Degradation and Reshapes Chlorinated Byproduct Formation during Electrochlorination
abstract: Abstract Electrochlorination is a promising technology for micropollutant degradation in decentralized water treatment. However, ammonia can alter chlorine chemistry. This study investigates the effect of ammonia on micropollutant degradation and chlorinated byproduct formation during electrochlorination using the RuO2/IrO2–Ti anode. Compared to electrochlorination at 10 mM chloride without ammonia, the presence of 1 mM ammonia increased the degradation rate constants of metronidazole and carbamazepine by 2.7- and 4.5-fold, respectively. This enhancement is consistent with interfacial breakpoint chlorination, defined as preferential chlorine–ammonia conversion within an anode-adjacent, chlorine-rich aqueous diffusion layer before complete bulk mixing. During electrochlorination with ammonia, dissolved HO• contributed to micropollutant degradation. Electron paramagnetic resonance provided qualitative evidence of HO• formation, whereas nitrobenzene was used as a probe to quantify its steady-state concentration. The ammonia-induced steady-state HO• concentration reached 2.4 × 10–13 M at 1 mM ammonia, whereas the HO• contribution was negligible without ammonia. Meanwhile, 1–5 mM ammonia reduced the total yields of chlorinated byproducts by only 25–31% during electrochlorination. The limited suppression is consistent with concurrent competition between ammonia and dissolved organic matter for locally generated chlorine within the anode-adjacent region. These findings identify near-anode chlorine–ammonia conversion as a route to reactive-species formation and micropollutant degradation, while showing that chlorinated byproducts remain a concern in ammonia-containing electrochlorination systems.

title: Source or Sink: Bioanalytical and Chemical Profiling of New and Field-Weathered Plastics
abstract: Abstract Plastics contain complex mixtures of chemicals that can leach into the aquatic environment. Conversely, the high sorption capacity of certain polymers renders plastics passive samplers for environmental pollutants from ambient waters. We evaluated whether effects from chemicals that are extractable or leachable from plastics from the North Pacific Ocean are dominated by plastic-associated or sorbed environmental compounds. First, bioanalytical profiling of chemical mixtures from solvent extracts of field-weathered marine plastics in cell-based bioassays was compared to that of chemicals from solvent extracts of newly purchased counterparts of the field plastics. Second, the new plastics were artificially UV-weathered and solvent-extracted, and the leachate waters were enriched with solid-phase extraction and dosed into a test battery of four in vitro bioassays where activation of the arylhydrocarbon receptor, oxidative stress response, and/or cytotoxicity were most responsive. Finally, chemical screening was performed using high-resolution mass spectrometry with subsequent mixture effect modeling to identify toxicity drivers. The results showed a multifaceted picture: Newly purchased high-durability outdoor products caused higher effects before weathering, whereas food packaging tended to show increased effects after field weathering. The analyzed chemicals could partially explain the observed effects (<0.1–98%). Our study underlines the relevance of field weathering for marine plastics and their potential to leach chemicals of concern into the environment.

title: Spatially Coupled •H-involved Reductive Decomplexation of Cu(II)–EDTA for Sludge-Free Copper Recovery
abstract: Abstract The electrochemical recovery of metals from stable complexes is often limited by the accessibility of coordinated metal centers at the electrode interface. Here, we develop a polyaniline-modified carbon felt (PANI@CF) cathode to regulate the interfacial microenvironment for selective Cu recovery from copper(II)–ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (Cu(II)–EDTA). The PANI interface couples Cu(II)–EDTA enrichment with •H generation through complementary nitrogen functionalities, thereby promoting Cu(II)–EDTA decomplexation while preserving ligand integrity. Under optimized conditions, PANI@CF achieves high Cu recovery (up to 99.9%) over a broad Cu(II)–EDTA concentration range (0.5–5 mM) and pH range (3–11), with a 32.75-fold enhancement in the apparent reaction rate compared with pristine carbon felt. Mechanistic investigations reveal that imine (–N═) functionalities contribute to interfacial Cu(II)–EDTA enrichment, whereas amine (–NH–) functionalities facilitate N–H activation and •H generation. This spatial coupling promotes interactions between short-lived •H and coordinated Cu centers, weakening Cu(II)–EDTA coordination and facilitating Cu reduction while preserving EDTA integrity. After ten consecutive treatment cycles, the cumulative Cu recovery reached 215.07 mg cm–2, and the PANI@CF electrode was regenerated by mild acid washing. The selective recovery of Cu and EDTA was further demonstrated in actual electroplating wastewater. This work highlights interfacial regulation through spatial coupling as a strategy for overcoming accessibility limitations in the electrochemical transformation of metal–ligand complexes and supports selective resource recovery from complexed industrial effluents.

title: Molecular Interactions between Styrene Oligomers and Human Serum Albumin: A Multiscale Computational Study of a Plastic-Derived Environmental Contaminant
abstract: Abstract Micro- and nanoplastics are pervasive environmental pollutants known to accumulate in human organs. While the hazards of larger plastic particles are under intense investigation, the toxicological impact of molecular-level plastic oligomers with dimensions around 1 nm is a critical and underexplored area. This study provides a comprehensive molecular-level in silico characterization of the binding interactions between styrene oligomers (1–7 units) and HSA, characterizing their molecular basis and its potential relevance to HSA’s ligand transport function. A multilevel computational approach was employed, integrating molecular docking, MD simulations, DFT, MM/PBSA binding free energy calculations, and ProLIF interaction fingerprinting. FA1 accommodated 82–95% of the most favorable docking poses for oligomers containing three to seven styrene units and exhibited the lowest docking scores, reaching −11.9 kcal·mol–1, compared with −6.4 kcal·mol–1 for the monomer. MD simulations confirmed the structural stability of oligomer-HSA complexes, further supported by dynamic cross-correlation, principal component, and solvent-accessible surface area analyses. Quantum biochemistry analyses further confirmed FA1 as the most energetically favorable binding pocket, with an average interaction energy of −117.47 kcal·mol–1 compared with −73.96 kcal·mol–1 for FA6, a hierarchy independently reproduced by MM/PBSA calculations (R = 0.82). For the hexamer and heptamer, FA1 exhibited energetic advantages of 27.39 and 21.84 kcal·mol–1, respectively. These findings indicate that HSA binds styrene oligomers with high stability and affinity at FA1, providing a molecular basis for further investigation of their potential relevance to ligand transport and systemic exposure to plastic-derived contaminants.

title: Soil Mineral Coatings on Biodegradable Microplastics: Formation and Control of Enzymatic Degradation
abstract: Abstract In agriculture, biodegradable plastics weather and fragment into microplastics that inevitably acquire mineral coatings. However, the impact of mineral coatings on microplastic degradation remains poorly understood. We examined coating formation and enzymatic degradation of pristine and photoaged poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) microplastics (PBAT-MPs) in loessial soil and red soil under drought, moist, alternate wetting-drying, and flooded regimes during 64 days. Soil type, moisture, and photoaging governed coating accumulation. Loessial soil produced greater Al and Fe loading on PBAT-MPs than red soil, while unsaturated regimes increased Al and Fe by 394%–1109% relative to flooding (p < 0.05). Synchrotron micro-X-ray fluorescence combined with absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy analyses showed heterogeneous elemental distributions and mineral speciation on PBAT-MPs that resembled those of the source soils. Unexpectedly, loessial-soil coatings increased PBAT-MPs’ terephthalic acid and adipic acid release by 9.1%–17.4% and reduced residual PBAT mass by 6.5%–23.5% (p < 0.05). Kinetic analyses showed that although mineral coatings slowed enzyme adsorption via diffusion limitations, localized leaching of Ca2+ from the coatings enhanced cutinase activity and outweighed this physical constraint. These findings demonstrate that mineral coatings can regulate the enzymatic degradation of PBAT, providing new insights into the environmental fate of biodegradable microplastics in agricultural soils.

title: Interfacial Triplet-Energy Funneling Directs Energy-Transfer-Mediated Singlet Oxygen Generation for Deep Toluene Mineralization
abstract: Abstract Photocatalytic oxidation is a promising strategy for volatile organic compounds (VOCs) abatement, but incomplete mineralization and carbonaceous intermediate accumulation remain major challenges, especially when conventional charge-transfer pathways generate nonselective radical reactive oxygen species. Selective activation of molecular oxygen toward singlet oxygen (1O2) offers a potential route to controlled oxidation, yet efficient energy-transfer-mediated 1O2 generation in solid-state photocatalysts remains difficult to achieve. Herein, a strongly coupled In(OH)3/ZnGa2O4 heterojunction with an electronic structure consistent with an S-scheme configuration is constructed to investigate interfacial excited-state regulation. Spectroscopic measurements indicate modified excited-state relaxation and a reduced effective singlet–triplet energy separation, which may favor singlet-to-triplet conversion. Combined spectroscopic analyses, quenching experiments, and density functional theory calculations support a proposed interfacial triplet-energy-funneling pathway involving ZnGa2O4-related/interfacial triplet-related states and subsequent energy transfer to adsorbed O2 for 1O2 generation. As a result, the optimized In(OH)3/ZnGa2O4 photocatalyst achieves 98.3% toluene removal and 92.4% mineralization in a continuous-flow gas-phase reactor, together with excellent cycling stability and humidity tolerance. Mechanistic results further suggest that a pathway involving 1O2 contributes to methyl oxidation and the subsequent conversion of oxygenated intermediates, potentially limiting carbonaceous residue accumulation. This work provides an excited-state-engineering strategy for selective molecular oxygen activation and offers a promising route toward efficient, durable, and deeply mineralizing photocatalytic VOCs abatement.

title: Suppressing Proton Affinity of Surface Oxygen for Enhanced N2 Selectivity in Mn-Based NH3–SCR Catalysts
abstract: Abstract Inferior N2 selectivity remains a critical challenge for Mn-based catalysts in NH3–SCR denitration. Here, using atomically dispersed Mn on anatase (Mn1/TiO2) and MnO2 as model catalysts, we elucidate the origin of surface oxygen activity and the role of surface oxygen in the formation of N2O. Both catalysts achieved >99% NO conversion in the temperature range of 175–300 °C (WHSV = 60,000 mL·g–1·h–1). Compared with the poor selectivity of α-MnO2 (1.2% at 300 °C), Mn1/TiO2 maintained >88.0% N2 selectivity in 50–300 °C. Density functional theory calculations revealed that the high affinity of surface oxygen for protons results in overoxidation of NH3-derived intermediates, thus promoting N2O formation. Orbital interaction analysis manifested that surface oxygen activity in octahedrally coordinated catalysts depends on the spin polarization in transition-metal 3d bands. Atomic dispersion of Mn sites on oxides with nonspin-polarized dxy orbitals was demonstrated as a universal strategy to boost N2 selectivity. This work deepens the fundamental understanding of surface oxygen activity in catalysts, paving a way for designing Mn-based catalysts with excellent N2 selectivity.

title: UV328 Promotes Plastisphere Formation on Microplastics through Quorum-Sensing-Associated Signaling Interference
abstract: Abstract Microplastics have created an expanding anthropogenic microbial niche known as the plastisphere, yet the mechanisms by which plastic additives influence these microbial assemblies remain poorly understood. Here, we show that UV328, a ubiquitous benzotriazole stabilizer recently listed in the Stockholm Convention, may be associated with quorum sensing signaling that accelerates plastisphere formation, biomass accumulation, and extracellular polymeric substance production on microplastics. In UV328-exposed polystyrene and polylactic acid plastisphere, the total expression levels of biofilm formation genes are upregulated by 1.38- to 2.94-fold compared to the control and quorum quenching manipulations. Molecular dynamics simulations predict that UV328 structurally mimics N-acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL) and may plausibly occupy ligand-binding domains of the quorum sensing receptor SdiA and CciR with favorable energetics. UV328 exposure was further associated with the upregulation of genes involved in bacterial chemotaxis, flagellar assembly, and central carbon metabolism. This physiological reprogramming alters community assembly trajectories and leads to a protein-rich plastisphere phenotype that was reversible by enzymatic quorum quenching, potentially supporting the involvement of AHL-sensitive processes. Our findings suggest that UV328 can alter plastisphere development through signaling-associated ecological processes, raising the possibility that microplastics may function as chemically active interfaces and highlighting microbial signaling interference as an overlooked dimension of the ecological risks associated with plastic additives in aquatic ecosystems.

title: Coal Tar-Based Driveway Sealant Extract Induces Mutations in Liver, Bone Marrow, and Germ Cells of MutaMouse Male Mice
abstract: Abstract Coal tar-based driveway sealants (CTS) are a widespread but underrecognized source of human exposure to mutagenic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). We used Duplex Sequencing, an error-corrected sequencing technology, to assess the mutagenicity of a complex PAH mixture extracted from a CTS in MutaMouse male mice. We observed significant dose-dependent increases in mutation frequency (MF) in liver and bone marrow, with mutation spectra dominated by C:G > A:T substitutions, closely resembling a mutational signature linked to human cancers associated with tobacco smoking. In germ cells, we did not observe a statistically significant increase in MF, although there was a positive dose–response trend and enrichment of C:G > A:T mutations at higher doses. The mutagenic effects of CTS in germ cells were supported by a statistically significant increase in mutant frequency measured using the plaque-based lacZ assay. Tissue-specific analyses revealed greater mutation susceptibility and potency in liver, likely reflecting its central role in PAH metabolism. Mutation spectrum analysis showed that the mutagenic profile of the CTS extract largely resembled that of benzo(a)pyrene; however, detailed spectral analysis indicated additional contributions from other PAHs or PAH metabolites that produced distinct mutational patterns. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that the CTS extract induces tissue-specific mutagenic responses driven by characteristic C:G > A:T mutations, offering mechanistic insight into how environmental PAH mixtures contribute to mutation burden and cancer risk.

Future environmental impacts of EU permanent magnet demand: a combined prospective MFA-LCA assessment
abstract: Advancing climate change necessitates a transformation of the mobility and energy sector towards low-carbon technologies. Rare earth element-containing permanent magnets (PMs), a key component in efficient electric machines, are currently produced in only a few countries and not efficiently recycled, motivating efforts to diversify supply by establishing domestic recycling routes. This study inspects the projected environmental impacts of PM value chains, thereby providing context to transitioning from a geographically concentrated, linear value chain towards a circular value chain in the European Union. Combining material flow analysis (MFA) and prospective life cycle assessment (LCA), the emissions from 2025 to 2100 are estimated under alternative production and recycling scenarios. Results show that i) future impacts of PM production will increasingly depend on the footprint of the material, ii) guaranteeing high magnetic performance during the use phase is key to achieving environmental benefits of circular value chains, iii) end-of-life products can become a relevant source for PM materials if recycling technologies and value chains are developed, and iv) recycling material substitution rates strongly influence overall results. The article showcases how to meaningfully combine LCA and MFA in dynamic system studies and demonstrates the cumulative environmental benefits of diversifying PM supply. Findings support ongoing EU efforts to strengthen domestic critical raw material supply and circular economy strategies.

Well-to-wake climate performance of e-fuels in aviation based on life cycle assessment
abstract: Aviation causes about 3.5% of effective anthropogenic radiative forcing. About two-thirds of this comes from non-CO 2 short-lived climate forcers (SLCFs), which current aviation policy does not yet regulate. This study compares the well-to-wake climate impact of e-kerosene, liquid hydrogen and ammonia, each made with wind or solar electricity, with that of conventional jet fuel (CJF). Contrail cirrus, NO x , water vapour, hydrogen and ammonia slip and N 2 O are included and assessed with four metrics: ATR 20 , ATR 100 , GWP 20 and GWP 100 . SLCFs cause 83% of the tank-to-wake impact of CJF under ATR 20 and 96–100% of that of the alternative fuels. Liquid hydrogen made with wind electricity has the lowest impact under all four metrics. It is 181.3 gCO 2 -eq·MJ −1 under ATR 20 (60% below CJF) and 58.0 gCO 2 -eq·MJ −1 under GWP 100 (66% below CJF). Per passenger-km, a long-range hydrogen aircraft that uses 42% more energy is still 46–59% below CJF if contrail cirrus is counted per kilometre. E-kerosene made with wind electricity is 26–53% below CJF. Ammonia made with wind electricity is only 7% (ATR 20 ) to 36% (GWP 100 ) below CJF at a NO x emission of 10 g·kg −1 , and above CJF under ATR 20 at more than 11.1 g·kg −1 . Under GWP 100 , the e-fuels are below CJF only with electricity below 126 (ammonia), 143 (e-kerosene) or 233 (liquid hydrogen) gCO 2 -eq·kWh −1 . At the 2025 EU grid average of 209 gCO 2 -eq·kWh −1 , e-kerosene and ammonia would therefore be worse than CJF. Fuel policy should include SLCFs and require additional renewable electricity.

title: Experimental analysis of effects of load, intake pressure and equivalence ratio on a Semi-Closed Cycle Oxy-Fuel Combustion engine for carbon capture purposes
abstract: In this paper, an experimental evaluation was conducted to determine the effect of engine load, intake pressure, and the O2-to-fuel ratio (λ) on a Semi-Closed Cycle Oxy-Fuel Combustion (SCC-OFC) reciprocating internal combustion engine (RICE). To this end, tests were carried out at low and mid-high loads in a commercial compression ignition (CI) RICE retrofitted to OFC, sweeping intake pressure and λ at a constant temperature while employing water injection for evaporative cooling. On the one hand, it has been demonstrated that the CI engine can operate across a very wide range of EGR rates—up to 95% at low loads—although with excessive O2 dilution, as inherently high cycle pressure means high EGR and high trapped mass. On the other hand, at mid-high loads, suitable O2 concentrations are achieved even at high cycle pressures, thereby enabling efficient combustion. The cycle operating intake pressure is identified as a key variable in the optimization and control of closed-cycle RICEs. Furthermore, it was shown that the exhaust dry CO2 concentration can be isolated from variations in load, water injection, or EGR, maintaining a constant level through the control of λinj. A critical correlation was observed between the quantity of liquid water ingested by the engine and the deterioration of combustion efficiency (an increase in CO and uHC emissions), presenting a fundamental challenge for closed cycles operating with high wet EGR rates. The extended ignition delay caused by OFC CI - RICE offers a promising avenue for the adoption of highly reactive fuels, such as high-cetane biodiesel, paving the way for the integration of biofuels with source CO2 capture directly from the highly concentrated flue gas of SCC-OFC RICEs.

title: Integrating hydrogen into Ontario’s energy hub: A robust, carbon-aware framework for power–heat–transport
abstract: Decarbonizing electricity generation, heating, and transportation simultaneously requires integrated planning tools that coordinate multiple energy carriers while remaining reliable under uncertainty. This paper develops a carbon-aware and uncertainty-resilient optimization framework for a grid-connected multi-energy hub that co-optimizes electricity, heating, cooling, and transportation services with an explicit hydrogen sub-hub. The model is formulated as a mixed-integer linear program over annual planning states from 2025 to 2050, representing 25 inter-year transition intervals. The hub integrates photovoltaic and wind generation, dispatchable natural gas-based conversion, storage, demand response, EV charging and V2G, and a storage-mediated hydrogen chain comprising an electrolyzer, hydrogen storage, FCEV demand, and stationary fuel-cell reconversion. Two policy archetypes are examined: a carbon tax, represented by an emissions-cost term in the objective, and a net-zero pathway, represented by a declining emissions constraint. Feasibility-critical operational uncertainty is treated through budgeted robust optimization with deviation bounds ± 30 % deviation bounds and a tunable uncertainty budget, applied to electricity and heat balances. Under the adopted representative-period design, the Ontario case yields an electrolyzer expansion from 300 MW in 2025 to 3800 MW in 2050, hydrogen-storage expansion from 2000 to 37,000 MWh, and a robustness premium of approximately 6.6%–9.0% in the policy cases. These numerical magnitudes are conditional on the compression of each planning year into a representative 48-hour window. Because this aggregation excludes sequences longer than that window, the 37-GWh result is not a validated seasonal-adequacy requirement and is likely downward-biased when multi-day low-renewable episodes are binding; the reported robustness premium should likewise be interpreted as conditional on the adopted temporal representation.

Decarbonization benefits of municipal solid waste recovery: A cross-country analysis of 32 countries
abstract: Municipal solid waste (MSW) recovery is critical to global decarbonization agendas. Existing studies have provided important insights into the environmental performance of alternative waste-treatment pathways through life-cycle and scenario-based assessments. However, less is known about whether recovery expansion translates into measurable reductions in observed carbon emissions. This study employs an instrumental-variable framework to estimate the economy-wide carbon-emission effects of MSW recovery using a 32-country panel from 1998 to 2023, addressing reverse-causality concerns in the recovery-emission relationship. The results show that, across the 32-country sample, a 10% increase in aggregate MSW recovery is associated with an average 0.95–1.15% reduction in per capita carbon emissions. This estimate reflects the net system-level effect of recovery expansion under the observed mix of recovery pathways and national conditions, rather than a common effect of individual recovery technologies. The effect varies substantially across recovery systems: energy-recovery-dominated systems show stronger mitigation effects than recycling-dominated systems, with further differences across recovery scale, energy structure, and socioeconomic conditions. Finally, selected non-sample countries are compared with the 32-country sample across key structural moderators to identify where recovery expansion is most likely to deliver large mitigation gains. Overall, the study provides cross-country causal evidence on how MSW recovery translates into economy-wide emission outcomes under different national conditions, offering a system-level basis for aligning recovery strategies with broader decarbonization goals.

title: The synergy of building information modeling and artificial intelligence for building carbon management: A systematic review
Modified Biochar for Wastewater Nutrient Recovery and Slow‐Release Fertilization in Sandy Agroecosystems
abstract: ABSTRACT Modified biochars are increasingly recognized as multifunctional materials for wastewater nutrient recovery and slow‐release fertilization in sandy agroecosystems. This review evaluates modified biochars, with particular emphasis on tyre‐derived biochar (TBC), for (i) recovery of nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) from wastewater and digestate and (ii) reuse of nutrient‐enriched biochar as a slow‐release fertilizer in sandy agroecosystems. Importantly, pristine biochar often shows limited affinity for anionic phosphorus species such as orthophosphate because its surface is commonly negatively charged, whereas chemical or mineral modification can markedly enhance P adsorption by introducing reactive sites and improving surface functionality. Across the literature, modified biochars generally outperform pristine materials in nutrient recovery due to increased surface area, porosity, and functional group density, with adsorption governed by ion exchange, electrostatic attraction, surface complexation, pore filling, and mineral precipitation. Following soil application, nutrient‐loaded biochars can improve nutrient retention, reduce leaching losses, and supply nutrients gradually, making them particularly relevant for sandy soils in arid and semi‐arid regions where low organic matter and rapid drainage constrain nutrient‐use efficiency and crop productivity. In this context, biomass‐derived biochars more directly support biogenic nutrient recycling, whereas TBC is more appropriately framed as a waste‐derived resource recovery material within a broader waste‐valorization pathway rather than a closed circular nutrient cycle. However, performance varies with feedstock, modification strategy, wastewater composition, nutrient form, and soil conditions, while contaminant risks including heavy metals, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and phytotoxicity remain important limitations, especially for waste‐derived chars. Overall, modified biochars show strong potential to link wastewater treatment, nutrient recovery, and improved fertilization efficiency in sandy agroecosystems, but future work should prioritize long‐term field validation, contaminant safety, and site‐specific biochar design for arid and semi‐arid farming systems.

Robust equilibria in cheap-talk games with fairly transparent motives
abstract: For cheap-talk games with a binary state space in which the sender has state-independent preferences, we characterize equilibria that are robust to introducing slight state-dependence on the side of the sender. Not all equilibria are robust, but the sender-optimum is always achieved at some robust equilibrium.

Non‐Traditional Roles and Unmet Care Need During Primary Care Appointments
abstract: ABSTRACT Primary healthcare systems worldwide face a shortage of General Practitioners and Nurses. One response by the English Health System to combat this shortage is to expand the role of non‐traditional roles in primary care, often shifting away tasks from Nurses. Non‐traditional practitioners, though less taxing on budgets, tend to have less formal training than Doctors and Nurses, which may affect quality of care. Using data from 614,115 respondents to a survey of primary care patients in England between 2018 and 2022, we assess the extent to which non‐traditional practitioners meet patients' needs in primary care appointments. Patients who see a non‐traditional provider have a 12.6 percentage points lower probability that their care needs were met, relative to those seeing a Nurse. Findings are consistent across linear, probit and instrumented recursive bivariate probit models, and concentrated amongst patients aged 35–54.

title: The Ubiquity of Business Groups around the World: A Property‐Rights Theory
abstract: Abstract Business groups (BGs) are collections of legally independent firms connected by ownership ties and are widely present in both developing and developed economies. We develop property‐rights theory (PRT) to explain this prevalence, extending its scope from the allocation of rights over a bundle of assets to the legal partitioning of assets as another allocative mechanism of property rights. Our conceptual framework complements traditional theories understanding BGs primarily as responses to institutional voids. Drawing on a large global dataset of firms, we examine how firm asset specificity and ownership sharing influence the controlling owners' decision to organize their economic activities as a BG or as a standalone firm. We find that the likelihood of adopting a BG organizational form over a standalone entity increases when (1) controlling owners rely on more firm‐specific assets, and (2) ownership is shared or potentially shared. Moreover, our findings are robust across three commonly observed firm strategic configurations: focused, vertically integrated, and diversified. Our study expands the PRT by developing a theory of property‐rights architecture, moving forward from the institutional voids perspective to explain BGs as efficient governance responses to asset and ownership complexities, hence contributing also to the strategic management and international business literatures.

title: An Integrated Three‐Phase Green Quality Function Deployment Framework for Evaluating Lean–Green Criteria Under Uncertainty
abstract: ABSTRACT Manufacturers need decision models that translate environmental and customer requirements into operational priorities while integrating lean and green practices within a unified programme. This study develops and applies an integrated decision framework to identify, structure and prioritise lean–green manufacturing criteria and to examine how their relative importance changes as strategic requirements are translated into technical, environmental and operational priorities. An initial literature‐derived set of 15 criteria and 55 subcriteria was refined through expert screening to eight criteria and 42 subcriteria. Fuzzy analytic network process (FANP) was first used to capture interdependencies among the retained criteria and derive their network‐based priorities. These priorities were subsequently carried through three linked green quality function deployment (GQFD) matrices, sequentially relating lean–green criteria to gearbox technical characteristics, environmental requirements and lean enablers. The resulting lean‐enabler weights were then incorporated into interval VIKOR to obtain the final compromise priorities under uncertainty. FANP ranked workforce, environmental performance and process highest, whereas the final analysis placed supply chain, performance outcomes and environmental performance in the leading positions. This cross‐stage reordering shows that structural importance within an interdependent decision network does not necessarily translate directly into implementation priority and demonstrates the value of tracing how lean–green priorities are reconfigured across successive deployment stages.

title: From Good to Green: Entrepreneurial Pathways to Eco‐Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT The connection between personal well‐being and planetary health is often overlooked. This study is aimed at researching into the effects of entrepreneurs' well‐being on eco‐innovation. More specifically, and grounded on the entrepreneurship literature, we argue that entrepreneurial orientation, as an internal factor, and ecosystem exploitation, as an external factor, mediate the relationship between well‐being and eco‐innovation. Based on a sample of 401 entrepreneurs and using an SEM analysis, results suggest that entrepreneurial well‐being does not directly promote eco‐innovation. Thus, feeling well is not an enough precondition to promote improvements for the environment. Instead, working internally toward more entrepreneurial attitudes, as well as working externally by leveraging the available mechanisms in the ecosystem, may help entrepreneurs to engage in eco‐innovation. Our research supports a holistic view of entrepreneurship as a human and ecological endeavor, contributing not only to economic value but also to the resilience of individuals, organizations, and their ecosystems.

title: Engagement is not enough: Unlocking the path from green leadership to environmental sustainability

Accounting and the fragmented self: institutional opacity, spiritual inequality and moral burden in Islamic finance
abstract: Purpose This study examines how Islamic financial institutions, despite claiming ethical legitimacy, may reproduce spiritual and moral inequalities. Drawing on Muhammad Iqbal's concept of khudi (Self), the study examines how institutional opacity, limited theological engagement and compliance-oriented practices displace moral responsibility onto individuals, forcing consumers to navigate financial choices amid guilt, uncertainty and fragmented ethical agency. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative interpretive approach, drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with UK-based Muslim consumers who currently hold or have previously held Islamic financial products. The data were analysed thematically to explore how individuals experience ethical ambiguity, self-surveillance and clerical authority, and how they resist the commodification of their faith within modern financial systems. Findings Rather than a transparent ethical alternative, Islamic finance asserts moral authority without substantive justification. Facing institutional opacity and limited theological reasoning, participants internalise moral risk through guilt and self-surveillance. This uneven clarity erodes trust in religious authority, intensifies spiritual disorientation, and exposes how institutions can privatise accountability while retaining institutional legitimacy. Research limitations/implications By introducing khudi as a counter-accountability framework to demonstrate that inequalities take spiritual and moral forms, the study offers a new ontological lens for reimagining accountability as a dialogical and emancipatory practice. It urges institutions, Shariah boards and standard-setters to move beyond formal, audit-driven compliance. It repositions accountability as a substantive ethical practice, demanding that claims of Islamic legitimacy be structurally transparent and publicly justified. Originality/value Extending critical accounting scholarship, the study reveals that inequality in Islamic finance is spiritual and moral. By introducing Iqbal's khudi (Self), it provides a novel framework demonstrating how calculative regimes can either fragment or sustain the transcendent Self, repositioning accountability as a site for reclaiming spiritual agency.

title: The impact of AI on tourist decision-making within the smart tourism ecosystem: Personalization towards satisfaction
Distributionally robust coordinated optimization of IES-HPP-SAP based on P2P network game
Türkiye’s gas market reform: A hybrid institutional pathway for competition and resilience
abstract: This paper analyzes Türkiye's natural gas market reform through the lens of institutional path dependence, demonstrating the failure of textbook liberalization strategies in a system marked by embedded support structures and geopolitical constraints. The delayed restructuring of BOTAŞ and the absence of a clear segmentation framework prevented the emergence of a well-functioning domestic market, constraining price formation and liquidity, and ultimately hindering Türkiye's hub potential.To address this structural gap, this study proposes a unique hybrid institutional pathway operationalized through a novel Dual-Ring Model. This model segments gas supply between a regulated Guardian Ring (for vulnerable consumers) and a market-based Competitive Ring, fostering traded liquidity and authentic benchmark pricing. Drawing on the "second-best" institutional approach and the principle of "embedded autonomy", the framework argues against full liberalization. The AggregateTR procurement mechanism coordinates strategic state bargaining power, notably leveraging the critical 2026–2030 contract rollover period, with transparent competitive allocation. Two original Structural Market Indicators (SSDI and TVR) monitor support targeting and traded liquidity.Scenario-based analysis demonstrates how disciplined segmentation and phased support recalibration, including the strategic release of Sakarya Domestic Gas Production into the Competitive Ring, progressively balance supply security, affordability, and benchmark credibility. This framework provides a resilient hybrid gas market architecture grounded in Türkiye's structural context, offering actionable insights for the critical 2026–2030 contract rollover window and the subsequent post-2030 market design. The approach offers replicable lessons for other gas import-dependent emerging economies, reconciling liberalization with strategic state coordination.

title: MXene-based heterostructures for hydrogen evolution reaction: Catalytic performance and environmental implications
Size- and Time-Resolved Emission Rates of Particulate Matter Mass, Chemical Constituents, and Oxidative Potential from Indoor Sources
abstract: Abstract We quantified the time- and size-resolved emission rates of particulate matter (PM) mass, its chemical constituents, and OP (via dithiothreitol assay) from six indoor sources in a test chamber (two types of incense, candle, toaster, humidifier, and cigarette). Both the chemical composition and mass-normalized OP (OPm) varied little temporally. However, both the chemical composition and OPm varied with particle size from <0.25 to 10 μm, with quasi-ultrafine particles (Q-UFPs < 0.25 μm) showing the highest OPm. The particle size distribution of the PM emitted from these sources was mostly unimodal, with both PM10 mass and OP emission rate concentrated in the Q-UFP size range. Given the abundance of Q-UFPs in the emitted PM with their high intrinsic OP, we find that 37 ± 3% of the emitted PM10 mass and OP from these sources has the potential to deposit in the respiratory tract, 45 ± 2% of which deposits in the alveolar region. An exploratory exposure assessment suggests that for an equal dose of PM10 mass and OP originating from these indoor sources vs ambient PM, the emissions from the tested indoor sources will likely result in a 76 ± 10% higher dose of alveolar-deposited mass and OP. Collectively, these results emphasize the need to better quantify the size-resolved toxicological properties of PM from myriad indoor emission sources to reliably estimate the resulting health risks.

title: Thermal analysis of a ground-mounted photovoltaic system coupled with the crop of a metal-hyperaccumulating plant using multiple modelling approaches
abstract: Understanding the operating temperature of photovoltaic (PV) modules is crucial for assessing their electrical performance, yet most agrivoltaic models focus on crop yield rather than PV thermal behaviour. This study addresses this gap by proposing a one-dimensional dynamic thermal model based on a nodal approach to simulate the PV modules’ temperatures. The model was validated using PV back-surface temperatures measured during a two-year experiment and integrate soil and vegetation surface temperatures and meteorological parameters. This model (Model 3) was evaluated against two simplified thermal models: the Ross thermal model (Model 1) and the Normal Operating Cell Temperature model (Model 2). Model 3 showed the greatest precision with a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) down to 1.6°C and a Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency coefficient (NSE) > 92 %, outperforming Models 1 and 2 by 20 % in NSE and 50-80 % in RMSE reduction. Model 1 performed better under cloudy conditions (RMSE 3.6-4.5°C; NSE 72-80 %), while Model 2 slightly improved sunny-day predictions (NSE up to 82 %). Model 3 consistently provided the best results (NSE > 92 %). Comparing simulated and measured electrical energy production of an opaque module, Models 1 and 2 overestimated output (+2 % to +3 %, more under sunny conditions), while Model 3 exhibited the closest agreement (deviation < 1 %). Parametric simulations with Model 3 also highlighted the potential of brownfield sites in southern France for ecovoltaic deployment. This work provides a robust thermal modelling framework for ecovoltaic systems, improving performance predictions and supporting sustainable energy integration.

Impact of global supply chain pressures on energy demand and stability: The role of global sustainability initiatives
abstract: Global supply chain pressures (GSCP) have become a major challenge for multinational enterprises (MNEs), influencing firm-level operational decisions, including evolving energy demand patterns. This paper investigates the impact of global supply chain pressures on energy consumption in Chinese MNEs from 2013 to 2022. Results from Double-Selection Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) linear regression indicate that GSCP increases the energy demand of Chinese MNEs. One possible explanation is that GSCP undermines production stability and operational efficiency, prompting firms to intensify production, extend operating hours, and adopt additional shifts to meet volatile demand conditions. Furthermore, global shocks (i.e., US-China Trade War and COVID-19) and global green initiatives (i.e., Montreal Protocol–Kigali Amendment, the EU Innovation Fund, and the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative) significantly moderate the relationship between GSCP and energy demand. The heterogeneity analysis exhibits that the GSCP impact is most pronounced among state-owned MNEs, firms with substantial overseas investment experience, and enterprises exhibiting lower degrees of internationalisation. This study contributes new empirical and theoretical insights into how global supply chain disruptions affect corporate energy demand and shape the strategic responses of Chinese MNEs.

title: Environmental catalytic characteristics of pyrolyzed oil sludge and the role of permanent radicals
Hydrological redistribution shapes structural mismatch between water–energy–food sustainability and ecosystem services in an arid inland river basin
