Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space
abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Here we report an ODT-based Bose-Einstein condensate created aboard the China Space Station, containing 2.0 × 10 4 atoms, reaching an equivalent temperature of 9.7 − 2.7 + 3.2 pK with a free expansion time of 7.0 s. This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space.

title: Stacked porous NiTi structure with low cost and ultrahigh fatigue life for elastocaloric cooling
abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake
abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
abstract: Abstract A longstanding challenge in developmental science is to understand how children learn language from naturalistic everyday input. To study this process, we leveraged the First 1,000 Days (1kD) dataset, which provides longitudinal, ultra-dense daily audiovisual recordings for individual children in their home environments. This unusually detailed, child-specific record of early experience enabled us to pair each child’s rich language input with a cognitively grounded learning agent, linking naturalistic experience (“nurture”) to internal learning mechanisms (“nature”). Trained incrementally on each child’s input without prior linguistic knowledge, the learning agent discovered speech units corresponding to the English phoneme inventory and acquired thousands of words, closely mirroring individual developmental trajectories. Learning generalized across children while preserving individual differences in rate and timing. Interestingly, learning relied not only on linguistic input but also on the rehearsal of past experiences at the end of each training day. These findings demonstrate that everyday environments provide sufficient structure for language acquisition and establish a unified mechanistic framework for studying development in real-world contexts.

title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients’ plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolven s, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.

title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

title: In the image of their tools
Denoising the US Census: Succinct block hierarchical regression
abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

title: Expanding global access to GLP-1s: Challenges and opportunities
Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
abstract: Abstract We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

title: Financial constraints and the transmission of monetary policy: Evidence from relaxation of collateral constraints
Shadow banks on the rise: Evidence across market segments
abstract: This paper examines the comparative advantages of shadow banks across market segments. Combining credit bureau data on retail loans in India with weather shocks as a proxy for credit demand, we show that Fintechs respond more in uncollateralized markets. In contrast, non-Fintech shadow banks exhibit stronger responsiveness in collateralized markets. Exploiting geographic heterogeneity in the adoption of digital payments, we identify technology as the key advantage for Fintechs. Leveraging four natural experiments, we document the significance of lower regulation for non-Fintech shadow banks. Our results suggest that the comparative advantage of shadow banks differs across market segments.

title: Perceived Political Bias of the Federal Reserve,
abstract: Abstract We conduct a survey experiment with a politically representative sample of more than 5,000 U.S. consumers to study how perceptions of the Federal Reserve’s (Fed) political stance shape macroeconomic expectations, trust, and information processing. Overall, 63.5% of respondents view the Fed as politically neutral, 9.4% as aligned with their own party (in-group), and 27.2% as opposed (out-group). The non-neutral minority differs sharply: out-group respondents report substantially higher inflation expectations and lower trust than neutral or in-group respondents, even after controlling for partisanship and demographics. They also pay more to avoid opposing media and are less likely to receive Fed communication—yet update their expectations by more once exposed to it, placing less weight on their priors when the same article carries a Fed label. In a hypothetical Trump presidency, the neutral share falls to 37.2%, with respondents in both parties shifting toward viewing the Fed as Republican-leaning, consistent with expected political capture. Perceived neutrality is thus central to the Fed’s credibility and the reach of its communication, and it can shift with changes in political leadership.

Are the Hedges of Funds Green?
abstract: Abstract Over the past decade, hedge funds have increasingly embraced green investing. We develop a novel return-based measure of fund greenness and find that greener funds earn higher average returns, consistent with capturing a positive green premium, and are associated with lower risks, especially during adverse periods. We further show that performance gains are greatest among directional funds, whereas risk reduction is most pronounced among nondirectional funds. We also provide evidence that managers of these funds exhibit superior green investment skills through green stock selection and green factor timing. Finally, investors reward greener hedge funds only when they demonstrate strong performance.

Developing technological expertise through ecosystem orchestration for industrial circularity
abstract: Research on circularity often assumes that the more technological expertise industrial firms build, the more circular they become. This study challenges this assumption by showing that technological expertise alone is insufficient; how firms orchestrate collaboration to build such expertise also matters. We examine collaborations between large industrial firms and specialist SMEs, using the ecosystem-as-structure perspective to understand how technological expertise and orchestration come together. Based on a qualitative multiple-case study of seven Indian industrial firms with global operations and their 12 SME partners, drawing on 46 interviews and a validation seminar, we identify three types of technological expertise: material traceability, resource foresight, and decision integration. Each is associated with a distinct orchestration mechanism: ecosystem protocol alignment, cross-boundary validation, and milestone-anchored co-specialization, respectively. We further identify three structural conditions that shape which pairing is viable: activity interdependence, position complementarity, and link transfer specificity. The study contributes to circular economy research by showing that circular value depends on the fit between technological expertise and orchestration, and that different configurations produce distinct forms of circular value rather than simply higher or lower levels of circularity. It extends the ecosystem-as-structure perspective by explaining how structural conditions shape this fit. For practitioners, the findings show how large firms can better align technological expertise development with partner orchestration, while SMEs can use these collaborations to progress from technical service providers towards more strategic co-creation roles.

title: China’s fiscal stimulus, global financial intermediaries, and international spillovers
Ancestor's Legacy? The Effect of Folklore on Corporate Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper investigates how ancestral narratives shape contemporary corporate innovation. Drawing on pre‐industrial folklore from 20 countries, we exploit within‐country variation in local cultural motifs to examine their impact on firm innovation. We focus on two types of motifs: narratives depicting heroes’ successful challenges relative to challenge‐losing ones and narratives containing supernatural entities. We show that firms located in societies whose local folklore prevalently features heroes overcoming challenges exhibit greater R&D investment and higher patent‐based innovation efficiency, with directionally similar but statistically insignificant evidence for citation‐based efficiency. In contrast, firms in societies where folklore emphasizes supernatural entities display lower R&D investment and lower innovation efficiency. Cross‐sectional analyses indicate that these effects are moderated by regional economic openness and national patent protection and are more pronounced in highly innovative industries and among firms with higher levels of corporate transparency. Our findings are robust after controlling for regional factors or alleviating large country sample bias. The relationship between folklore and R&D investment remains directionally consistent, albeit with lower statistical significance, after instrumenting the folklore measure with historical immigration patterns to the United States. We further show that the net prevalence of challenge‐encouraging motifs is associated with more radical innovation strategies and greater corporate risk‐taking, while supernatural motifs exhibit the opposite pattern. Overall, our findings support the view that folklore persists across generations and meaningfully influences firms’ contemporary economic decisions and outcomes.

title: The Jamaica life expectancy paradox: The role of the hookworm campaign
Climate exposure and the flight of inventors
The DNA of Neuroticism and Financial Decisions
abstract: A polygenic score (PGS) capturing genetic predisposition toward neuroticism predicts heterogeneity in risk aversion, return beliefs, and stock market participation. This approach addresses key methodological and interpretive concerns associated with phenotypic measures of neuroticism. Risk aversion and return beliefs are important, but incomplete, channels linking the neuroticism PGS to stock market participation. The neuroticism PGS also predicts heterogeneity in demographic and behavioral characteristics previously shown to influence financial choices. These characteristics serve as key channels through which the genetic propensity for neuroticism shapes financial choices.

title: Impartiality and inequality of resources: Edgeworth and utilitarianism
abstract: This paper analyses Edgeworth’s anti-egalitarian conclusions, which are based on utilitarianism and the hypothesis that individuals differ in their sensitivity to pleasure and pain. According to Edgeworth, the absence of perfect competition is a defining feature of the contemporary world. This necessitates the adoption of a principle of arbitration to reconcile conflicting individual interests. The purpose of this arbitration principle is to identify the means of achieving the greatest happiness, taking into account differences in capacity for pleasure and pain. However, the question remains as to what could motivate individuals to adopt the equilibrium point defined by utilitarianism.

title: Political uncertainty, social legitimacy, and nonmarket strategy
abstract: Abstract The Decade Award–winning article by Darendeli and Hill (2016) presents a novel yet nuanced approach to the question of whether and how foreign firms can strategically navigate a volatile and unpredictable political environment. Their 2026 retrospective builds on their earlier contribution by showing how their insights have contributed to a number of contemporary IB research streams, including those addressing political risk, political action, and political ties. Going beyond their earlier contribution, in the retrospective, they describe the relational and physical pillars of social legitimacy (Darendeli & Hill, 2026). They then assess the efficacy of their original perspective in an environment characterized by heightened geopolitical conflict and political polarization. Finally, they develop a model that delineates four strategic approaches to legitimacy building in host countries. In this commentary, I offer perspectives that complement and extend their contributions by discussing (1) the nature of political uncertainty and the use of real options in responding to that uncertainty, (2) the literature on substantive versus symbolic CSR and how that might further extend some of their insights, and (3) research regarding when and how multinational enterprises provide public goods and services typically provided by government. I conclude by outlining how Darendeli and Hill’s (2016, 2026) insights have relevance for contemporary practice and policy.

title: Co‐Constructing the Illusion of Progression: How Boundary Blurring and Affirming Reproduce Social Exclusion in Elite Professions
abstract: Abstract Social exclusion is a persistent problem in elite professions. While scholarship has emphasized structural and cultural barriers, less is known about the relational practices and mechanisms through which social exclusion is sustained. Drawing on interviews with 84 lawyers, paralegals, and managers in elite UK law firms, we develop a conceptual model of how the blurring and affirming of social and symbolic boundaries between higher‐status and lower‐status groups reproduces social exclusion. We show how both groups blur and affirm boundaries across three domains: professional work, professional space, and systems of professional advancement. Boundary blurring makes symbolic boundaries more permeable, positioning lower‐status actors as prospective professionals, while boundary affirming maintains social boundaries around professional membership. We identify and theorize the illusion of progression as a relational mechanism emerging from intertwined blurring and affirming, constructing lower‐status roles as pathways into the profession even though progression is rare. The illusion perpetuates liminality by sustaining hope, individualizing failure and undermining lower‐status groups' collective challenge to social exclusion. Our findings advance understanding of the relational mechanism through which social exclusion persists in elite professions, show how boundary blurring can sustain rather than threaten status distinctions, and help explain why organizational diversity and inclusion efforts have produced little substantive change.

title: The Anti‐SLAPP Statutes and Corporate Environmental Policies
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether legal protection for civic participation affects corporate pollution. Polluters may deter public discipline through strategic lawsuits. Anti‐SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) statutes mitigate this threat by enabling prompt dismissal and recovery of legal costs. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that enacting an anti‐SLAPP statute in a state significantly reduces toxic emissions from that state by increasing local public pressure. The reduction is greater when the statutes provide stronger protection, when local stakeholders have stronger incentives and abilities to discipline polluters, and when local public pressure increases more after the enactment. Plants lower emissions by improving abatement rather than by reducing output or relocating emissions. Our paper underscores the role of legal protection in environmental governance and informs policy debates over anti‐SLAPP legislation.

title: Board–CEO Trust and Concealing Adverse News
Overall Evaluation Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach
abstract: This paper discusses meta-analytic methods for estimating the value of marketing interventions given a database of historical A/B tests with multiple outcome variables.

title: Knowledge‐Based Institutional Work in the Circular Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT The circular economy ( CE ) literature has primarily focused on incremental additions to the linear economy, whereas understanding of institutional change towards the CE remains limited. This study explores knowledge‐based institutional work in small born‐circular businesses that possess advanced CE applications and fundamentally aim to drive change. Drawing on 28 interviews and extensive secondary data from the clothing and apparel industry in Northwest Europe, the study identifies three forms of knowledge‐based institutional work: operational, engagement‐based and altruistic institutional work. Creating CE solutions under operational institutional work creates the foundation of the other identified forms of institutional work, whereas acknowledgement of the businesses' CE expertise enables their further development. The study concludes that, in the CE , (1) knowledge intertwines institutional work and business operations, (2) knowledge‐based institutional work blurs the boundaries between businesses and their surroundings and (3) views of knowledge help explain the mechanisms and motivations underlying institutional work.

title: Organizational Capabilities for Sustainability‐Oriented Innovation in Multi‐Stakeholder Networks: An Integrative Framework and Future Research Agenda
abstract: ABSTRACT Organizational capabilities have become imperative for stakeholders to realize sustainability‐oriented innovation in multi‐stakeholder networks, where diverse stakeholders collaborate to address complex sustainability challenges. Yet, the literature remains fragmented, lacking a clear and integrative understanding of which organizational capabilities are required and how they jointly support sustainability‐oriented innovation. To address this fragmentation, we conduct a systematic literature review of 54 articles and synthesize existing literature into an integrative multilevel framework drawing on the dynamic capabilities and ecosystem perspectives. The framework conceptualizes 17 capabilities across macro‐, meso‐, and micro‐levels and across the higher‐order dynamic capability categories of sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring. Our analysis particularly highlights network orchestration capabilities at the macro‐level, collaboration capabilities at the meso‐level, and knowledge management capabilities at the micro‐level. The study further proposes a future research agenda focused on system‐level capability interdependencies and identifies four specific domains through which these interdependencies can be examined.

title: Sustainability as a Mediating Construct: Connection, Evaluative Openness, and the Risk of Capture
abstract: ABSTRACT Similar sustainability commitments can become organizationally consequential in markedly different ways, yet the relational architecture producing this variation remains under‐theorized. This conceptual paper theorizes sustainability as a mediating construct through representational, projective, and organizing forms. Recursive translation explains how changes within one form feed back into the others, generating varying degrees of connection. Because connection does not determine which sustainability claims retain capacity to challenge and revise mediation, the framework introduces evaluative openness as a second, analytically independent dimension. Their intersection yields four configurations: symbolic, exploratory, embedded, and captured sustainability. The embedded–captured distinction reveals the central implication: strongly connected mediation can sustain coordinated action while the range of values, actors, evidence, and possible futures capable of redirecting that mediation progressively narrows. By separating connection from evaluative openness, the framework extends research on decoupling, hybrid organizing, and performativity and explains why organizational incorporation alone does not establish transformative capacity.

title: AI‐Driven Marketing Strategy as a Catalyst for Circular Economy Participation
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how sustainable marketing communication and AI‐driven marketing personalization influence circular economy participation through marketing automation maturity, carbon‐aware digital infrastructure, and willingness to purchase low‐carbon products. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory, it explains the capability‐building mechanisms underlying digitally enabled sustainability. We collected data from 3253 middle‐ and senior‐level marketing and advertising managers across five countries. We tested the proposed model using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM). We also used Jeffreys's Amazing Statistics Program (JASP) to run machine learning analyses, including support vector machine regression, regularized linear regression, and random forest regression, to assess predictive performance. Marketing automation maturity and carbon‐aware digital infrastructure significantly mediate the relationship between sustainable marketing communication and circular economy participation. Low‐carbon product willingness to purchase emerged as the strongest market‐level mechanism, whereas AI‐driven marketing personalization primarily influenced circular economy participation through sequential capability pathways. Random forest regression demonstrated superior predictive performance and confirmed the dominant importance of willingness to purchase low‐carbon products. By integrating explanatory and predictive analytics, this study extends dynamic capabilities theory by demonstrating that circular economy participation stems from sequential development of digital capabilities rather than direct marketing effects, offering actionable implications for organizations pursuing AI‐enabled sustainability and circular transformation. JEL Classification: M31, Q56, O33

title: Shocks, recovery, and labour dynamics: Evidence from the accommodation sector
abstract: This study examines the long-term relationship between tourism demand and employment in Spain's accommodation sector during the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic. Using a dynamic System GMM panel model across fifty provinces over two decades, the analysis captures employment persistence and regime-specific responses to tourism demand. Findings reveal significant employment inertia, particularly for permanent contracts, while temporary employment acts as the primary adjustment margin. Employment sensitivity to tourism demand weakened during the Great Recession but rose during COVID-19, reflecting a shift in the margin of adjustment under Spain's furlough scheme. Disaggregated results highlight pronounced heterogeneity: temporary and male employment adjust rapidly to demand shifts, while permanent and female employment adjust more gradually. Long-run results suggest that employment growth tracks sustained tourism expansion, though female employment adjusts more rigidly, possibly reflecting occupational segregation. These findings underscore the need for labour policies promoting stability and gender equity to strengthen sectoral resilience against future shocks.

title: Aligning institutions and organizations for sustainable supply chains: the role of digital transformation and low-carbon practices
abstract: Purpose The transition toward carbon neutrality has become a global strategic priority for achieving sustainable development and a green economy. Despite growing interest in digital transformation among scholars and practitioners, achieving a balance between green supply chain performance and carbon performance within the context of carbon neutrality remains underexplored. Drawing on the technology acceptance model and change management theory, this research aims to provide solutions for achieving the zero-carbon target in 2060 through holistic digital transformation, and how institutional pressure and organizational readiness influence green supply chain and carbon performance through digital transformation, low-carbon operations management practices (LCOMP) and the moderating role of environmental proactivity. Design/methodology/approach Data from 442 Chinese manufacturing firms were analyzed using Smart PLS v4 to test the research hypotheses. Findings The results indicate that all three dimensions of LCOMP mediate the relationship between digital transformation, green supply chain and carbon performance. In addition, environmental proactivity strengthens the influence of digital transformation on the three dimensions of LCOMP. Originality/value The findings contribute to the literature by addressing a key gap in sustainable supply chain and digital transformation research, which has largely examined these relationships in isolation without fully explaining the mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: How can generative AI's conversational affordances drive firm performance? A service-dominant logic perspective
Conceptualising and designing experiential consumer logistics: a literature synthesis towards a value-based framework
abstract: Purpose The value of last-mile delivery is no longer confined to functional performance but increasingly involves consumers' experiences. Despite growing recognition of experiential value, research in this area remains fragmented and underdeveloped. Thus, this study aims to develop a value-based conceptualisation of experiential consumer logistics (ECL) through a synthesised literature review. Design/methodology/approach A two-study literature review design was employed. Study 1 synthesises the logistics literature to conceptualise the value configurations and experiential mechanisms underlying ECL. Building on this conceptualisation, Study 2 integrates insights from the service design literature to examine how experiential value can be systematically reinforced. Findings Study 1 conceptualises ECL based on two analytical dimensions, value proposition (high-touch vs high-tech) and value appreciation (individualised vs networked), leading to four principal value configurations labelled as: traditional, technology-based, ethical and platform-enabled logistics. Furthermore, Study 2 identifies two complementary service design approaches for reinforcing experiential value: accommodating (relationship building and design for invisibility) and empowering (design for visibility and community building), each aligned with distinct configurations of ECL. Originality/value By consolidating dispersed literature, this review proposes an initial conceptualisation of ECL that explains how experiential value is proposed, appreciated and reinforced through service design. The findings provide an integrated theoretical foundation for understanding experiential mechanisms in last-mile logistics, offer practical guidance for designing logistics services and identify directions for future research.
journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

title: Does access to credit improve labour productivity?
abstract: Abstract If credit rationing justifies public intervention in credit markets, it should be the case that unconstrained firms should result in higher productivity. In this paper, we use a longitudinal SME dataset for the UK to empirically test whether this is true. Our findings are nuanced and show that SMEs subject to quantity rationing suffer from productivity declines of up to 40%, which is more important than full rationing in the determination of labour productivity. We suggest that partial rationing forces firms to undertake second-best investment projects that limits their ability to become more productive. This implies that the returns to capital would increase if small firms that are of sufficient quality to pass banks screening tests received all the funds they applied for. This suggests that loan guarantee schemes may play a fundamental role in removing quantity rationing barriers for SMEs. We also find that discouragement can have a positive effect on productivity, and this suggests that firms reconfigure their capital structure by retaining more cash to avoid engaging with debt markets.

title: Compressed work week – predictors and outcomes: a systematic review using text mining
abstract: The digitalisation of work processes, fuelled by the COVID-19 pandemic and the expansion of hybrid work, has renewed interest in Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs), including Compressed Work Weeks (CWWs). However, prior reviews have not systematically investigated the predictors of CWW adoption or provided an integrated overview of their individual- and organisational-level outcomes. This systematic review addresses these gaps through a topic modelling analysis of 140 research papers. Findings indicate that CWW adoption is shaped by individual, work-related, and family-related predictors, including attitudes towards time use, commuting time and distance, supervisory and organisational support, and perceived work-life balance (WLB) benefits. CWWs are generally associated with higher job satisfaction, lower turnover intention, and improved WLB, although these benefits may be reduced when extended daily working hours are involved. Evidence regarding health, fatigue, sleep, productivity, and performance remains mixed, particularly depending on daily working hours and whether subjective or objective indicators are utilised. At the organisational level, evidence on absenteeism, turnover, productivity, performance, and financial outcomes remains limited, while emerging research suggests reductions in energy use. This review integrates predictors and outcomes, clarifies conceptual distinctions,demonstrates that CWW outcomes are contingent on contextual factors, and identifies directions for future research and HRM practice.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Explaining and mitigating hiring discrimination against transgender women: evidence from India
abstract: Despite legal and organizational recognition of transgender rights in India, transgender people continue to face exclusion from professional jobs. Prior research suggests that such exclusion is often framed in ostensibly job-relevant terms rather than explicit prejudice. Drawing on the Justification-Suppression Model (JSM), we argued that when overt discrimination is normatively constrained, cisgender hiring managers rely on stereotype-based justifications to rationalize unequal treatment. Integrating the JSM and the Stereotype Content Model (SCM), we proposed that diverse rejection rationales converge on a core evaluative structure: perceptions of low warmth and low competence. Using a between-participants in-basket experimental design with Indian professionals, we examined evaluations of a transgender woman and a cisgender woman applicant for a nursing role. In the no-individuating information condition, the transgender woman applicant received significantly lower hireability ratings than the cisgender woman applicant. When counterstereotypical individuating information indicating high warmth and high competence was provided, this disparity was eliminated. These findings demonstrate that discrimination operates through stereotype-based justifications grounded in warmth and competence and that bias attenuates when the justificatory basis is weakened. The study advances theory by empirically grounding JSM in a transgender woman professional hiring context and specifying low warmth and low competence as a potential justification factor through SCM.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Management control across complexity and dynamism: A synthesis of contingency-based research
abstract: More than five decades of contingency-based research have generated extensive evidence on how management control (MC) practices vary with organisational context, yet the diversity of contingency factors examined makes it unclear what cumulative knowledge the field has produced. This paper synthesises 1844 empirical associations from 266 studies published from 1969 to 2022, using a conceptual framework that relates contingency factors to two sources of uncertainty, complexity and dynamism, and to the distinct control problems they impose. Firms facing greater complexity or dynamism rely less on direct supervision and more on a common set of MC practices, including formal strategic planning, diagnostic measurement use, performance-based pay, decentralisation, lateral coordination, and personnel controls. Uncertainty is therefore associated not with less control, but with reliance on a wider range of MC practices. Complexity is associated with a control pattern termed distributed bureaucracy, in which formalised accountability structures are combined with delegation and lateral coordination to support integration. Dynamism is associated with bounded autonomy, in which formal controls guide and evaluate responses to changing conditions while preserving the local discretion needed for adaptation. The more limited evidence on contexts high in both complexity and dynamism suggests that firms combine the two patterns rather than prioritising one. The paper concludes by outlining priorities for advancing MC contingency theory through research on the functions and interdependencies of MC practices, the implications of digital technologies, and the evolution of MC over time.

title: Developing agile teams from the inside out: The role of team and individual psychological capital
Avoiding the AI knowledge trap: A simulation-based forecast of entry-level automation, talent pipelines, and innovation capacity
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of automating professional tasks traditionally performed by entry-level staff. While such automation may drive short-term efficiency and profitability, it risks disrupting the experience-based learning pipeline essential for developing a firm's long-term innovation capacity. This paper introduces the Knowledge Trap: a structural condition where immediate gains from AI adoption lead to the gradual degradation of the tacit knowledge and adaptive search capabilities required for future performance. Using an NK agent-based simulation model, the study examines how different sectors and governance horizons influence this risk. The model distinguishes between three adoption strategies - substitutive, hybrid, and complementary - to track their long-term effects on a firm's experience pool and innovation fitness. The findings demonstrate that the Knowledge Trap is most severe under substitutive adoption, particularly in sectors with high task interdependency. Conversely, adopting AI in a complementary mode can substantially mitigate these capability losses. This research contributes a forecasting framework to help organisations and policymakers identify structural risks and develop AI implementation strategies that protect the human talent pipeline.

title: The economics of bundling in casino markets: Theory and evidence from U.S. gaming destinations
When AI does too much: Generative AI vs agentic AI and traveller empowerment in travel planning
Rethinking the Anatomy of Passion: A Biopsychosocial Configurational Perspective on Antecedents of Work and Entrepreneurial Passion
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite over two decades of passion research, our understanding of how passion is construed remains fragmented and dominated by additive approaches that treat antecedents as isolated predictors (both theoretically and empirically). Drawing on the biopsychosocial (BPS) framework, we challenge prior research by reconceptualizing passion as a configurational phenomenon emerging through interdependent BPS conditions which combine in complex ways to form equifinal pathways to passion. In doing so, we comparatively analyze configurations associated with harmonious and obsessive passion across the two most frequently studied domains in the management literature: work and entrepreneurship. To empirically examine this configurational perspective, we employ fuzzy set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), which is well equipped to test the equifinal, compensatory, and interdependent nature of configural constructs. Using two time‐lagged samples of employees and entrepreneurs, we identify multiple distinct configurations that not only differentiate harmonious from obsessive passion but also distinguish passion across the work and entrepreneurial domains. Our results demonstrate that passion is largely domain‐contingent, such that work and entrepreneurial passion are each associated with mostly unique BPS configurations rather than universally operating antecedents. Our study advances passion research by shifting attention from isolated net effects toward a holistic view of passion as a system of interdependent BPS predictors.

title: Data Breach Risks of Adopting Interorganizational Data Exchange Systems: Evidence from Health Information Exchange Adoption
Pricing the Priceless? How Communities Challenge the Marketization of Public Goods and Services
Acts, Threats, and Regime Shifts: U.S. Policy Uncertainty, Global Geopolitical Risk, and Korean Sectoral Stock Returns
abstract: This paper examines how U.S. economic policy uncertainty (EPU) and global geopolitical risk (GPR) are priced in Korean sectoral stock returns across political regimes. EPU is inherently country-specific, reflecting the U.S. policy environment that most directly shapes Korean trade and industrial conditions. GPR is global in nature, capturing supply-chain disruptions, commodity shocks, and security threats that transcend national borders. Using monthly data from January 2015 to January 2026 for five industries—semiconductors, secondary batteries, automobiles, steel, and energy and chemicals—we find clear sectoral heterogeneity. In Trump’s second term, semiconductors respond positively to geopolitical acts but negatively to threats; secondary batteries and energy and chemicals react more negatively to realized shocks; automobiles are closely tied to exchange-rate movements; and steel responds more to regime shifts and long-term interest rates. CAPM excess-return results confirm that these effects survive risk adjustment, reflecting industry-specific transmission channels rather than aggregate market risk.

title: How Does Green Transformation Shapes Corporate Investment: The Conditional Role of Green Finance
abstract: Drawing on firm-level observations from China’s A-share market over the 2008–2023 period, we examine whether and how corporate green transformation shapes firms’ inefficient investment. The results show that corporate green transformation significantly increases firms’ inefficient investment. Further evidence suggests that the increase in inefficient investment associated with green transformation is largely attributable to greater corporate over-investment. Specifically, corporate green transformation exacerbates inefficient investment by alleviating firms’ financing constraints and fostering green investment bubbles. The strength of this relationship is also closely associated with the development of green finance. In addition, we find significant heterogeneity in this effect across regions, industries, and firms.

title: How Digital Governance Reshapes Corporate Fixed Asset Investment: Evidence from the Data Security Law
Ripple in Green: The Supply Chain Spillover Effects of Green Finance
Selective industrial policy for the EU open strategic autonomy: The role of products' relatedness
abstract: The European Union has adopted the concept of Open Strategic Autonomy (OSA) to reduce strategic dependencies while preserving openness to international trade. An important policy question is therefore which countries are best positioned to develop new trade advantages in strategic products. Building on the literature on relatedness and export diversification, we address this question by complementing the standard notion of product distance, measuring how close a country is to a product compared to other countries, and how close a product is to a country's productive structure compared to other products. We term these concepts absolute and relative distance advantages. We argue that relative distance advantages reflect countries' incentives to diversify into a product, whereas absolute distance advantages capture their ability to successfully develop new trade advantage in that product. Using trade data for EU countries, we show that both dimensions significantly predict the emergence of new export specializations in products identified by the EU as strategic.

title: Digging Into the Subsoil: Considering and Theorizing Human Services Delivery at the Sub‐Micro‐Level of the Public Service Ecosystem
abstract: ABSTRACT Public services are often delivered in partnership with families and communities, yet these relationships receive limited attention within public service ecosystem (PSE) theory. Responding to call to develop the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE, we introduce the concept of subsoil sensitivity to foreground the family and community ecosystems that underpin public service value creation. These informal systems are active sites of value creation and destruction with sensitivities arising from their alignment or misalignment with public services. We propose legislative and policy nodes as connectors that translate macrolevel policy into microlevel practice. Drawing on child protection vignettes, we show how nodes create the conditions for interaction, while subsoil dynamics influence whether value is cocreated or codestroyed amid power asymmetries and differing belief systems. The paper extends the sub‐micro‐level of the PSE and offers a framework for examining family and community ecosystems in public service delivery.

title: The difficulties of reducing administrative burden via the nonprofit sector: how sedimented governance stifles care coordination
abstract: Care coordination services are designed to reduce administrative burden. However, they may not always achieve this aim. This paper, which draws from care coordination service user experiences, provides insights concerning why policies designed to reduce administrative burden may struggle when embedded in existing institutional systems, and how they might inadvertently contribute to new costs. We thematically analyse a multi-modal dataset concerning dementia care navigation services provided by non-profits in two English counties and find that stakeholders’ efforts to deal with administrative burden-related costs may be unsuccessful and potentially counterproductive: attempts to maximize information provision, reduce psychological costs and avoid compliance costs may obscure the role of a care coordination service so that learning costs remain high or even increase. We show that while studies have argued that non-profits in pluralist, networked governance models can reduce burdens, the ways they interact with sedimented governance logics can stifle such efforts.

title: The only game in town: NPM’s resilience and depoliticizing effects in (r)urban sustainability transition
abstract: This article explains the resilience of New Public Management (NPM) by conceptualizing it as a ‘mobile assemblage’ of flexible ideas and practices translated across contexts. Drawing on a qualitative study of four Swedish municipalities undergoing (r)urban sustainability transition, we demonstrate how NPM is mobilized as a set of flexible resources – managerial tools, entrepreneurial identities, market-making devices, legitimizing discursive resources, and behaviour-prescribing scripts – to organize transition initiatives. NPM thus becomes raw material for four governing arrangements – temporary projects, consultant collaboration, municipally owned companies, and public-private partnerships. Through these arrangements, NPM embeds market and management logics into local governance, fostering silent depoliticization.

title: Assessing mediation of sexual orientation disparities in miscarriage by age at pregnancy, gravidity, and use of medically assisted reproduction in four national cohorts
abstract: Recent research has documented a higher miscarriage risk among sexual minority individuals than heterosexual individuals. These disparities may be partly mediated by age at pregnancy, gravidity, and use of medically assisted reproduction (MAR). We used data from four cohorts (Nurses' Health Study 2 and 3, Growing Up Today Study, and National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health) to estimate randomized interventional analogues of mediational direct and indirect effects of sexual orientation on miscarriage (pure natural direct effects [rPNDE], total natural indirect effects [rTNIE], and proportions mediated [rPM]). We found that pregnancies to sexual minority individuals were more likely to end in a miscarriage than those to heterosexual individuals. We found weak mediation of this effect by age (rPNDE: 1.23, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.15-1.32; rTNIE: 1.02, 95% CI: 1.01-1.03; rPM: 12%, 95% CI: 5%-19%), but not gravidity (rPM: 2%, 95% CI: -1%-6%) and MAR use (rPM: -1%, 95% CI: -4%-3%). While these factors impact miscarriage risk, our findings suggest that sexual orientation disparities in miscarriage are only minimally explained by age, and not explained by gravidity and use of MAR, contributing to the understanding of the role of pregnancy-related factors vs. structural factors in sexual orientation disparities in miscarriage.

title: Neighborhood deprivation and the risk of stillbirth in New York
abstract: Stillbirth (fetal death ≥ 20 weeks gestation) occurs in approximately 21,000 births each year in the United States. Previous studies have observed associations between neighborhood deprivation and adverse perinatal outcomes. We estimated associations between neighborhood deprivation and singleton stillbirth in New York. We performed a cross-sectional study of stillbirths and live births from hospital claims data from the Statewide Planning and Research Cooperative System (2022-2024). Neighborhood deprivation index (NDI) at the census tract level was assigned to geocoded addresses at delivery. Risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using a generalized estimating equations model adjusted for individual-level maternal variables of age at delivery, race/ethnicity, marital status, and primary health insurance payer. Our analysis included 3,128 stillbirths and 552,361 live births. The NDI quartiles were associated with stillbirth, with higher levels of deprivation corresponding to increased risk compared to the least deprived quartiles. We observed the highest risk of stillbirth among women in the most deprived quartile (RR 1.42; 95% CI 1.25-1.61). The association of NDI quartile on the risk of stillbirth did not differ by race/ethnicity. Our findings highlight that women residing in the most deprived NDI quartile could benefit from enhanced prenatal services and support.

title: Identification and dating of pregnancies in administrative healthcare claims databases: An updated, transparent, and transportable algorithm
abstract: Studies using routinely collected healthcare data are essential for understanding the benefit-risk profile of medications in pregnancy. However, reproducibility is limited by the lack of shared pregnancy identification algorithms, and generalizability is constrained by their development primarily in commercial insurance databases. A previously developed pregnancy identification algorithm was updated for ICD-10-CM and translated into a standardized format to support transport across diverse databases. Algorithm implementation characteristics were evaluated in three US health insurance claims databases (2000-2025), including commercially and publicly insured populations. Overall, 5.8 million and 3.0 million pregnancies were identified in two commercial databases (Merative™ and Optum) and 2.3 million pregnancies in Merative™ MarketScan® Multi-State Medicaid Database (MDCD). Across databases, live birth prevalence ranged from 76-83%, miscarriage/abortion 15-23%, ectopic pregnancy 1%, and stillbirth ≤0.5%, with a higher proportion of live births in MDCD. Pregnancy dating methods varied substantially across coding eras: use of gestational age records increased from 4-9% in the ICD-9-CM era to 87-92% during the ICD-10-CM era, with greater use in MDCD. Using a standardized algorithm, this study demonstrates how database characteristics and coding transitions influence pregnancy identification and dating in healthcare data, highlighting methodological considerations for reproducible pregnancy research across data sources.

title: A recipe for population-based doubly robust estimation via weighting, regression, calibration, and standardization
abstract: A large class of doubly robust estimators can be viewed as regression standardization augmented by a bias correction based on inverse probability of treatment weights. These estimators are often justified as solutions to augmented inverse probability weighted (AIPW) estimating equations. When regression standardization is based on a canonical-link generalized linear model fit via maximum likelihood estimation to an inverse probability of treatment weighted sample (IPTW-GLM), double robustness holds without any explicit bias correction. These estimators have usually targeted causal effects within a population represented by the study sample. Here, we present a unification and extension of these doubly robust estimators in terms of constructing a weighted pseudosample that represents a flexible target population with randomized exposures. This allows the bias correction to be understood and operationalized as calibrating the outcome model to match the group means within the balanced pseudosample, illuminating the connection between IPTW-GLM and other AIPW estimators. It also allows the straightforward construction of estimators that are doubly robust for target populations other than the study sample, which is useful when data come from studies where enrollment depends on exposure (e.g., observational cohort studies).

title: Compulsive Sexual Behaviour vs Problematic Pornography Use: Converging Evidence of Distinct Constructs from GGM, EGA and Bayesian Networks
abstract: For some people, intense and repetitive sexual urges/behaviours can cause distress and impair functioning across other life domains. Problematic Pornography Use (PPU) is often considered the most common manifestation of Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder (CSBD), yet their conceptual and diagnostic boundaries remain contested. This multi-method study examined whether CSBD and PPU reflect a shared syndrome or better represent distinct symptom structures. A community sample of adults from Australia and New Zealand (N = 632, Mage = 35.56, SD = 10.68, 58.5% women) completed the Compulsive Sexual Behaviour Disorder Scale (CSBD-19) and the Problematic Pornography Consumption Scale (PPCS). Complementary network and dimensional analyses were used to examine relationships and clustering among symptoms. Across analyses, CSBD and PPU demonstrated empirically separable networks, with minimal cross-construct connectivity. Dimensional analyses consistently identified symptom clusters composed exclusively of CSBD or PPCS items, even when accounting for gender or non-users of pornography. Symptom-level patterns suggested that reduced sexual satisfaction may represent a peripheral feature of CSBD, whereas mood modification and salience-related symptoms formed a stable cluster within PPU. These findings suggest that CSBD and PPU may represent related but distinct patterns of dysregulated sexual behaviour, and caution against treating PPU as a direct proxy for CSBD.

title: How Frequent is Sexual Exploitation Among Passengers of Ridehailing, Robotaxis, and Taxis? Prevalence, Relative Risk, and Comparison with Industry Disclosures
abstract: = .023). Despite differing prevalence, the most frequently reported behaviors within categories were similar across ridehailing and taxis. Among respondents using both modes during the past year, higher ridehailing-related prevalence persisted after adjustment for mode-specific frequency of use. Behaviorally specific surveys and publicly disclosed administrative case counts therefore provide complementary but non-equivalent information, and public disclosures may capture a narrower range of sexual exploitation than passengers report in surveys.

title: Burden of Disease Attributable to Violence in Childhood in the United Kingdom
abstract: Childhood exposure to violence is widespread in the UK and leads to significant long-term mental, behavioural, and physical health problems. While some violence types are recognised in the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) framework, many remain overlooked, and the complete burden in the UK had not been previously quantified. This study estimated the disease burden attributable to various forms of violence-including physical, emotional, and sexual abuse, neglect, domestic violence, bullying, and community violence-experienced before age 18. Using UK and Australian data, population attributable fractions (PAFs) were calculated for conditions like depression, anxiety, alcohol use disorder, smoking, and self-harm, and applied to 2021 GBD UK figures. Results showed that 7.9% of total Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs) were attributable to childhood violence, with men bearing a higher burden, particularly for smoking and self-harm, and women for depression and anxiety. These findings highlight the urgent need for stronger violence prevention and trauma-informed approaches in the UK.

title: Supernatural explanations and norm enforcement in nine societies
abstract: Historical and ethnographic evidence suggests that people around the world use supernatural beliefs to explain misfortune. The cross-cultural prevalence of this pattern may arise from our expectations that norm violations lead to sanctioning. In cases where an outcome seems punitive yet lacks an identifiable cause, individuals, motivated to fill this explanatory gap, may rely on beliefs in supernatural punishment to make sense of what has happened. If true, supernatural explanations for misfortunes should be more common when a victim is believed to have not cooperated in the past (i.e., in cases where misfortunes might be unexplained but otherwise appear deserved). Using a vignette experiment across nine diverse populations ( N = 714), including African hunter-gatherers and Melanesian horticulturalists, we tested if knowledge of past bad actions increased participants' endorsements of supernatural causes for misfortune. Across all populations, participants rated a misfortune as more likely to be supernaturally caused when the victim was known to have failed to reciprocate a favour or engage in generous actions towards others in the past. This was slightly increased when the behaviour was additionally labelled normative. Responses to open-ended free-listing questions provide additional evidence that when the victim was known to be uncooperative, participants were more likely to propose supernatural causes for misfortune as well as supernatural solutions. Additional normative labelling had only a small effect. Together, these findings suggest that when misfortunes lack clear causes, people's motivation to explain interacts with moral evaluations, leading them to invoke supernatural beliefs most commonly when misfortune appears deserved.

title: Framing Service-Learning Experiences: Evidence From a Survey Experiment Engaging Prosocial and Pre-Professional Identities
abstract: Universities are increasingly expected to integrate civic and social goals into their curricula, yet it remains unclear how to engage students whose motivations are primarily professional. Service-learning experiences (SLEs), which combine academic study with community service, are one strategy, but student self-selection complicates design and evaluation. Because SLEs help cultivate the voluntary sector’s future volunteers and donors, who gains access is a question for the sector, not only for educators. This study examines how prosocial and pre-professional identities shape students’ interest in SLEs and whether course framing influences engagement. In a preregistered survey experiment, students evaluated SLEs framed as descriptive, volunteer-focused, or career-focused. Altruistic values and pre-professional identity modestly but significantly predicted interest; volunteer identity did not. Course framing had no effect. These findings suggest civic and professional orientations may be more compatible than assumed, and engagement depends less on framing than on integration within broader curricular and developmental pathways.

title: Public policy and political trust within unequal societies: evidence from India
abstract: Deeply entrenched socioeconomic inequalities complicate public service delivery, especially for local governments in developing countries. In jurisdictions characterized by deep economic cleavages, it can be exceedingly difficult for local governments to fund and deliver public works that satisfy most citizens’ needs in a timely and efficient manner. However, one of the tragic consequences of extreme inequality is that it reduces people’s trust in their government. Here, we hypothesize that policy interventions that encourage the co-production of local public works, such as bottom-up, demand-driven rural development programs, help neutralize the negative effect of inequalities on trust in local governance institutions by improving perceptions of state responsiveness and building social capital. Using quasi-experimental methods, large-N panel data, and the case of the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) – the world’s largest rural employment guarantee initiative – our analysis finds support for these expectations.

title: Co-optimization of intraday and frequency containment reserve bids for battery energy storage
abstract: As renewable energy integration increases supply variability, battery energy storage systems (BESS) present a viable solution for balancing supply and demand. This paper proposes a joint bidding strategy that combines participation in the primary frequency reserve market with continuous trading in the intraday market, addressing a gap in the extant literature that typically considers these markets in isolation and simplifies the continuous nature of intraday trading. Our approach utilizes a mixed integer linear programming implementation of the rolling intrinsic algorithm for intraday decisions and state of charge recovery, alongside a learned classifier strategy (LCS) that determines optimal day-ahead capacity allocation between markets. A comprehensive out-of-sample backtest over more than one year of tick level historical German market data validates our approach: The LCS increases overall profits by over 4\% compared to the best-performing static strategy and by more than 3\% over a naive dynamic benchmark. Crucially, our method closes the gap to a theoretical perfect foresight strategy to just 4\%, demonstrating the effectiveness of dynamic, learning-based allocation in a complex, multi-market environment.

title: Data center cooling in the AI era: cross-scale challenges and system-level outlook
Capacity design in district energy systems with thermal energy storage – a new planning paradigm
abstract: Planning future district energy systems is increasingly challenged by uncertainties in demand growth and spatial development. Conventional planning resolves this by oversizing infrastructure to meet projected peak demand – tying up capital in assets used only a fraction of the year, with reactive upgrades still required where demand develops beyond projections. The result is a persistent trade-off between cost, emissions, and resiliency. This study proposes a new paradigm for capacity design that treats thermal energy storage (TES) – and particularly strategically placed decentralized TES (DecTES) – as an integrated design element that adds a degree of freedom to the capacity design problem. While centralized TES reduces peak production requirements, DecTES additionally resolves transmission bottlenecks by absorbing peak demand locally, adding a spatial dimension to system flexibility. The approach is demonstrated on district cooling and heating systems at Stanford, California, and Aalborg, Denmark. At Stanford, existing TES reduces OPEX by ~12% and CO₂ emissions by ~7% annually; doubling TES potentially adds ~2% OPEX and ~1.5% CO₂ savings, and DecTES enables 20-23% local demand growth without infrastructure expansion. In Aalborg, existing TES delivers ~10% OPEX savings and ~17% CO₂ reductions; DecTES enables 20-28% local demand growth at baseline and 54-62% under adaptive operation, potentially adds ~2.5% OPEX and ~5% CO₂ savings, and phases out decentralized fossil peak production. The analyses also indicate derived electricity-grid benefits, with connection capacity reducible by 24% and 39% respectively. Unlike conventional peak capacity, TES delivers year-round value from day one – reducing planning risk regardless of how demand unfolds.

title: Accelerating wind-farm AEP evaluation by exploiting near-low-rank wake structure

Arrow's shadow over climate governance
abstract: For thirty years, climate negotiations have failed to produce a stable and widely accepted rule for distributing mitigation burdens, even as finance, technology, and loss and damage have advanced. Political will, free-riding, and domestic constraints explain part of that, but not why the deadlock persists. This paper contends that the challenge is structural. It uses Arrow's voting paradox to diagnose the burden-sharing track of the climate negotiations and to draw the institutional consequences. Burden-sharing constitutes a preference-aggregation problem involving incompatible fairness principles. Arrow's impossibility theorem elucidates both the nature and direction of this difficulty: no procedure can transform divergent rankings of historical responsibility, capability, and equal per capita claims into a single, stable, and broadly accepted formula. Although the theorem does not establish formal impossibility within a treaty context or explain any specific negotiation breakdown, it highlights a constraint that neither improved analysis nor increased commitment has overcome.Because the constraint is structural and unsolvable, agreement proceeds by working around the aggregation problem. Issue linkage relaxes Arrow’s independence condition, while the Paris Agreement shifts aggregation from an ex ante distribution to self-differentiation, focal points, and an ex post stocktake of collective progress. Sen’s comparative justice helps explain why this works: parties need not agree on a fair allocation to agree that some outcomes are worse than others. The deeper threat to cooperation is therefore not disagreement over shares within the shared frame, but rejection of the frame itself.

title: Who owns the land after regime collapse? Shifting land claims and tenure governance in post-2021 Afghanistan
abstract: In Afghanistan, land ownership has long shifted with political power. Successive regime changes have reshaped who is recognised as an owner, who can occupy property, and how territorial resources are redistributed. The Taliban’s return in 2021 did not produce formal land reform, but it reopened a familiar pattern in which political transition unsettles property relations and enables new forms of control. Drawing on qualitative interviews with Afghan landowners now living in exile, this article examines how ownership moves between informal occupation and formal recognition. Houses, plots, and commercial spaces often remain legally tied to former owners while authority is renegotiated on the ground. In some cases, occupation becomes institutionalised through administrative approval, new documentation, or policy measures that regularise access for politically aligned actors. Property change therefore unfolds less as a single act of confiscation than as a layered process through which possession, mediation, and emerging governance practices redefine ownership. The analysis shows how struggles over land operate as a mechanism for reassembling political order. Ownership becomes increasingly difficult to exercise across distance, producing conditions in which property may persist on paper or be reassigned through governmental decree, while recognition and effective control shift in practice. By foregrounding absent owners and unsettled claims, the article contributes to land use policy debates on restitution, return, and post-conflict land administration, with implications for other fragile political environments.

title: From urban greenbelt to peri-urban ecological zone: A counterfactual evaluation of nature-based solutions under the Park City strategy
