Electric vehicle–integrated sustainable community microgrids: A review of control strategies, challenges, opportunities and pathways toward SDG 7
abstract: The demand for electricity continues to increase with economic growth and increasing end-use electrification, particularly in the transport sector. Despite ongoing progress, achieving Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7 by 2030, which aims to provide affordable and clean energy for all, remains uneven and structurally constrained. Electric vehicle (EV)-integrated community microgrids (MGs), operating in grid-connected or islanded modes are a promising solution that combines distributed energy resources, local electricity generation options and mobile energy storage systems (ESSs) through EV fleets. However, the high penetration of renewable energy resources, EVs and battery ESSs introduces significant challenges to system stability, power flow and operational reliability. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of recent developments in EV-integrated community MGs, energy management, decentralized EV fleet coordination and bidirectional EV charging/discharging into the electricity network. It also provides a framework for integrating MGs, EVs, and renewables, including grid-to-vehicle (G2V) charging, bidirectional vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and vehicle-to-everything (V2X) applications, to enhance grid flexibility and ancillary services. It further discusses the optimization mechanisms, control frameworks and their applications within the MG environment. In addition, the review evaluates the contribution of EV-integrated community MGs toward achieving SDG 7 in sustainable community energy systems. The analysis also addresses existing technical, economic, social acceptance and regulatory challenges that hinder large-scale deployments. The study outlines future research directions and proposes a conceptual framework for researchers and policymakers, offering actionable pathways to accelerate the global clean energy transition and support the achievement of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

title: Nanoconfinement Drives Non-Monotonic Methane Density in Shale Nanopores: Direct Observation of Competitive Water–Gas Exchange
abstract: Abstract The efficiency of unconventional gas recovery is fundamentally governed by the nanoscale partitioning and competitive exchange between methane and water in shale reservoirs, yet direct experimental insight into their coupled behavior under in situ conditions (pressure and temperature) remains elusive. Here, we integrate a first-of-its-kind approach, combining contrast-matching ultra- and small-angle neutron scattering (USANS/SANS) at 50 MPa with vapor sorption, cryo-microscopy, and molecular simulations, to achieve unprecedented direct visualization of methane–water distribution across the multiscale pore–fracture network of the Longmaxi Shale. We report a fundamental revision to classical models, discovering that methane density exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on pore size, increasing with nanoconfinement but peaking sharply at ≈2 nm before declining in sub-2 nm pores. Mechanistically, water forms continuous films on hydrophilic quartz surfaces but aggregates into distinct clusters on organic kerogen. The stronger affinity of water for quartz and its increasing interaction with kerogen at higher saturations enable it to displace adsorbed methane competitively, thereby directly controlling local gas saturation. Furthermore, we reveal that microfractures are the dominant pathways for early water flowback and subsequent gas migration, with pore–fracture connectivity dictating fluid accessibility and phase exchange efficiency. These results establish a mechanistic link between interfacial nanophysics and macro-scale reservoir performance, providing a scientific foundation for optimizing hydraulic fracturing and maximizing resource recovery in deep sedimentary systems.

title: Slippery Amphiphilic Antifouling Loose Nanofiltration Membrane with “Double-Defense” Functionalities for High-Salinity Organic Wastewater Sustainable Management
abstract: Abstract Loose nanofiltration (LNF) holds potential for sustainable management of high-salinity organic wastewater through precise organics/salts fractionation, but practical application is constrained by severe organic–inorganic combined fouling. Herein, we propose a “double-defense” antifouling strategy and develop a slippery amphiphilic LNF membrane via facile stepwise surface modification. A hydrophilic branched polyethylenimine (PEI) network was first cross-linked onto a polyamide (PA) substrate to form a fouling-resistant protection layer, followed by covalent grafting of liquid-like polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) brushes to confer a slippery, fouling-release surface. The PEI layer acts as a hydration and electrostatic barrier to repel organic-cation complexes and scale precursors, while the slippery PDMS layer with high mobility and low surface energy minimizes interfacial interactions and strengthens hydraulic shear responsiveness. During the concentration of authentic leachate membrane bioreactor (MBR) effluent, the optimized membrane showed superior antifouling performance: low flux decline ratio (FDR) of 41.6% and high flux recovery ratio (FRR) of 98.1%, outperforming a commercial PA membrane (FDR 91.2%, FRR 78.4%). It also delivered an organics/salts fractionation selectivity 7.8 times that of the commercial membrane, demonstrating multiple cycles stability. This rationally designed architecture offers a practical solution for challenging wastewater and is extensible to other PA-based membrane systems in environmental applications.

title: From Nontargeted Analysis to Toxicity: Revealing the Disinfection Byproduct Exposome
abstract: Abstract Chemical disinfection is essential for ensuring the microbiological safety of drinking water, but it inevitably generates disinfection byproducts (DBPs), introducing a complex and largely unresolved chemical burden. Trihalomethanes (THMs) and haloacetic acids (HAAs) have long underpinned DBP regulation, shaping monitoring and treatment strategies. However, recent analytical advances have fundamentally reshaped our understanding of DBPs. In this perspective, we examine how high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS)-based nontargeted analysis (NTA) has expanded the detectable DBP chemical space, while revealing key limitations that hinder translation from detection to identification. We then highlight emerging mass spectrometry and computational approaches as key pathways toward scalable DBP discovery and identification. We further examine the disconnect between rapid DBP discovery and limited toxicological understanding, highlighting key limitations of current toxicity assessments, including high-dose testing paradigms, fragmented end points, and overlooked mixture effects. To address these challenges, we propose an exposome-oriented framework as a conceptual model that integrates comprehensive chemical characterization with toxicity assessment, highlighting the need for future computational tools and prioritization strategies. Bridging chemical diversity to health relevance will be critical for prioritizing DBPs of concern and supporting risk-informed water quality management and public health protection.

title: Investigations of New Particle Formation Mechanisms in North China Plain during the Spring Campaign Based on Observations and Simulations
abstract: Abstract New particle formation (NPF) plays a critical role in atmospheric aerosol loading, yet the mechanisms controlling NPF under high-pollution conditions remain poorly understood. Ground-based measurements and GEOS-Chem-APM simulations were combined to investigate the factors governing NPF in a typical industrial city over North China Plain. During the spring campaign (3 May-2 June 2016), 10 NPF days were identified, each preceded by nighttime northwesterly ventilation and occurring under dry daytime conditions. The model reproduced 6 of 10 observed NPF events, whereas the remaining 4 showed substantially weaker simulated nucleation. Well-simulated events were generally associated with low relative humidity (RH) and condensation sink (CS) environment. NH3 remained in large excess throughout the campaign. In our test, increasing H2SO4 by up to a factor of 3 substantially enhanced nucleation rate (J) but did not fully reproduce the observed particle evolution, while replacing modeled RH and aerosol surface area with observations only moderately adjusted J. The model underestimated growth rates by 51% and 75% on well-simulated and poorly simulated days. These results indicate that nighttime ventilation reduces surface area and CS of pre-existing aerosol loading, favoring NPF, while successful reproduction of observed NPF depends jointly on diverse precursor-driven nucleation, aerosol scavenging, and subsequent particle growth.

title: Cross-Level Responses of Freshwater Zooplankton to Micro/Nanoplastics: A Meta-Analysis Integrating Individual- to Community-Level Evidence
abstract: Abstract Despite the known threats of micro/nanoplastics (MNPs) to freshwater ecosystems, their risks to zooplankton remain poorly resolved because existing evidence is fragmented across biological levels. Consequently, associations between lower-level responses and population- and community-level outcomes remain unclear. Here, we synthesized 3042 research cases from controlled experiments worldwide covering 12 response categories. We found significant overall negative effects of MNPs in systems without predators, with predators, and with predator-conditioned medium. Although molecular-level evidence remains limited, a consistent hierarchical response pattern emerged under predator-absent conditions. We therefore propose a conceptual hierarchical effect pathway (HEP) framework integrating effect sizes and cross-level associations. Within this framework, MNPs exposure was associated with increased ingestion of MNPs, physiological damage, feeding impairment, and reduced activity and defense. These responses formed an upstream tier associated with life-history impairments, including impaired growth and development, reduced reproductive capacity, and reduced survival, although these associations do not establish temporal ordering or causation. Under predator-present conditions, negative population- and community-level effects were also observed. Effect magnitudes also varied with MNPs characteristics, exposure duration, and zooplankton group. Together, the HEP framework clarifies cross-level associations and helps identify informative endpoints and incorporate food-web context into risk assessment of MNPs.

title: Global Potential of No-Tillage in Enhancing Soil Carbon and Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions While Sustaining Crop Yields
abstract: Abstract Pursuing the balance between environmental sustainability and agricultural productivity remains a critical challenge for achieving global sustainable development goals. No-tillage (NT), as a key measure of sustainable conservation and climate-smart agriculture, offers a promising approach to addressing this challenge. However, its comprehensive effects on soil carbon accumulation, greenhouse gas emissions, and crop yields remain unquantified at the global scale, limiting our ability to optimize both environmental and agronomic outcomes. Here, we conducted such a global synthesis by combining a meta-analysis of 8,303 paired observations from 1,371 studies with a random forest model to assess the influence of site conditions and management on NT effects. Our meta-analysis demonstrates integrated benefits of NT in enhancing soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks in 0–30 cm layer by 11.0% and mitigating greenhouse gas (the sum of CO2, CH4, and N2O in CO2-equivalent) emissions by 13.5%, without a significant impact on crop yields (−0.6% ± 1.5%). The integrated benefits are stronger in drier climates and coarser-textured soils, and they exhibit significant time-dependent patterns. Our prediction identifies 44% of global croplands as being optimal for NT’s integrated benefits, mainly in Africa, South Asia, and North America. Adopting NT in these areas would result in a 4.8% increase in major food-crop yields, a 15.2% increase in 0–30 cm SOC stocks, and a 6.4% reduction in global cropland emissions, respectively. These findings underscore the relevance of implementing NT in suitable regions by adopting it into Good Agricultural Practice Guidelines.

title: Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers (PRTRs) as a Cornerstone of Global Chemicals Management: Current Gaps and Future Directions
abstract: Abstract Pollutant Release and Transfer Register (PRTR) systems in different countries are key tools for global chemicals management and an important data source for measuring progress toward achieving Sustainable Development Goal 12 of sustainable consumption and production patterns. However, current implementations face several structural and functional limitations that hinder the broad applicability of the PRTR reporting data. These limitations can be categorized into two main aspects: within-system issues and between-system inconsistencies. Within systems, data gaps can result from limited monitoring of nonpoint sources, incomplete reporting, exemptions due to thresholds and confidentiality agreements, and other similar factors, while data inaccuracies can be caused by estimation errors, duplicated counts, and other related issues. Between systems, differences in chemical lists, threshold settings, emission source types, reporting methods, and other discrepancies can hinder data comparability and integration, limiting the effectiveness of global chemicals management. Addressing these issues, through unified pollutant lists, harmonized reporting methodologies, expanded source coverage, and improved data verification, can significantly strengthen the utility of PRTR systems, advancing an integrated and evidence-based global sound management of chemicals.

title: Direct Upcycling of Rare Earth Hyperaccumulator Biomass into Luminescent CaS:Ce Phosphors
abstract: Abstract Rare earth elements (REEs) are essential to high-tech industries and sustainable development, but traditional mining poses significant environmental challenges. Phytomining, which uses hyperaccumulators to recover REEs from soils or low-grade mines, has emerged as a sustainable alternative; however, the high cost and low efficiency of extracting and purifying REEs from harvested biomass remain major barriers to its practical application. Here, we propose a novel in situ doping strategy to directly convert cerium (Ce)-enriched hyperaccumulator biomass into color-tunable CaS:Ce phosphors and value-added syngas, bypassing complex separation of Ca and REEs. The results show that Ce, Ca, and S could be selectively enriched from hyperaccumulator biomass to the resulting char through solvothermal pretreatment with sulfuric acid and ethanol. Subsequent steam gasification of the char produces Ce-doped CaS phosphors with broad, green-yellow emission and high photoluminescence quantum yields of 18.5–37.4%. Our approach reduces energy use by 33.6%, carbon emissions by 22.4%, and costs by \$2.62 kg–1 biomass, outperforming conventional REE recovery in both environmental and economic sustainability. This strategy provides an environmentally sustainable and economically viable route for high-value utilization of REE-rich biomass, addressing a critical bottleneck in phytomining and advancing its development as a green REE recovery technology.

title: Fe(II) Speciation Regulates Microbial Metabolic Reprogramming and Phototrophic Fe(II) Mineralization in Rhodopseudomonas palustris SX2
abstract: Abstract Phototrophic iron mineralization (PIM) is a keystone biogeochemical process linking anoxic iron redox transformations to carbon sequestration. Although PIM is widely documented, how Fe(II) speciation impacts cell physiology and thus causes divergent mineralization phenotypes remains poorly understood. In this study, we systematically investigated the physiological, mineralogical, and molecular responses of a newly isolated photoferrotroph, Rhodopseudomonas palustris SX2, exposed to uncomplexed Fe(II) [Fe(II) without OM] versus organically complexed Fe(II) [Fe(II)-OM] under anoxic and illuminated conditions. We demonstrate that distinct Fe(II) speciation drives divergent metabolic reprogramming for rapid metabolic adaptation and phototrophic biomineralization phenotypes. Fe(II) without OM triggered cell-surface encrustation and activated stress-mitigation and metal-efflux systems, whereas Fe(II)-OM stimulated the formation of discrete intracellular iron nanoparticles while upregulating photosynthetic light harvesting and autotrophic CO2 fixation. Furthermore, genetic knockout and complementation confirmed that the pioABC operon constitutes the indispensable electron conduit driving Fe(II) oxidation across both speciation regimes, with organic complexation significantly enhancing its transcriptional activation. Our findings reveal how metabolic adaptation driven by Fe(II) speciation dictates the spatial distribution of biogenic iron minerals and regulates the efficiency of coupled carbon sequestration in anoxic ecosystems.

title: Wastewater Treatment Plants as Anchor Infrastructure for Geothermal Energy in Cold Regions
abstract: Abstract Thermal constraints in cold regions suppress biological treatment, increase energy demand, and elevate greenhouse gas emissions of existing wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), and remain a major barrier to the deployment of adequate sanitation infrastructure in many cold-region communities. Where geothermal resources exist, low-enthalpy hydrothermal heat is well matched to this energy gap. Yet, WWTPs are underrecognized anchors for broader geothermal deployment, providing a continuous, weather-independent thermal offtake through which subsurface CAPEX can be amortized. We reframe geothermal-WWTP integration as a system-level enabler that benefits both parts. Using three cascaded configurations for a full-scale WWTP, a rapid techno-economic analysis identifies three trends: energy and carbon savings/revenues alone are insufficient under realistic policy stacks, whereas crediting the upgrade-deferral value of geothermally enhanced treatment makes the project economically favorable across most policy scenarios. Globally, this triple intersection encompasses ∼11,600 catalogued WWTPs serving ∼280 million people, with a further estimate of ∼48 million people in the same regions beyond current service radii. The opportunity is greatest in cold, remote, and underserved communities, where local geothermal resources, treatment intensification, and community-scale demand together carry a case that no single driver could sustain alone.

title: Multi-Omics Gut Microbiome Species Communities and Functional Modules Linking Metal Exposures to Children’s Neurodevelopmental Health in a Canadian Birth Cohort
abstract: Abstract Early life metal exposure has been associated with adverse neurodevelopment, with gut microbiome disruption proposed as a potential pathway. However, most studies have focused on individual taxa or pathways, despite microbes functioning within ecological communities and coordinated functional networks. Here, we integrated stool metal measurements, shotgun metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, and neurodevelopmental assessments in 116 children aged 8–12 years from the GESTE birth cohort in Sherbrooke, Canada. Nineteen metals were quantified in stool samples, and neurodevelopment was assessed using parent-reported behavioral scales, attention performance testing, and resting-state fMRI. Using network-based community detection, we identified 10 co-occurring species communities (SCs) from metagenomic data and 16 coexpressed functional modules (FMs) from metatranscriptomic data and evaluated their associations with metal exposures and neurodevelopmental outcomes. Higher levels of lead, cadmium, aluminum, zinc, copper, and magnesium were associated with lower abundance of Streptococcus- and Veillonella-dominated SCs, while multiple metals were associated with lower abundance of amino acid metabolism and carbohydrate degradation FMs. Exploratory mediation analyses suggested potential indirect associations between stool metals and parent-reported ADHD-related traits througha methionine cycle-related FM or sequentially through a Clostridium spp. SC and a Factor 420 biosynthesis FM. These findings suggest that stool metal concentrations are associated with community-level variations in gut microbial composition and function, some of which were further associated with parent-reported ADHD-related traits.

Energy and carbon routing in hydrothermal conversion of lignocellulosic biomass: An uncertainty-aware machine-learning framework
abstract: Reliable assessment of hydrothermal lignocellulosic biomass conversion requires quantitative prediction of how feedstock mass, chemical energy, and carbon partition among bio-oil, solid residues, aqueous products, and gases under heterogeneous feedstock, solvent, catalyst, and severity conditions. We constructed a harmonized database of 3,693 HTL/HTC experiments from 187 scientific papers and 433 different biomass samples, with temperatures up to ∼ 600 ◦C and maximum residence times of up to 1,200 min. From this literature-scale dataset, we developed an uncertainty-aware machine-learning framework for predicting mass partitioning, energy and carbon allocation, and higher heating value (HHV) of condensed phases. Among the tree-ensemble regression methods examined, Random Forest (RF) provided the most stable cross-target compromise, with test R2 values for product yields around 0.8, energy/carbon allocation metrics between 0.8 and 0.9, and bio-oil HHV around 0.7 with root-mean-squared error ∼ 2–3 MJkg−1. The model recovers established severity, solvent, and composition trends while identifying regions where predictions are well supported or weakly constrained. SHAP attributions are interpreted as model-conditional associations: liquid-phase outcomes depend strongly on solvent and operating conditions, whereas solid-phase HHVs are more associated with feedstock carbon and ash content. Ensemble and conformal uncertainty methods distinguish relative epistemic uncertainty from calibrated scenario bounds. The framework is intended for uncertainty-aware process screening, scenario bounding, and experimental prioritization rather than unqualified point optimization in poorly represented regimes.

Who gets to govern local food? Knowledge, power, and participation in a post-socialist urban food system
abstract: Urban areas face intersecting challenges related to environmental sustainability, food security, and climate resilience, raising questions about who has the authority to define food-related problems and translate them into urban policy action. This study examines a community-led participatory governance process in Kraków (Poland) and explores how multi-stakeholder dialogue makes local food governable through unequal forms of knowledge, authority, and institutional positioning. Drawing on three structured workshops (February-May 2025) involving farmers, market organizers, municipal officers, public institutions, NGOs, and researchers, we ask: (1) What themes and priorities emerge from multi-stakeholder discussions on local food markets and urban environmental governance? and (2) How do stakeholder groups’ institutional positions, resource dependencies, and claims to legitimate knowledge shape the priorities they articulate and the governance options they treat as feasible? Using Framework Analysis, we identify six thematic frames – market infrastructure, institutional governance, consumer awareness, economic viability, promotion, and quality assurance/certification – and analyse how their salience differs across stakeholder groups according to actors’ institutional mandates, resource dependencies, exposure to risks, and claims to legitimate knowledge. The findings show that participatory food governance does not simply aggregate diverse priorities. It reveals how actors differently positioned within the food system seek to make their risks, responsibilities, and knowledge claims visible, while uneven authority shapes which problems appear actionable, which forms of expertise are recognised, and which governance options remain marginal or invisible. The Kraków case contributes to urban food governance debates by showing how general dynamics of participatory governance under capitalism intersect with post-socialist conditions of fragmented mandates, uneven trust in collective organisation, and weakly institutionalised food policy.

title: Community‐Managed Systems as Nature‐Based Solutions: Effects of Elevation and Size on Floral Richness and Carbon Stock of Sacred Groves in Kerala, India
abstract: ABSTRACT Limiting global warming to 1.5°C–2°C requires rapid reductions in atmospheric carbon, highlighting the need to conserve ecosystems with high carbon stock potential. Sacred groves are culturally protected forest fragments maintained through traditional practices and represent community‐managed landscapes with significant potential as nature‐based solutions. This study evaluated the influence of elevation and grove size on plant species richness, carbon stock and soil properties in 55 sacred groves (31 lowland, 19 midland and 5 highland; ranging from 0.025 to 20.2 ha and from 3 to 906 m above mean sea level) across different physiographic regions of Kerala, India. Aboveground biomass carbon was estimated using allometric equations, and soil organic carbon was quantified by wet digestion; these components were combined to estimate total carbon stock. Species richness, carbon stock and soil properties were analysed across elevation and grove‐size categories using one‐way ANOVA, Kruskal–Wallis tests and multiple linear regression. Total carbon stock ranged from 30.46 to 318 Mg ha −1 (mean 113 Mg ha −1 ) but showed no significant relationship with elevation or grove size. In contrast, plant species richness (5–177 species) varied significantly across both factors (elevation: p = 0.005, grove size: p < 0.001). Sacred groves in the midland region supported the highest mean species richness (70 species) among elevation classes, compared with 56 in highland and 37 in lowland groves, while larger groves harboured more species (71) than medium (67) and small (30) groves. Multiple regression identified soil nitrogen as the strongest predictor of species richness (adjusted R 2 = 0.19), with grove area showing a consistent positive but marginal effect, whereas total carbon stock was best explained by exchangeable potassium (adjusted R 2 = 0.13). Soil properties, particularly exchangeable potassium (highest in midland groves, 0.004%) and bulk density (highest in highland groves, 1.76 g cm −3 ), exhibited distinct physiographic patterns. The results demonstrate that sacred groves consistently store substantial carbon irrespective of size or elevation, whereas biodiversity conservation is strongly influenced by grove extent and elevation. These findings underscore the role of sacred groves as effective nature‐based solutions, where traditional stewardship supports both biodiversity conservation and climate change mitigation in human‐dominated landscapes. Integrating systematic management and ecological restoration practices into existing conservation frameworks, with active community participation, is recommended.

title: Quantifying uncertainty in deep learning models for urban safety perception: An MC Dropout approach
abstract: Deep learning models have revolutionized the automated analysis of urban perception. However, these models typically provide point predictions without associated uncertainty estimates, limiting their application in critical urban planning and policy decisions. This research explores the implementation of Monte Carlo Dropout (MC Dropout) as a method for quantifying uncertainty in deep learning models for urban safety perception. Using ResNet-based convolutional neural networks, we evaluated this approach on both global urban datasets (PlacePulse 2.0) and a specific case study of Santiago, Chile, focusing specifically on the safety dimension of urban perception. Our findings reveal that MC Dropout yields per-image uncertainty estimates without requiring significant architectural modifications, alongside a modest improvement in predictive accuracy (from 66.81% to 67.64%). We show that these estimates vary systematically with urban characteristics, with distinct patterns observed between different urban districts, and that the MC Dropout spread is systematically narrower than the discrepancy between the stochastic and deterministic predictions. We are explicit about what the study does not establish: none of our analyses tests the uncertainty estimates against predictive error, so we do not claim that they are calibrated or that they rank predictions by reliability, and we specify in detail the risk–coverage protocol and pairwise proper scoring rule that such a validation would require. The potential implications for urban analytics—triage of cases for human verification, mapping the spatial distribution of predictive dispersion within cities, and improved interpretability of model decision-making—are presented as prospective applications conditional on that validation. The methodological framework established here can be adopted and extended for future studies and practical applications in urban environments.

title: The Economic Sustainability of Intangible Cultural Heritage in the Platform Age With Global Evidence and Implications for Xinjiang
abstract: ABSTRACT Digital platforms lower market access costs for intangible cultural heritage but can concentrate visibility, weaken community control, and disconnect revenue from cultural reproduction. This global survey integrates platform and cultural economics with research on authenticity, intellectual property, and heritage governance. Its Platform Frictions, Cultural Rents, and Intergenerational Reproduction framework distinguishes living practices from their commercial products, recordings, and experiences. Economic sustainability requires four minimum conditions that cannot substitute for one another. These comprise adequate net market access, viable cultural reproduction, a sufficient practitioner value share, and meaningful community control. The framework distinguishes these conditions from the mechanisms through which platforms affect them. Rankings, provenance labels, copyright, and certification can improve discovery and bargaining while concentrating demand, excluding legitimate variants, or burdening small producers. Community authorization requires representation, reviewable delegation, and effective appeal. Distributional assessment separates individual earnings, collective transfers, unpaid contributions, and investment in transmission. Applications to Xinjiang differentiate crafts, performances, foodways, and community events by economic object and institutional responsibility. Longitudinal indicators of apprentice retention, repertoire in use, and contextual participation distinguish authorized adaptation from commercial hollowing. Platform growth sustains living heritage when returns support practitioners, learning, and community authority.

title: Exchange Rates and International Tourism Demand with Endogenous Prices and Capacity Constraints
abstract: ABSTRACT Why does destination depreciation sometimes expand tourism and sometimes leave demand almost unchanged? We develop a two‐destination equilibrium model with endogenous supplier prices, imported‐cost exposure, currency risk, and capacity constraints. Five propositions separate price transmission, destination reallocation, additional trips, and welfare. Depreciation expands demand only when its conversion benefit exceeds the associated increase in supplier costs. A binding capacity constraint absorbs further cost relief into scarcity rents and creates unequal quantity responses to favorable and adverse shocks. Destination gains can arise entirely from reallocation when total international travel is fixed. Risk protection raises demand only when its certainty‐equivalent benefit exceeds its price. These analytical results organize a critical synthesis of tourism‐demand evidence. A documented literature verification and a paired comparison of Mauritian studies distinguish measurement differences from changes in samples and estimators. Booking‐horizon alignment remains a theoretical implication requiring direct testing. The analysis identifies the observations needed to distinguish the mechanisms behind conflicting exchange‐rate estimates.

title: Natural Capital Measurement and Applications in Economic and Financial Analysis1
abstract: ABSTRACT Natural capital refers to environmental assets that produce economic goods or services used in production or consumption. Today, the concepts of natural capital and the associated ecosystem service flows are being applied beyond their traditional applications in cost‐benefit analysis to a range of topic areas in economics and finance. These broader applications include assessment of physical risks to real estate, insurance, and supply chains, and advancements in modelling economic growth, productivity, and financial risk. These developments have the potential to shift perspectives on economic measurement to include more comprehensive concepts of output and consumption, increase the accuracy of measured productivity and risks, and add precision to our understanding of tradeoffs in resource allocation. We provide an overview of the economic theory underlying natural capital valuation and recent initiatives in natural capital measurement and discuss how new data sources, modeling advances, and frameworks are broadening the application of natural capital concepts and metrics. We include open questions integrated throughout to inform or prompt future scholarly research, model development, and economic measurement.

title: Fisher Dynamics, Monetary Policy, and Household Indebtedness
abstract: Abstract Growth in household debt‐to‐income ratios reflects nominal debt changes or “Fisher dynamics” due to interest income and expenses, real income growth, and inflation. Using two decades of microdata on all Norwegian households, we decompose these channels' roles in how debt‐to‐income evolves over time and in response to monetary policy shocks. On average, debt changes outsize Fisher dynamics, except among highly leveraged households. After interest rate hikes, the channels pull in opposite directions, but the debt changes dominate, so debt‐to‐income ratios decline. This holds across subgroups, including highly indebted households, recent movers, and those facing liquidity constraints or high unemployment risk.

title: Water‐Conscious Governance: The Role of Co‐Opted Members in Water Withdrawal
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the impact of co‐opted board directors on water withdrawal. Based on a U.S. sample of 4194 firm‐year observations between 2008 and 2022, we find that the presence, independence and tenure of co‐opted directors reduce firm water withdrawals. Co‐opted directors can play a constructive role in improving corporate water management by aligning with the CEO environmental initiatives, responding to legitimacy pressures, and supporting strategies that balance profit with stakeholder concerns. Additional analyses reveal that this relationship is stronger when the CEO and board chair roles are separated and in firms with strong corporate governance and environmental performance, as well as in firms that link executive compensation to CSR performance. Also, we show that the effect is prevalent in firms with CSR and nomination committees. Our findings offer new insights for regulators and managers seeking to address water management issues and encourage firms to improve their board structure by increasing board co‐option to better align board decisions with CEO water management policies.

title: Sustainable Innovation Management: From Knowledge Creation to Resource Efficiency
abstract: ABSTRACT This study aims to uncover the internal organizational mechanisms driving sustainable innovation and to develop a unified conceptual framework. To address the theoretical fragmentation in current research, a systematic review of 128 recent empirical articles was conducted, combining conceptual mapping of keyword co‐occurrences with qualitative thematic synthesis. The findings reveal a sequential organizational architecture comprising four interdependent pillars: cognitive foundations, strategic orchestration (driven by dynamic capabilities and strategic agility), technological amplification, and sustainable materialization, all supported by a transversal human and relational substrate. Based on these insights, the study proposes the capability‐based sustainable innovation (CBSI) framework. By integrating the resource‐based view, the knowledge‐based view, and the dynamic capabilities framework, the model explicates the operational sequence required to execute the twin transformation and achieve verifiable circular economy and environmental performance. The framework provides a structured agenda for future research and offers managers a practical blueprint for appropriately aligning human capital with digital investments.

title: Does the Facial Trustworthiness of Hosting Staff Lead to Forecast Bias? Evidence from Analysts’ Site Visits
abstract: We use unique data about corporate site visits in China to examine whether face‐to‐face interactions introduce bias in analyst forecasts. We find that analysts tend to issue more optimistic forecasts when accompanied by hosting staff with high facial trustworthiness, indicating a cognitive bias. This effect is amplified when firms convey more positive information during visits, but is attenuated for firms with high disclosure quality, for experienced and star analysts, for analysts with science, technology, engineering, and mathematics backgrounds, and for analysts visiting industry peers concurrently. Furthermore, the bias is stronger for sole‐visiting analysts but diminishes over time as additional information becomes available or with repeated interactions. Additional analyses show that forecast accuracy also declines, but the effect of facial trustworthiness does not extend to analysts’ stock recommendations or market reactions. Overall, our findings highlight that even sophisticated analysts are susceptible to cognitive bias in face‐to‐face interactions, while alternative information sources, professional experience, and repeated engagement help mitigate such bias.

title: Regional Service Trade Agreements and Manufacturing Global Value Chains: Evidence from 60 Economies
abstract: This study uses the data of 60 countries (regions) from 2000 to 2018 to test the impact of regional service trade agreements on the participation of a country (region) in the global value chain of manufacturing. (1) Overall, signing regional service trade agreements can promote the forward participation of a country’s (regional) value chain, and enhance the division of labour status of a country’s (regional) manufacturing GVCs. (2) After a series of robustness tests, the results remain consistent with the benchmark results. The impact of signing regional service trade agreements on the participation of a country’s (regional) manufacturing GVCs division of labour varies due to the heterogeneity of the country (region), income level and multilateral resistance. (3) The signing of regional service trade agreements between countries (regions) enhances the participation of a country (region) in the GVCs division of manufacturing industry. (4) Trade network status and dynamic evolution process.

title: “Planning” Or Decentralization? Strategic Choices for Business Groups Under Economic Policy Uncertainty
abstract: This paper investigates the impact of EPU on the allocation of decision rights among business groups. We find that when EPU increases, business groups encourage decentralization in order to leverage information from lower-level managers. Furthermore, when the top managers of business groups have an information advantage, the negative relationship between EPU and business group centralization is less pronounced. Moreover, group decentralization promotes corporate innovation and technology acquisition propensity when EPU increases, which enhances firm value. Overall, the findings of this study empirically support traditional decentralization theory while also establishing a trade-off relationship between top managers' and decentralized information advantage.

title: Sovereign Risk Mitigation Mechanism in Emerging Markets
abstract: This paper explores a mechanism for mitigating sovereign risk in emerging markets without risks mutualization. The mechanism involves pooling diversified portfolios of sovereign bonds and issuing them in tranches, with the senior tranche offering low-risk payoffs protected by the subordination of the junior tranches. We argue that this mechanism is feasible for emerging markets. The senior bonds issued by the securitization vehicle attain the properties of a safe asset. The risk level of the junior bonds depends on the structure of the underlying sovereign bonds portfolio. Nevertheless, the properties of the synthetic bonds are, arguably, acceptable for the practical application of the proposed mechanism in promoting the development of financial markets in emerging markets and for practical tasks such as intergovernmental aid or lending.

title: Trade Tariffs and Corporate Greenwashing: Evidence from Chinese A-Share Listed Firms
abstract: Using data on Chinese A-share firms from 2009 to 2023, we examine how import tariff exposure is related to corporate greenwashing. We combine tariff and customs data with annual reports and environmental penalty records. Greenwashing is measured by the gap between environmental disclosure and penalties relative to peers. Random-effects logit estimates show that lower tariff exposure is associated with a higher likelihood of this gap. This relationship varies with media attention, managerial incentives, and fund occupation. The findings do not prove that firms intend to mislead or that tariffs improve the environment.

Scaling up to the cloud: Cloud technology use and growth rates in small and large firms
abstract: Using a unique combination of micro-level data sources on French firms, this paper explores the relationship between cloud technologies and firm growth. Whereas digital technologies have generally been found to disproportionately benefit larger firms, we document that cloud use is positively associated with firm growth, and this association is significantly stronger for smaller firms. Distinguishing cloud services between Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS), we find that the size-contingent association is driven entirely by SaaS. Crucially, this small firm advantage is conditional on complementary assets as it emerges only among firms endowed with ICT capabilities. Our results are robust across a range of specifications, including instrumental variable strategies. SaaS cloud use is further associated with internal workforce reorganisation toward ICT, managerial, and intermediate occupations and away from manual and clerical ones, particularly among smaller firms, consistent with SaaS cloud operating as an organisational innovation enabling digitalisation and scaling. Finally, we present descriptive sectoral evidence of a negative correlation between cloud and market concentration.

title: When the music changes, so must your dance: Technology-forcing regulation and the shifting geography of automotive invention
Who Goes Toxic? Understanding Political Toxicity on Social Media Across Individuals and Contexts
abstract: As political toxicity has become widespread on social media, scholars have sought to understand what drives it. While studies often emphasize platform-level explanations, such as algorithmic amplification, they offer limited insight into which users are more likely to produce toxic content. Even less is known about how the relationship between individual-level factors and toxicity varies across political contexts. Using data from 184,354 randomly sampled U.S. Twitter (now X) users, their original tweets (25M), and the accounts they follow, we link users’ inferred characteristics and political context to their real-life toxic behavior. Results show that Republican, male, and older users are consistently more likely to post both impolite and intolerant content, whereas education shows no clear association. We also find that state-level electoral competitiveness increases overall toxicity and, in some cases, conditions individual-level relationships. The age gap in impolite behavior significantly narrows in more competitive states, while the corresponding moderation for intolerance is only marginally significant. There is also some indication that partisan differences in impoliteness become larger in more competitive states, but this moderation is only marginally significant. Together, these results demonstrate that political toxicity is shaped jointly by users’ individual characteristics and the political contexts in which they operate.

Genetic Background and Metabolic Influence on Long-Term Lithium Bioaccumulation in Mytilus Mussels and Their Hybrids
abstract: Abstract Marine mussels are widely used as sentinel organisms in coastal biomonitoring, yet the biological mechanisms controlling the bioaccumulation of emerging metals remain poorly constrained. Climate change and anthropogenic disturbances are reshaping species distributions and contact zones, promoting mussel hybridization that may alter physiological traits and contaminant-handling capacities. Lithium (Li) remains largely overlooked despite its potential toxicity and rapidly increasing global demand. Here, we investigate the influence of critical factors on Li bioaccumulation by mussels combining genetic background and isotopic approaches. Progenies of two Mytilus species and their hybrids were transplanted to the same Atlantic coastal site for 12 months. Over this in situ exposure period, Li concentrations show comparable temporal trends across all progeny groups, with an initial uptake-dominated phase followed by biodilution. Lithium isotope ratios (δ7Li) display a coherent temporal trend across all groups (decrease at early exposure, increase during later growth), and the magnitude of the shift differs slightly among genetic backgrounds. Across samples, δ7Li is coupled to growth-related metrics (dry weight) and inversely related to Li concentrations, indicating a metabolic control on Li isotope compositions of these organisms. Li concentrations are also positively correlated with lithogenic-associated elements (e.g., aluminum), consistent with the influence of particle associated Li. A simplified biodynamic modeling including Li isotopes data further indicates a more efficient Li depuration after 5 months, combined with a relatively stronger contribution from dissolved Li. Overall, growth-related factors emerged as the primary biological drivers of Li concentration and isotope variability, with the relative contributions of dissolved and particulate exposure pathways varying in association with physiological growth. Hybridization may modulate Li bioaccumulation and δ7Li values, but its influence appears secondary and does not compromise the use of Mytilus mussels as bioindicators in established frameworks such as “Mussel Watch”.

title: Building-Stock Turnover Reshapes Mitigation Priorities in China’s Building Sector
abstract: Abstract China’s building sector is pivotal to the 2060 carbon-neutrality ambition, yet prospective assessments often insufficiently capture regional heterogeneity and life-cycle emission dynamics. Here, we develop a provincial-level dynamic framework integrating material flow analysis, life-cycle assessment, and machine-learning-informed parameter trajectories to project emissions through 2060. Under a business-as-usual (BAU) scenario, China’s building life-cycle emissions are projected to peak in 2031–2033, while carbon neutrality remains challenged by persistent pressures from both material use and building operations. These pressures arise from the existing stock, whose continued use sustains energy demand while increasing building retirements shift construction from stock growth to the replacement of retired buildings. Implementing a high-efficiency scenario with regionally differentiated deployment of material- and energy-efficiency strategies could reduce China’s building-sector life-cycle emissions by 90% in 2060 relative to the BAU scenario. Provincial analysis further reveals that similar overall mitigation potential masks substantial differences in the composition of effective mitigation portfolios, reflecting local building-stock and energy-use characteristics. To close the remaining gap, deeper operational decarbonization should be coupled with stock-management strategies that extend building lifetimes, avoid premature demolition, and prioritize renovation and reuse.

title: Can the Spatial Planning of Livestock Production Tackle Future Nitrogen Pollution in China?
abstract: Abstract Nitrogen (N) pollution from livestock production significantly threatens China’s air and water quality, necessitating innovative solutions to balance food security and environmental sustainability. Studies have mostly overlooked the spatial heterogeneity of N-related environmental impacts and the trade-offs between reducing ammonia (NH3) emissions and N concentrations in water. This study develops a spatially explicit multiscale model system encompassing 13,000 polygons across China to assess soil N balance, NH3 emission intensity, and N concentrations in surface water, aiming to explore integrated spatial-planning (SP) strategies that maximize synergy and minimize trade-offs. Our findings reveal that single-purpose SP scenarios (e.g., reducing NH3 emissions or instream N concentrations) can effectively address one N-related issue but produce substantial trade-offs, leaving >50% of China’s population exposed to at least another N-related problem. However, an integrated SP approach could reduce harmful N exposures for 90% of China’s population while ensuring food security. This approach involves reallocating 14% of livestock production, reducing livestock numbers by one-third relative to the 2050 baseline, and implementing advanced technologies to mitigate N pollution hotspots. Thus, our findings emphasize the importance of spatially explicit N boundaries and multicriteria planning to tackle N pollution in air and water simultaneously, supporting cross-media N management policy-making and region-specific strategies.

Layered double hydroxides functionalized electrospun recycled polyamide 6 from fishing nets: structure–property relationships for antimicrobial non-woven fabrics
abstract: Plastic pollution, particularly marine plastic waste from discarded fishing nets, represents a significant environmental challenge and highlights the need for effective strategies to recover and valorize end-of-life polymers. Polyamide 6 (PA6) fishing nets are an underexploited source for the development of high-value functional materials. This work develops antimicrobial non-woven fabrics (NWFs) from recycled PA6 (rPA6) incorporating organo-modified Mg/Al layered double hydroxides (LDHs) intercalated with antimicrobial anions, namely ascorbate (ASA), ferulate (FER), salicylate (SAL), and citrate (CA), into rPA6, followed by electrospinning. The resulting nanofibrous NWFs were characterized by Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM), Fourier Transformed Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Wide Angle/Small Angle X-ray Scattering with micro-beam (μWAXS/μSAXS), thermal analysis and tested against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus . Homogeneous nanofibers were obtained and LDH incorporation preserved rPA6 chemical structure while reducing crystallinity. rPA6/LDH-FER, rPA6/LDH-ASA, and rPA6/LDH-CA, showed 96.7 to 99.9% bacterial mortality. After thermal aging at 115 °C, LDH-containing NWFs exhibited improved structural stability. These results demonstrate the feasibility of converting recycled PA6 fishing-nets into functional antimicrobial nanofibrous fabrics through LDH functionalization and electrospinning, supporting circular and sustainable applications of marine recycled polyamides.

title: Multi‐Objective Spatial Optimization of Cropland Layouts in Highly Urbanized Regions: Evidence From Dongguan, China
abstract: ABSTRACT Cropland protection in highly urbanized regions requires reconciling stable quantitative‐qualitative targets with the functional optimization of extremely fragmented spatial structures. This study develops a patch‐level multi‐objective spatial reconfiguration framework of cropland layouts based on the Non‐dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm‐II (NSGA‐II) to balance fragmentation mitigation and land conversion costs under constraints of quantity balance, cropland quality non‐degradation, spatial feasibility, and adjustment priorities. The method integrates multi‐scenario cropland adjustment scales with three patch‐level adjustment modes, that is, internal filling, edge expansion, and patch connection. Validation in Dongguan, a representative highly urbanized city in China, demonstrates the framework's effectiveness in generating spatially realistic layouts through a well‐distributed Pareto front. Results indicate that while larger adjustment scales substantially improve landscape aggregation, land conversion costs escalate non‐linearly; the highest‐intensity scenario incurred costs over six times those of the smallest. Across all scenarios, edge expansion served as the primary cost‐effective pathway for consolidation, while internal filling contributed to resolving patch perforations and stabilizing core areas. Patch connection remained indispensable for bridging isolated fragments and ensuring systemic landscape integrity. However, sensitivity analysis showed that optimization outcomes were more responsive to the connection distance than to the relative cost coefficients, and increasing the connection distance did not necessarily improve the overall landscape structure. These findings emphasize that coupling patch‐level mechanisms with multi‐objective optimization provides a robust, actionable tool for precise spatial planning and targeted cropland policy in high‐density urban environments.

ON THE CCE ESTIMATION OF THREE-DIMENSIONAL PANELS WITH MULTI-LEVEL FACTORS
abstract: Abstract We consider the common correlated effects estimation of a three-dimensional panel data model with heterogeneous slope coefficients and multi-level interactive fixed effects. We study the asymptotic properties of the heterogeneous slope coefficient estimators and the mean group (MG) estimators. We find that bias correction is indispensable for the MG estimator and show that the MG estimators exhibit different convergence rates depending on the degree of heterogeneity in the slope coefficients. We propose a bias correction procedure and inference method that is uniformly valid irrespective of the degree of slope heterogeneity. We conduct Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the performance of our estimators and inference methods in finite samples. We apply our new methods to international trade data and find significant heterogeneity in the gravity model even after we control for the multi-level factors.

The Impact of Corporate Social Irresponsibility in the Agri‐Food Sector and Its Policy Implications
abstract: ABSTRACT The financial impacts of Corporate Social Irresponsibility (CSI) on publicly traded agricultural firms are analysed using an EGARCH event‐study framework and 18,635 CSI incidents. We find that CSI events are associated with significantly lower stock returns and elevated market volatility. The clearest and most persistent return penalties arise for novel, sharp, broad‐reaching, and lower‐severity incidents, while high‐severity incidents are associated primarily with large and significant increases in volatility in the immediate post‐event windows. Larger firms are more resilient to CSI shocks than smaller firms, highlighting the role of firm size in absorbing reputational damage. The findings show that agri‐food firms are financially exposed not only to catastrophic ESG failures but also to more routine and unexpected incidents, with implications for ESG governance, disclosure and crisis management.

title: Intergenerational transmission of education: evidence from school construction in Indonesia
Stuck in place? Intergenerational occupational mobility in Türkiye
abstract: Abstract This study analyzes intergenerational occupational mobility in Türkiye using 2021 Family Structure Survey data (N = 13,076). Applying mobility matrices, Altham's statistics, and rank-rank correlations across four birth cohorts (1951 1994), we separate structural economic change from genuine social fluidity. Results reveal a stark divergence. While absolute mobility rose significantly due to de-agrarianization and service-sector expansion, relative mobility stagnated or declined after controlling for these shifts. This implies a "compositional illusion" economic transformation created movement without improving equality of opportunity. We identify "asymmetric permeability": a "sticky top" where the children of professionals are protected by a "glass oor," and a "slippery bottom" where origins in agricultural or low-status positions lead primarily to manual labor. The analysis uncovers profound heterogeneity. Mobility is highly gendered, with daughters facing stronger status persistence than sons, and spatially fractured. Econometric results confirm education as the key engine for upward mobility, while paternal education buffer against social descent. JEL Classification: J31, J24, D31, J21, O15

title: Real incentives really matter
abstract: Abstract Incentivizing behavior, a core principle of economic experiments, is currently under scrutiny due to a series of papers that find little to no difference in choices made under real or hypothetical incentives. We experimentally assess the effectiveness of hypothetical incentives to induce participants’ real effort – an integral aspect of reliable experimental data. We find that although linking behavior to hypothetical incentives generates modest additional effort compared to no reference to such incentives, hypothetical incentives fall substantially short of real ones, even when their nominal value is radically inflated. To understand the mechanism behind these effects, we systematically vary base pay and piece-rate magnitudes across incentive conditions and structurally estimate a model of costly effort. Although higher base pay increases effort both by increasing non-pecuniary motivation and by enhancing responsiveness to hypothetical incentives, incentive-compatible real payments are far more cost-effective.

title: Sustaining cooperation with correlated information: an experimental test
abstract: Abstract In infinitely or indefinitely repeated games with noisy signals about others’ actions, sustaining cooperation is difficult. Theoretical work shows that cooperation can be maintained if the signals are correlated and the degree of correlation depends on the actions. In this study, we implement such an information structure in a laboratory experiment and investigate whether subjects are able to sustain cooperation by conditioning their behavior on it. A substantial number of subjects adopt strategies accounting for the correlation, but this does not increase cooperation compared to a control treatment without correlation, as behavior with independent signals is more lenient when players can communicate, while without communication cooperation remains low in both settings.

title: The use of armed conflict as a bargaining tool against unsophisticated opponents
abstract: This paper studies the role of conflict as a bargaining instrument and its impact on dispute termination. We explore an infinite-horizon bargaining game where limited conflicts reveal information about the contenders relative strength. We study the case where the uninformed party learns from battlefield outcomes but does not learn fully from diplomacy. The equilibrium of this bargaining game displays several features observed in real-world disputes. First, convergence in expectations about relative strengths is not suffcient for dispute termination. Second, defeats lead to gambles for resurrection when limited conflicts are not too costly. Finally, disputes display non-monotonic termination probabilities over time.

title: Tantalus curse? Multigenerational persistence of welfare dependency in Switzerland
abstract: We study welfare dependency in a multigenerational horizontal framework that exploits family links among siblings and cousins. Leveraging population-wide administrative data from Switzerland, we document how family resemblance in welfare receipt is distributed between the nuclear and the extended family. Individuals with a welfare-dependent sibling show about a 22-percentage-point higher probability of welfare receipt. Conditional on sibling receipt, having a welfare-dependent cousin is associated with a further increase of about 5 percentage points. Conditional analyses indicate that most predictive content is concentrated within the nuclear family while the cousin association remains economically meaningful given a baseline prevalence of about 4 percent. Sibling resemblance is stronger for welfare receipt than for income, while the additional predictive content of cousins is similar for both outcomes, implying that this heterogeneity is confined to the nuclear family.

When does digital transformation pay off? A contingent knowledge-combination logic of digital breadth and depth in SME innovation
abstract: Digital transformation expands firms’ access to knowledge while increasing the work needed to integrate it. Drawing on the knowledge-based view, we examine when digital breadth and depth complement or substitute for one another in SME innovation. We combine panel regressions with static and dynamic fsQCA using 3,170 firm-year observations of Chinese GEM-listed SMEs from 2013 to 2023. Breadth and depth are each positively associated with innovation, but their average interaction is negative. Six high-innovation configurations combine these dimensions with digital incentives, the digital environment, state ownership, and political connections. Their annual consistency varies, with several configurations receiving sustained support. We develop a contingent knowledge-combination logic in which the value of combining broader search with deeper integration depends on the resources needed to connect them. Institutional and digital conditions matter because they can help firms meet these demands.

Does College Education Promote Healthier Behaviors? Evidence From Demographic Distortion Caused by Japanese Superstition
abstract: ABSTRACT We investigated the causal effects of a college education on smoking, drinking alcohol, sleeping, and site‐specific cancer‐screening behaviors in Japan. To adjust for endogeneity, we leveraged a unique instrument—demographic distortion caused by a behavior based on a superstition. A superstition held by some Japanese people caused a demographic shift in 1967 that led to an increase in college educational attainment among a certain cohort. Using a recursive bivariate probit approach, we found that having a college education reduced smoking and increased some types of cancer‐screening behaviors. Additionally, we found that the causal relationship may be mediated by an improvement in economic and social resources.

title: Distribution Regression for Partially Observed Discrete, Ordered Outcomes—The Case of Adolescent Substance Abuse
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies Distribution Regression (DR) for ordered and discrete outcomes that are only partially observed due to misreporting. Such outcomes frequently occur in self‐reported surveys eliciting socially undesirable, illegal or stigmatised behaviours like substance abuse, domestic violence or anti‐social behaviour. We demonstrate that DR can offer a flexible way to study the distribution of these outcomes. Specifically, we analyse the asymptotic properties of the DR estimator and derive simultaneous confidence bands for unconditional ‘survival’ probabilities generated by that estimator as well as for counterfactual functionals thereof. The method is illustrated by examining possibly underreported lifetime marijuana consumption behaviour among US high‐school students. We find significant, positive differences across some consumption frequencies in lifetime marijuana use between students residing in states with and without recreational marijuana laws.

title: EXPRESS: Are Exposure Bucks Worth It? Evidence from Instagram
abstract: Using Instagram's recently introduced collaborative post feature, which lets brands credit creators in shared posts seen by the brand's followers, this study quantifies the value of exposure to a brand's audience for small-to-mid-tier sized creators. We assemble a novel dataset linking all collaborative posts from 260 leading fashion and beauty brands to a daily panel of follower counts for the participating creators. To identify causal effects, we exploit rigidity in brands' posting schedules together with high-frequency daily data, attributing the discrete jump in follower growth on the exact post date to brand exposure. To address post content endogeneity, we match treated and control posts on visual content using GPT-4o embeddings and additional aesthetic features. On average, a collaborative post increases a creator's follower count by 0.52%--roughly one week of organic growth--and yields a conversion rate from brand followers to creator followers comparable to online display advertising. We find no effect on engagement or on creators' subsequent sponsored work with other brands. Although larger brands offer greater reach, their followers are less engaged and their collaborative content deviates further from creators' typical style, resulting in roughly constant treatment effects across brands ranging from 0.7 to 8.6 million followers.

title: EXPRESS: So Near Yet So Far: The Unexpected Role of Near Misses for Salesperson Turnover
abstract: Quota attainment is critical for salespeople because it determines their income, recognition, and career progression. Accordingly, salespeople who frequently fail to meet quota may become more inclined to turn over and try their luck elsewhere. However, not all quota failures carry the same weight. Drawing on the expected utility model of turnover, we argue that salespeople who repeatedly miss quota by a narrow margin are especially likely to turn over. This is because such near misses erode a salesperson’s confidence that they will yield valued outcomes in their current job while increasing the perceived attainability of those outcomes elsewhere. We validate these predictions using a seven-year cross-industry panel of 13,277 salespeople across 44 companies, three experiments, and multiple auxiliary studies. The effect is stronger when hitting quota is more important due to high variable pay and group performance homogeneity. Furthermore, we establish expected utility of switching as the mechanism underlying these effects. Our research introduces near misses as a novel antecedent of turnover and as a new trigger that can reshape expected utilities. Furthermore, our research allows managers to implement targeted interventions to retain valuable talents, such as preventing near misses or reframing salespeople’s expected utility once near misses occur.

title: EXPRESS: The Enjoy-Able Effect: Consumer Enjoyment Inflates Self-Evaluations of Ability
abstract: This research establishes the enjoy-able effect . Enjoyment (whether experienced, anticipated, or relative) increases consumers’ self-evaluated ability, leading them to act more like self-perceived experts (e.g., choose more expert-targeted products) and exhibit better-than-average biases for more enjoyable activities. Two waves of archival data (Ns = 559,370 and 491,791), normed associations across 100 consumer activities (N = 397), and six experiments (Ns = 251–593) document these outcomes of consumer enjoyment, establish that they operate independently of actual ability, and provide evidence that consumers’ inferences about their ability are driven by their overgeneralization of a lay theory about the relationship between enjoyment and expertise. The enjoy-able effect therefore depends on the diagnosticity of enjoyment as an input to subjective expertise, relative to other accessible inputs. Accordingly, this work highlights when and for whom other accessible inputs (e.g., an alternate lay theory associating effort and expertise) reduce reliance on the “enjoyment = expertise” lay theory. Overall, this research documents a previously unrecognized influence of enjoyment on consumer behavior, offers new insights on classic theories (e.g., flow and self-determination theory), and identifies a new and robust antecedent to subjective expertise. Managerial implications for product development and promotion, consumer targeting, and gamification are discussed.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
abstract: We quantify the short-term impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on sales performance through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading crossborder online retail platform. Over 2023–2024, the platform integrated GenAI into seven business workflows spanning customer service, consumer-product matching, advertising, and seller services. We find that GenAI adoption increases sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3% depending on GenAI’s marginal contribution relative to baseline firm practices. Across the four GenAI applications with positive sales effects, the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer—an economically meaningful impact given the retailer’s scale and the early stage of GenAI adoption. The gains operate primarily through higher conversion rates rather than larger cart values, consistent with GenAI improving the shopping experience by reducing search, information, communication, and personalization frictions. Importantly, these effects are not associated with worse postpurchase outcomes as product return rates and customer ratings do not deteriorate. Finally, we document substantial demand-side heterogeneity, with larger gains for less experienced consumers. Our findings provide novel, large-scale causal evidence on how GenAI shapes sales productivity in online retail, highlighting both its immediate value and broader potential. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: L.
