Z. Yuan acknowledges financial support from the National Key Research and Development Project [Grant 2024YFB3312900], the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72141305 and 72203202], the National Social Science Fund of China [Grants 26ZDA030 and 25&ZD149], and the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities. K. Zhang, D. Donati, and M. Sarvary have no funding to report. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2026.00623 .

title: The Asymmetric Nature of Social Hierarchies: Unpacking the Dynamic Relationship Between Power and Status
abstract: Scholars and practitioners alike have long presumed that power and status, two foundational bases of social hierarchy, share a symmetric, mutually reinforcing relationship. However, support for this presumption has largely taken the form of theoretical accounts due to the prevalence of static research designs and a dearth of dynamic methodology in organizational research. Drawing on the Dual Perspective Model, we propose that one’s status is more likely to drive changes in one’s power than vice versa because status has a stronger connection to communion—an important component of interpersonal evaluations—than does power, and communality is an important predictor of both power and status. Using data from two studies involving project teams and a contemporary methodology from developmental psychology for modeling dynamic relationships (bivariate dual change score models), we illustrate that there is indeed a mutually reinforcing relationship between power and status over time, but this relationship is asymmetric. In three additional experiments, we find that perceptions of communality explain this asymmetry. We also find similar effects whether power is formal—attached to a position or role—or involves control over informal resources. Across all studies, we find that the path from status to changes in power is stronger than the path from power to changes in status.

title: Using Financial Accounting Information to Estimate the Income Shifting of US Multinationals
abstract: ABSTRACT Existing estimates of how much income US multinational corporations (MNCs) shift out of the United States differ dramatically, and most cannot identify which specific firms do the shifting. We use data from firms' public financial reports to derive firm‐year estimates of US MNCs' outbound income shifting. We find that aggregate US outbound income shifting is substantially lower than widely cited macroeconomic‐based estimates, with the gap driven primarily by double counting of foreign income in macroeconomic data rather than by differences in firms' sensitivity to tax rates. Income shifting is also highly concentrated among a small number of firms, primarily in intangible‐intensive industries such as computers and pharmaceuticals, while most MNCs shift little or no income. This concentration implies that size‐based thresholds embedded in the OECD's Pillar 2 and the US corporate alternative minimum tax will capture the most active income shifters but may also impose compliance burdens on many firms that shift minimal income. These findings have direct implications for policy‐makers designing international tax rules, tax authorities prioritizing audit resources toward high‐risk income shifters, and investors and lenders assessing MNCs' tax‐related exposures.

title: When and How the Implementation of Green HRM Analytics and Open Eco‐Innovation Collaboration Improves Firm Net‐Zero Performance?
abstract: ABSTRACT The understanding of how manufacturing companies can successfully incorporate collaborative eco‐innovation strategies to reach challenging environmental objectives represents one of the main challenges in sustainable operations management. Given this lack of knowledge, the present study aims to research the mechanisms by which Open Eco‐Innovation Collaboration (OEIC) can be used to develop circular learning capability (CLC) and, in turn, improve net‐zero performance (NZP). Further, the moderating influence of green human resource management analytics (GHRMA) is examined and the challenging relationship between them is reinforced. This study presents and empirically tests a new conceptual model, based on the theoretical frameworks of open innovation and natural‐resource‐based view (NRBV). The model assumes that the relationship between OEIC‐NZP is mediated by CLC, which is also a positive moderator for the relationship between the firm's proficiency in GHRMA‐CLC. The data were gathered from 274 manufacturing companies in Pakistan through structured questionnaire and analyzed by partial least square structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM). The results demonstrate the important role of OEIC in improving a firm's CLC, which in turn is an important determinant of NZP. In addition, the findings show that the positive impact of OEIC on NZP through CLC is significantly enhanced if companies have good GHRMA capabilities, helping them to make the most of people as a resource for circular and decarbonization actions. This research adds to the sustainable operations management body of knowledge by shedding light on the organizational learning processes and enablers that make the shift from an open eco‐innovation to concrete net zero results. The study provides practical implications for practitioners by highlighting the importance of building external partnerships, developing circular learning processes, and investing in data‐driven green HRM practices in order to speed up their journey toward a sustainable and net‐zero future.

title: Investigating Associations Between Media Sentiment Surrounding Climate Change Engagement (SDG 13) and Performance Measures: A Study of FTSE 100 Listed Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether media coverage of climate change action (SDG 13) by FTSE 100 firms is associated with business performance in the following year. Drawing on 406,052 news articles published between 2013 and 2022, the study adopts a novel bibliometric keyword‐extraction approach to identify the valence of SDG 13‐related coverage of these firms. A dynamic panel model estimated by the generalized method of moments estimator shows that adverse SDG 13 media coverage of a firm is negatively associated with its sales, net profit, and Tobin's Q . In contrast, positive coverage is associated with improved sales and Tobin's Q . Viewed through the lens of integrated thinking as a holistic framework linking institutional and stakeholder theories, the findings suggest that SDG 13‐related media coverage is associated with corporate reputation and performance. Several implications are extracted from the study and avenues for future research.

title: Big Data and Predictive Analytics Capability and Triple Bottom Line Sustainability Performance: A Resource‐Based Perspective From BRICS Nations
abstract: ABSTRACT This study aims to investigate the relationship between big data and predictive analytics (BDPA) capability and triple bottom line (TBL) sustainability performance in BRICS manufacturing firms. Grounded in the resource‐based view (RBV), we conceptualise BDPA capability as a third‐order hierarchical construct comprising tangible resources (data infrastructure and technology), intangible resources (organisational culture, organisational learning and data‐driven culture) and human‐related skills (technical skills and management skills). Survey data have been used from 304 IT and analytics professionals representing different organisations across BRICS economies and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM) with 5000 bootstrap samples; we test six hypotheses examining both the resource‐capability link and the capability‐performance link. Results reveal that all three resource categories significantly contribute to BDPA capability, with human‐related skills exerting the strongest influence. BDPA capability, in turn, significantly predicts environmental performance, social performance and economic performance, explaining 40%, 50% and 55% of variance, respectively. The study contributes to the literature by providing an empirically validated, multi‐level resource‐capability‐performance framework for analytics‐driven sustainability in emerging economies.

title: Regulatory Relief Under Uncertainty: Market Reactions to the EU's Omnibus CSRD Reform
abstract: ABSTRACT This article investigates the stock market reaction to the European Commission's Omnibus package, released on 26 February 2025, which seeks to amend the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). To explore whether investors interpret this proposal as a regulatory relief or as a signal of heightened policy uncertainty, we conduct an event study on 3292 publicly listed European firms. The release was not associated with the positive reaction expected by the Commission. The evidence points instead to a negative, though modest, reaction. This may reflect uncertainty about the announcement and its timing, close to the first reporting date, which left compliance costs sunk. The most negative reactions concentrate among firms most exposed to uncertainty and compliance investments, and among firms in countries that had already transposed the CSRD into national law. These findings underline the need for clear, coherent and credible rules regarding European sustainability regulatory framework.

title: The Influence of Board Gender Diversity on ESG Controversies: Do Family Control and CSR Committee Matter?
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how board gender diversity relates to firms' exposure to ESG controversies and how this relationship depends on ownership structure and governance formalization. Drawing on an attention‐based perspective, we argue that women directors influence corporate responsibility not only through monitoring but also by shaping what boards notice and address. Relying on a panel of 69 French firms listed on the SBF 120 index over the 2011–2023 period (897 firm‐year observations), we estimate dynamic panel models using a system GMM estimator. A greater representation of women on corporate boards is associated with higher ESG controversy scores, which denote lower exposure to controversies. This association becomes more pronounced in firms under family control, where reputational exposure heightens the salience of issues raised at the board level, although this moderation is sensitive to how the dependent variable is measured. By contrast, the effect diminishes when a dedicated CSR committee is in place. This pattern is consistent with a substitution logic, whereby the formalization of sustainability oversight concentrates responsibility within a specific structure and, in doing so, attenuates collective engagement with ESG‐related risks across the board. The findings indicate that governance mechanisms do not operate cumulatively and that their effectiveness depends instead on how attention and accountability are distributed within the board.

title: Aspect-level sentiment and review helpfulness across satisfied and dissatisfied restaurant reviews: Does reviewer spatial distance matter?
I trust, therefore I act? How green mindful leadership relates to green behavior in the hospitality industry
When a robot fits the role: Service robot appearance and consumers’ emotional and functional expectancies across relationship orientations
Leading for green: how organizational support and intellectual agility drive sustainable innovation
abstract: Purpose The Purpose of this mixed-methods study is to investigate the relationship between leadership styles and employees’ green behavior within the context of Egyptian five-star hotels. Specifically, it examines the mechanisms through which entrepreneurial and resilient leadership influence an innovation climate and employees’ intellectual agility to foster sustainable outcomes. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a sequential mixed-methods design. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the hypothesized relationships using survey data from 349 hotel employees. This is supplemented by the qualitative phase, which involves semi-structured online interviews with 25 hotel professionals to get more insight into leadership practices that have contributed to sustainability. The theoretical foundations of this investigation include social cognitive theory and dynamic capabilities theory. Findings Resilient and entrepreneurial leadership can enhance employees’ intellectual agility by fostering an innovation-oriented climate, which, in turn, strengthens their green organizational citizenship behavior and green innovative behavior. In the presence of green knowledge sharing, the climate of innovation has a greater impact on intellectual agility; perceived organizational support (POS) also enhances the impact of intellectual agility on each of the two green behaviors. The qualitative results show that leaders promoting an innovation-oriented culture enhance agility and knowledge transfer. Employees consequently invest more in environmental initiatives, bringing tangible benefits to the hotel, including cost savings and positive recognition from guests. Practical implications The findings indicate that an integrated managerial approach is needed: developing resilient and entrepreneurial leadership, establishing an innovation-supportive climate, using human resources (HR) practices to improve employees’ intellectual agility and creating formal mechanisms for green knowledge sharing. Providing tangible organizational assistance could also enable employees to harness their abilities and expertise into enduring green conduct and innovation. Originality/value This study contributes to the hospitality sustainability literature by integrating entrepreneurial and resilient leadership perspectives. The research establishes a sequential mediation chain in which innovation climate and intellectual agility transmit the effects of leadership to employees’ green behaviors, while demonstrating how green knowledge sharing and POS act as boundary conditions. The dual-theory framework, together with mixed-methods research in an emerging market setting, provides fresh theoretical and practical insights for promoting employee-led green innovation.

title: Nurturing sales leads: How early-stage behaviors shape salesperson customer need knowledge and sales outcomes
Inside the service work ecosystem: a lived account of young workers
abstract: Purpose Existing service work ecosystem research primarily examines how systems are structured and managed, offering limited insight into how they are experienced by workers. This study addresses that gap by providing the first empirical, worker-centered account of how the service work ecosystem is lived, interpreted and navigated from within. Design/methodology/approach Five Lego® Serious Play® (LSP) workshops were conducted with 80 participants aged 18–26, all with frontline service experience and originating from Global South contexts (Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos). Visual, narrative and observational data were analyzed using an abductive, iterative approach, examining participants' interpretations and recurring visual patterns alongside transcripts, with Psychology of Working Theory (PWT) as a sensitizing lens. Findings Findings reveal a systemic pattern of constraint rather than opportunity. Work is experienced not as a pathway to mobility, but as a site where all three PWT needs (survival, social connection, self-determination) are persistently compromised through macro-level forces, organizational practices and relational dynamics. Pursuing self-determination carries a moral cost, conceptualized here as the guilt of aspiration. Navigating these conditions is itself invisible, uncompensated labor that depletes the very resources on which service quality depends. Originality/value Findings reveal a systemic pattern of constraint rather than opportunity. Work is experienced not as a pathway to mobility, but as a site where all three PWT needs (survival, social connection, self-determination) are persistently compromised through macro-level forces, organizational practices and relational dynamics. Pursuing self-determination carries a moral cost, conceptualized here as the guilt of aspiration. Navigating these conditions is itself invisible, uncompensated labor that depletes the very resources on which service quality depends.

title: Caste, Exclusion, and Humiliation in Indian Markets: Moving Beyond the Bottom of the Pyramid Paradigm
abstract: Recent inclusion-oriented approaches in business and management studies, such as bottom-of-the-pyramid and subsistence marketplace, aim to alleviate poverty but often overlook the socio-historic realities of marginalized groups. These approaches frequently depoliticize inequality by failing to adequately engage with ascriptive hierarchies, such as caste, which shape access to resources, opportunities, recognition, and dignity. We address this gap by advancing the Bottom of the Caste Pyramid (BOCP) as a relational and processual lens to examine how caste structures market participation. Drawing on in-depth interviews with 31 BOCP participants, our analysis reveals graded ascription of status, systemic misrecognition, and problematic inclusion as mechanisms of exclusion and humiliation faced by them, alongside their context-specific agentic responses to sustain market participation in the form of valorization, oscillating between erasures, calculated survival, and normalization of inequality. These practices enable survival yet maintain caste-based hierarchies through ongoing negotiation. By foregrounding caste as a foundational principle organizing market relations, the study calls for historically anchored, dignity-centered approaches to inclusion in management scholarship.

title: Sustainable HRM through a justice lens: identifying a leverage point for systemic impact
abstract: Contemporary HRM scholarship recognizes that sustainable HRM plays a salient role in addressing global grand challenges. However, largely attributable to the complexity of sustainability agendas and the ambiguity surrounding sustainable HRM’s scope and role in organizations, its potential to do so is constrained. To address this, our paper explores how sustainable HRM can meaningfully and holistically contribute to sustainable development. Employing a socio-ecological lens we argue that social justice, because it aligns with and supports sustainable HRM’s core competencies and is essential for sustainable development, affords a key leverage point for advancing and optimizing HRM’s potential to effectively contribute to current social and ecological challenges. Additionally, drawing on sustainability research, we identify and discuss some of the key principles and enablers needed to guide the development of social justice within sustainable HRM.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: From Pitch to Partnership: Startup Engagement Strategies for Securing Corporate Interest
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the early formation stage of corporate–startup collaborations (CSCs). Using fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), we uncover four collaboration‐enabling configurations: Plug‐and‐play, targeted co‐development, and emergent. Each configuration is contingent on the corporation's goals (need‐driven vs. discovery‐driven) and involvement preferences (transactional vs. developmental). Our findings show that corporate interest in a startup is not determined by a single factor in isolation; instead, it is shaped by specific configurations of pitch style, collaboration opportunity, and characteristics of the technology being presented. Taken together, this study advances a configurational approach to early‐stage CSC formation, moving beyond assessments of a pitch detached from its substantive content.

title: Does Corporate Accountability Towards Biodiversity Loss and Species Extinction Protection Account for Audit Efforts: New Insights from External Auditing
abstract: This study investigates whether and how corporate biodiversity disclosure affects external audit efforts. Using a deep‐learning‐expanded text analysis of corporate social responsibility reports for heavily polluting Chinese companies from 2009 to 2021, this paper examines the relation between biodiversity disclosure and audit efforts. The empirical evidence reveals that firms with more extensive biodiversity disclosure exhibit significantly greater external audit efforts. The results remain robust to a series of endogeneity checks, including two‐stage least squares estimation and a combined propensity score matching and difference‐in‐differences analysis. Further analyses show that this positive relation is more pronounced for non‐state‐owned enterprises and firms located in eastern China. Mechanism tests reveal that biodiversity disclosure by heavy polluters triggers a ‘horn effect’, which elevates auditors' perceptions of composite audit risk, thereby driving greater audit effort. Interestingly, while biodiversity disclosures increase audit duration, they do not translate into higher audit fees. Collectively, the findings demonstrate that corporate biodiversity accountability increases audit risk and effort, highlighting the economic consequences of sustainability reporting within the auditing context.

title: Symbolic or substantive? Discursive features of moral legitimation in CSR communication
Effectiveness of daily deal acquisition campaigns and reactions by existing customers
abstract: This research investigates the effectiveness of acquisition-oriented daily deals and reactions by existing customers to such campaigns. Utilizing purchase history data from a company that ran a Groupon acquisition campaign targeted at only prospective customers, we find that the campaign’s long-term return on investment was substantial despite losses for the company during the redemption period. Although Groupon customers had lower lifetime value than those acquired via other channels, their relationship with the company was front-loaded. Consequently, they were similarly valuable as organically acquired customers in the first year, and their relative value increased with a firm’s discount rate of future incomes. Moreover, the campaign did not lead to a reduction in existing customers’ lifetime value, due to the company’s approach to minimizing potential resentment and enhancing fairness perception by honoring Groupon redemption requests of existing customers. Our research offers empirical evidence that daily deals can be an effective acquisition tool without alienating existing customers.

title: How to develop organizational resilience using digital technologies
Harnessing Neuroscience in Social Advertising: From Emotional Impact to Cognitive Understanding and Intentional Behavior in Children and Adolescents
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines emotional responses and their associations with Cognitive Understanding and Intentional Behavior following exposure to a social advertising video featuring historical female role models. Using a mixed‐methods approach that combines near‐infrared spectroscopy with survey data, it investigates how emotional responses observed during exposure to a femvertising stimulus are associated with subsequent Cognitive Understanding and Intentional Behavior. The research contributes to the understanding of emotional and cognitive responses to social advertising among children and adolescents and examines whether these relationships differ between male and female respondents. The model analyzes the relationships among emotional responses, cognitive engagement, and behavioral predisposition, using gender as a grouping variable. Results highlight the critical influence of both positive and negative emotions in responding to social messages and the potential of femvertising narratives to engage gender‐related awareness among young audiences. Practical implications for marketing and education are discussed, along with directions for future research.

title: Beyond the office: How workation fosters individual creativity
Pathways, Strategies, and Conditions: A Resource Reservoir Framework for Tourism Startup Ecosystems
abstract: Tourism startups are increasingly positioned as agents of renewal, yet existing theory offers limited insight into how these ventures navigate external resource environments they depend on. Resource-based perspectives privilege internal capabilities, while ecosystem approaches treat entrepreneurial contexts as relatively undifferentiated. Drawing on 57 in-depth interviews, conducted in 2025, with founders and ecosystem coordinators across 26 countries, this study develops the Startup Ecosystem Resource Reservoir (SERR) framework. This framework theorizes tourism entrepreneurial environments along three analytical layers: a pathway layer distinguishing Endowed-Access Resources (allocated through gatekeeper selection) from Ambient-Access Resources (worked out through participation and relational labor); a strategy layer identifying three founder postures (substantive engagement, performative conformity, and pathway avoidance) through which ventures engage these pathways; and a conditioning layer in which a structurally bifurcated legitimacy regime (investor-track and industry-incumbent-track) and infrastructural conditions shape availability and posture viability across the reservoir.

title: The Penalty of Anticipated Motherhood in the Boardroom: Fertility Policy and Corporate Risk-Taking
Uncovering the Mechanisms of Policy Interventions: A Difference‐In‐Differences Framework for Mediation Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Although mediation analysis is widely used in human resource management to explain how practices shape outcomes, most cross‐sectional approaches rely on the strong assumption of sequential ignorability. We develop a two‐period difference‐in‐differences framework that accommodates time‐invariant unobserved confounders of the mediator and outcome. Rather than requiring independence in levels, identification rests on restrictions on change, including parallel untreated trends and change‐based mediator–outcome exchangeability. The framework clarifies the assumptions needed to identify total and mediator effects as distinct from those required for controlled direct and natural indirect effects. With observed heterogeneity, the natural indirect effect equals the treated‐population average product of the mediator's effect on the outcome and the treatment's effect on the mediator; the full natural indirect effect adds an unidentified residual covariance term, assessed through sensitivity analysis. We extend the method to multi‐period staggered designs and provide estimation, bootstrap inference, diagnostics, and an open‐source R package.

title: The Signal Transmission Effect of Environmental Regulations: A Perspective from Punishment Signals and Reputation Signals
abstract: This study investigates how distinct environmental regulatory signals—punitive versus reputational—affect firms’ green innovation from a signaling theory perspective. Based on a sample of Chinese listed firms, we show that both types of signals significantly stimulate green innovation. However, the two environmental signals operate through distinct transmission mechanisms. Punitive signals drive innovation primarily by forcing firms to finance additional R&D from their own resources. In contrast, reputational signals facilitate innovation by enabling firms to obtain government subsidies from public funds. We further document considerable heterogeneity in these effects across firms. Specifically, firms with less political connection respond more strongly to regulatory signals. Stringent environmental enforcement and greater investor attention also strengthen firms’ incentives to undertake green innovation. Our results underscore the complementary roles of deterrence-based and incentive-based policy instruments. Importantly, we highlight the need to design differentiated regulatory approaches that account for firm-specific characteristics and external conditions in order to effectively foster firms’ green innovation.

title: How Does Digital Risk Exposure Affect Corporate Debt Structure in China? Further Analysis on Debt Default Risk
abstract: The digital economy’s continued expansion not only brings opportunities to enterprises but also exposes them to increasingly prominent digital risks, while evidence regarding how digital risk exposure shapes corporate debt structure is still scarce. Using a sample of Chinese A-share listed companies from 2010 to 2024, this paper analyzes the effects of digital risk exposure (DRE) on corporate debt structure and debt default risk. Baseline estimates show that digital risk exposure is associated with a lower long-term debt ratio, with this association more pronounced among non-high-tech firms. Further analysis shows a negative association between digital risk exposure and corporate debt default risk. This paper broadens existing research into the drivers of corporate debt default risk by treating digital risk exposure as a distinct explanatory dimension and provides empirical evidence and practical implications for firms seeking to manage digital uncertainty and prevent debt risk.

title: Data Security Risk Exposure in Chinese Enterprises: A Large Language Model Approach
abstract: With the rapid expansion of the digital economy, data security risk has become an increasingly important economic concern. Using large language models to analyze more than 560,000 analyst reports from 2006 to 2022, we develop firm-level measures of data security risk exposure for Chinese listed companies. Extensive empirical tests show that the measures capture systematic variation in exposure across time, regions, and industries and significantly predict firms’ subsequent vulnerability status. Firms with higher exposure tend to be larger, more profitable, and more liquid and to have greater growth opportunities. This study provides a forward-looking quantitative tool for enterprises and regulators to identify and mitigate potential risks during the digital transformation process.

title: Impact of Knowledge Maturity on Corporate Green Technological Innovation: Empirical Evidence from China
abstract: Based on knowledge integration theory, this study explores the influence of knowledge maturity on corporate green technological innovation. Using panel data of Chinese A-share non-financial listed firms, we find an inverted U-shaped relationship between the two variables: moderate knowledge maturity facilitates green technological innovation by balancing integration costs and commercial value. Regulatory pressure steepens this U-shaped curve, while normative pressure and imitative pressures exert no significant effects. Furthermore, the above relationship presents evident heterogeneous characteristics in different firms. These findings extend knowledge management and green innovation theory, revealing the nonlinear mechanism and boundary conditions of knowledge maturity, and provide practical implications for managers to rationally allocate knowledge and formulate green innovation strategies.

title: Climate Policy Uncertainty and Corporate Risk-Taking Behavior: Evidence from China
abstract: Uncertainty surrounding climate risks has led governments to adjust climate policies frequently, potentially affecting corporate risk-taking behavior. Combining firm-level data for Chinese A-share companies with city-level CPU, we document a decline in subsequent corporate risk-taking when local climate-policy conditions become more uncertain. Firms respond with lower leverage, larger cash buffers, and lower stock-return volatility, while R&D spending and ESG performance increase, consistent with selective adaptation rather than greater overall risk appetite. This contraction is particularly pronounced among financially constrained firms, Big 4-audited firms, and firms receiving greater media scrutiny. Province-based instrumental-variable estimates yield similar results. The findings show how institutional conditions shape corporate responses to climate-policy uncertainty in an emerging market.

title: How Trade Policy Uncertainty Influences the Digital Transformation of Commercial Banks? Evidence from China
abstract: Amid intensifying global trade protectionism and rapid digital transformation, trade policy uncertainty (TPU) has become an important external factor shaping banks’ strategic behavior. Yet bank-level evidence on whether TPU accelerates or inhibits banks’ digital transformation remains limited. Using an unbalanced panel of Chinese commercial banks from 2010 to 2018, this study links macro-level trade policy shocks to banks’ digitalization decisions. The results show that higher TPU significantly promotes banks’ digital transformation across strategic, business, and managerial dimensions. Mechanism analysis indicates that market competition, innovation capability, and operational efficiency strengthen this relationship, whereas higher risk-taking weakens it by inducing strategic contraction under uncertainty. Heterogeneity tests show that the promoting effect is significant across bank types, with larger estimates for large state-owned and nationwide joint-stock banks, and varies regionally, being significant in the eastern, western, northeastern, and national groups but not in the central region. Overall, the study provides bank-level evidence that TPU can promote rather than impede digital transformation, offering insights into how financial intermediaries adjust strategic decisions under macroeconomic uncertainty.

title: Agricultural Socialized Service Pilot Policies and Corporate Green Total Factor Productivity—An Empirical Analysis Based on the Double Machine Learning Framework
abstract: Agricultural socialized services (ASS) constitute an important policy arrangement for promoting the specialization, large-scale development, and green transformation of agricultural production, and their policy effects can generate further green development spillover effects at the firm level. This study examines its impact on corporate green total factor productivity (GTFP) and the underlying mechanisms. The results indicate that the ASS pilot policy significantly enhances firms’ GTFP. Mechanism analyses reveal that the policy improves executives’ green awareness, strengthening managerial attention to green competitive advantages and environmental responsibility, thereby promoting firms’ green production efficiency. And the policy enhances resource allocation efficiency and reduces investment inefficiency, providing more effective resource support for firms’ green technological upgrading and green transformation. Heterogeneity analysis indicates the policy generates larger GTFP gains for firms with low green media coverage, heavily polluting industries, and non-state-owned enterprises.

title: Dividend Juicing in Mutual Funds: Catering to Retail Investors in China
abstract: This study investigates mutual funds’ hidden flow-induced trading associated with the juicing strategy, a practice characterized by purchasing stocks shortly before dividend payments to boost dividend yields and pass the resulting dividends through to investors. Given China’s distinctive retail-investor-dominated market structure, we show that the juicing strategy appears to cater primarily to retail investors and exhibits strong persistence. Notably, juicing funds are associated with greater retail investor inflows when they pay substantially higher dividends than their underlying holdings imply, particularly during periods of underperformance or market turbulence. The juicing strategy imposes tangible costs on investors through excessive portfolio turnover and transaction costs, ultimately eroding their returns. Our findings challenge the traditional Homo Economicus view that investors value capital gains and dividends equally, regardless of their source. Instead, retail investors appear to regard fund dividends as a distinct and stable income stream. This susceptibility allows portfolio managers to strategically exploit investor preferences, highlighting the principal–agent problem between managers and investors.

title: Save for a Rainy Day: How Do Climate Risks Affect Corporate Cash Holdings?
abstract: Climate-related threats are becoming a more prominent constraint on corporate operations, making liquidity policy an important part of climate resilience. Using Chinese A-share listed companies from 2013 to 2022, we find that greater climate risk is associated with more conservative cash policies and higher cash balances. The association is stronger for non-state-owned firms, firms with less financialization, and firms led by less myopic managers. Mechanism tests suggest that climate risk heightens precautionary and transactional cash demand by curbing corporate investment and increasing transaction costs. The effect also intensifies with financing constraints, stricter environmental regulation, and greater managerial attention to environmental issues. The evidence adds to research on the firm-level financial consequences of climate risk and informs corporate liquidity management and regulatory design.

title: Could Artificial Intelligence Facilitate Digital Trade? Evidence from Cross-Country Data
abstract: This study investigates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on digital trade using cross-country bilateral data from 2005 to 2023. While AI can improve information processing, expand digital supply, and facilitate cross-border coordination, its effects may vary across product categories and national conditions. We measure AI development using AI-related patent data and examine its relationship with bilateral digital trade. Our empirical results show that AI significantly promotes digital trade. Mechanism analysis suggests that AI strengthens digital supply capacity, expands digital demand, and improves institutional arrangements that support cross-border digital connectivity. The positive relationship is strongest for communication equipment and is more pronounced in economies with higher institutional quality, income, and fixed-broadband penetration, as well as in OECD member economies. Our study contributes to the literature by providing bilateral cross-country evidence on the relationship between AI and digital trade, measuring AI-related technological capability with patent data, and identifying the channels and country conditions through which AI is associated with digital trade.

title: Staying on topic: How research knowledge spills over via university education to regional entrepreneurial activity
abstract: Entrepreneurship is an important driver of regional economic development. Universities contribute to this goal by conducting state-of-the-art research and educating talent. The academic and policy debate regarding innovative start-up firms has primarily focused on how the outputs of research can be translated into entrepreneurial activities. In contrast, the role of education in fostering entrepreneurial activity has received comparatively little attention. As such, it remains unknown which task of a university is more important for innovative entrepreneurship in a region: research or education. Further, existing research on academic entrepreneurship has largely focused on Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) or the life sciences (LS), but innovative start-up firms in the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) domain are understudied. Furthermore, while entrepreneurship education is seen as an important method to promote innovative entrepreneurial activity, little attention has been paid to its effectiveness in achieving this goal. Hence, we pose the following question: What is the influence of university education and research on the level of regional innovative entrepreneurial activities within a given topic? We make education, research, and entrepreneurship data comparable across specific topics in a region, by applying topic models to course descriptions and publication abstracts from two universities in the Netherlands, as well as to innovative start-up firm descriptions from the two regions in which these universities are located.We show that both research and education foster innovative entrepreneurial activity, but that the effect of education is much stronger than that of research. Second, we find that education mediates the positive effect of research on innovative entrepreneurship. Third, we observe that innovative entrepreneurial activities are highest in the SSH domain. Finally, we find evidence that providing practical entrepreneurship education is beneficial for innovative entrepreneurial activity. This effect appears particularly strong in the LS and, to a lesser extent, in the STEM domain. Our findings indicate that more attention to the impact of education and pedagogical approaches is warranted to promote innovative entrepreneurial activity.

title: Volatility in Evidence Use: A Computational Analysis of Punctuated Equilibrium Theory
When More Is More: Committee Overlap and the Diversity of Information in Problem Definition

Anti-corruption policies: examining and evaluating the integration of agencies and whistleblower systems
abstract: This article interrogates dominant anti-corruption evaluation models by foregrounding the integration between Anti-Corruption Agencies (ACAs) and whistleblower systems as a critical yet underexamined determinant of institutional effectiveness. Drawing on institutional theory, regulatory governance, and structured cross-country comparison, it develops a four-part typology of ACA–whistleblower integration regimes (complementary, substitutive, fragmented, and minimalist) based on document-based qualitative evaluation across 13 countries. The findings suggest that institutional coordination and interoperability, rather than the formal existence of anti-corruption institutions alone, are consistently associated with stronger enforcement capacity, greater institutional legitimacy, and higher public trust. The study challenges checklist-based global evaluation models that privilege institutional presence over institutional interaction and proposes an integration-centred framework for assessing integrity systems. By shifting attention from institutional design to institutional integration, the study offers a context-sensitive diagnostic approach for evaluating anti-corruption governance across diverse political and administrative settings.

title: Simulating the unseen: Crash prediction and prevention should learn from what did not happen
Multi-scale facility context and micro-spatial motor-vehicle–cyclist conflict risk at signalized intersections: a characterized spatial squares framework
Seeing trauma in the Mirror: Childhood sexual abuse and bodily expression in adulthood
abstract: Background Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is linked to disrupted body boundaries and difficulty inhabiting the body as an integrated part of self. Such disruptions are thought to be encoded procedurally rather than verbally, so self-report may not fully capture them. The Mirror Game, a nonverbal dyadic task, allows such functioning to be observed directly. Objective This study examined whether adult women with self-reported CSA differ from a comparison group in nonverbal behavior and dyadic coordination during the Mirror Game, and whether CSA severity is associated with these behaviors. Methods Thirty-nine Israeli women (23 survivors, 16 without reported CSA) completed a 15-min Mirror Game with a female expert player blind to group status. Interactions were coded with the Mirror Game Scales; the Together and Free composites were primary outcomes, and the 20 individual scales were exploratory. CSA severity was assessed with the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire sexual abuse subscale. Results Survivors scored lower than the comparison group on Together, g = 1.12, 95% CI [0.44, 1.80], and Free, g = 1.19, 95% CI [0.50, 1.88], and were more often classified as Difficult to Play With (87.0% vs. 37.5%). Across the full sample, sexual abuse scores correlated negatively with Together, r = −0.47, and Free, r = −0.50. Exploratory analyses showed lower scores among survivors on 15 of 20 scales. Conclusions Survivors showed a broad, though not uniform, pattern of constricted embodied and relational engagement. Findings support the Mirror Game as an observational complement to verbal report of the embodied consequences of CSA.

title: Dyadic adjustment in a clinical sample of adult victims of cumulative childhood interpersonal trauma: The role of complex posttraumatic stress and attachment insecurities
abstract: Background Cumulative childhood interpersonal trauma (CCIT) is highly prevalent and has been consistently associated with persistent relational difficulties in adulthood. Victims frequently report lower dyadic adjustment, a key determinant of health, well-being, and trauma recovery. However, the mechanisms linking CCIT to impaired couple functioning remain insufficiently understood. Objective This study examined a sequential model in which symptoms of complex posttraumatic stress disorder (C-PTSD) – including posttraumatic stress (PTS) and disturbances in self-organization (DSO) – and subsequent attachment insecurities (avoidance and anxiety) were tested as explanatory mechanisms in the association between CCIT and dyadic adjustment within a clinical sample. Participants and settings A total of 907 adults seeking therapy for sexual and relational difficulties completed validated measures as part of their intake assessment. Results Path analyses revealed significant sequential associations whereby CCIT was indirectly associated with lower dyadic adjustment through DSO then attachment avoidance (β = −0.034, 95% CI [−0.053, −0.020]), as well as through DSO then attachment anxiety (β = −0.008, 95% CI [−0.016, −0.003]). In contrast, CCIT was positively associated with dyadic adjustment through PTS alone (β = 0.060, 95% CI [0.032, 0.093]) but negatively associated with dyadic adjustment through the sequential association via PTS then attachment anxiety (β = −0.006, 95% CI [−0.013, −0.002]). Although statistically significant, the sequential indirect effects were small in magnitude and should not be interpreted as evidence of substantial clinical effects. The final model explained 24.8% of the variance in dyadic adjustment. Conclusion These results point to the relevance of addressing self-organization impairments and attachment dynamics in clinical interventions aimed at improving relational functioning among CCIT victims.

title: The Relationship Between Postpartum Sexual Well-Being and Parenting Sense of Competence Among Mixed-Gender, First-Time Parent Couples
abstract: Although sexual well-being often declines during the transition to parenthood, little is known about how couples' sexual experiences relate to parental adjustment. Sexual satisfaction and sexual distress are central indicators of sexual well-being and may be associated with parents' perceptions of competence through spillover within individuals and crossover between partners. Guided by Family Systems Theory, this study examined associations between sexual satisfaction, sexual distress, and parenting sense of competence among first-time parent couples during the postpartum period. Participants were 132 mixed-gender first-time parent couples from Portugal assessed at three months postpartum. Associations between sexual satisfaction, sexual distress, and parenting sense of competence were examined using dyadic Actor-Partner Interdependence Models (APIM). The results indicated that greater sexual satisfaction was associated with men's own greater sense of parental competence, greater own sexual distress was associated with lower parental competence for both partners, and men's greater sexual distress was associated with women's lower parental competence. After adjustment for contextual variables, only the actor associations for men's sexual satisfaction and sexual distress remained statistically significant. These findings highlight the associations of sexual satisfaction and sexual distress with couples' adjustment to parenthood, particularly among new fathers, and suggest that sexual experiences and perceptions of parenting competence may represent interconnected aspects of adjustment during the postpartum period.

title: The Impact of Methamphetamine on Sexual Behavior, Vulnerability, and Pleasure Among Sexual and Gender Minority Individuals: Implications for Harm Reduction and Improving Sexual Health
abstract: Methamphetamine (meth) use remains a persistent and evolving public health challenge among sexual and gender minority individuals, a population already disproportionately affected by human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Beyond its well-documented role in HIV transmission, meth fundamentally alters users' experiences of sex, intimacy, and pleasure. Understanding this intersection is critical to informing therapeutic and harm reduction approaches. We conducted semi-structured, in-depth interviews with 29 sexual and gender minority individuals assigned male sex at birth who used meth within the prior month. Interviews (mean = 54.9 min) were recorded, professionally transcribed, and analyzed using a reflexive thematic approach. Participants (mean age = 37.9 years) were racially and ethnically diverse (75% nonwhite) and 83% identified as gay. Nearly all described an initial non-sexual introduction to meth with use eventually becoming tightly intertwined with sexual behavior. Four major themes emerged: (1) from first introduction to "party-n-play" culture - a transition linking meth with sexual arousal and sexual networks; (2) meth shifting sexual behaviors - heightened arousal, prolonged encounters, and altered roles; (3) meth use and sexual violence during meth-related encounters - including being given meth without consent; and (4) "meth ruined sober sex" - diminished sexual pleasure without meth. Findings highlight that for many sexual and gender minority individuals, meth use and sexual experience may become inseparable, reshaping notions of desire, consent, and intimacy. Therapeutic and recovery interventions must explicitly address this fusion - acknowledging that reducing meth use often entails redefining sex itself. Clinicians should integrate trauma-informed, sex-positive frameworks to support recovery and reestablish healthy sexual functioning.

title: Scrolling through the noise: a cross-sectional analysis of Reddit posts discussing tamoxifen
With Thanks
Sexual Dimorphism in the Facial Morphology and Skin Color in Sub-Saharan Africa
abstract: Abstract In human faces, sexual dimorphism manifests itself in both morphological traits and skin color differences between males and females. Existing research has focused mainly on facial shape, but less is known about the interplay between dimorphism in facial structure and skin color, particularly in African populations. We investigated the degree of sexual dimorphism in facial shape and skin color in four sub-Saharan African populations (Cameroon, Mauritania, Senegal, and Sudan) using geometric morphometric analyses. We examined whether masculinization of facial morphology was consistently associated with darker skin tones, as would be expected given the influence of sex hormones on pigmentation, or whether this relationship varied across populations. Sexual dimorphism varied significantly in both shape and color across populations. The Sudan sample exhibited the strongest shape dimorphism in facial structure, while the Cameroonian and Mauritanian samples showed less pronounced differences. In contrast, the Senegal sample demonstrated the highest dimorphism in skin color, with men being notably darker than women. An unexpected pattern emerged in the Cameroonian and Mauritanian samples, where the most morphologically masculine men had a lighter skin than their less facially masculine peers. This challenges the expectation of skin darkening with increased masculinization. Given the drawbacks of highly masculine appearance, we discuss a possible compensatory mechanism where highly masculinized men have a lighter skin to offset the social or reproductive costs associated with morphological hypermasculinity. Our findings highlight the complexity of sexual dimorphism in African populations, emphasizing the need for further research into the impact of evolutionary, genetic, and sociocultural factors on facial diversity.

title: Mandatory Service Performance Reporting and Audit: Responses from Charities
abstract: Growing regulatory attention has extended to charity service performance reporting and its external audit, yet little is known about how charities respond when both are mandated. Drawing on a documentary analysis of 120 reports from large New Zealand charities and interviews with preparers and auditors, we examine the responses to these mandates. Using the decoupling theory, we find substantial formal compliance, but the audited statements of service performance were dominated by verifiable quantitative outputs, while qualitative outcome- and impact-oriented information was less prevalent. The audit process strengthened reporting routines, reducing policy-practice gaps, but contributed to means-ends tensions by encouraging reliance on quantitative information and shifting qualitative information to voluntary reporting mechanisms. By demonstrating charities’ emergent and deliberate responses to the mandates, we reveal how audit shapes reporting practices and the intentionality of responses.

title: Volunteer Motivation Fulfillment and Well-Being
abstract: If volunteering is associated with higher well-being, why might this be? Published correlations may reflect the influence of volunteering on well-being or the influence of well-being on volunteering, or both directions of influence. Moreover, volunteer motivation may serve as a boundary condition, with other-oriented goals more positively associated with well-being than self-oriented goals. However, motive fulfillment has yet to be examined in this context. We surveyed 406 current volunteers, registered with Prolific, from selected English-speaking nations, 3 months apart, assessing volunteer motivations, personality, and four types of well-being at T1 and motive fulfillment and well-being at T2. We found that greater fulfillment of important other-oriented motives was significantly more positively associated with well-being at T2 than greater fulfillment of important self-oriented motives; results remained significant when controlling for personality and, largely, T1 well-being. We conclude that fulfilling important other-oriented goals in volunteer work is associated with higher subsequent well-being.

title: The Rise of Tzu Chi: The Making of a Global Buddhist Movement Chengpang Lee. Vancouver: University of British Columbia Press, 2025. 276 pp. CA$34.95; £29.99 (pbk). ISBN 9780774871105
abstract: Chengpang Lee opens The Rise of Tzu Chi: The Making of a Global Buddhist Movement with an evocative account of the organization’s humanitarian response in Indonesia following the devastat- ing late-2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and earthquake. This narrative hook immediately situates the reader within the vast operational reach of the Compassionate Relief Tzu Chi Foundation, the largest nongovernmental social service organization in Asia and a global “charity superpower”.

Optimal co-planning of hybrid energy hubs and integrated electricity-hydrogen transmission infrastructure
abstract: Clusters of large-scale renewable energy projects, also known as renewable energy zones (REZs), are essential elements in the transition to net zero. Hybrid energy hubs (HEHs), which incorporate other energy vectors such as green hydrogen (H 2 ) into REZs, can further leverage economies of scale and diversity in electricity and H 2 production and demand to reduce the required capacity of connection assets and decrease overall operational and capital costs. This paper introduces a general, optimization-based framework for the co-planning of HEHs and integrated electricity and H 2 systems (IEHS), aiming to find the least-cost designs of HEHs, along with the electricity and H 2 transmission infrastructure required to connect them to the main grid. This framework features a modular HEH model that enables flexible technology selection and sizing without a predefined hub configuration, while minimizing the capacity of shared connection assets. Comprehensive case studies on the Australian National Electricity Market (NEM) that integrate HEH and system-level planning compare investment strategies between independent connection configurations and shared connection configurations within HEHs. The findings show that integrating HEHs with optimized shared connection assets into IEHS planning can not only displace investments in both electricity and H 2 transmission infrastructure, but also reduce renewable energy curtailment and enhance the utilization of existing and new assets. Moreover, although including H 2 transmission development can reduce system costs, HEHs with shared connection assets alone may provide greater cost reductions as an alternative investment strategy, enough to avoid all the uncertainty associated with building a new H 2 pipeline network.

title: Integrating land-use dynamics, climate change, and fiscal capacity into equitable ecological compensation: A county-level analysis in Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, China
The impact of the Swiss CO2 levy on residential heating emissions and energy demand
abstract: This paper assesses the impact of the Swiss CO 2 levy on residential heating energy demand and the associated CO 2 emissions. Using the synthetic control method, the results show that the levy led to an average annual reduction in CO 2 emissions of 6.5% during the post-treatment period (2008–2021), corresponding to a decrease of 0.1 metric tons of CO 2 per capita per year. Furthermore, the empirically estimated price elasticities for heating oil indicate that the short-run elasticity for the retail price is − 0.044 , while the elasticity for the CO 2 levy is − 0.997 , demonstrating that consumers respond more strongly to policy-induced price changes than to market-driven price changes. In the long run, these elasticities increase to − 0.054 (retail price) and − 1.215 (levy), highlighting that over time, households adjust their demand more significantly in response to sustained price changes. A similar pattern is observed for natural gas, with short-run elasticities of − 0.216 (retail) and − 0.547 (levy), increasing to − 0.552 and − 1.396 , respectively, in the long run. These findings are consistent with the Swiss CO 2 levy contributing to lower fossil-fuel demand and building-sector emissions, although the SCM inference does not reach conventional levels of statistical significance. The results underline the importance of policy-induced price instruments and highlight the necessity of high levy rates to ensure a measurable impact on consumption behavior.

Digital product passports for renewable energy assets: A lifecycle information framework
abstract: Digital Product Passports (DPPs) connect product identity with lifecycle information for compliance, circularity and stakeholder access. Positive energy districts (PEDs) require this information to remain useable as renewable-energy assets undergo maintenance, component replacement and ownership changes. This study synthesises passport and engineering literature, regulations, standards and initiative documents for photovoltaic systems (PV), small wind turbines (SWTs) and asphalt solar collectors (ASCs). It develops eight shared lifecycle categories with extensions for electrical performance, mechanical condition, and thermal-hydraulic and road-infrastructure information. Four layers organise complementary information responsibilities: identity and lifecycle baseline; operational data and connectivity; semantic and derived information; and governance and exchange. Illustrative records for inverter replacement, bearing inspection and road-work handover explain how asset configurations, observations, assessments and permissions remain connected across lifecycle events. Representative mappings connect the field profile to external information models, while district scenarios show how current capability, availability and constraint records can inform energy management alongside storage and demand coordination. Stewardship, skills and incentives sustain these exchanges. A staged pathway connects shared field definitions, operational tasks and longitudinal assessment to guide implementation for district operation, repair, reuse and recovery.

title: Review of hybrid ship propulsion systems: energy strategies, simulation platforms, and future challenges
abstract: With growing global attention to decarbonization and sustainable development, ship propulsion systems are undergoing a significant transition toward enhanced energy efficiency and reduced environmental impact. Hybrid ship propulsion systems, which integrate multiple energy sources such as LNG, hydrogen, and solar energy, have gained increasing attention in the maritime industry for their potential to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. However, the complexity associated with energy source configurations in hybrid ship propulsion systems, energy distribution and management, and simulation platform selection poses considerable challenges to the effective implementation of such systems. To address the above issues, this paper first reviews the development of ship propulsion systems. It then outlines the main energy sources applied in hybrid ship propulsion systems, including conventional fossil fuels, transitional fuels, and sources supporting zero-emission onboard operation. Furthermore, various types of energy management strategies (EMSs) for hybrid ship propulsion systems are summarized and compared. The simulation platforms, including GT-POWER, AVL Cruise M, Simcenter Amesim, and Simulink, are evaluated and compared to highlight their applicability and suitability under various scenarios. In addition, representative hybrid ship projects and their practical applications are introduced, including key demonstrations and their commercial use cases. Finally, the key challenges and future development trends of hybrid ship propulsion systems are discussed, providing a comprehensive reference for researchers, ship designers, and shipowners to further promote both academic research and practical deployment of hybrid ship propulsion systems.

title: Metatranscriptomics Reveals Potential Hybrid Electron Routing in Comammox Nitrospira and NO-Supplemented Cooperation in a Partial Nitritation-Anammox Bioreactor under Dynamic Aeration
abstract: Abstract Intermittent aeration drives partial nitritation-anammox (PN-A) systems, yet how microbiomes regulate aerobic and anaerobic respiration during rapid, oxygen-limited redox shifts remains poorly understood. Here, we applied genome-resolved metatranscriptomics to evaluate transcriptional dynamics in a long-term PN-A bioreactor treating low concentrations of ammonium. Under intermittent aeration, active populations did not follow strict metabolic switching, but instead exhibited complementary regulation by coordinately transcribing aerobic and anaerobic respiratory pathways. Notably, comammox Nitrospira exhibited a severe transcriptional bottleneck, with terminal oxidase expression 2–3 orders of magnitude lower than that of amo and nirK. Gene coexpression and pathway mapping support a novel hybrid electron transport chain where electrons from ammonia oxidation are directly routed to nirK. This alternative electron-transfer route functionally couples energy dissipation with obligatory nitrite detoxification. Concurrently, a severe transcriptional deficit of nirS relative to hdh in anammox Ca. Kuenenia indicates a partial bypass of intracellular nitrite reduction. Collectively, these patterns support a novel nitric oxide-supplemented cooperation: anammox bacteria scavenge extracellular nitric oxide generated by comammox Nitrospira, conserving their own electrons while acting as a vital sink to relieve comammox nitric oxide toxicity. These findings provide a mechanistic blueprint for optimizing advanced PN-A microbiomes through engineered aeration control.

title: Discovery of Emerging Aromatic Compounds with High Potential Risk from Coal-Fired Power Plants
abstract: Abstract Coal combustion releases aromatic compound (AC) mixtures far more complex than the 16 EPA-priority polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). Here, a high-resolution in-house database targeting 104 aromatic compounds prioritized by structural carcinogenicity alerts and structural analogy was developed to complement NIST library matching for screening fly ash, slag, and soil from five coal-fired power plants (CFPPs). This dual-database strategy increased the identification rate by 9.2% and captured 29 compounds previously unreported in the analyzed CFPP-related matrices. A total of 393 ACs spanning 24 structural classes were annotated. Cross-matrix profiling revealed distinct chemical shifts, from primary 1-ring products in slag to secondary chlorinated species in fly ash and ultimately to persistent high-molecular-weight PAHs in soils, suggesting that the observed AC patterns were associated with differences in unit efficiency, end-of-pipe control, and operational history across the five CFPPs. Incremental lifetime cancer risk assessment demonstrated that emerging PAHs contributed 60% of the total carcinogenic risk in fly ash despite comprising only ∼2% of total AC concentrations, with 4-ring compounds identified as the predominant risk drivers. Sensitivity analysis confirmed that assessments restricted to literature-derived toxic equivalency factors underestimate the full carcinogenic potential. These findings reveal a critical yet underrecognized toxic fraction in CFPP fly ash, underscoring the need for risk-oriented management strategies that explicitly incorporate emerging PAHs.

title: ES&T Next 60 Years: Sustainability and Climate Change
Energy Supply and Demand Coordination Can Advance Both Climate Goals and Sustainable Development in the Global South
abstract: Abstract Reconciling climate mitigation with sustainable development is a critical imperative in the Global South, where rising emissions coincide with persistent development deficits. Here, we develop an integrated assessment framework linking nationally determined contribution (NDC)-aligned supply-side, demand-side, and coordinated supply–demand policy packages to greenhouse-gas trajectories and a six-goal Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) scorecard. We show that supply-focused renewable expansion or demand-focused efficiency improves selected SDG-related dimensions but creates trade-offs involving energy-cost pressure, water use, and ecosystem protection. By comparison, an integrated supply–demand strategy maximizes the SDG score (69 versus 65 under REF in 2050), enhances clean-energy penetration and efficiency, and averts approximately 485,000 annual premature deaths in 2050 relative to REF. These findings highlight the potential of coordinated supply–demand strategies to reduce climate–SDG trade-offs across the Global South.

title: Divalent Cations and Chlorine Synergistically Reshape T6SS-Mediated Microbial Competition in Water Distribution System Biofilms
abstract: Abstract Microbial interactions shape the community structure and function in drinking water distribution system (DWDS) biofilms, yet how the dynamic competition is regulated in biofilms remains poorly understood. Here, we show that divalent cations (Ca2+, Mg2+) and chlorine in drinking water synergistically activate the type VI secretion system (T6SS) in opportunistic pathogens within biofilms. Field-collected biofilms serve as ecological hotspots that selectively enrich specific T6SS-harboring pathogens. Using simulated pipe systems and mutant validation, we further establish that divalent cations and chlorine enhance c-di-GMP signaling to promote T6SS-mediated colonization. This activation stimulates EPS production, whose polysaccharides mitigate T6SS attack, dampening the competitive advantage during mid-stage maturation but allowing gradual resurgence over extended succession. This divalent cation-chlorine-driven interplay shapes ecological succession, selectively retaining T6SS-proficient cells and establishing a “biofilm reservoir effect.” Under chlorine decay, T6SS-active pathogens can be released into bulk water, elevating exposure risks. Conversely, reducing divalent cations via nanofiltration suppresses T6SS across multiple pathogens, limiting reservoir accumulation and release. Our findings identify divalent cation availability as a key environmental signal associated with T6SS-mediated competition, linking water chemistry to pathogen persistence. This work suggests integrating membrane-based divalent cation removal with chlorine management as a chemistry-based strategy to mitigate microbial risks, advancing an integrated water quality paradigm for drinking water safety.

title: Embedding Environmental Science and Technology into Sustainability
abstract: E nvironmental science and technology have contributed much to a better world.However, a new understanding of their role is urgently needed.Recently, human-made and mobilized material have exceeded natural materials.1 Planetary boundaries have been transgressed for synthetic chemicals.A steep increase in the diversity, complexity, and volume of chemicals and materials on all levels from atomic to molecular, material, and product levels can be observed, and this development is expected to continue.Products such as alloys, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, personal care products, dyes, fibers, plastics, electronics, textiles, furniture, buildings, tires, cars, etc., are made up of complex combinations of different atoms, molecules, and materials.Moreover, the products and their constituents mix during use and at the end of their life at various rates and locations, e.g., in waste streams, the technosphere, the anthroposhere, and the natural environment.Legacy chemicals are still present in materials and products in use, waste, brown fields, soils, sediments, and the environment.During use, circulation, recycling, and treatment of effluents and exhausts and in the environment, chemicals and materials often undergo changes in composition and form non-intentionally added substances (NIAS) and transformation products (TPs).One parent compound often leads to many such reaction products.TPs and NIAS are often not commercially available as analytical standards and therefore need to be synthesized.How can we assess these substances if they are not available as pure compounds?All of these chemicals, materials, and products generate local, regional, national, and global flows with varying dynamics in terms of volume, composition, and lifetime.Each successful treatment or removal depends on optimum conditions for each individual compound, material, or product.Therefore, treatment is often demanding and incomplete. title: Structure-Dependent Maternal-Fetal Transfer and Fetal Hepatic Accumulation of PFOA and Hexafluoropropylene Oxide (HFPO)-Based Alternatives: Implications for Fetal Liver Metabolic Disruption
abstract: Abstract Hexafluoropropylene oxide (HFPO)-based compounds have been increasingly adopted as replacements for legacy per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), yet evidence on developmental toxicity remains limited. This study investigated structure-dependent maternal-fetal transfer, fetal tissue distribution, and hepatic effects of PFOA and four HFPO-based alternatives, including hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid (HFPO-DA) and hexafluoropropylene oxide trimer acid (HFPO-TA) homologues, in gestational mice. All compounds were detected in maternal serum, fetal tissues, and amniotic fluid in a dose-dependent manner, but transplacental transfer efficiencies varied markedly. C9 HFPO-TA showed the greatest fetal accumulation, indicating enhanced fetal retention. Desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry imaging revealed preferential hepatic localization of PFOA and HFPO trimers, with fetal hepatic burden increasing with van der Waals volume, suggesting structure-dependent enrichment. Metabolomics showed broad alterations of fetal hepatic metabolism, dominated by altered lipids and lipid-like molecules. 5-Aminolevulinic acid, a key heme precursor, was consistently reduced, whereas ALAS1 and ALAD protein levels increased, indicating perturbation of heme biosynthesis. The provisional, study-specific developmental reference doses derived from fetal or placental endpoints were comparable to or lower than those based on maternal hepatomegaly, suggesting greater developmental sensitivity. These findings reveal structure-dependent fetal liver accumulation and support incorporating fetal-specific endpoints into PFAS risk assessment.

Numerical assessment of the environmental impact of hydrogen-powered vehicles under realistic driving conditions
abstract: This study evaluates the cradle-to-grave (CTG) greenhouse-gas (GHG) emissions of a light-duty hydrogen internal combustion engine (HICE) vehicle by combining vehicle simulations, which estimate fuel consumption and GHG emissions under real-world driving conditions, and a life-cycle assessment (LCA) covering the vehicle’s lifetime up to 2050 under four different hydrogen production scenarios. The environmental performance of this vehicle is compared with that of its gasoline-fueled counterpart, considering both conventional and hybrid powertrains, to assess the potential of hydrogen fuel and hybridization to decarbonize the road-transport sector. The results show that HICE vehicles can achieve substantially lower CTG GHG emissions than their gasoline counterparts, although their environmental performance is highly dependent on the hydrogen production pathway. Under the assumptions adopted for the 2050 scenarios, SMR-based hydrogen production pathways incorporating CCS and biogenic feedstocks exhibit the lowest life-cycle GHG emissions. However, when considering the worst-case scenarios under maximum uncertainty, the situation is reversed, with the scenarios dominated by renewable water electrolysis yielding the lowest emissions, suggesting that these findings should be interpreted with caution. Hybridization generally improves fuel efficiency, but its environmental benefits strongly depend on the carbon intensity of hydrogen production and driving conditions, with potential advantages for the selected hybrid architecture only under urban driving. These results highlight the importance of considering representative driving conditions when evaluating the environmental performance of alternative fuels and powertrain configurations, and demonstrate the value of linking vehicle-level driving-cycle analysis with LCA to assess their life-cycle GHG emissions.

A “cradle-to-grave” life-cycle assessment of biokerosene production through chemical looping gasification for use in jet engine: Comparing second and third generation biomasses
abstract: Current biofuels are mainly derived from second and third generation biomasses. When used in chemical looping gasification (CLG), biomasses can be converted to undiluted syngas that is ready for conversion to biofuels, while the energy-intense air separation needed in conventional gasification is avoided. This work performs a “cradle-to-grave” life-cycle assessment (LCA) for biokerosene production and use in jet engines. The syngas for kerosene synthesis is generated through CLG technology with ilmenite as oxygen carrier and tablets of two types of microalgae and pellets of wheat straw and forest wood as feedstocks. These biomasses are representative precursors of two generations of biofuels. The LCA model covers all steps from biomass cultivation/growth to the final biokerosene combustion in jet engines. The four biomasses and ilmenite originate from inside Spain, and after production and mining they are transported to produce syngas in a CLG plant that is assumed near Zaragoza in Spain. Downstream syngas processing includes catalyzed Water-Gas Shift, Fischer-Tropsch (F-T) synthesis, Dry Reforming and uncatalyzed Pressure Swinging Adsorption and Refining. The syntheses of catalysts and adsorbents are also considered. The biokerosene is finally transported to a nearby airport for use in jet engines. The European Commission’s Environmental Footprint method with sixteen indicators is employed to study the process’s potential life-cycle impacts to climate, atmosphere, ecosystem, biodiversity, human health and natural resource depletion. Among the four biomasses, the microalgae produced from raceway pounds have the highest global warming potential (19.4 kg CO 2 eq. emissions), and this is followed by the microalgae from photobioreactors (16.6 kg CO 2 eq. emissions). Microalgae from the photobioreactor use the least land (only 83.7Pt), while wheat straw occupies the most land (1770Pt) for production of 1 kg biokerosene. Hotspot analyses are done through subprocesses’ contributions, and the most influencing flows and parameters are identified. A series of sensitivity and Monte Carlo analyses are made to study the indicators’ sensitivity and robustness. Finally, a scenario analysis is performed to find options that could be used to lower the life-cycle impacts with microalgae.
