title: Carbon removal and the politics of asset revaluation
abstract: The political economy of climate change mitigation has variously been conceptualized as a struggle between fossil and ‘green’ coalitions or capital fractions. More recently, Colgan et al. (Citation2021) have reconceptualized climate politics as an existential struggle over asset revaluation between holders of climate-forcing and climate-vulnerable assets. In this commentary, we argue that the anticipated role of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) and the renewed attention to carbon capture and storage (CCS) in climate change mitigation have the potential to profoundly reshape these dynamics – a factor which has not yet been adequately considered. Specifically, we contend that expectations of CDR and CCS enable claims to residual and ‘hard-to-abate’ emissions as a political strategy to resist decarbonization and avoid asset stranding, while simultaneously creating opportunities to revalue fossil assets as indispensable to net-zero pathways. To develop this argument, we critically review the literature on asset stranding and the politics of asset revaluation and propose four research avenues to foreground the underexplored role of CDR, CCS, residual emissions, and hard-to-abate-ness. In doing so, we connect critical CDR scholarship to broader political economy debates on climate change mitigation, including asset revaluation, fossil fuel phase-out, green industrial policy, and the distributive politics of climate policy.

title: Occupational choice, human capital formation and life-cycle earnings
Revisiting Momentum Through Dynamic Kernel Learning
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper revisits momentum through a dynamic kernel framework that links return continuation to the speed at which return‐relevant shocks propagate through prices. Using nearly 60 years of US equity data, we estimate nonnegative and geometric kernels that govern how past returns are weighted over time. The estimated decay parameter rises sharply after 2000, indicating faster dissipation of return persistence and a shorter effective horizon for continuation, coinciding with the documented weakening of traditional 12–1 momentum. In out‐of‐sample tests, the structured kernel models match or outperform common machine‐learning benchmarks while retaining economic interpretability, and these gains remain robust after controlling for volatility timing and trading frictions. The framework provides a parsimonious tool for tracking time variation in return propagation and for adapting momentum implementations to changing market conditions.

title: The other China shock: EU critical and strategic minerals dependency in comparative-historical perspective
abstract: The current geopolitical saliency of critical and strategic minerals (CSMs) in Europe is not novel, but a cyclical phenomenon which has waxed and waned through several iterations since World War I. A comparative-historical analysis of these cycles reveals both recurrent and unique features of the current resurgence. I identify two broad repeating vectors of contestation since WWII. First, Europe has at times faced a threat to conditions of access for critical minerals, whereby peripheral producers have sought a greater share of the surplus from extractive industries (a challenge from the South). Second, great power rivals (principally the Soviet Union during the Cold War and now China) have at times been perceived as threatening Europe’s access per se to CSMs via potential disruption of physical supply lines for geopolitical advantage (a peer challenge, or challenge from the East). The contemporary Chinese challenge synthesises both axes of contestation. China has already successfully parlayed CSM market power into the development of technologically advanced downstream industries, while the overwhelming concentration of extraction and/or processing of many CSMs within China provides the capability to disrupt physical supply. This unique combination presents a new and distinct threat to European positions within key value chains.

title: The emperor has no batteries: internal protection and Europe's uneven bid for electromobility
abstract: This article refines the developmental network state (DNS) concept by arguing that DNS functions are not generic capabilities but fundamentally growth stage-specific, particularly in capital-intensive, technology-intensive sectors undergoing rapid scaling. The key theoretical contribution is that internal protection against the structural risks of hyperscaling (solvency risk, demand volatility, operational errors and cost cliff dynamics) operates independently from external protection against unfair competition. While external protection (tariffs, trade remedies) receives substantial theoretical and policy attention, internal protection remains undertheorised despite being equally consequential. By looking at the case of EV battery scale-ups in Sweden and France, we show that internal protection operates through two analytically distinct mechanisms: ex-ante institutional embedding, which makes firm failure politically more costly by anchoring firms within state-coordinated value chains and strategic ownership structures; and ex-post crisis support, which provides refinancing, demand stabilisation and restructuring capacity when hyperscaling collides with macroeconomic shocks. The article argues that neither mechanism alone suffices; effective DNS requires both forms of credible commitment signalled across political cycles. This theoretical framework enables a more precise diagnosis of why industrial policy succeeds or fails in high-stakes technological transitions, moving the literature towards analysis of institutional alignment between protection mechanisms and firm lifecycle stages.

title: Structural Breaks in the Taylor Rule
abstract: ABSTRACT Stillwagon (this issue) tests extensively for structural breaks in a dynamic Taylor rule for US data and finds no breaks over 2001–2025, whether using Bai–Perron tests or multiplicative indicator saturation. The current paper complements and builds on Stillwagon by focusing on features specific to three Fed chairs (Bernanke, Yellen, and Powell) during 2006–2025, and on the zero lower bound. The Taylor rule is chair‐specific; and the zero lower bound affects the Taylor rule for Yellen's and Powell's tenures. These economically significant structural breaks are detectable by multiplicative indicator saturation that focuses on those features, whereas the broad‐spectrum multiplicative indicator saturation in Stillwagon misses these breaks. Such structural breaks limit the interpretability and usefulness of the Taylor rule for monetary policy.

title: Benefiting from Culture Wars: Resource Mobilization in Polarized Issue Domains
abstract: Organizations engaging with contested social issues may struggle to mobilize resources due to disapproval from hostile audiences. Yet, some may benefit from increased support from sympathetic audiences, leaving unclear when such support will outweigh opposition. We propose that variation in audience reactions depends partly on how contestation is structured. We theorize that ideological polarization—the extent to which opposing stances on an issue sort along ideological lines—may enhance resource mobilization in contested issue domains. As polarization increases, contested issues pit opposing identities against each other and heighten threats to sympathetic audiences’ worldviews. New ventures in more polarized domains may attract greater support as sympathetic audiences respond by investing in aligned ventures, a mechanism we term “compensatory investment.” This relationship strengthens under conditions that heighten identity threat: when issues are highly salient, making them central political battlegrounds, and when audiences on both sides rely on core moral foundations to evaluate the issue, so that disagreements are experienced as moral violations. Analyses of U.S.-based Kickstarter campaigns (2009–2020) support our predictions and provide evidence consistent with compensatory investment. Our study highlights polarization as a key source of issue heterogeneity, introduces the mechanism of compensatory investment, and specifies when polarization enhances resource mobilization.

title: Leaders as Theorists
abstract: Abstract Research on leadership has long focused on two extremes, either on individual traits (or styles and behaviours) or on relationships and context. We argue that neither extreme explains where leadership originates from or how it produces the collective outcomes it is credited with. We propose a third view that is neither a compromise between nor a variant of these extremes. We argue that leaders are theorists. Leaders are forward‐looking actors who, at any level of an organization, formulate causal theories and frame problems. The value of leader theories is realized, amplified or constrained through social mechanisms. Theorizing is not one activity among many – it is the act that constitutes leading itself. The very factors foregrounded by recent work in leadership (like context, trust, and relationality) are not the starting point of leadership but emerge as leaders advocate, adopt, test, and scale theories. The leader‐as‐theorist agenda is normative and interventionist, highlighting how leader theorizing and causal reasoning can be improved and taught. We close by laying out a research agenda for studying leaders as theorists.

title: Making ‘Gender‐Lens Investing’ Work: Cultivating Proto‐Infrastructure for Alternative Financial Futures
abstract: Abstract This study examines how elites engage in prefigurative organizing and construct the institutional infrastructure for enacting alternative futures. We investigate their engagement in gender‐lens investing (GLI) within the global movement for gender equality in finance and investment. Using fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) of 28 GLI mutual funds and exchange‐traded funds, we diagnose how fund managers combine available resources to prefigure GLI as investment products, identifying distinct configurations of symbolic, relational, and material resources through which GLI is enacted and made recognizable and actionable in the present. In doing so, we show that prefigurative efforts are not exclusive to grassroots activism, and demonstrate that the infrastructure supporting alternative practices is built through elites' efforts to recombine existing institutional resources into proto‐infrastructure. We therefore contribute a combinatorial perspective of prefigurative organizing that highlights the role of elites, and introduces proto‐infrastructure as a conceptual device for theorizing how prefigurative practices begin to acquire an incipient institutional form prior to the full consolidation of institutional infrastructure. This combinatorial perspective offers a new and timely lens for understanding GLI, impact investing, and the gender equality movement under current political backlash.

title: List of People Who Reviewed for this Special Issue
Issue‐Centric Orchestration of Climate Transition: The Case of Transition Risk Governance
abstract: Abstract A decade ago, climate transition fell outside the mandates of financial regulators, central banks, accounting standard‐setting bodies, and financial‐market actors. Today, it is central to financial‐market governance aimed at steering business conduct toward a low‐carbon economy. Drawing on a longitudinal study of climate transition as a financial governance concern from 2010 to 2021, we show how governance authority over emerging sustainability concerns is assembled when no actor has an established mandate to address those concerns. Informed by Latour's concept of matter of concern, our analysis reveals how climate transition became constituted as transition risk, was stabilized through the private industry‐led Task Force on Climate‐related Financial Disclosures, and was translated across interconnected governance sites. We develop a three‐phase process model of issue‐centric orchestration – issue emergence, stabilization, and translation – unpacking how governance authority is progressively assembled through the trajectory of transition risk. The study contributes to public–private governance research by showing how private governance initiatives can reshape and extend, rather than displace or reduce, public authority. It further advances orchestration research by showing how interdependent governance arrangements form around shared concerns across governance domains and jurisdictions.

title: Generative AI and the architecture of knowledge work: Expertise bypass, exchange governability, and shifting bottlenecks
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Research on GenAI and work has largely focused on tasks. We ask when task‐level effects alter knowledge‐work industry architecture: the allocation of activities across firm boundaries. Using a three‐stage abductive design—an executive roundtable, a panel of 626 firm websites (2017–2025), and 33 interviews plus two further roundtables with C‐level executives and corporate directors—we document divergent repositioning: professional services firms foreground relational value, while interface‐oriented technology firms emphasize scalable interfaces. We find that activity reallocation is shaped by two independently varying dimensions: expertise bypass and exchange governability. Their intersection yields four configurations: contestable reallocation, persistent bundles with selective insourcing, federated expert provision, and integrated expert provision. We extend industry architecture theory by explaining change when production and exchange conditions shift separately. Managerial Summary GenAI is not simply making knowledge work more efficient—it may be changing which organizations perform which work. We document that professional services firms are emphasizing relationship‐driven, judgment‐intensive work, while interface‐oriented technology firms are extending scalable delivery. Our framework explains why task exposure alone does not determine where work moves. We distinguish between expertise bypass—whether GenAI can produce an output without the expertise previously required—and exchange governability—whether that activity can be specified, verified, priced, and warranted across firm boundaries. Where both are present, work becomes contestable and may be reallocated. Where they diverge, highly exposed activities may remain bundled, while less exposed, human‐intensive work may move through federated specialist models. These conditions shape which organizational forms become viable.

title: Private Firm Disclosures and Public Firms' Debt Choice
Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal acknowledges the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. Y. Lin gratefully acknowledges financial support from the NUS Research Grant [Grants A-8001725 and A-8004426]. R. Lu and X. Zhang acknowledge the financial support of the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 71903005, 72402005, and 72472001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01919 .

title: Recommender Systems Under Privacy Protection
Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty
abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: A. Delavande acknowledges funding from the Economic and Social Research Council Research Centre on Micro-Social Change [Grants ES/L009153/1 and ES/S012486/1] and the National Institute on Aging [Grant P01AG008291]. J. Ganguli acknowledges research support from the Economic and Social Research Council [Grant ES/K00168X/1]. F. Mengel acknowledges support from the European Research Council [Grant DYNNET-805017]. Ethical approval was obtained by the Ethics Social Sciences subcommittee at the University of Essex in August 2015. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06232 .

title: Growth Paths in Early Machine Learning Ventures: Technical Configuration and Competitive Advantage Over Time
abstract: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them. Through an inductive, multicase study tracking six early-stage machine learning ventures in an accelerator program, we explore how their phases of specialization and exploration may be constrained by properties of the underlying technology. Our findings show how training data, learning paradigms, and model outputs depend on one another and on the applications they serve, and how these relationships change over time. This interdependence shapes firms’ growth paths, alternately expanding or limiting the strategic options available to them. Characteristics that confer an early competitive advantage can constrain later growth. We discuss the implications for strategy research on competitive advantage and path dependence in machine learning ventures.

title: Signaling Corporate Resilience Under Extreme Weather Shocks: Strategy, Visibility, and Market Responses
abstract: ABSTRACT Extreme weather provides a negative public signal about firms' operating conditions, while their capacity to withstand disruption remains difficult for external evaluators (including investors) to observe. We develop a signaling game in which costly, observable strategic commitments can convey otherwise latent resilience. Using Chinese A‐share firm data (2011–2022), we examine annual stock price limit‐down events under the conventional approximately 10% daily price limit with panel Poisson regression and a complementary generalized additive model. Extreme‐weather exposure is positively associated with limit‐down incidence, particularly among firms with greater public visibility. The association is weaker among firms with AI‐related patents, declining accounts payable, or improving environmental (E‐pillar) performance. These findings are consistent with technological, supply‐chain liquidity, and environmental commitments serving as positive, countervailing resilience signals. By examining realized downside events at an exchange‐defined boundary, we extend climate–finance research and highlight the role of strategic resilience decisions and credible disclosure in market evaluation.

title: Logistics Services in a Circular Economy: Finding the Fit Between Logistics Service Buyers and the Providers
abstract: ABSTRACT Logistics is essential for the circular economy, yet little is known about whether the services that logistics service providers offer align with the logistics service buyers need. Drawing on contingency theory, this study examines this fit at three levels: strategic (the circular strategy a service supports), functional (the logistics processes it performs) and capability (the resources and know‐how behind it). This study employs qualitative content analysis of corporate reports and websites of 45 large Swedish companies including 35 buyers across seven sectors and 10 providers of two types, traditional logistics service providers and waste management companies. The findings show that logistics services in the circular economy extend well beyond returns and reverse logistics. Across the sectors, the buyers need logistics services strategically to support prevention, life extension and material circularity and functionally for logistics optimization, reverse‐flow coordination, material processing, service logistics and platform coordination. And these logistics service needs are dependent on governance, specialized assets, circular know‐how, data‐handling and decarbonization. Logistics service providers address these needs in two ways. Traditional providers' services are more product centric, and waste management companies' services are more materials centric. No single provider type meets the needs of every sector, and the three‐level framework shows where fit and misfit arise. For buyers, it guides whether to rely on one provider, combine providers or keep functions in‐house. For providers, it shows where circular offerings are missing and where joint service bundles are needed.

title: A Meta‐Analysis of the Twin Transition: The Impact of Digitalization on Firms' Eco‐Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT In the twin transition, firms pursue digitalization and environmental sustainability simultaneously, an effort that draws growing academic interest. However, empirical insights into the relationship between digital technologies and eco‐innovation remain lacking. With a quantitative synthesis and meta‐regression of 38 empirical studies published in high‐impact journals, encompassing 587 effect sizes, the current research clarifies the heterogeneous nature of this relationship across technology types and environmental outcomes. Digitalization is positively and statistically significantly associated with eco‐innovation. Across technology types, artificial intelligence, digital innovation, and smart product platforms show the strongest positive associations, while robotics and Industry 4.0 technologies yield weaker evidence. Across environmental outcomes, the results indicate robust positive associations with green innovation but negative or null associations on average for decarbonization. In revealing that digitalization alone might not be sufficient to achieve emissions reductions without complementary environmental strategies, this study contributes to twin transition literature and clarifies the heterogeneous nature of the digitalization‐eco‐innovation relationships. For managers seeking to balance digital investments with environmental objectives, it also offers practical recommendations.

title: Digital Intelligence for Environmental Governance: How Analytics, IoT, and AI Foster Sustainability‐Oriented Innovation and Interconnectivity
abstract: ABSTRACT Emerging digital technologies are transforming how governments sense, interpret, and respond to environmental challenges. In this study, we develop and test a dynamic capability‐based model that explains how analytics insight capability, Internet of Things (IOT) intensity, and artificial intelligence (AI) assimilation, collectively termed emerging technological capabilities, enhance environmental governance through sustainability‐oriented innovation and digital interconnectivity. We utilize the dynamic capabilities view and the resource‐based view frameworks to conceptualize the technological capabilities that enable organizations to integrate knowledge, reconfigure resources, and deploy digital assets toward sustainable outcomes. Using survey data from public‐sector agencies, we use PLS‐SEM to test the sequential paths from digital capabilities to knowledge integration, innovation, interconnectivity, and governance effectiveness. The results demonstrate that well‐coordinated analytics, IoT, and AI capabilities stimulate sustainability‐oriented innovation and foster interagency data integration, leading to more transparent, adaptive, and evidence‐based environmental governance. This paper makes a theoretical contribution by bridging dynamic capabilities view and resource‐based view in the context of digital sustainability, demonstrating how the configuration of digital resources into higher order dynamic capabilities transforms technological potential into environmental governance value. From a managerial perspective, this study positions digital intelligence as an engine of sustainable public management.

title: A Sequential Process Framework for ESG Activation: Translating Platform Capabilities Into Organizational Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT This study proposes a sequential process through which organizations translate data collected and managed by environmental, social, and governance (ESG) platforms into institutionalized sustainability performance shifting the attention from ESG measurement for reporting to data activation for the organizational strategy. We develop an integrated framework and empirically test it using survey data from 580 corporate entities headquartered in EU‐27 countries and subject to Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD)‐related disclosure obligations. The data are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM). The empirical results highlight, on the one hand, the ability of the ESG platform to act as a critical technological antecedent capable of significantly driving ESG–management by objectives (MBO) integration ( β = 0.542); and, on the other hand, how the integration of sustainability metrics into performance management systems directly promotes the rigorous alignment of managerial incentive structures ( β = 0.612), while exerting a significant direct effect on overall sustainability performance ( β = 0.276). The paper highlights how it is possible to turn double materiality and regulatory demands into integrated control mechanisms, showing that ESG tracking delivers value only when coupled with data‐driven MBO and ESG‐linked compensation.

title: Bridging ESG and Financial Performance: A Balanced Scorecard and AHP Approach to Strategic Assessment
abstract: ABSTRACT Aligning environmental, social, and governance (ESG) objectives with financial performance remains a critical challenge for organizations committed to responsible and transparent operations. This study presents a structured approach to integrating ESG and financial key performance indicators (KPIs) using the balanced scorecard (BSC) and the analytic hierarchy process (AHP). The BSC provides a comprehensive framework, anchored in stakeholder, resource‐based, legitimacy, agency and triple‐bottom‐line perspectives, that connects ESG metrics with financial outcomes across four strategic perspectives: financial, customer, internal business processes (IBP), and learning & growth (L&G). The AHP complements this by enabling the prioritization and weighting of KPIs through expert input and stakeholder preferences, offering a transparent and data‐driven method for decision‐making. Together, these tools support a clear strategic alignment between sustainability goals and business performance, identifying key areas where ESG efforts deliver measurable value. This integrated approach contributes to the field of sustainability assessment and policy modelling by offering a replicable, stakeholder‐focused framework for performance management. It enables organizations to make informed decisions that advance ESG commitments while maintaining financial accountability.

title: Informality and the Business Environment as Drivers of Carbon Emissions: The Moderating Role of Environmental Regulatory Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT A low‐carbon transition cannot succeed while a substantial share of business activity remains beyond the effective reach of regulation. This study examines how informality and the business environment shape carbon emissions and whether regulatory quality conditions the environmental consequences of informal production. The analysis uses an annual panel of 145 economies over 2005–2020, combining data from the World Development Indicators and World Bank. Informality is measured using dynamic general equilibrium and Multiple Indicators Multiple Causes estimates, while nine disaggregated business‐environment dimensions capture firm entry, infrastructure, finance, taxation, trade and commercial institutions. Standard negative binomial regression constitutes the principal estimator, with Poisson regression, alternative informality measurement and income‐group estimations used for robustness. The results show that informality is consistently associated with lower aggregate CO 2 emissions, with the relationship strongest in low‐income economies and weakest in high‐income countries. This apparent environmental advantage reflects the small‐scale, labour‐intensive and capital‐constrained nature of informal production rather than inherently cleaner business practices. Most business‐environment indicators are associated with higher emissions, particularly in lower‐ to middle‐income economies, suggesting that enterprise expansion and energy demand may outpace the diffusion of cleaner technologies. Environmental regulatory quality moderates the negative informality–emissions relationship. The findings show that neither informality, formalisation nor business‐environment reform is intrinsically green. Governments should therefore align formalisation and business reforms with proportionate environmental regulation, green finance, cleaner energy and supply‐chain accountability to reconcile enterprise development with climate objectives.

title: A COM-B and conservation of resources view of employees’ pro-environmental behavior in hospitality: The conditioning role of well-being
Affective hospitality: A new framework for applying ability emotional intelligence to hospitality
abstract: Extensive research shows that hospitality workers’ emotional intelligence (EI) impacts key work outcomes, including performance and satisfaction. However, the underlying emotional skills remain poorly understood because scholars have primarily studied emotion-related hospitality competencies in isolation, rarely examining the mechanisms that could link and explain them. In the present article, we introduce a new framework called “Affective Hospitality” to provide an integrated and systematic approach to emotional skills in hospitality based on the Four-domain model of ability EI. Specifically, we discuss how the EI abilities to perceive, use, understand, and manage emotions may be the underlying skills that enable critical emotion-related competencies in hospitality, namely service delivery , conforming to display rules, employing emotional labor , as well as workers’ customer-orientation , resilience, and co-creation of emotional value . Through this new framework, we propose new lines of research in hospitality that emerge directly from this integrated approach. For example, researchers could investigate specific emotional skills covered by ability EI theory, such as emotional sensitivity to explain adaptive service delivery or interpersonal emotion regulation to better understand value co-creation.

title: Strengthening service research through replication: contributions, guidelines, and a checklist
abstract: Purpose Despite increasing recognition of the importance of replication studies in confirming or refining our understanding of established phenomena, they remain relatively scarce in service research. This paper has two primary objectives. First, it aims to enhance conceptual clarity by developing a taxonomy of replication studies and their respective contributions to the service literature. Second, it provides practical guidance for conducting and publishing quantitative replication studies that generate meaningful value for the service management field. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts a conceptual and reflective approach rooted in the broader replication literature and existing replication studies in service research. Findings This paper classifies replication studies along three dimensions – replication fidelity, researcher independence, and claim provenance and demonstrates that such studies can yield substantial contributions that extend beyond mere verification. In particular, we develop an integrated framework that distinguishes four complementary contribution pathways and associated goals – theory-confirming (validating), theory-extending (extending), methodological (refining), and practical contributions (translating), and illustrate each with examples from the service literature. In addition, we propose a five-step set of guidelines for conducting, writing, and evaluating replication studies. Originality/value This paper is the first to systematically examine the key dimensions of replication studies and to develop a comprehensive framework that delineates the diverse contributions such studies can generate. In addition, it offers practical guidance for conducting replication studies in service research, thereby lowering the barriers for service scholars to engage in replication work. To support this effort, we develop a comprehensive checklist that enables authors, reviewers, and editors to systematically assess the quality of replication studies.

title: How does home region focus boost international performance for INVs in the international post-entry phase? The mediating role of international opportunity-pursuing orientation
abstract: Purpose This study aims to improve our understanding of international opportunity pursuing orientation (IOO) through which home region focus affects international performance. Design/methodology/approach The authors collected a sample of 360 International New Ventures (INVs) in the international post-entry phase from a two-wave survey in China. They tested the mediating effects of IOOs using structural equation modeling. Findings Both existing and envisaged IOOs are positively associated with international performance. Home region focus is positively related to existing IOO but negatively related to envisaged IOO. Existing and envisaged IOOs play a significant mediating role between home region focus and international performance. Research limitations/implications This study advances the regionalization hypothesis literature and international entrepreneurship perspective by introducing two new mediators, existing and envisaged IOOs, to link home region focus to international performance. Practical implications Managers should foster existing (envisaged) IOO to transform high (low) home region focus into superior international performance. Policymakers should help firms develop IOOs by organizing managers to visit abroad and formulating the function of embassies and consulates to collect foreign information. Originality/value While home region focus is essential for performance, there is a dearth of research explaining the underlying mechanisms through which home region focus affects performance. IOO is a novel antecedent of international performance among INVs at the international post-entry stage.

title: Universities’ knowledge exchange efficiency and regional innovativeness: an empirical analysis
abstract: Abstract This study examines the relationship between universities’ knowledge exchange (KE) activities and regional innovation. Using panel data on UK universities from 2008 to 2019, we first estimate activity-specific stochastic frontier models to assess KE efficiency of both formal research commercialisation activities and informal academic engagement activities. We then employ Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood regression to examine the associations between universities’ KE efficiency and regional innovativeness. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity in universities’ KE efficiency across activities. Licensing and spin-off efficiency exhibit positive associations with regional innovation in both the main and two-year lag specifications, while consultancy efficiency is positively associated with regional innovation only in the two-year lag analysis. Patenting efficiency becomes statistically significant in the two-year lag analysis, whereas other KE activities generally exhibit no significant associations with regional innovativeness. These findings highlight the heterogeneous relationships between different KE activities and regional innovation. The study advances Regional Innovation Systems theory by demonstrating that KE efficiency, rather than KE volume, is an important factor associated with regional innovation outcomes. It also provides policy-relevant insights into the importance of prioritising high-efficiency KE channels and aligning KE strategies with regional absorptive capacity and industrial structure.

title: Does Releasing Earnings When the Audit Is Less Complete Increase Audit Costs?
journal_name: Auditing: A Journal of Practice & Theory

title: Credibility displacement in algorithmic financial reporting: a critical review of AI, disclosure credibility and capital-market consequences
abstract: Purpose This review examines how financial-reporting credibility is shaped when algorithmic systems enter the reporting chain. It asks where credibility is produced, tested and understood when artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, large language models, eXtensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL) analytics and related tools affect reporting information. Design/methodology/approach The paper combines a search and screening procedure informed by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) with a concept-centric synthesis. The evidence base comprises a 226-paper curated core and a 144-paper close-synthesis subset. Sensitivity analyses re-examine the 39-record outlet boundary and the close-synthesis threshold. Findings The evidence remains dispersed across research on textual disclosure and natural language processing (NLP), audit analytics and assurance, structured reporting using XBRL, market interpretation, accounting information systems (AIS) implementation and AI governance. Across these streams, algorithms can improve reporting processes but may also alter the grounds on which reporting assertions are accepted. We describe the latter possibility as credibility displacement: model-related output, provenance or validation partly substitutes for scrutiny of the underlying assertion or for identifiable professional and institutional safeguards. Originality/value The review defines algorithmic financial reporting as a reporting-chain phenomenon rather than a general label for technology adoption. It distinguishes four sites: preparation, assurance, machine-readable presentation and algorithmic interpretation. Governance operates across these sites as a cross-cutting condition, making the proposed displacement mechanism more focused and empirically testable.

title: The evolution of power asymmetries in interorganisational open strategy
Collaborative tie termination and focal inventors’ exploratory and exploitative innovation
How Access‐Based Consumption Turns Abusive: A Self‐Destruction Account of the Extended Self
abstract: ABSTRACT Prior research has examined consumer–product relationships across ownership and access contexts, but less is known about why temporary access may lead consumers to use products harshly or excessively. This research develops fear of ephemerality as an additional psychological mechanism explaining why abusive product use may be more likely in temporary access than ownership contexts. We focus on abusive product use, which refers to harsh use or overuse that can harm the product or consumer, and compare abusive usage behaviors toward consumer‐owned products and consumer‐accessed products. Drawing on self‐preservation and self‐destruction theories within the extended‐self framework, the present research employs both field data collection and experimental evidence. We find that accessed products, compared to owned products, are more prone to abusive use. This pattern is consistent with a fear‐based shift from self‐preservation toward self‐destruction when the temporary nature of access becomes salient. Furthermore, fear of ephemerality explains why accessed products are more prone to abuse than owned products. We also examine how self‐esteem and self‐extension tendency shape the strength of this effect as boundary conditions.

title: Less Disclosed, More Minimal: How Soft Launches of Romantic Relationships Promote Minimalist Consumption
abstract: ABSTRACT Soft and hard launches of romantic relationships have become increasingly prevalent forms of relationship disclosure in digital environments, yet little is known about whether these forms of disclosure influence subsequent consumer behavior. Across four experiments, we show that soft (vs. hard) relationship disclosures increase consumers' preference for minimalist consumption. We identify preference for subtle self‐presentation as a potential explanatory mechanism underlying this effect: soft relationship disclosures increase preference for subtle self‐presentation, which subsequently enhances preference for minimalist consumption. Relationship privacy orientation moderates this process, such that the indirect effect of soft launch on minimalist consumption via preference for subtle self‐presentation strengthens as relation privacy increases. A marketplace urgency cue also moderates this process, such that the indirect effect holds when the cue is absent but diminishes when it is present. These findings demonstrate how romantic relationship disclosure types influence subsequent marketplace preferences.

title: AI error or AI creativity? Attributional ambiguity in AI-generated expectation-violating prerolls
Tourism Development and Rural Income Growth: A Micro-Macro Dual Perspective
abstract: This study examines whether household income gains from tourism aggregate into regional growth. Drawing on structural transformation theory and Stolper–Samuelson factor-price logic, it treats tourism as a sector-specific demand shock. A time-varying difference-in-differences design applied to China Family Panel Studies data (2012–2022) estimates the household-level effect of the National Rural Tourism Demonstration County policy, while spatial panel models on provincial data (2011–2023) account for province-specific trajectories and exposure to the National Rural Revitalization Strategy. Tourism raises rural household income and is positively associated with provincial rural income. The regional relationship is predominantly spatially indirect; only wage income shows a significant positive local association. Human capital and consumer-market development strengthen the tourism–wage relationship, but bootstrap tests find no evidence that employment reallocation mediates it. Evidence for an income channel, therefore, does not establish the employment reallocation mechanism. Tourism strategies should pair destination promotion with workforce development and interprovincial coordination.

title: Digital transformation of service ecosystems: an orchestration perspective
abstract: Purpose This study investigates how digital transformation unfolds within logistics service ecosystems and how inter-actor operational connections and coordinating roles change over time from an orchestration perspective. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted a case study of three international inland ports in China. Data were triangulated through interviews, observations and documents to capture ecosystem-level orchestration practices and transformation evolution. Findings The authors developed a process model that identifies three evolutionary stages of the digital transformation of service ecosystems: developing digital connectivity, tapping digital service potential and co-creating digital value. The model demonstrates how actors employ resource and network orchestration at each stage. The analysis reveals how these two forms of orchestration interact and how orchestration dynamics change over time. Originality/value This study shifts the focus of digital transformation research from a few focal firms to service ecosystems overall. It theorizes a three-stage transformation process, reveals the evolving interplay between resource and network orchestration, shows that different actors can assume orchestration leadership, and provides actionable recommendations for managers seeking to digitally transform logistics and supply chain service ecosystems.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: Walk the talk: how procurement professionals' interpretations shape social sustainability cascading
abstract: Purpose Procurement professionals shape how firms translate their commitments to social sustainability into supplier-facing governance, which can vary markedly, even within the same firm. This study explains this variation by theorizing how procurement professionals interpret their role and translate engagement with suppliers into governance practices. Design/methodology/approach The study draws on constructivist grounded theory and interviews with 27 professionals across organizational contexts. The analysis combines iterative coding, constant comparison, theoretical sampling, and abductive engagement with sensitizing literature. Findings The study develops a process model that explains cascading depth from a people-centric perspective. The interviewed procurement professionals differed on whether they construed their remit to include social sustainability, whether supplier-facing action appeared worth pursuing, and whether more improvement-oriented engagement appeared feasible. This situated judgment shaped whether cascading is enacted predominantly through procedural compliance or through more generative supplier-facing practice. Prospective paradoxical sensemaking helped explain how more generative supplier-facing responses could remain actionable under competing commercial demands, as professionals saw anticipated social and commercial consequences as relevant to their judgment in the present. Originality/value The study reframes cascading depth as a matter of how procurement professionals enact governance mechanisms. It specifies interpretive and relational conditions that remain underexplored in the literature on sustainable behavioral supply chain management. It extends paradoxical sensemaking research on how tensions are framed to include how more generative responses may be established and sustained in practice.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: The end of laissez-faire leadership? Problematizing and revitalizing a neglected construct
abstract: Leadership approaches defined by inaction, such as laissez-faire leadership, remain understudied, leaving theory ill-equipped to address organizational challenges where knowing when to step back may be as important as knowing when to act. Where such work exists, it largely frames leader inaction as dysfunctional, reducing laissez-faire leadership to a one-dimensional negative construct. This framing constrains theoretical development by obscuring when, why, and under what conditions leader non-intervention might be appropriate or effective. To address this gap, we conduct a problematizing review of the laissez-faire leadership literature to examine how implicit assumptions have constrained theoretical development. We identify six such assumptions: (1) leadership necessarily involves action; (2) existing definitions adequately capture the construct; (3) negative findings are independent of measurement choices; (4) laissez-faire leadership is inherently negative; (5) current theoretical approaches sufficiently capture leader inaction; and (6) laissez-faire leadership reflects a stable leader tendency. We argue that these assumptions have restricted theoretical development and reinforced a pattern of largely unchallenged negative findings. Drawing on signaling theory and leader role theory, we reconceptualize laissez-faire leadership as leader behavioral non-intervention. Building on this reconceptualization, we outline a step-by-step agenda for future research that advances new conceptual, theoretical, and methodological approaches to studying leader non-intervention and clarifies when and why laissez-faire leadership may produce a range of outcomes. Together, this framework opens new avenues for theory development, empirical research, and leadership practice.

title: Housing Price Pressure and Employee Lawsuits: Evidence From China
abstract: ABSTRACT This study explores how rising housing prices affect employee–employer conflict through the lens of employee lawsuits. Using a sample of Chinese listed firms from 2013 to 2019, we find that the likelihood of employee lawsuits against a firm increases with housing prices in the city where the firm is located. To establish causality, we employ a staggered difference‐in‐differences approach based on the implementation of home purchase restriction policies designed to curb housing price growth, and we also use land supply as an instrument for housing prices. Mechanism and cross‐sectional analyses show that psychological pressure can be the key mechanism driving employee lawsuits. Additional analyses demonstrate that housing price pressure leads to substantiated employee lawsuits instead of vexatious lawsuits. Also, it does not significantly increase other types of litigation, indicating that the psychological pressure primarily affects internal labor relations rather than external stakeholder disputes. These findings indicate that external cost‐of‐living pressures can erode workplace relations and escalate labor conflict. Overall, our paper provides novel evidence on how macroeconomic housing market conditions shape employee–employer dynamics and labor litigation.
journal_name: Journal of International Financial Management & Accounting

title: Retail depositor strategies in Russian regions during the pandemic shock: whether to withdraw and why
Hiding in the green fog: Climate policy uncertainty, greenwashing, and stock price crash risk
Environmental tax reform and corporate group debt distribution: Empirical evidence from Chinese listed companies in heavy pollution industries
Public scrutiny and the strategic pivot toward green innovation in multinational enterprises
The cost of the buzz? A sufficiency threshold perspective on digital transformation disclosure and cost of equity capital
abstract: Firms disclose information about complex internal activities to keep capital markets informed about their long-term value. We engage two rival predictions, the 'more-is-better' assumption in information risk theory and the 'more-is-noisy' assumption in technological fad perspectives, and ask what shape best characterizes the association between firms' digital transformation (DT) disclosure and the cost of equity capital. Using FTSE350 firms from 2010 to 2020 and adopting a question-driven, phenomenon-based approach, we document a non-linear association in which both traditions describe the same relationship over different ranges of disclosure. Where disclosure is sparse, capital markets cannot separate commitment from fashion and additional disclosure in this range is associated with a higher cost of equity capital; where disclosure becomes substantively informative, the information benefit dominates and the association reverses. The estimated sufficiency threshold, 0.0149% of annual report text, is reached by almost no firm in our sample. Prevailing disclosure practice therefore sits on the ascending portion of the association, while the descending portion is identified from a thin upper tail. The concavity of this relationship is robust to excluding the highest-disclosing firms, to winsorisation, to selection correction, and to leaving out any single firm. We discuss implications for theories of corporate disclosure of complex internal activity and for the design of DT disclosure policy.

title: From dual-use to omni-use: How firms' strategic responses reproduce institutional lock-in in European technology governance
Investigating the Sensitivity of Growth Mixture Model Results to Covariate-Informed Scoring
abstract: Growth mixture models (GMMs) are commonly used to identify heterogeneous developmental trajectories in longitudinal data. When GMMs are estimated using a two-step approach—first scoring instruments via item response theory (IRT) and then fitting mixture models—scoring decisions can influence class enumeration and growth parameter estimates. An unresolved methodological question is whether covariates should be incorporated during the IRT scoring stage. Using Monte Carlo simulations and an empirical application, we examined whether covariate-informed scoring improves class enumeration and parameter recovery relative to unconditional scoring. Results indicate that covariate-informed scoring provides an advantage when covariates influence the measurement model.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: Longitudinal Sentiment Analysis with Social Media Text Data: A Tutorial and New Methods
abstract: Longitudinal social media text data provide important opportunities for studying how sentiment changes over time, but they also create methodological challenges because unstructured text data need to be transformed into analyzable sentiment score before statistical modeling can be applied. The current study is designed as a methodological tutorial that provides a practical workflow for longitudinal sentiment analysis. Specifically, we illustrate how researchers can move from raw social media posts to cleaned text, extract sentiment scores using both lexicon-based and large language model (LLM)-based approaches, aggregate irregular post-level scores into person-period longitudinal data, and fit statistical models to examine sentiment trajectories over time. Using longitudinal Twitter/X data as an empirical example, we compared AFINN and LLaMA as representative sentiment extraction methods and apply several longitudinal models, including the Heteroscedastic Linear Mixed Model (HLMM), Growth Curve Model (GCM), First-Order Autoregressive Model (AR(1)), and the proposed Trajectory model with Recurrent Autocorrelation and Cumulative Event-triggered effects (TRACE). Using AFINN-based sentiment scores in the empirical illustration, the TRACE showed better performance than traditional longitudinal models across three evaluation criteria (i.e., RMSE, WAIC, and LOOIC). Overall, these findings suggest that the choice of sentiment extraction method can influence later statistical modeling results, and TRACE provides a useful alternative for modeling both temporal dependence and event-driven changes in longitudinal text data.

title: Frailty Models in the Structural Equation Modeling Framework
abstract: Frailty models extend survival analysis models to accommodate recurrent events by incorporating random effects to account for the dependence among clustered event times. Despite their relevance for behavioral and social science research, frailty models remain underutilized, in part due to limited integration with commonly used analytic frameworks. This paper presents a comprehensive treatment of frailty models and their specification and estimation in structural equation modeling (SEM) programs using multilevel and multivariate model specifications. We review discrete-time and Cox survival models and demonstrate how each is specified using SEM software. We then extend these models to include random effects and outline multiple specification strategies along with their associated data structures. Using empirical data on adolescent sleep latency, we illustrate the implementation of six alternative frailty model specifications and compare their parameter estimates. Recommendations for model specifications are discussed.

title: Distal Outcomes in Latent Transition Analysis: Linking Later Outcomes to Transition Histories
abstract: Latent transition analysis (LTA) is widely used to study movement among latent classes over time, yet distal outcomes are often modeled as a function of final class memberships, resulting in a relatively static representation of the dynamic developmental process. Although distal outcomes can, in principle, be conditioned on combinations of latent class variables or transition histories, such specifications may be underused, difficult to implement, or insufficiently documented. This paper presents a practical, theory-guided approach for relating distal outcomes to longitudinal transition histories in LTA. We focus on a grouped-pattern approach in which theoretically meaningful transition patterns are specified using Mplus dot-language constraints while adjusting for classification uncertainty. Using math and science attitudes across high school, we illustrate how stability and change relate to later STEM career attainment.

title: Exploring the Comparability of Measurements – Empirical Benchmarks and Detectability Thresholds for Configural Invariance with EGA Trees
abstract: Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA) trees detects configural non-invariance without a priori group specifications, yet interpreting the Network Difference (ND) index remains challenging due to a lack of empirical benchmarks. To address this, we conducted a large-scale Monte Carlo simulation (18,500 repetitions) using the ADEMP framework to evaluate detection sensitivity. By manipulating violation types, intensity (δ), number of affected items, and sample size (N), we modeled detection probability as a function of ND and N. Results revealed a conservative empirical Type I error rate (.008). Crucially, we derived sample-size-specific critical thresholds (τND) for 80% statistical power, demonstrating that required ND significantly decreases as sample size increases. We identify N = 400 (τND = .517) as the minimum functional baseline for detecting common configural non-invariance. To support research design and measurement validation, we complement these benchmarks with annotated R code and step-by-step tutorials, providing a ready-to-use resource for empirical and instructional applications.

Healthcare professionals' experiences of using an Artificial Intelligence training tool to practice asking questions about child abuse
abstract: Background Children with chronic diseases face an increased risk of child abuse. The aim was to explore healthcare professionals' experiences with an artificial intelligence (AI)-based training tool for practicing questions to identify potential child abuse as well as their overall experiences of asking such questions. Methods An exploratory qualitative study was conducted at a pediatric hospital in Sweden. Fifteen healthcare professionals participated. Following a brief educational session on child abuse and its consequences, participants used an AI-based training tool to practice asking questions about potential child abuse in simulated conversations. Semi-structured interviews analyzed using Systematic Text Condensation, a thematic cross-case analysis method. Results Four categories emerged from the analysis, ‘Perceptions of interaction and support in the training tool’, ‘An opportunity to practice asking questions about child abuse’, ‘Organizational support for learning and development’, ‘Difficulties and uncertainty in asking questions about child abuse’. The training tool was perceived as credible and engaging, and useful for practicing difficult conversations. The analysis revealed a need for practice in asking difficult questions and a need for managerial guidance to allocate time. Regular follow-up visits increase opportunities to build trust and are perceived to make it easier to ask sensitive questions. Conclusion Healthcare professionals described uncertainty regarding how to ask about child abuse. Practicing with an AI-based training tool in simulated conversations appeared to increase their confidence and preparedness for addressing potential child abuse in clinical encounters.

Basalt Application Alters the Nitrogen Budget of Midwestern U.S. Agricultural Soils through Reduced Nitrous Oxide Fluxes and Increased Nitrogen Leaching
abstract: Abstract Land-based enhanced rock weathering (ERW)─applying ground silicate rock to soils─is being explored for sequestration of CO2 from the atmosphere, with impacts beyond carbon storage. Weathering of basalt releases base cations increasing alkalinity and soil pH, which we hypothesized would reduce N2O emissions. Repeated applications of basalt to a heavily fertilized annual Zea mays and Glycine max rotation (maize and soybean) and the low-fertilized perennial bioenergy grass Miscanthus x giganteus (miscanthus) in Illinois raised soil pH from 6.6 to 7.1 in maize/soybean and from 5.4 to 6.3 in miscanthus and consistently reduced annual N2O emissions by 16–40% over 7 growing seasons. Although not statistically significant for any given crop, our results indicate an emerging trend of increased N leaching (23% pooled across crops and years), suggesting a potential shift in N loss from the atmosphere to groundwater. Crop yields increased or remained unchanged, indicating enhanced weathering is compatible with conventional farming practices. Regional land model simulations show that ERW deployment across the US Corn Belt could reduce soil N2O emissions by 11% under a moderate deployment pathway and by 24% under a more intensive deployment pathway. The effects of enhanced weathering extend beyond CO2 sequestration and may benefit both greenhouse gas mitigation and bioenergy crop production, with a potential trade-off of increased N mobility in fertile, organic matter-rich US Midwestern soils.

title: Issue Editorial Masthead
Issue Publication Information
Microplastics Rapidly Sink and Beach in a Whole-Lake Experiment
abstract: Abstract Although advances in oceanographic and limnological modeling have increased our understanding of microplastic transport and persistence, we require more knowledge to effectively protect biodiversity. We initiated a whole-lake experiment (the pELAstic project) to measure the real-world fate and transport of microplastics. We added microplastics to a boreal lake, simulating stormwater input, at loading concentrations predicted to achieve environmentally relevant concentrations. Here, we introduce our experiment and describe the particle budget from the first microplastic addition. We observed rapid transport of microplastics to different ecosystem compartments. Transport patterns could not be fully explained by initial particle size and density, highlighting how natural processes modify plastic fate in real-world systems. Microplastic fragments rapidly redistributed─exiting the water column and settling on the bottom and shorelines. A particle budget across the water column, bottom sediments, and beaches accounted for 77% of the polyethylene, 48% polystyrene, and >100% polyethylene terephthalate. “Missing” plastic was likely in the nearshore littoral. Our observations suggest that if we prevent further inputs to aquatic ecosystems, microplastics will quickly disappear from the water column─washing up on shorelines and settling on the bottom. Thus, understanding rates of microplastic deposition and burial is critical to forecast the legacy of microplastic pollution.

title: Emerging CRISPR Technologies for Environmental Protection: From Genetic Engineering and Biosensing to Environmental Deployment
abstract: Abstract Since its discovery, Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR) has revolutionized biomedical science and engineering with its ability to recognize and edit gene sequences with high specificity and precision. Despite the growing interest in using these capabilities to address environmental and sustainability challenges, the broader potential of CRISPR in environmental systems remains unexplored relative to its biomedical applications. Here, we provide a critical perspective on the emerging use of CRISPR for pollution management, ecological conservation, and environmental monitoring. Rather than viewing CRISPR solely as a gene-editing or biosensing technology, we consider both capabilities together to examine how advances in CRISPR engineering can translate into practical environmental solutions. We highlight the fundamental principles behind CRISPR-based editing and sensing and evaluate the challenges that constrain their transition from proof-of-concept experiments to field deployment, including off-target effects, delivery methods, ecological risks, and low sensitivity. Addressing these hurdles requires a multifaceted approach that integrates emerging technologies such as reversible CRISPR technology, amplification and cascade reactions, and machine learning, with strict regulatory oversight and rigorous risk assessments. This perspective identifies critical strengths, weaknesses, and research priorities for advancing CRISPR from laboratory technology toward robust tools for environmental applications.

title: Abnormal Event Monitoring of Drainage Pipelines Based on Distributed Optical Fiber Vibration Sensing
abstract: Abstract Urban drainage networks are critical infrastructure for modern cities, yet their complex and concealed nature makes real-time monitoring of abnormal events a persistent challenge. To address this, this work proposed a distributed optical fiber vibration sensing system based on phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (Φ-OTDR) for drainage pipeline monitoring. To accurately capture abnormal events from complex environmental noise, a two-tier intelligent processing architecture comprising localization and classification modules was developed. The localization module employed an enhanced You Only Look Once (YOLO) model integrating anchor-box optimization, a channel-attention module, and an additional small-target feature layer, achieving a mean average precision of 96.8% in laboratory tests. The classification module utilized a hybrid model combining convolutional neural network, bidirectional long short-term memory, and attention classifier, achieving an overall accuracy of 98.1% for five abnormal events. During two-week of continuous field monitoring, the system localized simulated events with errors below 2.60 m and distinguished internal leakage, knocking, and drilling from walking, running, and vehicle interference with precision and recall exceeding 99.6% for the tested classes. Notably, the system successfully detected and accurately localized an actual branch pipe leakage event, demonstrating its practical effectiveness under real-world operating conditions.

title: Technological Substitution in Pesticide Application Reduces Occupational Risk but Fails to Mitigate Dietary Residue Burden: Field Evidence from UAV versus Manual Spraying in Paddy Rice
abstract: Abstract UAV spraying has been widely promoted as superior to manual application in Asian rice production, yet its combined implications for food safety and occupational exposure have never been evaluated within a single integrated framework. Here, we report a full-season field trial comparing UAV and manual imidacloprid (IMI) application in paddy rice, simultaneously tracking grain residue dynamics and occupational exposure in 29 applicators through to harvest. Grain IMI concentrations at harvest were comparable between regimes (86−115 μg/kg) and exceeded the EU maximum residue limit (MRL, 10 μg/kg) in both groups. More critically, on an LC-HRMS-derived relative-concentration basis, parent IMI accounted for 30.4% of the detected IMI-related profile in grain, whereas transformation products collectively accounted for 69.6%. Among these, 6-hydroxynicotinic acid was the single highest-abundance compound, surpassing parent IMI itself, yet none of the detected transformation products are included in China’s residue definition for imidacloprid in plant-derived foods. Regarding occupational exposure, urinary IMI rose approximately 9-fold from pre-exposure baseline in UAV operators compared with 17-fold in manual applicators. Manual application also induced markedly greater lipid peroxidation stress, with median baseline-normalized MDA fold changes of approximately 3.8- and 2.6-fold in the manual and UAV groups, respectively (p = 0.001). These findings establish that application technology substitution effectively reduces occupational exposure risk but confers no advantage at the food safety end point. Current parent-compound-centered residue surveillance frameworks systematically underestimate the true IMI-related burden in harvested grain, and expansion of regulatory monitoring beyond the parent compound is warranted.

title: Chemically Stratified Urban Boundary Layer: Seasonally Reversing Vertical Changes in the Underlying Chemistry of Atmospheric Oxidation Capacity
abstract: Abstract The vertical structure of atmospheric oxidation capacity (AOC) and its underlying radical chemistry within the urban boundary layer remains poorly characterized, yet it governs secondary pollutant formation. Here, we combined tower-based vertical observations with process-resolved model simulations in Beijing across winter and summer. We find that AOC generally declined with height in both seasons, but radical concentrations exhibit opposite vertical gradients. Notably, enhanced biogenic volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emissions in summer suppress near-surface OH levels, creating a mid-altitude maximum. However, sharp vertical NO gradients drove an increase in ROx with height in winter. The underlying chemistry of vertical AOC variation shifts with the seasons. In winter, the photolysis of HONO dominates ROx production, and NOx-driven ROx loss prevails. In summer, the photolysis of oxygenated VOCs takes over, with radical self-reactions as the primary ROx sink. These findings demonstrate that surface observations alone may provide an incomplete representation of the whole boundary-layer chemistry.

title: Ionizing Radiation Sustains Fenton Oxidation through Radiolytic Fe Redox Cycling for Deep Mineralization of Refractory Pollutants
abstract: Abstract The limited regeneration of Fe(II) from Fe(III) constrains sustained oxidation and mineralization in conventional Fenton processes. Here, we investigate an ionizing radiation-assisted Fenton process (IRFP) in which radiolytic Fe redox cycling sustains Fe-mediated oxidation. Using sulfasalazine as a model pollutant, we demonstrate that radiolytically generated hydrated electrons support two coupled pathways: rapid H2O2 activation and the conversion of Fe(III) to Fe(II). The resulting Fe redox cycling dynamically replenishes the Fe(II) pool alongside radiolytic H2O2 activation, thereby sustaining oxidative transformation beyond the initial degradation stage. Compared with irradiation and conventional Fenton treatment, IRFP promoted deeper fragmentation of azo, sulfonamide, and aromatic structures, resulting in enhanced mineralization. Transformation-product analysis further showed that continued transformation in IRFP reduced the persistence of complex intermediates with elevated predicted toxicity. In real pharmaceutical and coking wastewaters, IRFP achieved effective treatment under near-neutral conditions with substantially lower H2O2 and Fe(II) requirements than Fenton treatment and lower absorbed doses than irradiation alone. Although its electricity demand remained higher than short-time Fenton treatment, the markedly lower dosage of chemicals reduced the potential iron sludge burden and resulted in lower estimated COD-normalized treatment costs under the investigated conditions. These findings establish radiolytic Fe redox cycling as a strategy for sustaining Fe-mediated oxidation and promoting deeper transformation and mineralization of refractory pollutants.

title: Far-UVC Activation of Performic Acid Enables Concurrent Oxidative and Reductive Micropollutant Abatement
abstract: Abstract Conventional UV-driven advanced oxidation and reduction processes generally emphasize one redox regime and can be inhibited by wastewater constituents. Here, we characterize the photochemistry of performic acid (PFA) under 222 and 254 nm irradiation and evaluate the capacity of PFA solution, prepared from H2O2 and formic acid and thus containing residual H2O2 and formate, to generate concurrent oxidative and reductive pathways. Relative to 254 nm, 222 nm irradiation increased the fluence-normalized photodecay rate constants of neutral PFA (PFA0) and its conjugate base (PFA–) by 1.21- and 3.81-fold, respectively. The increase arose from 16.1- and 10.1-fold larger molar absorption coefficients at 222 nm, despite lower fitted innate quantum yields (0.367 and 0.804 molecule photon–1 at 222 nm versus 0.587 and 0.819 molecule photon–1 at 254 nm). The UV222/PFA solution system generated the reductant •CO2– together with oxidative HO• and oxygen-centered organic radicals. Pathway analysis attributed 34% of carbamazepine removal to •CO2– and 19% of naproxen removal to R-O• at 222 nm. Chloride and bromide enhanced fluence-normalized degradation through reactive-halogen chemistry; the largest increases were observed for carbamazepine (47.5-fold at 254 nm and 21.9-fold at 222 nm). In real municipal wastewater, UV222/PFA solution decreased total organic carbon by 33.5% within 60 min, compared with 21.6% under UV254/PFA solution, at an initial PFA concentration of 80 μM. These results suggest far-UVC activation of PFA solution as a dual-redox treatment platform, with the observed advantages maintained in the tested wastewater effluents.

Alternative finance for critical minerals: Ecosystem maturity and project-finance capability
abstract: Australia has developed capital markets and experienced mining investors, yet critical minerals projects can require substantial investment before developers can demonstrate processing performance or secure long-term sales. This conceptual Perspective examines how alternative finance can become a repeatable financing option under those conditions. It draws on selected international cases and 198 publicly disclosed qualifying Australian critical minerals alternative-finance transactions identified between January 2016 and July 2026. The framework links legal predictability, institutional de-risking and specialist market depth to the financing terms that sponsors can negotiate and boards and investment committees can approve. The Australian transactions show that sponsors have secured royalties, offtake-linked prepayments and hybrid capital from a market in which domestic private providers are active and offshore firms account for much of the specialist participation. For a developer seeking comparable terms, those precedents can help establish how financiers will price risk. Some constraints remain specific to the project, particularly where lenders need evidence that the proposed process can deliver a product buyers will accept. In those circumstances, support for testing and qualification can bring a project closer to financing. The case for developing Australian specialist capability is strongest where it enables domestic investors to underwrite projects alongside experienced offshore providers or gives sponsors access to financing terms they could not otherwise secure.
