Collusion through Common Leadership
Banking on jobs: Impact of a workfare program on formal credit
Introduction to Special Issue: Integrating Earth Observation into Impact Studies in Agriculture and Climate Change
Bimodality everywhere: International evidence of Deep Momentum
State-conditioned equity stress around FOMC and ECB meetings
journal_name: Journal of International Money and Finance

title: Changing bodies changes minds—and behavior? An economist’s guide to embodiment interventions
The social–ecological system framework for farming adaptation: the influence of social capital on eco-practices
abstract: Climate change has intensified the urgency of ecological transitions, particularly within small-scale farming systems, which are vital for food supply but highly vulnerable to environmental pressures. This study applies the Social-Ecological System framework to examine how different forms of social capital (bonding, bridging, and linking) shape ecological practices and identifies climate change as a collective action issue. Using survey data from Sardinian sheep farmers, a Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) disentangles the effects of social capital on the adoption of ecological innovations. Results show that bonding social capital reinforces traditional ecological practices, while trust in agricultural institutions ( agro-linking ) is the most consistent predictor of adoption across both traditional and innovative pathways. In contrast, bridging and institutional linking show no statistically significant effect in this context. Productivity expectations and eco-technical knowledge further mediate adoption, highlighting both economic and cognitive drivers of the adoption process. The findings provide empirical evidence of the multidimensional effects of social capital on distinct ecological pathways, offering policy-relevant insights. Sustaining traditional practices requires leveraging local networks and community knowledge, whereas innovation-oriented policies should focus on building institutional trust, technical knowledge, and closer farmer–institution linkages.

title: Climate regulation and civil society activism
abstract: This paper examines how climate public regulation shapes NGO activism against firms. We develop a private-politics framework where regulation alters campaign incentives through two opposing mechanisms: a cost-reducing channel lowering monitoring costs, and a value-diminishing channel where state compliance substitutes for private pressure. When the cost-reducing channel dominates, public regulation crowds in civil-society activism. Testing these predictions on a novel monthly panel of NGOs across 76 countries (2010–2023) within an event-study design, we show that executive regulations trigger a persistent increase in firm-targeted activism without pre-trend anticipation. Textual evidence shows that NGOs explicitly invoke regulatory benchmarks in their campaigns and that their use around enactment is not confined to campaigns already underway. Mobilization is strongest in weaker regulatory environments and concentrated among national NGOs targeting domestic firms. Together, these findings demonstrate that public regulation mobilizes civil society as an informal enforcement layer, extending climate governance beyond formal state action.

title: Gender in Micro‐Enterprise Research: Recent Trends, Thematic Inquiry, and Future Directions
abstract: ABSTRACT Gender is increasingly visible in micro‐enterprise research, although its conceptual role within the wider literature remains unclear. This study examines how gender has been positioned and repositioned across three periods: 1988–2018, 2019–2023, and 2024–2025. A longitudinal bibliometric analysis of 12,252 publications combines keyword‐frequency analysis, multiple correspondence analysis, and period‐specific thematic maps. The findings show that gender initially occupied a peripheral cluster associated with entrepreneurship and the entrepreneur. During the middle period, it became a basic theme linked to entrepreneur and India, indicating high relevance but limited internal development. In the most recent period, gender, entrepreneur, and microenterprise formed a motor theme, indicating growing conceptual importance. Across the corpus, gender was positioned closest to financial inclusion, education, social capital, and women, between the microfinance instruments and the innovation‐and‐performance vocabulary that anchor opposite ends of the conceptual structure. The study shows that gender is becoming more relevant to how micro‐enterprise scholarship conceptualizes the enterprise actor, while exposing the continuing separation between resource‐access explanations and accounts of entrepreneurial action and outcomes.

title: Does Digital Technology Enhance New Quality Agricultural Productivity? A Quantitative Meta‐Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT This study employs meta‐analysis to assess the effect of digital technology on new quality agricultural productivity, defined as a systemic construct driven by technological innovation and factor reallocation and encompassing output, efficiency, and green performance. Based on 853 estimates from 48 studies, all effect sizes are converted into partial correlation coefficients. The results show a small positive average effect that remains robust across publication‐bias and sensitivity tests. The positive effect does not vary significantly across digital technology types, productivity measures, transmission mechanisms, region, or analytical scales, but is influenced by climate and environmental risks, temporal contexts, and econometric methods. Climate risk significantly strengthens the contribution of digital technology, particularly in the 2010s, whereas this effect was relatively weak in the 1990s. No significant differences emerge across technology types under climate risk, suggesting that coordinated digital systems may enhance agricultural climate resilience more effectively than individual technologies. This study integrates fragmented microlevel, regional, and cross‐country evidence within a comparable framework, distinguishes average from conditional effects, and incorporates climate risk into research on new quality agricultural productivity.

title: Valuation Risks and Mitigation in Data Intellectual Property Pledges: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: ABSTRACT The value of data intellectual property depends on its application scenario and can change rapidly, challenging conventional collateral valuation and control. Drawing on a qualitative review of the literature and China's pilot practices in data intellectual property pledge financing, this paper examines how scenario‐dependent returns, changing dataset boundaries, and non‐exclusive use generate valuation and enforcement risks. The analysis identifies gaps in legal rules, the definition and control of collateral, and judicial review and disposal. It proposes a framework of scenario‐based rights allocation encompassing pledge creation, the parties’ obligations, regulatory coordination, and judicial review. Registration would specify the intended use, while valuation would assess provenance, authorization chains, and lawful processing. The pledgor would warrant scenario compatibility, and the pledgee would exercise proportionate control that preserves legitimate commercial use. Material changes would trigger reassessment, registration updates, and measures to restore collateral coverage where necessary. Coordinated supervision and structured judicial review would connect valuation assumptions with asset eligibility and recoverability. The framework offers a basis for aligning market valuation with the legal conditions governing data use and disposal in China.

title: National preparedness for food supply shocks: An economic efficiency approach
Neural and behavioral probability weighting function
Heterogeneous trends of animal product consumption in the US: Evidence from grocery purchase data
Forecast Horizon and Peer‐Disclosure Effects: Quarterly Versus Annual Management Forecasts
abstract: ABSTRACT Managers often look to industry peers when deciding whether to issue earnings guidance, but peer‐communication effects can differ across forecast horizons. We examine how the association between peer disclosure and a firm's guidance decision varies for quarterly versus annual management forecasts. Using US management forecast data from 2005 to 2024, we estimate dynamic linear probability models in which a firm's disclosure decision depends on the proportion of industry peers issuing guidance for the same time horizon in the prior period. The evidence indicates a clear horizon split—where a higher proportion of peers issuing guidance in the previous period is associated with a higher likelihood that the focal firm will issue quarterly guidance and a lower likelihood that it will issue annual guidance. Additional analyses indicate that these horizon‐specific associations vary in uncertainty‐related settings, consistent with peer disclosure strengthening short‐horizon disclosure pressure while enabling greater substitution with longer horizons.

title: On evolution of marginal distributions for Markov processes
abstract: We provide a study of the time evolution of the marginals of Markov processes. If this evolution can be controlled by an associated function, the process is said to satisfy the FoED property. This property is used to derive a theorem for an Itô–McKean diffusion, which states that the distribution of the process, under mild conditions, is determined by its one-dimensional marginals. Moreover, the FoED property together with the notion of bridge operators determines the backward dependence structure of a Markov process, providing an alternative to the usual forward dependence structure determined by the semigroup operators. This paves the way for a new approach to dealing with the finite-dimensional distributions of Markov processes. This approach is illustrated by new convolution formulas for Lévy processes. Additional examples illustrating the approach are also presented.

title: Where are we headed? Traverse analysis à la Hicks, Lowe, and Pasinetti
abstract: Hicks’s positive traverse and Lowe’s instrumental traverse are reconsidered through Pasinetti’s structural economic dynamics. Traverse analysis examines real capital adjustment as the economy transitions between growth paths. Pasinetti does not offer a traverse theory directly; instead, he treats non-uniform structural change as permanent and continual. He investigates the structural conditions required for full employment and concludes these cannot be maintained in dynamic economies. Together, the three approaches imply that dynamic economies are always in traverse, and that full employment cannot be a one-time policy endpoint but must be structural, dynamic, and continuous.
journal_name: The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought

title: Pareto and the logico-experimental method: interpretations and overruns
abstract: This article re-evaluates the methodological approaches used by Pareto in economics and sociology. The first part presents the state of the art on this issue. The second part evaluates Pareto’s logico-experimental method in terms of its analytical stakes compared with Walras’s rational method, and then from the perspective of its practical forms. The third part examines the stages that define Pareto’s experimentalism in sociology. A fourth part shows that the author uses Mill’s concrete deductive method in economics and sociology. The fifth part highlights that Pareto favours a more hypothetical and deductive approach in pure economics, close to the “null hypothesis” method advocated by Popper. A sixth part emphasises, however, that Pareto also uses, in sociology, the inverse deductive method that Mill also envisages for this discipline.
journal_name: The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought

title: CEO environmental communication, speech acts, and firm value
abstract: Abstract Signaling theory predicts that communication, such as by CEOs, might complement observable environmental engagement by a firm, by reducing information asymmetry. Yet it remains unclear whether firms with stronger environmental engagement communicate more about these efforts and the potential implications for firm value. To analyze 14,523 firm-quarter earnings call Q&A sessions held by 364 publicly listed firms between 2007 and 2022, the current research measures CEO communication about firm environmental engagement and the communicative intent behind such communication by combining MSCI Environmental Pillar Scores, Compustat data, and a fine-tuned DeBERTa model. Firms with stronger environmental engagement communicate less, rather than more, about their efforts during earnings call Q&A sessions. Yet CEO communication about firm environmental engagement can be positively associated with firm value, depending on the communicative intent the CEO indicates, such that assertive and directive speech maintain this positive association, but expressive and commissive speech acts are negatively associated with firm value.
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: EXPRESS: Biological Age and its Value to Marketing Theory and Practice
abstract: Aging has profound effects on how we consume, yet marketers often simplify aging to the mere passage of time (chronological age; ChronAge), overlooking biological and psychological aspects and meaningful variation within ChronAge segments. This paper highlights the need for multidimensional approaches to studying aging consumers and pioneers a framework integrating biological aging into consumer behavior theory. It introduces a measure of biological age (BioAge), derived from epigenetic data, to marketing. Using Health and Retirement Study data, the analyses demonstrate that BioAge captures distinct aspects of aging, not reflected in ChronAge, and improves prediction of consumer activities and spending. BioAge is most useful in domains where functional capacity, energy, cognition, and health-related constraints shape engagement, including technology use, social and physical activity, and discretionary entertainment spending, and is limited in more routinized or necessity-based domains. The analyses further show that BioAge mediates the impact of time on consumer behavior through objective physiological pathways, including chronic disease, cognitive functioning, and physical vitality, rather than subjective perceptions of health. The paper concludes with implications and best practices, including how BioAge can improve segmentation and customer lifetime value optimization, and the ethical and legal challenges of its use in research and practice.

title: EXPRESS: Causal Alignment: Augmenting Language Models with A/B Tests
abstract: We develop a framework for improving the effectiveness of marketing communications by aligning a language model to the causal signal in A/B tests. The core idea is that randomized experiments reveal not just which content performs best, but directions of improvement that can serve as supervision for a generative model. Using within-experiment comparisons, we fine-tune a language model to create an improver architecture that transforms lower-performing content into higher-performing content. The resulting model can be composed with any baseline decision-maker, e.g. a human expert, to suggest improvements to new content. We validate our framework through a large-scale field experiment in email marketing spanning 36 new campaigns and 283 million impressions. Subject lines improved by our aligned model achieve click-through rates 32% higher than those from unassisted human experts, while a general-purpose language model with 30 times as many parameters as our fine-tuned model does not improve outcomes. This suggests that alignment to experimental data adds value beyond model capabilities alone. Our findings provide the first field evidence that aligning language models to A/B tests improves outcomes in real marketing campaigns and show that integrating AI with experimentation can train systems that make better future decisions.

title: The Effect of Non‐US Tax Authority Monitoring on Income Shifting by Affiliates of US Multinationals: Evidence From EDGAR Search Activity
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments worldwide are concerned that multinational enterprises (MNEs) shift profits across borders to avoid taxes. While prior research shows that home‐country tax enforcement can reduce tax avoidance, far less is known about whether foreign tax authorities (FTAs) can constrain income shifting by MNE affiliates. We measure FTA monitoring using data on FTAs' downloads of US MNEs' annual reports filed with the SEC. We find that FTA monitoring is more intensive in higher‐tax‐rate countries with a larger MNE presence, consistent with those jurisdictions facing stronger incentives to monitor income shifting. More importantly, we find that monitoring by an affiliate's local tax authority does not systematically reduce income shifting by US MNE affiliates, whereas aggregate monitoring in the MNE group affects an affiliate even when its own local FTA is not observably monitoring it. This result is consistent with a spillover effect of FTA monitoring. This association is stronger when FTAs operate under information‐exchange treaties, when company disclosures are more detailed, and when enforcement capacity is greater. We also find positive associations between aggregate FTA monitoring and subsequent tax avoidance and tax settlements of US MNEs. Our findings suggest monitoring by multiple FTAs effectively combats MNE tax avoidance and have implications for how tax administrations design and coordinate monitoring efforts.

title: EXPRESS: From Trends to Tweets: The Impact of Trendjacking on Consumer Engagement on Social Media
abstract: Brands increasingly insert themselves into trending online cultural moments, a practice known as trendjacking, yet evidence on its effectiveness is mixed. Combining over 660,000 posts from 356 Fortune-listed companies (2018–2022) with trending topic data from X, we find that trendjacking increases social media engagement by 120.8%. We further find that trendjacking’s effectiveness varies by timing, trend type, and brand personality. Engagement is highest when brands post on the day following and on the day a trend first enters X’s top five trends. Effectiveness also varies by trend type, with pop culture trends generating the most engagement. Brand personality further shapes these effects, as exciting brands do best with pop culture trends, whereas rugged brands perform better with political trends. We further conduct two controlled experiments across different product categories, controlling for post and topic characteristics, and find consistent evidence that trendjacking increases engagement. These findings offer important implications for managers seeking to leverage trending topics in their social media strategy.

title: From Board Cultural Diversity to Environmental Innovation: The Mediating Role of Diversity and Opportunity Policies and the Moderating Roles of R&D Intensity and Institutional Quality
abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental innovation requires firms to recognize complex environmental opportunities and integrate heterogeneous knowledge, stakeholder perspectives, and technological expertise. Board cultural diversity (BCD) may facilitate this process by bringing together directors with different cultural backgrounds, international experiences, and cognitive perspectives; however, these potential benefits may depend on whether diverse knowledge is effectively integrated and implemented within the firm. This study examines the association between BCD and environmental innovation and investigates the mediating role of diversity and opportunity policies (DOP) and the moderating roles of R&D intensity and institutional quality. Using a global dataset of 3250 nonfinancial firms across 58 countries over 2018–2024, we employ firm fixed‐effects regressions supplemented by System Generalized Method of Moments estimation and additional sensitivity analyses. The results show that BCD is positively associated with environmental innovation. DOP exhibits a statistically significant indirect association, consistent with complementary partial mediation, whereas the positive BCD–environmental innovation relationship is stronger at higher levels of R&D intensity and institutional quality. Theoretically, the findings support a capability‐conversion perspective in which board diversity represents a potential knowledge resource whose value depends on organizational integration, technological capacity, and institutional support. Practically, the results suggest that board diversity alone may be insufficient; firms should combine diverse boards with substantive inclusive practices and adequate R&D capacity, whereas supportive institutional environments can facilitate the translation of heterogeneous knowledge into environmental innovation.

title: Legitimacy Strategies for Animal Welfare in Dyadic Supply Chains: An Evidence‐Based Business Strategy Typology
abstract: ABSTRACT Firms at food supply chains have increasingly been concerned with their environmental and social business strategies, such as animal welfare adoption. However, we know little about how to set boundaries to manage these strategies. This article thus explores how buyer–supplier relationships build market legitimacy in the cage‐free table egg supply chain. Grounded on legitimacy theory, a case study was conducted through six buyer–supplier relationships. Data were collected from a table egg supplier, retailers, hybrid wholesale‐retailers, a certifier, and a nongovernmental organization over a 1‐year timespan and then codified using an inductive content analysis. Our results reveal three objects formed from supplier's and buyers' legitimacy strategies (animal welfare scheme, certification, and product mix), with only the first one being successfully adopted across all dyadic relationships analyzed. Our analysis led to an evidence‐based business strategy typology for legitimacy organized into four quadrants (i.e., sleeper, explorer, passenger, and driver). This study builds theory on how dyadic supply chains legitimize animal welfare practice and offers the concept of object legitimation . By doing so, we explain why and how the legitimacy‐as‐process leads to shift from actions (legitimacy strategies) to outcomes (types of legitimacy) in the cage‐free table egg supply chain.

title: Iterative Causal Loop Diagrams for Theory Building: Mapping the Dynamics of Sustainable Open Business Models
abstract: ABSTRACT Complex organisational phenomena emerge from dynamic interactions between multiple variables, yet existing qualitative approaches often struggle to build explanatory theory that captures these dynamics while integrating insights from multiple theoretical domains. This paper develops and demonstrates an iterative causal loop diagram (CLD) method for qualitative theory building in complex organisational settings. Applied to an analysis of six sustainable open business models in the energy sector, the method progressively refined system boundaries, abstracted recurring causal structures and integrated concepts drawn from business model theory, sustainability, collaborative innovation and organisational design. The resulting common model linked diverse empirical observations into a shared explanation of how societal value is created and sustained over time. Findings suggest that sustainability in open business models is not simply a product of business model design, but emerges from interacting feedback processes involving governance, innovation, stakeholder alignment and external collaboration. More broadly, the study demonstrates how iterative CLD development can support integrative middle‐range theory building from qualitative case evidence.

title: Beyond Technocratic Optimism: A Systematic Review of Repair in the Circular Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT Repair is increasingly promoted as a key strategy within the circular economy, yet research on repair remains fragmented. This article provides a systematic review of management and social science research on repair, combining a critical thematic review with bibliometric analysis. We map key features of the field and integrate research streams related to governance, consumer behaviour, repairability, business models and outcomes. Our study shows that the literature is structured around four assumptions related to policy effectiveness, repairability, sustainability outcomes and scalability. By critically examining these assumptions, we challenge the technocratic optimism that dominates the field and reconceptualise repair as a context‐dependent socio‐technical and political‐economic phenomenon shaped by institutional constraints and competing value logics, rather than an inherently beneficial circular economy strategy. We conclude by deriving implications for managers and policymakers and by outlining a research agenda to better understand when and under what conditions repair contributes to circular economy objectives.

title: Green and Smart HRM for Eco‐Innovation: Disruptive Technology, Organisational Digital Capability and Boundary Conditions in Nigerian Manufacturing
abstract: ABSTRACT Manufacturers once pursued dividends and competitive advantage with little regard for environmental harm, a legacy that now compounds global warming. Disruptive technology (DT) and digitalisation both intensify and complicate firms' current eco‐innovation agendas. Drawing on a three‐wave survey of 485 managers in 192 Nigerian manufacturing firms, we examine how organisational digital capability (ODC) and smart HRM and its green counterparts shape eco‐innovation. The results show that ODC and DT are positive predictors of eco‐innovation, whereas smart HRM on its own suppresses eco‐innovation. Among green HRM practices, only green recruitment and selection (GRS) yields a direct positive contribution. Interaction effects reveal that GRS dampens the relationship between DT and eco‐innovation yet strengthens the relationship between ODC and eco‐innovation. Green training, inclusion and development (GTID) displays a similar pattern, amplifying ODC's influence while muting DT's. Smart HRM reverses the negative moderations of GRS and GTID on the relationship between DT and eco‐innovation and intensifies GTID's positive moderation of the relationship between ODC and eco‐innovation. These findings emphasize the importance of aligning specific green HRM functions with digital capability and judicious smart HRM policies to help firms navigate technological disruption while advancing environmental sustainability. Managerial and policy implications are discussed.

title: Green Research and Development Experience Congruence at the Apex of the Firm: Boards of Directors, Top Management Teams and Green Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how board‐top management team (TMT) green research and development (R&D) congruence influences green innovation from the strategic leadership system (SLS) perspective. Specifically, it distinguishes between supplementary congruence, reflecting green R&D experience similarity across the board and the TMT and complementary congruence, reflected in the interaction between green R&D directors and managers. Using panel data from Chinese listed firms, it demonstrates that both forms of congruence promote green innovation. Green strategic attention mediates the effect of complementary congruence. Moreover, the effectiveness of the two forms of congruence varies across ownership type, technological intensity and green investor coverage. By conceptualising the board and the TMT as an integrated leadership system and distinguishing two forms of cross‐level congruence, this study extends the SLS perspective to environmental management and refines its explanation of corporate green innovation.

title: Energy Transition, Trade Structure and Green Productivity Within Global Value Chain Production Networks
abstract: ABSTRACT Integration into global production networks does not necessarily translate into green productivity gains. This study examines the associations of renewable electricity and global value chain (GVC) participation with green productivity in BRICS economies during 1990–2024. Green productivity is measured using Malmquist–Luenberger total factor productivity change, incorporating carbon emissions as an undesirable output. CS‐ARDL provides the principal estimates, accounting for common influences and dynamic adjustment, whereas CS‐DL and FGLS provide supplementary checks. Extensions examine energy efficiency as a control and an outcome, alongside sensitivity to country‐specific linear trends. GVC participation is negative but statistically insignificant in the principal estimates and remains insignificant after trend adjustment. Renewable electricity is positively associated with green productivity in the baseline estimates, but its coefficients decline and lose statistical significance after introducing country‐specific trends. Energy efficiency findings vary across estimators: GVC participation is positively associated with efficiency in FGLS, whereas renewable electricity exhibits negative associations in FGLS and long‐run CS‐DL estimates. The study contributes macro‐level evidence distinguishing cleaner electricity, energy efficiency, and environmentally adjusted productivity within BRICS production networks. Its findings inform coordinated energy and industrial policy, whereas specification sensitivity and unresolved endogeneity warrant interpretation as conditional associations.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian modeling of hotel availability using high-resolution panel data: Application to post-earthquake accommodation market dynamics following the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake
Family Offices: Governing Transgenerational Wealth Across Organizational and Generational Boundaries
abstract: Family offices have become increasingly important organizational actors in the governance and deployment of private family wealth. Yet, despite growing scholarly attention, family office research remains fragmented across research traditions that build on different conceptualizations of family offices as wealth managers, governance mechanisms, investment vehicles, professional service organizations, or infrastructures of dynastic wealth. This definitional plurality has generated valuable insights, but it also inhibits cumulative theory building and empirical comparison. We synthesize existing theoretical and empirical evidence and propose a theoretical definition and a definitional taxonomy of family offices, thereby developing a conceptual baseline for family office research. We then develop an analytical framework that connects family goals and willingness, organizational forms, activities and ability, boundary mechanisms, and multidimensional outcomes. By positioning contemporary research within this framework, we identify priorities for cumulative scholarship and practical challenges in family office design and renewal.

title: Single-Family Offices or Venture Capitalists? Entrepreneurs’ Perceptions of Investor Attractiveness at the Deal-Origination Stage
abstract: Deciding whom to initially contact for potential venture funding is an important entrepreneurial choice, particularly at the deal-origination stage when limited information makes signals about investor characteristics essential. Grounded in signaling theory, this study builds on an experiment exploring entrepreneurs’ perceived attractiveness of single-family offices (SFOs) compared to venture capitalists (VCs). The findings reveal that SFOs are perceived as more attractive to initial contacts than VCs, identifying humanization and a feeling of closeness as underlying psychological mechanisms. The study contributes to a nuanced understanding of the psychological mechanisms driving entrepreneurs’ perceptions of the family signal, bridging family business and psychology research.

title: Drivers and outcomes of harmonious environmental passion: a self-determination theory approach in the hotel industry
abstract: Purpose Despite growing interest in employee-driven environmental sustainability in hospitality, limited research explains how personal, social and organizational factors jointly shape harmonious environmental passion (HEP) and how this passion translates into diverse green work outcomes. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study aims to develop and test a conceptual model that examines key antecedents and consequences of HEP among hotel employees. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from frontline and supervisory employees working in four- and five-star hotels. A structured questionnaire was used, and the proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings The results indicate that individual green values, personal environmental norms, nature connectedness (NC) and corporate environmental ethics positively influence HEP, while green psychological climate shows no significant effect. HEP positively affects in-role green behavior, extra-role green behavior, green voice behavior and green recovery performance. Proactive personality (PP) moderates the relationship between NC and HEP, such that the relationship is stronger among highly proactive employees. Practical implications Hotel managers can enhance employee-driven environmental sustainability by recruiting and developing employees with strong green values, reinforcing ethical environmental practices and strengthening employees’ connection with nature. Nature-related sustainability initiatives may be particularly effective among employees with higher PP. Originality/value This study applies SDT by integrating personal, social and organizational antecedents of HEP and by demonstrating its impact on both behavioral and performance-based green outcomes in hospitality settings.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Advancing and integrating value-based selling research in industrial marketing: New theories, methods, and perspectives
Perceived fairness, accountability and transparency toward ML-based AI service delivery: conceptualization and measurement
abstract: Purpose This study conceptualizes and validates a multidimensional framework of consumers' perceived fairness, accountability and transparency (FAT) in machine learning (ML)-based AI service delivery. Addressing inconsistent conceptualizations and limited service-oriented measures, it examines how FAT perceptions emerge across goal-setting, coding and developing and implementation stages. A formative FAT scale is developed and tested for its predictive validity on trust and usage intention. Design/methodology/approach A multi-stage scale development process was used. Items were generated through literature review and 20 interviews, and face validity was assessed via an expert focus group. Two surveys (n = 448; n = 535) supported exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) validation of a reflective–formative FAT structure. A third survey (n = 455) established convergent and nomological validity with established FAT scales, trust and intention to use. Findings Results confirm FAT as a multidimensional construct shaped across goal-setting, coding and developing and implementation phases. All nine first-order factors significantly form the three higher-order FAT dimensions. The scale demonstrates strong reliability and validity, and fairness and transparency exhibit the strongest effects on trust and intention to use. Findings support a stage-based view of ethical perception in AI service delivery. Originality/value This research provides the first stage-based conceptualization and validated scale of perceived FAT in ML-based service AI. It integrates attribution theory with a socio-technical lens to disentangle how ethical judgments form throughout the AI lifecycle. The study advances theoretical clarity and offers actionable guidance for designing, developing and deploying ethically aligned AI services.

title: Food insecurity as a source of supply chain risk? An alternate perspective on a vicious cycle
abstract: Purpose The objective of this paper is to provide a perspective on food insecurity as an antecedent and enabling condition of supply chain risk. The goal is to scope a research landscape for evaluating this relationship and to encourage future research in this underexplored direction. Design/methodology/approach Building on extant literature on food security and supply chain risk management, we conceptualize food insecurity as a social condition that generates or intensifies existing supply chain risks. Findings We provide a framework and propositions to explore the mechanisms through which food insecurity may become operationally consequential across the micro-meso-macro levels. We also discuss different interventions for mitigation. Practical implications Using real-world examples, we illustrate how the impact of food insecurity-related disturbances may affect supply chain performance. We discuss reactive, active, and proactive interventions involving business decision-making and policymaking. Originality/value We explore an underexplored pathway of how food insecurity affects supply chain performance. We position food insecurity not only as an outcome but as an antecedent of supply chain risk.
journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

title: Innovators and Transformers: When supplier counts mislead about pharmaceutical supply resilience
abstract: Purpose Approved supplier counts are used as signals of supply capacity in pharmaceutical markets. This article shows that such counts record administrative visibility, measure the gap between administrative and operational visibility in the US drug shortage records, and show that neither count is a valid measure of operational redundancy without normalization by market type and volume. Design/methodology/approach The analysis links United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) drug shortage records, Orange Book approvals, drug listing records and inspection classifications for 3,344 active ingredient-by-dosage form markets in a cross-section. It tabulates the share of approved applications with no active listing and no linked firm. A temporally aligned comparison measures approved applicants for shortage markets at shortage onset and for comparison markets at pseudo-onset dates drawn from the same onset distribution. Findings Across markets, 12.8% of approved applications that are not formally discontinued are absent from the drug listing directory and 59.6% of all approvals are either discontinued or unlisted; the shares are nearly identical in shortage and comparison markets. Under temporal alignment, shortage markets have a median of seven approved applicants at onset against a pseudo-onset median of one for comparison markets and the count of linked firms shows the same inversion: markets with no linked firm are the least likely to be in shortage. Among approvals that predate onset, the median lead is 20 years (83% of approvals in shortage markets). Practical implications Shortage-risk classification should not rest on approval counts, and a count of linked firms is not a substitute without normalization by market type and volume; a low linked-firm count in a high-volume generic market is the configuration to watch. Originality/value The article separates administrative visibility from operational visibility as distinct constructs. It quantifies the wedge between the public approval register and the active counts that the regulator and the Government Accountability Office build internally. It documents that statute, policy metrics, guidance and published studies use register counts as the count of competitors.
journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

title: When small meets big: Who fears coopetition most?
abstract: Coopetition between small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and large firms (LFs) is increasingly common in innovation-driven industries, yet the risks associated with these asymmetric relationships remain poorly understood. Drawing on a 3-year qualitative study in the French defence industry, we ask how risks differ between SMEs and LFs in coopetition and how these differences shape coopetitive tensions. Our findings reveal qualitatively different risks for these partners. SMEs face structural dependency, knowledge appropriation, constrained value capture and exclusion risks. LFs fear strengthening SMEs as competitors, losing market control and the redeployment of technologies. Coopetition with SMEs also generates internal tensions within LFs. We challenge the assumption that risks are unilaterally borne by SMEs, showing that coopetitive tensions differ in content across partners and that SME–LF coopetition acts as a double-edged trajectory-shaping mechanism that simultaneously enables and constrains entrepreneurial growth.
journal_name: International Small Business Journal: Researching Entrepreneurship

title: Dude, Where's Our Stuff? A Systematic Literature Review of Shortages in Supply Chain Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain shortages (SCSs) arise when firms cannot access enough inputs to meet demand, and the resulting gap cannot be closed through routine operational responses or price adjustments. SCSs are practically important because they occur frequently and are disruptive, motivating this systematic literature review of supply chain management studies examining the causes and consequences of SCSs. Based on the systematic literature review, this research develops a holistic model that categorizes the sources of SCSs; recognizes the reciprocal relationship between realized and anticipated SCSs; proposes a 2 × 2 framework grouping firms' actions in response to SCSs along dimensions concerning internal versus external orientation and whether actions improve resource access versus reduce resource importance; and postulates that firm traits and product/service attributes moderate the impact that SCSs have on firms' actions. We suggest several directions for future research to extend understanding of SCSs.

title: Cultural diversity and team-based case learning in a sustainability accounting course in Colombia: an exploration of cultural intelligence
abstract: This study explores the extent to which cultural diversity in team-based case learning contributes to the achievement of learning goals in accounting courses. Understanding cultural diversity is increasingly recognised as central to addressing challenges in classroom interaction and communication. We combine a self-study approach with an exploratory qualitative case study of a sustainability accounting course in Colombia. Drawing on a cultural intelligence framework, the findings provide empirical evidence of cross-cultural capabilities among a Vietnamese educator and Colombian learners, which play a crucial role in effective team-based case learning. Motivation is reflected in the accumulation of international experience, the expansion of professional networks, and exposure to sustainability knowledge. Cognition is demonstrated through a willingness to acquire both culture-general and context-specific knowledge. Metacognition is evident in the use of varied instructional strategies (i.e. teaching methods and materials), cultural awareness (i.e. punctuality and learning approaches), and reflective practices. Behaviour is observed in a respectful classroom climate, efforts to learn and cooperate, and supportive actions. Together, these cultural intelligences contribute to achieving three learning outcomes: teamwork skills, communication skills, and a sustainability mindset. This study contributes to the literature on cultural diversity in accounting education by conceptualising and providing empirical evidence on the application of an integrated framework of cultural intelligence and team-based learning. It recommends culturally responsive strategies for accounting educators. Finally, it also contributes to research on social issues in organisations by advancing understanding of cultural diversity from an accounting education perspective.

title: The Rose and Its Hidden Thorn: Patterning and Evolution of Consumer Vulnerability in Transformative Service Initiatives
abstract: Transformative Service Initiatives (TSIs) aim to reduce consumer vulnerability (CV), yet they can reproduce the harm they seek to address. We investigate this paradox in TSIs offering entrepreneurship support to refugees. Study 1, drawing on interviews with forty-two managers from thirty-three TSIs, identifies three service models (access-dominant, balanced-constrained and control-dominant) that organise consumers’ access to resources and control over their use. Each model positions consumers differently, as passive recipients, conditional agents or autonomous strivers, and sustaining each position makes a distinct CV pattern likely: a recurrent form of constrained agency or unmet need. Study 2, a three-year ethnography of a TSI provider (70 interviews, 144 observational sessions), shows how consumers contest their assigned positions within the service relationship: testimonial repositioning (making the lived costs of service participation visible) and prefigurative repositioning (demonstrating what greater enabling resources could make possible). It then traces how these acts contributed to service-model reconfiguration under particular organisational and institutional conditions. Theoretically, findings explain how service models can recurrently pattern vulnerability through consumer positioning and how consumers’ within-relationship responses may contribute to service-model reconfiguration. Managerially, the typology enables managers to diagnose CV risks in their service models and develop organisational capacity for service reconfiguration.

title: Connected Friction—Collectively Designing Service Ecosystems Through Reflexive Relations
abstract: Designing service ecosystems is a collective endeavor in which interdependent actors intentionally reconfigure the social structures coordinating their value cocreation. Because actors experience structures differently, however, they often disagree about how to reconfigure them. Although reflexivity has been identified as a key enabler for service ecosystem design, research has primarily treated it as an individual capacity. Yet transformation guided only by reflexive individuals risks unintended consequences for others and rupturing the relations on which value cocreation depends. In response, we examine how reflexive relations can be stewarded to support service ecosystem design in pursuit of desirable collective outcomes. We define reflexive relations as a form of interaction in which differently positioned actors jointly render the institutionalized social structures coordinating their value cocreation observable, contestable, and open to reconfiguration. Through a two-year cooperative inquiry in Norwegian child welfare, we explicate connected friction as the core dialectic dynamic through which reflexive relations emerge, with uniformity and rupture as hindering dynamics. We also identify four situated conditions—practical distance, actor perspectives, emotional effort, and institutional legitimacy—that require continual attunement to steward reflexive relations in practice. This research reconceptualizes reflexivity as emerging through actors’ relations and shows how ongoing stewardship can leverage conflicting interdependencies as a generative resource for designing service ecosystems.

title: How Private Enterprises Improve Their ESG Performance: An Examination Based on the Reverse Mixed‐Ownership Reform
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This paper exploits the introduction of minority state ownership into private firms (i.e., reverse mixed‐ownership reform) as a quasinatural experiment and employs a staggered difference‐in‐differences model to identify the causal effect on the ESG performance of private firms. Research Findings/Insights Using a sample of private firms listed on China's A‐share market over the period 2009–2021, this study finds that reverse mixed‐ownership reform significantly improves the ESG performance of private firms. Minority state ownership serves as a means of filling institutional voids, with its core mechanism operating through the alleviation of financing constraints and the acquisition of government subsidies and tax incentives. This effect is more pronounced among firms that simultaneously face high financing constraints and high ESG investment opportunities, and it weakens as the regional financial institutional environment improves. Further analysis shows that the promotional effect of minority state ownership exhibits an optimal ownership range and is driven primarily by the initial introduction of state capital. Tests of economic consequences indicate that the resulting improvement in ESG performance significantly enhances the long‐term value of firms with both high financing constraints and high ESG investment opportunities, while reducing their cost of debt capital. Theoretical/Academic Implications Drawing on institutional theory, this study proposes that minority state ownership performs a governance function of filling institutional voids in transition economies, offering a new theoretical explanation for the ESG effects of reverse mixed‐ownership reform and deepening the understanding of the mechanisms through which state ownership operates within the mixed‐ownership reform literature. In addition, by identifying boundary conditions at both the micro and macro levels, this study reveals the context‐dependent nature of the ESG effect of minority state ownership, providing empirical evidence on how the institutional environment shapes the effectiveness of governance mechanisms. Practitioner/Policy Implications This study reveals the optimal ownership range within which minority state ownership influences the ESG performance of private firms, providing a basis for the government to strategically advance reverse mixed‐ownership reform and ESG policies, as well as practical guidance for private firms to optimize their corporate governance structures and equity arrangements.

title: Enlightened Egoism and Its Discontents: Mapping the Business Case for Doing Good
The dual challenge of contextualization in leadership research: A systematic review, critical assessment and future research agenda
abstract: Although context is widely seen as essential for leadership research, the field is thought to suffer from a context deficit. Building on Johns (2006) and Rousseau and Fried (2001), this systematic review investigates whether empirical leadership studies go beyond merely acknowledging context and engage in contextualization by truly embedding context in the research design, analysis, and interpretation. We argue that contextualization is best assessed as a research practice in its own right. Yet, the value of contextual findings also depends on how a study handles two further challenges in leadership research: conceptual proliferation and causal ambiguity. We systematically review 209 empirical leadership studies (2003−2023), coding them not only on a large set of context variables, but crucially also on the degree of contextualization, and as complementary diagnostics, on conceptual clarity and causal inference. Our review shows that many leadership studies do typically incorporate context, but the degree to which they engage in high levels of contextualization remains limited. In addition, and irrespective of the degree of contextualization, the review brings to the fore that the analysis of the leadership concepts used or of causal inference in our sample of 209 papers is underdeveloped. The dual challenge that emerges from our review for leadership scholars is therefore not only to deepen contextualization as such, but to do so while also strengthening leadership conceptualization and causal inference.

title: Environmental Regulation and Corporate Green Innovation Bubbles: Evidence from China’s Green Shield Action
abstract: Firms’ strategic decisions concerning green innovation are shaped by environmental regulation. We investigate whether corporate green innovation bubbles are associated with the implementation of China’s Green Shield Action. Firms exposed to the policy exhibit fewer green innovation bubbles; this association is stronger when firms have more female executives or higher levels of executive green awareness. Increased public environmental concern and green investment may be potential channels. As an extension, the findings are also consistent with a reduction in debt maturity mismatch associated with the suppression of green innovation bubbles.

title: Digital Resources and Corporate Internal Control from the Perspective of Resource Empowerment and Interaction: Evidence from China
abstract: Digital resources (DR) provide new drivers for the effectiveness of internal control (IC). This study examines how DR empowers IC. Digital system resources (DSR) and digital human resources (DHR) positively affect IC effectiveness and achieve empowerment through the mediation of control activities and the information and communication process. DSR and DHR interact negatively in enhancing IC effectiveness, which may be due to functional overlaps, competence mismatch, and lack of collaborative management. DHR prompts IC effectiveness more significantly in non-state-owned, manufacturing, and high-tech enterprises; DSR has a broadly positive effect across enterprise types. This study promotes application of resource empowerment in IC.

title: ESG Competitive Advantage and the Cost of Equity: A Competitor-Based Perspective
abstract: This study examines the association between ESG competitive advantage (ECA) and the cost of equity (COE) in an emerging-market setting. Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2012 to 2024, this study identifies product-market competitors through textual similarity and constructs a competitor-relative ESG measure. While ECA is negatively associated with the capital asset pricing model-based (CAPM-based) COE, the estimated economic magnitude is modest. ECA is also positively associated with analyst coverage and green innovation, which are treated as related outcomes rather than as identified transmission mechanisms. In joint specifications, the relative component of ECA does not provide statistically-supported incremental explanatory power beyond firms’ own ESG (environmental, social, and governance) performance. The observational design cannot exclude reverse causality or omitted variables. Accordingly, the results represent conditional associations, rather than causal effects. The China-based evidence is not directly generalizable, but the framework supports comparative research across emerging markets.

title: The Impact of Rural Digital Infrastructure on New Quality Productive Forces: Spatial Heterogeneity Analysis
abstract: This study examines whether rural digital infrastructure (INF) is associated with new quality productive forces (NQP) in China. Using a provincial panel of 30 regions from 2013–2024 and two-way fixed-effects models, we find a positive and statistically significant INF–NQP association. The mechanism results are consistent with partial mediation through patent R&D and household consumption, while science and education expenditure strengthens the association. Associations appear larger in less industrialized, less urbanized, less open, and less developed regions. The spatial models indicate positive dependence, with the strongest coefficient under the economic–geographic nested matrix. The findings support differentiated rural digital policy.

title: Impacts of Administrative Penalties for Digital Technology on AI Entrepreneurship: Evidence from China
abstract: Administrative penalties for digital technology (APDTs) may either deter entrepreneurship by raising compliance costs or promote it by reducing regulatory uncertainty. Using panel data for 282 Chinese cities from 2008 to 2023, we examine their effects on AI entrepreneurship. We find that stronger APDT intensity is associated with higher levels of AI entrepreneurship, with results remaining robust to instrumental-variable estimation and alternative specifications. Digital and non-digital technological innovation constitute important transmission channels. These findings highlight the signaling role of regulatory enforcement in supporting entrepreneurship in emerging digital markets.

title: Analysis of Monetary Policy’s Impact on Corporate Risk-Taking: Evidence from China
abstract: Drawing on a sample of Chinese main-board listed firms from 2011 to 2022, this study investigates the association between Monetary policy and corporate risk-taking. Theoretically, we distinctively categorize corporate risk-taking motives as either active or passive, thereby offering a more comprehensive analysis of how monetary policy shapes corporate risk-taking. Empirical research has found a negative correlation between accommodative monetary policy and firms’ risk-taking levels; that is, loose monetary policy reduces corporate risk-taking levels, while the risk-incentive effect was not substantiated. Mechanism tests indicate that accommodative monetary policy reduces corporate risk-taking levels by alleviating financing constraints through the financial channel and lowering default risks, while simultaneously enhancing operational efficiency through the efficiency channel. Heterogeneity analysis based on a moderating effects model indicates that the negative correlation between accommodative monetary policy and risk-taking levels is more pronounced among private enterprises, small and micro enterprises, and high-tech enterprises. This study further enriches the research on the risk-taking channels of monetary policy.It provides empirical evidence for how monetary policy can effectively serve the real economy and alleviate the pressure on firms to bear risks.

title: Cultural Identity, Financial Development, and Higher Education Innovation
abstract: This study examines how regional cultural identity affects higher education innovation and how fiscal and financial conditions shape this relationship. Using Chinese provincial panel data from 2009 to 2023 and province and year fixed effects, we find that stronger cultural identity is associated with greater university invention patent applications. Education fiscal support and financial development further strengthen this relationship. Mechanism analysis suggests that cultural identity promotes innovation through enhanced social cooperation, knowledge diffusion, and technology transfer capacity. The findings highlight the complementarity between informal institutions and formal fiscal and financial conditions in fostering higher education innovation.

title: Investment Strategy in a Supply Chain Featuring an Entrant Supplier
abstract: This paper studies strategic supply chain interactions when a retailer invests in reducing an incumbent supplier’s production cost and may introduce a competing supplier. Analyzing scenarios with and without investment spillovers yields three insights: (1) supplier entry can boost retailer investment; (2) contrary to conventional wisdom, when production cost and competitive pressure are high, an entrant supplier can uniquely benefit the incumbent supplier; (3) a novel revenue and cost-sharing contract can serve as a strategic tool for the incumbent supplier to deter entry. Numerical analysis confirms the robustness of these results under partial spillovers.

title: Population Aging and GVC Upgrading in China: Firm-Level Associations and Provincial Patterns
abstract: China is aging rapidly as manufacturing firms seek higher positions in global value chains (GVCs). Using firm-level data for 2000–2013, we find a negative association between the provincial old-age dependency ratio and firm GVC upgrading under year fixed effects. The coefficient is economically non-trivial but does not reach conventional significance under wild-cluster bootstrap inference. Firm fixed effects attenuate it to near zero, pointing to a between-firm (compositional) pattern rather than weaker upgrading among continuing firms. Only human capital shows a detectable indirect association; saving, R&D, and inward FDI do not. A provincial panel for 2014–2023 shows no robust negative link between aging and log export technological complexity. Because the two analyses differ in unit, period, outcome, and design, the contrast is a descriptive divergence, not an identified paradox or a test of policy compensation. The within-versus-composition distinction is relevant for other economies aging before affluence.

title: Climate risk and corporate financial reporting practices: evidence from earnings comparability
Policy green light, biodiversity bright? How green monetary policy innovation drives corporate biodiversity engagement in emerging markets
Quantifying undetected severe misconduct in medical research
Understanding AI Adoption in Local Government: Capacity Constraints or Political Caution?
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been widely adopted by governments, but whether and to what extent governments adopt AI varies. A key question is whether variation in AI adoption across local governments stems from differences in capacity or political constraints. Understanding this has implications for the kinds of policies officials may want to adopt to ensure that local governments have access to the technologies that they want and need. This paper combines data from the International City/County Management Association (ICMA) Survey, American Trends Panel (ATP), the Current Population Survey (CPS), and other public data sources, to examine how capacity and political constraints influence local government AI adoption in the United States. Using logistic and Poisson regression models, we find that AI adoption at local governments is associated with citizens’ attitudes toward AI, public employee unionization, local governments’ financial capacity, and infrastructure support. Notably, political factors (citizens’ attitudes and public sector unionization) are equally influential as capacity factors in explaining government AI adoption, and in some cases, more powerful. These findings suggest that variation in AI adoption across local governments results not only from capacity barriers but also from political constraints due to the power of public employees and concerns of the public.
journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

title: Upstream-consistent traffic state representation for real-time crash risk prediction using vehicle-anchored flow entropy
Stationary and non-stationary extreme value models for pedestrian–vehicle conflicts incorporating movement type and vehicle conflict speed
Harmonizing police crash registers for cross-border fatal-crash modelling: Poland and Queensland
abstract: Road safety researchers and agencies may seek to compare crash patterns or evaluate the applicability of severity models developed in other jurisdictions. However, differences in police crash data definitions, coding, and reporting coverage can undermine such comparisons. This study examines whether independently maintained police crash datasets can be harmonized into a common set of indicators that preserves sufficient information for cross-jurisdiction fatal-crash model evaluation, and identifies the limitations of transferring models between these datasets. Event-level casualty-crash records from Poland (SEWIK) and Queensland, Australia (TMR), covering 2015–2024, were harmonized using documented deterministic mapping rules. A structural-support audit excluded seven indicators without counterparts in both datasets, leaving 20 binary indicators describing weather, collision type, road surface, and location (401,805 crashes). Logistic regression and CatBoost models were trained on 2015–2022 data and evaluated on 2023–2024 records, both within and across jurisdictions. Logistic-regression AUC was 0.71 for Poland-to-Queensland transfer and 0.67 for Queensland-to-Poland transfer, compared with 0.76 and 0.73 for locally trained models evaluated on the corresponding test records. Raw predictions from class-weighted models were poorly calibrated; target-jurisdiction Platt recalibration reduced expected calibration error from 0.43 to 0.005 in Queensland and from 0.36 to 0.019 in Poland. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the principal discrimination findings persisted under alternative modelling and sample definitions. The results demonstrate that, for this dataset pair, harmonization preserves partial fatal-crash ranking information but does not establish equivalence of crash characteristics, reporting practices, or predicted probabilities. The study provides a documented procedure for assessing cross-jurisdiction comparability and model transfer; local validation and recalibration remain necessary before operational use.

title: Tensions between policy and practice: Implementation challenges of mandatory reporting for child sexual abuse in China
Child aggression before and after a national ban on corporal punishment: A longitudinal, cross-national study
abstract: Background Preventing violence against children is prioritized in Target 16.2 of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals guiding international priorities to improve health and wellbeing globally through 2030. One way that countries have attempted to protect children from violence is by outlawing corporal punishment. What is lacking is evidence of how these legal bans of corporal punishment are related to children's behavior. Objective This study tested how outlawing corporal punishment is related to change in children's aggression from before to after a ban. Participants and setting Longitudinal data were from 1086 families in seven countries over nine years, extending from before to after corporal punishment was outlawed in Kenya. Corporal punishment was not outlawed over this period in the comparison countries (Colombia, Italy, Jordan, Philippines, Thailand, and United States). Methods Mothers reported on corporal punishment used by members of their household, and children reported on their own aggression annually at ages 8–16. Results Analyses demonstrated (1) a decrease in corporal punishment following national outlawing of corporal punishment in Kenya, compared to before the ban; (2) children's aggression significantly decreased in Kenya from before to after the legal ban, predicted by a decrease in corporal punishment; (3) children's aggression increased over this period in six comparison countries (Colombia, Italy, Jordan, Philippines, Thailand, United States) that did not outlaw corporal punishment over this time period. Conclusions National laws against corporal punishment serve the human rights function of protecting children from violence and can decrease parents' use of corporal punishment and children's aggression.

title: Behavioral and physiological immunity under constraint: Pathogen disgust sensitivity relates to protein balance in chronic cardiovascular disease patients
Tamoxifen on the web: accessible, but can anyone understand it?
Gender Gaps in AI Skill Acquisition and Labor Market Returns
abstract: ABSTRACT Using resumes from a major Chinese online recruitment platform, we document gender gaps in reported AI skills and their labor‐market associations. Women are less likely to report AI skills. Gelbach decompositions show that major choice, occupational sorting, and complementary skills account for part of this gap, while a sizable residual remains. Reported AI skills are associated with higher wages, but the association is weaker for women. Women with AI skills also sort less into AI‐requiring jobs. Employer responses improve when applicants' reported AI skills match job requirements, with no statistically significant gender difference detected.

title: Comparative assessment of angular-selective radiative cooling performance for urban buildings under future climate scenarios
Urban pollution island and urban heat island jointly worsen solar PV power potential in China
The Iberian blackout: A black swan or a gray rhino? A protection-aware dynamic voltage security assessment
abstract: On 28 April 2025, the Iberian power system collapsed after a rapid voltage rise that led to widespread generation disconnections and loss of synchronism. The final report of the ENTSO-E Expert Panel attributes the blackout to several interacting factors including ineffective voltage control, fixed power factor operation, misaligned protection settings, manual shunt reactor switching, and limited observability. These factors raise a general question: given the current state, can the next trip, ramp, topology action, or shunt switching raise the voltages measured by overvoltage relays above their settings before voltage controls respond? We answer this with a protection-aware dynamic voltage security assessment. For each candidate event, the method computes the voltage at every overvoltage relay over the relay time window from a dynamic model of the network, its controls, and its relays. It predicts which relays trip after a first trip, identifies assets whose relay or measurement data are insufficient for a safety conclusion, and, when one exists, computes a minimum-cost fast reactive power action that keeps all relay voltages below their settings. Case studies on four benchmark systems and a 2000-bus system that reproduces the mechanism of the Iberian blackout show that the method flagged every event that caused a secondary trip within the relay window, never declared safe a plant that tripped within that window, and, on the benchmarks, found fast reactive power actions that prevented the trips within the relay window whenever it judged such actions feasible. These results were validated with nonlinear time-domain simulations. The implementation code and a visual guide of this work are publicly available.

title: Decoupling instantaneous and cumulative stress: Physics-guided capacity prediction for lithium-ion batteries under stochastic cycling
Integrating social perceptions into spatial planning for conservation and restoration in the Colombian Coffee Region
